modules.title: SOC operations
modules.description: How a security operations centre is organised and run: the tiered team and its roles, how an alert moves from detection to closure, the analyst's daily workflow and shift handover, the service levels and metrics that measure the SOC, and the tooling that connects it all.

lessons.title: 1.1 SOC tiers
lessons.summary: Why a SOC is organised in tiers, what Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 each own, how cases escalate up and lessons flow back down, and how functional teams and automation reshape the classic model.
learning_objectives: Explain the SOC's mission and why a tiered structure is used to handle alert volume
Describe the responsibilities and decision rights of Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 3 and the SOC lead
Apply written escalation criteria to decide whether a Tier 1 analyst should close or escalate an alert
Compare the classic tiered model with functional-team SOCs and automation
Interpret a prioritised Tier 1 queue from the course lab and group related alerts into a case

lessons.title: 1.2 Roles
lessons.summary: The roles in and around a SOC: analysis and response roles, the engineering roles that keep detection working, the outside teams that hold authority to act, RACI matrices, and how roles are split with MSSP and MDR providers.
learning_objectives: Describe the responsibilities and decision rights of analyst, shift lead, incident responder and specialist roles
Explain why detection, threat intelligence, SOAR and platform engineering roles are essential to a SOC
Identify the SOC's interfaces with IT operations, identity, legal and compliance, communications and external parties
Construct a RACI matrix with exactly one Accountable role per activity
Evaluate what an MSSP or MDR contract must specify about roles and responsibilities

lessons.title: 1.3 Alert lifecycle
lessons.summary: Follows an alert from generation through queueing, triage, investigation, disposition, escalation and closure to feedback, using the Banyan lab queue to show why priority order is not event order.
learning_objectives: Describe the eight stages of the alert lifecycle and the output of each
Distinguish true positive, benign true positive, false positive and undetermined dispositions and the action each requires
Explain alert states, ownership and acknowledged escalation in a case system
Group the minisiem and triage.py alerts into cases and reconstruct them in event-time order
Write a closure note that answers what happened, what evidence supports it, what was done and what should change

lessons.title: 1.4 Analyst workflow
lessons.summary: The analyst's shift as a repeatable workflow: orientation and log-source health checks, the per-alert loop, time boxes and early escalation, documentation as you go, evidence preservation and escalation notes.
learning_objectives: Carry out start-of-shift orientation, including a log-source health check in minisiem
Apply a consistent per-alert loop inside a time box and escalate early when impact may be high
Write a defensible case note with UTC times, exact queries, evidence references and labelled assessments
Preserve case evidence with a hash and custody record using evidence_export.py
Recognise anchoring, confirmation bias and alert fatigue and the workflow habits that counter them

lessons.title: 1.5 Shift handover
lessons.summary: How a SOC transfers situational awareness, open work and case ownership from one shift to the next without losing anything, using a written note, a verbal briefing with read-back and acknowledged reassignment.
learning_objectives: Explain why shift boundaries are a point of operational risk and the failure modes that cause handover gaps
Carry out a handover in the correct order: update cases, publish the note, brief with read-back, reassign and acknowledge ownership
Write a handover note using the seven-section template, separating facts from assessments
Check platform health with the course mini-SIEM and report it in a handover
Describe controls that make handover failures visible, such as alerts on unacknowledged critical cases

lessons.title: 1.6 SLAs
lessons.summary: What a SOC service level agreement defines, how its timers start, stop, pause, warn and breach, how severity sets the targets, and how SLAs fit regulatory clocks such as CERT-In's six-hour reporting rule.
learning_objectives: Distinguish an SLA from SLOs, OLAs, underpinning contracts and aggregate SOC metrics
Define start, stop and pause events for acknowledgement, triage, notification and resolution targets
Build a severity-based SLA matrix and apply it to cases in the queue
Check per-case SLA compliance from the lab kit's synthetic case data and interpret breaches
Identify ways SLAs are gamed and the quality controls that counter them

lessons.title: 1.7 Metrics
lessons.summary: How a SOC measures speed, quality, coverage and capacity, computing MTTA, MTTR and false-positive share from synthetic cases with soc_metrics.py and showing why the median and mean must be read together.
learning_objectives: Define MTTD, MTTA, MTTR, false-positive share and coverage with explicit start and stop points
Compute MTTA and MTTR means and medians from case records using soc_metrics.py
Interpret the effect of outliers and identify the cases behind an average
Explain how metrics change behaviour and pair speed metrics with quality measures

lessons.title: 1.8 SOC tooling map
lessons.summary: The SOC's tools as a connected system: telemetry and collection, SIEM, EDR and NDR, case management, SOAR and context sources, the data flows between them, and how each maps onto the course lab kit.
learning_objectives: Describe the function of each major SOC tool category
Trace an alert across the tooling map from telemetry to closure and metrics
Build a tooling map with owners, health checks and failure impact for each integration
Explain how SOC tools are protected and how attempts to blind the SOC are detected
Map each course lab kit script to its real-world tool category

modules.title: Telemetry
modules.description: The raw material of security operations: what endpoint, network, identity and cloud sources record, which event fields matter and how to read them, why timestamps and time zones make or break an investigation, and how collection pipelines move telemetry reliably into the SIEM.

lessons.title: 2.1 Endpoint logs
lessons.summary: What endpoints record about execution, change, access and their own defences: Windows Security and PowerShell logs, Sysmon, Linux auth logs and auditd, and EDR, read through the lab's WS-104 events.
learning_objectives: Explain what execution, change, access and defence evidence endpoint telemetry provides and why it complements network logs
Identify the core Windows Security, PowerShell and Sysmon event IDs and the fields each carries
Describe how audit policy, Sysmon configuration and forwarding decide which endpoint events reach the SIEM
Apply parent-child stacking to the lab dataset to isolate an anomalous process
Interpret a per-host endpoint timeline and recognise the gaps left by missing sources

lessons.title: 2.2 Network logs
lessons.summary: What firewall, proxy, DNS, DHCP, flow, NSM/IDS and packet-capture telemetry record, how vantage points decide what is visible, what encryption hides, and how proxy metadata exposes a beacon and an exfiltration in the lab.
learning_objectives: Describe the fields and limitations of firewall, proxy, DNS, flow, NSM/IDS and packet-capture telemetry
Explain how vantage-point placement determines which traffic paths are observed
Distinguish what TLS encryption hides from the metadata that remains visible
Attribute a network event to a host and user using DHCP and endpoint evidence
Analyse proxy logs from the lab for rare destinations, beaconing and large uploads

lessons.title: 2.3 Identity logs
lessons.summary: How Windows and Active Directory authentication events, identity provider sign-in logs and VPN records show who authenticated, how, from where and with what result, read through the Banyan dataset's password spray.
learning_objectives: Explain which machine writes 4624, 4625, 4768, 4769, 4771 and 4776 during a domain logon
Interpret logon types and common 4625 failure status codes
Describe the fields and categories of an identity provider sign-in log
Detect password spraying by counting distinct users per source in VPN logs
Distinguish benign authentication failures from attack patterns during triage

lessons.title: 2.4 Cloud logs
lessons.summary: How AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity and resource logs and Google Cloud Audit Logs record control-plane and data-plane activity, what is collected by default, and how to read and route cloud audit records.
learning_objectives: Distinguish control-plane from data-plane logging and explain why the difference matters
Read a CloudTrail record field by field and resolve assumed roles to the real identity
Compare the equivalent audit logs, default retention and SIEM routes in AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
Identify high-signal cloud events such as logging tampering, new credentials and permission changes
Assess cloud log coverage gaps and map cloud fields to a normalised schema

lessons.title: 2.5 Event fields
lessons.summary: How to read security event fields correctly, why the same field name can mean different things in different sources, and how ECS-style normalisation gives every source one searchable vocabulary.
learning_objectives: Classify the fields of an event into when, where, who, what, how, outcome and provenance families
Identify field-semantics traps such as perspective, subject versus target, placeholders and encoded values in the Banyan dataset
Choose stable identifiers for joining events across sources and explain when a time window is required
Map source-specific fields to ECS-style normalised names and justify each mapping
Run normalise_demo.py and interpret how normalisation links a firewall drop and a VPN login from the same address

lessons.title: 2.6 Timestamps
lessons.summary: Why timestamps make or break an investigation: UTC versus local time (IST +05:30), ISO 8601 and other log formats, clock drift and NTP, event versus ingest time, and the pitfalls of ordering events.
learning_objectives: Convert timestamps between IST and UTC and write them in ISO 8601 / RFC 3339 form
Explain why naive timestamps, classic syslog times and epoch values need explicit handling at ingestion
Describe clock drift, skew and NTP synchronisation, including the CERT-In requirement for NIC/NPL-traceable time
Distinguish event time from ingest time and explain how late-arriving events can evade scheduled rules
Build a correctly ordered multi-source timeline, accounting for precision, ties and cross-host skew

lessons.title: 2.7 Collection pipelines
lessons.summary: How collection pipelines move telemetry from source to SIEM: agent-based and agentless collection, WEF, syslog and Beats/Elastic Agent forwarders, buffering and delivery guarantees, parsing at ingest, and source-health monitoring to detect silent loss.
learning_objectives: Explain the stages of a collection pipeline and how each can lose, delay or duplicate events
Compare agent-based and agentless collection and choose a method for each source type
Describe how WEF, syslog and Beats/Elastic Agent forward events and their reliability limits
Explain buffering, back-pressure and at-most-once versus at-least-once delivery
Design source-health checks for presence, volume, completeness and ingestion lag

lessons.title: 2.8 Telemetry lab
lessons.summary: A hands-on telemetry lab with the C08 kit: regenerate and hash the Banyan dataset, ingest it with minisiem.py, run source-health checks for inventory, volume, silence, per-host gaps and field completeness, watch normalise_demo.py parse two raw formats, and inject an outage, a malformed record and duplicates.
learning_objectives: Regenerate and verify the lab dataset and confirm events written equal events loaded
Run source-health searches for inventory, hourly volume, silence and per-host gaps with minisiem.py
Interpret field-completeness results against a baseline, including placeholder values
Explain how normalise_demo.py converts a local-time syslog line and a JSON record into one UTC schema
Inject outage, parse-failure and duplicate faults and show which checks detect each

modules.title: SIEM fundamentals
modules.description: How a SIEM turns raw telemetry into answers: ingestion and parsing, normalisation to a common schema, correlation rules that join events across sources and time, dashboards and search for investigation, and retention that balances cost, compliance and forensic need - finishing with a hands-on SIEM lab.

lessons.title: 3.1 Ingestion
lessons.summary: What a SIEM does between receiving an event and making it searchable: receiving, event breaking, source labelling, event and ingest time, routing and indexing, with volume and cost decisions, explored by loading and deliberately breaking the Banyan dataset in minisiem.
learning_objectives: Describe the stages of SIEM ingestion and the filing decision each one makes
Compare how Splunk, Elastic, Microsoft Sentinel and Wazuh name the same ingestion stages
Explain why routing to an index or table is a retention, access and detection control
Estimate ingest volume from EPS and event size and assess the detection risk of volume reductions
Interpret minisiem load results, including duplicate and malformed-input failures

lessons.title: 3.2 Parsing
lessons.summary: How parsers turn raw syslog, key-value, CSV, JSON, XML and CEF records into typed fields, why positional patterns break, and how to build, test and monitor parsers that tag failures instead of losing events, shown by stress-testing the kit's firewall parser.
learning_objectives: Match raw format families to suitable extraction techniques such as regex, grok, dissect, key-value and structured decoding
Explain how anchoring, greediness and backtracking affect regex parser correctness and performance
Diagnose parse failures from test-harness output and identify the assumption that failed
Design a parser that tags and keeps failed and partial events and exposes a failure metric
Apply golden-sample testing and defences against log injection and regex denial of service

lessons.title: 3.3 Normalization
lessons.summary: How a SIEM maps many vendors' field names, values and event types onto one common schema (ECS concepts, field mapping) and adds asset, identity, geo and intelligence context through enrichment.
learning_objectives: Explain why normalisation is needed and how ECS field sets, categorisation fields and other schemas (OCSF, CIM, ASIM) organise events
Write a field mapping for a new source, covering names, values, types, case, placeholders and time
Build and interpret a field coverage matrix to see which sources fill each correlation key
Design enrichment from asset, identity, geolocation and threat-intelligence sources, choosing ingest-time or search-time lookup
Identify normalisation and enrichment failures that create silent detection gaps

lessons.title: 3.4 Correlation
lessons.summary: How correlation rules join events across sources, time windows and shared entities, studied through the lab SIEM's six rules (R1-R6) and windowed, cross-source, entity-aggregation and absence variants.
learning_objectives: Distinguish single-event, threshold, sequence, combination, absence and entity risk aggregation rules
Read a sequence rule line by line and explain its entity join, order condition, distinct count and threshold
Choose and test time windows, and explain the trade-offs of sliding and tumbling windows
Write a cross-source correlation query on a normalised entity and interpret its result
Explain how adversaries try to stay outside rule assumptions and how layered rules and preventive controls respond

lessons.title: 3.5 Dashboards
lessons.summary: How to design purpose-driven SOC dashboards from operational questions, what to show and what to leave out, and why dashboards inform rather than detect, using real minisiem panels from the Banyan dataset.
learning_objectives: Distinguish the three jobs of SOC dashboards and match dashboard families to their audiences
Design a panel from a question, audience, action, baseline, threshold and owner
Build queue, health, activity and top-N panels as minisiem queries and interpret their output
Explain why the Banyan intrusion hour is invisible on a volume chart and which panels to avoid
Assess dashboards for data exposure, search load, time-zone and integrity risks

lessons.title: 3.6 Searching
lessons.summary: Query thinking for investigations: time ranges, filters, aggregations, stacking and pivoting across sources, practised with minisiem's SQL search over the Banyan dataset and related to pipeline languages such as SPL, KQL and ES|QL.
learning_objectives: Apply the question, time range, filter, inspect, aggregate, pivot and record loop to an investigative question
Diagnose search errors caused by letter case, wildcards, null fields and time zones
Use COUNT DISTINCT, MIN/MAX, HAVING and stacking to find rare and regular values
Pivot on hosts, users and addresses across proxy, Sysmon, Windows and VPN events to scope an incident
Explain the security and privacy controls that SIEM search access requires

lessons.title: 3.7 Retention
lessons.summary: How long SIEM data is kept and where: hot, warm, cold and archive tiers, their cost, legal floors such as the CERT-In 180-day log retention and privacy ceilings, and the forensic value lost when retention is too short.
learning_objectives: Explain the four purposes of telemetry retention and the minimum each sets
Describe how hot, warm, cold and archive tiers and lifecycle policies trade search speed for cost
Apply legal and regulatory requirements, including the CERT-In 180-day direction and DPDP limits, to a retention schedule
Demonstrate with the lab kit how a retention purge removes an intrusion's root cause and breaks lookback rules
Design a per-data-class retention schedule with protected, tested archives

lessons.title: 3.8 SIEM lab (Wazuh, Elastic)
lessons.summary: A hands-on investigation in the course's minisiem: load and orient, run rules, pivot, write and test a cross-source correlation rule, build a timeline and dashboard panels, export hashed evidence, then map the exercise onto Wazuh and Elastic.
learning_objectives: Run and interpret saved correlation rules over a multi-source dataset
Pivot from an alert by IP and host to reconstruct a cross-source incident timeline
Write and boundary-test a time-windowed correlation rule
Export case evidence with a SHA-256 hash and custody record
Map each lab stage onto the components of a Wazuh or Elastic single-node lab

modules.title: Log analysis
modules.description: Reading the logs an analyst meets every day - Windows events, Linux authentication, web server, firewall, DNS and proxy logs - recognising normal from suspicious in each, and writing precise queries across them, ending with a hands-on log analysis lab on the course dataset.

lessons.title: 4.1 Windows event analysis
lessons.summary: How to analyse Windows Security events rather than just recognise them: a seven-step reading method, actor-versus-target field reading, normal and suspicious patterns per event family, the four shapes of failed logons, and a worked analysis of the Banyan WS-104 chain with dwell gaps and absence checks.
learning_objectives: Apply a repeatable method (question, inventory, baseline, deviation, chain, absence, context) to a Windows alert
Distinguish the actor from the target in 4624, 4720, 4732 and 1102 events
Classify groups of failed logons as typing errors, stale credentials, brute force or password spraying
Reconstruct and interpret an event chain on one host using dwell gaps and peer baselines
State accurately what the absence of an event does and does not show

lessons.title: 4.2 Linux auth logs
lessons.summary: Reading Linux authentication logs in auth.log, secure and the journal: the anatomy of a syslog line, how one SSH login appears across sshd, PAM and systemd-logind, sudo and account-tool lines, separating internet noise from targeted guessing, and a worked analysis of an illustrative compromised server.
learning_objectives: Interpret sshd, PAM, sudo, su, logind and account-tool lines field by field
Reconstruct an SSH session using the sshd PID and the logind session number
Separate background SSH noise from targeted guessing and from a success after failures
Extract failures, successes, sudo commands and account changes with grep, awk and journalctl
Identify the limits of auth.log evidence, such as SSH keys written as files

lessons.title: 4.3 Web server logs
lessons.summary: How to read web server access and error logs as an analyst: the Combined Log Format field by field, status codes and response sizes, client addresses behind proxies and self-declared user agents, and how to recognise content discovery, path traversal and injection attempts and judge from the server's answer whether they succeeded, while ruling out benign look-alikes.
learning_objectives: Interpret each field of a Combined Log Format access-log line and of an nginx error-log line
Explain what each HTTP status class reveals about how far a suspicious request reached
Recognise content discovery, path traversal and injection attempts in encoded request lines
Distinguish scanning and injection attempts from crawlers, health checks, authorised scans and ordinary user input
Analyse an access log with command-line counts to reconstruct one source's activity and decide the next action

lessons.title: 4.4 Firewall logs
lessons.summary: How to analyse firewall logs: stateful logging of decisions, drop versus reject, netfilter and session-log fields, tracing a host through source NAT, and recognising vertical scans, horizontal sweeps, blocked outbound attempts, beacons, large transfers and out-of-state drops against their benign look-alikes.
learning_objectives: Interpret netfilter log lines and next-generation firewall session records field by field
Explain how state tracking, logging configuration and drop or reject actions shape what a firewall records
Trace an external report about the public address back to an internal host through NAT session logs
Identify port scans, sweeps, blocked outbound attempts and beaconing from counts of ports, hosts, intervals and bytes
Separate suspicious connection patterns from background scanning, update traffic, backups and expired sessions

lessons.title: 4.5 DNS logs
lessons.summary: How to read DNS resolver, sensor and endpoint DNS records, what normal DNS looks like, and how NXDOMAIN bursts, long high-entropy labels, many unique subdomains, TXT volume and resolver bypass reveal domain generation algorithms and DNS tunnelling from the defender's side.
learning_objectives: Interpret the fields of a DNS query record and pivot from name, answer and timestamp to other evidence
Explain how recursive resolution carries a query name to the zone's authoritative server and why that enables DNS tunnelling
Recognise DGA, tunnelling and resolver-bypass patterns and distinguish them from their benign look-alikes
Evaluate Shannon entropy and rarity as detection features using real output from the lab domains
Design DNS logging and egress controls that make resolver logs complete

lessons.title: 4.6 Proxy logs
lessons.summary: A method for analysing web proxy logs: record anatomy and field pitfalls, what TLS inspection changes, and a six-question workflow (rarity, content, rhythm, volume, scope, endpoint pivot) applied with minisiem.py and hunt.py to the WS-104 beacon and upload in the lab dataset.
learning_objectives: Interpret proxy log fields, including byte direction, status-code origin and CONNECT records
Compare the evidence available with and without TLS inspection
Apply rarity, content, rhythm, volume and scope queries to proxy data with minisiem.py and hunt.py
Build a source-cited case timeline joining proxy and endpoint events
State conclusions from proxy evidence at the strength the evidence supports

lessons.title: 4.7 Query writing
lessons.summary: Turning an analytical question into a precise, tested query: specification, type-safe and anchored conditions, half-open time ranges, grain, bounded joins, anti-joins and window functions, with real SQL on the Banyan dataset and SPL/KQL equivalents.
learning_objectives: Write a query specification (population, condition, grain, window, output) from an analytical question
Avoid false and missed matches caused by types, substrings, time boundaries and NULLs
Write bounded joins and NULL-safe anti-joins without fan-out errors
Use CTEs, time buckets and window functions such as LAG() to compare periods and measure intervals
Test a query against known positives and negatives and express its precision and recall

lessons.title: 4.8 Log lab
lessons.summary: A guided multi-source analysis of the Banyan dataset: baseline Windows, endpoint, VPN and proxy logs separately, merge the exceptions into one timeline, run scope checks and write a findings note.
learning_objectives: Baseline Windows Security, Sysmon, VPN and proxy events with aggregation queries
Classify exceptions in each source as noise, suspicious or unexplained, with evidence
Build a merged timeline joined on host, user, address and time
Run scope checks and record their negative results and limits
Write a findings note that separates facts, confidence, gaps and recommended actions

modules.title: Alert triage
modules.description: The core analyst skill: deciding quickly and defensibly what each alert is. Severity and prioritisation, enrichment with context, validating whether an alert is real, handling false positives without blinding the SOC, escalation criteria, and case notes that another analyst can trust - practised in a hands-on triage lab.

lessons.title: 5.1 Severity
lessons.summary: What an alert's severity claims (harm if the alert is true), how a consequence-based scale is designed and anchored, how base, alert and case severity differ and are revised with recorded reasons, and an audit of the lab kit's rule severities.
learning_objectives: Distinguish severity from confidence and priority and explain the harm each level asserts
Design a consequence-based severity scale with definitions and anchoring rules
Justify a rule's base severity using intrusion stage, breadth, reversibility and what the behaviour touches
Reclassify an alert or case severity from triage evidence and record the reason
Audit the lab kit's RULE_META values against its Sigma rule levels and resolve a discrepancy

lessons.title: 5.2 Prioritization
lessons.summary: How a SOC decides what to work next: decomposing the triage.py score, the effects of a multiplicative model, measuring confidence and maintaining criticality, tie-breaking, entity risk aggregation, time and capacity, and recorded analyst overrides.
learning_objectives: Decompose a priority score into severity, confidence and asset criticality and identify what it omits
Compare multiplicative, weighted-sum and matrix prioritisation models
Explain how the kit's sort breaks ties and define an explicit tie-breaker
Calculate entity risk for the Banyan queue with per-rule de-duplication
Justify and record an override of the score order using time and context

lessons.title: 5.3 Enrichment
lessons.summary: How an analyst enriches an alert during triage: extracting its entities, adding asset, identity, network (geolocation and ASN), threat-intelligence and history context with provenance, interpreting ioc_match.py matches by validity, confidence and fit, and respecting privacy and operational limits on lookups.
learning_objectives: Identify the entities in an alert and the context source that answers each question about them
Enrich lab alerts with asset, identity and prevalence context using triage.py and minisiem.py searches, recording provenance
Interpret threat-intelligence matches, expired indicators and non-matches from ioc_match.py
Explain the limits of geolocation and ASN data as evidence
Apply privacy and operational limits to enrichment lookups

lessons.title: 5.4 Validation
lessons.summary: Testing whether an alert is real: stating its claim, reproducing the rule logic, reading the raw event, corroborating across independent sources, seeking refuting evidence and concluding confirmed, refuted or undetermined, practised on the Banyan R1 and R2 alerts with minisiem.py.
learning_objectives: Apply the six-step validation workflow to a SIEM alert
Reproduce a correlation rule's logic to expose its assumptions, thresholds and missing time windows
Use raw events to recover fields that the normalised view omits
Distinguish corroboration by independent sources from mere time alignment
Recognise query and evidence pitfalls such as NULL exclusions, time-zone errors and double counting

lessons.title: 5.5 False-positive handling
lessons.summary: How to tell a false positive from a benign true positive, record false positives as tuning evidence, and write scoped suppressions with an owner, reason and enforced expiry, shown by running triage.py's CHG-1042 suppression and a deliberately over-wide one that hides the attacker's svc_update account.
learning_objectives: Classify a non-malicious alert as a false positive or a benign true positive by testing rule intent before authorisation
Write a false-positive closure record and tuning request that detection engineering can act on
Design a suppression scoped to one rule and the narrowest fields, with reason, reference, owner and expiry
Demonstrate in the lab how over-suppression and unenforced expiry create blind spots
Evaluate tuning options, preferring data and logic fixes and lower priority over hiding alerts

lessons.title: 5.6 Escalation criteria
lessons.summary: Criteria for escalating a triaged alert (hard triggers, impact-based triggers, beyond-remit cases), how to escalate with acknowledged transfer of ownership, the fields an escalation must carry, and why the CERT-In six-hour reporting requirement makes the time noticed essential, applied to the WS-104 lab case.
learning_objectives: Apply hard-trigger and impact-based criteria to decide whether, how urgently and to whom an alert is escalated
Choose between hierarchical and functional escalation routes and complete a hand-off with recorded acknowledgement
Write a structured escalation stating what, so what, evidence, confidence, time noticed, done and need
Explain the CERT-In six-hour reporting requirement and the analyst's role in recording the time noticed and flagging reportability
Distinguish queue priority from escalation decisions using the lab triage queue

lessons.title: 5.7 Case notes
lessons.summary: How to write case notes that another analyst, an incident handler and an auditor can trust: a fixed record structure, facts kept apart from inferences, UTC timestamps and evidence referenced by SHA-256 hash.
learning_objectives: Structure a case record into header, summary, entities, timeline, analysis, actions, evidence and disposition
Distinguish observed facts from inferences and state a confidence level for each inference
Record every time in UTC using ISO 8601 and explain why local or unmarked times corrupt timelines
Reference exported evidence by name, location, SHA-256 hash and method, and verify it with sha256sum
Rewrite a weak case note into one the next analyst and a reviewer can rely on

lessons.title: 5.8 Triage lab
lessons.summary: A hands-on lab that works the full triage.py queue on the Banyan dataset: prioritise, enrich, validate, disposition and document every alert, then group them into cases and export hashed evidence.
learning_objectives: Build and interpret a prioritised alert queue, including the fields the helper inferred rather than observed
Validate each alert against raw events with minisiem.py searches and the kit's intelligence and hunt outputs
Assign a disposition with a confidence level to every alert and group related alerts into cases
Export and verify case evidence with SHA-256 and record what the export does not contain
Write per-alert notes, case records and a queue summary from real lab output

modules.title: Threat intelligence
modules.description: Threat intelligence as the SOC uses it: indicator types and their shelf life, confidence and source grading, enrichment workflows, MISP basics, feeds and their pitfalls, the limits of intelligence, and responsible sharing under TLP - ending with an intel lab on the course dataset.

lessons.title: 6.1 IOC types
lessons.summary: Classifies threat indicators as atomic, computed or behavioural, ranks them on the Pyramid of Pain and explains why each type has a different shelf life, using the C08 lab feed and rules.
learning_objectives: Classify an indicator as atomic, computed or behavioural and name the field and log source it must match
Place indicator types on the Pyramid of Pain and explain the cost each imposes on an adversary
Estimate an indicator's shelf life from its type and set a sensible validity window
Interpret ioc_match.py output by indicator type, including expired and unmatchable indicators
Climb from a low-level indicator to durable artefact and behavioural detections

lessons.title: 6.2 Confidence
lessons.summary: Grades intelligence with the Admiralty system, builds a local confidence score from producer confidence, corroboration and thresholds, and ages it by hard expiry or decay, using the C08 lab feed.
learning_objectives: Distinguish producer confidence, source reliability and information credibility
Grade indicators with the Admiralty A-F / 1-6 system and justify each grade
Identify genuine corroboration and recognise circular reporting
Apply a local scoring policy and thresholds to decide block, alert or context only
Compare hard expiry with gradual decay and explain how age lowers the weight of a match

lessons.title: 6.3 Enrichment workflow
lessons.summary: Intelligence-driven enrichment as a repeatable pipeline: canonicalising and deduplicating entities, a privacy gate, a lookup cascade from internal sources to approved external services, caching with type-specific TTLs, rate-limit and failure handling, and provenance records, shown on the Banyan data and ioc_match.py.
learning_objectives: Design an enrichment pipeline that extracts, canonicalises, gates, looks up, records and attaches intelligence context
Order a lookup cascade by cost and exposure and define when it stops
Specify a cache policy keyed on value and source, with type-specific and negative TTLs and validity re-checks
Handle rate limits, refusals and timeouts without recording missing answers as clean
Record provenance that makes an enrichment result reproducible and respects privacy and TLP

lessons.title: 6.4 MISP basics
lessons.summary: The MISP data model and sharing mechanics: events, attributes and the IDS flag, objects, taxonomy tags, galaxy clusters, distribution levels and sharing groups, publishing, correlation and its control, sightings, feeds and automation, applied by modelling the Banyan case.
learning_objectives: Explain how MISP organises intelligence into events, attributes, objects, tags and galaxy clusters
Choose attribute types, categories and IDS flags for indicators from a real case
Distinguish platform-enforced distribution and sharing groups from TLP handling instructions
Interpret correlations and control over-correlation with warninglists and exclusions
Use sightings and publishing review to share safely and return feedback to producers

lessons.title: 6.5 Feeds
lessons.summary: Where threat intelligence feeds come from, the formats they arrive in, how to judge their quality, and how normalisation, deduplication, allowlisting, scoring and ageing keep them useful, shown on the lab feed on two dates.
learning_objectives: Compare open, commercial, community/ISAC and internal intelligence sources by context, confidence and obligations
Explain how STIX 2.1 indicators and TAXII collections carry and transport feed content compared with CSV lists
Evaluate a feed against measurable quality criteria such as relevance, accuracy, uniqueness and terms
Apply normalisation, deduplication, allowlisting and scoring to indicators before they drive action
Interpret ioc_match.py output on two dates to separate an indicator's expiry from the evidence it already produced

lessons.title: 6.6 Limitations
lessons.summary: What an indicator match can and cannot prove: stale indicators, collateral matches on shared infrastructure, telemetry gaps, circular reporting, attribution limits and bias, worked through an expired lab indicator matching routine VPN activity.
learning_objectives: Distinguish expired from stale indicators and explain why each matters when reading a match
Assess an indicator match against shared infrastructure and the surrounding events before acting
Explain why no match can mean no data or new infrastructure, and how behaviour-based detection covers the gap
Identify circular reporting, attribution limits and cognitive bias in intelligence use
Write case judgements with explicit confidence that cite the evidence actually justifying the action

lessons.title: 6.7 Sharing
lessons.summary: How a SOC shares intelligence responsibly: TLP 2.0 labels, ISACs and CERT-In, what to strip under the DPDP Act 2023, and the legal and contractual limits on a release.
learning_objectives: Apply the five TLP 2.0 labels to incoming and outgoing intelligence, including combined products
Choose the right community or authority (ISAC, CERT-In, NCIIPC, source) for a given release
Summarise the CERT-In April 2022 reporting, log-retention and clock-synchronisation requirements
Identify and remove personal data and internal identifiers before sharing, in line with the DPDP Act 2023
Recognise feed-licence, contractual and legal limits that narrow a release

lessons.title: 6.8 Intel lab
lessons.summary: Hands-on lab: match the course feed against the Banyan dataset, verify, grade and age each indicator, derive first-party indicators and release a checked TLP:GREEN note and a TLP:AMBER sighting.
learning_objectives: Run ioc_match.py and verify each match in the raw events with minisiem.py
Grade indicators by source reliability and credibility, recording analyst overrides with reasons
Make ageing decisions that separate validity from confidence
Derive first-party indicators from an incident and set their validity
Write a shareable intel note that passes a pre-share check and respects every inherited TLP label

modules.title: Detection engineering
modules.description: Writing detections the SOC can trust: detection logic and its trade-offs, Sigma rules as portable detection-as-code, ATT&CK mapping, testing rules against known-good and known-bad data, tuning, finding coverage gaps and reviewing rules - ending with a hands-on detection lab on the course dataset.

lessons.title: 7.1 Detection logic
lessons.summary: Signature, behavioural and anomaly detection logic, the precision-recall trade-off and the design questions to answer before writing a rule, using the kit's minisiem rules R1-R6.
learning_objectives: Distinguish signature, behavioural and anomaly detection logic and the logical shapes that express them
Calculate precision and recall for rule variants run against the Banyan dataset
Identify the attacker-controlled values and legitimate look-alikes of a detection rule
Apply the five design questions to harden a rule such as R1 before it is written
Explain why detection families should be layered and how the base rate affects alert quality

lessons.title: 7.2 Sigma rules
lessons.summary: The structure of a Sigma rule, how selections, modifiers and conditions match events, and how sigma-cli validates rules and converts them to Splunk queries through processing pipelines.
learning_objectives: Describe the fields of a Sigma rule using the kit's two rules
Interpret selections, value lists, modifiers and conditions, including filters
Validate rules with sigma check and interpret its errors and issues
Convert rules to Splunk with and without a processing pipeline and explain the difference
Evaluate a rule's ATT&CK tags and exceptions for correctness and evasion risk

lessons.title: 7.3 ATT&CK mapping
lessons.summary: How ATT&CK organises adversary behaviour into tactics, techniques, sub-techniques and procedures, and how to map detections and data sources to it and build an honest, versioned coverage matrix for the Banyan rules.
learning_objectives: Explain the relationship between ATT&CK tactics, techniques, sub-techniques and procedures
Map a detection rule to the technique its observation actually supports, with version and rationale
Identify the data sources and fields each mapped technique depends on
Build a coverage matrix that separates data, rule and test status
Recognise mapping errors and coverage theatre, including unverified technique IDs in rule tags

lessons.title: 7.4 Rule testing
lessons.summary: Testing detections as code: positive, near-miss, boundary and regression cases with the kit's test_rules.py, two real defects found by negative cases, and where historical replay and end-to-end lab checks fit.
learning_objectives: Design positive, near-miss and boundary test cases from a rule's decision points
Run and interpret the kit's unittest suite, including failure reports
Use failing tests to find and fix rule defects without losing true positives
Explain how tests guard tuning changes against silent regressions
Distinguish unit testing from historical replay and authorised end-to-end checks

lessons.title: 7.5 Tuning
lessons.summary: How a detection engineer tunes a rule: measuring per-rule precision and volume, diagnosing whether noise comes from data, logic, numbers or an authorised instance, narrowing R6 instead of suppressing, setting thresholds and R2's window from evidence with tests as the guard, and controlling every change.
learning_objectives: Measure a rule's precision and volume from dispositions and explain why precision says nothing about recall
Diagnose the cause of a noisy rule and choose between fixing data, narrowing logic, re-setting numbers and a scoped suppression
Run a threshold sweep on stored data and set thresholds and windows from baseline and attack-step evidence
Narrow a rule and update its unit tests so that the reason for the change is recorded and enforced
Apply a change-control path of reproduction, tests, replay, review, staged deployment and monitoring

lessons.title: 7.6 Coverage gaps
lessons.summary: How to find and prioritise coverage gaps: telling data-source, field and scope gaps from logic gaps, proving the Banyan dataset's real gaps by query (no DNS or flow, Sysmon process events only until 06:14, an untraceable VPN session), and ranking gaps by the threat they hide in a gap register.
learning_objectives: Distinguish data-source, field, scope and logic gaps and name the owner and fix for each
Measure what a SIEM actually collects per source, host and time period with inventory and scope queries
Identify the real coverage gaps in the Banyan dataset and the incident questions they leave unanswered
Prioritise gaps by likelihood, harm, compensating detections and cost, and record decisions in a gap register

lessons.title: 7.7 Rule review
lessons.summary: Review detections against a six-area peer review checklist and apply it to the course kit's two Sigma rules, raising real findings on severity, tests, data and ATT&CK tags.
learning_objectives: Explain why rule review is needed even when automated gates and unit tests pass
Apply the six-area checklist (logic, data, tests, metadata, ATT&CK tags, severity) to a detection change
Identify inconsistencies between a Sigma rule, its SIEM translation and the triage configuration
Verify ATT&CK tags against a pinned ATT&CK version before raising or closing a finding
Write classified review findings that an author can act on

lessons.title: 7.8 Detection lab
lessons.summary: Hands-on lab: design, implement, test, mutate and integrate a correlation rule that links a macro-document download to an Office-spawned shell on the Banyan dataset.
learning_objectives: Turn a detection requirement into SQL logic and matching positive, negative and boundary tests
Run test_rules.py and minisiem.py rules and interpret the results
Diagnose and fix a time-window boundary bug exposed by a test
Integrate a new rule with triage metadata and confirm its queue position
Review your own rule with the six-area checklist, including its Sigma correlation version

modules.title: Incident handling
modules.description: How a SOC analyst takes part in incident response: the incident response lifecycle, communication under pressure, giving containment advice, preserving evidence, the severity matrix, post-incident review and tabletop exercises - finishing with an incident response lab built on the course dataset.

lessons.title: 8.1 Incident response lifecycle
lessons.summary: How an incident moves through the NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle and its CSF 2.0 framing in Rev. 3, and what the SOC analyst does in each phase, traced through the Banyan intrusion.
learning_objectives: Describe the four phases of the NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 lifecycle and its feedback paths
Map the classic phases onto the CSF 2.0 Functions and Categories used by SP 800-61 Rev. 3
Explain the SOC analyst's responsibilities in preparation, analysis, containment and post-incident activity
Scope an incident from lab hunt output and state the telemetry the scope rests on
Place each Banyan alert and action in its lifecycle phase

lessons.title: 8.2 Communication
lessons.summary: Communicating during an incident: audiences, the incident log, status updates and cadence, out-of-band channels, need-to-know, and the facts the SOC supplies for CERT-In and other notifications.
learning_objectives: Identify internal and external incident audiences and route communication through the IR lead and designated roles
Write technical and executive status updates from one incident log with confidence labels and a next-update time
Decide when to move to an out-of-band channel and apply need-to-know, codenames and TLP
Supply legal and the CERT-In point of contact with the time noticed, six-hour point and confidence-labelled facts

lessons.title: 8.3 Containment advice
lessons.summary: How a SOC analyst recommends short-term and long-term containment, weighs each action's harm reduction, evidence cost, business impact and tip-off risk, and applies it to WS-104, gopal and svc_update.
learning_objectives: Compare host, account, network and persistence containment actions by their effect, cost and signal to the attacker
Distinguish short-term from long-term containment and give each measure an owner and end condition
Explain why all known footholds should be contained together and when to act immediately instead
Describe who recommends, approves, executes and verifies containment under a containment authority
Write and verify a containment recommendation for the Banyan incident from SIEM evidence

lessons.title: 8.4 Evidence preservation
lessons.summary: Preserving incident evidence in order of volatility, with SHA-256 integrity and a chain of custody, using the kit's evidence_export.py, plus log preservation, legal hold and Indian evidence law basics.
learning_objectives: Apply the RFC 3227 order of volatility to a live compromised workstation
Explain what a SHA-256 match proves and what it does not
Export, verify and tamper-test log evidence with evidence_export.py and record its chain of custody
Identify limitations of an evidence tool and compensate with documented queries
Describe log preservation, legal hold and the SOC's role in them

lessons.title: 8.5 Severity matrix
lessons.summary: How an incident's severity is derived, as distinct from alert severity: functional, information and recoverability impact, scope and urgency combined in a matrix with floor rules, applied to the Banyan cases and re-rated as evidence arrives.
learning_objectives: Distinguish incident severity from alert severity and identify who owns each
Rate functional impact, information impact and recoverability using defined categories
Derive a base severity from impact and scope with a severity matrix and adjust it for urgency and floor rules
Apply the matrix to the Banyan cases, rating unknowns on the reasonable worst case and recording confidence
Separate severity of record from operating severity and from regulatory reportability

lessons.title: 8.6 Post-incident review
lessons.summary: Running a blameless post-incident review of the Banyan incident: reconstructing the attacker and defender timeline from the dataset, separating root cause from contributing factors, writing owned and verifiable actions, and computing dwell time and related metrics from real timestamps.
learning_objectives: Explain the principles of a blameless review and rewrite blameful findings as system findings
Reconstruct a sourced UTC timeline of attacker and defender activity from minisiem queries and the case record
Distinguish the root cause from contributing factors, each supported by evidence
Write action items with one owner, a due date and a verification method
Compute and interpret dwell time and related intervals from the dataset's timestamps

lessons.title: 8.7 Tabletop
lessons.summary: Designing, facilitating and evaluating a tabletop exercise - objectives, scenario, injects and the MSEL, roles, facilitation, hotwash and after-action report - with a ready-to-run Banyan Microfinance scenario that tests declaration, containment authority, the CERT-In deadline and out-of-band communication.
learning_objectives: Distinguish a tabletop from seminars, drills, functional, full-scale and red or purple team exercises
Write evaluable exercise objectives and an MSEL with timed injects, expected actions and branches that do not depend on one decision
Facilitate a tabletop with role-directed questions, time management and a visible decision log
Evaluate an exercise through evaluator notes, a hotwash and an after-action report and improvement plan with owned actions
Run the Banyan tabletop and calculate the CERT-In deadline in UTC and IST

lessons.title: 8.8 IR lab
lessons.summary: Working the Banyan incident end to end with the C08 kit: declaring and starting the CERT-In clock, scoping with hunts and negative checks, building a reproducible timeline, writing ordered containment advice, assembling and verifying a hashed evidence package, and writing the incident report.
learning_objectives: Declare an incident from a triaged queue and record the noticed time and CERT-In deadline in UTC and IST
Scope an incident with hunt.py and negative checks, stating the limit of each check
Build an incident timeline from one reproducible query and label each line as observed or inferred
Write ordered, owned, evidence-aware containment advice for both incident threads
Assemble an evidence package with evidence_export.py, rebuild and verify the SHA-256 manifest, and demonstrate tamper detection

modules.title: Phishing and malware triage
modules.description: Handling the alerts SOCs see most: suspicious emails and the malware they carry. Email header analysis, safe URL and attachment checks, sandbox use, handling user reports, signs of account compromise, containment and reporting - practised in a phishing triage lab, all from the defender's side.

lessons.title: 9.1 Email header analysis
lessons.summary: Interpret message headers and authenticate the source of each observation.
learning_objectives: Identify trusted Received hops
Distinguish envelope, signing and visible From identities
Explain alignment and document next verification steps

lessons.title: 9.2 URL and attachment checks
lessons.summary: Triage suspicious links and attachments from preserved artifacts without opening them on an analyst workstation.
learning_objectives: Separate display text from the recorded destination
Interpret static file metadata with its limitations
Route evidence to the approved analysis environment

lessons.title: 9.3 Sandbox use
lessons.summary: Interpret sandbox observations with attention to coverage, privacy and provenance.
learning_objectives: Trace observations to their monitoring source
Explain the limits of a single execution report
Make a policy-based decision about sample handling

lessons.title: 9.4 User reports
lessons.summary: Receive user-reported phishing and turn the initial report into an actionable incident record.
learning_objectives: Preserve the original submission and record user actions
Prioritise reports by observed interaction and possible impact
Close the feedback loop with the reporter

lessons.title: 9.5 Account compromise signs
lessons.summary: Correlate account activity across sign-in, mailbox, endpoint and network telemetry.
learning_objectives: Distinguish deviations from confirmed compromise
Correlate account and device evidence across sources
Document gaps and justify escalation

lessons.title: 9.6 Containment
lessons.summary: Recommend and verify scoped containment for suspicious mail, accounts and endpoints.
learning_objectives: Choose controls based on confirmed exposure and activity
Preserve evidence and obtain decision authority
Verify effective containment and record residual risks

lessons.title: 9.7 Reporting
lessons.summary: Write audience-appropriate phishing incident reports with clearly bounded claims.
learning_objectives: Separate observed facts from assessments and scope limits
Present time-sensitive decisions with owners and evidence
Preserve the source record and adapt distribution to each audience

lessons.title: 9.8 Phishing lab
lessons.summary: Apply the module workflow to Banyan's synthetic phishing case using the course kit.
learning_objectives: Preserve and evaluate evidence from the fictional case
Infer bounded scope from the dataset
Produce a defensible containment recommendation and incident report

modules.title: Threat hunting
modules.description: Learners plan and run hypothesis-driven threat hunts against saved, fictional Banyan Microfinance records and small synthetic fixtures. They check data coverage, write read-only hunt queries, build baselines, frame hunts around ATT&CK behaviors, document scope and reasoning, and validate findings into positive, benign or no-data outcomes.

lessons.title: 10.1 Hypothesis design
lessons.summary: Turn a hunt trigger into a testable hypothesis that names a behavior, scope, observable predictions and the evidence that would refute it.
learning_objectives: Write a hunt hypothesis that states a behavior, an entity scope, a time window and at least two observable predictions
Identify the refuting evidence for a given hypothesis before any data is examined
Rank three candidate hypotheses by impact, plausibility and data feasibility and justify the ranking
Rewrite an untestable or conclusion-shaped hypothesis into a falsifiable one

lessons.title: 10.2 Data needs
lessons.summary: Map each hypothesis prediction to the sources, fields, time coverage and quality it requires, and record what the hunt cannot see.
learning_objectives: Build a data-needs matrix that links each hypothesis prediction to a source, required fields and time coverage
Classify a hunt question as answerable, partially answerable or unanswerable from a stated data inventory
Distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence when a source is missing or incomplete
Describe how clock skew, retention and missing join keys limit a hunt conclusion

lessons.title: 10.3 Hunt queries
lessons.summary: Design read-only hunt queries that stack, filter, window and join records on shared entities, then check them by hand against a small fixture.
learning_objectives: Write pseudocode hunt queries using stacking, filtering, time windows and entity joins
Trace a query by hand over a synthetic fixture and state the exact rows it returns
Identify query defects such as time zone mismatch, null-field exclusion and join fan-out
Document a query with its purpose, inputs, assumptions and expected positive and negative results

lessons.title: 10.4 Baselines
lessons.summary: Establish what normal looks like using time windows, peer groups and frequency analysis, and judge whether an observation departs from it meaningfully.
learning_objectives: Choose a baseline window and peer group appropriate to a stated hunt question
Use stacking and frequency counts to separate common, rare and first-seen values
Compare an observation to a baseline and explain whether the deviation is meaningful
Explain why a baseline describes the past and is not an allowlist of safe behavior

lessons.title: 10.5 ATT&CK-driven hunts
lessons.summary: Use ATT&CK as a shared vocabulary to move from adversary behaviors to observable records and hunt hypotheses without overclaiming technique matches.
learning_objectives: Translate an ATT&CK tactic and behavior description into observable data predictions
Select hunt behaviors using threat relevance and data visibility rather than matrix coverage
Map an observation to ATT&CK with stated confidence and an alternative benign explanation
Explain why sequential tactic labels do not prove a connected intrusion

lessons.title: 10.6 Documentation
lessons.summary: Record hunts so another analyst can reproduce the scope, data, queries, results, confidence and limitations, including negative results.
learning_objectives: Complete a hunt record with hypothesis, scope, data sources, queries, results and limitations
Write findings in calibrated language that separates source observations, enrichment and analyst inference
Cite evidence by source and record identifier so another analyst can reproduce a finding
Produce handoff notes for incident response and detection engineering from a hunt record

lessons.title: 10.7 Validation
lessons.summary: Test hunt findings and hunt queries: corroborate across sources, weigh benign explanations, check for false negatives and assign defensible outcomes.
learning_objectives: Validate a hunt query against a seeded synthetic positive and a known negative
Corroborate a finding using independent sources and identify when sources are not independent
Assign a positive, benign or no-data outcome with a confidence level and justify it
Decide whether a validated finding should be escalated, closed or carried forward

lessons.title: 10.8 Hunt lab
lessons.summary: Run a complete paper hunt over supplied saved records: form hypotheses, check data, trace queries, compare baselines, document scope and defend findings.
learning_objectives: Form and prioritize hypotheses from the supplied Banyan and synthetic lab records
Trace hunt queries by hand and cite the exact records that support each result
Reach a defensible positive, benign or no-data outcome for each lab case
Write a scoped hunt report that separates observations, enrichment, inference and gaps

modules.title: SOC automation
modules.description: Operate defensive SOC automation as an auditable workflow: case management, orchestration, bounded enrichment, approval gates, metrics, and offline playbook testing.

lessons.title: 11.1 SOAR concepts
lessons.summary: Learn how a SOC workflow turns inputs into observable, reviewable decisions.

lessons.title: 11.2 TheHive and Cortex

learning_objectives: Distinguish an alert, case, task and observable

lessons.title: 11.3 Shuffle workflows

learning_objectives: Trace trigger data through actions and branches

lessons.title: 11.4 Approval gates
lessons.summary: Design a human gate that approves a specific defensive action with scoped authority.
learning_objectives: Capture a complete approval request

lessons.title: 11.5 Enrichment automation
lessons.summary: Build an enrichment workflow that records provenance, freshness and uncertainty.
learning_objectives: Normalize a typed observable without losing the original
Apply approved data handling and cache boundaries
Distinguish no-match, stale, error and unknown

lessons.title: 11.6 Metrics
lessons.summary: Measure workflow performance and outcomes without mistaking automation volume for effectiveness.
learning_objectives: Define comparable metric endpoints and denominators
Interpret queue, approval and verification metrics

lessons.title: 11.7 Safe playbooks
lessons.summary: Design playbooks with bounded authority, safe failure, duplicate handling and an audit trail.
learning_objectives: Specify preconditions and safe failure states

lessons.title: 11.8 Automation lab
lessons.summary: Test an offline automation playbook using a fictional case and check its outcome record.
learning_objectives: Run a local fixture through the simulated workflow

modules.title: Capstone
modules.description: Complete a defensive SOC shift from synthetic alert triage through case investigations, detection review and a documented change of watch.

lessons.title: 12.1 Capstone: triage alerts 1-15
lessons.summary: Build a first-pass triage queue for the first 15 synthetic alerts and document priorities.
learning_objectives: Read the case inputs and source fields
Prioritise alerts using impact and confidence

lessons.title: 12.2 Capstone: triage alerts 16-30
lessons.summary: Complete triage for alerts 16?30 and reconcile the queue with the first batch.
learning_objectives: Group duplicate items while preserving auditability

lessons.title: 12.3 Capstone: case 1
lessons.summary: Investigate the first capstone case and separate evidence of execution from unverified scope.

lessons.title: 12.4 Capstone: case 2
lessons.summary: Investigate the second capstone case using authentication evidence and identity context.
learning_objectives: Interpret failed and successful authentication events

lessons.title: 12.5 Capstone: case 3
lessons.summary: Investigate the third capstone case and decide whether verified benign context resolves the alert.
learning_objectives: Test the benign hypothesis with independent records

lessons.title: 12.6 Capstone: detection 1
lessons.summary: Specify and test a defensive detection from the capstone evidence using offline fixtures.
learning_objectives: State a relationship, window and grouping field

lessons.title: 12.7 Capstone: detection 2
lessons.summary: Review a second capstone detection for context, duplicates and gaps.

lessons.title: 12.8 Capstone: shift report
lessons.summary: Write a shift report with decisions, evidence, operational risks and clear ownership.

lessonFiles.content:
## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Every organisation of any size produces a continuous stream of security-relevant events: a user signs in over the VPN, a laptop starts a process, a proxy forwards a request, a domain controller adds someone to a group. Almost all of these events are harmless. A very small number are the first visible traces of an intrusion. A **security operations centre (SOC)** is the team, process and technology that watches this stream, decides which traces matter, and acts on them quickly enough to limit the damage.

MITRE's guide *11 Strategies of a World-Class Cybersecurity Operations Center* (Knerler, Parker and Zimmerman, 2022) describes a SOC as a team primarily composed of security analysts, organised to detect, analyse, respond to, report on and prevent cybersecurity incidents. Each verb in that definition is a distinct activity. **Detect** means noticing that something may be wrong, usually because a rule or model raised an alert. **Analyse** means establishing whether the alert is real, what happened and how far it reaches. **Respond** means containing and recovering, usually in partnership with IT teams who own the systems. **Report** means telling management, regulators and sometimes customers what happened. **Prevent** means feeding what was learned back into controls and detections so that the next attempt is caught earlier or fails altogether.

In the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, the SOC lives mainly in the **Detect** and **Respond** Functions, but it cannot work without **Identify** (an asset inventory that tells the analyst whether a host is a test laptop or the payments server) and **Protect** (the controls whose logs the SOC reads). A SOC that does not know what the organisation owns, or which systems matter most, will treat every alert as equally important and will drown.

That last word is the central problem of security operations, and it is the reason this lesson exists. The events that reach a SOC as alerts are still far too many for every one to receive expert attention. Experienced investigators are scarce and expensive; alerts are plentiful and cheap. The **tier model** is the organisational answer: it arranges the team so that a large number of alerts can be handled consistently at the first level, and only those that need deeper skill move upward to people who can provide it. The alert lifecycle, shift handover, service levels and metrics in the rest of this module are all defined in terms of tiers.

> [!NOTE]
> The tier model is a way of organising work, not a ranking of people's worth. Tier 1 analysts make the highest number of decisions in the SOC, and a wrong Tier 1 closure can hide an entire intrusion. The tiers differ in the depth and duration of the work, not in its importance.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| SOC | Security operations centre: the team, processes and tools that detect, analyse, respond to, report on and help prevent incidents. |
| Event | A single recorded occurrence, such as a log-on, a process start or a proxy request. |
| Alert | An event or combination of events that a rule, model or analyst has flagged for human review. |
| Case | The record in the case-management system that holds an alert (or several related alerts), the analyst's notes, evidence and decisions. |
| Incident | A confirmed or strongly suspected security breach or attempt that needs a coordinated response. |
| Triage | Rapid assessment of an alert to decide whether it is real, how urgent it is and who should handle it. |
| Escalation | The formal transfer of a case to a higher tier or another team, with evidence and a reason. |
| Disposition | The conclusion recorded when an alert is closed: for example true positive, benign true positive, false positive or inconclusive. |
| Playbook | A documented set of steps for handling a particular type of alert or incident. |
| Tier 1, 2, 3 | Levels of the classic SOC model: triage, investigation and response, and specialist work respectively. |

## Why a SOC is organised in tiers

Imagine a SOC with no structure at all: every analyst picks alerts from one shared queue and takes each one as far as it needs to go. On a quiet day this works. On a normal day it fails in three predictable ways.

First, **the queue stops moving**. An analyst who picks up an alert that turns out to be the start of a real intrusion may spend the rest of the shift on it, quite rightly. While they do, the dozens of other alerts they would have looked at wait. One of them may be the more urgent case.

Second, **the work is inconsistent**. Without agreed boundaries, one analyst closes a certain alert type after a thirty-second check and another spends an hour on the same pattern.

Third, **expertise is wasted**. The colleague who can reverse-engineer a malicious document spends most of the day closing alerts caused by a misconfigured backup job, because that is what the queue contains.

Tiers solve these problems by **separating breadth from depth**. The first tier works the whole queue quickly and consistently, using playbooks, and has a clear duty to pass on anything that needs more time or skill. The second tier takes the smaller number of cases that are probably real and investigates them fully. The third tier provides specialist skills that are needed occasionally but intensely, and also works proactively on problems the queue never shows. Because each tier receives fewer, harder cases than the one below it, the team as a whole behaves like a funnel: wide at the top where alerts arrive, narrow at the point where specialists apply scarce expertise.

## The tiers in depth

### Tier 1: triage and first response

Tier 1 analysts watch the alert queues that the SIEM (security information and event management system), EDR (endpoint detection and response) and other tools populate. For each alert they answer a small set of questions as quickly as accuracy allows:

1. **Is it real?** Does the evidence in the alert actually show what the rule claims, or did the rule fire on something it was not designed for?
2. **What does it touch?** Which host, which user, and how important is each? A finance workstation used by a payments approver is not the same as a kiosk in the reception area.
3. **Is there an obvious benign explanation?** A scheduled change, a known administrative tool, an approved test.
4. **What happens next?** Close with a documented disposition, or escalate with evidence.

To answer these questions Tier 1 **enriches** each alert: it pulls asset context from the configuration management database (CMDB), identity context from the directory, reputation from threat intelligence, and the surrounding events from the SIEM. It follows playbooks, which tell it what to check for a given alert type and what conditions require escalation. It closes false positives and documented benign activity, and it escalates true or probable positives.

Tier 1 typically has a **time budget** per alert, and that budget is the reason the tier exists. If a case cannot be resolved within it, or if the playbook's escalation criteria are met, the correct action is to escalate rather than to keep digging.

Tier 1 also often handles **first-response actions** that the playbook pre-authorises: for example, isolating an endpoint through the EDR when a high-confidence ransomware detection fires out of hours, or disabling an account that is clearly compromised. These are deliberately limited, reversible actions, agreed in advance with the system owners, so that the SOC does not have to wait for a meeting while an attack spreads.

### Tier 2: investigation and incident response

Tier 2 receives escalated cases and investigates them in depth. Where Tier 1 asked "is this real?", Tier 2 asks "what exactly happened, how far does it go, and what must we do about it?" Typical Tier 2 work includes:

- **Scoping**: building a timeline, finding related alerts and events, identifying every affected host and account.
- **Root-cause analysis**: working out how the activity started, for example a phishing email or a reused password on an external service.
- **Containment recommendations**: deciding which accounts to disable, which hosts to isolate, which indicators to block, and agreeing those actions with IT operations and the identity team.
- **Coordination**: keeping the case record current, informing the SOC lead, and providing facts for any notification decisions.

Tier 2 analysts need a broader and deeper knowledge of operating systems, networks, identity systems and attacker techniques than Tier 1. They are also the people who decide, together with the SOC lead, whether a case is declared an **incident**, at which point the organisation's incident response plan takes over (Module 7 of this course).

### Tier 3: specialists and proactive work

Tier 3 is less a queue than a pool of specialist capability. Its members are called in by Tier 2 for problems that need particular skills, and in between they work proactively. Typical Tier 3 functions are:

- **Threat hunting**: searching for attacker activity that no rule has alerted on, starting from a hypothesis (Module 8).
- **Malware analysis**: examining a suspicious file to learn what it does and to extract indicators.
- **Digital forensics**: acquiring and analysing disk, memory and log evidence in a way that preserves its integrity.
- **Detection engineering**: designing, testing and tuning the rules that generate alerts in the first place (Module 6).

The last item is important for understanding the whole structure. Tier 3 does not only sit at the top of the funnel; it also reaches back to the bottom of it. When Tier 2 or Tier 3 learns something from an investigation, for example that a rule fires on a legitimate backup tool or that an attacker technique went undetected, that lesson becomes a change to a rule or a playbook, and Tier 1 receives a better queue tomorrow.

### The SOC lead

Above or alongside the tiers sits the **SOC manager or SOC lead**, who owns staffing and shift rotas, the quality of analysis, metrics, and communication with stakeholders: the CISO, IT leadership, legal and compliance, and external bodies. In India, the lead must make sure the SOC can support the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022, which require covered entities to report specified cyber incidents to CERT-In within six hours of noticing them and to retain logs for 180 days. A six-hour clock is a strong argument for clear tier boundaries and an out-of-hours escalation path: an alert that waits for the morning shift may already have used up the reporting window. Lesson 2 examines the lead and the other supporting roles in detail.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Escalation is a duty, not a failure. A Tier 1 analyst who escalates a case that Tier 2 later closes as benign has done the job correctly if the evidence at the time met the escalation criteria. A Tier 1 analyst who closes a real intrusion because escalating "looked weak" has not.

## How work flows through the tiers

The tiers are connected by two kinds of flow. **Escalation** moves cases upward: from the alert queue to Tier 1, from Tier 1 to Tier 2 when a case is probably real or exceeds the Tier 1 time budget, and from Tier 2 to Tier 3 when it needs specialist skills. **Feedback** moves knowledge downward: from investigations back to the rules and playbooks that Tier 1 uses. Both flows pass through the **case-management system**, which is the single place where an alert becomes a case, where notes and evidence accumulate and where ownership is recorded. A SOC that escalates by chat message or by tapping a colleague on the shoulder has no record of who owns a case, and cases fall through the gaps, especially at shift change.

The figure below shows this structure as one picture: where alerts come from, how they enter case management, how they move between tiers, where most of them leave the funnel, and how lessons return to the start.
