## Key takeaways

- Linux authentication is recorded as text sentences from sshd, PAM, sudo, logind and the account tools; the wording is the meaning.
- The sshd PID joins a connection's lines; the logind session number tracks the session.
- Separate internet noise (invalid users, no success) from targeted guessing (real accounts) and above all from a success after failures.
- Read every `Accepted` line for method, account and source against the account's baseline.
- sudo and account-tool lines show what a session did with privilege; account creation plus group membership is the Linux persistence pattern.
- `auth.log` cannot see SSH keys written as files; state that limit when reporting absence.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

A web server is one of the few systems in an organisation that is deliberately exposed to everyone on the internet. Anyone, anywhere, can send it a request at any time, and most of the requests it receives are not from customers. Search-engine crawlers index it, uptime monitors poll it, automated scanners probe it for forgotten files and known weaknesses, and occasionally a person tries to make the application do something it was never meant to do. The web server writes down every one of those requests. Its logs are therefore the defender's most direct record of what the outside world tried to do to a public application, and of how the application answered.

This lesson teaches you to **read** that record as an analyst. Lesson 1 of this module worked through Windows events and Lesson 2 through Linux authentication logs; both describe what happened *on* a host. Web server logs describe what happened *at* a host's front door: each line is one HTTP request and one response. The new element is the content of the requests: you must recognise attempts to read files or alter database queries in encoded form, judge from the server's answer whether they achieved anything, and tell them apart from harmless requests that look similar.

Throughout the lesson we use the customer portal of Banyan Microfinance, the course's fictional company, at `portal.banyan.example`. The C08 lab kit contains no web server data (its dataset holds Windows, Sysmon, VPN and proxy events), so every access-log line here comes from a small **illustrative** sample written for this lesson with documentation addresses. The analysis commands were run against that sample, and their output is shown exactly as produced.

> [!NOTE]
> A web server log is not the same as the proxy log you met in Module 2. A proxy log records requests that *your users* make to other people's websites, on the way out. A web server log records requests that *other people* make to *your* website, on the way in. Lesson 6 of this module returns to proxy logs.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Access log | The web server's record of every request it handled: one line per request, written when the response is complete. |
| Error log | The web server's diagnostic log: start-up and configuration problems, denied requests, failures of modules or upstream applications. Not one line per request. |
| Common Log Format (CLF) | The original NCSA access-log layout: client, identity, user, time, request line, status and response size. |
| Combined Log Format | CLF plus two quoted fields at the end: the `Referer` and `User-Agent` request headers. The default in most Apache and nginx installations. |
| Request line | The first line of the HTTP request: method, path with query string, and protocol version, for example `GET /login HTTP/1.1`. |
| Status code | The three-digit HTTP response code (RFC 9110), grouped into classes 1xx to 5xx. |
| User agent | A free-text header in which the client describes itself. It is chosen by the client and proves nothing. |
| Referer | A header (spelled with one "r" in the standard) naming the page that linked to the requested resource. Also chosen by the client. |
| Percent-encoding | Representing a character as `%` and two hex digits, for example `%27` for an apostrophe and `%2F` for a slash, so that it can travel inside a URL. |
| Reverse proxy / load balancer | A system in front of the web server that receives the client's connection and forwards the request, so the web server sees the proxy's address unless it is configured to trust a forwarded header. |
| X-Forwarded-For | A request header in which proxies record the original client address. Any client can also set it, so it is trustworthy only when written by your own proxy. |

## Why web server logs matter to a SOC

Three properties make these logs valuable.

**They are the record of the attack surface.** Firewalls in front of a public web server must allow ports 80 and 443 to everyone, so firewall logs show only that connections happened. The access log shows what each connection asked for.

**They record the server's answer.** Every line contains the status code and the number of bytes returned. A request for `/.git/config` that received a `404` and 196 bytes is a failed probe. The same request receiving a `200` and 2,400 bytes means the repository configuration was handed over, which is a finding in its own right.

**They are high-volume and noisy.** A modest portal can write millions of lines a day, and a large share of them come from automation. Separating crawlers, monitors and background scanning from targeted activity is much of the skill.

There is also a regulatory reason to keep them well. The CERT-In directions issued in April 2022 under section 70B of the IT Act 2000 require organisations to maintain logs of their ICT systems for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction. Because the logs hold client addresses and sometimes personal data in query strings, the DPDP Act 2023 also applies to them.

## Anatomy of an access log line

Both Apache HTTP Server and nginx ship with the Combined Log Format as their usual default. In Apache it is defined with format directives:

```text
LogFormat "%h %l %u %t \"%r\" %>s %b \"%{Referer}i\" \"%{User-agent}i\"" combined
```

In nginx the built-in `combined` format is defined with variables:

```text
log_format combined '$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] '
                    '"$request" $status $body_bytes_sent '
                    '"$http_referer" "$http_user_agent"';
```

The two definitions produce the same layout. Here is one line from the illustrative portal sample:

```text
198.51.100.23 - - [03/Nov/2026:10:04:33 +0530] "GET /account/statement?month=10%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20NULL-- HTTP/1.1" 500 531 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64)"
```

Reading it field by field:

- `198.51.100.23` is the **client address** (`%h` in Apache, `$remote_addr` in nginx): the address of whatever opened the TCP connection to the server. Behind a load balancer this is the load balancer, not the visitor.
- The first `-` is the **identity** field from the old RFC 1413 ident protocol. It is almost always `-`; nginx writes a literal hyphen.
- The second `-` is the **authenticated user** (`%u`, `$remote_user`). It is filled only for HTTP authentication handled by the web server itself (for example Basic authentication). Users who log in through the application's own login form do **not** appear here, which surprises many analysts.
- `[03/Nov/2026:10:04:33 +0530]` is the **time**, in the server's local time with its UTC offset. This server runs on Indian Standard Time; the line happened at 04:34:33 UTC. Module 2, Lesson 6 explained why you normalise to UTC before correlating.
- `"GET /account/statement?month=10%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20NULL-- HTTP/1.1"` is the **request line**: method, path including the query string, and protocol. It is logged as received, still percent-encoded.
- `500` is the **final status code** (`%>s`; the `>` asks Apache for the status after any internal redirects).
- `531` is the **response body size in bytes** (`%b`; a `-` means zero bytes). It excludes headers.
- `"-"` is the **Referer**: no referring page was sent.
- `"Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64)"` is the **User-Agent**: a short, generic browser-like string.

Decoded, the query string reads `month=10' UNION SELECT NULL--`. The apostrophe closes a string in a SQL statement, `UNION SELECT` asks the database to append the results of a second query, and `--` starts a comment that hides the rest of the original statement. The application answered with a server error. We will come back to what that answer means.

Microsoft IIS uses a different layout, the **W3C Extended Log File Format**: space-separated fields whose order is declared in a `#Fields:` header line at the top of each file, with times in UTC by default. The content is similar, but read each file's header rather than assume an order.

![Figure 4.5: Anatomy of a Combined Log Format access-log line](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M04-L03-F1.svg)

*Figure 4.5: Anatomy of a Combined Log Format access-log line. The nine positional fields of one portal access-log line, with the Apache format directive for each and the two fields Combined adds to the Common Log Format.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The figure lays the example access-log line out as a row of segments, one per field, so that you can see the Combined Log Format as a structure rather than a string. Analysts who know which position holds which field can read thousands of lines quickly and write parsing and search logic that does not break.

**Components.** From left to right the segments are: **Client address** ("198.51.100.23", top label `%h`), **Identity** ("-", `%l`), **User** ("-", `%u`), **Time** ("[03/Nov/2026:10:04:33 +0530]", `%t`), **Request line** ("GET /account/statement?month=10%27...", `"%r"`), **Status** ("500", `%>s`), **Bytes** ("531", `%b`), **Referer** ("-") and **User-Agent** ("Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64)"), both topped "Combined". The first seven, in blue, slate, orange and red tones, form the original Common Log Format; the last two, in violet, are the fields the Combined format adds. The request line is drawn widest because it is the longest and most interesting field, and the status is drawn in red because in this line it is the evidence that matters.

**Relationships.** The segments are positional: there are no field names in the log itself, only order. The request line and the two headers are wrapped in double quotes because they can contain spaces; everything else is space-separated. That is why the illustrative commands later in this lesson can use `awk '{print $9}'` for the status but must split on the quote character to extract the user agent.

**Execution flow.** The server fills these fields at different moments. Client address, time of arrival and request line are known as soon as the request is read; status and bytes only once the response has been sent. The line is written at the end, which is why a request that never completes (a client that disconnects mid-download) may be logged with a smaller byte count, and why the timestamp is the time the request was received.

**Technical interpretation.** Each field is under the control of a different party. The client address comes from the TCP connection and is hard to forge for a completed request. Status and bytes come from the server. The request line, Referer and User-Agent come entirely from the client, who can write anything. A good analyst weighs fields by who controls them.

**Practical example.** In the portal sample, the analyst reads this segment row for the 10:04:33 line and notes: an external client, no HTTP authentication, a query string carrying SQL syntax, a 500 status and a small, error-sized response, with a generic user agent and no referer. Each segment adds a fact; together they say "an injection probe reached code that failed".

**Security implications.** If an administrator changes the log format, every parser and saved search built on positions silently breaks; monitor for that. Because the request line is logged as received, attackers can use encoding to hide keywords from naive searches, so detection must decode before matching.

**Key learning.** Read a Combined Log Format line as nine positional fields, and trust each field only as far as you trust the party that wrote it.

## Status codes from the analyst's side

HTTP status codes are defined in RFC 9110. For a defender each class answers a different question about a suspicious request: was it served, redirected, refused, or did it break something?

| Code | Meaning | What it tells the analyst |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 200 OK | The resource was returned. | The request was served. For a probe of a sensitive path, this is the line that matters; check the bytes. |
| 206 Partial Content | Part of a resource was returned (range request). | Normal for media and resumable downloads; many 206s for one large file can indicate a download manager or bulk retrieval. |
| 301 / 302 | Redirect elsewhere. | Common after a login (`POST /login` then `302` to the account page) and for HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects. A 302 after a login attempt does not by itself prove success; read where the application redirects failures. |
| 304 Not Modified | The client's cached copy is still current. | Normal browser behaviour; zero body bytes. |
| 400 Bad Request | The server could not parse the request. | Malformed or deliberately mangled requests; often produced by scanners and by the server's own path normalisation rejecting traversal. |
| 401 / 403 | Authentication required / access forbidden. | Access controls working. Many 401s for one path from one source suggests password guessing against HTTP authentication. |
| 404 Not Found | No such resource. | Broken links, old bookmarks and, in bursts, content discovery: a client guessing paths. |
| 405 / 429 | Method not allowed / too many requests. | 429 shows rate limiting has triggered: a control firing, worth counting per source. |
| 500 Internal Server Error | The application failed while handling the request. | The input reached application code and caused an error. After an injection-shaped request, this is a strong prompt to read the error and application logs. |
| 502 / 503 / 504 | Upstream failure, unavailable, timeout. | Back-end or capacity problems; bursts can mark denial-of-service or a crashed application server. |

Two habits follow. First, always read **status and bytes together**. Error pages and "not found" pages tend to have a fixed size, so a run of `404 196` lines is one page repeated, and a line that breaks the pattern (a `200` with a much larger size for a path that usually fails) is the one to investigate. Second, remember that the status describes what the **web server** returned, not what the application did internally. An application that catches every error and returns a friendly page with `200` hides failures from the access log entirely; that is a logging weakness you should raise with the application owner.

## The error log

The error log is the server's diagnostic channel. It records start-up messages, configuration problems, requests the server itself refused, and failures talking to the application behind it. It is not one line per request, so it is far smaller, and that is its value: when the access log shows something unusual, the error log at the same second often explains it.

An nginx error log line for the probe of `/server-status` in our sample would look like this (illustrative):

```text
2026/11/03 10:04:14 [error] 2211#2211: *57 access forbidden by rule, client: 198.51.100.23, server: portal.banyan.example, request: "GET /server-status HTTP/1.1", host: "portal.banyan.example"
```

The fields are the local timestamp (no offset is written, so you must know the server's time zone), the severity in brackets, the worker process and thread identifiers, a connection number (`*57`), the message, and then key-value context: client, virtual server, request line and the `Host` header. "Access forbidden by rule" means an `allow`/`deny` rule in the configuration refused the request: the `403` in the access log was a deliberate control, not an accident.

For a `500` the web server's error log often says only that the upstream application returned an error. The detail lives in the **application log** (the framework's own log, or the database's error log). When the application is the target of an injection attempt, a database syntax error logged at the same moment as the access-log line is strong evidence that the input reached the query unsanitised, even though nothing was returned to the client. Make sure application and database logs are forwarded to the SIEM alongside the web server's, or this correlation is impossible.

## Who is really asking: addresses, proxies and user agents

### Client addresses behind proxies

Most production portals sit behind a load balancer, a content delivery network or a reverse proxy. The web server then sees every request coming from the proxy's address, and the access log's first field becomes useless for attribution unless the server is configured to take the real client address from a header such as `X-Forwarded-For`. Two errors are common. Some teams never configure it, so all traffic appears to come from two internal addresses. Others trust the header from anyone, so an attacker who adds `X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.1` to their requests appears in the log as that address. The correct design is to trust the header **only** when the connection comes from your own proxies, and to log both the connecting address and the forwarded address.

On an unfamiliar web log, first ask the platform team what the first field contains.

### User agents

The User-Agent header is whatever the client chooses to send. Browsers send long strings beginning `Mozilla/5.0`; command-line tools and libraries send their own names by default; well-behaved crawlers identify themselves and give a URL. Because it is self-declared, a user agent is **evidence about intent, never about identity**:

- A scanning tool's name in the user agent hints at automation, but anyone can copy or change it.
- A browser-like string proves nothing about a browser. In our sample the scanner sends the short string `Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64)`, which looks like a browser and is not one: it lacks the engine and version tokens real browsers send, and it requested no images, stylesheets or scripts.
- An empty user agent (`"-"`) is unusual for people and common for scripts, health checks and some API clients.
- A crawler claiming to be a major search engine can be verified by reverse DNS lookup of its address followed by a forward lookup of the name, as the search engines themselves recommend; a claim that fails the check is an impersonator.

Behaviour is more reliable than the header. Real browsers fetch a page and then its assets (stylesheets, scripts, images) within a second or two, send a Referer for those assets, and keep cookies. Automation tends to request pages without assets, at machine-regular intervals, with no Referer.

## Recognising scanning and injection attempts

Recognising an attack in a log needs a set of **shapes** and the habit of checking each against the server's answer.

### Content discovery

A content-discovery scan requests many paths the site does not have, looking for something left behind: environment and configuration files (`/.env`), source-control metadata (`/.git/config`), backups (`/backup.zip`), administration interfaces (`/admin/`, `/phpmyadmin/`), the login pages of popular content management systems the site may not even run (`/wp-login.php`), and server diagnostics (`/server-status`). In the log the shape is unmistakable: one source, a burst of `404`s within seconds, each for a different well-known path, usually with a fixed error-page size. It happens daily on any public server. The questions that turn background noise into a case are: did any of those paths answer `200`? Did the same source go on to do something else?

### Path traversal

Traversal attempts try to escape the web root by inserting `../` sequences into a path or parameter, aiming at files such as `/etc/passwd` on Linux or system files on Windows. Because servers normalise plain `../`, attempts are usually encoded: `..%2F`, `%2e%2e%2f`, or double-encoded `%252e%252e%252f`. In the sample, `GET /download?file=..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd` received a `400`. A `400` or `404` means the attempt was rejected or found nothing; a `200` with a response size similar to a system file is a likely compromise and an immediate escalation.

### Injection into parameters

Injection attempts place syntax from another language into a parameter so that the application passes it on to a database, a shell or a browser. In logs you see characteristic fragments, nearly always percent-encoded:

- **SQL injection**: an apostrophe (`%27`), keywords such as `UNION SELECT`, always-true comparisons such as `OR '1'='1'`, comment markers (`--`, `%23`), or time-delay functions.
- **Cross-site scripting**: script tags and event-handler attributes, usually encoded as `%3Cscript%3E` and similar.
- **Command injection**: shell metacharacters such as `;`, `|` and `$(` in parameters that should hold a number or a name.

The access log can only show injection in the **URL**. Data sent in the body of a `POST` request, which is where login forms and most API calls put their parameters, is not logged by default (and should not be logged wholesale, because it contains passwords and personal data). For that you rely on a web application firewall's logs, application-level logging of rejected input, or the database's error log.

### The server's answer decides the severity

The same suspicious request can be noise or an incident depending on what came back. The figure below turns this into the triage logic an analyst applies to any suspicious line.

![Figure 4.6: Triage of a suspicious web request by the server's answer](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M04-L03-F2.svg)

*Figure 4.6: Triage of a suspicious web request by the server's answer. The order of questions an analyst applies to a suspicious access-log line: authorised source first, then the status class, then the deeper logs.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The figure is a decision graph for one suspicious access-log line. It exists because analysts tend to react to the request (it looks alarming) when the deciding evidence is the response. It encodes the order of questions that separates background probing from a real compromise.

**Components.** The orange starting box is **Suspicious request in access log** ("scan path, traversal or injection marker"). Two violet decision boxes follow: **Known authorised source?** ("own scanner, monitor, crawler (verified)") and **What did the server return?**. Three outcome classes hang from the second: blue **4xx: 400, 403, 404** ("rejected or not found"), orange **5xx: 500, 502** ("input reached code that failed") and red **2xx / 3xx** ("the request was served"). The end states are green **Benign: document and tune**, slate **Record; watch source and volume**, orange **Read error and app logs** ("same second, same client") and dark **Escalate as possible compromise** ("bytes, follow-on requests, host").

**Relationships and arrows.** Every arrow points forward through the analyst's reasoning. From the authorisation check, the arrow labelled "yes" leads to the benign outcome and "no" leads to the status question. Each status class has its own arrow to an action. The orange error-log box has an arrow labelled "evidence it reached the query" into the dark escalation box, and the red served class goes straight there.

**Execution flow.** First rule out sources you know about, then read the status, then act. Authorisation comes first because a scheduled scan by your own vulnerability team produces exactly the same lines as an attacker's.

**Decision logic.** A 4xx means the control or the absence of the resource stopped the request; it is worth recording and counting, but it is not an incident alone. A 5xx means the input reached application code; it is a reason to look deeper but not yet proof. A 2xx or 3xx means the server answered successfully, and for a sensitive path or an injection-shaped parameter that is presumed serious until shown otherwise.

**Technical interpretation.** The status classes stand for layers of the stack: 4xx usually comes from the web server or framework before the business logic runs, 5xx from inside the application, and 2xx from a completed response. The decision graph is really asking "how deep into the system did this input get?".

**Practical example.** In the sample, 198.51.100.23's six 404s and one 403 go to the slate box. The traversal attempt's 400 joins them. The two SQL-shaped requests with 500 go to the orange box: the analyst opens the application and database error logs for 10:04:33 and 10:04:35. The same source's later `GET /api/v1/branches` with `200` is a public endpoint, but its timing (directly after the probes) means it is included in the case.

**Security implications.** A SIEM rule that alerts on every injection pattern will fire all day on a public site; one that alerts on injection patterns *with* 2xx or 5xx responses is far more useful. Unknown sources should never be assumed authorised: verify the scanner's address against the vulnerability team's schedule.

**Key learning.** Judge a suspicious web request by the server's answer, read in the order: authorised source, status class, then the deeper logs.

## Worked example: ten minutes of the portal's access log

The illustrative sample holds 23 lines written by the portal between 10:02 and 10:05 IST on 3 November 2026. Standard command-line tools show the method; Lesson 7 does the same in SIEM queries. The first three lines are an ordinary customer visit:

```text
203.0.113.14 - - [03/Nov/2026:10:02:11 +0530] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:132.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/132.0"
203.0.113.14 - - [03/Nov/2026:10:02:12 +0530] "GET /static/app.css HTTP/1.1" 200 18432 "https://portal.banyan.example/" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:132.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/132.0"
203.0.113.14 - - [03/Nov/2026:10:02:30 +0530] "POST /login HTTP/1.1" 302 - "https://portal.banyan.example/" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:132.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/132.0"
```

This is what normal looks like: a page, then its stylesheet one second later with the page as Referer, then a login form submitted as `POST` and answered with a redirect. A full browser user agent is consistent throughout.

### Step 1: the shape of the responses

```terminal
$ awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
     10 200
      7 404
      2 500
      1 403
      1 400
      1 304
      1 302
```

`awk '{print $9}'` prints the ninth space-separated field, which in the Combined format is the status (the request line counts as three fields: method, path, protocol). `sort | uniq -c` counts identical values and `sort -rn` orders them by count, highest first. Seven 404s and two 500s in three minutes is worth a closer look; on a busy site, compare with previous days.

### Step 2: who is receiving the errors

```terminal
$ awk '$9 ~ /^4/ {print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      8 198.51.100.23
      1 192.0.2.10
```

The condition `$9 ~ /^4/` keeps only lines whose status begins with 4, and `{print $1}` prints the client address. One source holds eight of the nine client errors. The single 404 for `192.0.2.10` is the crawler following an old link (`/branches/old-office`), a typical benign 404.

### Step 3: who the clients say they are

```terminal
$ awk -F'"' '{print $6}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
     11 Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64)
      4 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:132.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/132.0
      3 Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; ExampleBot/2.1; +https://bot.example/)
      3 HealthCheck/1.0
      2 Mozilla/5.0 (Linux; Android 14) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/130.0 Mobile Safari/537.36
```

`-F'"'` makes the double quote the field separator, so field 6 is the text inside the third pair of quotes: the user agent. The busiest client is the short, generic string, all eleven of its lines from 198.51.100.23. `HealthCheck/1.0` belongs to Banyan's uptime monitor at 192.0.2.200, which requests `/health` once a minute and receives a two-byte answer; it is the most regular source in the log, and it is benign.

### Step 4: injection and traversal markers

```terminal
$ grep -Ei '%27|union|%2e%2e|\.\.%2f|\.\./' access.log | awk '{print $1, $7, $9}'
203.0.113.52 /search?q=O%27Brien 200
198.51.100.23 /download?file=..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd 400
198.51.100.23 /account/statement?month=10%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20NULL-- 500
198.51.100.23 /account/statement?month=10%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271 500
203.0.113.52 /static/app.js 304
```

`grep -Ei` searches case-insensitively with extended regular expressions for an encoded apostrophe, the word `union`, or encoded and plain traversal sequences; `awk` then prints the client, path and status. Five lines match, and two of them are false positives worth studying:

- `/search?q=O%27Brien` is a customer searching for the surname O'Brien. Apostrophes are part of real names and addresses; a rule that alerts on `%27` alone will alert on customers.
- `/static/app.js` matched because `grep` searched the **whole line**, and this line's Referer was the O'Brien search page. Matching must be done on the right field, decoded.

The three remaining lines are the probes from 198.51.100.23: traversal rejected with `400`, and two SQL injection attempts (`10' UNION SELECT NULL--` and `10' OR '1'='1`) on the statement parameter, both answered with `500` and a 531-byte error page.

### Step 5: the source's whole story

In order, 198.51.100.23's eleven lines read: seven discovery paths in three seconds (all `404` except `/server-status`, refused by rule), one traversal attempt (`400`), two injection attempts (`500`), then the public API (`200`, 1,874 bytes), all without a Referer or any assets.

The analyst's conclusion: an automated probe of the portal by an unknown external source, with no evidence of success in the access log, and **one open question**: the two 500s. The next action is to pull the application and database error logs for 10:04:33 to 10:04:35. If they show a syntax error, the statement page builds its query from the parameter unsafely; that is a vulnerability to fix even though this attempt returned nothing, and it should go to the application team as a priority. The source address is then searched across the other logs in the SIEM.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The analyst in this example investigates by **reading logs** of requests other people sent. Reproducing the requests against the portal to "check" the vulnerability is testing, which requires written authorisation and belongs to the application security team under its rules of engagement, never to an analyst acting on their own initiative.

## Benign look-alikes

Most alarming-looking lines in a web log are harmless.

| Looks like | Usually is | How to tell |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Burst of 404s from one source | A crawler or a user following stale links; a broken page referencing a missing asset | Paths are real site paths, often with a Referer from your own site; the same 404 from many different clients points to a broken link |
| Regular requests every N seconds | Uptime monitoring, load-balancer health checks | A single fixed path (`/health`), tiny responses, a known source address agreed with operations |
| `%27` or `--` in a query | Names, addresses, product codes, pasted text | Appears in search or form fields, from clients with full browsing behaviour; no SQL keywords around it |
| Many requests with an unfamiliar bot user agent | A legitimate crawler, partner integration or SEO tool | Fetches `robots.txt` first; verifiable by reverse and forward DNS; respects disallowed paths |
| Discovery paths from one address | Your own vulnerability scanner or an authorised penetration test | The address and window match a scan schedule or a signed authorisation; confirm, do not assume |
| Spike of 5xx | A deployment or back-end outage | 5xx across all clients and paths at once, not one source; matches a change record |

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"The user field shows who logged in."** It shows only users authenticated by the web server itself. Application logins appear nowhere in the access log; you need the application's own authentication log.
- **Treating the first field as the visitor.** Behind a proxy it is the proxy, and a trusted `X-Forwarded-For` may be the attacker's invention if trust is misconfigured.
- **Alerting on the request alone.** A rule for "SQL keywords in URL" produces thousands of alerts a day on a public site. Combine pattern, status and source behaviour.
- **Searching encoded text with plain keywords.** `UNION SELECT` written as `UNION%20SELECT`, `UNION/**/SELECT` or with mixed case will defeat a naive search. Decode, normalise case, then match.
- **Forgetting the body.** No injection in the access log does not mean no injection: POST parameters are not there.

## Security implications, detection and defence

From the defender's side, web server logs support three kinds of detection:

1. **Behavioural rules**: one source producing many distinct 404 paths in a short window (content discovery); many 401s on one path (password guessing against HTTP authentication); a sudden rise in 5xx from one source (input reaching failing code); a sensitive path such as `/.git/` or `/.env` answering `200` from any source (a misconfiguration being exploited, or about to be).
2. **Pattern rules on decoded fields**: traversal sequences and injection keywords in the decoded path and query, scoped to parameters that should never contain them, and raised in severity when the status is 2xx or 5xx.
3. **Correlation**: a source that probed the portal and then appears in VPN or firewall logs, or a probe followed by new processes started by the web server account on the host.

Defensive controls that make the logs more useful and the attacks less effective:

- Put a **web application firewall** in front of public applications and forward its logs; it sees request bodies the access log does not.
- Configure **real client IP** handling correctly, with trust limited to your own proxies, and log both addresses.
- Remove what discovery scans look for: no `.git` directories, environment files, backups or diagnostic pages in the web root; restrict `server-status` and administration paths to internal addresses.
- Fix injection at the source with parameterised queries and input validation; the log tells you where to look, it does not fix anything.
- Apply **rate limiting**, and log its decisions (429s).
- Forward access, error, application and database logs centrally and retain them for at least 180 days.

## Key takeaways

- Access logs record one line per request in a positional format; the Combined Log Format adds Referer and User-Agent to the Common Log Format.
- The request line, Referer and User-Agent are written by the client; status and bytes are written by the server. Weigh evidence by who controls the field.
- Read suspicious requests through the server's answer: 4xx rejected, 5xx reached code and needs the error and application logs, 2xx served and needs escalation.
- Scanning looks like bursts of 404s for well-known paths; traversal and injection look like encoded syntax in parameters. Decode before matching.
- Apostrophes in names, crawler 404s, health checks and authorised scans are the everyday look-alikes; rule them out with evidence, not assumption.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

A firewall sits on a boundary and makes one decision, over and over: should this connection be allowed to cross? Every decision it logs becomes a line that says who tried to talk to whom, on which port, and what the firewall did about it. Module 2, Lesson 2 surveyed firewall logs as one network telemetry source among several. This lesson goes further and teaches you to **analyse** them: to read a raw line field by field, to understand what the firewall's state table and address translation do to what is recorded, to recognise the connection patterns that scans, malware and data theft leave behind, and to separate those from the far larger volume of harmless traffic that produces similar lines.

Firewall logs have a particular character. They are **content-blind**: a firewall that is not inspecting applications sees addresses, ports, protocol flags, byte counts and durations, never URLs, file names or commands. They are **voluminous**: a perimeter firewall on a modest network logs millions of decisions a day, and anything exposed to the internet receives a constant background of unsolicited probes. And they are **independent**: an attacker who controls a workstation cannot edit the firewall's log. That combination makes them poor at explaining *what* happened inside a connection and excellent at establishing *that* it happened, when, how often, and how much data moved. Analysts who understand that trade-off use firewall logs to confirm, scope and time-box activity first seen elsewhere, and to find patterns (regular beacons, outbound attempts on blocked ports, unusual volumes) that no single host log reveals.

Examples in this lesson use Banyan Microfinance's perimeter firewall `fw01`. Banyan's internet-facing address is `203.0.113.10` and its office network uses `10.40.0.0/16`. The C08 kit contains one real firewall line, in `LAB_ASSETS/C08/normalise_demo.py`, which we use first. Everything else is an **illustrative** sample written for this lesson with documentation addresses; the analysis commands shown were run against that sample and their output is reproduced exactly.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 5-tuple | Source address, source port, destination address, destination port and protocol: the identity of a connection. |
| Stateful firewall | A firewall that tracks connections in a state table, evaluating the rule base for the first packet and then matching later packets to the existing session. |
| Allow / accept | The connection is permitted. |
| Drop / deny | The packet is discarded silently; the sender receives nothing. |
| Reject | The packet is refused with a reply: a TCP reset or an ICMP unreachable message. |
| Implicit (default) deny | The rule at the end of a rule base that refuses everything not explicitly allowed. Its logging often has to be switched on separately. |
| Session log | A log entry per connection, typically written at session start, end or both; the end record carries bytes and duration. |
| SNAT / PAT | Source NAT: rewriting internal source addresses (and ports, for port address translation) to the firewall's public address on the way out. |
| DNAT / port forward | Destination NAT: rewriting the public destination address of inbound traffic to an internal server's address. |
| Zone / interface | The network segment a packet arrived on or leaves by (for example `eth0` outside, `eth1` inside); it gives a log line its direction. |

## How a firewall decides, and what it writes

### State changes what gets logged

Almost every modern firewall is stateful. When the first packet of a new TCP connection arrives (a `SYN`), the firewall walks its rule base from the top and applies the first matching rule. If the rule allows the connection, the firewall creates an entry in its state table, and every later packet of that conversation, in both directions, is matched against the table rather than the rules. When the connection ends with `FIN` or `RST`, or sits idle past a timeout, the entry is removed.

This has a direct consequence for analysis. A firewall does not log every packet: it logs **decisions**. Next-generation firewalls usually write one record when a session starts, one when it ends, or both, depending on configuration. A Linux netfilter firewall logs only the packets that hit a rule with the `LOG` target, which administrators normally place in front of the rules that drop traffic. If you are asked "did 10.40.0.23 talk to 198.51.100.80 at 10:02?", the firewall can only answer if the relevant rule had logging enabled, and the most frequent gap in real investigations is exactly that: denied traffic was logged, allowed traffic was not.

### Drop, reject and what the other side sees

Drop and reject both refuse a connection, but they look different from outside. A dropped `SYN` gets no answer, so the sender eventually times out; a port scanner reports such a port as *filtered*. A rejected `SYN` gets an immediate reset or ICMP unreachable, so the sender knows at once; a scanner reports it as *closed*. Many perimeter policies drop rather than reject inbound traffic, both to give scanners less information and to avoid generating replies to spoofed packets. In the log both appear as refusals; the action field and the absence or presence of a reply in session records tell you which was used.

### The real line from the kit

The lab kit's line is in the netfilter `LOG` style, received through syslog:

```text
Nov  3 12:16:21 fw01 kernel: DROP IN=eth0 SRC=203.0.113.66 DST=10.40.0.5 PROTO=TCP DPT=3389
```

Module 2 read its fields once; three points matter for analysis. First, the word `DROP` is **not** written by the kernel's packet filter as a verdict. Netfilter's `LOG` target only logs; the text that precedes `IN=` is a prefix the administrator chose (`--log-prefix`) when writing the rule, and the packet was dropped by a separate rule. A prefix is only as truthful as the person who configured it, so rule names and prefixes should be checked against the rule base. Second, `IN=eth0` with no `OUT=` field shown means the packet arrived on the outside interface. Third, the destination is a private address, `10.40.0.5`: an inbound packet addressed to an internal host means the rule that logged it was evaluated after destination NAT, or on a path that routes to the internal network, so the analyst must know where in the rule chain the logging rule sits.

The kit's `normalise_demo.py` turns that line into ECS-style fields. The script's own output, run on an unchanged copy of the kit, is:

```terminal
$ python normalise_demo.py
{"@timestamp": "2026-11-03T06:46:21Z", "destination.ip": "10.40.0.5", "destination.port": 3389, "event.action": "drop", "event.module": "firewall", "host.name": "fw01", "network.transport": "tcp", "source.ip": "203.0.113.66"}
{"@timestamp": "2026-11-03T06:46:00Z", "event.action": "login", "event.module": "vpn", "event.outcome": "success", "source.ip": "203.0.113.66", "user.name": "gopal"}
```

The firewall timestamp `12:16:21` (IST, assumed by the script) becomes `06:46:21Z`. The second line is the VPN event from the same kit. Read together they make a short, important story: at 06:46:00 UTC the address `203.0.113.66` logged in successfully to the VPN as `gopal`, and 21 seconds later the same address tried to reach an internal host on RDP from the outside and was dropped. A single drop of port 3389 from the internet is background noise; the same address succeeding at the VPN seconds earlier turns it into part of a case. That is the analyst's basic move with firewall logs: an individual line rarely means much, but a line joined to other evidence by address and time often does.

### A fuller netfilter line

Real netfilter log lines carry more fields than the kit's abbreviated one. A line from the illustrative sample, written by a rule with the prefix `FW-DROP-IN`:

```text
Nov  3 10:20:01 fw01 kernel: FW-DROP-IN IN=eth0 OUT= SRC=192.0.2.77 DST=203.0.113.10 LEN=44 TTL=52 PROTO=TCP SPT=61000 DPT=21 SYN
```

`OUT=` is empty because the packet was destined for the firewall's own address (input) rather than forwarded. `LEN` is the IP packet length, `TTL` the remaining time-to-live, `SPT` the source port, and `SYN` the TCP flag that was set: this was the opening packet of a connection attempt. Real kernels write further fields (MAC addresses, TOS, IP ID, TCP window and others), which this sample omits for readability.

### Session logs from a next-generation firewall

Commercial firewalls write richer, session-oriented records, each vendor in its own format. The illustrative sample uses a vendor-neutral key-value layout to show the fields most of them share:

```text
2026-11-03T10:02:41+05:30 fw01 action=allow rule=OUT-WEB src=10.40.0.23 spt=51290 dst=198.51.100.80 dpt=443 proto=tcp nat_src=203.0.113.10 nat_spt=40112 bytes_out=1840 bytes_in=52211 duration=12 reason=tcp-fin
```

It records the decision (`action=allow`) and the rule that made it (`OUT-WEB`), the internal 5-tuple, the translated source address and port, the bytes in each direction, the duration in seconds, and why the session ended (`tcp-fin`: a normal close). The direction of the byte counters is defined relative to the initiator in this sample; in real products check the documentation, because "sent" and "received" are defined differently by different vendors, and getting it backwards turns a download into an exfiltration.

## Address translation: one connection, two identities

Network address translation is where many firewall investigations go wrong. Banyan's workstations use private addresses, and every outbound connection leaves with the firewall's single public address. To the outside world, every Banyan user is `203.0.113.10`.

![Figure 4.7: One outbound connection through source NAT](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M04-L04-F1.svg)

*Figure 4.7: One outbound connection through source NAT. How fw01 rewrites a workstation's connection to its public address, reverses the translation for replies, and records both identities in its session log.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The sequence diagram follows one outbound HTTPS connection through source NAT, showing that the same conversation is known by two different 5-tuples on either side of the firewall, and that the firewall's own session log is the only record that holds both. This is the fact an analyst needs when an external party reports activity "from your address".

**Components.** There are four lanes. The blue **Workstation WS-104** lane is labelled with its internal address "10.40.0.23". The orange **Firewall fw01** lane is labelled "SNAT to 203.0.113.10". The slate **Web server** lane is the external destination "198.51.100.80". The dark **SIEM** lane on the right receives the log.

**Relationships and arrows.** Solid arrows are requests and dashed arrows are replies, all in time order from top to bottom. The first arrow runs from the workstation to the firewall, "SYN 10.40.0.23:51290 to 198.51.100.80:443". The second runs from the firewall to the web server, "SYN from 203.0.113.10:40112 (after SNAT)": the same packet, with source address and port rewritten. The dashed reply "SYN/ACK to 203.0.113.10:40112" comes back to the firewall, which sends the dashed "SYN/ACK to 10.40.0.23:51290 (reversed)" to the workstation, undoing the translation by looking it up in the state table. The arrow "data, then FIN: session closes" shows the conversation completing, and the final arrow from the firewall to the SIEM is the "Session-end log: src, nat_src, bytes, duration".

**Execution flow.** The translation is created when the first packet passes and is reversed for every reply until the session ends; only then, in a session-end configuration, is the record written.

**Decision logic.** There is one implicit decision: the first packet must match an allowing rule (`OUT-WEB` in the sample) before any translation entry exists. A denied first packet is never translated, so outbound denies are logged with the internal source address only.

**Technical interpretation.** Port address translation lets thousands of internal connections share one public address by giving each a distinct public source port. The pair "public address plus public port plus time" therefore identifies one internal connection, but only for as long as the firewall's records keep that mapping.

**Practical example.** A partner reports that `203.0.113.10:40112` connected to their server `198.51.100.80` at 10:02:41 IST. Searching the firewall's session log for `nat_spt=40112` around that time returns the line above, naming `10.40.0.23` and source port 51290. DHCP logs then tie `10.40.0.23` to WS-104 at that moment.

**Security implications.** Without translation records, every external report about Banyan's address is unattributable. Keep NAT session logs with accurate, synchronised time; a few minutes of clock error can map a report onto the wrong connection, because public ports are reused quickly.

**Key learning.** After NAT the outside world sees only the firewall's address and a port; the firewall's session log, joined on public port and time, is how you find the internal host.

## Connection patterns and what they mean

Single firewall lines are rarely conclusive. Analysis works on **patterns across many lines**: how one source's attempts spread across ports and hosts, how regular its timing is, how many bytes move and in which direction. The patterns below are the ones every SOC analyst should recognise, each paired with the benign activity that produces the same shape.

**Vertical port scan.** One source tries many destination ports on one host in a short time. In the log: the same `SRC` and `DST`, a run of different `DPT` values, `SYN` flags, all dropped, often within seconds. It is reconnaissance: the scanner is mapping which services a host offers.

**Horizontal sweep.** One source tries the same port on many hosts. In the log: the same `SRC` and `DPT`, many `DST` values. Sweeps look for one service (remote administration, file sharing, a newly vulnerable product) across an address range. Internet-wide sweeps of every public address are continuous, so a sweep against your public range is normal background; a sweep from an **internal** source across internal hosts is not, because it suggests a compromised machine looking for its next target.

**Outbound attempts on blocked ports.** An internal host repeatedly tries to reach the internet on a port policy forbids: SMB (445) or mail (25) from a workstation are classic examples. In the log: an internal `SRC`, the outbound interface, a deny, repeated. Malware that spreads over SMB or sends spam produces this pattern; so do misconfigured applications and laptops trying to reach a file share that is only available inside a home network.

**Regular small sessions (beaconing).** An internal host opens a short connection to the same external destination at a fixed interval, with nearly identical byte counts. In allowed-session logs this is the signature of command-and-control check-ins. Software update checks, telemetry and time synchronisation produce the same rhythm, which is why destination reputation, rarity across the estate and the presence of jitter matter.

**Large outbound volume.** A session with far more bytes sent than received, to a destination rarely seen before. It may be data theft; it is more often a backup, a cloud-storage sync or a video call.

**Out-of-state denies.** Packets with `ACK` or `PSH` flags but no matching state-table entry are dropped as invalid. They usually come from sessions that outlived the firewall's idle timeout, or from asymmetric routing where the firewall saw only one direction of a connection. They are noise to be understood, not attacks.

![Figure 4.8: Connection patterns in firewall logs and their look-alikes](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M04-L04-F2.svg)

*Figure 4.8: Connection patterns in firewall logs and their look-alikes. Six connection patterns an analyst recognises in firewall logs, the log signature of each and the benign activity that produces the same shape.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The table collects the six connection patterns of this lesson in one place, with the log signature that identifies each and its most common benign look-alike. It is a reference an analyst can hold against a set of firewall lines to decide which story the lines might tell, and what has to be ruled out before deciding.

**Components.** There are three columns: **Pattern**, **Log signature** and **Benign look-alike**. The six rows are **Vertical port scan**, **Horizontal sweep**, **Outbound to blocked port**, **Regular small sessions**, **Large outbound bytes** and **Out-of-state deny**. The first two rows are red because they are direct evidence of probing. The next three are orange: they can indicate compromise but need context. The last is slate: it is usually operational noise.

**Relationships.** Each row reads left to right as a hypothesis test. The signature column says what to count ("one SRC, one DST, many DPT, seconds"; "one SRC, one DPT, many DST"; "internal SRC, DPT 445 or 25, denied, repeated"; "same DST, fixed interval, similar bytes"; "bytes out far above bytes in, rare DST"; "ACK or PSH without SYN, dropped"). The look-alike column names what produces the same counts innocently ("authorised vulnerability scan"; "internet background scanning"; "misconfigured app or roaming laptop"; "update checks, telemetry, NTP"; "backup, cloud sync, video call"; "idle timeout, asymmetric routing").

**Execution flow.** In practice an analyst works down the table after an initial count of drops or sessions by source: group by source, count distinct ports and destinations, measure intervals and byte ratios, then compare with the look-alike column before raising severity.

**Decision logic.** Direction is the branch that matters most. The same vertical scan is background when the source is on the internet and the target is a public address, and a serious finding when both are internal. Likewise, regular sessions to a well-known update service are expected, while the same rhythm to a destination no other host contacts is suspicious.

**Technical interpretation.** All six signatures use only fields a content-blind firewall records: addresses, ports, flags, timing and byte counts. That is why they work across vendors and survive encryption, and also why each needs corroboration from content-aware sources (proxy, DNS, endpoint) before it becomes a conclusion.

**Practical example.** In the illustrative sample, `192.0.2.77` matches the first row against `203.0.113.10`; `198.51.100.140` matches the second across Banyan's public addresses; `10.40.0.31` matches the third; `10.40.0.23` matches the fourth with its five-minute sessions to `198.51.100.200`, and also the sixth with one invalid `ACK PSH` packet. The worked example below derives each of these from the raw lines.

**Security implications.** Detection rules built from these signatures should carry the look-alikes as explicit exclusions with owners and expiry, so that the authorised scanner or the backup server does not become a permanent blind spot.

**Key learning.** A firewall pattern is a shape in addresses, ports, timing and bytes; name the shape, then rule out its benign twin before you call it an attack.

## Worked example: analysing a burst of drops

The illustrative netfilter sample contains 25 dropped packets logged by `fw01` between 10:20 and 10:27 IST. Three representative lines:

```text
Nov  3 10:20:01 fw01 kernel: FW-DROP-IN IN=eth0 OUT= SRC=192.0.2.77 DST=203.0.113.10 LEN=44 TTL=52 PROTO=TCP SPT=61000 DPT=21 SYN
Nov  3 10:25:05 fw01 kernel: FW-DROP-OUT IN=eth1 OUT=eth0 SRC=10.40.0.31 DST=198.51.100.9 LEN=44 TTL=128 PROTO=TCP SPT=49831 DPT=445 SYN
Nov  3 10:26:30 fw01 kernel: FW-DROP-INVALID IN=eth1 OUT=eth0 SRC=10.40.0.23 DST=198.51.100.80 LEN=44 TTL=128 PROTO=TCP SPT=51544 DPT=443 ACK PSH
```

The prefixes tell you which rule logged each packet: inbound drops, outbound drops and invalid-state drops. The interfaces confirm direction: `IN=eth0` is from the internet, `IN=eth1 OUT=eth0` is from the office towards the internet.

### Step 1: who is being dropped

```terminal
$ grep -o 'SRC=[^ ]*' fw.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
     12 SRC=192.0.2.77
      8 SRC=198.51.100.140
      3 SRC=10.40.0.31
      1 SRC=203.0.113.66
      1 SRC=10.40.0.23
```

`grep -o` prints only the matching part of each line, here the `SRC=` field; the rest of the pipeline counts and ranks as in Lesson 3. Two external sources dominate. Two internal sources appear, which deserves more attention than their small counts suggest, because internal hosts should rarely be dropped at all.

### Step 2: how many ports, how many hosts

```terminal
$ awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){if($i~/^SRC=/)s=substr($i,5); if($i~/^DPT=/)d=substr($i,5)} print s, d}' fw.log | sort -u | awk '{n[$1]++} END{for(s in n) print n[s], s}' | sort -rn
12 192.0.2.77
1 203.0.113.66
1 198.51.100.140
1 10.40.0.31
1 10.40.0.23
```

The first `awk` walks every field of a line and keeps the values after `SRC=` and `DPT=`; `sort -u` removes duplicate source-port pairs; the second `awk` counts distinct ports per source. Changing `DPT=` to `DST=` in the same pipeline counts distinct destinations instead:

```terminal
$ awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){if($i~/^SRC=/)s=substr($i,5); if($i~/^DST=/)d=substr($i,5)} print s, d}' fw.log | sort -u | awk '{n[$1]++} END{for(s in n) print n[s], s}' | sort -rn
8 198.51.100.140
1 203.0.113.66
1 192.0.2.77
1 10.40.0.31
1 10.40.0.23
```

Now the sources sort themselves into the table's rows. `192.0.2.77`: twelve ports, one host, within three seconds: a **vertical scan** of Banyan's public address (ports 21, 23, 25, 110, 135, 139, 445, 1433, 3306, 3389, 5900 and 8080). `198.51.100.140`: one port (23, Telnet), eight hosts `203.0.113.11` to `203.0.113.18`: a **horizontal sweep**. Both were dropped and both are internet background unless something else connects them to Banyan. `203.0.113.66`: one RDP attempt, but the analyst recognises the address from the kit's VPN event and adds the line to that case. `10.40.0.31`: three outbound attempts on port 445 to one external address within nine seconds: **outbound to blocked port**, which needs an owner's explanation or an endpoint check. `10.40.0.23`: one invalid `ACK PSH` to a web server it had a session with: **out-of-state**, almost certainly an expired session.

### Step 3: timing in allowed sessions

Drops show what failed. To look for beaconing you need allowed-session logs. The illustrative session sample holds nine `allow` records; counting destinations gives:

```terminal
$ grep -o 'dst=[^ ]*' session.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      6 dst=198.51.100.200
      2 dst=198.51.100.80
      1 dst=192.0.2.150
```

Extracting the time and outbound bytes of each session to `198.51.100.200`, and the gap in seconds from the previous one:

```terminal
$ grep 'dst=198.51.100.200 ' session.log | awk '{split(substr($1,12,8),a,":"); t=a[1]*3600+a[2]*60+a[3]; for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i~/^bytes_out=/) b=substr($i,11); if(p) print substr($1,12,8), t-p, b; else print substr($1,12,8), "-", b; p=t}'
10:00:04 - 612
10:05:04 300 612
10:10:05 301 618
10:15:04 299 612
10:20:04 300 612
10:25:05 301 612
```

`substr($1,12,8)` takes the `HH:MM:SS` part of the ISO timestamp, which is converted to seconds; the loop extracts `bytes_out`; each line prints the time, the gap since the previous session and the bytes sent. Six sessions from `10.40.0.23`, 300 seconds apart give or take one, each sending 612 or 618 bytes and receiving 1,460, each lasting one second. That is a **beacon**: a program on the host checking in every five minutes. The analysis does not say whether it is malicious. The next steps are to ask whether any other Banyan host talks to `198.51.100.200` (rarity), what the proxy and DNS logs say about the destination name, and what process on WS-104 owns the connection (endpoint telemetry).

> [!TIP]
> Regularity is easiest to see as gaps, not timestamps. A list of times looks random to the eye; a column of `300 301 299 300 301` does not. Real implants often add random jitter, so look for a narrow spread of gaps rather than identical ones.

## Benign look-alikes

| Looks like | Usually is | How to tell |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thousands of inbound drops a day | Internet background scanning of every public address | Many unrelated sources, spread across ports, none followed by allowed sessions or other evidence |
| Vertical scan from one source | Your own vulnerability scanner or an authorised test | Source address and time window match the scan schedule or signed authorisation |
| Regular outbound sessions | Update checks, antivirus signatures, NTP, monitoring agents | Destination is contacted by many hosts, is a known vendor service, often on its documented port |
| Large outbound transfer | Backups, cloud sync, video conferencing | Known destination, scheduled time, known host role; confirm with the system owner |
| Outbound denies on 445 or 53 | A laptop or application configured for another network; a device using a hard-coded DNS server | Same host, same destination over days, matching a known application; endpoint confirms the process |
| Invalid-state drops | Expired idle sessions, asymmetric routing, failover between firewalls | Destinations the host had legitimate sessions with; spikes coincide with network changes |

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"The firewall would have logged it."** Only rules with logging enabled write lines, and allowed traffic is the usual gap. Check the logging configuration before concluding that a connection did not happen.
- **Treating every inbound drop as an attack.** A drop means the control worked. Inbound drops matter when they connect to other evidence, as `203.0.113.66` did.
- **Ignoring internal sources.** An internal host being dropped, or scanning other internal hosts, is far more significant than an external scan, and perimeter firewalls never see east-west traffic at all.
- **Trusting prefixes and rule names blindly.** A netfilter prefix is free text chosen by an administrator; confirm against the rule base.
- **Losing the NAT mapping.** Searching for the public address alone cannot identify an internal host; join on public port and time.
- **Misreading byte directions.** Vendors define sent and received differently. Confirm before calling a transfer an exfiltration.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Useful firewall detections, all built on fields a content-blind firewall records:

1. **Internal scanning**: one internal source contacting many internal hosts or ports within minutes (lateral movement reconnaissance). Needs internal firewall or flow logs.
2. **Outbound policy violations**: repeated denied outbound connections from one internal host, especially on SMB, SMTP, or direct DNS that bypasses the resolver.
3. **Beaconing**: sessions from one host to one rare destination with a narrow spread of intervals and similar byte counts, over hours.
4. **Volume anomalies**: outbound bytes from one host to one rare destination far above that host's baseline.
5. **Correlated external sources**: an external address that is dropped at the firewall and also appears in VPN, web or authentication logs.
6. **Allowed after denied**: a source with many drops followed by an allowed session, which can mean it found an open path.

Controls that make firewall evidence better:

- Log allowed **and** denied traffic at least for the perimeter and for sensitive internal zones, including the default deny rule.
- Keep NAT session records and synchronise firewall clocks with NTP; forward logs centrally with time zones recorded, and retain them for the 180 days the CERT-In directions require.
- Apply **egress filtering**: permit only the outbound ports the business needs, so that malware's attempts become denies you can see.
- Segment the internal network with logging between zones, so east-west movement crosses a firewall.
- Keep the rule base documented, with meaningful rule names and log prefixes, and review it for rules that allow more than intended.

## Key takeaways

- Firewalls log decisions, not packets: what is recorded depends on which rules have logging enabled, and allowed traffic is the common gap.
- Drop gives no reply and reject gives a reset or ICMP unreachable; netfilter prefixes such as `DROP` are labels chosen by the administrator.
- After source NAT, the internal host is found only through the firewall's session log, joined on public port and time.
- Analyse patterns across lines: vertical scans, horizontal sweeps, outbound attempts on blocked ports, beacons, large outbound volumes and out-of-state drops.
- Every pattern has a benign twin; direction (internal or external), rarity and corroboration from other logs decide which story is true.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Almost every connection a computer makes starts with a question: *what is the address of this name?* Before a browser opens `https://mail.banyan.example/`, before an update agent checks for a new version, and before a piece of malware contacts its controller, something on the machine asks a DNS resolver to translate a name into an address. The Domain Name System is therefore the most universal piece of network behaviour in any estate, and a resolver that records the questions it is asked holds a running diary of what every host is trying to reach.

Module 2, Lesson 2 introduced DNS logs as one network telemetry source among several and listed what a query log contains. This lesson is about **analysis**: reading DNS records field by field, knowing what normal looks like, and recognising the handful of patterns that mean something is wrong. Those patterns fall into three families:

1. **Failure patterns.** A burst of NXDOMAIN ("this name does not exist") answers, especially for names that look random, is the classic trace of malware that generates candidate domains with an algorithm and tries them until one answers.
2. **Shape patterns.** Query names with unusually long, high-entropy labels, or a host asking for hundreds of different subdomains of one parent domain, suggest that data is being carried *inside* the names themselves: DNS tunnelling.
3. **Volume and type patterns.** A workstation making a steady stream of TXT queries, or querying an outside resolver directly instead of the company resolver, is behaving unlike an ordinary desktop.

DNS is attractive to an adversary for the same reason it is valuable to a defender: it is everywhere and rarely blocked. Even a strict firewall lets workstations ask the internal resolver about names, and the resolver forwards the question to whichever server is authoritative for that name. If the adversary controls that server, the question itself becomes a message, as the first figure shows.

DNS analysis also has honest limits. The resolver sees *names and answers*, not the traffic that follows; encrypted DNS to an outside provider and hard-coded IP addresses leave no trace in its log. And a strange-looking name is not proof of compromise, because CDNs and cloud services generate random-looking names constantly. The analyst combines the shape of the name with **who asked, how often, what the answer was and what happened next**.

> [!NOTE]
> The Banyan Microfinance lab dataset (`LAB_ASSETS/C08/banyan_events.jsonl`) contains proxy, Sysmon, Windows and VPN events, but **no DNS resolver events**. ## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Stub resolver | The DNS client built into the operating system; it sends queries to a configured recursive resolver and caches answers. |
| Recursive resolver | The server (internal DNS server or a provider's) that finds an answer on the client's behalf by asking root, top-level-domain and authoritative servers in turn. This is where query logging normally happens. |
| Authoritative server | The server that holds the records for a zone (for example `banyan.example`) and gives the definitive answer for names in it. |
| QNAME, QTYPE | The queried name and the record type requested (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, PTR, SRV and others). |
| RCODE | The response code in the answer header: NOERROR (0), SERVFAIL (2), NXDOMAIN (3), REFUSED (5) are the ones an analyst meets daily. |
| NXDOMAIN | "Non-existent domain": the authoritative data says the name does not exist. |
| TTL | Time to live: how many seconds a resolver may cache an answer. |
| Label | One dot-separated part of a name. `ping.cdn-telemetry-sync.example` has three labels. |
| Registered domain | The part of a name that an organisation registers, for example `banyan.example` in `mail.banyan.example`; analysis often groups by it. |
| DGA | Domain generation algorithm: code that derives many candidate domain names (often from the date and a seed) so that malware can find its controller without a fixed name (MITRE ATT&CK T1568.002). |
| DNS tunnelling | Carrying data inside DNS queries and responses, usually by encoding it into subdomain labels and record data of a zone the adversary controls (ATT&CK T1071.004 for DNS as a command channel; T1572 for protocol tunnelling generally). |
| Shannon entropy | A measure of how unpredictable the characters of a string are, in bits per character; random strings score higher than words. |
| Encrypted DNS | DNS over TLS (DoT, TCP port 853) or DNS over HTTPS (DoH, inside ordinary HTTPS on port 443); both hide queries from on-path observers and from resolvers they bypass. |
| Passive DNS | A historical database of observed name-to-address answers, used to see what a domain resolved to in the past and which other names shared its addresses. |

## Where DNS records come from

DNS evidence reaches a SOC from three kinds of vantage point, and each answers a slightly different question.

**The recursive resolver.** An internal DNS server (Windows DNS, BIND, Unbound) or a protective DNS service can log every query it receives: one log covers every host that uses it. Its weakness is identity: it sees the **source IP address**, and behind a local forwarder every query appears to come from the forwarder, so attribution needs the forwarder's logs or DHCP leases.

**The network sensor.** A passive sensor such as Zeek, watching a copy of traffic, writes a `dns.log` with one entry per query and response pair. Its standard fields include `ts`, `uid`, the connection's `id.orig_h` / `id.resp_h` addresses and ports, `query`, `qtype_name`, `rcode_name`, the `answers` list and their `TTLs`, and flags such as `RD` (recursion desired) and `RA` (recursion available). A sensor sees DNS that bypasses the internal resolver, for example a workstation sending queries straight to an outside server on UDP port 53, which the resolver itself never sees.

**The endpoint.** Sysmon event ID 22 (DNSEvent), introduced in Module 2, Lesson 1, records a query made through the Windows DNS client with `QueryName`, `QueryStatus`, `QueryResults` and, crucially, the `Image` that made it. It is the only one of the three that can say *which process* asked. A resolver log can tell you that WS-104 looked up a strange name; Sysmon event 22 can tell you it was `powershell.exe` rather than the browser.

The analyst's working record is the same regardless of source. Normalised into the SIEM, a DNS event should carry at least: timestamp (UTC), client address and, if known, host and user, the queried name, the query type, the response code, the answers and their TTLs, and the resolver or sensor that observed it.

### Reading one record

The illustrative record below is written in the normalised style used in this course (it is not lab output; field names follow ECS-like conventions from Module 3):

```json
{
  "@timestamp": "2026-11-03T06:16:58Z",
  "source.ip": "10.40.0.23",
  "host.name": "WS-104",
  "dns.question.name": "cdn-telemetry-sync.example",
  "dns.question.type": "A",
  "dns.response_code": "NOERROR",
  "dns.answers": [{"data": "203.0.113.80", "ttl": 300}],
  "observer.name": "dns-resolver-01"
}
```

Read it as a sentence: *at 06:16:58 UTC, workstation WS-104 asked resolver dns-resolver-01 for the IPv4 address of `cdn-telemetry-sync.example`; the name exists and resolved to 203.0.113.80, cacheable for 300 seconds.* Every part of that sentence is a pivot. The name can be stacked across the estate (who else asked?). The answer address can be searched in firewall and proxy logs (who connected to it?). The timestamp can be lined up against the endpoint timeline (what process started just before?). The TTL hints at infrastructure: very short TTLs on names whose answers change constantly are one trait of fast-flux hosting (ATT&CK T1568.001), though many legitimate load-balanced services also use short TTLs.

### How recursion carries a question to its owner

To understand both DGA failures and tunnelling, you have to follow a query beyond the resolver. The internal resolver does not know the answer to most names; it finds the authoritative server for the zone and asks it. For a name under a zone the organisation does not control, the question is delivered, by design, to whoever runs that zone's authoritative server.
