## Key takeaways

- MISP stores intelligence as events containing typed attributes and template objects, labelled with taxonomy tags and linked to galaxy clusters such as ATT&CK techniques.
- Category, type and the IDS flag decide whether a value reaches the right control; the IDS flag follows specificity and validity, not severity.
- Distribution is enforced by the platform; TLP instructs people. Use sharing groups for precise audiences and keep the two consistent.
- Correlation links events by exact value; warninglists, exclusions and disabled correlation keep it meaningful.
- Sightings, feeds, synchronisation and the API connect MISP to the SOC pipeline and return feedback to producers.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

A threat intelligence feed is a stream of indicators, and sometimes of richer objects such as reports and relationships, that a producer publishes on a schedule so that consumers can load them into their tools. To a SOC, a feed looks like a simple promise: subscribe, import, and your SIEM will start telling you when known-bad infrastructure appears in your logs. In practice the promise is only kept by teams that manage their feeds as carefully as they manage their detection rules. A feed that is imported blindly does three kinds of damage. It floods the queue with matches on addresses that were bad two years ago and now belong to someone else. It hides the few indicators that matter among thousands that do not. And, when it drives automatic blocking, it can take down a business service because a content delivery network address was once listed next to a phishing page.

Lessons 1 to 4 covered indicator types, confidence, enrichment and MISP. This lesson is about the inbound side of the platform: **where feeds come from, what formats they arrive in, how to judge whether a feed is worth having, and the four routine operations that keep a feed useful: normalisation and deduplication, allowlisting, scoring, and ageing out.**

The organising idea is the one the intelligence cycle starts with: *requirements first*. A SOC should be able to say, for every feed it consumes, which question that feed helps answer. "Which infrastructure is being used against finance-sector users in India this quarter?" is a requirement; "more indicators are better" is not. A feed with no requirement behind it is noise with a licence fee.

> [!NOTE]
> The feed in this course's lab kit (`LAB_ASSETS/C08/ioc_match.py`) is a small fictional list whose fields mirror STIX ideas (type, value, confidence, valid_until, source, context, TLP). It is a teaching structure, not STIX JSON, and its five entries deliberately come from the four kinds of source this lesson describes.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Feed | A regularly updated, machine-readable publication of indicators or intelligence objects from one producer. |
| Open feed | A feed published free of charge, often by researchers or community projects, usually with little context per indicator. |
| Commercial feed | A paid feed from a security vendor, typically with curation, context, confidence scores and a support contract. |
| Community / ISAC feed | Intelligence shared among members of a trust community such as a sector Information Sharing and Analysis Center, usually under TLP. |
| Internal intelligence | Indicators produced by your own SOC from its own incidents and investigations. |
| STIX 2.1 | Structured Threat Information Expression, an OASIS standard JSON format for intelligence objects such as indicators, malware and relationships. |
| TAXII | Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information, the companion protocol for transporting STIX content over HTTPS. |
| Normalisation | Converting indicator values to one canonical form so that the same indicator from two feeds compares as equal. |
| Deduplication | Merging records that describe the same indicator into one, while keeping every source and sighting. |
| Allowlist | A curated list of values (own domains, critical services, shared infrastructure) that must never raise alerts or be blocked on indicator evidence alone. |
| Ageing out | Lowering the weight of, and finally retiring, an indicator as it gets older or passes its `valid_until` time. |
| Hit rate | The share of a feed's indicators that ever match your telemetry; a measure of relevance, not of quality on its own. |

## Where feeds come from

Every feed is shaped by who produces it and why. Knowing the producer's incentives tells you what to expect from the content.

### Open feeds

Open feeds are published free by researchers, non-profit projects and community volunteers. Typical content is a list of addresses, domains, URLs or file hashes associated with a category of activity: scanning, botnet command and control, phishing pages, malware distribution. Their strengths are cost, breadth and speed; their weaknesses follow from how they are produced. Many open lists are generated automatically from honeypots or sandboxes, so an entry means "this address did something we classify as bad, at some point" and little more. Context is thin, confidence is rarely stated, and entries are not always removed when the address is reassigned. An open-feed entry should normally be treated as a lead for enrichment, not a reason to block.

### Commercial feeds

Commercial feeds are sold by security vendors, either on their own or bundled with a product such as an EDR, firewall or threat intelligence platform. You are paying for curation: analysts who vet indicators, attach context (malware family, campaign, first and last seen), assign confidence and expire entries. Quality varies by vendor, and the contract matters as much as the data: licensing may forbid sharing the indicators onward. Commercial feeds also overlap heavily with open sources; part of evaluating one is measuring how much of it you already have.

### Community and ISAC feeds

Information Sharing and Analysis Centers and similar trust communities exist so that organisations facing the same threats can warn each other. Their content is often the most relevant you will receive, because it was seen against organisations like yours, and it usually carries context written by an analyst who handled the incident. It also carries obligations: community intelligence is normally shared under the Traffic Light Protocol, and breaking a TLP:AMBER restriction can cost you your membership as well as tip off the adversary. In India, CERT-In advisories play a related role.

### Internal intelligence

The best source of indicators for your organisation is often your own SOC. Every confirmed incident produces infrastructure, file hashes and behaviours that were proven to be used against you. Internal intelligence has the highest relevance and, if the investigation was sound, high confidence. Its weakness is coverage: it only contains what you have already seen. Record it in the same platform and fields as external feeds, so it is matched, aged and shared the same way.

### The lab feed by source

The five entries in the lab kit cover all four kinds of source:

| Indicator | Source in the feed | Kind of source | Confidence | TLP |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` | ISAC-A | Community / ISAC | 85 | TLP:AMBER |
| `banyan-payroll-update.example` | internal | Internal | 70 | TLP:GREEN |
| `203.0.113.66` | ISAC-A | Community / ISAC | 60 | TLP:GREEN |
| `198.51.100.104` | open feed | Open | 40 | TLP:CLEAR |
| `9f2c...e1a0` (SHA-256, truncated) | vendor | Commercial | 90 | TLP:AMBER |

Confidence and source kind do not line up neatly: the commercial hash has the highest confidence, the open-feed address the lowest. Confidence belongs to each indicator, not to the feed, so indicators are scored one by one.

## Formats: from CSV lists to STIX and TAXII

Feeds arrive in a few recurring formats. The format decides how much context survives the journey from producer to your SIEM.

### Plain lists and CSV

The simplest feeds are text files with one value per line, or CSV files with a few columns such as value, type, first seen and a category. They are trivial to parse and to load into a lookup table, which is why so many open feeds use them. Their limitation is that each consumer must guess the meaning of the columns, there is no standard way to express confidence, validity or relationships, and a value with no type column is ambiguous (is `example.com` a domain or part of a URL?).

### STIX 2.1

STIX 2.1 (Structured Threat Information Expression), an OASIS Standard since 10 June 2021, defines a set of JSON objects for exchanging intelligence. Domain objects include `indicator`, `malware`, `threat-actor`, `intrusion-set`, `campaign`, `attack-pattern`, `infrastructure`, `vulnerability` and `report`; relationship objects connect them, for example "indicator *indicates* malware". For a SOC the most important object is the indicator, because it carries a detection pattern and the properties that a feed-management process needs. A minimal indicator for the ISAC domain in the lab feed might look like this (the identifier is a placeholder UUID):

```json
{
  "type": "indicator",
  "spec_version": "2.1",
  "id": "indicator--00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
  "created": "2026-11-01T09:00:00.000Z",
  "modified": "2026-11-01T09:00:00.000Z",
  "name": "Loader C2 domain (finance-sector phishing)",
  "pattern": "[domain-name:value = 'cdn-telemetry-sync.example']",
  "pattern_type": "stix",
  "valid_from": "2026-11-01T09:00:00Z",
  "valid_until": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z",
  "confidence": 85
}
```

Read it field by field. `type`, `spec_version` and `id` identify the object; an id is the object type, two hyphens and a UUID, and it stays the same across updates so that a consumer can recognise a revised version of the same indicator. `created` and `modified` record when the producer created and last changed it. `pattern` is the detection logic, written in the STIX patterning language and announced by `pattern_type`; here it says "a domain-name object whose value equals this string". `valid_from` and `valid_until` bound the period in which the producer considers the indicator meaningful, which is exactly the information ageing out needs. `confidence` is an integer from 0 to 100. The lab feed's value, confidence and valid_until fields each have a STIX home here.

### TAXII

TAXII is the protocol for moving STIX content between systems over HTTPS. A TAXII server publishes a discovery endpoint, one or more API roots, and within them **collections**: named sets of objects that a client can be granted permission to read or write. A consumer polls a collection and asks for objects added after the time of its last request, so that it only downloads what changed. TAXII therefore answers "how do I get the feed, securely and incrementally?", while STIX answers "what does each item mean?". Many ISACs and commercial providers offer TAXII collections, and threat intelligence platforms such as MISP and OpenCTI can act as TAXII clients, servers, or both.

> [!TIP]
> When a provider offers both CSV and STIX/TAXII, prefer STIX/TAXII even if you only use the indicators today. The validity window, confidence and relationships it carries are exactly the fields your ageing and scoring logic will need later, and they are lost the moment the data is flattened into a list.

## The feed-management pipeline

Between a feed's arrival and an analyst seeing a match, every indicator should pass through the same sequence of operations. Platforms name the stages differently, but the stages are the same.

1. **Collect** from each source on its own schedule: TAXII polling, a downloaded CSV, an ISAC portal export, your own case notes.
2. **Normalise** values and field names into one internal schema.
3. **Deduplicate and merge** records that describe the same indicator.
4. **Filter against the allowlist**, so that your own infrastructure and known shared services never become alerts or blocks.
5. **Score** each indicator from its confidence, its source's reliability and its age.
6. **Age out** indicators past their validity, keeping them for history but removing them from action.
7. **Distribute** by score: high scores to detection and, with change control, to blocking; lower scores to enrichment and hunting only.
8. **Feed back** what happened: false matches to the producer, confirmed sightings to your community.

Ageing is applied last, at match time, because age changes every day even when the feed does not.

**Decision logic.** The visible branch is the split at the end: only current, high-scoring indicators go to detection and blocking; expired, low-confidence or context-free indicators go to enrichment and hunting, where a human reads them in context. The allowlist filter is an implicit branch: matching entries leave the action path entirely, but are logged for review.

**Technical interpretation.** In a platform such as MISP or OpenCTI these stages correspond to feed connectors, warning lists, decay or scoring models, and export rules that publish selected attributes to the SIEM. In the lab kit the stages are compressed: the feed is a hand-curated list, scoring is the stated confidence, and ageing is the comparison of `valid_until` with the fixed `AS_OF` date.

**Practical example.** The ISAC domain `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` (confidence 85, valid until 31 December 2026) passes every stage and is fit for detection and, after review, blocking. The open-feed address `198.51.100.104` (confidence 40, valid until 30 June 2026) is already past its validity on the lab date of 3 November 2026, so it may only be used for history and enrichment.

**Security implications.** The pipeline is also a control against poisoning: an adversary or a careless producer who inserts a popular domain into a feed is stopped by the allowlist, and an indicator that is never corroborated decays instead of living forever.

**Key learning.** Never connect a feed straight to a blocklist; every indicator must be normalised, deduplicated, allowlist-checked, scored and aged before it is allowed to act.

## Judging a feed: quality criteria

Before subscribing, and at every renewal, evaluate a feed against criteria you can measure, not against the size of its indicator count.

| Criterion | Question to ask | How to measure it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relevance | Does it describe threats to organisations like ours? | Hit rate against your telemetry; overlap with your own incidents. |
| Timeliness | How long after activity does an indicator appear? | Compare first-seen times with your own sightings and with other feeds. |
| Accuracy | How often is a match a false positive? | Share of matches closed as false positives over a review period. |
| Context | Does each entry say what it was seen doing, and when? | Proportion of entries with category, first/last seen and confidence. |
| Uniqueness | Does it add indicators we do not already have? | Overlap analysis against existing feeds after normalisation. |
| Ingestibility | Can we load it reliably without manual work? | Format (STIX/TAXII, CSV), stability of the schema, parsing errors. |
| Terms | What may we do with the data? | Licence and TLP: can it be shared, sent to cloud tools, used in reports? |

Two of these deserve comment. **Hit rate** is often misread. A feed with a very high hit rate may simply contain popular shared infrastructure; a feed with zero hits may be excellent intelligence about threats that have not reached you yet. Hit rate tells you a feed is relevant to your traffic, and the false-positive share of those hits tells you whether the relevance is useful. **Uniqueness** matters because feeds copy each other. Know how much of a paid feed you already have before you renew it.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Record every evaluation: date, feed, the measurements above and the decision. A feed review that is not written down cannot be repeated next year, and a SOC that cannot say why it consumes a feed cannot defend the cost or the false positives it produces.

## Normalisation and deduplication

The same indicator reaches you in many spellings. One feed lists `CDN-Telemetry-Sync.example.` with a trailing dot, another `cdn-telemetry-sync[.]example` in "defanged" form so that it cannot be clicked by accident, a third embeds it in a URL. Unless they are reduced to one canonical form, one real connection may raise three alerts that look like independent confirmations.

Normalisation rules are simple and should be applied in code, once, at ingestion:

- **Domains:** convert to lower case, remove a trailing dot, re-fang defanged notation (`[.]` back to `.`, `hxxp` back to `http`), and store internationalised names in one consistent form.
- **URLs:** split into scheme, host and path so that the host can also be matched as a domain; normalise the host as above.
- **IP addresses:** store in canonical text form; keep CIDR ranges as ranges rather than expanding them; record IPv4 and IPv6 under separate types.
- **Hashes:** convert to lower-case hexadecimal and record the algorithm as the type (`md5`, `sha1`, `sha256`); never compare a SHA-1 value with a SHA-256 value.
- **Field names:** map each producer's columns into your schema (type, value, confidence, first seen, valid until, source, context, TLP).

Deduplication then merges records whose canonical type and value are identical. The merge must **keep** information, not discard it: the merged record lists every source, keeps the earliest first-seen and the latest last-seen, keeps every context string, and carries the **most restrictive** TLP of the contributing records. What it must not do is add the confidences together. Two feeds reporting the same address may both have copied it from a third, so two entries are not two independent confirmations; Lesson 6 returns to this problem as circular reporting.

Matching needs the same discipline. The kit's matcher builds its domain search as the pattern `%://<domain>/%`, with the domain passed as a query parameter rather than pasted into the SQL. Requiring the scheme separator before the domain and a slash after it means that `evil.example` does not match `notevil.example`, or a URL that merely mentions the name in its path, as a naive substring search would. As the kit's own notes point out, the pattern also does not match subdomains; a production matcher would extract the hostname from each URL and compare it with the indicator and with its parent domains.

## Allowlisting

An allowlist (also called a warning list or exclusion list) is the set of values that must never raise an alert or be blocked on indicator evidence alone. It exists because feeds contain popular legitimate infrastructure far more often than newcomers expect: a malware sample contacts a well-known search engine to test connectivity, a phishing kit is hosted for a few hours on a large cloud provider's address, a sandbox records the public DNS resolver its malware used. Automatically generated feeds pick all of these up.

A good allowlist has layers:

- **Your own estate:** your public address ranges, your domains (in the lab, `banyan.example` and its subdomains such as `mail.banyan.example`, `intranet.banyan.example` and `crm.banyan.example`) and your private RFC 1918 ranges.
- **Critical business services:** the SaaS, payment, update and partner services the business depends on.
- **Widely shared infrastructure:** major cloud and CDN ranges, public DNS resolvers, well-known top domains. MISP ships curated warning lists of these.
- **Documented exceptions:** specific values excluded after an analyst confirmed a false positive, each with a reason, an owner and a review date.

The allowlist is a control with its own risk. Legitimate services can be abused, and attackers deliberately host content on trusted platforms because they expect to be allowlisted. So an allowlist entry should **remove a value from automatic action**, not from visibility: the match is still logged and can still be hunted. And, like the suppressions in Module 5, every exception needs an owner, a reason and an expiry that someone actually reviews.

> [!WARNING]
> Blocking straight from a feed without an allowlist is how SOCs cause outages. A single feed entry for a shared CDN address can cut off every site hosted behind it. Put blocking behind change control, apply it only to high-confidence, current, allowlist-checked indicators, and monitor what the block actually stops.

## Scoring and ageing out

Indicators lose value with time at different rates. An IP address can be reassigned to a new customer within days of an attacker abandoning it. A domain lasts longer, though it can expire and be re-registered by someone else. A file hash never matches a different file, but the attacker can produce a new hash at will, so an old hash simply stops matching anything. A feed-management process expresses this as an **age policy**: a default lifetime per indicator type, overridden by the producer's own `valid_until` where one is given, and a score that falls as the indicator ages without fresh sightings. There is no universal correct lifetime; the right values come from your own measurements of how long matches on each type stay useful, and should be written down as SOC policy.

Scoring combines what you know about the indicator into one number that decides where it goes. A simple, explainable model multiplies three factors: the producer's confidence, your assessment of the source's reliability (Lesson 2), and a recency factor that falls from 1 towards 0 as the indicator approaches and passes its validity limit.

Ageing out does **not** mean deleting. An expired indicator keeps value for retrospective work: if an incident is later found to have started months ago, you want to know whether its infrastructure appeared in your logs at the time. The rule is that expired indicators stay in the platform for history and hunting, and leave the paths that alert or block automatically. The kit implements exactly this rule: expired entries are still matched and reported, with a warning, but marked so that they cannot trigger action.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"More feeds mean better coverage."** Overlapping feeds multiply duplicates and false positives faster than they add unique, relevant indicators. Measure uniqueness and relevance before adding a feed.
- **Deduplicating by adding confidence.** Two copies of one report are not two confirmations. Merge sources, do not sum scores.
- **Deleting expired indicators.** You lose the ability to look back. Retire them from action, keep them for history.
- **Reading "no match" as "clean".** The lab hash cannot match because the dataset holds no hashes. A feed is only as useful as the telemetry it is matched against.
- **Ignoring licence and TLP at ingestion.** Pushing a TLP:AMBER feed into a third-party cloud enrichment service or a public sandbox may breach its terms; record TLP on every indicator from the start.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Feeds are an input to your security tools, so they are also part of your attack surface. A compromised or careless producer can push indicators that cause outages (blocking shared or business infrastructure) or blind spots (an adversary who can influence an allowlist can hide). Defend the feed path like any other integration: authenticate TAXII and portal connections, monitor for sudden changes in feed size or in the share of entries hitting your allowlist, keep the allowlist under change control, and require a human decision before any feed-driven block reaches production. Count matches per feed, the share closed as false positives and the blocks rolled back; they are the evidence for the next feed review.

## Key takeaways

- Feeds differ by producer: open feeds are fast and broad but thin; commercial feeds sell curation and context; ISAC feeds are relevant but bound by TLP; internal intelligence is the most relevant but narrowest.
- CSV lists lose context; STIX 2.1 indicators carry pattern, validity and confidence, and TAXII transports them securely and incrementally.
- Judge a feed by relevance, timeliness, accuracy, context, uniqueness, ingestibility and terms, measured against your own telemetry.
- Normalise, deduplicate, allowlist, score and age every indicator before it may act; never wire a feed directly to a blocklist.
- Expiry removes an indicator from action, not from history: the lab's spraying address is expired on 15 November, yet its matches on 3 November remain evidence.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Threat intelligence is evidence about adversaries, and like all evidence it has a scope, an age and a source, each of which limits what it can prove. The previous lessons treated intelligence as something to collect, score and match. This lesson asks the opposite question: **when an indicator matches, or fails to match, what does that actually tell you, and what does it not?**

The question matters because intelligence is persuasive. A match against a feed arrives with a label such as "malicious", a confidence number and often the name of a threat actor, and it is tempting to read that label as a verdict about your own environment. It is not. A feed entry is a statement by someone else, about activity they saw, at some time in the past, through their own telemetry. A match tells you only that a value in your logs equals a value in that statement. Everything else (whether the activity in your logs is malicious, whether it is the same actor, whether you are compromised) is an inference that the analyst must make, and which the match alone cannot make for you.

Experienced SOC analysts hold two ideas at once. Intelligence is enormously useful: in the lab dataset of this course, the ISAC indicators turned a handful of ambiguous events into a confirmed phishing, beaconing and password-spraying case within minutes. And intelligence is routinely wrong for your environment: the same feed matched an ordinary employee's VPN session through an address that had been listed months before. The skill is telling the two situations apart, and saying how sure you are.

The limitations fall into a small number of families, which this lesson takes in turn:

1. **Perishability:** indicators go stale as infrastructure is abandoned and reassigned.
2. **Shared infrastructure:** one address or domain can serve thousands of unrelated users.
3. **Absence of evidence:** "no match" is often "no data".
4. **Circular reporting:** feeds copy each other, so one observation can look like many.
5. **Attribution limits:** naming who is behind activity is hard, contested and usually unnecessary for defence.
6. **Bias:** analysts and producers see what they expect, and vendors have incentives.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> An indicator match is a lead, not a finding. It becomes a finding only when the events it points to make sense in your own context, and the conclusion you write should say how confident you are and why.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Stale indicator | An indicator that no longer reliably identifies malicious activity because the infrastructure has been abandoned, reassigned or changed. |
| Expired indicator | An indicator whose stated validity period (`valid_until`) has passed; a formal marker that it should no longer drive action. |
| Shared infrastructure | Addresses, domains or services used by many unrelated parties at once: cloud and CDN ranges, shared web hosting, VPN providers, Tor exit relays, mobile carrier gateways. |
| Collateral match | A match caused by legitimate activity that happens to use the same shared value as listed malicious activity. |
| Circular reporting | The same original observation reaching an analyst through several sources that copied it, so that it falsely appears independently confirmed. |
| Attribution | Assigning responsibility for activity to a named actor, group or state. |
| Cognitive bias | A systematic error in judgement, such as confirmation bias (favouring evidence that fits an existing belief) or anchoring (over-weighting the first information received). |
| Estimative language | Standardised wording ("low", "moderate", "high confidence") that tells the reader how strongly the analyst holds a judgement. |

## Perishability: stale and expired indicators

An indicator describes infrastructure at a moment in time, and attackers change infrastructure constantly. Some rotate domains and addresses per campaign, some per victim. Cheap cloud servers are rented for hours and returned; the address then goes back into the provider's pool and is handed to the next customer, who may be a bakery, a university or your own payroll provider. Domains expire and are re-registered by someone else, sometimes by a security researcher who sinkholes them, so that connections to the "malicious" domain are now connections to a defender's server. A file hash cannot be reassigned, but it decays in a different way: the attacker recompiles or changes one byte, the old hash stops matching anything new, and the feed keeps it forever.

Two terms are easily confused. An indicator is **expired** when its producer's stated validity has passed; that is a formal, checkable property, and Lesson 5 showed how the lab matcher evaluates it against a date. An indicator is **stale** when it no longer reliably identifies malicious activity, whatever its label says. Many stale indicators have no expiry at all, because the producer never set one; and an indicator can expire while it is still correct, as the lab's spraying address showed when the date moved to 15 November. Expiry is a policy tool for removing indicators from automatic action. Staleness is a judgement the analyst makes about a specific match.

The practical consequence is that the age and validity of an indicator must be visible at the moment an analyst reads a match. A match line that says only "malicious IP" invites the wrong action. The lab matcher prints confidence, source and TLP on every line, and puts `EXPIRED` in the status column where nobody can miss it.

## Shared infrastructure and collateral matches

Most internet infrastructure is shared. A single cloud address may host many customers' services over a year; a single CDN edge address serves thousands of websites at the same moment; a shared web-hosting server holds hundreds of small sites, one of which may be compromised and used for phishing; commercial VPN services and Tor exit relays carry traffic for large numbers of users, a few of whom misbehave; mobile carriers place many subscribers behind a small number of public addresses using carrier-grade NAT. When any of these addresses appears in a feed, every legitimate user of the same infrastructure becomes a potential collateral match.

Shared infrastructure explains why IP addresses and domains sit low on the Pyramid of Pain from Lesson 1, and why they produce most false positives in indicator matching. It also explains why the context field matters so much. An entry that says "scanning (old, shared hosting)" is warning you, in its own words, that the address was shared and the observation was old: two separate reasons to doubt any match.

Defences against collateral matches are partly technical and partly analytical. Technically, the allowlist from Lesson 5 removes known shared ranges from automatic action, and IP indicators should carry shorter lifetimes than domains and hashes. Analytically, an analyst seeing an IP match should ask what kind of address it is (cloud, hosting, VPN, residential, mobile) before asking what it did, and should look for corroboration from a different kind of evidence: a process, a user behaviour, a second indicator that is not on the same infrastructure.

## Worked example: an expired indicator matching routine activity

The lab kit contains a deliberately awkward match. In a temporary copy of `LAB_ASSETS/C08` (never inside the course library), load the dataset and run the matcher:

```terminal

loaded 340 events
$ python ioc_match.py

MATCH    domain banyan-payroll-update.example    conf= 70 hits=  1 first=2026-11-03T06:12:00Z src=internal TLP:GREEN
```

```python
("ipv4", "198.51.100.104", 40, "2026-06-30", "open feed",

```

Everything about the indicator argues for caution: an open feed, confidence 40 out of 100, validity that ended on 30 June 2026, more than four months before the lab date, and a context string that itself says the observation is old and the address is shared hosting. The matcher has already done its part, labelling the line `EXPIRED` and printing the warning instead of treating it as a detection.

Now look at the event it matched. The kit's `minisiem.py search` command runs one read-only SQL query against the loaded table and prints the columns and rows:

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT ts, user, src_ip, outcome FROM events WHERE source='vpn' AND src_ip LIKE '198.51.100.%' ORDER BY ts"
ts | user | src_ip | outcome
2026-11-03T13:33:00Z | gopal | 198.51.100.104 | success
```

One successful VPN session for the user gopal at 13:33 UTC. The raw event in `banyan_events.jsonl` adds one more field, `"country": "IN"`, consistent with an employee of an Indian microfinance company connecting from home. The dataset generator, `make_dataset.py`, confirms what this event is. In its "Routine activity" section, each user has a chance of an evening VPN session from a random address in the documentation range:

```python
if random.random() < 0.4:
    t = start + timedelta(hours=10)
    add(t, source="vpn", user=u, src_ip=f"198.51.100.{random.randint(10, 200)}",
        outcome="success", country="IN")
```

So the match is a collateral match: ordinary activity that happens to come from an address an open feed listed months earlier for something unrelated. In a real SOC you would not have the generator's source code, but you would have equivalent evidence: the user's normal working pattern, the address's ownership and type, and the absence of any other suspicious behaviour linked to that session.

### The right action, for the right reason

Acting on this indicator, for example by disabling gopal's account or blocking the address because "threat intelligence flagged it", would be wrong. It would disrupt a legitimate user on the strength of stale, low-confidence, shared-infrastructure evidence, and it would teach the business that the SOC's alerts are unreliable.

There is a twist that makes this example worth studying. Query all of gopal's VPN activity:

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT ts, source, src_ip, outcome FROM events WHERE user='gopal' AND source='vpn' ORDER BY ts"
ts | source | src_ip | outcome
2026-11-03T06:42:42Z | vpn | 203.0.113.66 | failure
2026-11-03T06:46:00Z | vpn | 203.0.113.66 | success
2026-11-03T13:33:00Z | vpn | 198.51.100.104 | success
```

Earlier the same morning, gopal's account was one of the targets of the password spray from `203.0.113.66`, and the spraying address logged in successfully as gopal at 06:46. That is exactly what rule R2 (`vpn_spray_then_success`) in `minisiem.py` detects, and it is supported by a current ISAC indicator whose context ("password spraying against VPNs") fits exactly. gopal's account therefore does need action: a credential reset, a review of what the 06:46 session did, and a check of the 13:33 session as part of that case. The expired indicator plays no part in that decision. **The account is at risk because of the spray, not because of the stale address.** An analyst who disabled the account "because of 198.51.100.104" would have done roughly the right thing for the wrong reason, and would write a case record that misleads everyone who reads it later.

**Purpose.** The figure is the question sequence an analyst should follow whenever an indicator matches, so that the match is weighed rather than obeyed. It matters because every collateral match in this lesson is caught by one of its three questions.

**Components.** The slate starting box is **Indicator match** ("value in our logs equals a feed value"). Three violet decision boxes ask **Indicator current?** ("within valid_until, not stale"), **Shared infrastructure?** ("cloud, CDN, hosting, VPN, Tor") and **Events fit the context?** ("user, host, time, behaviour"). The outcome boxes are **No automatic action** in slate ("history and enrichment only"), **Seek corroboration** in orange ("a different kind of evidence"), **Record collateral match** in green ("report to the producer") and **Act proportionately** in dark ("alert, hunt, block via change control").

**Relationships and arrows.** Solid arrows labelled "yes" and "no" are the answers to each question. From **Indicator current?**, "no" leads to **No automatic action** and "yes" leads on to **Shared infrastructure?**. From there, "yes" leads to **Seek corroboration** and "no" goes straight to **Events fit the context?**; corroboration also feeds into that final question. The dashed arrow labelled "still review the events" runs from **No automatic action** to **Events fit the context?**: an expired match is removed from automation, not from the analyst's attention.

**Execution flow.** Ask about the indicator first (age), then the infrastructure (sharing), then your own events (context). Only the last question looks at your environment, and only it can lead to action.

**Decision logic.** From **Events fit the context?**, "yes" leads to **Act proportionately** and "no" leads to **Record collateral match**. No path reaches action without passing that question.

**Technical interpretation.** The first two questions can be partly automated (validity checks, warning lists of shared ranges); the third needs an analyst with access to the surrounding telemetry and asset context.

**Practical example.** The `198.51.100.104` match takes the "no" branch at **Indicator current?**, then the dashed arrow: the event is gopal's routine evening VPN session, so the answer at **Events fit the context?** is "no" and the outcome is **Record collateral match**, with a note to the open-feed producer if a feedback channel exists. The `203.0.113.66` match on 3 November follows "yes", "no", "yes" to **Act proportionately**: eight failures and one success fit the ISAC context exactly.

**Security implications.** Skipping the first two questions produces false accusations against users; skipping the third lets a current, plausible indicator drive action against activity that does not fit.

**Key learning.** Judge the indicator, then the infrastructure, then your own events; only the events can justify action.

## Absence of evidence: "no match" is not "clean"

The last line of the matcher output is as instructive as the expired one. The vendor's SHA-256 indicator for the malicious `invoice.docm` has the highest confidence in the feed (90) and reports `no match`. Read the code and the reason is plain: for hash indicators the matcher sets `rows = []`, with the comment that the dataset has no file hashes. The SOC never collected the field, so the indicator could not have matched whatever happened. Yet the same dataset shows divya downloading `invoice.docm` from the look-alike domain at 06:12, and Word spawning PowerShell on WS-104 two minutes later. The file was almost certainly present; the telemetry simply could not see its hash.

A match can only occur where three things line up: the adversary used the indicator against you, your telemetry recorded the field it lives in, and your matcher compared that field with the feed. A "no match" result therefore has at least three explanations: the activity did not happen, it happened but was not logged in a form you can match, or it happened with different infrastructure that no feed has listed yet. The last is the normal case for a targeted attack: an adversary who builds fresh infrastructure for each victim will never appear in anyone's feed before they reach you. This is why the module keeps returning to behaviour-based detection. Rule R1 (Office spawning a shell) fired on this intrusion without any intelligence at all, and it would still fire if the attacker changed every domain and file.

## Circular reporting and feed overlap

Feeds and reports copy each other. A researcher publishes a blog post with ten indicators; an open feed scrapes them; two commercial vendors include the open feed in their products; an ISAC member forwards the vendor's alert to the community; a national advisory cites the ISAC. Your platform now shows the same address from five sources and the score climbs, although there is still exactly one original observation behind it, and nobody downstream re-checked it. If the original was wrong, or was an address of shared hosting, five sources agree on the error.

Defend against circular reporting in three ways. Record provenance, not only source: where possible note the original report each feed entry derives from. Merge duplicates without summing confidence (Lesson 5). And treat agreement between sources as strong only when they observed the activity independently, for example your own proxy log and a different organisation's incident.

## Attribution: who is behind it, and does it matter?

Attribution means naming the actor responsible for activity. Intelligence reports often lead with it, and it can be useful at the strategic level: knowing that a group with a history of targeting financial services is active in your region helps leaders prioritise investment. For the analyst handling a case, attribution is limited in three ways.

**It is hard and uncertain.** Infrastructure is rented and shared, tools are sold, leaked and reused, and capable actors sometimes plant misleading clues. Reliable attribution usually needs evidence that a SOC does not have, and public attributions are often made with stated or unstated uncertainty.

**Names do not line up.** Each vendor names the groups it tracks in its own scheme, and their boundaries differ. One well-known group is called APT29, Cozy Bear or Midnight Blizzard depending on whose report you read, and the groups behind those names do not necessarily overlap completely. MITRE ATT&CK group pages list associated names reported by others, which helps translate between reports, but a shared name is a claim about overlap, not proof of identity.

**It is rarely needed for defence.** Whether the spray from `203.0.113.66` was run by a named group or by an opportunist, the response is the same: reset the credential, review the session, require multi-factor authentication for VPN access, and block the address while it is current. Act on behaviour and evidence; leave attribution to those whose decisions depend on it, and never state it in a case record more firmly than the evidence allows.

## Bias in producers and analysts

Intelligence passes through people twice: the producer who wrote it and the analyst who reads it. Both are subject to cognitive bias. **Confirmation bias** leads an analyst who already suspects an incident to read every match as support and to explain away the expired flag. **Anchoring** gives undue weight to the first piece of information, such as an alert title naming an actor. **Availability bias** makes a dramatic recent breach in the news seem more likely to be behind today's alert than it is. Producers have their own pressures: vendors compete for attention, and a report that names a sophisticated actor attracts more of it than one describing an ordinary password spray. A feed's selection of what to publish also reflects what that producer can see, which may be very different from your sector and region.

Structured techniques help. Richards Heuer's *Psychology of Intelligence Analysis*, published by the CIA's Center for the Study of Intelligence, describes **Analysis of Competing Hypotheses**: list every plausible explanation, list the evidence, and look for the evidence that is inconsistent with each hypothesis rather than the evidence that fits your favourite. Applied to the `198.51.100.104` match, the hypotheses "attacker reusing old infrastructure" and "employee working from home" both fit the bare match; only the second is consistent with the session timing, the country, the user's normal pattern and the absence of any other suspicious activity from that address. A simple **key assumptions check** works too: write down what you are assuming (for example "the feed entry is still accurate") and ask what would happen if it were false.

## What intelligence can and cannot tell you

Pulling the limitations together gives a clear division of labour between intelligence and your own investigation.

![Figure 6.12: What threat intelligence can and cannot tell you](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M06-L06-F2.svg)

*Figure 6.12: What threat intelligence can and cannot tell you. Intelligence supplies others' observations, context and confidence; whether you are compromised can only be answered from your own evidence.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The figure separates the questions threat intelligence can help answer from those only your own evidence can answer. It matters because most misuse of intelligence comes from asking a feed a question from the right-hand column.

**Components.** Two columns are separated by "vs". The left, green column is titled **Intelligence can tell you** and lists: "what others saw, where and when"; "context: C2, spraying, phishing"; "the producer's confidence and validity"; "which values to hunt for first"; "TTPs worth detecting". The right, red column is titled **It cannot tell you** and lists: "whether you are compromised"; "that no match means clean"; "that an old value is still bad"; "who is really behind it"; "what your own users were doing".

**Relationships.** The "vs" between the columns signals that each item on the right is the limit of the matching item on the left. Intelligence says what others saw; it cannot say whether you are compromised. It supplies confidence and validity; it cannot say that an old value is still bad. It tells you which values to hunt for; it cannot promise that a hunt with no results means you are clean.

**Execution flow.** In practice an analyst moves from left to right: start from what intelligence offers (a list of values to look for, with context), then answer the right-hand questions with your own telemetry, asset knowledge and user context.

**Decision logic.** If a question you are asking appears on the right, intelligence alone cannot decide it, and any case note that answers it must cite evidence from your own environment.

**Technical interpretation.** Left-column items are properties of the feed entry: its pattern, context string, confidence, `valid_until` and associated TTPs. Right-column items are properties of your environment and of the world beyond any one producer's view, which no feed can encode.

**Practical example.** For the lab case, the left column supplies "`203.0.113.66` was used for VPN password spraying, confidence 60, valid until 10 November" and "`198.51.100.104` was seen scanning on shared hosting, confidence 40, expired". The right column is answered from the logs: gopal's 06:46 session came from the spray, the 13:33 session was routine, and the missing hash match reflects a telemetry gap, not a clean host.

**Security implications.** Over-trusting intelligence causes false accusations and outages; under-using it wastes the speed it offers. Keeping the two columns distinct prevents both.

**Key learning.** Intelligence tells you what to look for and how much others trust it; only your own evidence tells you what happened to you.

## Stating confidence in your own conclusions

Because intelligence is uncertain, conclusions built on it must say how uncertain they are. Use a fixed vocabulary, such as low, moderate and high confidence, defined once in your SOC's procedures, and give the reasons in the same sentence. For the lab case a well-formed set of judgements reads:

- High confidence that gopal's VPN credential was compromised by password spraying: eight failed logins across all users from `203.0.113.66` within a minute, followed by a successful login as gopal, matching a current ISAC indicator with the same context.
- High confidence that the `198.51.100.104` match is collateral: expired, low-confidence open-feed entry on shared hosting, matching a routine session consistent with the user's normal behaviour.
- Moderate confidence that the spray and the WS-104 phishing are the same actor: they share timing on the same morning but no infrastructure.
- No assessment of attribution: the evidence does not support one.

Each sentence separates what was observed from what was inferred, and a reader can see exactly what would change the judgement.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"The feed says malicious, so it is."** A feed entry is someone else's past observation; it needs your own evidence before it becomes a finding.
- **Treating expiry and staleness as the same.** Expired indicators can be historically correct; unexpired ones can be stale. Judge each match.
- **Counting sources as confirmations.** Five feeds repeating one blog post are one observation.
- **Reading "no match" as "clean".** Check that your telemetry records the indicator's field before drawing any conclusion.
- **Leading with attribution.** Naming an actor adds little to the response and much risk to the case record if it is wrong.
- **Doing the right thing for the wrong reason.** Record the evidence that actually justifies an action, as with gopal's account and the spray.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Intelligence limitations become operational risks when indicators drive automation. Collateral matches on shared infrastructure lead to outages and to users being locked out; stale indicators produce alert fatigue until analysts stop reading intelligence matches at all; an empty match list creates false assurance. The defences are those of this module combined: expiry evaluated at match time, allowlists of shared infrastructure, human review before blocking, behaviour-based detections alongside indicators, telemetry coverage checks for each indicator type you consume, and explicit confidence in every written judgement. Measure the result: track the share of intelligence matches closed as collateral, by feed and by indicator type, and use it at the next feed review.

> [!CAUTION]
> Even a collateral match involves real people. A case record that says a named employee "matched a malicious IP" can follow them long after the match is shown to be stale. Write the conclusion precisely, and correct the record when the assessment changes.
