**Execution flow and decision logic.** The table has no arrows, but there is an implied decision for each row: if the "Easiest evasion" is cheap for the attacker, the rule needs a partner that covers that evasion; if the "Legitimate look-alike" is common in your estate, the rule needs context or tuning before it can page anyone.

**Technical interpretation.** Notice that the evasion column names a *field the attacker controls* for R1 (the child image), R4 (request size), and R6 (size and timing), but an *operating-system fact* for R3 and R5. That is the deeper reason R5 can be both signature-shaped and durable. Notice also that the anomaly rules have the broadest look-alike column: they describe "unusual", and plenty of benign things are unusual.

**Practical example.** In the Banyan storyline, R1 fired at 06:14 on WS-104 when Word started PowerShell. Had the macro started `wscript.exe` instead, R1 would have stayed silent, but R6 would still have caught the 220-byte check-ins that followed, and R5 would still have caught the log clearing at 08:17. Layering, not any single rule, gave the SOC the intrusion.

**Security implications.** A rule whose evasion is trivial and whose look-alike is common (a pure name match on a popular tool, for example) gives both false confidence and noise. Writing this table during design review exposes such rules before they reach production.

**Key learning.** For every rule, name what it relies on, how it is most cheaply evaded and what benign activity looks the same; those three answers predict its false negatives, its durability and its false positives.

## Precision and recall: measuring the trade-off

Two numbers summarise how a rule behaves against reality. Using the counts defined in the terminology table:

$$\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

Precision answers the analyst's question: *when this rule fires, how often is it real?* Recall answers the defender's question: *when the threat happens, how often does this rule fire?* They pull against each other because almost every change to a rule moves the boundary between "alert" and "no alert". Make the condition looser and more true events fall inside it (recall rises) but so do more benign ones (precision falls). Make it tighter and the benign ones drop out (precision rises) but some true events drop out with them (recall falls).

The kit lets you see this with real numbers. R6 has two conditions in its `HAVING` clause: at least ten requests, and a size spread under 50 bytes. You can run variants of it with `minisiem.py search` against the loaded dataset. First, drop the spread condition and keep only the volume threshold:

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT host, url, COUNT(*) AS hits FROM events WHERE source='proxy' GROUP BY host, url HAVING hits >= 10"
host | url | hits
WS-103 | https://cdn.example.org/ | 10
WS-103 | https://intranet.banyan.example/ | 11
WS-104 | https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping | 18
```

`search` runs the quoted SQL against `minisiem.db` and prints a header row and one line per result. Three host-and-URL pairs now qualify, and only one of them (the WS-104 beacon) is the intrusion. The two WS-103 rows are a busy user on the intranet and a content-delivery site. Precision has fallen to one in three. Now restore the spread condition but raise the volume threshold from 10 to 20:

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT host, url, COUNT(*) AS hits FROM events WHERE source='proxy' GROUP BY host, url HAVING hits >= 20 AND MAX(bytes_out)-MIN(bytes_out) < 50"
host | url | hits
```

Only the header is printed: no rows. The beacon made 18 requests between 06:17 and 07:42, so a threshold of 20 misses it entirely. Recall for this storyline is now zero, and there is no alert to have a precision at all. The rule as shipped, with `hits >= 10 AND max_b - min_b < 50`, returns exactly the one true pair, as `python minisiem.py rules` showed in earlier modules:

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py rules
...
R6 beacon_regular_small: 1 hit(s)
    ('WS-104', 'https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping', 18, 220, 220)
```

(The `...` stands for the lines printed for R1 to R5, omitted here.) Figure 2 places the three variants side by side.

![Figure 7.2: One rule, three variants: precision against recall](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M07-L01-F2.svg)

*Figure 7.2: One rule, three variants: precision against recall. Alerts produced on the Banyan dataset by three variants of R6, and how many of them were the WS-104 beacon.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The chart shows, with the lab's real results, how changing a single condition in one rule moves it along the precision-recall trade-off. It exists to make an abstract formula concrete: the same data, the same intent, three different outcomes.

**Components.** There are three horizontal bars, each labelled with a variant of R6 and a value equal to the number of alerts it produced on the Banyan dataset. The first bar, slate, is **Volume only (hits >= 10)** with **3 alerts, 1 true**. The second bar, green, is **R6 as shipped** with **1 alert, 1 true**. The third bar, red, is **Volume >= 20 + spread < 50** with **0 alerts, beacon missed**. The note under the chart states the conclusion.

**Relationships.** Bar length is the alert count, which is what the analyst experiences as workload. The text after each count is what the detection engineer cares about: how many of those alerts were the intrusion. Reading from the first bar to the last, the rule becomes stricter at every step.

**Execution flow.** Start with the first bar: the loosest rule catches the beacon but buries it among two benign pairs, giving a precision of $1/3 \approx 0.33$ with recall of 1 for this storyline. Move to the second: adding the spread condition removes both benign pairs without losing the beacon, so precision is $1/1$ and recall is still 1. Move to the third: raising the volume threshold above the beacon's 18 requests removes the true pair as well, so recall drops to 0.

**Decision logic.** The second variant is better than the first because the extra condition encodes something *true about beacons* (constant size) that is *rarely true of people* (varied sizes). The third variant is worse because its extra strictness encodes nothing about beacons; it merely demands more of them. Good tightening adds discriminating information; bad tightening just raises a number.

**Technical interpretation.** The dataset is small and synthetic, so these counts are illustrations, not estimates for a real estate. In production, "1 true" becomes an unknown you estimate through testing (Lesson 4) and analyst feedback (Lesson 5), and recall is especially hard to measure because you rarely know about the attacks you missed.

**Practical example.** Imagine a vendor's update agent on every Banyan workstation that polls a fixed URL with identical 300-byte requests every few minutes. All three variants would fire on it, on every host. R6 would need an allowlist of known agents or a further condition (for example, a destination first seen recently) before deployment.

**Security implications.** An attacker who understands the rule can add random padding to each request so that the spread exceeds 50 bytes, moving the beacon out of all three variants. Knowing the trade-off includes knowing which condition the attacker can cheaply defeat.

**Key learning.** Tighten rules with conditions that describe the threat, not with bigger numbers; every threshold you raise should be checked against the real volume of the behaviour you are trying to catch.

### The base-rate problem

Precision is harsher in production than intuition suggests, because the threat is rare. Suppose, purely as an illustration, that a rule examines one million process-creation events a day, that ten of them are malicious, and that the rule catches all ten while wrongly flagging just 0.1% of the benign events. 0.1% of 999,990 is about 1,000 false positives. The rule's precision is $10 / (10 + 1000) \approx 0.01$: ninety-nine alerts in every hundred are noise, even though the rule is "99.9% accurate" on benign events.

So rules that page analysts need very low false-positive *rates*, while broad anomaly rules usually feed a risk score or hunting queue instead.

### Which error is worse?

Decide per rule and write it down. A missed log clearance (an R5 false negative) means an attacker removed evidence undetected, a serious loss for a rare and high-value event, so R5 is tuned for recall and accepts the occasional maintenance false positive. A beacon detector on a network full of update agents may have to accept lower recall to stay usable, provided another layer covers the gap. A false positive costs analyst time and trust; a false negative costs dwell time. Let severity and compensating detections decide.

## Designing a rule: the questions to answer first

Syntax is the last and easiest part. First answer five questions in writing; they become the rule's documentation and the basis of its tests later in this module.

1. **What exactly is the behaviour?** State it in one sentence, in terms of the technique, not the tool: "a document editor starting a command interpreter", not "detect the invoice malware".
2. **Where does it appear in telemetry, and which fields carry it?** Which source (Sysmon process creation, Windows Security, proxy, VPN), which event type, which fields? If the data is not collected, the rule cannot work, however good its logic.
3. **Which of those values does the attacker control?** Anything the attacker can choose (file names, paths, command-line text, URL paths, request sizes, timing) can be changed to evade the rule. Prefer fields the attacker cannot easily change.
4. **What is the legitimate look-alike, and how often does it happen here?** Name the benign activity that produces the same pattern and estimate its volume in *your* estate.
5. **What context would make it more or less suspicious?** An unusual parent, a rare host, a privileged account, a first-seen destination, an out-of-hours time, a combination with another alert on the same entity.

### Worked example: hardening R1 on paper

Apply the questions to R1.

**The behaviour** is "Word starts a script interpreter", which is technique-level: it maps to user execution of a malicious file and to the use of a command or script interpreter. **The telemetry** is Sysmon event 1 (process creation), using the `parent_image` and `image` fields. In the Banyan dataset, Sysmon recorded 33 process creations. Grouping them by parent and child:

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT parent_image, image, COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE source='sysmon' AND event_id=1 GROUP BY 1,2"
parent_image | image | COUNT(*)
C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE | C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe | 1
C:\Windows\explorer.exe | C:\Program Files\App\excel.exe | 8
C:\Windows\explorer.exe | C:\Program Files\App\explorer.exe | 8
C:\Windows\explorer.exe | C:\Program Files\App\msedge.exe | 8
C:\Windows\explorer.exe | C:\Program Files\App\outlook.exe | 8
```

`GROUP BY 1,2` groups by the first and second selected columns. Thirty-two of the 33 starts are ordinary applications launched from the Windows shell, `explorer.exe`; one is Word starting PowerShell. In this (synthetic) estate, the parent-child pair is a near-perfect discriminator, which is exactly what you want from a behavioural rule. In a real estate, first measure how often `WINWORD.EXE` legitimately has any child at all.

**Attacker-controlled values** are where R1 is weakest. The rule matches *names* in the image path. An attacker cannot easily make Word not be Word, but they can choose which interpreter to start, and they can copy an interpreter to a new name. The course library's fictional teaching scenario has an authorised red team copying PowerShell to `updater.exe` past a name-based rule. Three design improvements address this, each at the level of what to look for rather than how to evade:

- **Match on a property the attacker cannot rename.** Sysmon and most EDR products record the executable's embedded original file name (Sysmon's `OriginalFileName` field), which stays `PowerShell.EXE` when the file is copied to another name. The kit's dataset does not include that field, so R1 cannot use it; a production rule should.
- **Widen the child list deliberately.** PowerShell and `cmd.exe` are the most common, but Windows has other script hosts (`wscript.exe`, `cscript.exe`, `mshta.exe`). Each addition raises recall and needs a look-alike check.
- **Widen the parent list deliberately.** The kit restricts R1 to Word; Excel and PowerPoint macros are equally capable. Measure Excel's own children in your estate before widening.

**The look-alike** is an approved macro that starts a script, which the kit's Sigma version of this rule records under `falsepositives` (Lesson 2). **Context** that raises suspicion includes a document recently downloaded from an external domain (in the storyline, `invoice.docm` from `banyan-payroll-update.example` at 06:12), a command line with an encoded payload, and the same host producing a beacon shortly afterwards.

There is also a subtle **semantic** detail in the SQL. Windows paths are case-insensitive: `WINWORD.EXE`, `WinWord.exe` and `winword.exe` are the same program. R1 therefore lowercases the field with `lower()` and compares it with a lowercase pattern. In SQLite the `=` operator is case-sensitive, and although `LIKE` ignores the case of ASCII letters by default, that default can be changed and other query languages behave differently; writing the normalisation explicitly makes the rule's intent survive translation. In the dataset the parent path is stored as `...\Office16\WINWORD.EXE` in capitals, so a case-sensitive comparison against `winword.exe` would miss it. Note too that `LIKE '%winword.exe%'` is a *contains* match: it would also match a hypothetical `notwinword.exe`. The Sigma version in Lesson 2 uses an *ends-with* match on `\WINWORD.EXE`, which is stricter.

### Baselines for real anomaly rules

R4's fixed 10 MB threshold works on the dataset because ordinary proxy requests there are small: a summary by host shows that every workstation except WS-104 sent at most 3,999 bytes in a single request, and WS-104's maximum was the 48,200,000-byte upload. In a real business a single number rarely fits everyone. A per-entity baseline asks "is this large *for this host or user*?", typically by comparing the new value with that entity's own history (for example, its recent maximum or a high percentile of its past values) over a defined learning period.

Learning periods, recalculation and entities with no history are tuning questions for Lesson 5; at design time, record which baseline the rule assumes.

## Layering the families

Because each family fails differently, mature detection sets combine them on purpose:

| Family | Typical role | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Signature on attacker infrastructure | Fast, cheap confirmation of known campaigns; feeds from intelligence (Module 6) | The attacker changes the indicator |
| Signature on operating-system facts | High-value single events (log cleared, audit policy changed) | Telemetry is missing or disabled first |
| Behavioural | Main alerting layer for techniques | The attacker uses a different technique or an unlisted variant |
| Anomaly | Catch the unknown; feed risk scores and hunts | The baseline is wrong or the attacker blends in |

In the storyline, a signature (the ISAC's domain list matched the beacon destination in Module 6), behaviours (R1, R2, R3), an operating-system fact (R5) and anomalies (R4, R6) each saw part of the intrusion. Removing any single layer would still have left enough to open a case; that redundancy is the goal.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"Behavioural rules have no false positives."** They have different false positives: the legitimate version of the same behaviour. Measure it before deployment.
- **Matching on names the attacker chooses.** Process names, file names and URL paths are suggestions, not facts. Prefer original file names, signatures, hashes of known tools, or relationships.
- **Tightening by raising numbers.** As the R6 variants showed, a higher threshold can remove the true positive while adding no discriminating power.
- **Designing without the data.** A rule for a field that is not collected, or is parsed under a different name, will pass review and never fire.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Detection logic is itself an attack surface. Attackers study public rules and common SIEM content and choose techniques that fall between them; the "Easiest evasion" column of Figure 1 is what a capable adversary will try. Defenders prefer values the attacker cannot change, layer families, and keep some logic (thresholds, allowlists) out of public view.

The second implication is dependency on telemetry. Every rule in this lesson assumes the data arrives. An attacker who disables Sysmon, stops log forwarding or clears logs blinds the rules that rely on that data. That is why R5 matters beyond its own alert, and why absence rules (Module 3) that notice a source going quiet are part of a sound detection design.

Finally, detections process personal data. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, keep rules and alert payloads to the fields an analyst needs.

## Best practices

- Write the five design answers (behaviour, telemetry, attacker-controlled values, look-alike, context) before the logic, and keep them with the rule.
- Prefer conditions that describe the threat over conditions that merely demand more of it.
- State each rule's precision target and its role: page an analyst, contribute risk, or feed a hunt.
- Normalise case and field names explicitly, and check the semantics of every comparison (contains, ends with, equals).
- Record which error is worse for each rule, and which other rule compensates for its blind spot.

## Key takeaways

- Detection logic falls into three families: signatures match known values, behaviours match what a technique must do, anomalies match departures from normal. Shapes (single event, threshold, sequence, aggregation) express them.
- What matters most is who controls the value you match: operating-system facts (event 1102) are durable even as signatures; attacker-chosen names are brittle even inside a behavioural rule.
- Precision is TP / (TP + FP) and recall is TP / (TP + FN). Loosening a rule usually raises recall and lowers precision; tightening does the reverse.
- On the Banyan data, dropping R6's size condition gave 3 alerts with 1 true; raising its volume threshold to 20 missed the 18-request beacon entirely.
- Because threats are rare, a tiny false-positive rate can still mean that most alerts are noise; decide per rule whether it pages, scores or hunts.
- Layer families so that each cheap evasion lands in another rule's field of view, and design around the telemetry the attacker may try to remove.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Lesson 1 designed detections as ideas: a family, a fact to rely on, a trade-off between precision and recall. To run, an idea has to be written in a query language, and every SIEM has its own. The kit's R1 is SQLite SQL; the same logic in Splunk is SPL, in Elastic it is KQL or EQL, in Microsoft Sentinel it is KQL of a different kind. If a SOC writes its detections directly in one product's language, its detection knowledge is locked into that product, cannot be shared with peers who use another, and must be rewritten every time the platform changes.

**Sigma** solves this by separating *what to detect* from *how a particular SIEM searches for it*. A Sigma rule is a YAML file that describes a log-based detection in generic terms: which kind of log it applies to, which field values to look for, how to combine them, how serious a hit is and what benign activity may trigger it. Tools convert that description into a specific SIEM's query. The open-source project maintains the specification, a large public rule repository, and the Python library **pySigma** with its command-line front end **sigma-cli**, which validate and convert rules through pluggable **backends** (one per target query language) and **processing pipelines** (which adapt generic field names and log sources to a particular deployment).

For a SOC, Sigma is more than a file format. It makes **detection as code** practical: rules live in version control as small readable text files, changes are reviewed as diffs, automated checks run on every change, and the same rule can be deployed to more than one platform. It also gives analysts a shared language: a Sigma rule published in an advisory can be read, judged and adapted before anyone converts it.

This lesson takes the kit's two Sigma rules, `rk_office_spawns_shell.yml` (the Sigma form of R1) and `rk_security_log_cleared.yml` (the Sigma form of R5), field by field. You will see how the detection section expresses AND, OR and NOT, how `logsource` decides where a rule applies, how `sigma check` catches mistakes, and why converting a rule without the right pipeline can silently produce a query that searches the wrong data.

> [!NOTE]
> All commands in this lesson run on your own machine against rule files in a copy of the kit. Converting a rule only produces query text; nothing is sent to any system. The outputs shown were produced with sigma-cli 4.0.1, pySigma 2.1.0 and pysigma-backend-splunk 3.0.1 (the course library records the same results with sigma-cli 4.0.0). Other versions may word their messages differently.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Sigma rule | A YAML document describing one log-based detection in a platform-independent way. |
| Log source (`logsource`) | The section that states which kind of log the rule applies to, using `category`, `product` and/or `service`. |
| Detection (`detection`) | The section holding named search identifiers (selections) and the `condition` that combines them. |
| Selection | A named search identifier: a map of field names to values that a single event must match. |
| Modifier | A suffix after a field name, separated by `\|`, that changes how values match (for example `endswith`, `contains`). |
| Condition | The Boolean expression over selection names (`and`, `or`, `not`, parentheses, `1 of`, `all of`) that decides a match. |
| Level | The rule's severity: `informational`, `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical`. |
| Status | The rule's maturity, for example `experimental`, `test` or `stable`. |
| pySigma | The Python library that parses, validates and converts Sigma rules. |
| sigma-cli | The command-line tool built on pySigma (`sigma check`, `sigma convert`, `sigma list`). |
| Backend | The pySigma component that renders a rule into one target query language (Splunk SPL in this lesson). |
| Processing pipeline | A set of transformations applied before rendering: mapping generic field names and log sources to a specific deployment. |

## Anatomy of a Sigma rule

Here is the complete file `LAB_ASSETS/C08/rk_office_spawns_shell.yml`, exactly as it ships in the kit:

```yaml
title: Office Application Spawning Script Interpreter
id: 6c0f4d2b-9a1e-4f53-8a3e-2f7b7e9c1a01
status: experimental
description: Detects Microsoft Word starting PowerShell or cmd.exe, a common
  sign of a malicious document (RedKross Academy teaching rule).
references:
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: RedKross Academy
date: 2026-11-07
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\WINWORD.EXE'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate macros that launch scripts (rare; document and allow-list)
level: high
```

The fields fall into five groups, which Figure 1 shows as a tree: identity, context, the log source, the detection logic, and triage hints.

![Figure 7.3: Anatomy of a Sigma rule: five groups of fields](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M07-L02-F1.svg)

*Figure 7.3: Anatomy of a Sigma rule: five groups of fields. The kit's rk_office_spawns_shell.yml broken into identity, context, log source, detection logic and triage hints.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The diagram breaks one Sigma rule into the five groups of fields that make it up, so you can see which parts a converter actually uses to build a query and which parts exist for people and tooling. When you review a rule, you check each group for a different kind of error.

**Components.** The dark root box at the top is **Sigma rule (YAML)**, with the subtitle naming the kit file `rk_office_spawns_shell.yml`. Five child boxes sit beneath it. **Identity**, slate, lists `title, id, status, author, date`. **Context**, blue, lists `description, references, tags`. **logsource**, violet, lists `category, product, service`. **detection**, orange, lists `selections + condition`. **Triage hints**, green, lists `falsepositives, level`. The note under the diagram says that only logsource and detection become query text.

**Relationships and arrows.** Each arrow runs from the root to one child: the rule *is composed of* these five parts. There are no arrows between the children, but in practice two of them work together: **logsource** says *where* to look and **detection** says *what* to look for. The other three groups travel with the rule into the SIEM as metadata (rule name, severity, references) but do not change which events match.

**Execution flow.** When a converter processes the rule it reads **logsource** first, to decide which pipeline transformations apply (for example which index or log name to add), then renders **detection** into the target query language. **Identity**, **Context** and **Triage hints** are read by validators and by the people and platforms that manage the rule.

**Decision logic.** The diagram has no branches, but the colours encode the review questions. Violet and orange (**logsource**, **detection**) answer "will it match the right events?". Green (**Triage hints**) answers "what should an analyst do with a hit?". Slate and blue (**Identity**, **Context**) answer "can we track, version and justify this rule?".

**Technical interpretation.** `id` is a UUID that identifies the rule permanently, even if its title changes; deployment and deduplication tooling relies on it, so a copied rule must get a new one. `status: experimental` tells consumers that the rule is new and not yet proven in production. `tags` follow the `attack.` namespace convention: a tactic name (`attack.execution`) or a technique ID in lower case (`attack.t1204.002`, User Execution: Malicious File; `attack.t1059.001`, Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell). `level: high` is the base severity that Module 5 compared with the triage helper's values.

**Practical example.** When R1 fired on WS-104 at 06:14, an analyst looking at a Sigma-based alert would see the title, the `high` level and the false-positive note about legitimate macros. That note tells the analyst what to rule out first: is there an approved macro for this user and document?

**Security implications.** Weak triage hints or a missing `falsepositives` entry push the cost of understanding a rule onto every analyst who meets it. Wrong `tags` distort coverage reports (Lesson 3). A wrong `logsource` is the most dangerous error, because it changes which data the query searches while the rule still looks correct.

**Key learning.** A Sigma rule is a detection plus its documentation: logsource and detection become the query, and everything else is what makes the rule reviewable, traceable and usable at triage time.

## logsource: where the rule applies

The `logsource` section names the kind of log a rule is written for, using up to three keys:

- **`category`** describes a type of event independent of the tool that records it, such as `process_creation`. Sysmon event 1, an EDR process event and Windows Security event 4688 can all be "process creation".
- **`product`** names the platform, such as `windows` or `linux`.
- **`service`** names a specific log within the product, such as `security` for the Windows Security event log.

The kit's two rules use the two common styles. `rk_office_spawns_shell.yml` uses `category: process_creation` with `product: windows`: it applies to *any* Windows process-creation source that provides `Image` and `ParentImage`. `rk_security_log_cleared.yml` uses `product: windows` with `service: security`: it applies to one specific log. Category-style rules are more portable; service-style rules are more precise about which log is meant.

The key point is that `logsource` is a *statement*, not a filter that the rule enforces by itself. Whether the resulting query actually restricts the search to that log depends on the processing pipeline used at conversion time. You will see the consequence in the conversion section below.

## detection: selections, values and modifiers

The `detection` section holds one or more named **selections** and exactly one `condition`. The names are your choice; prefixes such as `selection_` and `filter_` are conventions that make the condition readable. Three structural rules decide how a selection matches:

1. **A map is AND.** All field-value pairs inside one selection must hold for the same event.
2. **A list is OR.** A list of values under one field means "any of these".
3. **Plain values match the whole field, ignoring case.** `EventID: 1102` matches the value 1102 exactly; a string such as `'\WINWORD.EXE'` would have to equal the entire field unless a modifier says otherwise. Sigma string matching is case-insensitive by default, which matters for Windows paths (Lesson 1 showed the minisiem SQL achieving the same with `lower()`).

**Modifiers** change how values match. They are appended to the field name after a pipe. The kit uses `endswith`; others in everyday use include:

| Modifier | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `endswith` | The field ends with the value | `Image\|endswith: '\cmd.exe'` |
| `startswith` | The field begins with the value | `CommandLine\|startswith: 'powershell'` |
| `contains` | The value appears anywhere in the field | `CommandLine\|contains: ' -enc'` |
| `all` | Combined with a list: every value must match (AND instead of OR) | `CommandLine\|contains\|all:` followed by a list |
| `re` | The value is a regular expression | use sparingly: costly and backend-dependent |
| `cidr` | The field is an IP address inside the given range | `SourceIp\|cidr: '192.0.2.0/24'` |

Applying the rules to the kit file: `selection_parent` has one field, so it matches when `ParentImage` ends with `\WINWORD.EXE`. `selection_child` has one field with a two-item list, so it matches when `Image` ends with `\powershell.exe` *or* `\cmd.exe`. The leading backslash matters: `endswith: '\cmd.exe'` matches `C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe` but not a hypothetical `notcmd.exe`. This is stricter than the minisiem SQL's `LIKE '%cmd.exe%'`, which is a contains match.

### The condition

The `condition` combines selections with `and`, `or`, `not` and parentheses. In the kit rule, `selection_parent and selection_child` means both selections must hold for the same event, which is exactly the parent-child relationship that Lesson 1 identified as the behaviour.

Two shorthand forms keep rules with many selections readable: `1 of selection_*` (at least one selection whose name matches the pattern) and `all of selection_*` (every such selection); `them` refers to all selections in the rule. The most important pattern in practice is the **filter**: a selection describing known-benign activity, removed with `and not`. Filters are how a rule records an approved exception instead of leaving every analyst to rediscover it.

Why two selections rather than one map with both fields? In this rule a single map with `ParentImage|endswith` and `Image|endswith` would mean the same thing, because a map is AND. Separate, named selections make the intent clearer, give each part a name that reviewers can discuss, and make it easy to add more parents or a filter later.

## The second kit rule: Security log cleared

`LAB_ASSETS/C08/rk_security_log_cleared.yml` is the Sigma form of R5:

```yaml
title: Windows Security Event Log Cleared
id: 3b8e5a71-2c4d-4e9f-b0a6-7d1c9e2f4a12
status: experimental
description: Detects clearing of the Windows Security event log (event 1102),
  which attackers use to remove evidence (RedKross Academy teaching rule).
references:
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1685/005/
author: RedKross Academy
date: 2026-11-07
tags:
  - attack.t1685.005
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 1102
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Administrators clearing logs during approved maintenance (should be rare
    when logs are forwarded to a SIEM)
level: high
```

The detection is the simplest possible: one selection with one field and one value, and a condition that is just that selection. All of the rule's precision comes from the combination of `service: security` and `EventID: 1102`; the same number in a different log could mean something else entirely. The `falsepositives` entry makes a useful operational point: when logs are forwarded to a SIEM, administrators rarely have any reason to clear them, so every hit deserves a question.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Pin and record the ATT&CK version, because IDs change (this one did).** This file is tagged `attack.t1685.005` and its reference points to that technique. That tag is current: in ATT&CK content version 20.1 the former Defense Evasion tactic was split into Stealth (TA0005) and Defense Impairment (TA0112), and clearing Windows event logs is now **T1685.005 Clear Windows Event Logs** under **Defense Impairment** (a sub-technique of T1685 Disable or Modify Tools). Older material, and many existing rules, cite the former ID **T1070.001**. The rule does not say which ATT&CK version it was mapped to, so before using its tag in a coverage report, check it against the version your team has pinned and record that version with the mapping. Lesson 3 covers mapping and versioning in detail.

Notice also that the rule has *no tactic tag*, while the first rule carries `attack.execution` alongside its technique IDs. Consistency of tagging across a rule set is a review item in Lesson 7.

## From rule to query: check, pipeline, backend

A Sigma rule does nothing until it is converted. Conversion in pySigma has three stages: the rule is parsed and validated, a processing pipeline adapts it to a deployment, and a backend renders the result as query text. Figure 2 shows the path, with the real outputs from the kit's rules.

![Figure 7.4: From Sigma rule to SIEM query](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M07-L02-F2.svg)

*Figure 7.4: From Sigma rule to SIEM query. pySigma parses and validates a rule, a processing pipeline adapts it to your data, and a backend renders the query text.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The diagram traces one Sigma rule from a YAML file to a query a SIEM can run, and marks the stage where the most consequential decision (which pipeline to use) is made. It explains why the same rule can produce different, and sometimes wrong, queries.

**Components.** The flow runs from top to bottom through six steps. **rule.yml**, slate, is the input file. **Parse**, blue, turns YAML into a rule object. **Validate (sigma check)**, green, runs validators over structure, condition and tags. **Processing pipeline**, violet, maps `logsource` to log or index conditions and generic fields to platform fields. **Backend (Splunk)**, orange, renders the condition in SPL. **Query text**, dark, is the result, with the subtitle `source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=1102`.

**Relationships and arrows.** Each arrow passes the rule object to the next stage, so every stage works on the output of the one before. Validation does not change the rule; the pipeline does, by adding conditions and renaming fields before the backend sees them.

**Execution flow.** `sigma check` exercises the first three steps and stops. `sigma convert` runs the whole chain: with `-p splunk_windows` the pipeline stage is active; with `--without-pipeline` it is skipped and the backend renders the generic rule as it stands.

**Decision logic.** The key branch is at the pipeline step. For the log-cleared rule, skipping it produced `EventID=1102`, which searches every event with that ID in any log. Applying `splunk_windows` turned `service: security` into `source="WinEventLog:Security"` and renamed `EventID` to Splunk's `EventCode`. Validation is a second gate: a rule with a condition error fails at **Validate** and conversion refuses to continue.

**Technical interpretation.** The backend knows the query language but not your data; the pipeline is where knowledge of your data lives. A pipeline that matches someone else's indexing produces syntactically valid queries that miss your events.

**Practical example.** A Banyan analyst converts the log-cleared rule for the SOC's Splunk. If Banyan's Security log really is indexed with source `WinEventLog:Security` and field `EventCode`, the `splunk_windows` output is right. If Banyan's collector stores it differently, the analyst must use or write a pipeline that matches, then confirm with a test search that the query finds a known 1102 event.

**Security implications.** A wrong pipeline creates a silent false negative: the rule is deployed, reviewed and green on the dashboard, and never fires. A missing pipeline can create the opposite, an unscoped query that matches unrelated events. Both are found only by testing against real data (Lesson 4).

**Key learning.** `logsource` states intent; the processing pipeline makes it true for your data. Always convert with a pipeline that matches how your logs are stored, and verify the output.

### Validating with sigma check

Install the tools in a Python virtual environment inside your working copy of the kit, never system-wide:

```bash
python -m venv sigvenv
# Windows: sigvenv\Scripts\activate    Linux/macOS: source sigvenv/bin/activate
pip install sigma-cli pysigma-backend-splunk
```

`python -m venv sigvenv` creates an isolated environment in the folder `sigvenv`; activating it makes `pip` and `sigma` refer to that environment. `pip install` fetches sigma-cli and the Splunk backend. Then check the first kit rule:

```terminal
$ sigma check rk_office_spawns_shell.yml
Parsing Sigma rules
Checking Sigma rules

=== Summary ===
Found 0 errors, 0 condition errors and 0 issues.
No rule errors found.
No condition errors found.
No validation issues found.
```

`sigma check` takes one or more files or directories. It reports three classes of problem: **errors** (the YAML is not a valid rule), **condition errors** (the condition cannot be resolved) and **issues** (validator findings such as malformed tags or naming problems). The log-cleared rule produces the same clean summary.

To see the checker earn its keep, introduce two deliberate mistakes in copies of the rule. In the first copy, misspell a selection name in the condition (`selection_childs`):

```terminal
$ sigma check rk_office_cond_typo.yml
...
Found 0 errors, 1 condition errors and 0 issues.
...
| 1     | Detection 'selection_childs' not defined in detections in ...
```

(Output abridged; the tool prints the rule's full path where `...` appears.) Trying to convert that file fails with the same message, so a broken condition cannot reach a SIEM through the converter. In the second copy, shorten the technique tag to `attack.t1059.01`:

```terminal
$ sigma check rk_office_tag_typo.yml
...
issue=InvalidATTACKTagIssue severity=medium description=Invalid MITRE ATT&CK tagging rule=... tag=attack.t1059.01
...
Found 0 errors, 0 condition errors and 1 issues.
```

The tag validator catches malformed or unknown technique IDs using the ATT&CK data bundled with your pySigma version. Two limits follow. A clean check does not mean a tag is the *right* mapping for the behaviour; that is a judgement (Lesson 3). And because the bundled ATT&CK data changes between pySigma releases, the result for a given tag may differ between versions, which is one more reason to record the ATT&CK version a rule was mapped against.

### Converting to Splunk

```terminal
$ sigma convert -t splunk --without-pipeline rk_office_spawns_shell.yml
Parsing Sigma rules
ParentImage="*\\WINWORD.EXE" (Image IN ("*\\powershell.exe", "*\\cmd.exe"))
```

`-t splunk` selects the Splunk backend; `--without-pipeline` tells sigma-cli to render the rule with no field or log-source mapping. Read the output against the YAML: `endswith` became a leading `*` wildcard, the two-item list became `IN (...)`, and the `and` between selections became Splunk's implicit AND (a space). The backslashes are doubled because SPL string escaping requires it; this is correct, not a bug.

Without either option, sigma-cli refuses:

```terminal
$ sigma convert -t splunk rk_office_spawns_shell.yml
...
Error:
Processing pipeline required by backend! Define a custom pipeline or choose a predefined one.

Get all available pipelines for splunk with:
sigma list pipelines splunk
...
```

The refusal is deliberate: the tool makes you choose between a pipeline and an explicit statement that you do not want one. `sigma list pipelines` showed three Splunk pipelines in the tested installation: `splunk_windows` ("Splunk Windows log source conditions"), `splunk_sysmon_acceleration` and `splunk_cim` ("Splunk CIM Data Model Mapping"). Converting the log-cleared rule both ways shows why the choice matters:

```terminal
$ sigma convert -t splunk --without-pipeline rk_security_log_cleared.yml
Parsing Sigma rules
EventID=1102
$ sigma convert -t splunk -p splunk_windows rk_security_log_cleared.yml
Parsing Sigma rules
source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=1102
```

`-p` names the pipeline. The first query contains nothing from `logsource`: it would match an event 1102 from any log. The second restricts the search to the Security log and uses Splunk's field name. Pipelines can also remap fields entirely. With `-p splunk_cim`, the office rule became a query on Splunk's Common Information Model process fields:

```terminal
$ sigma convert -t splunk -p splunk_cim rk_office_spawns_shell.yml
Parsing Sigma rules
Processes.parent_process_path="*\\WINWORD.EXE" (Processes.process_path IN ("*\\powershell.exe", "*\\cmd.exe"))
```

Same rule, same backend, different field names, because the pipeline describes a different way of storing the same data. Use a pipeline only if it matches how your own data is indexed.

## Worked example: extending the rule with a filter

Lesson 1 suggested widening R1 to Excel and recording approved exceptions. In Sigma, both are small, reviewable edits. Copy the kit rule to `rk_office_spawns_shell_v2.yml`, give it a new `id` (generate one with `python -c "import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())"`), and change the detection:

```yaml
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\WINWORD.EXE'
      - '\EXCEL.EXE'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
  filter_approved:
    CommandLine|contains: '\finance\approved\'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and not filter_approved
```

The tested variant passed `sigma check` with no issues and converted as follows:

```terminal
$ sigma convert -t splunk --without-pipeline rk_office_spawns_shell_v2.yml
Parsing Sigma rules
(ParentImage IN ("*\\WINWORD.EXE", "*\\EXCEL.EXE")) (Image IN ("*\\powershell.exe", "*\\cmd.exe")) NOT CommandLine="*\\finance\\approved\\*"
```

The parent list became an `IN`, `contains` became wildcards on both sides, and `and not` became `NOT`. The change is easy to review as a diff: one new parent, one named filter.

The filter is also a deliberate teaching flaw. `CommandLine` is an **attacker-controlled value**: anyone who can start a process can include that folder string in its command line, and the filter would then hide the alert. A better exception keys on things the attacker controls less, such as the specific signed script, the approved host group or a combination of user and document, and is documented with an owner and an expiry date. Tuning and exceptions are developed in Lesson 5.

## Sigma and minisiem side by side

The kit expresses the same detection twice, and comparing them shows what translation must preserve:

| Aspect | minisiem R1 (SQL) | Sigma rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | `source='sysmon' AND event_id=1` | `category: process_creation`, `product: windows` |
| Parent match | `lower(parent_image) LIKE '%winword.exe%'` (contains) | `ParentImage\|endswith: '\WINWORD.EXE'` |
| Child match | Two `LIKE` tests joined by `OR` | A two-item list (OR) |
| Case | Explicit `lower()` | Case-insensitive by default |
| Metadata | Rule name only | Title, id, tags, level, false positives |

The SQL hard-codes the source and event ID that the Sigma rule leaves to a pipeline, and it uses a looser contains match. Neither is wrong for its purpose, but a translation that silently changes match semantics (contains versus ends-with, case-sensitive versus not) changes the rule's precision and recall. Check semantics after every conversion, not only syntax.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"Sigma is a SIEM" or "Sigma runs queries."** It is a description format; pySigma converts it, and the SIEM runs the result.
- **Assuming `logsource` filters the data.** It only does so through a pipeline. `EventID=1102` with no source restriction is the classic result.
- **Using any pipeline that makes the error go away.** A pipeline must match your indexing; otherwise you deploy a valid query that never fires.
- **Reusing an `id`.** Copied rules need a new UUID, or deployment tools will treat two rules as one.
- **Confusing map and list.** Two fields in one selection mean AND; two values under one field mean OR. Use `|all` when every value must match.
- **Filtering on attacker-controlled fields.** Exceptions written against command lines or file names can be imitated.
- **Treating a clean `sigma check` as proof of correctness.** It proves structure and tag syntax, not that the rule detects the behaviour or that tags are the right mapping.
- **Mixing tabs and spaces.** YAML requires consistent space indentation; a tab is a common parse error.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Sigma rules shape what the SOC can see, so treat the rule repository as a security asset. Restrict who can merge changes, require review, and run `sigma check` and conversion automatically on every change, so a broken condition or malformed tag never reaches production. A malicious or careless filter is effectively a blind spot that looks like a tuning decision.

Public rules carry the same risk as public code. A rule from a community repository or an advisory encodes someone else's log sources, field names and assumptions. Read it, convert it with your own pipeline, and test it on your data before trusting it. Conversely, publishing your own rules helps peers but also tells adversaries exactly what you match on; many SOCs share the behaviour while keeping thresholds and exceptions internal.

Converted queries also carry personal data concerns. Rules that pull user names, command lines or URLs into alerts should be limited to what triage needs, consistent with the DPDP Act 2023 principle of processing only what is necessary for the stated purpose.

## Best practices

- Keep one rule per file, named descriptively, with a unique UUID and an honest `status`.
- Name selections and filters for what they mean; prefer separate named selections over one large map when it aids review.
- Prefer `endswith` on full path components (with the leading backslash) to loose `contains` matches.
- Write `falsepositives` that tell an analyst what to rule out first; keep exceptions in named filters with an owner.
- Store rules in version control; run `sigma check` and conversion with your production pipeline in an automated pipeline on every change.
- Record the ATT&CK version used for tags, and re-check tags when ATT&CK releases change (Lesson 3).
- After conversion, compare the query's semantics with the rule's intent and test it against known data (Lesson 4).

## Key takeaways

- Sigma describes a log-based detection in portable YAML; pySigma and sigma-cli validate it and convert it into SIEM queries through backends and pipelines.
- A rule has five groups of fields: identity, context, `logsource`, `detection` and triage hints. Only `logsource` and `detection` shape the query.
- In `detection`, a map is AND, a list is OR, plain values match the whole field case-insensitively, and modifiers such as `endswith` and `contains` change matching. The `condition` combines named selections and filters.
- `sigma check` catches structural, condition and tag-format problems; it does not prove a rule detects what it claims.
- Without a pipeline, the log-cleared rule became `EventID=1102`; with `splunk_windows` it became `source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=1102`. The pipeline must match your data.
- The kit's `attack.t1685.005` tag is current: log clearing is T1685.005 Clear Windows Event Logs under Defense Impairment (TA0112); T1070.001 is the former ID found in older material. IDs change, so pin the ATT&CK version you map to and record it.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

By the end of Lesson 2 you could write a Sigma rule, check it and convert it into a query. A rule on its own, however, answers only a narrow question: "does this pattern appear in my data?" A SOC manager, an auditor or a threat-intelligence team asks wider questions. Which attacker behaviours can we see at all? Which ones would we miss? If a report says a ransomware group uses a particular way to gain persistence, do we have anything that would fire? Answering those questions requires a shared vocabulary for attacker behaviour that every rule, every log source and every intelligence report can be attached to. In modern security operations that vocabulary is **MITRE ATT&CK**.

ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) is a freely available knowledge base maintained by MITRE. It describes how adversaries behave once they target an organisation, and it is built from observed, publicly reported intrusions rather than from theory. Its central idea is that an intrusion is a sequence of **goals** (tactics) achieved by particular **methods** (techniques and sub-techniques), carried out in concrete ways by real groups and tools (procedures). Because the entries are numbered and stable enough to cite, a detection engineer in Pune, an incident responder in Singapore and a vendor's research team can all say "T1059.001" and mean the same thing: use of PowerShell as a command and scripting interpreter.

**ATT&CK mapping** is the practice of attaching those identifiers to your own artefacts. In this module the artefacts are detection rules, but the same practice is used for log sources, incident timelines, threat-intelligence reports, red-team findings and security controls. Mapping turns a pile of rules into something you can reason about as a whole: you can count, compare and colour your detections against a common grid and see where the empty squares are. That grid is the **coverage matrix**, and it is the bridge between this lesson and Lesson 6 (Coverage gaps).

Mapping is also easy to do badly: a coverage heat map that shows a technique as green because one untested rule mentions it creates false confidence. This lesson therefore treats mapping as a judgement with rules of evidence. You will learn how ATT&CK is structured, how to decide which technique a rule genuinely detects, how to link techniques to the data sources that make detection possible, how to build an honest coverage matrix, and how to keep mappings correct as ATT&CK itself changes.

Throughout, the worked examples use the course's Banyan dataset (`LAB_ASSETS/C08/banyan_events.jsonl`, 340 synthetic events) and the six correlation rules in the teaching SIEM `LAB_ASSETS/C08/minisiem.py`, together with the two Sigma rules in the kit.

> [!NOTE]
> Every technique ID in this lesson was chosen because it is long-established in ATT&CK Enterprise. ATT&CK is versioned and changes over time (techniques are added, renamed, split, deprecated or revoked), so the professional habit is to look an ID up in the version you are mapping to and record that version with the mapping. Never copy an ID from a blog post, a vendor rule or even a course file without checking it.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Matrix | A view of ATT&CK for one technology domain. Enterprise (Windows, Linux, macOS, cloud, network, containers and identity platforms), Mobile and ICS are the three domains. |
| Tactic | The adversary's tactical goal: the *why* of an action, such as Execution or Persistence. Identified as `TA` plus four digits, e.g. TA0002 Execution. Tactics are the columns of the matrix. |
| Technique | A general method of achieving a tactic: the *how*, such as T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter. Identified as `T` plus four digits. |
| Sub-technique | A more specific variant of a technique, written as the parent ID plus a three-digit suffix, e.g. T1059.001 PowerShell. |
| Procedure | A specific, observed implementation of a technique by a group or tool, for example "a macro in a Word document starts hidden PowerShell with an encoded command". Procedures are what logs actually show. |
| Group / Software | ATT&CK entries for named threat groups (`G` IDs) and malware or tools (`S` IDs), each linked to the techniques they have been reported using. |
| Mitigation | A preventive control category linked to techniques (`M` IDs), such as restricting Office macros. |
| Data source | The kind of telemetry in which a technique can be observed (for example process creation, logon sessions, network traffic). ATT&CK's own way of modelling data sources has changed between versions; the idea of "which data shows this behaviour" is what matters here. |
| Mapping | Associating one of your artefacts (rule, log source, finding, report sentence) with the ATT&CK tactic and technique it represents, with a stated version and rationale. |
| Coverage matrix | A table or heat map that shows, per technique relevant to your threats, whether the data is collected, whether a detection exists and whether it has been tested. |
| ATT&CK Navigator | MITRE's open-source web tool for annotating and colouring the matrix; an annotated view is saved as a JSON "layer" file that can be shared and version-controlled. |

## How ATT&CK is organised

### Tactics: the adversary's goals

The Enterprise matrix arranges tactics roughly in the order in which an intrusion tends to unfold, although real intrusions loop back and skip steps. The long-standing Enterprise tactics, with their identifiers, are listed below. Notice that the numeric IDs are not in kill-chain order: TA0043 Reconnaissance and TA0042 Resource Development were added later and placed at the front, and TA0011 Command and Control comes before TA0010 Exfiltration in the matrix even though its number is higher. IDs are identifiers, not sequence numbers.

| Tactic ID | Tactic | The adversary is trying to... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TA0043 | Reconnaissance | gather information to plan the operation |
| TA0042 | Resource Development | establish infrastructure, accounts or capabilities |
| TA0001 | Initial Access | get into your network |
| TA0002 | Execution | run malicious code |
| TA0003 | Persistence | keep their foothold across restarts and credential changes |
| TA0004 | Privilege Escalation | gain higher-level permissions |
| TA0005 | Stealth | avoid being noticed (formerly part of Defense Evasion) |
| TA0112 | Defense Impairment | disable or weaken defences such as logging and security tools (formerly part of Defense Evasion) |
| TA0006 | Credential Access | steal account names and passwords |
| TA0007 | Discovery | learn about your environment |
| TA0008 | Lateral Movement | move through your environment |
| TA0009 | Collection | gather data of interest |
| TA0011 | Command and Control | communicate with compromised systems |
| TA0010 | Exfiltration | steal data |
| TA0040 | Impact | disrupt, destroy or manipulate systems and data |

Two things about tactics matter for mapping. First, a tactic is a *goal*; a detection observes an action, and the tactic is inferred from what that action achieves. Second, one technique can serve more than one tactic. T1078 Valid Accounts appears under several tactics, among them Initial Access, Persistence and Privilege Escalation, because logging in with a stolen but genuine password can achieve each of them (check the current release for its full tactic list: ATT&CK content version 20.1 split the former Defense Evasion tactic into Stealth and Defense Impairment, and older material still shows the old name). When you tag such a technique, choose the tactic that matches what *your rule* sees in context, or list several only when the rule genuinely covers each.

### Techniques and sub-techniques: the methods

Each tactic column contains techniques. Many techniques are split into sub-techniques that describe more specific variants. T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter, for example, has sub-techniques for PowerShell (T1059.001) and the Windows Command Shell (T1059.003) among others. T1110 Brute Force includes T1110.003 Password Spraying, where the attacker tries one or a few common passwords against many accounts instead of many passwords against one account.

The sub-technique level is usually the right level for a detection tag, because detections are specific. A rule that watches for `powershell.exe` starting under Word observes PowerShell specifically, so tagging T1059.001 says more than tagging T1059. Conversely, if you genuinely cannot tell which variant an event represents, tag the parent technique and say why; a precise-looking sub-technique that you guessed is a false statement.

### Procedures: what the logs actually show

Below the sub-technique sits the procedure: the concrete way a particular adversary performed the technique. Detection rules are written against procedures and their artefacts (a parent-child process pair, an event ID, a request pattern), and then mapped *upwards* to the technique and tactic. This is the core movement of mapping, and the figure below follows one rule from the Banyan case through every level of the hierarchy.

*Figure 7.5: From tactic to detection: one Banyan chain through ATT&CK. The ATT&CK hierarchy as a stack, from the Execution tactic down to the observed procedure on WS-104 and the rule that recognises it.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The diagram shows the ATT&CK hierarchy as a stack, from the most abstract level at the top to the most concrete at the bottom, using one real chain from the course dataset. It exists to make one point concrete: you write rules at the bottom of the stack and map them upwards, never the other way round.

**Components.** There are five stacked bands. The dark top band, **Tactic: TA0002 Execution**, carries the sub-label "the why: run malicious code". The violet band below it, **Technique: T1059**, is labelled "Command and Scripting Interpreter". The orange band, **Sub-technique: T1059.001**, is labelled "PowerShell". The red band, **Procedure**, reads "Word macro starts hidden PowerShell (WS-104, 06:14)". The green band at the bottom, **Detection: minisiem R1 / Sigma rule**, reads "WINWORD.EXE parent + powershell.exe child". The note under the stack states the direction of mapping.

**Relationships.** Each band is a more specific case of the band above it. Execution can be achieved by many techniques; T1059 is one of them; PowerShell is one variant of T1059; the macro-launched PowerShell on WS-104 is one observed instance of that variant; and the rule is the logic that recognises the instance in telemetry.

**Execution flow.** Read the diagram bottom-up when you map. The Sysmon event at 06:14 on WS-104 records `WINWORD.EXE` as the parent of `powershell.exe` with `-W Hidden -EncodedCommand`. The rule fires on that parent-child pair. You then ask: what technique does this observation demonstrate? A scripting interpreter being run, specifically PowerShell, so T1059.001. And what goal does that serve? Running code, so TA0002 Execution.

**Decision logic.** The stack also shows where to stop. If the rule could not tell PowerShell from other interpreters, you would stop at the violet T1059 band. If the rule saw only "Word started something", you would not be entitled to the T1059 bands at all. The narrower the observation, the lower in the stack you can tag with confidence.

**Technical interpretation.** The upper bands are stable and shared across the industry; the lower bands are specific to your environment and change with each campaign. This is why a coverage matrix is organised by the upper bands while rules are built from the lower ones.

**Practical example.** The kit rule `rk_office_spawns_shell.yml` carries the tags `attack.execution`, `attack.t1204.002` and `attack.t1059.001`. The second tag, T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File, sits beside T1059.001 in the same Execution column: the user opening a malicious document is a separate technique observed in the same event, because Word is the parent.

**Security implications.** Mapping downwards ("we need something for T1059, so search for the string PowerShell") produces brittle rules that match on names. Mapping upwards from a well-understood procedure produces tags that are true.

**Key learning.** Detections live at the procedure level; ATT&CK IDs are the labels you attach to them after asking what the detection actually observes.

## Mapping a detection: the rules of evidence

Mapping a rule means answering three questions in order, and writing the answers down.

1. **What does the rule observe?** State it in terms of fields and values, not intentions. R1 observes "a Sysmon process-creation event (event ID 1) whose parent image contains `winword.exe` and whose image contains `powershell.exe` or `cmd.exe`". It does not observe phishing, a macro or malicious intent.
2. **Which technique does that observation demonstrate?** Look the candidate technique up and read its description. Does the observed artefact meet the definition on its own, or only when combined with other evidence you do not have? Tag only what the artefact demonstrates on its own.
3. **Which tactic does it serve in this context?** For techniques that appear under several tactics, choose by what the action achieves in the scenario the rule targets.

Three principles follow from those questions.

**Tag what the rule detects, not what the attacker did.** The attacker in the Banyan case phished a user, ran code, beaconed, sprayed VPN passwords, created an account, uploaded data and cleared a log. R1 detects one moment of that story. If R1 were tagged with every technique in the incident, the coverage matrix would claim that one rule covers exfiltration, which it plainly does not.

**Prefer the most specific technique the evidence supports.** R1 sees `powershell.exe` by name, so T1059.001 is supported. But R1 also fires for `cmd.exe`, which is the Windows Command Shell, T1059.003. The kit rule tags only T1059.001. That is an under-mapping: the rule genuinely covers both sub-techniques, and a coverage matrix built from its tags will miss the second one. Small inconsistencies like this are exactly what a rule review (Lesson 7) should catch.

**When the evidence is ambiguous, tag the parent and record the doubt.** R4 fires on any proxy upload larger than 10,000,000 bytes. In the dataset it found 48,200,000 bytes sent to `https://files-share-drop.example/upload`. If you know the destination is a cloud storage service, T1567.002 Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage fits. If you only know it is an HTTPS web service, the parent T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service is the honest tag. The rule itself cannot tell what kind of site it is talking to; that is enrichment, not detection.

| Observation (rule) | Evidence in the dataset | Technique | Tactic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Download of `invoice.docm` from a look-alike domain (no rule) | proxy, 06:12, WS-104 | T1566 Phishing (sub-technique unconfirmed) | Initial Access |
| Word is the parent of PowerShell (R1) | Sysmon EID 1, 06:14 | T1204.002 Malicious File; T1059.001 PowerShell | Execution |
| Word is the parent of cmd.exe (R1, second branch) | not present in the dataset | T1059.003 Windows Command Shell | Execution |
| 18 identical 220-byte HTTPS requests (R6) | proxy, from 06:17 | T1071.001 Web Protocols | Command and Control |
| 8 users fail from one IP, then one succeeds (R2) | VPN, 203.0.113.66, 06:42-06:46 | T1110.003 Password Spraying | Credential Access |
| The success itself: a real password over the VPN (R2 output) | gopal at 06:46 | T1078 Valid Accounts; T1133 External Remote Services | Initial Access |
| Account `svc_update` created, event 4720 (R3) | Security log, 07:02 | T1136.001 Create Account: Local Account | Persistence |
| `svc_update` added to Administrators, event 4732 (R3) | Security log, 07:03 | T1098 Account Manipulation | Persistence; Privilege Escalation |
| 48.2 MB upload (R4) | proxy, 08:12 | T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567.002 if the site is cloud storage) | Exfiltration |
| Security log cleared, event 1102 (R5) | Security log, 08:17 | T1685.005 Clear Windows Event Logs (formerly T1070.001) | Defense Impairment |

Several judgements in this table deserve a sentence each, because they are the kind you will make every week.

**The phishing row has no sub-technique.** The proxy shows a web download of a macro-enabled document from `banyan-payroll-update.example`. T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment describes a file attached to a message; T1566.002 Spearphishing Link describes a link the user follows. A web download is more consistent with a link, but the lab collects no mail logs, so we cannot see how the URL reached the user. Tagging the parent T1566 and writing "delivery vector unconfirmed: no mail telemetry" is accurate; picking a sub-technique would be a guess. Notice also that *no rule* fires here. R1 catches the next step, which is a common and acceptable design, but the matrix must show that the initial-access step itself is undetected.

**R2 maps to two moments.** The failures are password spraying. The success afterwards is the use of a valid account through an external remote service. A rule that only counted failures would support T1110.003 alone; because R2 requires the success, its alert is evidence of T1078 and T1133 as well. Whether to tag all three is a team decision; many teams tag the technique the rule is *designed* to find (T1110.003) and mention the others in the rule's documentation.

**R3 maps to two techniques because it matches two event IDs.** Event 4720 is account creation; event 4732 is a member being added to a security-enabled local group. Mapping also exposed a limitation: minisiem's table has no `group` column, so R3 fires on *any* 4732, not only additions to Administrators, despite its name `new_local_admin`. Mapping forces you to read the logic closely enough to see such gaps.

**R5 and the kit's Sigma tag.** The kit's Sigma rule `LAB_ASSETS/C08/rk_security_log_cleared.yml` detects the same behaviour as R5 (Security event 1102) and carries the tag `attack.t1685.005`. That tag is current. In ATT&CK content version 20.1 the former Defense Evasion tactic was split into Stealth (TA0005) and Defense Impairment (TA0112), and clearing Windows event logs is now T1685.005 Clear Windows Event Logs under Defense Impairment, a sub-technique of T1685 Disable or Modify Tools. Older material, and older rules, cite the former ID T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs under Defense Evasion. The kit rule's weakness is not the ID but the missing record of which ATT&CK version it was mapped to: the next reviewer has no way to tell a current tag from a stale one. Pin the ATT&CK version your organisation maps to, record it with every mapping, and re-map older content that still uses the former ID. If the rule repository and the ATT&CK reference disagree, automated coverage reports silently drop or misplace the rule.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A mapping is a claim. Write it down with its evidence: the ATT&CK version, the technique ID and name, and one sentence explaining why the rule's observation demonstrates that technique. A tag without a rationale cannot be reviewed.

### Writing the mapping into the rule

In Sigma, ATT&CK mappings go in the `tags` list using lower-case identifiers: `attack.` followed by the tactic name (`attack.execution`, `attack.defense-impairment`) or the technique ID (`attack.t1059.001`). Applying the judgements above to the kit's first rule would give:

```yaml
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003   # the rule also matches cmd.exe
```

and to the log-clearing rule, mapped against ATT&CK 20.1 (record that version in the rule's description):

```yaml
tags:
  - attack.defense-impairment
  - attack.t1685.005   # formerly T1070.001
```

`sigma check` validates the *form* of tags (that they follow the naming convention), but it cannot tell whether a technique is the right one for the logic. Correctness of a mapping is a human review responsibility.

## Mapping data sources

A detection needs three things to work: the behaviour must produce an observable artefact, the artefact must be collected and parsed, and logic must recognise it. Rules map to techniques; **data sources** map to the first two conditions. For every technique you care about, you should be able to say which telemetry would show it and whether you collect that telemetry with the fields the logic needs.

For the Banyan techniques the data requirements are concrete:

| Technique | Telemetry needed | Fields the logic depends on | Collected in the lab? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T1204.002, T1059.001, T1059.003 | Process creation with parent (Sysmon event 1 or EDR) | `Image`, `ParentImage`, ideally `CommandLine` and `OriginalFileName` | Yes (image, parent image, command line) |
| T1071.001 | Web proxy or HTTP logs | host, URL, bytes out, timestamp | Yes |
| T1110.003, T1078, T1133 | VPN or remote-access authentication logs | user, source IP, outcome, time | Yes |
| T1136.001, T1098 | Windows Security log, account management | event ID, target account, group | Partly: the group is in the raw event but not a minisiem column |
| T1567 | Proxy logs with upload sizes; ideally destination categorisation | URL, bytes out, category | Sizes yes; category no |
| T1685.005 | Windows Security log, forwarded off-host | event ID, host, user | Yes |
| T1566 | Mail gateway logs (sender, attachment, links) | sender, recipient, attachment hash, URL | No |

The last column is where data-source mapping earns its keep. It shows, without writing a single rule, that the lab cannot see phishing delivery at all and cannot distinguish cloud storage from other upload destinations. Those are telemetry gaps, and no amount of clever logic closes them.

> [!TIP]
> Event 1102 is written when the Security log is cleared, into the log that has just been cleared. If that log is stored only on the host, an attacker who clears it has also removed most of the evidence you would use to investigate. Forwarding to a SIEM in near real time is what makes the 1102 detection useful. Mapping the data source is how you notice such dependencies.

## Versions and the life of a mapping

ATT&CK is updated regularly, typically with two major releases a year. Releases add techniques, refine descriptions, split techniques into sub-techniques, and sometimes deprecate or revoke entries. A revoked entry has been replaced by another one, so an ID that was right when a rule was written can become wrong without anyone touching the rule. This has practical consequences:

- **Record the version.** Each mapping, and each coverage report, should state the ATT&CK version it was made against. A heat map without a version is not reproducible.
- **Re-validate on upgrade.** When you move to a new version, check every tag in the rule repository against the new dataset. Tools that read ATT&CK's published data (MITRE publishes it in the STIX 2.1 format) can flag tags that no longer exist or have been revoked.
- **Expect disagreement between sources.** Vendor content, community rules, course material and threat reports may cite different IDs for the same behaviour; the kit tag above is a live example. Resolve disagreements against the official ATT&CK site for your chosen version, not by majority vote.

## Coverage matrices

Once rules and data sources are mapped, you can combine them into a coverage matrix. The simplest useful form is a table with one row per technique that matters to your organisation and, at minimum, three yes/no columns: **data collected**, **rule exists**, **rule tested**. A fourth column records the resulting status in words that do not overstate it.

Each column fails in a different way. A technique with no data cannot be detected, whatever the rule repository says. A technique with data but no rule is a quick win: the telemetry is already paid for. A technique with an untested rule may or may not be detected; you do not know until the rule has been shown to fire on a known-bad case and stay quiet on a near miss, which is the subject of Lesson 4. Collapsing the three into one colour hides exactly the information you need to plan work.

Which techniques belong in the rows? Not all of ATT&CK, whose empty squares would drown the important gaps. Rows should come from your threat model: the techniques used by the groups and malware that target your sector (ATT&CK's Group and Software pages list them, with references), techniques seen in your own incidents and in red-team or purple-team exercises, and techniques your auditors or regulators ask about. For a teaching environment like Banyan, the incident itself defines the rows.
