## Key takeaways

- The NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 lifecycle has four phases, Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; and Post-Incident Activity, with feedback from containment to analysis and from review to preparation.
- SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) supersedes Rev. 2 and frames incident response within CSF 2.0: preparation in Govern, Identify and Protect, response in Detect, Respond and Recover, and improvement throughout.
- The SOC analyst builds preparation, does most of detection and analysis, advises on and verifies containment, and supplies the timeline and detection review afterwards.
- Scoping comes before containment where possible, and every scoping statement must name the data it rests on.
- In Banyan, more than two hours passed between the first malicious event and noticing; shortening that gap is what good preparation buys.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Module 5, Lesson 6 taught you how to escalate: a structured message that transfers ownership of a case to the IR lead and is complete only when it is acknowledged. That escalation is the first communication of an incident, not the last. Once an incident is declared, many more people need information: the teams who will contain it, the executives who must make business decisions, legal and compliance staff who must judge reporting duties, the affected users, and possibly regulators, customers and the police. Each needs different information, at a different time, through a different channel, and some must not receive certain information at all.

Poor communication is one of the most common reasons incidents go badly even when the technical work is sound. The classic failures are easy to recognise once named. An executive hears about the incident from a journalist. Three teams receive three different versions of the facts. A manager emails the compromised mailbox to ask what is happening, and the attacker reads it. A regulator's deadline passes because nobody told legal when the SOC first noticed the problem. A status update promises "contained" an hour before a second infected host is found.

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 treats communication as part of the response itself. In the CSF 2.0 structure covered in Lesson 1, Incident Response Reporting and Communication (RS.CO) is a Category of the Respond Function and Incident Recovery Communication (RC.CO) a Category of Recover. Communication is not something done once the "real work" is finished; it is real work.

This lesson covers audiences, status updates, out-of-band channels, need-to-know and regulatory notifications. The SOC analyst is rarely the person who briefs the board or talks to the regulator. But almost every message that goes out during an incident is built on facts the SOC supplied, and the quality of those facts decides the quality of everything downstream.

> [!NOTE]
> The Banyan Microfinance case from the course dataset is the running example. Event times come from `LAB_ASSETS/C08/banyan_events.jsonl`. SOC actions and their times (noticed 08:25Z, acknowledged 08:31Z, status updates) are illustrative and continue from Module 5, Lesson 6. IST is UTC+05:30.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Audience | A person or group that needs information about the incident, defined by what they must decide or do. |
| Status update (situation report) | A periodic, structured summary of the incident's current state, sent to an agreed list at an agreed cadence. |
| Cadence | The agreed interval between status updates, normally set by severity and stated in every update ("next update 10:00Z"). |
| Incident log | The single, time-ordered record of facts, decisions, actions and communications for one incident, kept by a named scribe or in the case system. |
| Single source of truth | The one place (usually the case or incident log) that holds the authoritative current facts; every update is drawn from it. |
| Bridge | A call (or dedicated meeting room) where the incident's working group coordinates in real time. |
| In-band | Using the organisation's normal communication systems (corporate email, chat, ticketing). |
| Out-of-band (OOB) | Using a channel independent of the systems that may be compromised: a separate tenant or platform, phone bridges, pre-agreed numbers. |
| Need-to-know | The principle that information is shared only with those who require it to perform their role in the incident. |
| Codename | A neutral name for the incident used in messages and calendars so that its nature is not revealed to casual readers. |
| TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) | FIRST's labelling scheme for how far information may be shared: TLP:RED, TLP:AMBER+STRICT, TLP:AMBER, TLP:GREEN, TLP:CLEAR. |
| Holding statement | A short, pre-approved external statement acknowledging an issue without detail, prepared by communications and legal. |
| Tipping off | Letting the attacker (or, in an insider case, the subject) learn that they have been detected, through careless communication. |

## Who needs to know: internal and external audiences

The first communication task in an incident is to work out the audiences. A useful test for each candidate is: **what will this person decide or do with the information?** If there is no answer, they do not need it yet.

### Internal audiences

- **The IR lead (incident commander).** Owns the incident and coordinates all communication. Every other internal audience is served through, or with the agreement of, this role.
- **The SOC and technical responders.** Need full technical detail: indicators, hosts, queries, the timeline. They usually work from the case itself and the bridge.
- **IT operations, identity and network teams.** Need specific, actionable requests: "isolate WS-104", "reset and revoke sessions for divya and gopal", "block these two domains". They need just enough context to act correctly, plus explicit instructions about evidence ("do not reboot or reimage").
- **Executives and business owners.** Need impact, risk, decisions required and business workarounds, in plain language. In Banyan, the head of finance needs to know that a payments approver's laptop is out of action and that payments may need a second approver today.
- **Legal, compliance and the data protection function.** Need precise facts and times to assess obligations: when the incident was noticed, what systems and data may be involved, whether personal or financial data may have left. They decide reportability, not the SOC.
- **Human resources.** Involved when an employee's conduct is in question or when staff are affected. Not every incident needs HR; an insider case always does.
- **Corporate communications.** Prepares holding statements and customer or media messaging, always with legal.
- **The affected users and their managers.** Need to know what to do and not do (stop using the device, expect a password reset, report anything unusual), not the investigative detail.
- **The help desk.** Needs a script: callers reporting symptoms linked to the incident should be routed to the IR team, and the help desk must not "fix" affected machines. The fictional scenario in this course's case material, where a technician's helpful reboot destroyed memory evidence, is what happens when the help desk is forgotten.

### External audiences

- **CERT-In**, for incidents of the types listed in its Directions of 28 April 2022, reported through the organisation's designated point of contact (POC) within six hours of noticing.
- **Sector regulators**, for regulated entities. Banyan, as a microfinance company, would need to check its regulator's own requirements; these vary by sector and are for compliance to identify.
- **The Data Protection Board of India and affected Data Principals**, where a personal data breach falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Whether and how this applies is assessed by legal and the data protection function.
- **Law enforcement**, at the organisation's decision, typically through legal.
- **Customers and partners**, where their data or services are affected or contracts require notice.
- **Insurers**, if a cyber insurance policy requires prompt notification.
- **An IR retainer or external forensics firm**, engaged by the IR lead.
- **Information-sharing communities** such as an ISAC, under the appropriate TLP label, once the organisation agrees to share.

The common feature of every external audience is that the SOC analyst does not contact them directly. External communication goes through the designated roles: the POC for CERT-In, legal for regulators and law enforcement, communications for customers and media. The analyst's contribution is accurate facts delivered quickly to those roles.

**Purpose.** The diagram maps who communicates with whom during an incident. It matters because most communication failures are routing failures: the right facts reach the wrong person, or an external body hears from someone not authorised to speak for the organisation.

**Components.** The diagram reads from top to bottom. Below the IR lead is a row of five boxes it serves: **IT ops, identity, network** (orange, "specific actions"), **Executives, business owners** (violet, "impact, decisions"), **Legal, compliance, DPO** (violet, "facts for obligations"), **Affected users, help desk** (slate, "instructions") and **Corporate communications** (violet, "with legal"). The next row holds the **CISO / CERT-In POC** (violet, "designated point of contact"), which is the authorised voice to CERT-In, and two external audiences in slate: **Other regulators, Data Protection Board** and **Customers, media**. At the bottom is **CERT-In** (slate, "within 6 h of noticing").

**Relationships and arrows.** The arrow from the SOC analyst to the IR lead, labelled **status, facts**, is the analyst's main communication path. Arrows from the IR lead fan out to each internal audience, each carrying the version of the facts that audience needs. Legal, compliance and the data protection officer (DPO) send **reportability advice** to the CISO / CERT-In POC, who sends the **report** to CERT-In. Legal also connects to other regulators, and corporate communications sends **approved statements** to customers and media.

**Execution flow.** Facts originate in the SOC, are consolidated by the IR lead, and are tailored for each internal audience. Legal assesses obligations from those facts; the authorised roles then speak externally.

**Decision logic.** There is no arrow from the SOC analyst to any external body. That absence is the main decision the diagram encodes: technical staff do not notify regulators, customers or media, however urgent the situation appears.

**Technical interpretation.** The hub-and-spoke shape keeps a single source of truth. If every team pulled facts from different analysts, versions would diverge within an hour.

**Practical example.** In Banyan, the analyst updates the IR lead that the beacon stopped after isolation. The IR lead tells the network team to keep the domain blocks in place, tells the head of finance that WS-104 will be rebuilt, and gives legal the time noticed (08:25Z) and the size of the upload. The POC uses those facts in the CERT-In report.

**Security implications.** Routing through authorised roles limits the spread of sensitive detail, stops inconsistent statements and prevents an analyst's unverified hypothesis from appearing in a regulatory filing.

**Key learning.** The SOC feeds facts to the IR lead; only designated roles speak to external bodies.

## The incident log: one source of truth

Before looking at messages to other people, consider the record they are drawn from. Every incident needs one **incident log**: a time-ordered record of facts as they are established, decisions and who made them, actions and who carried them out, and communications sent. In a mature SOC this lives in the case-management system; in a smaller one it may be a controlled shared document kept by a named scribe. What matters is that there is exactly one, that everyone knows where it is, and that every entry has a UTC time and an author.

The log does three jobs. It is the **source for status updates**, so different audiences receive consistent facts. It is the **memory of the incident**, which the post-incident review (Lesson 6) depends on. And it is **evidence**: if a regulator, insurer or court later asks when the organisation knew something or why it chose to isolate a host at a particular time, the log answers.

A few entries from the Banyan log show the style. Each is short, dated, attributed and either a fact, a decision or an action, never a mixture:

```text
08:25Z  SOC-T1   FACT     R5 alert opened: Security log cleared on WS-104 (event 1102, 08:17Z). Time noticed.
08:31Z  IR-LEAD  DECISION Incident declared, codename HERON. IR lead owns. Severity SEV1.
08:40Z  SOC-T2   FACT     hunt.py H3: no other host contacted the case domains (proxy telemetry).
08:52Z  IR-LEAD  DECISION Isolate WS-104; block both domains and 203.0.113.66; reset divya, gopal.
09:05Z  IT-OPS   ACTION   WS-104 network-isolated via EDR.
09:20Z  SOC-T2   FACT     No requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example since 09:05Z.
```

The times after 08:25Z are illustrative. Notice that the analyst's entries are facts with their source ("proxy telemetry"), and that decisions are recorded under the name of the person who made them.

## Status updates: structure and cadence

Once an incident is running, people who are not on the bridge still need to know what is happening. Without a planned rhythm of updates, they ask, by phone and chat, constantly, and every question interrupts a responder. A **status update** at a known **cadence** answers the questions before they are asked and gives everyone the same picture.

### What a status update contains

A good update is short and always follows the same structure, so readers can find what they need:

| Section | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Header | Codename, update number, time (UTC and local), severity, current phase, author. |
| Summary | Two or three sentences: what is happening and the current state. |
| Changes since last update | What is new: findings, actions completed, scope changes. |
| Impact | Systems, users, data and business processes affected, with confidence. |
| Actions in progress and next steps | Who is doing what, with expected times. |
| Decisions needed | From whom, by when. |
| Next update | The time of the next update. |

The last line matters more than it looks. A promised time lets everyone stop asking. Missing it, even with nothing new to report, damages trust in the whole process; "no material change, next update 10:30Z" is a perfectly good update.

The update must keep the discipline of the escalation in Module 5, Lesson 6: **separate fact from hypothesis** and **label confidence**. The temptation in updates is to sound reassuring. "Contained" is a strong word. If the beacon has stopped but scoping is incomplete, the accurate statement is "The known command-and-control channel has stopped since WS-104 was isolated at 09:05Z; scoping of other systems continues."

### Cadence

Cadence is set by severity and phase, in the IR plan. A typical pattern is frequent updates in the first hours of a serious incident, when facts change quickly, then longer intervals as it stabilises. Each organisation sets its own intervals; what matters is that they are defined in advance, stated in each update, and changed only by the IR lead. A significant change, such as discovering a second infected host, triggers an immediate update outside the cadence.

![Figure 8.4: The status update cycle](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M08-L02-F2.svg)

*Figure 8.4: The status update cycle. Each update is drawn from the incident log, separates fact from hypothesis, is tailored and reviewed, sent on a safe channel, logged, and followed by the next at the promised time.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The diagram shows the cycle every status update goes through, from the incident log to the record of what was sent. It matters because updates written in a hurry, from memory, are where inconsistent facts and premature reassurances come from.

**Components.** Seven rounded boxes run from top to bottom. **Pull facts from the incident log** (slate, "single source of truth") is the starting point. **Separate confirmed from hypothesis** (blue, "label confidence") is the analytical discipline. **Write the update** (orange, "changes, state, actions, next update") is the drafting step using the fixed structure. **Tailor per audience** (violet, "technical, executive, user") and **Review** (violet, "IR lead; legal for anything external") are the control steps. **Send on an approved channel** (green, "out-of-band if in-band may be compromised") is delivery. **Log what was sent** (dark, "to whom, when, which version") closes the record.

**Relationships and arrows.** Solid arrows run downward in order; each step depends on the previous one. A dashed arrow, labelled **next update at the stated time, or sooner on a major change**, returns from the last step to the first, making this a loop rather than a one-off task.

**Execution flow.** Facts are taken from the log, never from memory or chat. They are sorted by confidence, written into the fixed structure, rewritten for each audience, reviewed, sent through the channel the incident plan approves, and logged. Then the cycle waits for the next scheduled time.

**Decision logic.** Two conditions shape the flow. If the update goes outside the organisation, legal must review it in the Review step. If there is any sign that email or chat is compromised, the Send step uses the out-of-band channel. The loop has its own condition: a major change restarts the cycle early.

**Technical interpretation.** Tailoring changes the presentation, never the facts. The executive version of "48,200,000 bytes uploaded to files-share-drop.example at 08:12Z" is "about 48 MB of data left the network to an unknown file-sharing service; content not yet known", and both versions must come from the same log entry.

**Practical example.** At 09:30Z the Banyan analyst drafts update 2 from the log: isolation at 09:05Z, no beacon since, gopal's credentials reset, scoping continuing. The IR lead reviews it, it is sent over the out-of-band bridge's chat, and the log records "Update 2 sent 09:32Z to HERON core list". The next is promised for 10:30Z.

**Security implications.** The Review step stops an analyst's hypothesis being presented as fact to executives or regulators. The channel condition stops an update from tipping off an attacker reading mail. Logging what was sent means the organisation can later show exactly what it knew and said at each time.

**Key learning.** Every update comes from the log, labels its confidence, is reviewed, goes out on a safe channel, is logged and promises the next one.

### One set of facts, several versions

Here is update 2 in its technical form, for the incident working group:

```text

SUMMARY   Finance workstation WS-104 compromised via a malicious document; isolated
          09:05Z. Separate VPN compromise of account gopal from 203.0.113.66.
CHANGES   - WS-104 isolated 09:05Z (IT-OPS). No requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example
            since then (proxy, checked 09:20Z).
          - Blocks in place: cdn-telemetry-sync.example, files-share-drop.example,
            203.0.113.66.
          - divya and gopal: passwords reset, sessions revoked 09:15Z.
IMPACT    48,200,000 bytes uploaded 08:12Z to files-share-drop.example. Content NOT
          yet known (confidence: unknown). No other host seen contacting case
          domains (proxy telemetry; endpoint sweep pending).
NEXT      Evidence export of WS-104 events (SOC-T2, 10:00Z). Review gopal VPN session
          activity (identity team, 10:15Z).
DECISIONS Legal: reportability assessment in progress; noticed 08:25Z, CERT-In
          six-hour point 14:25Z (19:55 IST).
NEXT UPDATE 10:30Z
```

And the same facts for executives:

```text
HERON update 2, 15:00 IST. A finance laptop was infected through a fake invoice
document and has been disconnected; the attacker's link to it has stopped. A sales
employee's VPN password was also misused; it has been reset. About 48 MB of data
left the network to an unknown file-sharing site; we do not yet know what it
contained, and this is our main open question. Business impact: one payments
approver is without a laptop; a replacement is being prepared. Legal is assessing
reporting duties, with a deadline of 19:55 IST today. Next update 16:00 IST.
```

The executive version drops indicators and hostnames, converts times to local time, states impact in business terms, and makes the biggest unknown explicit. It does not soften it. The deadline appears in both, because both audiences may need to act on it.

## Out-of-band communication

Module 5, Lesson 6 introduced the rule: do not discuss an incident on a channel the attacker may be able to read. During incident handling that rule becomes a practical question of what channel to use instead, and the answer must be prepared before the incident.

### When to go out of band

Move incident communication off normal systems when any of these is true or plausible:

- A **mailbox** involved in the incident may be compromised. In Banyan, the malicious document ran as divya, so anything in or reachable from her mailbox, including threads she is copied on, may be visible to the attacker.
- **Identity infrastructure** may be compromised: a directory or identity-provider administrator account, a new privileged account. An attacker with administrative access to the tenant can read anyone's mail and chat.
- The **collaboration platform** or its administrators are in scope.
- The incident is an **insider** case and the subject has access to normal channels or their logs.
- Normal systems are **unavailable**, as in ransomware that has encrypted servers.

In Banyan, a new local administrator account on one workstation does not by itself prove tenant compromise, but the compromise of a user with mail access and an attacker with an unexplained VPN session make out-of-band communication the prudent default until scoping says otherwise. The decision, and its reason, goes in the incident log.

### What an out-of-band channel looks like

An out-of-band channel is independent of the systems that may be compromised: separate accounts and authentication, ideally a separate provider. Common forms are a pre-arranged phone bridge, a collaboration space hosted outside the corporate tenant with separate credentials, and printed or offline contact lists with phone numbers. Whatever is chosen must meet three conditions:

1. **Prepared in advance.** Setting up a new channel during the incident, by emailing invitations from the compromised mail system, defeats its purpose.
2. **Identity-checked.** Participants must be sure who they are talking to. An attacker with mail access may know the bridge exists; join codes should not be sent in-band, and unfamiliar voices or new participants should be verified by calling back on a known number.
3. **Recorded.** Decisions made on the bridge still go into the incident log. Out of band does not mean off the record.

> [!WARNING]
> Never use an affected device or account to communicate about the incident. In Banyan, nobody should message divya on WS-104 or at her corporate mailbox about the case. Reach her by phone, through her manager, and give instructions verbally: do not use the laptop, do not delete anything, expect a replacement device.

## Need-to-know in practice

Need-to-know protects the investigation, the people involved (an employee whose account was used is a victim until proven otherwise) and the organisation. Practical techniques:

- **Use a codename.** "HERON" in a calendar invitation, ticket title or bridge name reveals nothing; "WS-104 data theft finance" reveals a great deal to anyone browsing the ticket queue.
- **Keep distribution lists small and named.** A core list for full updates, a wider list for summaries, and nothing to all-staff lists unless communications and legal decide to.
- **Give action teams what they need to act, not the whole story.** The network team needs the domains and the address to block, not the identity of the finance user.
- **Use restricted case access.** The incident case should be visible only to its working group; ordinary tickets for related tasks should not contain the details.
- **Label shared information with TLP.** When indicators are shared with partners or an ISAC, the TLP label tells recipients how far they may pass it on. The ISAC indicator for `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` arrived as TLP:AMBER, which limits sharing to the recipient's organisation and its clients on a need-to-know basis; it should not appear in a public statement.
- **Avoid tipping off.** Do not change visible things before containment is coordinated: blocking the beacon domain an hour before isolating the host tells the attacker they are seen while their foothold is still live. Communication and containment timing must be planned together, which Lesson 3 develops.

Need-to-know is not secrecy: people who must act must still be told enough to act correctly.

## Regulatory notifications: the SOC's part

The legal detail of Indian reporting obligations belongs to Course 01 and to the organisation's legal team. What the SOC must understand is how communication inside the incident makes timely notification possible.

**CERT-In.** Under the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022, issued under section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, covered entities must report the incident types listed in the Directions within six hours of noticing them or being brought to notice of them, through their designated point of contact. Six hours is short. The report will be based on what is known at that moment, so the facts the SOC supplies must carry their confidence labels, and the SOC must keep supplying facts as the investigation develops.

**Personal data.** The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires a Data Fiduciary, in the event of a personal data breach, to intimate the Data Protection Board of India and each affected Data Principal. The form, content and timing are set by rules whose application legal must confirm at the time of the incident. In Banyan, the unknown content of the 48 MB upload is exactly the question that decides this, which is why update 2 called it "our main open question".

**Others.** Sector regulators, contracts and insurance policies may impose their own notifications; compliance identifies them. The SOC's duties are concrete:

1. **Get the time noticed to legal and the POC immediately**, in UTC and IST, together with the derived CERT-In six-hour point. For Banyan: noticed 08:25Z (13:55 IST), six-hour point 14:25Z (19:55 IST).
2. **Supply the facts reports need**: incident type as the evidence shows it, affected systems, indicators, time of first malicious activity, actions taken, and what data may be involved.
3. **State unknowns explicitly**, with what is being done to resolve them and when an answer is expected.
4. **Update legal whenever a fact changes** that could alter reportability or the content of a report: a second host, evidence that personal data was in the upload, or evidence that it was not.
5. **Never notify, estimate obligations, or promise outcomes yourself.** As Module 5 warned, legal interpretations in a case note mislead.

> [!CAUTION]
> A regulator's deadline is measured from the organisation's noticing, not from the end of the investigation. If the SOC sits on facts while it "gets them right", the people accountable lose time they cannot recover.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **Reassuring too early.** "Contained" or "no data lost" before scoping is complete becomes a false statement that must later be retracted, often in front of a regulator.
- **Different facts for different audiences.** Tailoring changes language and detail, never the facts; every version comes from the log.
- **Discussing the incident in-band.** Emailing the compromised user, or creating the bridge invitation from a mailbox the attacker can read.
- **Unprepared out-of-band channels.** A channel created during the incident, with invitations sent in-band, is not out of band.
- **Missing a promised update.** Silence prompts interruptions and rumours; a "no change" update keeps trust.
- **Forgetting the help desk and the affected user.** Well-meaning fixes destroy evidence.
- **Holding facts back from legal** until they are certain, which consumes the reporting window.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Communication channels are part of the attack surface during an incident: an attacker who reads the investigation can accelerate or destroy evidence. Attackers also exploit the confusion of an incident with impersonation: a message apparently from the IR lead asking someone to "disable the EDR agent for testing" or to send credentials. Defences are mostly preparation: a tested out-of-band channel, pre-agreed identity checks, an IR plan that names who may instruct whom, and a rule that instructions affecting security controls are confirmed through a known channel. The SOC can also monitor the incident itself: watch for logons to mailboxes of incident participants from unusual sources, mailbox rule changes and access to the incident case by unexpected accounts. In Banyan, any new mailbox forwarding rule on divya's account during the incident would be a strong sign that the attacker was watching.

## Best practices

1. Keep one incident log with UTC times, authors and labels (fact, decision, action, communication).
2. Identify audiences by what they must decide or do; route everything through the IR lead.
3. Use a fixed status update structure with confidence labels and a stated next-update time, and keep the cadence.
4. Tailor wording per audience, never the facts.
5. Prepare the out-of-band channel, contact lists and identity checks before an incident, and switch to them on any sign of mail, chat or identity compromise.
6. Use codenames, small named lists and restricted case access; respect TLP labels.
7. Send legal and the POC the time noticed and six-hour point at once, and update them on every material change.
8. Never let the SOC notify external bodies or estimate legal obligations.

## Key takeaways

- Communication is part of the response (RS.CO and RC.CO in CSF 2.0), built on facts the SOC supplies.
- One incident log is the single source of truth; every status update is drawn from it, labels confidence and promises the next update.
- Audiences are defined by what they must decide or do; the IR lead coordinates them, and only designated roles speak externally.
- Use prepared, identity-checked out-of-band channels whenever mail, chat or identity systems may be compromised, and never contact the affected device or mailbox about the incident.
- Need-to-know, codenames and TLP protect the investigation and the people involved without leaving action teams uninformed.
- Under the CERT-In Directions, reportable incidents must be reported within six hours of noticing; the SOC's job is to give legal and the POC the time noticed and accurate, confidence-labelled facts at once.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Detection tells you that something is wrong. Containment is the first thing the organisation does about it. It is the set of actions that limit the harm an incident can still cause: stopping an intruder from reaching more systems, cutting off a command-and-control channel, preventing more data from leaving, and taking away the credentials an attacker is using. Containment is not the same as fixing the problem. The malware may still be on the disk, the account the attacker created may still exist, and the weakness that let them in may still be open. Those are the jobs of eradication and recovery. Containment buys time and stops the damage from growing while those jobs are planned and done properly.

In most organisations the SOC analyst does not press the containment buttons alone. The analyst, who understands the evidence best, **recommends**: which actions, in which order, against which hosts, accounts and indicators, with what risks. An authorised person, usually the incident lead, **decides**, and IT operations, identity or network teams **execute**. Containment interrupts real people and processes (isolating a laptop stops its owner working; disabling an account may stop a payments run), so someone with authority to accept that impact must make the call.

A good recommendation is specific (exact host, account and indicator), complete (every foothold the evidence shows), ordered (what happens together, what waits), honest about trade-offs and reversible where possible. A poor one is "please isolate the machine", sent by email, about one host, while the attacker still holds a VPN session and a privileged local account.

This lesson builds that skill on the Banyan Microfinance dataset: the menu of containment actions, short-term versus long-term containment, the risk of tipping off the attacker, who decides, and a recommendation for WS-104, gopal and svc_update. Lesson 4 deals with the evidence that containment must not destroy.

> [!NOTE]
> NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 (2012) described a lifecycle with a combined "containment, eradication and recovery" phase. Rev. 3 (April 2025) reorganises incident response around the CSF 2.0 functions, but the containment vocabulary used in this lesson remains standard in playbooks and in practice.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Containment | Actions that limit the further harm of an incident: spread, data loss, misuse of access, damage to systems. |
| Short-term containment | Fast, usually reversible actions that stop the immediate harm (isolate a host, block an indicator, disable an account) while investigation continues. |
| Long-term containment | Interim measures that let the business keep operating safely until eradication and recovery are complete (rebuilt or replacement systems, tightened access, enhanced monitoring). |
| Eradication | Removing the attacker's presence: malware, persistence, unauthorised accounts, and closing the entry weakness. |
| Recovery | Restoring systems to normal operation from known-good sources and confirming that the attacker has not returned. |
| Foothold | Any means by which the attacker can still act: a compromised host, a live session, a valid credential, a persistence mechanism, an open C2 channel. |
| Tipping off | Alerting the attacker that they have been detected, so that they change behaviour, accelerate, destroy evidence or hide. |
| Network isolation (EDR) | An endpoint security feature that blocks a host's network traffic except to the security management console, keeping the host running and reachable for investigation. |
| Session revocation | Invalidating existing sessions and tokens issued to an account, so that a password reset is not undermined by sessions that are already authenticated. |
| Containment authority | The pre-agreed statement of who may approve which containment actions, at which severity, and which actions the SOC may take on its own. |

## Why containment is a decision, not a reflex

The instinctive reaction to a compromised machine is to pull the plug. The professional reaction is to ask what the plug is connected to. Every containment action has three effects at once, and the analyst's job is to make all three visible before anyone acts.

**It reduces harm.** This is the reason for acting at all. An isolated host can no longer reach its command-and-control server or the file server next to it. A disabled account can no longer be used to sign in. A blocked domain can no longer receive exfiltrated data.

**It costs something.** Business costs (a user who cannot work, a process that stops), investigation costs (a powered-off host loses its memory, a deleted account loses its history) and response costs (a blocked domain may push the attacker to one you do not know yet).

**It sends a signal.** An attacker watching their access notices a silent beacon, a failed password or a closed session. What they do next may be worse than the activity you were trying to stop.

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 lists criteria for choosing a containment strategy that capture this balance: potential damage to and theft of resources, the need to preserve evidence, service availability, the time and resources needed, effectiveness (partial or full containment) and duration (emergency workaround or permanent solution).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Never let the search for perfect evidence delay containment of serious, ongoing harm. If data is leaving or systems are being encrypted right now, stopping it comes first. Evidence preservation (Lesson 4) shapes *how* you contain, not *whether* you contain.

## The containment menu

Containment actions fall into a few families, each with a characteristic strength, cost and signal.

### Host containment

**Network isolation through EDR** is the default first action for a compromised workstation in organisations that have endpoint detection and response. The EDR agent blocks all network traffic except the connection to its own management console. The host stays powered on, so running processes and memory are preserved for collection; the analyst and forensic team can still reach it through the console to collect evidence; and the attacker loses the network path to and from the host. Its costs are user disruption and the fact that a beacon that stops checking in is noticeable to the attacker.

**Switch-port or VLAN isolation** is the fallback without EDR; it usually also cuts the management channel, making live collection harder.

**Powering off** stops everything, including the attacker, but destroys volatile evidence: memory contents, running processes, open network connections and decrypted material that exists only in memory. It is rarely the right first choice. The exception is ongoing destruction, for example ransomware actively encrypting a file share, where every minute running costs more than the evidence is worth.

### Account and credential containment

**Disabling an account** stops new sign-ins with it. **Resetting a password** stops the old password working. Neither, on its own, necessarily ends sessions that are already authenticated: an attacker who holds a live VPN session, a valid web session cookie or an issued access token may keep working until that session expires. Effective credential containment therefore pairs a reset or disablement with **revoking sessions and tokens**, and, where multi-factor authentication methods may have been tampered with, reviewing and resetting the registered MFA methods. The exact mechanisms differ by identity platform, and your playbook should name them.

Account actions also carry business cost (disabling a payments approver mid-run is a financial decision) and a strong signal: the attacker's next sign-in fails.

**Local accounts** need special care. An account created on one workstation exists only in that machine's local account database, not in the central directory. Disabling it requires action on the host itself (through the EDR console, endpoint management or a forensic responder), and the same account name may need to be searched for on every other host.

### Network containment

**Blocking domains and IP addresses** at the proxy, DNS resolver or firewall stops known command-and-control and exfiltration destinations for every host at once, including hosts you have not yet identified as compromised. It is cheap, fast and reversible, and the business impact is usually negligible when the destinations are attacker-controlled. Its weakness is that it is only as good as your indicators: an attacker with other infrastructure can switch to it. Blocking also has a scoping benefit. With the block logging enabled, any other host that tries to reach the same destination identifies itself.

**Blocking a source IP** at the VPN or perimeter stops further attempts from a known address, but complements account containment rather than replacing it.

### Persistence and access containment

**Disabling persistence** (unauthorised accounts, scheduled tasks, services, startup entries) removes the attacker's way back in. Disabling is usually preferred to deleting during containment: a disabled account keeps its creation record, group memberships and profile for investigation, while a deleted one loses them. Full removal belongs to eradication, after evidence has been captured.

## Short-term and long-term containment

Widely used incident-handling training, such as the SANS six-step model, divides containment into two stages, and the distinction is useful even where your playbook uses other words.

**Short-term containment** happens in minutes to hours. Its goal is to stop the immediate harm with actions that are fast and, ideally, reversible: isolate the host, block the destinations, disable the accounts, close the sessions. Short-term containment accepts disruption because the alternative is continuing damage. It is designed so that evidence collection can proceed straight afterwards: an EDR-isolated host is still running and reachable for memory and disk capture.

**Long-term containment** covers the period, often days, between stopping the immediate harm and completing eradication and recovery. The organisation must keep working while the investigation finishes and clean systems are prepared. Typical long-term measures are: giving the affected user a clean replacement device rather than returning the original; moving a critical function to a standby system; applying a temporary firewall rule or conditional access policy; requiring step-up authentication for a group of accounts; and running enhanced monitoring (extra detections, shorter review intervals) on the affected users and hosts. Long-term containment measures are temporary by definition, so each needs an owner and an end condition, or they become permanent technical debt.

| Aspect | Short-term containment | Long-term containment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goal | Stop harm now | Operate safely until eradication and recovery |
| Timescale | Minutes to hours | Days to weeks |
| Typical actions | EDR isolation, block indicators, disable accounts, revoke sessions | Replacement device, standby systems, temporary rules, enhanced monitoring |
| Evidence stance | Keep systems running for collection | Preserve images and records before rebuild |
| Who usually executes | SOC (if pre-authorised), IT ops, identity team | IT ops, application owners, identity and network teams |
| End condition | Harm stopped and footholds controlled | Systems rebuilt or restored and monitoring shows no return |

## The risk of tipping off

An attacker who has invested in access to an organisation watches that access. Commodity malware may simply stop working when blocked, but a hands-on-keyboard intruder notices when a beacon goes silent or a credential fails, and reacts. The reactions that matter to a responder are:

- **Acceleration.** Taking whatever data can still be reached, or triggering destructive payloads, before access is lost entirely.
- **Destruction of evidence.** Clearing logs, deleting tools and staged archives, removing accounts that would reveal how they operated.
- **Migration.** Moving to a foothold the defenders have not found: another compromised account, another host, a different command-and-control domain.
- **Dormancy.** Going quiet on the known footholds while keeping a hidden one, so that the defenders declare victory too early.

The practical rule that follows is: **contain all known footholds at the same time**, and do not take a visible action against one of them while the others remain open. Isolating the workstation but leaving the attacker's VPN session alive tells them which part of their access has been found and leaves them a route to react. Resetting a password an hour before isolating the host gives the attacker an hour of warning.

Tipping off also happens through communication: emailing a compromised user about the investigation, or discussing containment in a chat platform the attacker may be reading. Use the out-of-band channels from Lesson 2.

The opposite temptation also exists: delaying containment to observe the attacker, learn their infrastructure and contain more completely later. This can be legitimate in mature teams, sometimes at the request of law enforcement, but it means knowingly leaving an intruder active inside the organisation. It is a decision for the incident lead with legal and business owners, never for the analyst alone, and it is not appropriate when data is actively leaving or harm is ongoing.

> [!WARNING]
> Coordinated containment does not mean slow containment. If evidence shows serious harm in progress, such as a large upload under way or encryption starting, contain the active foothold immediately and accept the tip-off risk. Coordination is for the minutes you have, not a reason to wait.

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The figure is a decision aid. It sets six common containment actions side by side so that their trade-offs can be compared at a glance, which is exactly what an incident lead needs from a recommendation. It matters because the action that stops the attacker most completely is not always the right first choice: the best plan combines actions whose strengths cover each other's weaknesses.

**Components.** The table has five columns: **Action**, **Stops attacker**, **Keeps evidence**, **Business impact** and **Tip-off signal**. Each of the six rows is one action from the containment menu. **EDR network isolation** rates high for stopping the attacker on that host, high for keeping evidence (the host keeps running), medium for business impact and noticeable as a signal. **Block domain / IP** rates partial for stopping the attacker, high for evidence, low for business impact and low as a signal. **Disable + revoke sessions** rates high (for credential misuse), high for evidence, medium for impact and strong as a signal. **Disable persistence account** rates partial (it removes the way back, not current access), high for evidence because the account is kept, low for impact and medium as a signal. **Power off** rates high for stopping, low for evidence, high for impact and strong as a signal. **Wipe and reimage** rates high for stopping on that host, very low for evidence, high for impact and strong as a signal. Rows are tinted by their overall standing: green for the default first actions, orange for the action that needs care, and red for the two actions that destroy evidence.

**Relationships.** Reading across a row gives one action's profile; reading down a column compares actions on one criterion. The **Keeps evidence** column is where the two red rows stand out: they are the only options rated low or very low, which is why they are reserved for special cases.

**Execution flow.** In practice you assemble a plan by choosing a set of rows that together cover every foothold, then ordering them so that the signalling actions happen at the same time. For a typical workstation compromise that means EDR isolation, indicator blocks and account actions together, with persistence disabled through the isolated host's management channel.

**Decision logic.** The implicit rule is: prefer green rows; use the orange row with a stated reason; use red rows only when harm is ongoing and cannot be stopped another way (power off) or when evidence has already been captured (wipe and reimage, which belongs to recovery rather than containment).

**Technical interpretation.** Isolation and blocking act on the network path; disable-and-revoke acts on authentication; disabling persistence acts on the attacker's re-entry. They are complementary layers, not alternatives, which is why the table has no single winner.

**Practical example.** For the Banyan case, the green rows map to isolating WS-104, blocking the three attacker domains and 203.0.113.66, and disabling and revoking the sessions of the affected accounts. The orange row maps to disabling svc_update on WS-104. Neither red row is recommended.

**Security implications.** The **Tip-off signal** column is the reason for coordination. Four of the six actions send a noticeable or strong signal; taking them minutes apart rather than together gives the attacker time to react.

**Key learning.** No single containment action is best on every criterion; a sound recommendation combines several, keeps evidence, and times the signalling actions together.

## Who decides

Containment interrupts the business, so its authority must be settled before an incident, not argued about during one. Mature organisations write a **containment authority** into their incident response plan or playbooks, stating which actions the SOC may take on its own and which need approval, from whom, at which severity.

A common pattern is:

- **Pre-authorised SOC actions.** Low-impact, reversible actions the SOC may take immediately, often for any confirmed incident: blocking a confirmed-malicious domain or IP, isolating a standard workstation through EDR at the highest severities, disabling a clearly unauthorised account. The analyst still records each action and informs the incident lead.
- **Incident lead approval.** Actions with real business impact or wider consequences: isolating a critical user's device or a server, disabling a staff account, mass password resets, segmentation changes.
- **Business owner consultation.** Where an action stops a business process (a payments run, a production line, a customer-facing service), the owner of that process is consulted on timing and workarounds. They do not usually have a veto over stopping active harm, but they own the business continuity plan.
- **Executive and legal involvement.** Decisions such as deliberately delaying containment to observe the attacker, shutting down a business service entirely, or acting on a law-enforcement request.

The analyst's part is to make the decision easy: name the action, target, reason, impact, evidence consideration and suggested owner, so the incident lead can approve in one reply. Every approval and execution is recorded with a time in the incident log, which is itself evidence and the basis of the post-incident review (Lesson 6).

> [!TIP]
> If you are unsure whether an action is pre-authorised, treat it as not pre-authorised. Recommend it, state the time pressure, and escalate. A two-minute wait for approval rarely decides an incident; an unauthorised outage of a business-critical system can become an incident of its own.

## Worked example: containment advice for the Banyan incident

The Banyan Microfinance dataset (`LAB_ASSETS/C08/banyan_events.jsonl`, synthetic) records one intrusion on 3 November 2026. Earlier modules triaged it; here you turn the evidence into a containment recommendation. The first task is to list every foothold, because a plan that misses one is the plan that tips the attacker off.

### Step 1: establish the footholds from evidence

In a temporary copy of the kit (never the kit folder itself), load the dataset and query the three entities the incident lead asked about: the VPN activity behind R2, gopal, and svc_update.

`load` reads the JSONL file into a local SQLite database; `search` runs the quoted SQL against its `events` table and prints the columns separated by `|`. The `WHERE` clauses select the VPN source and the attacker's address, the VPN events for one user, and any event in which svc_update is the actor or the target.

Interpretation, fact by fact:

- **The VPN spray.** Eight different accounts failed from 203.0.113.66 at seven-second intervals, one attempt each: the shape of password spraying (ATT&CK T1110.003). Four minutes later gopal's account **succeeded** from the same address, with the VPN's country field unknown (`??` in the raw events). That successful session is a foothold: a valid credential with remote access to the network.
- **gopal's other activity.** A further success at 13:33Z from 198.51.100.104 (country `IN`) may be the real gopal working remotely, so a reset will interrupt a genuine user who must be given new credentials out of band. His own device, WS-107 (sales laptop), was on the internal network at 10.40.0.26 through the morning.
- **svc_update.** Created on WS-104 (event 4720) at 07:02Z and added to the local Administrators group (4732) at 07:03Z, with divya recorded as the acting account. It is a **local** account: disabling it in the central directory would do nothing.
- **WS-104 itself.** From earlier modules: `invoice.docm` from banyan-payroll-update.example at 06:12Z, Word spawning hidden encoded PowerShell at 06:14Z, 18 regular 220-byte requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example from 06:17Z to 07:42Z, a 48.2 MB upload to files-share-drop.example at 08:12Z, and the Security log cleared at 08:17Z.

Is the VPN session connected to WS-104? The evidence does not say: the activities overlap in time but share no host or address (divya's account was among those sprayed, but that attempt failed). Treat the VPN session as a **separate foothold** and state the link as an open question.

### Step 2: list footholds and map each to actions

| Foothold | Evidence | Short-term action | Owner | Evidence consideration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WS-104 host | Office-spawned PowerShell, beacon, upload, log cleared | EDR network isolation (not power-off) | IT ops / SOC if pre-authorised | Keeps memory and disk for Lesson 4 collection |
| C2 and exfiltration infrastructure | Three `.example` domains in proxy logs | Block at proxy and DNS, with block logging | Network team | Block logs reveal any other host that tries |
| Spray source | 203.0.113.66 in VPN logs | Block at VPN and perimeter | Network team | Keep VPN logs for the address |
| gopal credential and VPN session | Spray then success at 06:46Z | Disable or reset, terminate VPN sessions, revoke tokens, review MFA methods | Identity team | Export VPN logs before session data ages out |
| divya credential | Account used to run the payload and create svc_update | Reset, revoke sessions and tokens | Identity team | Note: the reset does not clean WS-104 |
| svc_update local admin | 4720 / 4732 on WS-104 | Disable on the host through the EDR or management channel; do not delete | IT ops | Deletion would lose the account's profile and records |

### Step 3: decide the order and the timing

All six actions send some signal to an attacker, and three of them (isolation and the two staff-account actions) send a noticeable or strong one. The recommendation is therefore one coordinated window, preceded only by the steps that do not signal anything:

1. **Before the window (silent).** Confirm the SOC's own channels are out of band (Lesson 2). Export the relevant logs, as Lesson 4 describes, so that containment cannot age them out. Brief the identity, network and IT operations executors by phone or the out-of-band bridge. Ask the finance head for a payments workaround.
2. **In the window (together, within minutes).** Isolate WS-104; apply the domain and IP blocks; disable and reset gopal, terminate his VPN sessions and revoke tokens; reset divya and revoke her sessions; disable svc_update through the isolated host's management channel.
3. **Straight after.** Verify (Step 5), then hand over to evidence collection on WS-104 and to scoping hunts: search every host for an account named svc_update and for any traffic to the three domains.

One caveat: the upload completed at 08:12Z. Had it been noticed while still running, the advice would change: isolate WS-104 at once, accept the tip-off risk, and coordinate the rest immediately afterwards.

### Step 4: write the recommendation

```text
CASE-0001 CONTAINMENT RECOMMENDATION (for incident lead approval)
Coordinated window: all items together; executors briefed out of band.
1 WS-104       EDR network isolation. NOT power-off, NOT reimage.
               Impact: payments approver offline -> deputy approves;
               clean replacement device for divya.
2 Domains      Block banyan-payroll-update.example,
               cdn-telemetry-sync.example, files-share-drop.example
               at proxy + DNS; log block hits.
3 IP           Block 203.0.113.66 at VPN + perimeter.
4 gopal        Disable/reset, end VPN sessions, revoke tokens,
               review MFA methods. Contact gopal by phone.
5 divya        Reset, revoke sessions and tokens.
6 svc_update   Disable (not delete) on WS-104 via EDR console.
Evidence:      WS-104 events exported and hashed before the window;
               memory and disk capture after isolation (forensics).
Open question: link between VPN session and WS-104 unproven.
After:         verify silence; hunt for svc_update and the domains
               on all hosts; eradication and rebuild plan to follow.
Decision requested within 15 minutes.
```

Each line names a target, an action and, where it matters, the impact and evidence consequence; the open question keeps a hypothesis from being read as a finding.

### Step 5: verify

Containment is complete only when confirmed. Check the SIEM for successful requests to the three domains after the block (block hits are expected and useful), VPN authentication from 203.0.113.66, sign-ins by gopal or divya not made by the real users, and the EDR console's confirmation that WS-104 is isolated. Log each check and result.

## Long-term containment for Banyan

WS-104 stays isolated until memory and disk have been collected, and is then rebuilt from a known-good image rather than cleaned. divya works on a replacement device with enhanced monitoring of her account. Finance reviews any payments approved from divya's account after the first malicious activity, because a compromised approver's workstation is an obvious route to payment fraud; the SOC recommends that review and finance owns it. The VPN gains near-real-time detection on the logic of rule R2, and the organisation reviews whether VPN access needs phishing-resistant MFA. Each item gets an owner and an end date, and all of them feed the post-incident review in Lesson 6.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"Containment means powering it off."** Powering off loses memory, running processes and network state. Isolate instead unless destruction is under way.
- **"A password reset locks the attacker out."** Existing sessions and tokens may survive it. Revoke sessions, end VPN connections and review MFA methods in the same action.
- **"Contain the first host, then look for more."** Containing one foothold while others stay open warns the attacker.
- **"Delete the malicious account."** Disable it during containment; deletion destroys its history. Removal belongs to eradication.
- **"The analyst should just do it."** Unless the action is pre-authorised, the analyst recommends and the incident lead decides.
- **"Containment ends the incident."** It stops the harm growing; eradication, recovery and lessons learned still follow.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Containment advice is only as good as the preparation behind it: EDR with network isolation on every supported host, central domain and IP blocking with logging, a practised identity procedure for disable, reset, session revocation and MFA review, a written containment authority, out-of-band channels, and continuity plans for the critical users whose interruption containment will cause. The tabletop in Lesson 7 tests these without an attacker present.

After containment, detection keeps working. Block-log hits, sign-in attempts on reset accounts and the scoping hunt's results are how you learn that containment was incomplete. The containment actions themselves (isolation events, rule changes, account administration) are security-relevant changes and must be logged, so that the post-incident review can reconstruct exactly what was done and when.

## Best practices

- Map every foothold to an action before recommending any, and say which may still be unknown.
- Prefer reversible, evidence-preserving actions: isolate rather than power off, disable rather than delete.
- Do the silent steps first, then take all signalling actions in one window, unless harm is in progress.
- Write each line with target, action, impact, evidence consideration and owner, and ask for a decision by a stated time.
- Verify after execution and record every approval, action and check with a UTC time.

## Key takeaways

- Containment limits further harm and is distinct from eradication and recovery; short-term containment stops harm now, long-term containment keeps the business running safely until rebuild.
- Every action stops, costs and signals; a recommendation states all three.
- Contain all known footholds together after the silent preparation, unless harm is ongoing.
- The analyst recommends and verifies; the incident lead decides under a pre-agreed authority; operations teams execute.
- For Banyan: isolate WS-104, block three domains and 203.0.113.66, contain gopal and divya including their sessions, and disable svc_update on the host, with the VPN-to-WS-104 link stated as unproven.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Every decision in an incident rests on evidence: what happened, when, on which systems, through which accounts, and what left the organisation. That evidence is fragile. Memory disappears when a machine is switched off. Network connections close. Logs roll over when local storage fills, SIEM retention expires, and an attacker who has administrative rights can clear the Security log, as the Banyan attacker did on WS-104 at 08:17Z. Evidence that is not preserved deliberately and early is often not available later, and evidence that was preserved carelessly may not be trusted when it matters.

**Evidence preservation** is the discipline of capturing information about an incident in a way that keeps it available, unchanged and explainable. Available means it still exists when the investigation, the regulator, the insurer or a court needs it. Unchanged means you can show that what you present today is bit-for-bit what you collected. Explainable means you can say who collected it, from where, how, when, and who has handled it since. The three map onto three practices this lesson teaches: collecting in **order of volatility**, protecting **integrity with cryptographic hashes**, and recording a **chain of custody**. Around them sit two organisational practices: **log preservation** (making sure the records the investigation depends on are not deleted by routine retention) and **legal hold** (a formal instruction suspending deletion when litigation or regulatory action is possible).

A SOC analyst is not usually a forensic examiner. Disk and memory imaging, and the analysis of those images, are specialist work covered in Course 09. But the SOC is present at the start of almost every incident, often hours before anyone else, and it controls the logs. What the SOC does in the first hour decides what forensics can do on the first day. The analyst's responsibilities are therefore to avoid destroying evidence, to request volatile capture before it is too late, to preserve log evidence with integrity and custody records, and to document every action taken on live systems. Lesson 3 showed that containment should be chosen with evidence in mind; this lesson shows what that evidence is and how to keep it.

You will work through these practices with the course kit's `LAB_ASSETS/C08/evidence_export.py`, run in a temporary working copy, exporting the Banyan WS-104 events, verifying them, detecting a deliberate change, re-running the export to show it is reproducible, and discovering one real limitation of the tool that matters for practice.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Evidence preservation | Capturing incident information so that it remains available, unchanged and explainable. |
| Volatile data | Data that is lost when a system is powered off or changes quickly while it runs: memory, processes, network connections. |
| Order of volatility | Collecting the most short-lived evidence first, as described in RFC 3227. |
| Cryptographic hash | A fixed-length digest computed from data such that any change to the data produces a different digest; SHA-256 produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters). |
| Manifest | A file listing evidence items with their hashes, for example a `SHA256SUMS` file. |
| Chain of custody | The documented history of an evidence item: who collected it, when, how, where it has been stored and every transfer since. |
| Forensic copy | A copy made with methods that do not alter the source and whose integrity is verified by hash. |
| Log preservation | Actions that stop routine retention or rotation from deleting logs an investigation needs. |
| Legal hold | A formal instruction, usually from legal counsel, to preserve information relevant to actual or anticipated litigation or regulatory action, suspending normal deletion. |
| Write-once storage (WORM) | Storage that prevents modification or deletion for a set period, such as object lock in cloud storage. |

## Why the SOC must care about evidence

Evidence serves more audiences than the courtroom, and most incidents never reach one. The SOC preserves evidence because several later decisions depend on it.

**Scoping and eradication.** The investigation must establish every system and account the attacker touched. If the logs showing the attacker's other footholds have expired, eradication is incomplete and the attacker returns.

**Regulatory reporting.** A report to CERT-In or a data protection notification must state facts: what happened, when it was noticed, what data was affected. Statements that cannot be backed by preserved records are risky to make and hard to defend.

**Impact assessment.** Whether the 48.2 MB upload from WS-104 contained personal or financial data decides much of the legal and business response. Answering it needs the proxy record, the files accessed on WS-104 before 08:12Z and, ideally, forensic analysis of the host.

**Insurance, disputes, discipline and prosecution.** Insurers and counterparties may ask what happened and when the organisation knew; disciplinary or criminal proceedings test evidence against people who want to show it was altered or mishandled.

Because the SOC cannot know at the start which of these will matter, the professional default is to preserve as though any of them might.

## Order of volatility

Not all evidence disappears at the same rate. RFC 3227, *Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving* (2002), sets out an order of volatility for a typical system, from most to least volatile: registers and cache; the routing table, ARP cache, process table, kernel statistics and memory; temporary file systems; disk; remote logging and monitoring data relevant to the system; physical configuration and network topology; and archival media. The principle is simple: collect what will vanish first before collecting what will last.

The order matters to a SOC analyst in two ways. First, it decides what you ask for, and how urgently. If WS-104 is still running, its memory may hold the decoded PowerShell that the process log shows only as `-EncodedCommand <redacted-for-course>`, the beacon's configuration, and network connections at the moment of capture. None of that survives a reboot. The analyst's request to the forensic team, made at the same time as the isolation recommendation, is "capture memory before anything else happens to this host". Second, it decides what you must stop other people doing. A helpful technician who reboots the machine, runs a clean-up tool or reimages it destroys the most volatile evidence first. A clear "do not touch, do not reboot" instruction to the help desk and the user is an evidence-preservation action.

The order also explains why EDR isolation, rather than power-off, is the default containment for a workstation: isolation preserves every layer of the order, while power-off destroys the top layers.
