### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The figure shows the order of volatility as a stack, most volatile at the top, applied to the Banyan incident. It matters because it turns an abstract list into a collection priority: work from the top down, and never take an action that destroys an upper layer before it has been captured.

**Components.** There are six layers, listed top first. **CPU registers and cache** (red) has the sub-label "nanoseconds; only by specialist tools", because it is rarely collected in practice. **Memory, processes, network connections** (red) has "lost at power-off: decoded PowerShell, beacon config". **Temporary file systems** (orange) has "lost at reboot or clean-up". **Disk** (orange) has "invoice.docm, svc_update profile, local logs". **Remote logs: SIEM, proxy, VPN** (blue) has "durable but subject to retention". **Archives and backups** (slate) has "longest-lived". Red marks layers that are gone the moment a host is switched off; orange marks layers that survive power-off but not routine clean-up or reimaging; blue and slate mark the more durable layers held away from the host.

**Relationships and arrows.** The stack has no arrows; position is the relationship. Each layer is more durable than the one above it, so the vertical position is both a durability scale and the collection order.

**Execution flow.** Collection proceeds from the top down. On WS-104 that means memory first (by the forensic team through the EDR channel after isolation), then disk imaging, while the SOC preserves the remote logs in parallel, because they are held on different systems and can be preserved without touching the host.

**Decision logic.** Before any action on a live host, ask which layers it would destroy. Power-off destroys the two red layers; a clean-up tool damages temporary files and disk; reimaging destroys everything on the host. Only the blue and slate layers survive all of these.

**Technical interpretation.** Volatility is about how long data persists without deliberate capture. Memory changes continuously while a system runs and is lost at power-off. Disk content persists but is altered by normal use, which is why imaging tools are designed not to write to the source. Remote logs are durable but bounded by retention periods and storage limits.

**Practical example.** WS-104's Security log was cleared at 08:17Z (event 1102). The local disk layer for that log is therefore damaged, but the remote layer survived: the SIEM had already collected the events, which is why the Banyan timeline still exists. That is the value of the blue layer.

**Security implications.** Attackers know the order too. Clearing local logs, running tools only in memory and deleting files are attacks on the lower and upper layers respectively. Central log collection and quick memory capture are the defences.

**Key learning.** Capture from the top of the stack down, protect the remote logs in parallel, and never let a well-meant reboot or reimage destroy the layers you have not yet collected.

## Integrity: what a hash proves

Once evidence is collected, you must be able to show that it has not changed. The standard tool is a **cryptographic hash**. SHA-256 takes any input and produces a 256-bit digest, written as 64 hexadecimal characters. Two properties make it useful as evidence: any change to the input, even one character, produces a completely different digest; and it is computationally infeasible to construct a different input with the same digest. Recording the digest at collection time and recomputing it later therefore shows whether the item is identical to what was collected.

Be precise about what a matching hash proves. It proves that the file is unchanged **since the hash was recorded**. It does not prove that the file was complete or accurate when it was collected, that the source system's logs were intact, or that the collection query selected the right events. A hash recorded after someone had already edited a file proves only that the edited file is unchanged. This is why the hash must be computed at the moment of collection and recorded somewhere the evidence handler cannot silently alter, and why the custody record also stores how the item was produced.

Older algorithms such as MD5 and SHA-1 have known collision weaknesses and should not be relied on alone for new evidence work; SHA-256 is the common default today.

## Chain of custody

A hash tells you whether an item changed. A **chain of custody** tells you who could have changed it. It is the continuous record of an item's life: who collected it, from which source, by what method, at what time (in UTC), with what hash; where it was stored; and every time it was accessed, copied or transferred, by whom and why. A gap in the chain, such as a period when nobody can say who held the file, invites the argument that the evidence could have been altered in that gap, even if the hash still matches.

In practice a chain of custody record holds, for each item: a unique item identifier and the case number; a description; the source (host, system, query); the collection method and tool; the collector's name; the date and time of collection; the hash and algorithm; the storage location; and a transfer log with dates, names, purpose and the hash verified at each hand-over. In mature SOCs this lives in a case-management system with access control and an audit trail, and the evidence itself is stored on write-once or tightly controlled storage.

## Worked example: preserving the WS-104 log evidence

The course kit's `LAB_ASSETS/C08/evidence_export.py` implements hashing and custody for log evidence in about forty lines. It exports the raw events for one host and time window from the teaching SIEM, writes a SHA-256 manifest and appends a custody entry. The run below was made in a temporary working copy of the kit with CPython 3.14.4 on Windows, using Git for Windows bash for `sha256sum`. Never run lab scripts inside the kit folder itself.

### Step 1: export and verify

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py load
loaded 340 events
$ python evidence_export.py CASE-0001 WS-104
exported 32 events -> evidence\CASE-0001\WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
sha256 8521c97cab10c667d87b01db92fa9c45a5f130dfc314fb49c622eaf1f2919acf
$ cd evidence/CASE-0001
$ cat SHA256SUMS
8521c97cab10c667d87b01db92fa9c45a5f130dfc314fb49c622eaf1f2919acf  WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
$ sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl: OK
$ cat custody.jsonl
{"case": "CASE-0001", "item": "WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl", "sha256": "8521c97cab10c667d87b01db92fa9c45a5f130dfc314fb49c622eaf1f2919acf", "events": 32, "query": {"host": "WS-104", "start": "2026-11-03T06:00:00Z", "end": "2026-11-03T09:00:00Z"}, "action": "exported from minisiem", "by": "analyst.t2", "utc": "2026-11-20T15:47:43Z"}
```

The script takes two arguments, the case identifier and the host; the time window is fixed by its defaults at 06:00Z to 09:00Z on 3 November 2026. It selects the `raw` column (the original JSON of each event, not the parsed fields) with a parameterised query ordered by timestamp, writes the rows to a JSONL file with Unix line endings, hashes the file in 65,536-byte blocks, writes `SHA256SUMS` in the two-space format that `sha256sum -c` expects, and appends one JSON line to `custody.jsonl`. The `-c` option of `sha256sum` reads the manifest, recomputes each listed file's digest and prints `OK` or `FAILED`. The export path prints with backslashes because the run was on Windows. Your digest must match the one above exactly, because the dataset and export are deterministic; only the `utc` field will differ.

Read the custody entry as a colleague would. It names the case and item, gives the digest and event count, records the **exact query parameters** (host and window) so that anyone can re-run the export and compare, says what was done and by whom, and gives the UTC time of the action. The `by` value is hard-coded as `analyst.t2` in this teaching script; a real system takes the identity from the authenticated user.

On Windows without `sha256sum`, PowerShell gives the same digest in upper case:

```terminal
PS> Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 .\WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl | Format-List Algorithm,Hash
Algorithm : SHA256
Hash      : 8521C97CAB10C667D87B01DB92FA9C45A5F130DFC314FB49C622EAF1F2919ACF
```

`-Algorithm SHA256` selects the hash function; `Format-List` prints only the two named properties. Hexadecimal digests are compared case-insensitively.

### Step 2: show that a change is detected

To see what the hash protects against, copy the export and its manifest to a separate folder, change one value in the copy, and verify it:

```terminal
$ cp evidence/CASE-0001/WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl evidence/CASE-0001/SHA256SUMS ../tamper/
$ cd ../tamper
$ sed -i 's/48200000/482000/' WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
$ sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl: FAILED
sha256sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
$ sha256sum WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
3401cb180d5cda71ca8e6a154994b99f1e8f02302295f3a4837f6092a01b4b4f *WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
```

`sed -i` edits the file in place, replacing the upload size of 48,200,000 bytes with 482,000: the kind of change that would turn a 48.2 MB exfiltration into a harmless-looking 0.5 MB transfer. Verification fails, `sha256sum` exits with a non-zero status, and the recomputed digest shares nothing visible with the original. (The `*` before the file name marks binary mode in this build of `sha256sum`.) Always tamper with a copy in a separate folder; never alter the original evidence, even in a lab.

### Step 3: show that the export is reproducible

```terminal
$ python evidence_export.py CASE-0001 WS-104
exported 32 events -> evidence\CASE-0001\WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
sha256 8521c97cab10c667d87b01db92fa9c45a5f130dfc314fb49c622eaf1f2919acf
$ wc -l evidence/CASE-0001/custody.jsonl
2 evidence/CASE-0001/custody.jsonl
```

The second run produces the identical digest, because the query, the ordering and the line endings are fixed, and it appends a second custody line rather than replacing the first. Reproducibility is a strong form of trust: anyone with access to the same SIEM data can re-run the recorded query and obtain the same bytes. Note that the second run also overwrote the export file; a production evidence system would refuse to overwrite an existing item and would instead create a new, separately identified one.

### Step 4: a second item, and a limitation

The Lesson 3 recommendation also covered gopal. Exporting his laptop's events into the same case shows a real limitation of the teaching tool:

```terminal
$ python evidence_export.py CASE-0001 WS-107
exported 10 events -> evidence\CASE-0001\WS-107_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
sha256 1ab3194ca5e6e692dfb9ea7331a969ec47240968555aad3711427edfec4f1868
$ cat evidence/CASE-0001/SHA256SUMS
1ab3194ca5e6e692dfb9ea7331a969ec47240968555aad3711427edfec4f1868  WS-107_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
```

Two lessons follow. First, the manifest now lists **only the WS-107 file**: the script rewrites `SHA256SUMS` on every run instead of appending to it, so the WS-104 digest has disappeared from the manifest. It still exists in `custody.jsonl`, which now has three lines, and that is why the custody log, not the manifest, is the authoritative record here. In practice, keep one manifest entry per item and never let a tool silently replace a previous record. Second, the WS-107 export contains gopal's ordinary proxy and process events, but **not** the suspicious VPN events: VPN records in this dataset carry no host field, so a host-based export cannot select them. Preserving them needs a separate, documented query (for example on `source='vpn'` and `src_ip='203.0.113.66'`), hashed and recorded in the same way. Always check that the export method actually covers the evidence you mean to preserve.

*Figure 8.8: Integrity chain for exported log evidence. How evidence_export.py makes the WS-104 export reproducible, tamper-evident and accountable, and how it is re-verified at every use.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The figure shows how a piece of log evidence becomes trustworthy: from the query that selects it, through hashing and recording, to the verification that anyone can repeat later. It matters because each step answers a different challenge that could be raised against the evidence.

**Components.** There are six steps, top to bottom. **Documented query** (violet) has the sub-label "host WS-104, 06:00Z-09:00Z, raw events": the control step that defines what is collected. **Raw export** (blue) has "WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl, 32 events". **SHA-256 digest** (orange) has "8521c97c...19acf", the key step that fixes the content. **Manifest + custody entry** (green) has "SHA256SUMS; custody.jsonl: who, when, query". **Store and transfer** (slate) has "restricted or write-once storage; log every hand-over". **Re-hash and compare** (dark) has "OK = unchanged; FAILED = altered copy", the outcome on which trust rests.

**Relationships and arrows.** Each downward arrow means "the output of this step is the input to the next". The query determines the export; the export's bytes determine the digest; the digest is written into both the manifest and the custody record; the stored item is later re-hashed and compared with the recorded digest. The dashed loop arrow labelled "every hand-over and every use" returns from the last step to **Store and transfer**, because verification is repeated each time the item moves or is used.

**Execution flow.** Steps one to four happen once, at collection time, in seconds. Steps five and six repeat for the life of the evidence.

**Decision logic.** The final step has two outcomes. **OK** means the item is identical to what was collected and can be used. **FAILED** means it is not; the copy is set aside, the discrepancy is recorded, and a verified copy is obtained from storage or the export is re-run from the documented query.

**Technical interpretation.** The query step gives reproducibility, the digest gives integrity, the custody record gives accountability, and controlled storage limits who could have changed the item. Remove any one and a challenge succeeds: without the query no one can reproduce the export; without the digest no one can detect alteration; without custody no one can say who held it.

**Practical example.** In the lab, the original verified **OK**, the copy with 48200000 changed to 482000 returned **FAILED**, and a re-run of the documented query gave the identical digest. The WS-107 run showed why the custody entry, not the overwritten manifest, carries the record.

**Security implications.** The chain begins at the SIEM, so it inherits the SIEM's integrity: if events were lost or altered before ingestion, a perfect hash of the export will not reveal it. Protecting the collection pipeline and the SIEM's own storage is part of evidence preservation.

**Key learning.** Query, export, hash, record, store and re-verify: each link answers a different challenge, and the custody record ties them together.

## Log preservation

For a SOC, logs are the evidence most directly under its control, and the most often lost to routine operation rather than to attackers. Retention periods expire, indexes are rolled over, endpoint logs overwrite themselves when they reach their size limit, and cloud platforms keep some activity logs for limited periods by default. An investigation that starts days after the intrusion can find that the first and most revealing events have already gone.

Log preservation therefore starts at the first sign of an incident and runs in parallel with containment. Its steps are:

1. **Identify the sources** that cover the incident: for Banyan, Sysmon and Windows Security events from WS-104, proxy logs for the three domains, VPN logs for 203.0.113.66 and gopal, and identity platform sign-in logs for divya and gopal.
2. **Export the relevant records** with integrity and custody, as in the worked example, so that they no longer depend on retention.
3. **Extend or suspend retention** on the source systems for the affected period, through the SIEM's index management or the platform's retention settings, so that the wider data set remains available for scoping.
4. **Protect the copies** on restricted or write-once storage.
5. **Record clock information** for each source (time zone and any known offset), because timelines built from several sources are only as good as their clocks (Module 2).

The Banyan case shows why central collection matters. The attacker cleared the Security log on WS-104 at 08:17Z. Locally, that destroyed the record of what had happened. Centrally, the events had already been collected, and the clearing itself was logged as event 1102, which became one of the strongest indicators in the case. Anti-forensic actions on a host are far less effective against an organisation that collects its logs elsewhere promptly.

In India, the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 require service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government organisations to maintain logs of their ICT systems securely for a rolling period of 180 days within Indian jurisdiction. That baseline is a minimum: a case may need specific logs preserved for much longer than routine retention.

## Legal hold

A **legal hold** (also called a litigation hold or preservation notice) is a formal instruction, normally issued by legal counsel, that information relevant to actual or reasonably anticipated litigation, regulatory investigation or dispute must be preserved, and that normal deletion, rotation and clean-up must be suspended for it. It applies to every form of the information: logs, emails, chat messages, tickets, case notes, disk images and backups.

The SOC's part in a legal hold is practical. Legal decides whether a hold is needed and what it covers; the SOC and IT operations implement it on the systems they run. That means identifying where the relevant data lives, stopping automated deletion for it (retention policies, mailbox clean-up, log rotation, scheduled reimaging of devices), confirming in writing that this has been done, and keeping the hold in place until legal releases it. A hold also binds the SOC's own records: the case notes, chat logs and tickets of the investigation itself may fall within it.

Two misunderstandings cause trouble. The first is waiting for a hold before preserving anything: the SOC's own evidence preservation should start at once, and a hold formalises and extends it. The second is assuming a hold is a technical setting; it is a legal obligation, and failure to honour it can have serious consequences in proceedings.

## Electronic evidence in Indian law

In India, electronic records are admissible as evidence under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 with effect from 1 July 2024. Section 63 of the new Act governs the admissibility of electronic records and, like section 65B of the old Act that it replaces, provides for a certificate accompanying the electronic record. Course 01 Module 7 notes that the prescribed certificate format refers to hash values; that detail, and how the certificate applies in a given case, is for legal advisers to determine. For the SOC analyst, the practical implication is clear: records exported with a documented method, a recorded hash and a complete custody record are exactly the material such a certificate needs, while records copied informally are not.

> [!CAUTION]
> The SOC preserves and documents evidence; it does not decide its legal sufficiency. Questions of admissibility, certification and disclosure belong to legal counsel.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"We will collect evidence after containment."** Containment chosen without evidence in mind (power-off, reimage) destroys the most volatile layers. Request memory capture with the isolation recommendation.
- **"The hash proves the evidence is genuine."** It proves the item is unchanged since the hash was recorded, nothing more. Completeness depends on the query and the source's integrity.
- **"The SIEM keeps everything."** Retention expires. Export case evidence and extend retention for the affected period.
- **"Screenshots are evidence."** A screenshot of a query result is a picture of evidence. Preserve the underlying records with a hash and custody entry.
- **"The manifest is the record."** As the WS-107 run showed, a tool can overwrite a manifest; the custody record, kept append-only, carries the history.
- **"Tidy up the analyst's working files."** Case notes and working copies may fall under a legal hold. Do not delete them until the case's retention rules allow it.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Evidence systems are targets. An attacker with administrative access may clear logs, as at Banyan, stop logging agents, or tamper with stored data. Defences include forwarding logs off the host promptly, alerting on log clearing and agent stoppage (event 1102 is a high-value detection, and the course's `rk_security_log_cleared.yml` rule detects it), storing evidence on write-once storage with tightly limited access, and keeping the custody record in a system with its own audit trail. Access to evidence stores should itself be logged and reviewed: an unexplained access is a break in the chain of custody.

Evidence also contains sensitive data. The WS-104 export holds user names, internal addresses and browsing history; a full disk image may hold personal data of customers. Preserved evidence must therefore be protected like any sensitive data set: encrypted at rest, shared on a need-to-know basis, and deleted when the case's retention period ends, in line with the DPDP Act's data protection obligations where personal data is involved.

## Best practices

- Preserve from the first hour, in order of volatility, in parallel with containment.
- Issue a clear "do not reboot, do not clean, do not reimage" instruction to the help desk and the user.
- Export raw records with a documented query, hash them with SHA-256 at collection time, and record a custody entry for every item.
- Verify the hash at every hand-over and before every use; record each verification.
- Keep custody records append-only, one entry per item and action, with UTC times.
- Extend retention for the affected sources and period; implement legal holds promptly when legal issues them.
- Record clock sources and offsets for every log source used in a timeline.

## Key takeaways

- Evidence must stay available, unchanged and explainable: order of volatility, hashing and chain of custody deliver those three properties.
- Collect from the most volatile layer down; isolation preserves every layer, power-off and reimaging destroy the top ones.
- A SHA-256 match proves an item is unchanged since its hash was recorded, not that it was complete; the documented query supplies reproducibility.
- In the lab, the export verified OK, a one-value change FAILED, a re-run reproduced the digest, and a second item exposed a manifest that is overwritten rather than appended.
- Preserve logs before retention removes them, implement legal holds when legal issues them, and leave admissibility questions (Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, section 63) to legal counsel.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Module 5 taught you to rate an *alert*: how much harm the detected behaviour would cause if the alert is true, how a rule's base severity becomes an alert severity, and how linked alerts produce a case severity. That lesson ended at a doorway. Once a case is confirmed as an incident, the question changes from "how bad is this behaviour?" to "how bad is this incident for the organisation, and how hard should we respond?". This lesson walks through that doorway.

An incident severity is not a bigger alert severity. It is a different kind of statement, made by a different person, for a different audience. The alert severity helps an analyst choose what to look at next. The incident severity decides who is woken up, whether an incident commander is appointed, whether executives and legal are briefed, how often status updates go out, how much disruption the organisation will accept to stop the attacker, and how the incident will be counted in next quarter's metrics. Because so much hangs on it, it has to be produced by a method that two incident leads on different nights would apply the same way. That method is the **severity matrix**.

A severity matrix combines three questions:

1. **Impact**: what has the incident done, or what is it reasonably shown to be doing, to the organisation's services, information and ability to recover?
2. **Scope**: how much of the organisation is involved: one host or account, a team, or a critical service and many systems?
3. **Urgency**: how much time is there before further harm happens, and is the attacker still active?

Module 5 Lesson 1 introduced the three impact questions (functional, information, recoverability) as a checklist. Here you turn the checklist into a defined scale, combine it with scope in a matrix, add urgency and floor rules, and apply the method to the Banyan incident, at the moment it was noticed and at each earlier stage.

> [!NOTE]
> The Banyan severity matrix in this lesson is a teaching design for the course's fictional SOC, not a published standard. Real organisations write their own, and the structure shown here (impact levels, scope bands, urgency, floor rules) is what you should look for when you read one. All data comes from the synthetic `banyan_events.jsonl` in `LAB_ASSETS/C08/`. The time the SOC noticed the incident (08:25Z) is the illustrative time used in Module 5 Lesson 6; the dataset itself contains events, not SOC activity.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Incident severity | The organisation's rating of how serious a confirmed incident is, which sets the scale and tempo of the response. Owned by the incident lead. |
| Severity matrix | A documented table that derives a base severity from an impact level and a scope band, so that the same facts always give the same rating. |
| Functional impact | The effect on the organisation's ability to deliver its services and business functions. |
| Information impact | The effect on the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information, especially personal, financial or proprietary data. |
| Recoverability | The effort, resources and time needed to return to normal operations, and whether full recovery is possible at all. |
| Impact level | One value (1-4 in the Banyan playbook) that summarises the three impact dimensions, taken as the highest of the three. |
| Scope | The breadth of the incident: the number of hosts, accounts, teams or services involved, and whether a critical service is among them. |
| Urgency | The time pressure: whether harm is ongoing or imminent, or the incident is contained and only recovery remains. |
| Floor rule | A rule that sets a minimum severity for a defined situation (for example confirmed attacker access) regardless of the matrix result. |
| Severity of record | The highest severity the incident reached. It is the value used for reporting, metrics and the post-incident review, and does not fall after containment. |
| Operating severity | The severity currently driving staffing and update cadence. It may fall after verified containment, with a recorded reason. |
| Reasonable worst case | The most serious interpretation that the evidence actually supports, used when a fact (such as the content of an upload) is not yet known. |

## Why incidents need their own severity

Consider three situations a Banyan analyst could face in one week. A phishing email reaches thirty mailboxes, and two people click; their browsers are blocked by the proxy and no code runs. A developer's laptop is found running a cryptocurrency miner. A payments approver's workstation shows a macro-launched PowerShell, a new administrator account, a 48.2 MB upload to an unfamiliar site and a cleared Security log. All three are true positives that High alerts could have produced, yet they deserve a mail clean-up, a rebuild, and a full response with legal and executives respectively.

Alert severity cannot make that distinction, for three reasons.

**It describes one behaviour, not the incident.** The phishing wave touches thirty mailboxes but stops at the click; the Banyan workstation touches one host but reaches the attacker's objectives.

**It is set before the investigation.** Incident severity is revised as scoping, forensics and the business reveal which data the host held, whether the account was used elsewhere and whether a process has stopped.

**It answers a different audience.** An executive, a legal adviser or a regulator needs to know what the organisation has lost or might lose, so the scale is defined by consequences for the organisation rather than by detection logic.

The incident lead (sometimes called the incident commander) owns the incident severity. The analyst proposes a rating with reasons, because the analyst knows the evidence best, but the decision belongs to the person accountable for the response. This mirrors the separation of roles in Module 5 Lesson 6, where the analyst flags reportability and the designated point of contact decides it.

## The three impact dimensions in depth

NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 (2012), the long-standing *Computer Security Incident Handling Guide*, described three factors for prioritising incidents and gave each a small set of categories. Revision 3 (April 2025) reorganised incident response guidance around the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and does not prescribe these tables, but the categories remain widely used in playbooks because they are short, consequence-based and easy to apply. The Banyan playbook adopts them and maps each to a number from 1 to 4.

### Functional impact

Functional impact asks what the incident has done to the organisation's ability to work. NIST's categories run from **None** (no effect on the ability to provide services) through **Low** (all critical services are still provided to all users, but with lost efficiency) and **Medium** (a critical service cannot be provided to a subset of users) to **High** (some critical services can no longer be provided to any users).

Two points need care. First, the impact of the *response* counts: if the isolated workstation is the one from which payments are approved, that function is degraded until a workaround exists. Record both the attacker's impact and the response's. Second, functional impact is the easiest dimension to observe and the easiest to over-weight; quiet data theft often has none at all.

### Information impact

Information impact asks what has happened to data. NIST's categories are **None** (no information was exfiltrated, changed, deleted or otherwise compromised), **Privacy breach** (sensitive personally identifiable information was accessed or exfiltrated), **Proprietary breach** (unclassified proprietary information, such as protected critical infrastructure information, was accessed or exfiltrated) and **Integrity loss** (sensitive or proprietary information was changed or deleted).

The Banyan playbook turns these into levels by sensitivity and by how strongly the evidence shows that data was affected:

| Level | Banyan definition |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | No evidence that information was accessed, changed or removed. |
| 2 | Information was exposed to the attacker (for example an attacker session on a system holding data) but there is no evidence of removal or change. |
| 3 | Information of limited sensitivity was removed or changed, or removal of sensitive data is possible but weakly evidenced. |
| 4 | Personal, financial or proprietary information was removed or changed, confirmed or strongly indicated by the evidence. |

At Banyan Microfinance, a lender, personal data about borrowers and financial records sit on many systems. A privacy breach also brings in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, under which personal data breaches must be intimated to the Data Protection Board and to affected individuals; the timing and content are for legal and the data protection function to determine. The analyst's job is to state what the evidence shows about which data may be involved, as precisely as possible.

### Recoverability

Recoverability asks how hard the way back will be. NIST's categories are **Regular** (recovery time is predictable with existing resources), **Supplemented** (predictable with additional resources), **Extended** (unpredictable; additional resources and outside help are needed) and **Not recoverable** (recovery is not possible, for example when sensitive data has been exfiltrated and published; the organisation can only investigate and manage the consequences).

Recoverability is where evidence destruction and attacker persistence show up. A host whose Security log was cleared, which carries a new administrator account and which has been talking to an external server, cannot be "cleaned" with confidence; it must be rebuilt, and the question of what else the attacker touched may need forensic help. Data that has left the organisation can never be recalled. Both push recoverability towards Extended or Not recoverable, even when the number of affected systems is small. The Banyan playbook maps the four categories directly to levels 1 to 4.

### One impact level, not three added together

The Banyan playbook takes the **highest** of the three levels as the incident's impact level. It does not add or average them. The reason is simple: an incident that is catastrophic on one dimension and harmless on the others is still catastrophic. A ransomware attack that encrypts every server but steals nothing (functional 4, information 1, recoverability 3) should not be rated lower than a moderate incident that scores 3 on everything. Averaging would hide the dimension that matters; adding would make scores depend on how many dimensions happen to be touched rather than on how bad the worst one is.

The impact levels are named to keep conversation precise: **Severe (4)**, **Significant (3)**, **Limited (2)** and **Minimal (1)**.

## Scope and urgency

### Scope

Scope measures breadth: how much of the organisation the incident reaches. The Banyan playbook uses three bands.

- **Contained**: one host, or one account, or one host and the account that uses it.
- **Several**: two to ten hosts or accounts, or the systems of a single team or department.
- **Widespread**: a critical business service (core banking, the payments platform, email for everyone, the identity provider), or more than ten hosts or accounts, or several departments.

Scope is not the same as impact. A single compromised domain controller is narrow in host count but, because it controls identity for everyone, it is treated as Widespread; the playbook lists such systems by name so that the decision does not depend on the analyst's memory. Scope is also the dimension most likely to grow during an investigation. The first host is where the SOC noticed the attacker, not necessarily where the attacker started or stopped, and every scoping hunt (for the same indicators, the same technique, the same account) can move the band.

### Urgency

Urgency measures time pressure. It is the dimension that separates "serious, and we have days" from "serious, and every minute counts".

- **Immediate**: harm is happening now or is expected within hours. Examples: an attacker session or beacon is live, data is being moved, files are being encrypted, an attacker holds privileged access that has not been revoked.
- **Pressing**: the attacker may still have access, but no current activity is observed and further harm is expected over days rather than hours.
- **Deferred**: the incident is contained and containment has been verified; what remains is eradication, recovery and review.

In the Banyan playbook, **Immediate** urgency raises the base severity by one level (to SEV1 at most). **Pressing** leaves it unchanged. **Deferred** never lowers the severity of record; it may only lower the *operating* severity, which governs staffing and the frequency of updates, and only with a recorded reason. Lesson 6 explains why the peak value must survive: a post-incident review that sees "SEV3, closed" for an incident that was SEV1 for six hours will draw the wrong conclusions about detection and response.

Urgency is not the reporting deadline. The CERT-In six-hour clock (Directions of 28 April 2022) runs whatever the severity; it belongs on the task list with an owner, not in the rating.

### Floor rules

A matrix built from impact and scope under-rates an attacker who holds access but has done no visible damage yet, such as a VPN session obtained by password spraying. Floor rules fix this by setting a minimum. The Banyan playbook has three:

1. Confirmed attacker execution on a host or confirmed attacker use of valid credentials: **at least SEV2**.
2. Destructive or extortion activity (encryption, wiping, a ransom note): **SEV1**.
3. A possible personal data breach: **at least SEV2**, so that legal and the data protection function are engaged early.

Floor rules are deliberately few. Each one is a judgment the organisation has made in advance, in calm conditions, so that nobody has to argue it at three in the morning.

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The diagram shows the derivation of an incident severity as a small pipeline with defined inputs. It matters because an incident severity that cannot be traced back to its inputs is an opinion, and opinions differ between shifts, between people and under pressure. With the pipeline, a reviewer can ask "which input moved this incident to SEV1?" and get an answer.

**Components.** The top row holds three blue boxes, the facts gathered by investigation: **Functional impact** ("none / low / medium / high"), **Information impact** ("none / privacy / proprietary / integrity") and **Recoverability** ("regular / supplemented / extended / not recoverable"). Their sub-labels are the NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 categories. The second row holds the orange **Impact level** ("highest of the three, 1-4"), the slate **Scope** ("contained / several / widespread"), the red **Urgency** ("immediate / pressing / deferred") and the violet **Floor rules** ("e.g. confirmed attacker access: at least SEV2"). Below them is the violet **Base SEV from the matrix** ("impact x scope"), and at the bottom the dark box **Incident severity of record** ("SEV1-SEV4, owned by the IR lead").

**Relationships and arrows.** The three blue boxes all point into Impact level: they are reduced to one value, and the sub-label says how (the highest, not the sum). Impact level and Scope both point into Base SEV, which is the matrix lookup shown in the next figure. Base SEV points into the severity of record, and two further arrows modify it: Urgency, labelled **adjust by one level**, and Floor rules, labelled **never below**.

**Execution flow.** Investigation answers the three impact questions; the highest answer becomes the impact level; the matrix combines that with scope into a base severity; urgency raises it by one level if harm is immediate; and finally the floor rules are checked, so that the result is never below the minimum they set. The incident lead records the outcome with the inputs that produced it.

**Decision logic.** Each box is a decision with a small set of defined answers, which is what makes the method repeatable. Two asymmetries are built in. Urgency can raise the severity of record but never lower it. Floor rules can only raise the result. Both protect against the most dangerous failure, under-rating, while the "highest of three" reduction protects against an incident being diluted by its harmless dimensions.

**Technical interpretation.** The pipeline separates *what has happened* (impact and scope) from *how fast we must move* (urgency) and from *policy decided in advance* (floor rules, hence violet). When a fact changes, only its box is revisited.

**Practical example.** For the WS-104 case at 08:25Z, investigation answers functional Low, information 4 (a 48,200,000-byte upload from a payments approver's machine to an unfamiliar domain) and recoverability Extended (cleared log, new administrator account). The impact level is therefore Severe. Scope is Contained (one host, one user). The matrix gives SEV2; urgency is Immediate because the attacker's administrator account still exists and the host is not isolated, so the severity of record becomes SEV1.

**Security implications.** A traceable derivation resists two pressures: the pressure to downgrade an incident because a high rating is inconvenient, and the pressure to upgrade every incident to the top so that it gets attention. Both destroy the meaning of the scale. Recording the inputs is also what makes the post-incident review of severity decisions possible.

**Key learning.** Incident severity is derived, not felt: the worst of three impacts, combined with scope in a matrix, raised by urgency and protected by floor rules, with every input recorded.

## The matrix

The base severity comes from a single lookup. Rows are impact levels, columns are scope bands, and each cell holds the severity before urgency and floor rules are applied. The figure shows the Banyan matrix with the two Banyan cases placed where their 08:25Z assessments put them.

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The table is the heart of the method: the place where impact and breadth meet. It matters because it makes the trade-off between "how bad" and "how wide" explicit and fixed in advance. Without it, one incident lead would treat a severe single-host incident as the top level and another would reserve the top level for estate-wide events, and the organisation's severity statistics would mean nothing.

**Components.** The first column, **Impact level**, lists the four levels from the top: **Severe (4)** in red, **Significant (3)** in orange, **Limited (2)** in blue and **Minimal (1)** in slate. The other three columns are the scope bands: **Contained (1 host or account)**, **Several (2-10 or one team)** and **Widespread (critical service or many)**. Each cell is a base severity from SEV1 (most serious) to SEV4. Three cells carry markers for the worked example: **SEV2 (CASE-0001 base)** in the Severe row under Contained, **SEV1 (if CASE-0002 merges)** in the Severe row under Several, and **SEV4 (CASE-0002 base)** in the Limited row under Contained. The note under the table restates the adjustments: Immediate urgency raises one level, floor rules set a minimum, and a contained incident keeps its peak severity of record.

**Relationships.** There are no arrows; the relationships are positional. Moving down a column lowers severity as impact falls; moving right along a row raises it as scope widens. The diagonal is deliberate: a Severe incident on one host (SEV2) equals a Significant one across a team.

**Execution flow.** Find the row from the impact level, find the column from the scope band, read the base severity, then apply urgency and floor rules as in the previous figure. For CASE-0001: Severe row, Contained column, SEV2; Immediate urgency raises it to SEV1.

**Decision logic.** The matrix contains no "maybe" cells. Uncertainty is handled before the lookup, by rating each input on the reasonable worst case the evidence supports and recording the confidence. The markers show the most important decision the incident lead will make about the Banyan incident: whether CASE-0002 belongs to the same incident. If it does, scope moves from Contained to Several, and the Severe row gives SEV1 even before urgency is considered.

**Technical interpretation.** No cell in the Minimal row reaches SEV2 and no cell in the Severe row is below SEV2. That bounds the influence of scope: breadth alone cannot make a trivial incident serious (a phishing wave that stopped at the proxy stays low however many mailboxes it reached), and narrowness alone cannot make a severe one minor.

**Practical example.** CASE-0002, the password spray followed by a VPN login as gopal at 06:46:00Z, has no observed information or functional impact in the dataset and a regular recovery, so it sits at Limited and Contained: SEV4. The marker reminds the reader that this is only the base value; the floor rule for confirmed attacker use of valid credentials lifts it to at least SEV2 as soon as gopal confirms the login was not his.

**Security implications.** Publishing the matrix inside the SOC and to stakeholders makes severity predictable, and predictability is what lets people act on a severity without debating it. It also invites criticism in calm times: "a payments approver's machine leaking data should always be SEV1" is an argument for a floor rule, settled once.

**Key learning.** Read the base severity from impact and scope, then adjust; the markers show that the biggest severity decision is often a scoping decision, not an impact one.

## Worked example: the Banyan incident at 08:25Z

At 08:25Z, the illustrative time the SOC noticed the R5 alert, the analyst has the WS-104 timeline from the earlier modules and the separate VPN finding. Every value below is tied to an event in the dataset.

| Input | CASE-0001 (WS-104, divya) | CASE-0002 (VPN, gopal) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Key evidence | 06:12:00Z `invoice.docm` from `banyan-payroll-update.example`; 06:14:00Z Word started hidden encoded PowerShell; 06:17:00Z-07:42:02Z 18 requests of 220 bytes to `cdn-telemetry-sync.example`; 07:02:00Z `svc_update` created, 07:03:00Z added to Administrators; 08:12:00Z upload of 48,200,000 bytes to `files-share-drop.example`; 08:17:00Z Security log cleared | 06:42:00Z-06:42:49Z eight users fail once each from `203.0.113.66`; 06:46:00Z VPN success as gopal from the same address, country `??` |
| Functional | Low (2): one workstation; isolation will interrupt payment approvals until a workaround exists | None (1): no service affected |
| Information | 4: data removal strongly indicated from a payments approver's machine; content unknown | 2: an attacker session existed; the dataset holds no activity from it |
| Recoverability | Extended (3): log cleared, persistence, rebuild and forensic help needed | Regular (1): reset password, revoke session and tokens |
| Impact level | Severe (4) | Limited (2) |
| Scope | Contained (one host, one user) | Contained (one account) |
| Base SEV | SEV2 | SEV4 |
| Urgency | Immediate: administrator account still present, host not isolated, attacker active until at least 08:17Z | Immediate until the session is confirmed ended and revoked |
| Floor rules | Rule 1 (confirmed execution) and rule 3 (possible personal data breach): at least SEV2 | Rule 1 applies once gopal confirms the login was not his |

In the CASE-0001 column the functional answer is honest (no service has stopped), and the information answer carries the weight on the reasonable worst case. Nobody yet knows what the 48,200,000 bytes contained, but an attacker in control of a payments approver's session, a fresh administrator account, an upload to a never-used domain and a cleared log strongly indicate data theft. The analyst records "content unknown; reasonable worst case; confidence moderate". If forensics later cleared the upload, the information value would be revised, but the severity of record would still truthfully show SEV1.

Recoverability is rated Extended rather than Not recoverable: there is no sign of publication or extortion at 08:25Z, and the host can be rebuilt. A reviewer could argue for the higher level, but it would not change the result, because the impact is already Severe from the information dimension.

The CASE-0002 column shows why floor rules exist. The matrix alone gives SEV4, yet the spray pattern (eight users, one attempt each, seven seconds apart, then one success) strongly suggests an attacker holds gopal's password. Until gopal confirms by phone that the session was not his, the case stands at SEV3 with Immediate urgency; after that, the floor rule lifts it to SEV2.

### The merge decision

The two cases are linked by timing only: the spray began at 06:42:00Z, 28 minutes after the PowerShell on WS-104, and one of the failed accounts was divya's, tried at 06:42:21Z while she was logged on at WS-104. That is suggestive, not proof. Running them as one incident moves scope to Several and the base severity to SEV1; running them as linked incidents keeps CASE-0002 a separate SEV2. Either is defensible if recorded. Ignoring the link is not: containing WS-104 alone would warn an operator who still holds a VPN identity, so containment for both is planned together.

## Severity changes over time

Incident severity is not set once. It rises as evidence arrives and, for the operating severity only, falls after verified containment. The Banyan dataset lets you see what the matrix would have produced at each stage if the SOC had been working each alert as the matching event occurred. This is a retrospective exercise: in the scenario nobody looked until 08:25Z, and Lesson 6 examines why.

| Time (UTC) | New evidence | Assessment | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 06:14:00 | R1: Word starts hidden encoded PowerShell on WS-104 | Information 2, recoverability 2 (rebuild), impact Limited, Contained: SEV4; Immediate: SEV3; floor rule 1 (confirmed execution) | SEV2 |
| 06:46:00 | R2: VPN success as gopal after a spray (separate case) | As CASE-0002 above | SEV3, SEV2 on confirmation |
| 07:03:00 | R3: `svc_update` created and added to Administrators | Recoverability 3 (persistence), impact Significant, Contained: SEV3; Immediate: SEV2 | SEV2 |
| 08:12:00 | R4: 48,200,000 bytes uploaded to `files-share-drop.example` | Information 4, impact Severe, Contained: SEV2; Immediate | SEV1 |
| 08:17:00 | R5: Security log cleared | Recoverability already 3; confirms attacker privilege and intent | SEV1 |
| After verified containment | Host isolated, accounts disabled, sessions revoked | Urgency Deferred: operating severity may fall to SEV2; severity of record stays SEV1 | SEV1 of record |

Three lessons follow. The incident was SEV2 from its first alert, so a SOC that took R1 at 06:14 would have run a SEV2 response nearly two hours before the data left. SEV1 arrived with the upload, the first irreversible harm. And staffing can relax after containment, but the record keeps the peak.

## Severity, reportability and communication

Severity and reportability are separate decisions made by different people. Severity is the incident lead's judgment of seriousness; reportability is the designated point of contact's and legal's judgment of whether a legal obligation applies. They are correlated but not the same. A SEV3 incident can be reportable to CERT-In if its type is on the list in the Directions, and a SEV1 outage caused by a non-malicious failure may not be a cyber incident at all. The analyst's contribution to both is the same: accurate facts, the time noticed, and an early flag. Coupling them ("we only consider reporting for SEV1") is a design error that can make an organisation miss a six-hour deadline.

Severity is also a communication device. Each level should carry its consequences in writing (who is paged, whether a bridge opens, the update cadence), and every status update should give the severity, a one-line reason and what would change it, so the rating stays a hypothesis under test.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Record every severity change with the time, the person, the old and new values, the inputs that changed and the reason. This is the incident-level version of the reclassification record from Module 5, and it is the raw material for the post-incident review in Lesson 6.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

**"Incident severity is the highest alert severity in the case."** The WS-104 case contains no alert above base severity 4 (High), yet the incident is SEV1. Incident severity comes from consequences for the organisation, assessed across the whole case.

**"Count the hosts."** One payments approver's workstation leaking data outranks a dozen kiosks with adware.

**"Wait until we know what was taken."** Forensics may take days. Rating on the reasonable worst case the evidence supports, with the confidence recorded, lets the response start at the right scale; waiting for certainty means responding late.

**"Downgrade after containment."** Lowering the severity of record makes the incident look smaller in every later report. Lower the operating severity if staffing allows, and keep the peak on record.

**"Severity decides reportability."** Reportability depends on the incident type and the law, assessed by the point of contact and legal; it must be considered for every confirmed incident.

**"Add up the scores."** Summing functional, information and recoverability scores rewards incidents that touch many dimensions mildly and dilutes ones that are catastrophic on one. Take the highest.

## Security implications, detection and defence

A severity matrix is a control on the response itself. Its job is to make sure that serious incidents receive serious responses quickly and that the organisation's attention is not exhausted by minor ones. It fails in predictable ways. **Inflation**: if every incident is SEV1, executives stop reading the updates, and the one that matters is lost. **Suppression**: if a high severity brings unwelcome scrutiny, people learn to find reasons to rate lower; the recorded inputs and a review of severity decisions in every post-incident review are the defence. **Stale inputs**: the playbook's list of critical services and the data held on each system must be maintained, or scope and information impact will be rated from memory.

Slow severity decisions help attackers. The Banyan operator moved from execution to persistence in 48 minutes and on to clearing the log in 74; an hour of debate gives away a stage of the intrusion.

## Best practices

- Write the matrix, the level definitions, the urgency rules and the floor rules into the incident response playbook, with examples from your own estate, and review them after every SEV1 and SEV2.
- Name critical services and the systems that hold personal or financial data in the playbook, so scope and information impact are looked up rather than remembered.
- Rate every input on the reasonable worst case the evidence supports, and write the confidence and the open question beside it.
- Keep severity of record and operating severity as separate fields; never overwrite the peak.
- Assess reportability separately for every confirmed incident.

## Key takeaways

- Incident severity is the organisation's rating of a confirmed incident; it is owned by the incident lead and sets the scale and tempo of the response, unlike alert severity, which orders an analyst's queue.
- Impact has three dimensions (functional, information, recoverability, with the NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 categories as a well-known scale); the impact level is the highest of the three, never the sum.
- The matrix combines impact with scope; urgency raises the result by one level when harm is immediate, and floor rules set minimums for situations such as confirmed attacker access.
- Rate unknowns on the reasonable worst case the evidence supports and record the confidence; revise as facts arrive, but keep the peak as the severity of record.
- For Banyan, CASE-0001 is Severe and Contained (SEV2 base) with Immediate urgency, giving SEV1; CASE-0002 is SEV4 by the matrix but at least SEV2 by floor rule once the login is confirmed as not gopal's; merging them would make scope Several.
- Severity and reportability are separate decisions; every confirmed incident needs both, and the time noticed travels with each.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

An incident is not finished when the attacker is removed and the systems are rebuilt. Until the organisation has understood why the incident happened, why it was not stopped sooner and what will change, the same weaknesses are still in place, waiting for the next operator who finds them. The **post-incident review** (also called a lessons-learned review, retrospective or post-mortem) is the structured process that turns one bad day into lasting improvement.

The idea is old and well established. NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 made "post-incident activity" the final phase of its incident response lifecycle and recommended a lessons-learned meeting after major incidents. Revision 3 (April 2025) places incident response inside the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, where improvement is a standing activity of the Identify function (the Improvement category) informed by incidents, tests and exercises, rather than a phase that happens once at the end. The two views agree on the essential point: an incident that produces no change was paid for and wasted.

A good review produces four things:

1. **A reconstructed timeline** that everyone accepts as the factual record: what the attacker did, what the defenders saw, decided and did, and when.
2. **An analysis of causes**: the root cause that started the incident and the contributing factors that let it go as far as it did.
3. **Actions**: specific changes, each with one owner, a due date and a way to check that it was done and worked.
4. **Metrics**: measured intervals (dwell time, time to notice, time to acknowledge, time to contain) that show how the response performed and allow comparison over time.

All four depend on one cultural condition: the review must be **blameless**. People will only describe their real decisions, including their mistakes, if describing them is safe. A review that hunts for someone to blame learns only what people are willing to admit.

This lesson builds all four outputs for the Banyan incident, CASE-0001, using the synthetic dataset in `LAB_ASSETS/C08/`. Lesson 5 established that the incident was SEV1 of record; here you ask why it reached that point, measure the response with timestamps taken from the data, and write the actions that would make the next attempt fail earlier.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Post-incident review | A structured examination of an incident after it is contained, producing a timeline, causal analysis, actions and metrics. |
| Blameless review | A review that treats errors as products of the system people worked in, and asks why decisions made sense at the time rather than who is at fault. |
| Timeline reconstruction | Building one ordered, sourced record of attacker activity and defender activity, in UTC, from logs, case notes and interviews. |
| Root cause | The earliest point in the chain where a change under the organisation's control would have prevented the incident from starting. |
| Contributing factor | A condition that did not start the incident but allowed it to progress further, last longer or cause more harm. |
| Action item | A specific change with one owner, a due date and a verification method, recorded in a tracker. |
| Dwell time | The time an attacker was active before the organisation noticed: from the first malicious event to the time noticed. |
| Time noticed | The moment the organisation first became aware of the incident; also the start of the CERT-In six-hour reporting clock. |
| Hindsight bias | The tendency, once the outcome is known, to believe the warning signs were obvious at the time. |
| Detection opportunity | An event that an existing rule matched or could have matched, at which the incident could have been noticed earlier. |

## Blameless review: why and how

### Why blame defeats learning

Imagine the Banyan review opening with the question "Why did divya open the document?" The answer is already known, it is uncomfortable, and it leads nowhere useful: the next person will open the next convincing document, because opening invoices is part of a payments approver's job. Worse, every participant now knows what the meeting is for. The Tier 1 analyst who worked the queue in priority order, and therefore reached the R5 alert only at 08:25, will describe the shift in the most defensive terms possible. The detection engineer who rated the beacon rule R6 at severity 2 will explain why that was reasonable rather than examine it. The review ends with a warning to staff and an unchanged system.

The blameless approach, borrowed from aviation safety, healthcare and site reliability engineering, starts from a different assumption: people generally make decisions that seem reasonable given what they know, the tools they have and the pressures on them at the time. If a reasonable person made a decision that turned out badly, the useful question is what about the situation made that decision reasonable. Change the situation and you change the decision for everyone, not just for the person who happened to be there.

### What blameless does not mean

Blameless does not mean that nothing was wrong, that no-one is responsible for improvement, or that deliberate misconduct is ignored. Accountability moves from the past to the future: each action has a named owner who is accountable for delivering it. Deliberate wrongdoing, such as an insider who disabled logging on purpose, is a matter for a separate disciplinary or legal process and should be taken out of the review, not mixed into it.

### Practices that make it work

- **Ask "how" and "what", not "why did you".** "What did the queue look like at 07:00?" and "What information did you have when you chose the next alert?" produce facts. "Why didn't you look at R1?" produces defence.
- **Reconstruct the local view.** For each decision, record what the person could see at the time, not what the timeline shows now. This is the direct antidote to hindsight bias.
- **Name systems, roles and controls, not people, in findings.** "The queue ordered R6 last" rather than "the analyst ignored the beacon".
- **Use a facilitator who was not in the response.** A neutral facilitator keeps the discussion on the system and makes sure quieter participants are heard.
- **Separate the review from performance evaluation.** If the review document is used in appraisals, people will stop being candid in the next one.

> [!TIP]
> A useful test for every finding: would a different competent person, in the same seat with the same information, plausibly have done the same thing? If yes, the finding belongs to the system, and so does the action.

## Running the review

A review is a short project with three stages.

**Before the meeting.** The incident lead appoints a facilitator and a scribe, and schedules the meeting soon after containment, while memories are fresh, typically within days. The SOC prepares a draft timeline from the case record and the logs, and circulates it as a pre-read with a request for corrections. Legal is consulted on how the review is documented and shared, because findings can be sensitive and the incident may be reportable; in some organisations legal asks to direct the review.

**The meeting.** The agenda follows the outputs: confirm the timeline, walk through the decisions, identify what helped and what hindered, agree the causes, and agree actions and owners. Participants include everyone who did meaningful work in the response (the Tier 1 and Tier 2 analysts, the IR lead, IT operations who executed containment, detection engineering), the business owner of the affected function (for Banyan, the finance operations manager) and, where relevant, legal and the data protection function.

**After the meeting.** The facilitator writes the review report, actions go into the tracker with owners and dates, and a follow-up date is set to check that the actions were done and work. The report and the metrics feed the SOC's quarterly reporting (Module 1) and the next tabletop exercise (Lesson 7).

**Purpose.** The diagram is the reconstructed timeline drawn to scale. Tables list events; a scaled timeline shows *gaps*, and gaps are what a review is about: the time between the attacker's actions, and above all the time between the attacker's first action and the defenders' first action.

**Components.** The horizontal axis runs from 06:00 at the left to 08:40 UTC at the right on 3 November 2026. There are four rows. The green row, **SOC response (illustrative)**, carries two ticks near the right edge: noticed 08:25 and IR lead acknowledgement 08:31.

Read horizontally to see gaps: the red row has a 48-minute gap before persistence, then a long quiet stretch before the upload.

**Execution flow.** Delivery and execution happen within two minutes; the beacon starts three minutes later and runs regularly; persistence follows; the beacon stops at 07:42; the upload and the log clearing come half an hour later. Only then does the green row begin.

**Decision logic.** The diagram makes one decision visible: the SOC's first tick is to the right of every red tick. The review's central question follows directly: at which of the earlier ticks could the SOC have started, and what prevented it? Each red tick with a rule match (R1 at 06:14, R3 at 07:02, R4 at 08:12) is a detection opportunity.

**Technical interpretation.** The beacon stopping at 07:42 while the upload happens at 08:12 suggests that the attacker's tooling changed mode or that the operator worked interactively for the final steps; the data cannot say which, and the review should record it as an open question, not a finding.

**Practical example.** Measure on the figure: from the first red tick (06:12) to the first green tick (08:25) is 133 minutes, the dwell time computed below. From the R1 tick (06:14) to the green tick is 131 minutes of available but unused detection.

## Root cause and contributing factors

### Two different questions

"Root cause" is a useful term with a misleading implication: that every incident has one cause, and that finding it is the goal. Security incidents almost never work like that. An intrusion succeeds when several defences each fail or are absent at the same moment. The review therefore asks two different questions.

- **What started it?** The root cause is the earliest point in the chain where a change under the organisation's control would have stopped the incident from beginning. It should be expressed as a condition of the system, not as a person's act.
- **What let it go so far?** Contributing factors are the conditions that allowed the incident to progress, last longer or do more harm. Each one is a separate opportunity to have stopped it, and most of the review's actions come from here.

A practical way to reach a root cause is to keep asking "what allowed that?" from the outcome backwards, stopping at the first answer that the organisation can change and that is supported by evidence. For Banyan: the data left because an attacker controlled WS-104; the attacker controlled WS-104 because PowerShell ran from a document; PowerShell ran because a macro-enabled document from the internet was able to start a script interpreter on that host. That last condition is within the organisation's control (Office macro and script-execution policy) and is supported directly by the Sysmon event at 06:14. "Because divya opened it" is not a root cause: it is a person's normal work, and the next person will do the same.

### Evidence discipline

Every causal statement in the review must cite evidence, and the review must separate what the data shows from what it suggests. The Banyan data shows that event 4720 and 4732 were recorded under divya's session, which means that session could create a local administrator; it does not show *why* the session had that right (divya may be a local administrator, or the attacker may have escalated). The review records the fact, lists the question, and assigns someone to answer it from the endpoint configuration. Writing "users have local admin rights" as a finding would be inventing a cause.

The figure shows the causal map the Banyan review agreed.
