### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The diagram separates the one condition that started the incident from the conditions that let it reach its outcome. It matters because reviews that name only a root cause produce one action, while the incident got through five other gaps; reviews that list everything as equal produce a long list nobody prioritises.

**Components.** The dark box at the bottom is the **Outcome: data likely taken, log cleared**, with its evidence "48.2 MB upload 08:12, event 1102 at 08:17". Above it are six boxes in two rows of three. In the top row: the red **Root cause: macro document ran PowerShell** ("internet .docm on a payments approver host"); the orange **Look-alike domain reachable** ("banyan-payroll-update.example, status 200"); and the orange **Session could create a local admin** ("4720 + 4732 under divya's session"). In the second row: the violet **R1 matched at 06:14, noticed 08:25** ("detection-to-response gap"); the violet **Beacon ranked last in the queue** ("R6 priority 3.6"); and the orange **Upload to never-seen domain allowed** ("files-share-drop.example, status 200").

**Relationships and arrows.** Every arrow points into the outcome: each box is a condition that fed it. The colours carry the distinction the review makes. Red marks the single root cause. Orange marks preventive gaps, where a control on the host or the network could have blocked a step. Violet marks detection and response gaps, where the SOC's own process let a visible step go unanswered.

**Execution flow.** Read the boxes in the order the attacker met them: the look-alike domain was reachable, the document's macro ran PowerShell, the session created an administrator, the beacon and R1 went unworked, and the upload to an unknown domain was allowed. Removing any one would have changed the outcome; removing the root cause would have prevented the incident.

**Decision logic.** The review applied two tests to each candidate factor: is it supported by an event in the data, and is it under the organisation's control? "The attacker was skilled" fails the second test. "Users have local admin rights" fails the first, which is why the box reads "session could create a local admin".

**Technical interpretation.** Both status-200 boxes come from the proxy log: the proxy saw and permitted both the download and the upload. The beacon box quotes the kit's own triage output, where `R6 beacon_regular_small` scores 3.6, the lowest in the queue, although the hunt later confirmed it as command-and-control. The R1 box uses the illustrative time noticed.

**Practical example.** In the review meeting, the detection engineer explains that R6's severity of 2 was chosen because regular small requests are often benign heartbeats (Module 5); the Tier 1 analyst explains that the queue was worked strictly by score. Both decisions were reasonable; together they placed the C2 channel at the bottom of a queue for over two hours. The finding goes to the system: priority by score alone does not group alerts by entity.

**Security implications.** Each box becomes an action. Preventive actions reduce the chance of the next incident; detection actions shorten the next one. A mature review produces both.

**Key learning.** One root cause starts an incident; contributing factors decide how far it gets. Name each as a condition supported by evidence.

## Actions with owners

An action is useful only if it is specific, has one owner (a role and a named person in the real report), has a due date, and states how completion and effectiveness will be checked. "Improve awareness" fails every test. The Banyan actions, from a review held on 10 November 2026 (fictional):

| # | Action | Addresses | Owner | Due | Verified by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | Block macros in documents from the internet and stop Office applications starting script interpreters on finance hosts | Root cause | Endpoint engineering lead | 2026-11-24 | Test document in the lab fails to start PowerShell; R1 hit count on finance hosts |
| A2 | Find out why divya's session could create a local administrator; remove standing local admin rights where present | Session could create a local admin | Endpoint engineering lead | 2026-12-01 | Configuration report for all finance hosts |
| A3 | Group alerts by host and user in the queue, so that an entity with three or more open alerts is surfaced as one item | R1 gap, beacon ranked last | SOC manager with detection engineering | 2026-12-08 | Replay of the Banyan dataset shows CASE-0001 as one item by 06:17 |
| A4 | Review R6's severity and description against its intent (C2 beaconing) | Beacon ranked last | Detection engineering | 2026-11-24 | Rule review record (Module 7) |
| A5 | Alert on, or require approval for, large uploads to domains first seen in the last 30 days | Upload allowed | Network and proxy team | 2026-12-15 | Replay: 08:12 upload produces an alert or a block |
| A6 | Add look-alike domain monitoring for Banyan's names and block newly registered look-alikes at the proxy | Look-alike reachable | Threat intelligence analyst | 2026-12-15 | Monthly look-alike report |
| A7 | Add timestamped fields for containment approval and execution to the case template | Metrics gap (below) | SOC manager | 2026-11-17 | Next SEV1/SEV2 case has both fields |
| A8 | Confirm MFA on the VPN for all users, and alert on a success after failures for many users from one address | CASE-0002 | IAM team | 2026-12-01 | VPN configuration review; R2 test (Module 7) |

Notice that the actions include changes to the SOC itself (A3, A4, A7), not only to other teams' controls. A review that only asks other teams to improve has not been honest about detection and response. Notice also what is absent: there is no action "retrain divya". Phishing awareness may still be part of a broader programme, but it is not a fix for a control gap that any recipient could fall through.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Track actions to completion. The follow-up date matters more than the meeting: an action list that is not reviewed at 30 and 90 days is mostly forgotten, and the next review of a similar incident will find the same factors.

## Metrics from the dataset

Metrics turn the timeline into numbers that can be compared across incidents. Module 1 defined MTTD, MTTA and MTTR across many cases; a review computes the same intervals for one incident, from real timestamps. A short script in your working copy of the kit reads the minisiem database (it is a helper you write, not part of the kit):

```python
"""Post-incident metrics for CASE-0001 from the minisiem database."""
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime

con = sqlite3.connect("minisiem.db")
q = lambda sql: con.execute(sql).fetchone()[0]
t = lambda s: datetime.fromisoformat(s.replace("Z", "+00:00"))

first_bad = q("SELECT MIN(ts) FROM events WHERE url LIKE '%banyan-payroll-update%'")
first_exec = q("SELECT MIN(ts) FROM events WHERE source='sysmon' AND lower(parent_image) LIKE '%winword%'")
last_bad = q("SELECT MAX(ts) FROM events WHERE host='WS-104' AND event_id=1102")
noticed = "2026-11-03T08:25:00Z"   # illustrative SOC time (Module 5 Lesson 6)

def gap(a, b):
    m = int((t(b) - t(a)).total_seconds() // 60)
    return f"{m} min ({m // 60} h {m % 60:02d} min)"

print("first malicious event ", first_bad)
print("first rule-matching   ", first_exec, "(R1)")
print("last attacker action  ", last_bad, "(R5)")
print("time noticed          ", noticed, "(illustrative)")
print("attacker active span  ", gap(first_bad, last_bad))
print("dwell time            ", gap(first_bad, noticed))
print("first alert to notice ", gap(first_exec, noticed))
```

```terminal
$ python pir_metrics.py
first malicious event  2026-11-03T06:12:00Z
first rule-matching    2026-11-03T06:14:00Z (R1)
last attacker action   2026-11-03T08:17:00Z (R5)
time noticed           2026-11-03T08:25:00Z (illustrative)
attacker active span   125 min (2 h 05 min)
dwell time             133 min (2 h 13 min)
first alert to notice  131 min (2 h 11 min)
```

The script takes each attacker timestamp from the data rather than typing it in, so the numbers can be re-derived by anyone with the evidence export. `fromisoformat` is given an explicit `+00:00` offset in place of the trailing `Z`, so every subtraction is between timezone-aware UTC times.

Interpret each number carefully.

- **Dwell time, 133 minutes.** From the first malicious event (the download at 06:12:00Z) to the time noticed. By industry standards this is short, but it was long enough: the attacker's active span was 125 minutes, so dwell time exceeded it. Every action, including the upload and the log clearing, happened before the SOC noticed.
- **First alert to notice, 131 minutes.** The first event that a kit rule matches came two minutes after the download. If R1 runs in near-real time, the SOC had a detection opportunity for 131 minutes. This number, not dwell time, is the one the SOC controls directly, and it is what A3 targets.
- **Notice to acknowledgement, 6 minutes** (08:25Z to 08:31Z, both illustrative). Good, and evidence that the paging process works; it does not offset the 131 minutes.
- **Time to contain: not computable.** The case record has no timestamp for containment approval or execution. Module 1 warned that a metric can only be computed from timestamps that are captured; this review discovered that the most important response metric for a SEV1 cannot be measured. A7 fixes it.
- **Time to report.** The six-hour CERT-In clock ran from 08:25Z to 14:25Z (19:55 IST). The review should record when the report was actually sent, from the point of contact's record, and compare.

> [!WARNING]
> Never compute dwell time from the first *alert* instead of the first *malicious event*: it hides exactly the period a review exists to examine. And never quote a dwell time without stating which two timestamps it runs between.

## The review report

The written report is short and structured, so that leadership can read the summary and engineers can find their actions:

1. Summary: what happened, severity of record, impact, in five lines.
2. Timeline: the merged table and figure, with sources.
3. What went well: for Banyan, the R5 hard trigger was escalated within minutes, the evidence was exported with a hash and custody record, and the escalation package separated fact from hypothesis.
4. Root cause and contributing factors, each with its evidence.
5. Actions: the tracker extract with owners and dates.
6. Metrics: with definitions and the timestamps used.
7. Open questions: what the data cannot answer (the content of the upload, why the beacon stopped at 07:42, whether CASE-0002 is linked).

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

**"The root cause was user error."** It names a person, not a condition, and produces no change in the system. Ask what allowed the action to cause harm.

**"One root cause, one action."** The Banyan incident passed six gaps; fixing only the macro policy leaves the detection and egress gaps for the next technique.

**"The timeline is obvious, skip it."** Without a sourced timeline, metrics are guesses and arguments about decisions have no common ground.

**"Hindsight shows the beacon was obvious."** It is obvious on the reconstructed timeline. In the live queue it was a priority 3.6 alert below six others. Reconstruct what was visible at the time.

**"Actions are done when the ticket is closed."** An action is done when its verification passes, for example when replaying the dataset produces the expected alert.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Post-incident reviews are among the most valuable sources of detection engineering work, because they come with confirmed attacker behaviour and real data to test against. Every Banyan detection action can be verified by replaying `banyan_events.jsonl` through the changed logic (the testing practice of Module 7). Reviews also contain sensitive material: attacker infrastructure, control weaknesses, personal data and the organisation's response times. Store the report with restricted access, share indicators externally only under the appropriate TLP marking, and keep it consistent with the regulatory reports already sent. Under the CERT-In Directions and the DPDP Act, regulators may ask further questions; a review whose timeline and metrics match the reports is far easier to defend than one that contradicts them.

## Best practices

- Hold the review soon after containment, with a neutral facilitator and a pre-read draft timeline.
- Keep the timeline in UTC with sources for every row, and keep attacker and defender lanes on one clock.
- State root cause and contributing factors as conditions supported by evidence; list open questions separately.
- Give every action one owner, a due date and a verification method, and include actions for the SOC itself.
- Compute metrics from captured timestamps with a reproducible query, state their definitions, and treat a missing timestamp as a finding.
- Follow up at 30 and 90 days, and feed the incident into the next tabletop exercise.

## Key takeaways

- A post-incident review produces a sourced timeline, a causal analysis, owned actions and metrics; without change, the incident's cost was wasted.
- Blameless means asking what made decisions reasonable at the time; accountability moves to the owners of the actions.
- Reconstruct the attacker lane from the logs and the defender lane from the case record, in UTC, on one clock.
- The root cause is the earliest controllable condition (for Banyan, a macro document from the internet could start PowerShell); contributing factors explain how far the incident got, and most actions come from them.
- From the dataset: attacker active span 125 minutes, dwell time 133 minutes to the illustrative time noticed, and 131 minutes from the first R1 match to notice; time to contain could not be computed because the case record lacks the timestamps.
- Verify actions by replaying the dataset, track them to completion, and keep the review consistent with any regulatory reports.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Earlier lessons in this module describe what an organisation should do during an incident. None of it is proven by being written down: an untested plan is a hypothesis. It assumes the contact list is current, people know their roles, the authority to isolate a payments workstation is clear, legal can be reached in the evening, and someone is watching the six-hour CERT-In clock. The first real incident is a poor time to find out which assumptions were wrong.

A **tabletop exercise** is the cheapest, safest way to test them. The people who would handle a real incident sit together while a facilitator walks them through a realistic scenario, releasing new information at intervals. At each step they discuss what they would do, who decides, what they need and whom they tell. Nothing is touched. The output is not a score but a list of gaps, each turned into an action with an owner and a date.

Tabletops matter for a SOC for three reasons. The SOC is usually where an incident starts, so its escalation, evidence and timeline are what every other participant works from; an exercise shows whether that material is good enough for a business owner, a lawyer or an executive. Many incident failures are not technical: organisations detect the problem but escalate late, tell the wrong people, or let a well-meaning technician destroy evidence, and a tabletop is designed to surface exactly those decision and coordination failures. And exercises are expected of a mature programme: NIST SP 800-84, *Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities* (2006), describes tabletop and functional exercises as ways to validate IT plans, and auditors increasingly ask not "do you have a plan?" but "when did you last test it, and what did you change?".

This lesson teaches you to design, run and evaluate a tabletop, and ends with a ready-to-run scenario built on the Banyan Microfinance incident. Lesson 8 then works the same incident in the lab: the discussion shows what decision-makers will ask the SOC for, and the lab shows whether the SOC can produce it.

> [!NOTE]
> A tabletop is a discussion exercise. Participants describe what they *would* do; they do not do it. Any exercise that touches live systems (isolating a test host, restoring from backup, calling the real CERT-In contact) is an operations-based exercise and needs its own authorisation, change control and safety plan.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Exercise | A planned event in which people practise or test a plan, procedure or capability against a scenario. |
| Tabletop exercise (TTX) | A discussion-based exercise in which participants talk through their responses to a scenario presented by a facilitator. |
| Discussion-based exercise | Seminar, workshop, tabletop or game: tests plans, policies and decision-making by talking. |
| Operations-based exercise | Drill, functional or full-scale exercise: participants perform actions with real or simulated systems. |
| Scenario | The storyline of the exercise: a plausible incident tailored to the organisation's threats and systems. |
| Inject | A piece of new information released during the exercise (an alert, a phone call, an email, a demand) that moves the scenario forward and forces a decision. |
| MSEL | Master Scenario Events List: the timed, ordered list of injects, with the expected player actions for each. |
| Facilitator | The person who presents the scenario, releases injects, asks questions and keeps the discussion on time and on objective. |
| Player | A participant who responds in their real role (incident lead, SOC analyst, legal, communications, IT operations, business owner). |
| Evaluator / note-taker | A participant who does not play but records decisions, times, gaps and quotes against the objectives. |
| Hotwash | The short, immediate debrief at the end of the exercise, while memories are fresh. |
| AAR / IP | After-action report and improvement plan: the written result of the exercise, listing strengths, gaps and owned actions. |
| Scenario time | The time inside the story (for example 08:30 UTC on the day of the incident), as opposed to the real time of the session. |

The terms MSEL, hotwash and AAR/IP come from the US Homeland Security Exercise and Evaluation Program (HSEEP), which is widely used as a reference model for exercise design well beyond the United States. You do not need to adopt HSEEP in full, but its vocabulary is what most exercise packages, including the free tabletop packages published by CISA, use.

## Where a tabletop fits among exercise types

Exercises sit on a ladder of increasing realism, cost and risk. **Seminars** and **workshops** explain or draft plans. The **tabletop** is the first rung that tests decisions against a developing scenario. Above it are operations-based exercises: a **drill** performs one task for real (an EDR isolation on a test machine, a call-tree test), a **functional exercise** has teams perform their functions in a simulated environment, and a **full-scale exercise** mobilises real people and systems.

| Type | What is tested | Touches systems? | Typical cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Seminar / workshop | Awareness of the plan; draft procedures | No | Hours |
| Tabletop | Decisions, roles, escalation, communication, authority | No | Half a day including preparation |
| Drill | One procedure performed for real (isolate, restore, call tree) | Yes, in a controlled way | A day |
| Functional | Teams performing their functions against a simulated incident | Simulated environment | Weeks of preparation |
| Full-scale | The whole response, with real resources | Yes | Months of preparation |

Security teams also run **red team** and **purple team** exercises, which are operations-based and need written authorisation and rules of engagement (Course 05). They test whether you *can detect and act*; a tabletop tests whether you *know what to decide and who decides it*. A purple team exercise might show that the Banyan beacon is detected within minutes, while a tabletop shows that nobody knew who could authorise isolating the payments approver's workstation.

Climb the ladder in order: tabletop a plan before you drill it, because practising a procedure whose decision points nobody has agreed has little value. Because tabletops are cheap, run them most often: at least yearly per major scenario, and after any significant change to the plan, the organisation or the threat picture.

## Designing a tabletop

Good tabletops are designed backwards from what you need to learn. The scenario is a means, not the end. A dramatic scenario that tests nothing in particular produces an entertaining afternoon and an empty improvement plan.

### 1. Set objectives

Start with three to five objectives, each naming a capability and how an evaluator will judge it, drawn from the plan and from known worries (a new reporting procedure, a reorganisation, an audit finding). "Participants agree a declaration and severity within 15 minutes of scenario time of the first escalation" can be evaluated; "test the IR plan" cannot, so it produces no actions. The Banyan objectives below are worked examples.

### 2. Define scope, participants and constraints

Scope says which teams are in play (for example the SOC, IT operations, finance, legal and communications) and which are simulated (the regulator, the media, the attacker). Invite the people who hold the real roles, and their deputies, because incidents happen when the primary is on leave. Keep to roughly six to twelve players; beyond that, quieter roles disappear. Fix the duration (60 to 120 minutes for one scenario) and constraints such as recording and the classification of materials.

### 3. Write the scenario

A good scenario is **plausible** (it matches the real threat profile and systems), **specific** (real host names, business processes and times) and **escalating** (it starts ambiguous and grows more serious). Build it from things that have happened: your own incidents, sector reports or relevant threat intelligence. For a SOC the best source is often an anonymised past investigation, whose details are known to be realistic.

Two rules prevent common failures. The scenario must not depend on players making one specific choice: if inject 3 only makes sense when the host was isolated at inject 2, phrase it so that it works either way. And the facts in each inject must be unambiguous, so that players debate decisions rather than what a badly written alert means.

### 4. Build the injects and the MSEL

Each inject is a short message in a realistic form: a SIEM alert line, an analyst's escalation, a call from a business head, a customer email. For each one the MSEL records the scenario time, the recipient, the content, the decision it should provoke, the expected actions (what the plan says should happen) and the objective it serves. Players never see the expected actions.

Aim for one inject every ten to fifteen minutes, with the key decisions mid-session rather than at the end, when time pressure cuts discussion short. Prepare **contingency injects**: one to raise the pressure if the group moves too fast, and a hint if it is stuck.

### 5. Assign roles

Besides players, appoint one **facilitator** (who does not play), at least one **evaluator** per objective group, and a **controller** who plays outsiders (the regulator, a journalist, a supplier) when players "call" them. A **trusted agent** in each team can help design the scenario without playing. Observers do not speak.

### 6. Prepare logistics and ground rules

Prepare a short briefing, the plan and contact lists as they really are (not cleaned-up versions), a visible scenario clock and the evaluation sheets. State the ground rules at the start:

- It is a no-fault environment: the plan and the organisation are being tested, not individuals.
- Respond as you would in your real role, with the authority and information you would really have.
- Do not "fight the scenario": accept the injects as given, even if you think the attack is unlikely.
- Decisions made in the room are discussion outcomes, not commitments, unless they are later approved through the normal process.
- What is said in the room stays in the exercise record and the AAR.

The design stage and the run stage form a lifecycle, which the figure shows end to end.

![Figure 8.13: The tabletop exercise lifecycle](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M08-L07-F1.svg)

*Figure 8.13: The tabletop exercise lifecycle. Seven steps from evaluable objectives to an owned improvement plan, with the improvements feeding the next exercise.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The figure shows the whole life of a tabletop exercise as seven ordered steps, from setting objectives to producing the after-action report, with a feedback arrow that closes the loop into the next exercise. It matters because most weak tabletops fail at the two ends of this chain: they skip step 1 (so nothing can be evaluated) or stop at step 6 (so the hotwash comments are never turned into actions).

**Components.** The steps run top to bottom. **1 Set objectives** (violet) is the control step: three to five capabilities with a test for each. **2 Scope + participants** (slate) fixes which teams play, which are simulated and who attends. **3 Scenario + MSEL** (blue) is the content: the storyline and the timed inject list with expected actions. **4 Roles + ground rules** (blue) assigns facilitator, players, evaluators and controller, and prepares the briefing. **5 Facilitate** (orange) is the live session, the step participants actually see. **6 Hotwash** (green) is the immediate debrief. **7 AAR + improvement plan** (dark) is the trust anchor of the whole process: the only durable output.

**Relationships and arrows.** Each solid arrow means "the output of this step is the input of the next". Objectives decide scope (you invite the people whose decisions the objectives test); scope constrains the scenario (it must exercise the teams that are in the room); the MSEL dictates which roles are needed; and so on. The dashed feedback arrow from step 7 back to step 1 carries the improvement actions: the next exercise should include an objective that tests whether last time's gaps were fixed.

**Execution flow.** Steps 1 to 4 happen in the weeks before the session and are invisible to players. Step 5 is the session itself, steps 6 and 7 follow immediately and within a few weeks respectively.

**Decision logic.** There are no branches in the lifecycle itself, but two judgements sit inside it. At step 3 the designer decides whether an inject needs a branch because the players' earlier choice might change its meaning. At step 7 the evaluators decide, objective by objective, whether each was met, partly met or not met, which determines what goes into the improvement plan.

**Technical interpretation.** The lifecycle is a small version of the plan-do-check-act loop that runs through security management: steps 1 to 4 plan, step 5 does, steps 6 and 7 check, and the feedback arrow acts.

**Practical example.** For Banyan, step 1 produced the objective "establish the CERT-In deadline in UTC and IST"; step 3 placed a legal inject at scenario time 08:50 UTC to test it; in step 5 the group calculated the deadline; in step 6 legal noted that nobody knew who held the CERT-In portal credentials; step 7 recorded that as an action with an owner and date, and the next exercise checks it.

**Security implications.** The MSEL and the AAR describe the organisation's weaknesses in detail and are sensitive documents; classify and store them accordingly.

**Key learning.** A tabletop is only as good as its first and last steps: evaluable objectives at the start and an owned improvement plan at the end.

## Facilitating the session

The facilitator keeps the group moving towards the objectives while letting the players do the thinking. It is a distinct skill: an incident lead often facilitates their own team badly because they cannot resist answering.

**Open with the frame.** Spend five to ten minutes on purpose, ground rules, roles and the starting situation, and warn that scenario time will jump: ninety minutes may cover six hours of incident.

**Release injects as the real channel would.** Read an alert aloud, hand out a printed escalation, or have the controller "phone" a player. An inject handed only to the service desk tests whether the service desk knows to escalate it.

**Ask, do not tell.** Ask open questions by role: "Incident lead, what is your decision and who must approve it?", "Legal, what do you need from the SOC first?", "SOC, how long would that query take, and how confident would you be?". Probe the plan: "Where is that written down?", "Who is your deputy?". When a player says "we would just do X", ask how, who and with what authority.

**Manage time and voices.** Time each inject; use a hint if discussion stalls and the pressure inject if it races. Direct questions by role so that one senior voice does not dominate.

**Do not rescue, do not punish.** Let an unsupported decision stand and ask what happens next: the gap is the finding. Restate the no-fault rule if blame starts.

**Capture decisions visibly** on a shared screen: scenario time, decision, decider, what was needed. It doubles as the single incident log of Lesson 2.

> [!TIP]
> Ask the SOC players to say aloud what they would need to run, and how long it would take, before you give them the answer in the next inject. It shows the other participants how long "just check the logs" really takes, and tests whether the SOC knows its own data (for example, that the VPN source carries no host field, so a VPN login cannot be tied to a device from VPN logs alone).

## Evaluating the exercise

Evaluation turns a discussion into evidence. It has three parts.

**During the session**, evaluators record against each objective what was decided, when (scenario time), by whom, with what information, what was missing, and notable quotes ("I don't know who has the CERT-In portal login"). They note strengths as well as gaps.

**At the hotwash**, immediately afterwards, go round the room asking each participant what went well, what did not, and the single most important change. Keep it to twenty minutes and capture observations rather than designing solutions.

**In the after-action report and improvement plan**, written within a few weeks, rate each objective met, partly met or not met with evidence; list strengths; and for each gap record the root cause (the plan was silent, wrong, or unknown, or a tool or access was missing) and an action with an owner and due date. Track the actions like any corrective action and test them in the next exercise.

Useful AAR measures are simple: the scenario time of declaration, the time to a containment decision, the decisions that needed someone not in the room, and whether the reporting deadline was calculated correctly. Like the SOC metrics of Module 1, they make exercises comparable year to year.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Classify the MSEL, evaluation notes and AAR. They describe exactly where the organisation's response is weak. Injects 5, 6 and 7 add business events that are **not** in the dataset; they are exercise material, invented to test communication and decision-making.

## Common mistakes and misconceptions

- **"A tabletop is a test the players pass or fail."** It tests the plan; treating it as an assessment of individuals hides the gaps.
- **Unevaluable objectives** produce no actions.
- **Over-clever scenarios** invite players to fight the scenario; plausible, local ones find more gaps.
- **Injects that depend on one decision** force the facilitator to steer.
- **The senior person answers everything.** Ask by role.
- **Stopping at the hotwash.** Without an AAR and owned actions the same gaps recur.
- **Using real data** in materials is a confidentiality risk for no benefit.

## Security implications, detection and defence

Exercise materials document weaknesses in detection, authority and communication, so protect them like any sensitive security document. Mark exercise messages clearly (many organisations prefix them "EXERCISE EXERCISE EXERCISE") so that nobody mistakes a scenario for a real incident, and never contact real external parties such as CERT-In, the RBI or the media during a discussion exercise; the controller plays them.

Exercises are themselves a control: they validate the plan, the contact list and decision authority, and they train people safely. Their actions often land in the SOC: a missing detection, a telemetry gap (Banyan shows that VPN events have no device field and that WS-104 process telemetry ends at 06:14 UTC), a playbook step or a faster evidence export. Track them to closure and re-test them.

## Best practices

- Derive objectives from real concerns; build local scenarios from your own incidents.
- Separate facilitator, evaluators and players, include deputies, and give every role an inject.
- Show scenario time in UTC and local time, and log decisions against it.
- Hold the hotwash immediately and the AAR within weeks; every gap gets an owner and a date.

## Practical application (discussion exercise)

Run the Banyan tabletop with your study group or colleagues. It needs no lab and touches no system.

1. Choose a facilitator and an evaluator; assign the player roles (one person may hold two).
2. Hand out the starting situation, objectives and evaluation sheet; keep the expected actions with the facilitator.
3. Brief for 10 minutes, then release injects 1 to 7 about every 10 minutes; hold C1 in reserve.
4. Keep a visible decision log, then hold a 20-minute hotwash.
5. Within a week, write a one-page AAR with each objective rated and at least five owned actions.
6. Keep the AAR: in Lesson 8 you can check whether the SOC could really produce, in time, what the players assumed.

## Key takeaways

- A tabletop tests decisions, roles, authority and communication by discussion; it touches no system.
- Design backwards from three to five evaluable objectives; the MSEL orders injects by scenario time with expected actions.
- Facilitators ask by role, manage time and let gaps stand rather than rescuing the group.
- Evaluation runs from notes, to the hotwash, to an AAR and improvement plan with owners and dates.
- Classify exercise materials and use synthetic data.
- The Banyan scenario tests declaration, containment authority, the CERT-In deadline (14:30 UTC, 20:00 IST from an 08:30 UTC noticed time) and out-of-band communication.

## Lab objective and scope

This lab closes the module by working the Banyan Microfinance incident end to end, as the SOC's part of incident handling. Earlier labs analysed the same data from other angles: Module 4 read each log source and built a findings note, Module 5 triaged the alert queue, Module 6 graded the intelligence. Here the question changes from "what happened?" to "what does the incident team need from the SOC, and can we give it to them in time?". You will declare the incident and start the reporting clock, scope it, build the incident timeline, write containment advice, assemble a verifiable evidence package and write the incident report. If you ran the Lesson 7 tabletop, keep your after-action notes beside you: this lab shows which of the players' assumptions about the SOC were realistic.

By the end of the lab you will be able to:

1. Turn a triaged alert queue into an incident declaration with a recorded noticed time and a CERT-In deadline in UTC and IST.
2. Scope an incident with hunts and negative checks, and state the limits of each check.
3. Build an incident timeline from a single reproducible query, separating facts from inferences.
4. Write ordered, owned containment advice that preserves evidence.
5. Produce an evidence package with a correct SHA-256 manifest and custody records, verify it, and show that tampering is detected.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Authorisation and scope.** This lab uses only the synthetic Banyan dataset (`banyan_events.jsonl`) and the kit's own scripts, run on your own computer in a copy of the kit. Every person, host, domain and address is fictional; external addresses come from the RFC 5737 documentation ranges and domains end in `.example`. Containment in this lab is *advice written in a report*: you do not isolate, block or disable anything. In a real organisation, the SOC recommends containment and an authorised owner approves and executes it.

## Key terminology

| Term | Meaning in this lab |
| --- | --- |
| Declaration | The recorded decision that a set of events is an incident, with severity and time. |
| Noticed time | The time the organisation became aware of the incident; it starts the CERT-In six-hour clock. Here it is set to 08:30 UTC. |
| Scope | Every host, account, address and data set involved, and the checks showing what is *not* involved. |
| Negative check | A query whose empty result is itself a finding (for example, no other host contacted the bad domains). |
| Incident timeline | The ordered list of incident events, in UTC, each with its source and an inference label. |
| Containment advice | Ordered actions the SOC recommends, each with owner, evidence precaution and business impact. |
| Evidence package | The exported records, a SHA-256 manifest (`SHA256SUMS`) and custody entries (`custody.jsonl`). |
| Incident report | The written record for the incident lead, legal and later reviewers: summary, timeline, scope, actions, evidence and open questions. |

## How the lab is organised

The lab follows the order in which an incident team asks for things. First it needs to know whether this *is* an incident and how serious it is, because that decides who is paged and starts the legal clock. Then it needs scope, because containment of one host while the attacker holds another foothold only warns them. Then a timeline, which every other participant (legal, communications, forensics) will quote. Then containment advice, then evidence that will survive scrutiny, and finally the report that ties it together.

![Figure 8.15: IR lab route: from alert queue to incident report](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M08-L08-F1.svg)

*Figure 8.15: IR lab route: from alert queue to incident report. The seven lab stages in the order the incident team needs them, with the kit tool or output behind each.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The figure is the lab's route map: seven stages, top to bottom, each naming the kit tool or output that produces it. It matters because an incident team consumes the SOC's work in this order, and a SOC that produces a perfect timeline after the reporting deadline has failed the team.

**Components.** **1 Load + alert picture** (slate) uses `minisiem.py load`, `minisiem.py rules` and `triage.py` to rebuild the prioritised queue. **2 Declare + start clock** (violet) is the decision step: the noticed time is 08:30 UTC and the CERT-In deadline is 14:30 UTC (20:00 IST). **3 Scope** (blue) runs `hunt.py` and three negative checks. **4 Timeline** (blue) is one merged query whose nine rows become the incident timeline. **5 Containment advice** (orange) is a written, ordered plan with owners. **6 Evidence package** (green) uses `evidence_export.py`, a rebuilt `SHA256SUMS`, `sha256sum -c` and a tamper test. **7 Incident report** (dark) is the deliverable that everything else feeds.

**Relationships and arrows.** Each arrow means "this stage depends on the one above". Declaration depends on the alert picture; scope depends on knowing which host and account to start from; the timeline needs scope so that it includes the VPN thread as well as WS-104; containment advice needs both scope and timeline; the evidence package must capture what the timeline cites; the report quotes all of them.

**Execution flow.** Stages 1 and 2 should take minutes, because the clock runs from stage 2. In a real incident, stages 3 to 6 overlap: evidence export (stage 6) often starts as soon as scope is clear, before containment, so that isolation or resets cannot change what is preserved.

**Decision logic.** Stage 2 is a yes/no decision with a severity attached. Stage 3 produces a branch in the story: the WS-104 thread is confirmed, while the VPN thread (gopal's 06:46 UTC login from 203.0.113.66) is linked only by timing, so it is carried as a hypothesis in every later stage rather than merged into the confirmed facts.

**Technical interpretation.** Every stage is reproducible: the same dataset and commands give the same counts and hashes, which is what makes the report defensible.

**Practical example.** Legal asks at 08:50 UTC whether reporting is required. Because stage 2 recorded the noticed time and deadline, the SOC answers in one line and returns to scoping.

**Security implications.** Skipping stage 3 risks partial containment; skipping stage 6 leaves a report whose claims nobody can verify later.

**Key learning.** Work in the order the incident team needs the answers, and record the noticed time before anything else.

### Step 2: Declare and start the clock

The queue meets any reasonable declaration criteria: malicious code execution (Word starting PowerShell), unauthorised privileged access (a new local administrator), possible exfiltration (48.2 MB to an external file-sharing look-alike) and anti-forensics (the Security log cleared), all on a payments approver's workstation. Declare an incident and grade it with the Lesson 5 severity matrix; with confirmed compromise of a business-critical asset and possible personal-data exfiltration, it belongs in the highest or second-highest band of most matrices.

Record the noticed time. For this lab the SOC became aware at **08:30 UTC**, when Tier 1 opened the queue. The CERT-In Directions of April 2022 require specified incidents to be reported within six hours of noticing them, so:

$$08{:}30\ \text{UTC} + 6\ \text{h} = 14{:}30\ \text{UTC} = 20{:}00\ \text{IST}\quad(\text{IST} = \text{UTC} + 05{:}30)$$

The SOC does not decide whether the incident is reportable; legal does. The SOC's job is to give legal the noticed time, the deadline and accurate facts quickly, and to note in the case record when and to whom it gave them.

### Step 3: Scope the incident

Scope answers two questions: what is involved, and what have we checked that is *not* involved. Start with the kit's hunts, which look beyond the known indicators.

```terminal
$ python hunt.py
H1 beaconing candidates (>= 8 requests, interval CV < 0.2)
  WS-104 https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping n=18 mean_gap=300s cv=0.004
H2 parent-child pairs seen on only one host
  WINWORD.EXE -> powershell.exe hosts=1 n=1
H3 other hosts contacting known-bad domains
  none found
```

H1 looks for *any* host and URL pair with at least eight requests at near-constant intervals, not just the known C2 domain; only WS-104's beacon qualifies, with a coefficient of variation of 0.004 (almost perfectly regular). H2 stacks parent-child process pairs across the estate; the only pair seen on a single host is Word starting PowerShell. H3 checks whether any host other than WS-104 contacted the three bad domains; none did. These are negative findings, and they go into the report as such.

Next, three checks of your own on the other entities: the spraying address, the new account, and the endpoint telemetry.

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM events WHERE src_ip='203.0.113.66' AND source<>'vpn'"
n
0
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM events WHERE user='svc_update' OR target_user='svc_update'"
n
2
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT MAX(ts) AS last_sysmon FROM events WHERE source='sysmon'"
last_sysmon
2026-11-03T06:14:00Z
```

The spraying address appears in no source other than the VPN. The account `svc_update` appears only in its own creation (4720) and group addition (4732): there is no record of it logging on. And the last endpoint process event in the whole dataset is the PowerShell start at 06:14 UTC. That last result is a **telemetry gap**, not a finding of innocence: from 06:14 onwards the dataset cannot show what ran on WS-104, so "no further processes" means "no further process telemetry". Every negative check must be reported with its limit.

**Purpose.** The figure is the incident's scope map: every entity the SOC has placed in scope, how each is connected, and which connections are confirmed versus hypothesised. It is the picture an incident lead needs before approving containment, because containment must cover every node at once.

**Components.** At the left, **banyan-payroll-update.example** (red) is the look-alike domain that served `invoice.docm`. The orange centre node, **WS-104 / divya**, is the compromised finance workstation and its user. Three red nodes hang off it: **cdn-telemetry-sync.example** (the C2 beacon), **svc_update** (the new local administrator) and **files-share-drop.example** (the 48.2 MB upload). In the second thread, **203.0.113.66** (red) is the spraying address and **gopal VPN session** (violet) is the successful login whose activity is unknown. The green node, **No other hosts**, records the negative results of H1 to H3. The slate node, **Telemetry gap**, records that endpoint process data ends at 06:14 UTC.

**Relationships and arrows.** Solid arrows are observed in the data and labelled with UTC times: the download at 06:12 points from the look-alike domain into WS-104; arrows from WS-104 point outwards to the C2 domain (18 beacons, 06:17-07:42), to `svc_update` (07:02-07:03) and to the upload domain (08:12), because WS-104 initiated each. The arrow from 203.0.113.66 to the gopal session is labelled "spray, success 06:46". The **dashed** arrow from the gopal session to WS-104 is labelled "link? timing only": it is a hypothesis, not an observation. Dashed arrows from the hunt and telemetry-gap nodes into WS-104 mark the boundaries of what the checks can show.

**Execution flow.** Read the WS-104 thread left to right in time order: delivery, execution and beaconing, persistence, exfiltration. The VPN thread runs in parallel between 06:42 and 06:46.

**Decision logic.** The dashed link decides containment scope. Because the cost of wrongly including gopal's account (a password reset and session revocation) is small and the cost of wrongly excluding it (a live attacker foothold) is large, the advice contains both threads together while the report keeps the link labelled as a hypothesis.

**Practical example.** When the Head of Finance asks "is it just Divya's PC?", the analyst points to the green node and its limit: no other host contacted the bad domains in the logged proxy traffic, but endpoint telemetry ends at 06:14 and the VPN session is unexplained.

**Security implications.** A scope map that draws only confirmed links invites partial containment; one that draws hypotheses as solid lines overstates the evidence in a report that legal will rely on.

**Key learning.** Draw every entity, mark every link as observed or hypothesised, and show the negative checks and their limits on the same picture.

### Step 4: Build the incident timeline

One query produces the timeline. It takes the incident window (06:00 to 09:00 UTC), keeps every non-proxy event on WS-104, every event from the spraying address, and only those WS-104 proxy URLs that no other host visited (the same "rare across the estate" idea as H2), then groups repeated activity into one row:

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py search "WITH k AS (SELECT ts, source, COALESCE(host, '-') AS host, user, CASE WHEN source='proxy' THEN url WHEN source='vpn' THEN 'vpn ' || outcome || ' from ' || src_ip WHEN source='sysmon' THEN 'process ' || image ELSE 'event ' || event_id || COALESCE(' ' || target_user, '') END AS activity FROM events WHERE ts >= '2026-11-03T06:00:00Z' AND ts < '2026-11-03T09:00:00Z' AND (src_ip = '203.0.113.66' OR (host = 'WS-104' AND (source <> 'proxy' OR url NOT IN (SELECT url FROM events WHERE source='proxy' GROUP BY url HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT host) > 1))))) SELECT MIN(ts) AS first_ts, MAX(ts) AS last_ts, COUNT(*) AS n, source, host, CASE COUNT(DISTINCT user) WHEN 1 THEN MIN(user) ELSE COUNT(DISTINCT user) || ' users' END AS user, activity FROM k GROUP BY source, host, activity ORDER BY first_ts"
first_ts | last_ts | n | source | host | user | activity
2026-11-03T06:12:00Z | 2026-11-03T06:12:00Z | 1 | proxy | WS-104 | divya | https://banyan-payroll-update.example/invoice.docm
2026-11-03T06:14:00Z | 2026-11-03T06:14:00Z | 1 | sysmon | WS-104 | divya | process C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
2026-11-03T06:17:00Z | 2026-11-03T07:42:02Z | 18 | proxy | WS-104 | divya | https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping
2026-11-03T06:42:00Z | 2026-11-03T06:42:49Z | 8 | vpn | - | 8 users | vpn failure from 203.0.113.66
2026-11-03T06:46:00Z | 2026-11-03T06:46:00Z | 1 | vpn | - | gopal | vpn success from 203.0.113.66
2026-11-03T07:02:00Z | 2026-11-03T07:02:00Z | 1 | windows | WS-104 | divya | event 4720 svc_update
2026-11-03T07:03:00Z | 2026-11-03T07:03:00Z | 1 | windows | WS-104 | divya | event 4732 svc_update
2026-11-03T08:12:00Z | 2026-11-03T08:12:00Z | 1 | proxy | WS-104 | divya | https://files-share-drop.example/upload

```

`COALESCE` supplies a dash for the VPN events' missing host; the `CASE` expression turns each event into a readable activity; the sub-query excludes any URL seen from more than one host; `GROUP BY source, host, activity` collapses the 18 beacons and the 8 spray failures into one row each. Nine rows cover 33 events. Keep the exact query in the case record, so that anyone can re-run it and get the same rows.

Turn the rows into the timeline the incident team will use, adding IST and an explicit label for each line: **observed** (directly in the log) or **inferred** (a conclusion drawn from observations).

| UTC | IST | Event | Source | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 06:12 | 11:42 | divya downloads `invoice.docm` from `banyan-payroll-update.example` | proxy | observed |
| 06:14 | 11:44 | Word starts PowerShell on WS-104 | sysmon | observed; malicious execution inferred |
| 06:17-07:42 | 11:47-13:12 | 18 x 220-byte requests every ~300 s to `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` | proxy | observed; C2 inferred (ISAC-A, conf. 85) |
| 06:42:00-06:42:49 | 12:12:00-12:12:49 | One failed VPN login for each of 8 users from 203.0.113.66 | vpn | observed; spray inferred |

Two features of the timeline deserve a sentence each in the report. The 4720, 4732 and 1102 events record divya's account as the actor: the actions ran in her logon session, which shows the attacker was operating as her, not that she performed them. And the beacon stops at 07:42:02, thirty minutes before the upload; the data does not say why, so the report lists it as an open question rather than explaining it.

### Step 5: Write the containment advice

Containment advice is ordered, owned and evidence-aware. Lesson 3's principles apply: preserve evidence first where it is safe to, never let collection delay stopping serious ongoing harm, and contain related footholds at the same time so that one action does not warn the attacker about the next. In the Banyan data the beacon has been silent since 07:42 and the upload finished at 08:12, so there is no sign of harm still in progress at 08:30; that allows a few minutes to start evidence collection before acting, but not hours.

| # | Action | Owner (approver) | Evidence precaution | Business impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | "Do not touch, do not reboot WS-104" instruction to IT ops and service desk | Incident lead | Prevents loss of memory and files | None |
| 1 | Export and hash SIEM evidence for WS-104, WS-107 and the VPN (Step 6) | SOC Tier 2 | The evidence step itself | None |
| 2 | Network-isolate WS-104 with EDR (not power off) | IT ops (incident lead) | Isolation keeps memory for forensic imaging | Divya loses her PC: issue a clean replacement |
| 3 | At the same moment: reset divya's and gopal's passwords, revoke sessions and MFA tokens | Identity team (incident lead) | Record the time; existing VPN and session logs are already exported | Both users re-enrol |
| 4 | Block `cdn-telemetry-sync.example`, `banyan-payroll-update.example`, `files-share-drop.example` at proxy and DNS; block 203.0.113.66 at the VPN | Network team (incident lead) | Keep logging hits on the blocks: later attempts are evidence of other footholds | Low |
| 5 | Disable `svc_update`; delete only after forensic imaging | IT ops (incident lead) | Deleting first destroys the persistence evidence | None |
| 6 | Memory and disk imaging of WS-104, then rebuild from a known-good image | Forensics (Course 09) | Hash images; custody records | WS-104 out of service until rebuilt |

Two points need to be stated explicitly in the advice rather than left to the reader. Resetting a password alone may leave existing sessions and tokens valid, which is why action 3 includes revocation. And the indicator blocks in action 4 will not stop an attacker who switches infrastructure; they are a containment measure, not a sign that the incident is over. The advice is a recommendation. Record who approved each action and when, in the single incident log.

### Step 6: Assemble the evidence package

`evidence_export.py` exports the raw stored JSON for one host and a time window (06:00 to 09:00 UTC by default), writes a SHA-256 manifest and appends a custody entry. Export WS-104 and, because the triage helper places gopal on WS-107, that laptop too:

```terminal
$ python evidence_export.py CASE-0001 WS-104
exported 32 events -> evidence\CASE-0001\WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
sha256 8521c97cab10c667d87b01db92fa9c45a5f130dfc314fb49c622eaf1f2919acf
$ python evidence_export.py CASE-0001 WS-107
exported 10 events -> evidence\CASE-0001\WS-107_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
sha256 1ab3194ca5e6e692dfb9ea7331a969ec47240968555aad3711427edfec4f1868
$ cat evidence/CASE-0001/SHA256SUMS
1ab3194ca5e6e692dfb9ea7331a969ec47240968555aad3711427edfec4f1868  WS-107_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
```

The WS-104 hash matches the hash published for this export in the course library text, because the query, ordering and line endings are fixed: reproducibility is part of trustworthiness. The 32 events are 28 proxy, 1 process and 3 Windows events; the 10 WS-107 events are all routine proxy requests.

The manifest, however, now lists only WS-107. The script writes `SHA256SUMS` with `write_text`, which *replaces* the file on every run, while `custody.jsonl` is opened in append mode and keeps one entry per export (it now has two lines, each with its item, event count, SHA-256, query and UTC time). An analyst who ran two exports and then shipped `SHA256SUMS` as the package manifest would hand over a manifest that silently omits the most important item. This is a real behaviour of the kit's tool, and exactly the kind of detail a tabletop never reveals.

The VPN events cannot be exported with this tool at all, because it selects by host and VPN events have none. Save them with a search instead, then rebuild the manifest over every item from inside the case folder:

```terminal
$ python minisiem.py search "SELECT raw FROM events WHERE source='vpn' AND ts >= '2026-11-03T06:00:00Z' AND ts < '2026-11-03T09:00:00Z' ORDER BY ts" > evidence/CASE-0001/vpn_2026-11-03_events.txt
$ cd evidence/CASE-0001
$ sha256sum WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl WS-107_2026-11-03_events.jsonl vpn_2026-11-03_events.txt > SHA256SUMS
$ cat SHA256SUMS
8521c97cab10c667d87b01db92fa9c45a5f130dfc314fb49c622eaf1f2919acf *WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
1ab3194ca5e6e692dfb9ea7331a969ec47240968555aad3711427edfec4f1868 *WS-107_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
7936f23ef9b779151e5500f4f577e83195406ffd6eb8ad91899dc67c344dccce *vpn_2026-11-03_events.txt
$ sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl: OK
WS-107_2026-11-03_events.jsonl: OK
vpn_2026-11-03_events.txt: OK
```

The `*` before each name is `sha256sum`'s binary-mode marker, which Git for Windows writes; `sha256sum -c` accepts it. The VPN file holds a header line `raw` and the 9 VPN events of the window. Because `search` prints through the console, on Windows the file has CRLF line endings, so the same query on Linux would give a different hash: record the platform, the exact query and that the file is a search output (not a `custody.jsonl`-tracked export) in a manual custody note. On PowerShell, `Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 <file>` gives the same digests in upper case.

Now prove that the manifest detects change. Work on a **copy**, never on the evidence itself:

```terminal
$ mkdir ../../check
$ cp WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl ../../check/
$ grep WS-104 SHA256SUMS > ../../check/SHA256SUMS
$ cd ../../check
$ sed -i 's/48200000/482000/' WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl
$ sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl: FAILED
sha256sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
```

Removing two digits from the upload size, the single most important number for the DPDP and CERT-In assessment, is detected at once. Delete the `check` folder afterwards (`cd .. && rm -r check`).

### Step 7: Write the incident report

The report is for the incident lead, legal and later reviewers. It states facts with sources, labels inferences, lists what is unknown and cites the evidence by hash. A model report, under 400 words:
