## Key takeaways

- A sandbox runs a suspicious object in an isolated, instrumented environment and reports its behaviour; it is the expensive step that comes after header checks, static checks and hash lookups.
- The report's evidence is the process tree, file activity, registry activity and network activity; the verdict is an opinion derived from signatures over that evidence.
- Every finding is limited to one environment, one run and one run time; long delays, environment and interaction checks, targeting and blocked networks all hide behaviour.
- A quiet run of an otherwise suspicious object is inconclusive, never proof of innocence.
- Uploading is a disclosure: look up the hash first, use private or contracted sandboxes for anything that may contain personal or business data, respect TLP and record every submission.
- Good case notes separate what the sandbox observed, what the real host confirms and what was not shown, and turn behaviour into searches, blocks and detections.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

A report from a colleague is a security observation. It can reveal suspicious messages the gateway delivered, an interaction the proxy cannot attribute, or an urgent payment conversation outside the normal alert feed. The report may arrive with very little context. An employee may say that an invoice looked strange, that their phone showed several authentication prompts, or that they entered information before noticing the address. The SOC needs an intake process that turns these different descriptions into useful, timely evidence. The quality of that process also determines whether people report the next suspicious message.

The first analyst should make it easy to do the right thing. Publish a known reporting route, give the reporter a clear acknowledgment, and ask only for facts that can change the response. Explain what will happen next in plain language. The employee should be able to continue the conversation without touching the suspicious content. A good exchange is brief enough for an anxious person to complete and specific enough that the next shift can understand why the case was escalated.

## Design the reporting route

Employees need a trusted way to reach the SOC from the applications where suspicious activity occurs. A reporting button can pair the user's intent with the original email and the organisation's normal case routing. A designated contact can help when the button is absent, such as on a phone or for a message received outside corporate mail. Publish these routes in onboarding and in a page employees can reach independently of any message. The route should explain how to report urgent credential, payment or endpoint events and whom to call if work communication is unavailable. A usability check should include mobile users, keyboard navigation and staff who need assisted reporting.

A supported reporting mechanism may preserve the original email and relevant metadata. Ordinary message forwards can change which content appears first, replace the original subject, or hide original routing information. If a reporter forwards a message to an unfamiliar person, the artifact can also reach an unintended mailbox. Accept the report you receive and record its acquisition method. Use policy to obtain the original, such as through a mail administrator's authorised export. A screenshot, pasted text or phone description can be enough to begin response. Each is better represented as a specific evidence type than treated as the same thing as preserved message bytes.

Treat work chat, messaging apps, voice and SMS reports similarly. Preserve the evidence that can be safely provided through the organisation's route. For example, document a reported phone call's time, apparent caller and claimed purpose, and note whether the employee disclosed information or acted. A phone number shown by caller ID is an observation of what was displayed. It does not establish who actually placed the call. Exposure affecting an employee's personal device requires the authorised incident and privacy process. Avoid taking custody of unrelated messages or devices when a more limited description can answer the response question.

## Ask questions that change the response

Capture the reported time, channel, account and affected device if relevant. Ask the reporter what they did after seeing the message and in what order. Useful questions include whether they replied, followed a link, entered information, approved a prompt, opened a file, or initiated a payment. Ask about time and the work service involved, without requesting sensitive values. A user can say that they entered a work password without telling anyone the password. A report that names an authentication prompt should say whether it was approved and what application it appeared to come from, as described by the user.

Requests should be concrete. ?Where did you see it and what did you do next?? is often better than ?Were you compromised?? The employee can report an action; the analyst will assess its security significance. Use neutral wording and allow for incomplete memory. People sometimes use ?opened? to mean they read the email, and sometimes mean they opened its file. Clarify that difference. If the employee estimates a time, record it as approximate. Later logs can corroborate or refine the timing, but they should not erase the source of the original statement.

A user may also be uncertain what information they entered. Ask about categories relevant to response, such as work credentials, financial information, or customer files, and route the answer to authorised owners. Do not ask them to re-create the action to see what happened. A second attempt can increase exposure, alter evidence and confuse the timeline. If continued contact in the original channel is risky, establish an independent recognised channel and record the handoff. The service desk, incident lead, identity team and finance team may each have a different safe channel, and predictable routing removes delay.

## Prioritise by the action and possible impact

The workflow links the type of reported interaction with the next responsible team. It is a triage aid for a first decision, followed by verification.

![Figure 9.6: Route a user report by interaction](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M09-L04-F1.svg)

*Figure 9.6: Route a user report by interaction. What the reporter did guides the first protective handoff and the checks that follow.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

Read each row as a combination of a reported action, a working risk and a request to an authorised owner. The first row says that a preserved suspicious message with no reported interaction needs delivery triage and classification. That remains worthwhile even if the individual reporter is safe. The message may have arrived in another inbox or the report may contain an important new artifact. The second row concerns a reported click with no information entry. The analyst asks which device and time, then compares the account with the available telemetry. A user statement can guide the search, and a request from an automated preview service does not verify that click.

The third row connects entry of a secret or approval of an unexpected authentication prompt with a prompt identity handoff. The analyst records the type of action and time, while the identity owner uses the organisation's response plan. The analyst gathering the original message can work in parallel with that response. The fourth row concerns an attachment the employee actually opened. Endpoint evidence can help assess what happened and whether another authorised action is needed. In that row, the initial action might be asking the endpoint owner to investigate the affected device without asking the employee to touch the file again.

The last row captures transfer of money or a change to payment instructions. Finance may have an immediate recovery or verification route and needs the report through an independent contact. This action can be urgent even when malware and sign-in signals are absent. Several rows can apply to a single report. If an employee clicked and approved a prompt, an identity escalation can occur before the mail action finishes. A support lead should keep the priorities and case links visible to each owner. What ties the rows together is the difference between the report and its later verification. Each report can justify careful response while the investigation determines which consequences the evidence supports.

## Link duplicates without losing details

An incident can produce many reports. Collapse repeat submissions by the same reporter into a single thread once you can show they refer to the same event. Group related recipient reports under a shared case when the evidence supports the relationship. Preserve the individual observations. The fact that one employee took no action is compatible with another submitting information. Retain the reported channel, time and affected identity for each record. Otherwise campaign grouping can hide exactly the exposure that requires a separate identity or endpoint handoff.

Avoid grouping only by subject text. Two campaigns may share a common subject, and automated prefixes or forwards can change it. Use available mail identifiers and trusted trace records to establish linkage. If only some attributes match, mark the relationship as a hypothesis. Revisit it as the mail team confirms message delivery and other sources show which systems or users were involved. Keep the original report accessible only within the approved case permissions. Campaign summaries can offer aggregate counts without unnecessary exposure of personal details.

The reported timestamp and the notice timestamp can matter for later review. Preserve both and record the time zone the user supplied, as well as your normalised timestamp where appropriate. If a precise event time is unknown, preserve an approximate window. This is often more honest than copying the ticket creation time into a field meant to record a click. Identify which part of the timeline comes from the source system and which comes from the reporter. A future review can then calculate intervals with meaningful endpoints rather than treating every field as equally reliable.

## Respond to the reporter

A useful acknowledgment confirms receipt and tells the employee what to do now. Thank them for reporting, give them a case or reference number if appropriate, and ask them to leave the suspicious message alone while the SOC works. Route urgent follow-up through the organisation's known channel. Keep the wording factual. A good reply can say ?We received your report and are reviewing the message. Please do not reopen it. If you entered information or acted on the payment request, contact the incident desk at the number in the company directory.? This keeps the employee oriented while protecting both the investigation and the user.

For a case with confirmed interaction, communicate the practical next step and owner. The responder may need the employee to stop using a device, wait for a call, or verify a business action through a separate process. Coordinate that message with the teams authorised to act. Fear and blame make people delay future reports or omit details. Focus on what the employee observed and what can be done to help. Avoid an expectation that the user will remember technical details or establish whether a security control worked.

Closing feedback can be simple. If policy permits, tell the reporter what category the SOC found, whether they need to do anything, and how they should report similar cases. Check that any message a person receives from the SOC is identifiable through a known route. If the evidence is incomplete, say the team reviewed the available records and state any remaining action; avoid reassuring them beyond what the records establish. The closure message can be generic in a broader incident and specific in a restricted case when the employee needs information about their own actions.

## Worked case: two reports and different priorities

Use a fictional finance campaign. At 08:05Z, a recipient in procurement presses Report suspicious on an apparent supplier notice. They viewed the subject but took no other reported action. The supported workflow saves the original and associates it with a case. The analyst records the employee's statement and asks the mail team to check the delivery trace. The account linked to the report is the mailbox recipient, not necessarily the device user or the person whose name appears in the message. The analyst acknowledges the report and gives a known route for updates.

At 08:09Z, an accounts payable employee calls the known service desk line about a notice with the same apparent supplier. They state that they used a work password on a linked page before seeing an unexpected prompt, which they did not approve. Payment records are unchanged as far as they know. The incident desk creates an identity handoff promptly with the interaction time and account. A mail analyst attempts to link the two reports using the trusted message trace and original artifacts. No password is copied into the ticket. The preliminary incident record treats them as possibly related, and the response to the second report does not wait for proof of that relationship.

At 08:14Z, the mail owner sees a preview request immediately after each delivery. That finding explains two automated observations; it cannot erase the employee's direct report that they took an action. Compare the device evidence and the reported window if such evidence exists. If telemetry misses the employee's mobile device, record this as a coverage gap. The identity owner can still act on the reported exposure and other authentication evidence. The correct resolution can include a tentative message classification, a definite protective response, and a statement of what additional data would be needed.

## Exercise and review criteria

Give one student the two fictional reports and another the role of incident lead. Have the intake analyst create one case entry per report and a short linking note. The first entry should make it easy to request the delivery check. The second should describe the reported credential interaction and a handoff to the identity owner. Give each entry a time and source. Then write an acknowledgment that can be shared without exposing the details of the other reporter. Swap roles and point out unclear or missing ownership.

Repeat the exercise with two changes. First assume the employee does not know whether the prompt was approved. Ask one question that reduces uncertainty without requesting a secret. Then assume the reporter used a private phone and offers to send an image of a page containing personal notifications. Decide which fields are necessary for the case and route collection through the organisation's approved process. The exercise tests whether you can retain useful evidence and reduce unnecessary disclosure at the same time. Finish with a shift note that distinguishes observed actions, possible impact and the pending verification request.

## Review the route with operational metrics

Track the time from report to acknowledgment and from reported exposure to an authorised handoff. Define each timestamp so repeat reports do not appear to speed up or slow down response inaccurately. Review cases that arrived through fallback routes to see whether the main route was available and understandable. Compare a sample of intake records with preserved artifacts and follow-up decisions. A reported increase can reflect improved trust in the reporting route rather than a change in incident frequency. Keep recipient-level details in the case and use aggregate counts in the process review.

## Key takeaways

- Offer a known, usable reporting route and preserve the best evidence available.
- Ask what the user did, when and in which channel, without collecting secrets.
- Group related cases while preserving each recipient's exposure and follow-up.
- Acknowledge useful reports promptly and route urgent risks to their authorised owners.

See [CISA's phishing tip sheet](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-09/Secure-Our-World-Phishing-Tip-Sheet.pdf) for general guidance on reporting suspicious messages.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

Phishing has two common goals. One is to put malware on a workstation, which is what happened to divya on WS-104 in the Banyan dataset. The other is to steal a credential, a session or a consent, so that the attacker can sign in as the victim and do whatever that person can do. The second kind of compromise is quiet. No process tree turns strange, no antivirus engine fires, and every action the attacker takes is, from the system's point of view, an authorised action by a legitimate user. ATT&CK files it under **Valid Accounts (T1078)**, and it is one of the most common ways intrusions start and persist.

Because an account compromise does not look like an attack, the analyst has to find it in the *pattern* of authentication and account activity. Somebody signs in from a place the user has never been, or from two places at once. A new authenticator app appears on the account the morning after a phishing campaign. A mailbox rule starts sending every message containing the word "invoice" to an external address and deleting the original. A user who only ever logs on interactively to one laptop suddenly authenticates over the network to a file server at three in the morning. None of these alone proves a compromise; each is a sign that raises a question the analyst must answer from other evidence.

This lesson teaches those signs, the telemetry each one lives in, the benign explanations that produce false positives, and how to combine weak signs into a defensible conclusion. The worked example uses the Banyan Microfinance dataset from the course lab kit, where gopal's VPN account (sales) authenticated from 203.0.113.66 after a burst of failures across eight accounts. You will rebuild that evidence with `minisiem.py` and see what the dataset can and cannot tell you about the session the attacker obtained. Lesson 6 turns the conclusion into containment; Lessons 1 to 4 covered the email itself, the links and attachments it carried, sandboxing and user reports.

> [!NOTE]
> All work in this lesson is defensive analysis of your organisation's own logs or the course's synthetic dataset. Investigating a user's sign-ins and mailbox is monitoring of personal data: do it under your organisation's acceptable-use and monitoring policy, record why you looked, and keep the findings on a need-to-know basis.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Account compromise | An unauthorised party holds the ability to act as an account: its password, a valid session or token, a registered authenticator, or a consent granted to an application. |
| Valid Accounts (T1078) | ATT&CK technique for using legitimate credentials to gain access, persist or move, rather than exploiting a flaw. |
| Password spraying (T1110.003) | Trying one or a few common passwords against many accounts, to stay under per-account lockout thresholds. |
| Impossible travel | Two sign-ins by one account whose locations are too far apart for the time between them to be covered by real travel. |
| Concurrent session anomaly | One account active from two incompatible places at the same time, for example an office workstation and an external VPN address. |
| Authenticator registration | Adding an MFA method (authenticator app, phone number, security key) to an account; attackers do it to keep access after a password reset (ATT&CK T1098.005, Device Registration). |
| MFA fatigue | Repeated push prompts sent in the hope that the user approves one (ATT&CK T1621, Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation). |
| Inbox rule | A mailbox rule that moves, deletes, marks or forwards messages automatically; attackers use them to hide replies (T1564.008, Email Hiding Rules) or to collect mail (T1114.003, Email Forwarding Rule). |
| Session token theft | Capturing a session cookie or token, for example through an adversary-in-the-middle phishing page, so that the attacker can replay a session that already passed MFA. |
| Baseline | The recorded normal behaviour of an account: usual devices, locations, hours, logon types and applications. Every sign in this lesson is a deviation from it. |

## Why compromised accounts are hard to see

An intrusion through malware leaves artefacts that are wrong in themselves: an Office application spawning PowerShell, a binary nobody installed, a beacon to a rare domain. An intrusion through a stolen credential leaves artefacts that are *right in themselves and wrong only in context*. A successful VPN logon is normal. A successful VPN logon for gopal, from an address that has just failed eight different accounts, while gopal's own laptop is browsing the intranet from inside the office, is not.

That shift has three consequences for the analyst.

**First, you need a baseline.** You cannot call a location unusual without knowing the usual ones, or a logon type rare without knowing which types the account normally uses. Identity platforms learn baselines automatically; in a smaller SOC the baseline may be a saved search of the last thirty days for that user.

**Second, you need several sources.** The identity provider records sign-ins and authenticator changes, the VPN gateway records remote sessions, the mail platform records rules and mailbox access, Windows records logons on each host, and the proxy shows where the user's device actually was. A sign that is ambiguous in one source is often resolved by another.

**Third, you reason in combinations.** Each sign has benign explanations. People travel, buy new phones, set up rules to file newsletters, and log on to servers for legitimate reasons. What turns a sign into a finding is coincidence with other signs and with a known trigger, such as a phishing campaign the user received or a spray that preceded the success.

## The four families of account compromise signs

### Impossible travel and location anomalies

The classic location sign compares two consecutive sign-ins. If the distance between their geolocated addresses, divided by the time between them, is faster than any realistic journey (commercial flight speeds are a common ceiling), at least one of the two sign-ins probably was not made by the user. Identity platforms ship this logic as detections named "impossible travel" or "atypical travel", usually combined with the account's learned locations so that a regular commute between two cities stops alerting.

The calculation is simple; the inputs are not. IP geolocation is an estimate, and it is often wrong for mobile carriers, satellite links and corporate egress points. A user on a corporate VPN or a cloud-hosted desktop appears to be wherever the provider's exit node is. Some sources do not record a usable location at all: in the Banyan VPN logs the attacker's session has the country field `??`. For that reason, the related **concurrent session anomaly** is often stronger evidence than distance. If one source shows the user's own device active on the internal network and another shows the same account authenticating from an external address in the same window, the two cannot both be the same person in the same place, whatever the geolocation database says.

Further location signs are a first sign-in from a country the organisation has no staff in, sign-ins from hosting providers or anonymising services instead of residential or corporate ranges, and sign-ins at hours the user never works.

### New MFA devices and authentication method changes

Multi-factor authentication raises the cost of a stolen password, so an attacker who gets past it once tries to make sure they never have to again. The most reliable way is to **register an authenticator of their own**: a new app instance, a phone number or a security key. After that, a password reset alone does not lock them out, because they can satisfy the second factor on their own device.

Authentication method changes therefore deserve attention far beyond their apparent severity. Course Module 4 cited the public account of how FireEye's 2020 investigation began: an alert that an employee's account had registered a second phone for MFA was followed up, the employee confirmed the device was not theirs, and the investigation uncovered a major intrusion. The lesson is that a low-priority identity alert, checked with the user through a known channel, can be the first thread of a large case.

Related signs include MFA methods removed or changed without a helpdesk ticket, a burst of push prompts that the user denies followed by one that is approved (MFA fatigue), a sign-in that satisfied MFA from a new device and a new location at once, and a self-service password reset followed within minutes by a method registration.

### Mailbox rules, forwarding and application consents

Once inside a mailbox, attackers commonly want two things: to read the victim's mail and to keep the victim from noticing. Mailbox rules deliver both. A **forwarding rule** sends copies of incoming mail, or mail matching keywords such as "invoice", "payment" or "bank", to an external address. A **hiding rule** moves replies from a particular correspondent, or anything containing words like "phishing", "hacked" or "suspicious", to a rarely viewed folder or deletes it, and may mark it as read. In business email compromise the pattern is classic: the attacker sends a fraudulent payment instruction from the real mailbox and a hiding rule makes sure the real user never sees the supplier's confused reply.

Rules are not the only mechanism. Many mail platforms also offer mailbox-level forwarding set by the user or an administrator, delegate permissions that give another account access to the mailbox, and organisation-wide transport rules. Cloud suites add **application consent**: an attacker who tricks a user into approving a malicious application gains a token that reads mail or files through the platform's API, which keeps working after the password changes (ATT&CK T1528, Steal Application Access Token). An analyst checking a suspect mailbox looks at all of these, not only at the rules list.

Signs in this family are a newly created rule that forwards externally or deletes, a rule with an odd name (single characters or punctuation are common), new forwarding settings, new delegates, and new application consents with mail or file permissions, especially when any of them appear soon after a suspicious sign-in.

### Unusual logons on hosts and services

On-premises and hybrid environments add Windows authentication to the picture. The Security log records successful logons (event 4624), failed logons (4625) and logons with explicitly supplied credentials (4648), and the logon type field says how the logon happened: type 2 is interactive at the console, 3 is network (for example a file share), 10 is RemoteInteractive (Remote Desktop), 11 is a cached interactive logon. Domain controllers add Kerberos events such as ticket requests (4768) and pre-authentication failures (4771).

The signs are deviations from the account's pattern: a user who only logs on interactively to one laptop appearing as a network or Remote Desktop logon on servers, logons to many hosts in a short time, logons outside working hours, failures with a status meaning "unknown user" (which suggests guessing names) rather than "wrong password", and an account used from a workstation that is not its owner's. For VPNs, the equivalents are a first VPN session for a user who never works remotely, sessions from unusual addresses, and a success from an address that has just produced failures for other users.

## Comparing the signs

The four families differ in where their evidence lives, how often they fire falsely and how directly they point to an attacker. The table below summarises them and records which ones the Banyan synthetic dataset can actually test, because a SOC that does not collect a source cannot see its signs at all.

![Figure 9.7: Account-compromise signs and visibility](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M09-L05-F1.svg)

*Figure 9.7: Account-compromise signs and visibility. Different activity requires different sources. The lab observes VPN and endpoint signals but omits provider and mailbox audit data.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

**Purpose.** The table is a field guide for the four sign families of this lesson. For each one it tells the analyst where to look, what most often causes a false alarm, how far the sign can be trusted alone, and whether the course dataset contains the telemetry to test it. It matters because analysts tend to reason from the signs their tools surface rather than from the signs the attacker leaves.

**Components.** The table has five columns: **Sign**, **Telemetry**, **Common benign cause**, **Weight alone** and **Banyan dataset**. Each of the four rows is one family. **Impossible travel / concurrent** draws on IdP and VPN sign-ins plus the proxy, is most often falsely triggered by VPN egress and geo-IP errors, has medium weight alone, and is testable in part through the available VPN and proxy sources. **New MFA device** draws on the IdP audit log, is most often benign because of a new phone, carries high weight, and is not testable in Banyan because the dataset has no IdP log. **Inbox / forwarding rule** draws on the mail audit log, is commonly benign for newsletter filing rules, carries high weight when the rule forwards externally or deletes, and is likewise absent from Banyan. **Unusual logon** draws on Windows 4624/4625 and VPN logs, is commonly benign for admin work and typing errors, carries low to medium weight, and is testable in Banyan.

**Relationships.** Rows are tinted by their tone: the two rows Banyan can test are blue, and the two it cannot are orange, to flag a telemetry gap rather than a weaker sign. The columns read left to right as a reasoning chain: from the sign, to the source to query, to the innocent explanation that must be ruled out, to how much the result is worth.

**Execution flow.** When an identity alert arrives, an analyst can use the table in order: identify the family, query the named telemetry, test the common benign cause first (call the user about the new phone, check the VPN egress list, read the rule), then weigh the result against the others.

**Decision logic.** The **Weight alone** column encodes the main judgement. A high-weight sign, such as an authenticator nobody in the helpdesk registered, justifies prompt escalation on its own once the benign cause is excluded. Low and medium signs are combined: an unusual logon plus a spray plus a concurrent session is far stronger than any of the three.

**Technical interpretation.** The benign causes are not random; they are the normal processes that use the same mechanism. Users legitimately register phones, file mail with rules and travel. That is why the detection must be followed by verification with the user or the owning team through a known channel.

**Practical example.** In Banyan, rule R2 fires for gopal. The blue rows say to look at the VPN and proxy sources, which the worked example does. The orange rows tell the analyst to record that MFA changes and mailbox rules for gopal could not be checked from the SIEM and must be requested from the identity and mail administrators.

**Security implications.** A SOC that ingests only the blue sources is blind to the two strongest signs. Collecting identity audit and mail audit logs is a detection investment, not a nicety.

**Key learning.** Each sign has a home in a specific log and a common innocent cause; weigh signs together, and record the families your telemetry cannot see as gaps, not as "nothing found".

## Worked example: reading the VPN evidence

In the synthetic Banyan records, the same source address appears on failed VPN authentications for eight different accounts from 06:42:00Z through 06:42:49Z. It then appears on a successful authentication for gopal at 06:46:00Z. The grouping across accounts matters more than the count on any one account. A bad password typed repeatedly by the owner of a single account would leave a different distribution. A shared gateway or a managed health-check process could also produce a cluster, so the source address, device context and normal use of that address remain important to the interpretation.

Start with the authentication rows in the training data. Record the precise observations: eight unique accounts, a 49-second observation span, and one later success for an account in that group from the same source. Record the inference separately: the failure pattern is consistent with password spraying, and the later success raises concern about unauthorised access. Ask the VPN owner whether the address belongs to known egress or a sanctioned testing system. If logs only identify the outcome, the SOC cannot say whether the successful connection established a usable session or what it did afterwards. Request session and network records when the exercise scenario assumes they exist. In the course kit, write down that these records are unavailable.

The queue associates the account with WS-107 from an inventory lookup. That lookup is useful for identifying the device owner and planning a check on the assigned laptop. The VPN record does not identify WS-107 as the device used for the successful login. An analyst who uses the lookup as observed client attribution may isolate the employee's legitimate device and still leave the actual session active. Ask the identity and VPN teams to verify and contain the observed session through their own approved controls. If endpoint checks show only routine traffic on WS-107, document the result with its time range. It limits a claim about the assigned workstation but cannot settle the origin of the independent VPN session.

## Writing the finding and the handoff

A practical escalation can be short. Identify the case and system, name the observed pattern, give the timestamp and reason for urgency, and specify what the receiving team should verify. For Banyan, the open questions are whether the VPN session was authorised, which client and session identifiers were attached to it, whether there were unrecognised authentication-method changes, and whether there are associated mailbox or workload changes. The SIEM has no mailbox audit trail in the exercise. Clearly assign that check to the mail administrator as a data request rather than presenting a clean result.

Consider a variation. An identity audit trail shows a new authenticator enrolled three minutes after the anomalous connection, but the employee says they recently replaced their phone. A helpdesk ticket matching the enrolment could explain the method change. Its existence does not explain the VPN pattern. Keep both hypotheses and look for a link in timestamps, device or event identifiers. Swap the variation: the employee denies both actions and the helpdesk has no enrolment record. That raises confidence and warrants prompt escalation even before you have confirmed later access. In either branch, record what the employee said and the channel used. A person responding on a mailbox or device under investigation may not be a reliable identity check.

## Practical application

Work from the saved R2 result and authenticated records printed in Module 8. Have a reviewer act as the identity owner and ask you for three observations and two next actions. Keep the observation format to timestamp, source, identity and result. Put the analyst's judgement in a separate sentence. Then repeat the drill after adding a fictional note that the source address is an approved corporate VPN exit. Decide what changes in your judgement and what evidence is still relevant. If the address is normal, the widespread sequence of failures followed by one success still deserves explanation. If the address is unknown, do not jump from suspicion to device attribution.

Finally, write a one-line data limitation for each unnecessary assertion you removed. An example is ?The course dataset provides VPN authentication outcomes but does not show command execution or application use inside the 06:46Z session.? This sentence lets the next reviewer decide what they need to request. The ability to describe where evidence ends is as important as the ability to recognise an account anomaly.

## Key takeaways

- Treat sign-in context, method changes, mailbox changes and endpoint behaviour as different sources of evidence.
- Check each deviation against known business activity and approved administrative changes.
- Use inventory enrichment as context and preserve the distinction between an assigned device and an observed client.
- Escalate actionable identity risk with evidence, confidence and precise questions for the owning team.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

In a phishing case, containment is the work of limiting further harm while the organisation confirms scope and prepares recovery. A message can remain reachable in a mailbox, a device can still communicate outward, an authenticated session can remain active, and a payment can still be awaiting approval. Different controls address these paths. An analyst's task is to translate evidence into a bounded recommendation, give it to an authorised owner and verify that it achieved the intended effect. Treat each action as a change with a purpose, an approval path and an observable result.

The right starting point depends on what is at risk. A report of suspicious delivery without evidence of interaction may call for mail-side actions and further scoping. An employee reporting a secret disclosure may need identity response at once. Endpoint evidence of harmful activity may justify urgent isolation. The mail team's exact classification can continue in parallel. A response can be both fast and evidence-aware when the teams agree who is responsible for each risk and what evidence collection can happen without delaying needed protection.

## Separate the response tracks

**Mail and content.** Work with the mail owner to locate the original and related deliveries. Confirm the precision of the search on known matching and benign examples before asking for a wide quarantine or purge. A subject line may be common. A display name can match both malicious and legitimate mail. Prefer trusted message, campaign or trace identifiers where they are available, and include an explicit time window. The owner should record how many objects matched, how many were acted on and why any were excluded. Quarantine may preserve a recoverable copy and limit exposure, depending on the platform and policy. Deletion requires particular care if records need to be preserved.

**Identity.** Ask the identity responder to establish which account and services are in scope. A password change and a session action address different forms of access. The organisation may also need to inspect unauthorised methods, changed recovery information, suspicious application grants or mailbox settings. The effect of a given action depends on the service and token type. Confirm it with that service's owner and request an effective timestamp. When employee communications are in doubt, coordinate verification through an independently known channel. Record the protective actions and how the user will regain approved access when it is appropriate.

**Endpoint.** When a verified device shows relevant execution or suspicious follow-on activity, involve the endpoint responder. An approved isolation mechanism can limit communication while retaining evidence for further assessment. The owner must check what communication the isolation mode permits, whether the management channel remains available and whether the response can affect critical operations. An offline device may queue an action until it connects again. Reporting ?action sent? is therefore a different claim from ?isolation is effective.? Record the user impact and provide a known way for the employee to get assistance or a clean replacement.

**Network and business process.** A destination restriction can reduce further access when the indicator is precise enough and the owner can verify the policy effect. Consider whether the domain or service is shared by legitimate work and whether the policy covers the relevant route and clients. Keep logs enabled when policy permits so the SOC can review later attempts. Independently, a suspected alteration of payment details may require verification or a hold through Finance. The response owner should confirm which transactions or vendors were affected and what downstream decisions remain under review. A mail control cannot resolve a payment action that already happened.

## Preserve evidence while limiting harm

Name the artifacts the decision depends on. These may include the original message and trusted delivery trace, relevant authentication and session records, endpoint observations and case notes. Save them in the approved evidence store and preserve collection details. Where authorised staff can do so safely, collect state that an action would erase or change. If a harmful action is ongoing, the incident lead may direct immediate containment ahead of additional collection. Document the reasoning, observed effect and resulting evidence gaps. The decision must be intelligible later to a reviewer who was not in the room.

Avoid treating a generic request such as ?block the campaign? as approval for any action that could fit the phrase. Specify which assets, time range and identifiers the proposed action applies to. Include how it will be executed and who can approve deviations. The responder should know whether they may take a reversible action while waiting for further confirmation and who decides if the tradeoff changes. If a case has only a suspicious message and no observed transaction, say that. If an employee reports approving an unexpected prompt, state that promptly and distinguish the reporter's statement from provider logs.

A decision record can fit in a brief text entry. Include the observed risk, effective scope, responder, approving role, expected effect, verification and next review. For example, a case can request temporary quarantine of message identifiers matched to three confirmed deliveries, with one preserved specimen and a search rerun to find additional copies. It should say who evaluates unintended matches and how a legitimate message could be restored. The count is a fictional example, but the fields are practical. Replace the count with confirmed values in the actual case instead of copying a sample recommendation.

## Verify the effect

The following decision path makes the difference between requesting a change and confirming its outcome visible.

![Figure 9.8: Containment from request to verification](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M09-L06-F1.svg)

*Figure 9.8: Containment from request to verification. A scoped, approved action is complete when its outcome is evidenced and remaining risk has an owner.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

The first step records a risk and its evidence. A mail delivery record, a reported credential entry and an endpoint process observation can each lead to a containment request, but they identify different assets and different effects. In the second step the incident lead identifies an owner and approves a bounded action. The plan says precisely which mail items, identities, devices or paths are in scope. It also identifies any evidence the action could change and any material operational cost. That preparation allows the team to choose a protective action without spending time debating ownership after it has triggered.

The third step combines evidence preservation with execution where circumstances permit. The responder records a request time and a result. The next step tests the effect from a source that can answer the question. If the mail team quarantines a set of messages, a disposition query can show which recipients are still exposed. If endpoint isolation was requested, look for the management result and review permitted endpoint and network observations. If the identity owner reports a session action, ask which services acknowledged it and what remains unknown. Do not ask a suspected user or a compromised system to perform a harmful action just to prove a block works. Use approved verification or safe test material.

The last step returns outstanding risks to the incident case. A control can succeed on two mailboxes and fail on a third, or a session action can complete while an unrelated account mechanism still needs review. The figure's loop sends that information back to the scoping step after recording the outcome. The owner can revise the plan when the evidence changes. For example, if the first search found two copies and a later message trace finds five, record the original decision's known scope and then approve the revised scope. This keeps the history auditable and gives the next shift a clear picture of effective protection and residual exposure.

## Worked example: the Banyan endpoint

The Banyan training dataset records an unusual download on WS-104 at 06:12Z and a suspicious Office child process at 06:14Z. Later records show unusual network activity and a 48.2 MB outbound transfer, whose contents are unknown. Those observations support prompt endpoint investigation and containment advice. In this dataset there is no original message or delivery trace, so it would be premature to list a campaign's recipients or claim a specific mailbox purge. The responding analyst should request authorised mail records from the owner if the scenario assumes they exist, and keep the endpoint case moving while that request is open.

A useful endpoint recommendation identifies WS-104 and references the process and network observations. Request isolation through the authorised endpoint owner under the incident lead's decision. Ask for an acknowledgment and timestamp, and confirm that continued collection is possible if needed. Capture available evidence according to the case procedure, without allowing optional collection to delay urgent protection. Include a plan for support to the legitimate user and for a clean route to essential duties. Make sure the report distinguishes the workstation's known signals from theories about the exact file content and the data in the transfer.

Separately, the training data records gopal's successful VPN authentication from an address associated with a burst of failures across users. A containment recommendation can ask the identity and VPN teams to review the session and act under the approved response plan. The data does not establish the endpoint used or show later activity inside that session. An inventory entry indicating gopal's usual workstation does not justify treating it as the observed client. Do not label the VPN and endpoint strands as one confirmed chain. The incident lead may coordinate the two responses while keeping the evidence and ownership distinct.

## Verify without making the case worse

Set a verification question before requesting each action. For mail, ask whether the correct objects were affected and how exceptions were handled. For endpoint, ask whether the targeted device reports the expected state and whether residual network evidence contradicts it. For identity, ask the owner to confirm which sessions and methods were acted on and to monitor for unexpected reappearance. For payment, ask Finance whether the identified case transaction is held or independently verified. A status field alone is insufficient when its definition is unclear. A completed request can still depend on a downstream system applying the change.

Use false-positive checks proportionate to the action. A proposed shared-domain restriction might affect many services, while a precise mail item quarantine may have a narrower cost. Start with the smallest scope that meaningfully reduces the identified risk when there is time and evidence to do so. Record why scope was expanded if related observations emerge. If the change causes an unrelated business outage, the incident lead needs a way to evaluate rollback, record the resulting risk and coordinate a safer control. A rollback is a decision with its own owner and timestamp, not an invisible erasure of the response.

Distinguish containment from recovery. A device may remain isolated for investigation. A user account may require a trusted re-enrolment and later monitoring. A transaction may remain held while Finance verifies it. Give each control a review owner and an end condition. If a closure criterion has not been met, retain the action and explain its operational impact. The case can move forward for other tracks. This discipline prevents an analyst from restoring an affected asset solely because the ticket has been open for a long time.

## Coordinate dependent actions

Two owners may need to act within the same response window. An identity action may prompt a user to contact the help desk, while the endpoint owner needs the user to leave a device in its current state. Agree on the order, the communication owner and the conditions under which either team should act immediately. The incident record should be clear about which step depends on which confirmation. If one central approver is unavailable and the response plan authorises a backup, record the route that was used. When different teams work from inconsistent asset names, reconcile them using approved inventory or evidence identifiers before applying a change.

A handoff is especially important on a shift boundary. Give the incoming analyst the current action states, the outstanding verifications, and the time each owner will next report. Include any time-limited access restriction or quarantine so the analyst can check whether it expires automatically. A temporary policy may be justified during an investigation but should have a review and an owner before it is left in place. Store the result next to the other case decisions. If the next shift concludes that the case requires wider scope, the prior record lets them expand the response with a clear reason rather than restarting the analysis.

## Key takeaways

- Recommend mail, identity, endpoint and business controls according to the evidence for each exposure.
- State decision authority, scope, preservation needs and operational effects.
- Verify observable outcomes and record any remaining gaps separately from the request.
- Give temporary controls a review owner and a clear end condition.

## Introduction and conceptual foundation

A phishing case is not finished when the malicious message has been purged from mailboxes and the affected workstation has been contained. Until the work is written down and sent to the people who need it, the organisation has learned nothing it can reuse, the people with legal duties cannot meet them, and the infrastructure that sent the message is still online, ready to target the next victim. **Reporting** is the step that turns one analyst's investigation into organisational knowledge, regulatory compliance and, through abuse reports, a small reduction in the attacker's capability.

Earlier lessons in this module took a phishing case through header analysis, URL and attachment checks, sandboxing, user reports, signs of account compromise and containment. Each of those steps produced facts: a sending IP address, a look-alike domain, a verdict from a sandbox, a list of recipients, the users who clicked, the hosts that ran something, the actions taken and their times. This lesson is about what happens to those facts next. It covers four reporting streams that leave the SOC after a phishing case:

1. **The phishing case report**, the internal record of what happened, what was done and what remains to do, written for the SOC, incident response, IT and management.
2. **Regulatory reporting**, which in India means assessing whether the incident must be reported to the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and supplying the facts for that report quickly.
3. **Abuse reports** to the providers whose services the attacker used: the registrar of a look-alike domain, the host serving a malicious file, the provider of a sending mail account.
4. **Metrics**, the numbers that show over time whether phishing defences, user reporting and SOC response are improving.

The streams share a source, the case record, but they differ in audience, content, timing and sensitivity. A case report can contain user names and internal host names because its readers are inside the organisation and need them. An abuse report to a hosting provider must contain enough evidence to justify a takedown and nothing more: no employee names, no internal addresses, no customer data. A regulatory report has its own content requirements and a clock. A metric strips away almost everything except times and counts. Learning to cut the same facts differently for each audience is the main skill this lesson teaches.

All names, domains and addresses are fictional or reserved for documentation. Lesson 8 works through this case hands-on.

## Key terminology

| Term | Precise meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Case report | The internal written record of a case: summary, timeline, indicators, scope, actions, impact and follow-up, kept in or attached to the case system. |
| BLUF | "Bottom line up front": the convention of putting the conclusion and the decision needed in the first lines, before the supporting detail. |
| CERT-In | The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, the national agency for incident response under section 70B of the Information Technology Act 2000. |
| CERT-In Directions | The directions issued by CERT-In on 28 April 2022 under section 70B(6) of the IT Act, which include reporting specified cyber incidents within six hours of noticing them. |
| Point of Contact (PoC) | The person an organisation designates to interface with CERT-In; usually in security or compliance, not the analyst on shift. |
| Abuse report | A notification to a service provider (registrar, host, mail provider) that its service is being used for malicious activity, with evidence, asking it to act under its own terms. |
| Defanging | Rewriting an indicator so it cannot be clicked or resolved by accident, for example `hxxps://banyan-payroll-update[.]example/invoice.docm`. |
| TLP | Traffic Light Protocol (version 2.0 published by FIRST in August 2022): labels CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER+STRICT and RED that tell recipients how far they may share information. |
| MTTA / MTTR | Mean time to acknowledge and mean (or median) time to resolve: the interval from alert creation to an analyst taking ownership, and to closure. |
| Report-to-purge time | For phishing, the interval from the first user report (or detection) to removal of the message from every mailbox. |

## Why reporting is part of the response, not paperwork after it

New analysts often treat the report as the boring end of a case. Three observations show why mature SOCs treat it as part of the response itself.

**Decisions depend on it.** The shift lead decides whether a phishing case becomes a declared incident, legal decides whether a regulatory notification is required, and IT decides whether to rebuild a workstation, all on the basis of what the analyst writes. A report that buries "PowerShell ran on a payments approver's workstation" in paragraph six can delay each of those decisions by hours.

**Clocks run while it is written.** The CERT-In Directions give six hours from noticing a reportable incident. That window covers detection, triage, escalation, a legal assessment and the submission itself. If the analyst's notes are scattered across chat messages and a half-filled case form, the people preparing the submission spend the window reconstructing facts instead of checking them.

**The attacker's infrastructure is still live.** A look-alike domain that delivered one macro document to Banyan Microfinance is probably being used against other organisations too. An abuse report to its registrar or host, sent the same day, can take it offline for everyone. Sent a week later, it often arrives after the campaign has moved on.

Reporting also feeds the module's earlier lessons in reverse. Indicators in the case report become blocklist entries and hunt queries; the timeline shows which detection fired first and which should have fired earlier; the metrics show whether user reporting is working. A SOC that does not report well cannot tune well.

## The phishing case report

The case report is the parent document: every other stream is derived from it. It is written progressively, from the first triage note onwards, and finalised when the case closes. A phishing case report has a recognisable structure because readers come to it with predictable questions.

### Structure

| Section | What it contains | Why it is there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Header | Case ID, title, severity, status, analyst, dates, TLP marking | Lets a reader find, file and handle the report correctly |
| Bottom line | Two to four sentences: what happened, current status, decision needed | Most readers stop here; it must stand alone |
| Message details | Sender, envelope sender, subject, delivery time, authentication results, number of recipients | Shows how the message arrived and why filters did or did not stop it |
| Indicators | Domains, URLs, IP addresses, file names and hashes, each defanged | Feeds blocking, hunting and sharing |
| Scope | Recipients, users who reported, users who clicked or opened, hosts with execution, accounts with suspicious sign-ins | Separates "delivered" from "engaged" from "compromised" |
| Timeline | UTC timestamps, one event per line, each with its source | Lets anyone re-check the sequence against the logs |
| Actions taken | Purge, blocks, isolation, resets, with time and who did it | The record of response, and the basis for later review |
| Impact | What data, systems or money were affected, or "none identified", with confidence | Drives the legal and business decisions |
| Notifications | CERT-In assessment, DPDP assessment, internal notifications, abuse reports sent | Shows obligations were considered, by whom and when |
| Root cause and gaps | Which control failed or was missing; which detection fired late or not at all | Turns the case into improvements |
| Follow-up | Open actions, each with an owner and due date | Prevents closed cases with open risks |
| Evidence appendix | Exported logs, the original message file, sandbox report, with SHA-256 hashes and custody entries | Makes the report verifiable |

Two distinctions in this table cause most of the arguments in real case reviews.

The first is the **scope ladder**: delivered, opened, clicked, executed, compromised. A phishing campaign that reached 40 mailboxes is a very different event from one where a single user ran a macro. Each rung needs its own evidence. "Delivered" comes from the mail gateway's message trace. "Clicked" requires interaction evidence, such as user confirmation or a qualified session event, with automated previews and normal resolver activity considered. "Executed" comes from endpoint telemetry such as Sysmon event 1. "Compromised" requires evidence of attacker activity after execution, such as a new account, persistence or command-and-control traffic. Writing "40 users compromised" because 40 received the message is the most common and most damaging overstatement in phishing reports.

The second is **fact versus assessment**. "WS-104 requested `invoice.docm` from `banyan-payroll-update.example` at 06:12:00Z (proxy log)" is a fact. "The document contained a malicious macro" is an assessment, supported by the fact that Word started a hidden, encoded PowerShell command two minutes later. Good reports label assessments and give their confidence, so that a reader can tell what would change if new evidence appeared.

### The bottom line, worked through

For the Banyan case at the point of escalation, a weak bottom line reads: "A phishing email was received and the user may have clicked a link. Investigation ongoing." It contains no host, no user role, no evidence of execution and no request.

A strong one reads:

```text
BOTTOM LINE (TLP:AMBER)
A payments approver (divya, WS-104) downloaded invoice.docm from the
look-alike domain banyan-payroll-update[.]example at 06:12Z; Word started
a hidden encoded PowerShell command at 06:14Z, and WS-104 then contacted
cdn-telemetry-sync[.]example every 300 s. Assessed: malicious document
executed, workstation compromised (high confidence). Available proxy records for the scoped period show no second host
contacting those domains. Requested: approval to isolate WS-104 and revoke
divya's sessions; legal to assess CERT-In reporting.
```

It names the asset and why it matters (a payments approver), gives the evidence for execution, states the assessment with its confidence, bounds the scope to the available proxy records and asks for specific decisions. Every claim in it can be checked against the dataset, which Lesson 8 does.

### Timelines in UTC

Write every timestamp in UTC with the `Z` suffix, because the logs, CERT-In and external providers all need a shared reference. Where management prefers Indian Standard Time, add IST (UTC+05:30) in brackets rather than replacing UTC; 06:12Z is 11:42 IST. Give the source of each line so that a reviewer can re-run the query. A timeline entry without a source is an anecdote.

### Handling marks and personal data

A phishing case report contains personal data: the names of recipients and clickers, their mailboxes and sometimes the content of their mail. Apply your organisation's privacy and retention procedures to this data and ask the privacy owner to determine applicable requirements. In practice: mark the report (TLP:AMBER is common for internal case reports), restrict access through the case system, and when you derive other reports from it, remove names unless the recipient genuinely needs them. A metric does not need to know who clicked; an abuse report never does.

> [!WARNING]
> Do not paste live malicious URLs into case notes, chat channels or email. Many clients render links automatically, preview services fetch them, and a colleague can click one by mistake. Defang every indicator in prose (`hxxps://`, `[.]`) and keep the original form only in the evidence file, where it is needed for blocking and searching.

## Communicating scope in stages

The figure gives an editor's checklist for the report. Use it to find the sources behind each claim before publishing a count or an impact statement.

![Figure 9.9: Evidence needed for phishing scope claims](/assets/courses/cyber-08/v2/C08-M09-L07-F1.svg)

*Figure 9.9: Evidence needed for phishing scope claims. Record the strongest claim supported by the available sources for each asset or identity.*

### Visual Walkthrough & Architectural Breakdown

Begin with delivery. A recipient appears in this stage when a trusted mail transport or store records a completed delivery, or another defensible record establishes that the message reached their mailbox. A rejected message or one held at the gateway belongs in a different disposition count. Several logs can describe the same message travelling through different internal systems. A combination of message identifiers, recipient and disposition can prevent double counting. This stage answers how widely the message was distributed, with the search interval and gateway coverage stated in the report.

The interaction stage uses a recipient's statement or a reliable event tied to the recipient's session. Some mail systems fetch previews automatically and security gateways can visit destinations during pre-delivery analysis. A proxy or DNS request by itself does not settle who acted or whether a browser followed the URL. Record automated checks separately where they can be identified. If the user reports opening an attachment and the device's audit trail is unavailable, write those two facts together. The report can proceed while the team tries to recover endpoint visibility.

The execution and compromise rows illustrate an evidentiary distinction. Device telemetry may show that an application ran or opened a file. To support a conclusion about compromise, append evidence of suspicious behaviour and tie it to the asset or identity under investigation. An identity compromise may also be supported by authentication and service audit evidence even when no payload ran on a workstation. The rows describe claims that can be tested independently. They do not require every incident to pass through the same progression. An analyst finishing the Banyan report can therefore say that the available proxy and endpoint records support one important execution finding while the total number of delivered messages cannot be established from this dataset. That leaves the mail team a clear question and avoids publishing a guessed denominator.

## Report variants and approval

The case record holds the most detailed account. Include the evidence references, the reviewer, the known gaps and the reasons for both actions taken and actions deferred. Attach approved exports or refer to their restricted location. Use incident and evidence identifiers instead of reproducing complete sensitive message bodies in an update. If a conclusion changes, preserve the prior version and explain the new evidence. Use explicit draft and approval dates so a reader can tell which conclusions were available at the time of each operational decision. A statement sent during first response usually has less context than the final assessment and should carry its own timestamp.

An executive summary needs the business impact, current response status, open decisions and the next time an update will be available. An analyst handoff needs time ranges, specific sources, identifiers, ownership and verification requirements. A report for an external recipient should contain only what the responsible organisational owner has approved for that audience. FIRST's Traffic Light Protocol helps express distribution expectations and does not itself authorise release. Native access controls, contracts and any other applicable requirements still govern what can be shared. The incident lead should resolve incompatible distribution constraints before the report leaves its current audience.

Record a notification decision separately from the technical severity. Capture who owns it, when the relevant facts and timestamps were passed to them, what was decided and whether follow-up is due. A SOC analyst can document the case timeline and supply evidence without treating a severity label as a legal opinion. Use the organisation's approved response plan for applicable duties and routes.

## Worked update

Consider the synthetic source records in Module 8. A proxy record shows that WS-104 sent 48.2 MB to an unfamiliar destination at 08:12Z. A Windows record subsequently indicates the Security log was cleared. A useful update states both events, their sources and the reason the lead should review the case promptly. It says the transferred content is unknown, and it asks which team can corroborate what the destination received. It also records which earlier claims about the endpoint were based on the process and network sequence.

A report should also state where the VPN thread stands. A suspicious authentication for a different identity overlaps the main event window. Timing supports further investigation, but no shared identifier in the course evidence establishes a common actor. A later lead might obtain a common session, a device fingerprint or another corroborating record, at which point the report can be revised. Until then, the response can assign a distinct owner to verify and contain that identity risk. Separate issue tracking can coexist with a single incident lead.

## Practical application

Write a four-sentence update for an incident manager. Sentence one identifies the affected business process and current risk. Sentence two gives two timestamped observations and their sources. Sentence three states one assessment and its confidence or one important uncertainty. Sentence four names an action owner, the requested decision and the next update time. Then write one paragraph for the technical analyst. Include the exact search interval and collection gaps that qualify your scope claim. Ask a colleague to highlight each unsupported assertion and each action missing an owner.

When comparing versions, pay special attention to negative results. Replace a broad claim about what did not happen with a precise description of the search, the result and its boundary. An example is ?The available proxy records for the six-hour review window show no second host requesting the observed destination.? That lets the reader compare a later search and understand whether a newly found host is a change in evidence or simply an expansion in search scope. Clear reporting supports collaboration, and it also protects the people whose data the incident team must review.

## Key takeaways

- Ground every impact and scope claim in a source and a defined window.
- Give the next reviewer the decision, owner and evidence needed to verify it.
- Keep evidence in the approved record and adapt each report to its audience.
- Update uncertainty as new records arrive, including what changed and when.

## Step 1: Count the matching proxy and VPN records

Run the following Python in the folder containing the extracted fixture. The script opens the saved data as text, parses JSON lines and groups exact host matches from proxy URLs. The URL parser only separates text fields. It does not open a connection. The resolved path is relative to your working folder, so check the filename and location if Python cannot read it.

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

rows = [json.loads(line) for line in Path("banyan_events.jsonl").read_text(
    encoding="utf-8"
).splitlines()]
case_hosts = {
    "banyan-payroll-update.example",
    "cdn-telemetry-sync.example",
    "files-share-drop.example",
}
for domain in sorted(case_hosts):
    hits = [
        row for row in rows
        if row.get("source") == "proxy"
        and urlsplit(row.get("url", "")).hostname == domain
    ]
    hosts = sorted({row["host"] for row in hits if row.get("host")})
    first = min((row["@timestamp"] for row in hits), default="-")
    last = max((row["@timestamp"] for row in hits), default="-")
    print(domain, len(hits), ",".join(hosts), first, last)

vpn = [
    row for row in rows
    if row.get("source") == "vpn"
    and row.get("src_ip") == "203.0.113.66"
]
failed_users = {row["user"] for row in vpn if row.get("outcome") == "failure"}
successes = sorted(
    (row["@timestamp"], row["user"])
    for row in vpn if row.get("outcome") == "success"
)
print("VPN distinct failed users:", len(failed_users))
for timestamp, user in successes:
    print("VPN success:", timestamp, user)
```

cdn-telemetry-sync.example 18 WS-104 2026-11-03T06:17:00Z 2026-11-03T07:42:02Z
files-share-drop.example 1 WS-104 2026-11-03T08:12:00Z 2026-11-03T08:12:00Z
VPN distinct failed users: 8
VPN success: 2026-11-03T06:46:00Z gopal

Every proxy match returned by this check names WS-104. That is a bounded statement about three exact hostnames in the available fixture. It says nothing about domains the search did not include, traffic that bypassed proxy collection, or additional mail recipients. The eighteen rows name one observed host, not eighteen affected users. Write the positive observations and the scope limit beside each other. A reviewer should be able to distinguish a low count caused by a narrow search from a true high-confidence exclusion.

The VPN results answer a different question. There are eight distinct identities with a failure from the selected address, and the data records a successful authentication for gopal. The query does not show the user behind the session or any later session activity. The VPN records do not name a host, and the ordinary workstation associated with an account in inventory is not the observed source device. Keep the authentication as an identity lead with a separate owner. A defensive analyst can ask the VPN team to verify session and source details without assuming it is the same actor as the workstation case.
