## Review and troubleshoot the work

If the proxy check produces zero rows for a hostname, first confirm that the file is the C08 fixture and that the parsed field is present. Compare the lane names in the fixture with those selected by the script. Checking the wrong file or a changed version can cause an empty result. Preserve a note of the version used and avoid changing only the query until it returns the expected count. If an event appears later or earlier than the course example, confirm UTC and check whether you copied the field from the source or from an enriched view.

Have a second student audit three conclusions. Ask them to point to the record that supports the endpoint action, the data gap that prevents definite mail scope and the evidence that bounds the VPN finding. Then ask them to locate the action owner, approval status and verification method for each proposed action. For a deliberate error, change ?available proxy records show one host? to ?one user received the message.? A reviewer should reject the second statement and be able to explain what source would be required. This is a check of reasoning and source coverage as much as a check of the answer.

For a second variation, suppose the authorised mail owner later confirms five deliveries and one blocked message in an additional hypothetical record. Update the handoff with the new source, time and disposition. Do not revise the proxy count. Then suppose the only observed access to a link from another mailbox was an automated preview. Record the preview as service activity and leave human interaction unknown. The updated exercise illustrates why later facts should add to or revise a particular assessment without silently changing the historical record of what the analyst knew.

## Check the evidence package as a second analyst

A complete practical submission includes the case worksheet, a copy of the observed output and a short record explaining how the check was reproduced. Include the fixture name, the selected sources and the three exact hostnames. If you also record a digest, include which copy it describes. A checksum can verify whether a later copy contains the same bytes. It cannot establish whether all necessary events were collected into the original fixture. The reviewer should be able to re-run the read-only check and point to the limits that remain even when the output matches.

Next compare the list of records with the written decision. Every affirmative claim should have a matching source, and every negative claim should have a time and collection boundary. Pay particular attention to statements that changed meaning when shortened for management. For instance, ?there was no additional matching proxy host in the supplied fixture? can become ?no other device was affected? if the source and match condition are dropped. Restore the shorter but accurate wording before approving the handoff. A comparison of claim, source and gap can be performed without exposing the full evidence record to every reader.

Finally, verify the response section against the case decision. The worksheet should identify who approves isolation, which endpoint is proposed for protection, and what record the responder would use to prove completion. It should also identify the outstanding request for mailbox evidence and the separate owner for the identity question. The reviewer can sign off the reasoning even when the simulated operational actions remain pending. Mark both outcomes clearly. In a training exercise, a conclusion that the evidence is insufficient for a particular claim is a useful result when it names the missing source and the person responsible for obtaining it.

## Key takeaways

- Read the saved records and preserve a traceable observation before drawing a conclusion.
- Report search scope and visibility explicitly, especially for negative results.
- Route the endpoint, identity and mail decisions to the appropriate owners.
- A verified lab output and a proposed operational response are different deliverables.

## Why hunting starts with a hypothesis

Threat hunting is the proactive search for adversary activity that existing detections did not alert on. A hunt is different from an alert triage: in triage, a rule has already fired and the analyst decides what it means. An earlier alert can motivate a wider hunt. The hunter decides what to look for, where to search and what evidence would support or refute the hypothesis. Without that decision made up front, a hunt drifts into browsing. The analyst opens a SIEM, scrolls through events, notices things that look odd, and spends an afternoon without being able to say what was tested or what was ruled out.

A hypothesis is the tool that prevents that drift. It is a short, testable statement about a behavior that might be present in a defined part of the environment, written so that the data can support it, contradict it, or fail to address it. The hypothesis does three jobs at once. It tells the analyst which records to pull. It tells a reviewer what the hunt was and was not about. And it tells the team what to do next, because a supported, refuted, or untestable hypothesis each leads to a different follow-up.

This lesson treats hypothesis design as its own skill. Later lessons in the module cover the data a hypothesis needs, the queries that test it, the baselines that give its predictions meaning, ATT&CK as a source of behaviors, documentation, and validation. All of those depend on getting the hypothesis right first. A weak hypothesis cannot be rescued by a clever query.

## The anatomy of a testable hypothesis

A useful hunt hypothesis has five parts. Not every team writes them in the same order, but a hypothesis missing any of them is usually hard to test.

**Behavior.** What would an adversary, or a misused account, actually be doing? Behaviors are verbs about systems: a document application starting a command interpreter, one source address failing authentication for many different accounts, a workstation sending far more data outbound than it usually does. A behavior is not a threat actor name, a malware family, or a feeling that something is wrong.

**Scope.** Which entities and which time window are in play? Scope might be "all Windows workstations in the finance subnet" or "VPN authentication events on 2026-11-03 UTC." Scope keeps the hunt finite and makes the result interpretable. A hypothesis about "the network" over "recent weeks" cannot be cleanly refuted.

**Observable predictions.** If the behavior happened in scope, what would the records show? A good hypothesis has at least two predictions, ideally from different sources, because one prediction alone often has many innocent causes. Predictions name fields and values, such as "a proxy request from the host to a domain not seen in the prior 30 days, followed within 10 minutes by an endpoint process event whose parent is an Office application."

**Refuting evidence.** What result would make the analyst say the hypothesis is not supported? Writing this before looking at data is the single most effective guard against confirmation bias. If the analyst cannot state what would refute the hypothesis, the hypothesis is not yet testable.

**Data feasibility.** Which sources would hold the predicted observations, and are they available for the scope? This part is covered in depth in the next lesson, but it belongs in the hypothesis statement because it decides whether the hunt can produce a supported or refuted outcome at all, or only a no-data outcome.

A compact template many teams use is: "If [behavior] occurred on [scope] during [window], we expect to see [prediction A] in [source] and [prediction B] in [source]. If we see [refuting result], the hypothesis is not supported."

## Where hypotheses come from

Hypotheses are not invented from nothing. They come from a handful of recurring sources, and knowing the source helps the analyst judge how much weight to give the result.

**Threat intelligence.** A report describes a behavior relevant to the organization's sector, such as attackers sending invoice-themed documents to finance staff. The analyst turns the reported behavior into a local question: did any finance workstation open an Office document and then spawn an unusual child process in the reporting window? Intelligence-driven hypotheses inherit the uncertainty of the report, so the hunt should test the behavior, not just the indicators in the report, which may have already changed.

**ATT&CK behaviors.** The ATT&CK knowledge base describes adversary tactics and behaviors in a common vocabulary. A hunter can pick a behavior that the organization has little detection coverage for and ask whether it is present. Lesson 5 covers this in detail.

**Situational awareness.** Something changed in the environment: a new remote access product was rolled out, a merger added unmanaged laptops, or a team began working from a new region. Changes create both new attack surface and new noise, and a hypothesis can target either.

**Prior incidents and near misses.** If an earlier incident involved a specific behavior, the team can hunt for the same behavior elsewhere to check whether it was isolated. This is one of the most productive hypothesis sources because the behavior is known to be realistic for the environment.

**Baseline anomalies.** A frequency analysis shows a rare value, such as a domain contacted by only one host. Anomalies are prompts, not hypotheses. The analyst still has to state what behavior the anomaly might represent and what else would be true if it did.

**Analyst observation during other work.** During triage of an unrelated alert, an analyst notices something that does not fit. Writing it down as a hypothesis, rather than chasing it immediately, lets the team prioritize it alongside other work.

## Hypothesis versus conclusion

The most common design error is writing a conclusion and calling it a hypothesis. "WS-104 was compromised by a phishing document" is a conclusion. It names a cause (phishing), a mechanism (a document), and an outcome (compromise), and in the saved Banyan dataset, none of the three can be directly observed. There is no mail gateway log, no mailbox audit, and no direct payload evidence. A hunt organized around that statement will either reach a conclusion it cannot support or quietly redefine success along the way.

The testable version narrows to what the records can show. The saved-record Banyan facts describe a proxy request from WS-104 to banyan-payroll-update.example at 06:12:00Z on 2026-11-03, an Office child process recorded by endpoint data at 06:14, eighteen requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example from 06:17:00Z through 07:42:02Z, and one request to files-share-drop.example at 08:12:00Z with 48,200,000 outbound bytes recorded by the proxy. A testable hypothesis would read:

"If a downloaded file led to code execution on WS-104 on 2026-11-03, we expect a proxy download shortly before an endpoint process event with an Office parent, and later outbound requests from WS-104 to destinations not seen on peer workstations. If no Office child process follows the download, or if the later destinations are common across peers, the hypothesis is not supported."

Notice what this version does not claim. It does not say how the file arrived, because the dataset cannot show mail. It does not say what was in the 48,200,000 bytes, because payload is unknown. It does not say the activity was malicious; it states what pattern would be consistent with execution and what would contradict it.

## Scoping: entities and time

Scope is where many otherwise good hypotheses fail. Two scoping decisions matter most.

**Entity scope.** Choose the population that the behavior could plausibly affect and that the data covers. If endpoint telemetry exists for workstations but not servers, a hypothesis about Office child processes should be scoped to workstations, and the documentation should say servers were out of scope because of data, not because they are safe. Entity scope also controls false linking. In the Banyan brief, the VPN thread involves identities authenticating from 203.0.113.66, including a successful authentication for gopal at 06:46, while the proxy and endpoint thread involves WS-104. No observed client or session identifies WS-104 as the source of gopal's successful VPN authentication: the VPN events carry no endpoint identifier and no later session activity. A hypothesis that assumes gopal used WS-104 has smuggled in a link the data does not contain.

**Time scope.** Choose a window wide enough to include the predicted sequence and its plausible precursors, but narrow enough that rare events remain rare. A window of a few hours around the Banyan proxy events is appropriate for testing a download-then-execution sequence. A baseline window, discussed in Lesson 4, is a separate and usually longer period used to decide what is normal. State all times in UTC and say so; mixing local time and UTC is a frequent source of false sequences.

## Writing predictions that discriminate

A prediction is useful when it is more likely to be observed if the hypothesis is true than if it is false. Analysts sometimes call this the discriminating power of a prediction. "WS-104 made proxy requests" has almost no discriminating power, because every workstation makes proxy requests. "WS-104 made a request to a domain first seen that day, followed within minutes by an Office application starting a child process" is much stronger, because benign workstations rarely produce that pair.

Three techniques improve discrimination:

1. **Combine sources.** A prediction that requires agreement between proxy and endpoint data is harder to satisfy by coincidence than one that requires a single source.
2. **Specify order and timing.** A download followed by execution within ten minutes is more specific than a download and an execution on the same day.
3. **Specify rarity.** A destination seen on one host is more interesting than one seen on every host. Rarity needs a baseline, which is why hypothesis design and baselining are linked.

Discrimination has a cost. Very specific predictions miss variants. If the hypothesis requires the Office parent to be a word processor, it will miss a spreadsheet parent. The analyst should write predictions at the level of the behavior, not the tool, and note deliberate exclusions.

## Writing refuting evidence first

Before pulling data, write down the results that would count against the hypothesis. For the WS-104 example, refuting results include: the endpoint process event precedes the download, which breaks the proposed order; the Office child process is a known update helper that appears on most workstations at that time each day; or the later destinations appear on many peer workstations with similar volumes.

For a VPN hypothesis such as "a single external source attempted authentication against many Banyan identities in a short period," refuting results include: the failures are spread across many source addresses, the identities are all the same account retrying, or the source address belongs to a known partner gateway that aggregates many legitimate users. Writing these first does two things. It keeps the analyst honest when a result is ambiguous, and it tells the reviewer what alternatives were considered.

Refutation is not failure. A refuted hypothesis is a completed hunt that has reduced uncertainty. The team now knows that, in the stated scope and window, the behavior was not present in the available data, and it can record that as a negative result.

## The three outcomes and what they mean

Every hypothesis should be designed so it can end in one of three outcomes, which the course uses throughout the module.

**Positive (supported).** The predictions were observed and the refuting results were not. A positive outcome is not proof of compromise; it means the pattern is present and warrants escalation or further validation.

**Benign (refuted or explained).** The predictions were not observed, or they were observed but a validated benign explanation accounts for them, such as a scheduled software update confirmed by an asset owner.

**No-data (untestable).** The required data was missing, incomplete, or could not be joined, so the hypothesis could not be tested. A no-data outcome is a real finding about visibility and should be recorded with the specific gap.

The Banyan VPN thread illustrates a likely no-data outcome for some questions. The hypothesis "the successful gopal authentication at 06:46 was followed by unusual session activity" cannot be tested because the VPN records contain no later session activity. The hunt can still test a narrower hypothesis about the authentication pattern itself, which the saved-record VPN summary does support: eight distinct identities failed from 203.0.113.66 and gopal succeeded at 06:46:00Z.

## Prioritizing hypotheses

Teams usually have more hypotheses than time. A simple scoring approach weighs three factors.

**Impact.** If the behavior were present, how bad would it be? Data leaving a finance workstation scores high at a microfinance organization.

**Plausibility.** How likely is the behavior given threat intelligence, prior incidents, and environment? A behavior seen in a recent sector report and consistent with saved anomalies scores higher than a theoretical one.

**Feasibility.** Can the available data test it? A high-impact hypothesis that only cloud identity audit logs could answer, when the dataset has none, scores low on feasibility. The analyst should still record it as a visibility gap, because the gap itself is worth fixing.

Ranking is a judgment call, and the justification matters more than the numbers. A short sentence for each factor is enough for a reviewer to agree or disagree.

## Bounded case reasoning

Consider three synthetic hypothesis drafts from a fictional review session. These are authored for this lesson and are not Banyan source data.

**Draft A:** "Check if anything bad happened on finance laptops last month." This names no behavior, no prediction, and no refuting result. Its scope is vague. It should be rejected and rewritten.

**Draft B:** "If an account was used from a new external address, we expect a successful VPN authentication from an address not seen for that account in the prior 30 days, and a failure burst from the same address within the preceding hour." This is testable if VPN data covers 31 days. It scores well on discrimination because it combines novelty with a preceding failure burst. Its refuting result is a successful authentication with no prior failures from the same address, which is more consistent with travel than with guessing.

**Draft C:** "Attackers exfiltrated customer data from WS-104 to files-share-drop.example." This is a conclusion. The proxy count of 48,200,000 outbound bytes shows volume, not content, and the payload is unknown. The testable rewrite asks whether WS-104's outbound volume to that destination departs from the peer baseline and whether the destination appears elsewhere.

The reasoning is bounded because each judgment refers to what the stated records could show. None of the drafts is improved by speculation about attacker intent.

## Common errors

- **Writing conclusions instead of hypotheses.** The statement names a cause the data cannot observe.
- **No refuting evidence.** Any result can be read as support, so the hunt cannot end.
- **Scope too broad.** "All systems, all time" produces unmanageable noise and an unfalsifiable result.
- **Tool-level predictions.** Predicting a specific filename misses variants of the same behavior.
- **Assumed links between entities.** Treating two threads as one intrusion without a shared entity in the records.
- **Indicators instead of behaviors.** Searching only for a reported domain finds nothing once the adversary changes infrastructure.
- **Ignoring feasibility.** Designing a hunt that the available data cannot answer, then reporting "nothing found" as if it were a negative result.

## Practical exercise

Work on paper or in a text file. No queries are run in this exercise.

The following hunt triggers are synthetic and authored for this lesson:

1. A sector intelligence note says invoice-themed documents are being used against microfinance lenders.
2. A frequency count shows one workstation contacted a domain that no other workstation contacted in the last 30 days.
3. A VPN summary shows a burst of failures across many identities from one external address, followed by one success.

For each trigger:

- Write a hypothesis using the five-part structure: behavior, scope, at least two observable predictions with sources, refuting evidence, and data feasibility.
- State which of the three outcomes would be most likely if the data inventory contained only proxy, endpoint process, Windows event, and VPN authentication records, with no mail, cloud identity, or session data.
- Rank the three hypotheses by impact, plausibility, and feasibility in one sentence each.

**Model answer notes.** Trigger 1 cannot be tested at the delivery step without mail data, so the hypothesis should shift to the observable consequence, an Office child process after a download, and record mail delivery as a gap. Trigger 2 needs a stated behavior: rarity alone is a prompt. A good rewrite predicts a download-then-execution sequence or unusual outbound volume. Trigger 3 is directly testable for the authentication pattern, but any prediction about post-authentication activity will produce a no-data outcome because session records are absent.

## Key takeaways

- A hunt hypothesis is a testable statement about a behavior in a defined scope, with observable predictions and stated refuting evidence.
- Write refuting evidence before looking at data to guard against confirmation bias.
- Predictions gain discriminating power by combining sources, specifying order and timing, and specifying rarity.
- Hypotheses must stay within what the records can show; in the Banyan data, mail delivery, payload content and post-VPN session activity cannot be observed.
- Every hypothesis should be able to end positive, benign or no-data, and each outcome is a legitimate result.

## From predictions to data requirements

A hypothesis tells the analyst what should be visible if a behavior occurred. Data needs analysis asks whether it can be visible, given what the organization actually collects. This is the step where many hunts quietly fail. An analyst writes an excellent hypothesis about credential misuse in cloud email, searches the SIEM, finds nothing, and reports that the behavior was not present. In fact, the SIEM never received cloud identity or mailbox audit logs. The hunt did not find a negative result. It found nothing because it looked in a place where the evidence could not be.

The purpose of this lesson is to make that gap explicit before any query is written. For every prediction in a hypothesis, the analyst identifies the source that would record it, the fields required to recognize it, the time coverage needed, the quality conditions that must hold, and the join keys needed to connect it with other predictions. The result is a data-needs matrix: a small table that shows, prediction by prediction, whether the hunt can answer its own question.

Data needs analysis also produces something valuable on its own: a list of visibility gaps tied to specific hunting questions. A gap phrased as "we have no mailbox audit data" is easy to deprioritize. A gap phrased as "we cannot test whether finance staff received invoice-themed documents, which sector intelligence flags as a current concern" makes the case for collection.

## The five questions for each prediction

For each observable prediction, ask five questions.

**1. Which source would record it?** Name the log source and, where it matters, the event type. "Endpoint data" is not specific enough; "Sysmon process creation events" or "Windows security log logon events" is. Different sources record the same behavior at different levels: a proxy sees a domain and byte count, an endpoint agent sees a process and its parent, a firewall sees addresses and ports.

**2. Which fields are required?** A prediction about an Office application starting a child process needs the child image, the parent image, the host, and a timestamp. If the endpoint source records process creation but not the parent, the prediction cannot be tested even though the source exists.

**3. What time coverage is needed?** The hunt window must be covered, and so must any baseline window. If a hypothesis predicts a destination "not seen in the prior 30 days," the source must retain at least 30 days before the hunt window. Retention shorter than the baseline period silently converts every destination into a first-seen destination.

**4. What quality conditions must hold?** Are clocks synchronized across sources? Are events complete, or does the collector drop events under load? Are fields normalized, or does one source write hostnames in uppercase and another in lowercase? Quality problems rarely make data unusable, but they change how confident a conclusion can be.

**5. What join keys connect it to other predictions?** If the hypothesis needs a proxy event and an endpoint event on the same host, both sources must carry a host identifier that can be matched. If one records a hostname and the other records only an IP address, the analyst needs a reliable mapping, such as DHCP records, for the time window.

## The Banyan data inventory

The C08 lab kit's saved Banyan dataset contains 340 rows: 284 proxy records, 33 Sysmon records, 13 Windows event records, and 10 VPN authentication records. The dataset omits several sources: there is no cloud identity audit, no mail gateway log, no mailbox audit, and no direct payload evidence. The VPN records have no endpoint identifier and no later session activity.

This inventory is small by design, but its shape is realistic. Many organizations have strong proxy coverage, partial endpoint coverage, sparse VPN detail, and nothing from mail or cloud identity sources. Reading the inventory before hunting allows the analyst to sort every question into one of three classes.

**Answerable.** The source exists, the fields exist, coverage spans the window, and quality is adequate. "Did WS-104 make a proxy request to banyan-payroll-update.example on 2026-11-03?" is answerable from proxy records, and the saved records contain one such request at 06:12:00Z.

**Partially answerable.** The source exists but lacks a field, a join key, or coverage needed for the full question. "What did WS-104 send to files-share-drop.example?" is partially answerable: the proxy records 48,200,000 outbound bytes, which answers how much, but there is no payload evidence, so what was sent is unanswerable.

**Unanswerable.** No source in the inventory could record the prediction. "Did WS-104's user receive an email containing the downloaded file?" is unanswerable because there is no mail gateway or mailbox audit data.

## Absence of evidence and evidence of absence

The distinction between these two phrases is the core idea of the lesson.

**Absence of evidence** means a search returned nothing. It says nothing about whether the behavior happened unless the search could have found it.

**Evidence of absence** means a search returned nothing and the analyst has shown that the search would have returned something if the behavior had occurred. That requires the right source, the right fields, adequate coverage and quality, and a query that has been validated against a known positive.

Consider the VPN thread. The saved records show that the VPN summary for 203.0.113.66 contains eight distinct identities that failed authentication and a successful authentication for gopal at 06:46:00Z. Suppose an analyst asks whether gopal's session then accessed internal file shares. A search of the VPN records returns no file share activity. That is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence, because the VPN records contain no later session activity at all. The correct result is a no-data outcome with a stated gap: "Post-authentication session activity is not recorded in the available VPN data."

Now consider a proxy question: "Did any workstation other than WS-104 contact files-share-drop.example on 2026-11-03?" If proxy coverage includes all workstations for that day and a query validated against the known WS-104 request returns only WS-104, that is evidence of absence for other workstations, within the proxy's coverage. The difference is that the analyst can show the search was capable of finding a positive.

## Coverage is not binary

Analysts often describe sources as "we have it" or "we don't." In practice, coverage varies along several dimensions.

**Population coverage.** Which hosts or identities send data? An endpoint agent may be installed on 90 percent of workstations. A hunt that finds no Office child processes across "all workstations" has really tested 90 percent of them. The documentation should say which.

**Event coverage.** Which event types does the source record? A Sysmon configuration may log process creation but exclude network connections to reduce volume. A Windows event log may record successful logons but not failures if the audit policy is narrow.

**Field coverage.** Which fields are populated? Proxy logs sometimes omit user identity for unauthenticated requests. A hunt that relies on the user field will miss those requests unless the query handles null values deliberately.

**Temporal coverage.** Which period does the data span, and are there gaps? A collector outage of two hours inside the hunt window means the hunt cannot speak to those two hours.

Coverage can be summarized per source as a short statement, for example: "Proxy: all workstations, request and byte fields populated, 2026-11-03 00:00 to 23:59 UTC, no known gaps." The Banyan inventory, as reported, supports statements at this level for proxy records on 2026-11-03, but the analyst should not assume coverage for other dates or hosts without checking the saved records.

## Time: synchronization, zones and windows

Time is the most common silent failure in data needs analysis.

**Time zones.** If one source writes UTC and another writes local time, a sequence can appear reversed. An Office child process recorded at 06:14 local and a download at 06:12 UTC may be hours apart. Every source should be normalized to UTC before sequencing, and the documentation should state that it was. The Banyan brief states times in UTC, which is the course convention.

**Clock skew.** Even when all sources use UTC, device clocks drift. A skew of a few seconds rarely matters for hour-scale patterns but can reverse an order that depends on seconds. If the hypothesis predicts that a download preceded execution by two minutes, a skew of up to a minute is tolerable; a skew of five minutes is not.

**Ingest time versus event time.** Many SIEMs record both the time the event occurred and the time it was received. Queries should use event time for sequencing. Ingest time is useful for spotting collection delays.

## Join keys and entity resolution

A hypothesis with predictions in two sources needs a way to say the predictions refer to the same entity. This is entity resolution, and it is where cross-source hunts often break.

**Host identity.** Proxy logs may record a hostname, an internal IP address, or both. Endpoint logs usually record a hostname. If the proxy records only an IP, the analyst needs a DHCP or asset mapping valid for the event time, because IP addresses move between hosts.

**User identity.** One source may write "gopal", another "BANYAN\gopal", another an email address. Normalization rules should be stated, not assumed.

**Missing keys.** Sometimes there is no join key at all. The Banyan VPN records have no endpoint identifier, so there is no field that links the gopal authentication to WS-104 or any other workstation. An analyst may notice that both threads occur on the same morning, but temporal proximity is not a join key. The correct statement is that the available records do not connect gopal's successful VPN session to WS-104.

**Enrichment is not observation.** An asset inventory may say WS-104 is assigned to a particular user or department. That is useful context, but it is enrichment: it describes the organization's records about the host, not something the proxy or endpoint source observed on 2026-11-03. When an inventory field is used, label it as enrichment and note its date. Do not use inventory ownership to create a link that the event data does not contain.

## Bounded case reasoning

The following cases use a small synthetic inventory authored for this lesson. It is not Banyan source data.

Synthetic inventory: proxy logs for all workstations with hostname, destination domain, bytes out and UTC timestamp, retained 14 days; endpoint process creation for workstations with parent image, retained 7 days; no DNS logs; no mail logs.

**Case 1: "Domain first seen in the last 30 days."** Proxy retention is 14 days, so the baseline cannot span 30. The question is partially answerable: the analyst can test "first seen in the last 14 days" and must record the reduced baseline as a limitation. Reporting a 30-day first-seen result would be wrong.

**Case 2: "Office child process within 10 minutes of a download, 10 days ago."** Endpoint retention is 7 days. The proxy half is answerable, the endpoint half is unanswerable for that date. The outcome for the full hypothesis is no-data, and the documentation should not report the proxy half as if it settled the question.

**Case 3: "Same host resolved a rare domain then connected to it."** No DNS logs exist. The proxy shows the request but not the resolution. The resolution half is unanswerable, though the request itself is visible; the analyst should consider whether the resolution step adds discriminating power at all, and drop it if not.

**Case 4: "No other workstation contacted the rare domain."** Proxy covers all workstations for 14 days, and a query validated against the known host returns only that host. This is evidence of absence within the proxy's population and time coverage.

## Building the data-needs matrix

The matrix has one row per prediction. Columns typically include: the prediction, the source, required fields, coverage needed, coverage available, join key, and status (answerable, partial, unanswerable). A final column states the consequence for the hunt, such as "test as written," "test with reduced baseline," or "record as gap."

Writing the matrix takes a few minutes and prevents hours of wasted querying. It also makes peer review faster, because a reviewer can check the matrix before reading any query.

The matrix should be revisited when the hunt uncovers something unexpected. If a query returns events from a host the analyst thought was out of coverage, that is a sign the coverage statement was wrong, and the matrix should be corrected before conclusions are drawn.

## Common errors

- **Treating an empty result as a negative result** without showing the source could have recorded a positive.
- **Assuming retention matches the baseline period** when the source keeps less history than the hypothesis needs.
- **Joining on time alone** when no shared host or identity field exists.
- **Using inventory enrichment as if it were an observation** to connect a user to a host.
- **Ignoring null fields** so that unauthenticated or unattributed events fall out of the result.
- **Mixing local time and UTC** and producing a reversed or invented sequence.
- **Describing coverage as "we have it"** without population, event, field and temporal detail.

## Key takeaways

- For each prediction, identify the source, fields, coverage, quality conditions and join keys before writing a query.
- Absence of evidence becomes evidence of absence only when the analyst shows the search could have found a positive.
- Coverage varies by population, event type, field and time; state it precisely.
- Normalize to UTC and use event time for sequencing.
- A missing join key means no link, and enrichment from inventory is context, not an observation.

## What a hunt query is for

A hunt query is the mechanism that tests a hypothesis's predictions against saved records. It differs from a detection rule in purpose and lifespan. A detection rule runs continuously, must keep false positives low enough for a queue, and is tuned for months. A hunt query runs a handful of times, is allowed to return a manageable set of candidates for human review, and is judged by whether it answers the hypothesis clearly. Many good detection rules begin life as hunt queries, but the analyst writing a hunt query should optimize for clarity and correctness first, not for alert volume.

Hunt queries in this course are read-only. They select, count, group, filter and join saved records. They never change data, contact external systems, or reproduce adversary activity. The examples are written in neutral pseudocode so the logic is visible regardless of which SIEM or log platform a team uses. No query in this lesson has been executed against a live system; the results shown are traced by hand against a small synthetic fixture so that any learner can verify them on paper.

This lesson covers four building blocks: stacking, filtering, time windows and entity joins. It then covers the defects that most often make a hunt query return the wrong answer, and how to document a query so another analyst can trust it.

## Building block 1: stacking

Stacking means grouping records by a field and counting. It is the simplest and most productive hunt technique, because rare values in a large population stand out without the analyst needing to know what to look for in advance. The hypothesis supplies the field to stack on; the stack shows the distribution.

```
FROM proxy
WHERE time_utc >= '2026-10-14T09:00:00Z' AND time_utc < '2026-10-14T10:00:00Z'
GROUP BY domain
COMPUTE rows = count(), hosts = count_distinct(host)
SORT hosts ASC
```

Traced by hand, the result is:

| domain | rows | hosts |
|---|---|---|
| invoice-viewer.example | 1 | 1 |
| sync-relay.example | 2 | 1 |
| updates.example | 4 | 4 |
| portal.example | 5 | 5 |

Two things deserve attention. First, the two rare domains, invoice-viewer.example and sync-relay.example, each appear on only one named host. Second, sync-relay.example shows two rows but only one distinct host. That mismatch is caused by P11, which has a null host. Most query engines exclude nulls from a distinct count, so P11 disappears from the host count while still counting as a row. If the analyst had stacked only on distinct hosts, the second source of traffic to sync-relay.example would be invisible.

Stacking choices shape what the analyst sees. Stacking by rows emphasizes volume; stacking by distinct hosts emphasizes prevalence. For rarity-based hunts, distinct hosts is usually the right measure, but the row count should be kept alongside it as a check.

## Building block 2: filtering

Filtering narrows records to those relevant to a prediction. Filters should express the behavior, not a single tool. A prediction about Office applications starting child processes should filter on a set of Office parent images, not on one.

```
FROM endpoint_process
WHERE lower(basename(parent_image)) IN ('winword.exe', 'excel.exe', 'powerpnt.exe', 'outlook.exe')
```

Against the fixture, this returns E01 (WS-203, WINWORD.EXE to cmd.exe) and E03 (WS-204, EXCEL.EXE to splwow64.exe). E04 is not returned because WINWORD.EXE is the child there, not the parent.

The filter alone does not discriminate between interesting and routine. E03 is a common printing helper started by Office applications when a user prints. A hunter who reported every Office child process would bury the useful result under routine ones. That is why filters are combined with stacking or joins rather than used alone, and why the analyst should know which Office children are routine in the environment, a question for the baseline lesson.

Case sensitivity is a frequent filter defect. If one source writes "winword.exe" and the filter expects "WINWORD.EXE", a case-sensitive engine returns nothing. Normalize case explicitly in the query, or confirm the engine's default behavior, and record the choice.

Path form is the other trap. The fixture stores bare file names, but many real sources (including the Banyan lab data) store the full path, such as `C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE`. An exact match on `WINWORD.EXE` returns zero rows against those records. That is why the filter above compares the file name at the end of the path (`basename`, written here as pseudocode; use your engine's equivalent), in lower case. In the same way, the Banyan proxy records hold a full `url`, not a `domain` field, so the hostname must be extracted from the URL before any domain filter or prevalence count.

## Building block 3: time windows

Many hypotheses predict a sequence: one event followed by another within a period. Time windows express that. They need a direction, a lower bound and an upper bound.

A window of "within 10 minutes" is ambiguous. Does it mean 10 minutes before or after, or either? For a download-then-execution hypothesis, the endpoint event should follow the proxy event, so the window is from 0 to 10 minutes after the proxy time. Using an absolute difference would also match process events that came first, which contradicts the hypothesis and would inflate the result.

Window width is a trade-off. Too narrow, and real sequences with a delay are missed, for example when a user downloads a file and opens it after a meeting. Too wide, and unrelated events on a busy host pair up by coincidence. The hypothesis should justify the width, and the documentation should note what a wider window would add.

## Building block 4: entity joins

A join connects predictions from different sources on a shared entity. The join key must exist in both sources and mean the same thing. In the fixture, host is the key between proxy and endpoint records.

The full hunt query combines all four blocks: stack proxy domains to find rare ones, then join those rows to Office child process events on the same host within 0 to 10 minutes after.

```
rare = FROM proxy
       WHERE time_utc >= '2026-10-14T09:00:00Z' AND time_utc < '2026-10-14T10:00:00Z'
       GROUP BY domain
       HAVING count_distinct(host) <= 1

candidates = FROM proxy AS p
             JOIN endpoint_process AS e
               ON lower(e.host) = lower(p.host)
              AND e.time_utc >= p.time_utc
              AND e.time_utc <= p.time_utc + 10 minutes
             WHERE p.domain IN rare.domain
               AND lower(basename(e.parent_image)) IN ('winword.exe', 'excel.exe', 'powerpnt.exe', 'outlook.exe')
             SELECT p.row, p.time_utc, p.host, p.domain, e.row, e.time_utc, e.parent_image, e.image
```

Traced by hand: the rare domains are invoice-viewer.example and sync-relay.example. Proxy rows for those domains are P06 (WS-203, 09:10:00), P10 (WS-203, 09:40:00) and P11 (null host, 09:45:00). For P06, E01 is on WS-203 at 09:11:30, ninety seconds later, with an Office parent: it matches. For P10, there is no Office child event on WS-203 between 09:40:00 and 09:50:00: no match. For P11, the host is null, so the join cannot match any endpoint row. The result is one candidate: P06 joined to E01.

E03 is not returned because WS-204 contacted no rare domain. That is the join doing its job: it filtered out a routine Office child process by requiring a rare download first.

P11 is not returned, but it has not been explained. It is a second source of traffic to sync-relay.example, identified only by 10.20.5.77. The query cannot say which host that was. Resolving it requires a DHCP or asset mapping for 09:45 UTC, which the fixture does not include. The analyst should record P11 as an unresolved row, not drop it silently.

## Common query defects

**Null-field exclusion.** Filters and joins on a field drop rows where the field is null. P11 demonstrates this. Check how many rows have nulls in key fields before trusting a result.

**Join fan-out.** A join on host alone, without a time window, pairs every proxy row on a host with every endpoint row on that host. In the fixture, WS-203 has three proxy rows (P03, P06, P10) and one endpoint row (E01), so a host-only join produces three candidate pairs, two of which are meaningless. On real data, fan-out can produce millions of rows and hide the real result.

**Time zone mismatch.** If the endpoint source wrote local time two hours ahead of UTC, E01 would read 11:11:30 and would not fall in any window after P06. The query would return nothing, and the analyst might wrongly report a negative. Confirm that every source is in UTC before joining on time.

**Wrong window direction.** Using an absolute time difference matches events in the wrong order. A process event at 09:08:00 would match P06 under an absolute 10-minute window even though it preceded the download.

**Over-specific indicators.** Filtering on a single domain or file name from a report finds only that indicator. The hunt should express the behavior, with indicators used as supplementary filters.

**Unbounded time ranges.** A query without explicit start and end times may run against whatever the platform default is, which can change between runs. Always state the range.

## Documenting a query

A hunt query should be documented well enough that another analyst can rerun it and expect the same result on the same saved data. The minimum record includes:

- **Purpose:** which prediction from which hypothesis it tests.
- **Inputs:** sources, time range in UTC, and any reference lists such as the set of Office parent images.
- **Assumptions:** for example, that host names are case-insensitive and that all sources are in UTC.
- **Expected positive:** what a matching row would look like.
- **Expected negative:** what a non-matching but similar row would look like, such as an Office child on a host with no rare download.
- **Known limitations:** rows the query cannot evaluate, such as null-host proxy rows.
- **Version:** a date or revision label, so changes are traceable.

The expected positive and negative are especially valuable. They let a reviewer check the query against a seeded example before trusting it on real data, a practice covered further in Lesson 7.

## Bounded case reasoning

Applying the same logic to the saved-record Banyan facts shows how a query result should be stated. The saved records show that WS-104 made one proxy request to banyan-payroll-update.example at 06:12:00Z on 2026-11-03, and the saved endpoint data records an Office child process at 06:14. If the saved endpoint row is on WS-104 and the destination is rare in the proxy data for that day, the join query above, adapted to that date, would return one candidate pair with a gap of roughly two minutes.

What the result would show is a rare download followed by an Office child process on the same host within the window. What it would not show is what the downloaded file was, how it arrived, or whether the child process did anything harmful. Those statements need further evidence, some of which the dataset does not contain. The query result is a candidate for validation, not a finding of compromise.

A learner using the Banyan data should confirm two things in the saved rows before relying on that reading: that the endpoint record's host field is WS-104, and that banyan-payroll-update.example is rare among workstations on that day. Neither should be assumed from the summary.

## Key takeaways

- Hunt queries are read-only tests of hypothesis predictions, optimized for clarity rather than alert volume.
- Stacking, filtering, time windows and entity joins are the core building blocks.
- Null fields, join fan-out, time zone mismatch and wrong window direction are the most common defects.
- Trace queries by hand on a small fixture before trusting them on real data.
- A query result is a candidate for validation, stated in terms of what the records show and do not show.

## What a baseline is and why hunts need one

Most hunt predictions contain a hidden comparison. "A destination not seen on peer workstations," "more outbound data than usual," "a child process that Office does not normally start": each of these depends on knowing what is normal. A baseline is the explicit, recorded description of that normal, built from a stated population over a stated period, so the analyst can judge whether an observation departs from it.

Without a baseline, analysts fall back on intuition. Intuition is useful for generating hypotheses but unreliable for testing them, because what looks strange to one analyst is routine to the team that runs the application. A file sync agent that sends tens of megabytes every hour looks alarming until someone checks how many workstations do the same thing. Equally, something that looks routine, such as a domain with "telemetry" in its name, may be unique to one host.

A baseline answers three questions: normal for whom, normal over what period, and normal by what measure. This lesson covers each, then explains how to compare an observation against a baseline, and why a baseline must never be treated as a list of safe behavior.

## Normal for whom: choosing a peer group

A peer group is the set of entities whose behavior the observation is compared against. Choosing it well is the most important baseline decision.

**Too broad.** Comparing a finance workstation to every device in the organization, including servers, build machines and kiosks, mixes populations with very different behavior. Servers send large volumes routinely, so a finance workstation sending a large volume looks ordinary by comparison.

**Too narrow.** Comparing a workstation only to its own history works for detecting change on that host, but it cannot tell the analyst whether a behavior is rare across the organization. If the host has always contacted a strange destination, its own history will call that normal.

**Well chosen.** Peers should share role, software build and usage pattern. For a finance workstation, a good peer group is other finance workstations on the same image. Many hunts use two baselines together: the entity's own history (has this host done this before?) and its peer group (do similar hosts do this?). An observation that is new for the host and rare among peers is far more interesting than one that fails only one comparison.

Peer groups depend on enrichment. The analyst usually decides which workstations are "finance" from an asset inventory, not from the logs. That is legitimate, but the documentation should label the peer group membership as enrichment with a date, because inventories go stale and a misfiled host can distort the baseline.

## Normal over what period: the baseline window

The baseline window is the period used to describe normal. It is separate from the hunt window, which is the period being tested, and the two should not overlap; otherwise the behavior under test helps define its own normal.

Window length involves trade-offs:

- **Short windows** of a few days reflect current behavior but miss weekly and monthly cycles. A month-end reporting job will look anomalous if the baseline covers only mid-month days.
- **Long windows** of several months capture cycles but include outdated behavior from before software changes or reorganizations.
- **Retention limits the choice.** A baseline cannot be longer than the data the source keeps. If proxy retention is 14 days, a 30-day baseline is impossible, and any "first seen in 30 days" result would be wrong.

Seasonality deserves explicit thought. Finance teams often have month-end, quarter-end and payroll cycles. A baseline that excludes those dates will flag them; one that includes them may hide an anomaly that happens to fall on a busy day. One practical approach is to compare like with like: compare a month-end day with previous month-end days, not with an average day.

The saved Banyan dataset contains 340 rows focused on 2026-11-03. If the saved records cover only that day, no multi-day baseline is available, and the only defensible comparison is a same-day peer comparison across the workstations present in the proxy data. The hunt documentation should say this plainly: "Baseline limited to same-day peer comparison; no historical baseline available in the saved records."

## Normal by what measure: choosing the metric

The metric is what is counted or measured. Different metrics answer different questions.

**Prevalence:** how many distinct entities show the value. This is the main metric for rarity: a destination contacted by one of forty workstations is rare by prevalence.

**Frequency:** how many times the value occurs. High frequency on one host with low prevalence across hosts is a common pattern for both beaconing malware and legitimate per-user software, so frequency needs context.

**Volume:** bytes, counts or durations. Volume is the natural metric for transfer hunts, but volume distributions are heavily skewed. A few large legitimate uploads dominate the upper end.

**Timing:** time of day, interval regularity, duration. A workstation active at 03:00 UTC when peers are idle may be interesting, depending on staff working patterns.

**Novelty:** whether the value appeared before in the baseline window. First-seen analysis is powerful but sensitive to the window length, as noted above.

For skewed metrics like volume, the mean and standard deviation are often misleading, because a single large legitimate value inflates both. The median and upper percentiles describe typical and high-but-normal values more robustly. A simple, explainable comparison is the ratio of the observation to the peer median, alongside whether it exceeds the highest value the peer group has shown.

## Stacking and the long tail

Stacking, introduced in Lesson 3, is the workhorse of baselining. Group by a field, count distinct entities, and sort. Real-world distributions almost always have the same shape: a short head of very common values, a long tail of values seen on only one or two entities.

The long tail is where hunts look, but most of it is benign. Personal browsing, one-off vendor portals and newly released software all live in the tail. The analyst's job is not to investigate every tail value but to use the hypothesis to decide which tail values matter. A rare destination that also received a large transfer, or that was followed by an unusual process, is worth attention. A rare destination that received a single small request with no other signal usually is not.

The saved records show that WS-104 made 18 requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example between 06:17:00Z and 07:42:02Z on 2026-11-03. That span is 85 minutes and 2 seconds, which would give an average gap of about five minutes across 17 intervals. Two baseline questions follow. First, prevalence: do other workstations contact this domain? If many do, it is likely a legitimate service, whatever its name. If only WS-104 does, its name says nothing about its legitimacy. Second, timing: are the intervals regular? An average says nothing about regularity; the analyst must read each timestamp in the saved rows before calling the pattern periodic.

## Comparing an observation to a baseline

The following tables are synthetic, authored for this lesson. They are not Banyan source data.

**Synthetic peer baseline: daily outbound bytes per finance workstation, 14 days from 2026-10-18 to 2026-10-31 UTC (includes the October month-end)**

| Host | Median daily MB | Max daily MB | Note from enrichment |
|---|---|---|---|
| WS-301 | 6.1 | 14.0 | Finance image |
| WS-302 | 5.4 | 11.2 | Finance image |
| WS-303 | 7.0 | 18.5 | Finance image |
| WS-304 | 4.8 | 9.9 | Finance image |
| WS-305 | 6.6 | 61.0 | Finance image; month-end report upload |
| WS-306 | 5.9 | 12.3 | Finance image |

**Synthetic observation, 2026-11-01 UTC:** WS-303 sends 52.0 MB in one request to a destination no peer contacted in the baseline window.

Step through the comparison.

**Against its own history:** WS-303's median is 7.0 MB and its maximum is 18.5 MB. 52.0 MB is about 7.4 times its median and nearly three times its previous maximum. It is new behavior for the host.

**Against peers by volume:** the peer group maximum is 61.0 MB, from WS-305. A naive threshold of "above the highest peer value" would not flag WS-303. Reading the note shows why that threshold is weak: WS-305's spike was a month-end upload, a known cyclic event. Including it in a single volume threshold lets any upload up to 61 MB pass.

**Against peers by destination:** no peer contacted the destination. That makes the destination rare by prevalence.

**Combined:** new for the host by volume, rare among peers by destination. Neither comparison alone is conclusive, and the volume comparison against the peer maximum is actively misleading. Together they support escalating the observation for validation. They do not establish what was sent or why.

This case illustrates the main skill of the lesson: an observation should be compared on more than one dimension, and each comparison should be read with its context.

## Baselines are not allowlists

A baseline describes what happened in the past. It does not certify that what happened was safe. This distinction matters in three ways.

**Pre-existing compromise.** If an adversary has been present for weeks, their activity is part of the baseline. A hunt that only looks for departures from baseline will never find them. Periodic hunts that examine the head of the distribution, such as common processes with unusual parents, help offset this.

**Common is not safe.** A behavior seen on every host could be a legitimate agent or a widespread problem. Prevalence lowers suspicion for a single host's anomaly; it does not clear the behavior itself.

**Allowlists go stale.** Teams sometimes convert baselines into suppressions: "these destinations are normal, exclude them from hunts." That can be reasonable for well-understood services, but each suppression should have an owner, a reason and a review date. A destination added because it was common in March may have changed hands by November.

The language in hunt documentation should reflect this. Write "consistent with the peer baseline" rather than "normal" or "safe."

## Bounded case reasoning

Apply the lesson to the saved-record Banyan transfer: one proxy request from WS-104 to files-share-drop.example at 08:12:00Z on 2026-11-03, with 48,200,000 outbound bytes, payload unknown.

What a defensible baseline statement could say, after checking the saved rows:

- Whether any other workstation in the saved proxy data contacted files-share-drop.example that day (same-day prevalence).
- How WS-104's 48,200,000 bytes compares with the outbound bytes of other workstations' requests that day (same-day volume).
- That no historical baseline exists in the saved records, if that is confirmed.

What it could not say: that WS-104 had never contacted the destination before, because the saved records may not include earlier dates; that the transfer was abnormal for the user, because there is no user history; or that the content was sensitive, because there is no payload evidence.

The outcome is likely a positive-for-validation result if the destination is unique to WS-104 and the volume is high among same-day requests, with an explicit limitation that the baseline is a single day.

## Common errors

- **Overlapping hunt and baseline windows**, so the behavior under test helps define normal.
- **Peer groups that mix roles**, such as workstations with servers.
- **Using the mean on skewed volume data**, inflated by a few legitimate large transfers.
- **Single-dimension thresholds** that pass anomalies hidden behind cyclic spikes.
- **Reading names as evidence**, such as trusting a domain because it contains "cdn" or "telemetry."
- **Calling an average interval regular** without checking the individual intervals.
- **Treating the baseline as an allowlist**, which hides pre-existing or widespread activity.
- **Baselines longer than retention**, which make every value look first-seen.

## Measure the interval and same-day comparison

The C08 kit's saved proxy records contain 18 matching requests for cdn-telemetry-sync.example, all attributed to WS-104. Sorting the matching timestamps produces 17 successive gaps. Legitimate business tasks and sparse source data can both affect what the analyst sees. Give the evidence source and baseline period when reporting an unusual measurement. Ask which additional source or period would support a stronger comparison. This exercise gives the analyst a reason to investigate a distinct outlier without treating size as proof of what was transferred.

## Key takeaways

- A baseline states normal for whom, over what period and by what measure.
- Use both the entity's own history and a well-chosen peer group.
- Keep baseline and hunt windows separate, and keep the baseline within retention.
- Prefer median and percentiles for skewed metrics, and compare on more than one dimension.
- A baseline is a description of the past, not an allowlist; write "consistent with baseline," not "safe."

## ATT&CK as a hunting vocabulary

MITRE ATT&CK is a publicly maintained knowledge base of adversary behavior, organized into tactics, which describe the adversary's goal at a stage of activity, and techniques, which describe how a goal is pursued. Examples of tactic names include Initial Access, Execution, Credential Access, Command and Control and Exfiltration. Under each tactic, technique entries describe behaviors, give examples of reported use, and list data sources that may help observe them.

For a hunter, ATT&CK is most valuable as a shared vocabulary. It gives a team a consistent way to say what behavior a hunt is about, to compare hunts over time, to communicate with threat intelligence and detection engineering, and to see which behaviors have received no attention. It is less valuable, and sometimes harmful, when it is treated as a checklist to complete or as proof that an observed event is malicious.

This lesson shows how to move from an ATT&CK behavior to a hunt hypothesis and observable predictions, how to choose which behaviors to hunt, and how to map an observation back to ATT&CK honestly. It deliberately does not cite technique identifiers. Technique IDs and names are revised between ATT&CK versions, and a lesson that quotes them from memory risks teaching outdated labels. When a hunt record cites a technique, the analyst should look up the current entry on the ATT&CK site at the time of writing and record the ATT&CK version used.

The lesson also stays on the defender's side of each behavior. It describes what a behavior looks like in saved records, not how to carry it out.

## From tactic to observable: the translation chain

An ATT&CK-driven hunt follows a chain with five links. Each link narrows the question and makes it more testable.

**1. Tactic.** The adversary goal, for example Credential Access: obtaining account credentials.

**2. Behavior.** A specific way of pursuing the goal, described in plain language. For example: trying a small number of common passwords against many accounts from one source, so that no single account locks out.

**3. Observable.** What that behavior leaves in records. For the example: many authentication failures across distinct identities from one source address within a short period, possibly followed by a success.

**4. Data source.** Where those records live. For the example: VPN or identity provider authentication logs with source address, identity and result fields.

**5. Hypothesis.** The testable statement for the local environment: "If guessing across many accounts from one external source occurred against Banyan VPN on 2026-11-03, we expect one source address with failures across several distinct identities within a short period. If failures are spread across many addresses, or one identity accounts for most failures, the hypothesis is not supported."

Each link is a place where the hunt can stop early. If no data source in the inventory records the observable, the chain ends at link four with a visibility gap. That is a useful result: it tells the team which ATT&CK behaviors it cannot currently hunt.

The chain also prevents a common mistake, which is jumping from tactic to query. A query written directly from "Credential Access" is either too broad to be useful or quietly assumes one behavior out of many. Writing the behavior and observable first makes the assumption visible.

## Choosing which behaviors to hunt

ATT&CK lists hundreds of behaviors. No team can hunt all of them, and trying to "cover the matrix" leads to shallow hunts that test nothing well. Selection should weigh three factors.

**Threat relevance.** Which behaviors are reported against organizations like yours? Sector intelligence, shared incident reports and the team's own incident history are the main inputs. A microfinance lender with remote staff on VPN has good reason to care about credential guessing against remote access and about data leaving finance workstations.

**Data visibility.** Which behaviors produce observables in sources you actually have? This is the data-needs analysis from Lesson 2, applied per behavior. A behavior that is highly relevant but invisible in current data is a collection priority, not a hunt.

**Detection gaps.** Which relevant, visible behaviors do current detections not cover? Hunting where a mature, tested rule already exists adds little. Hunting where no rule exists can both find activity and produce a detection candidate.

A coverage heat map that colors ATT&CK cells by "has a rule" or "was hunted" can help communicate these gaps, but its colors are easy to misread. A green cell for a technique might mean one narrow rule that catches one tool, while the behavior has many variants. Treat a heat map as a conversation starter, and record in the hunt documentation exactly which behavior variant was tested.

## Writing observables at the right level

ATT&CK technique entries often describe many procedures that share a goal. A hunt observable should be written at the level of the shared behavior, so that it catches variants, while staying specific enough to discriminate.

Consider document-driven execution, a behavior many intrusions begin with: a user opens a document, and the document application starts another program. The observables could be written at three levels:

- **Too specific:** a particular word processor starting a particular command interpreter with a particular argument. This catches one procedure and misses the rest.
- **Too general:** any process started on a workstation. This has no discriminating power.
- **Behavior level:** an Office application as parent of a process that is not a known routine helper, on a workstation, shortly after a download. This catches variants and still discriminates.

The behavior level depends on a baseline of routine Office children, which is why ATT&CK-driven hunts and baselining work together. The ATT&CK entry suggests the behavior; the baseline tells the hunter which instances of it are ordinary locally.

## Applying the chain to the Banyan threads

The saved-record Banyan facts can be examined through this chain. The aim is to generate hypotheses and observables, not to assign labels to events as findings.

**WS-104 proxy and endpoint thread.** The saved proxy and endpoint records show a proxy request from WS-104 to banyan-payroll-update.example at 06:12:00Z, an Office child process at 06:14, 18 requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example between 06:17:00Z and 07:42:02Z, and a request to files-share-drop.example at 08:12:00Z with 48,200,000 outbound bytes.

Each observation suggests a tactic that an analyst might hypothesize:

- The download and Office child process suggest hypotheses under Initial Access and Execution, specifically document-driven execution.
- Repeated requests to one destination suggest a hypothesis under Command and Control, if the destination is rare and the timing is regular.
- A large outbound transfer to a file-sharing destination suggests a hypothesis under Exfiltration.

These are candidate tactics, not conclusions. Each has a benign alternative. An Office child process may be a routine helper. Repeated requests to a telemetry-named domain may be a legitimate agent. A large upload may be a sanctioned file share used by the business. The hunt's job is to test each hypothesis against the data and the baseline.

**VPN thread.** The saved records show that the VPN summary for 203.0.113.66 contains eight distinct identities that failed authentication and a successful authentication for gopal at 06:46:00Z. This fits the observable for guessing across many accounts under Credential Access, and the success raises a hypothesis about a valid account being used for access. The benign alternatives include a shared egress address for a partner or a hotel network where several staff mistype passwords, though eight distinct identities failing in a short period from one address is not a common benign pattern. The VPN records contain no later session activity, so any hypothesis about what the gopal session did afterwards ends at link four with a no-data outcome.

## Sequence does not prove connection

ATT&CK tactics are often drawn left to right, and it is tempting to read a series of observations as a story that walks across the matrix. That reading is a hypothesis about connection, and it must be tested like any other.

In the Banyan data, the two threads sit near each other in time on the same morning. The WS-104 thread can be arranged as Execution, then Command and Control, then Exfiltration. The VPN thread can be read as Credential Access followed by account use. Putting them together suggests a single intrusion: guess a password, log in, reach WS-104, take data. But the available records do not connect gopal's successful VPN session to WS-104. The VPN events have no endpoint identifier, the proxy and endpoint events do not reference the VPN identity, and there is no session data showing the VPN user reaching any host. The failed accounts include divya, who is also named in the WS-104 evidence. That overlapping identity does not link gopal's successful VPN session to WS-104.

The correct position is that two separate hypotheses each have supporting observations, and the connection between them is untested and, with this data, untestable. Writing it any other way would turn ATT&CK's tactic ordering into evidence, which it is not. Many real intrusions skip tactics, repeat them or carry them out in an order different from the matrix layout, and many unrelated events fall near each other in time.

Even within one thread, sequence needs support. The WS-104 events share a host, which is a real link. But sharing a host does not prove the events are causally connected: a workstation can be used for unrelated tasks within two hours. The sequence strengthens the hypothesis; it does not settle it.

## Mapping observations back to ATT&CK with confidence

When a hunt produces a result, teams often record which ATT&CK behavior it relates to. Three practices make that mapping honest.

**State confidence.** Use a simple scale, such as low, moderate or high, and say why. A rare download followed within two minutes by a non-routine Office child process on the same host might be mapped to document-driven execution with moderate confidence. Without payload or command-line evidence, high confidence is not justified.

**State the benign alternative.** For each mapping, write the most plausible innocent explanation and whether it was ruled out. This keeps the mapping a hypothesis rather than a verdict.

**Map behaviors, not events.** A single proxy request is not a technique. A pattern of requests with rarity and regularity might be consistent with a Command and Control behavior. The mapping should describe the pattern and the evidence that supports it.

A mapping recorded this way is useful downstream. Detection engineering can see exactly which behavior variant was observed and in which data source. Threat intelligence can compare it with reporting. Incident response can see which parts are supported and which are inferred.

## Bounded case reasoning

Three synthetic mapping drafts follow, authored for this lesson; none is Banyan source data.

**Draft 1:** "Proxy row 118: Exfiltration." This maps a single event to a tactic with no confidence, no behavior and no benign alternative. It should be rewritten as: "WS-207 sent 39 MB in one request to a destination no peer used in the baseline window (proxy row 118). Consistent with an Exfiltration hypothesis, moderate confidence by volume and rarity; content unknown. Benign alternative: personal file sharing or an unsanctioned business tool; owner not yet contacted."

**Draft 2:** "Brute force attack from 198.51.100.40, user compromised." This states a conclusion and uses a label without stating the observable. A better version gives the count of distinct identities, the time span, whether any success followed and what data would show account use afterwards.

**Draft 3:** "Kill chain complete: Initial Access via VPN, Execution on WS-209, Exfiltration to sync-relay.example." This joins three observations into one intrusion. Unless a shared entity connects the VPN identity to WS-209, the draft should be split into separate observations with the link marked as untested.

## Common errors

- **Hunting the matrix instead of the threat**, spreading effort across behaviors with no local relevance.
- **Quoting technique IDs from memory** without checking the current ATT&CK version.
- **Mapping single events to tactics** without describing the behavior or pattern.
- **Treating tactic order as evidence** of a connected intrusion.
- **Writing observables at the tool level** so that variants of the behavior are missed.
- **Reading a green heat-map cell as complete coverage** when only one variant is detected.
- **Omitting confidence and benign alternatives** from mappings.

## Key takeaways

- Use ATT&CK as a vocabulary: tactic, behavior, observable, data source, hypothesis.
- Choose behaviors by threat relevance, data visibility and detection gaps, not by matrix coverage.
- Write observables at the behavior level so variants are caught and routine activity is excluded by baseline.
- Map observations with stated confidence and a benign alternative, and verify any technique citation against the current ATT&CK version.
- Tactic order is not evidence; observations need a shared entity before they are linked.
