options: Because domain controllers produce fewer false positives than other hosts
Because test machines are outside the SOC's monitoring scope by default
Because asset criticality is an escalation factor, so impact there is higher
Because the second alert to arrive is always the more reliable one
1.explanation: Escalation criteria combine evidence strength with asset and identity criticality; the same evidence on a domain controller carries far greater potential impact. This is why CMDB enrichment is a Tier 1 task. Test machines are still monitored.

1.q: Which escalation note gives Tier 2 the most useful starting point?
options: Looks suspicious on WS-104, several alerts fired overnight, please check urgently
R5 fired on WS-104 at high severity; escalating per playbook, priority 10.8
WS-104 might be compromised; user divya is a payments approver so treat as critical
Log cleared on WS-104 after new admins and a large upload; no change ticket found; meets critical-asset criteria
1.explanation: A good escalation states what was observed, what was checked, what was ruled out and why the criteria were met, so Tier 2 does not redo Tier 1's work. The other notes either give no evidence or give a score without the checks behind it.

1.q: A SOC treats an alert on a reception kiosk and one on the payments server with equal urgency because it has no record of what either system is. Under the NIST CSF 2.0, which Function's weakness is causing this?
options: Protect, because the kiosk should have been hardened before going live
Identify, because the asset inventory and criticality context are missing
Respond, because the containment playbooks have not been written yet
Recover, because the backup priorities of each system are undefined
1.explanation: The SOC lives mainly in Detect and Respond but depends on Identify for an asset inventory that says which systems matter most. Hardening (Protect) affects what happens, not how the SOC prioritises alerts it receives.

1.q: A covered entity in India has no out-of-hours escalation path; critical alerts raised overnight are read by the morning shift. How does the CERT-In Direction of 28 April 2022 make this especially risky?
options: Reporting is required within six hours of noticing, so an overnight wait may use up the window
Logs must be kept for 180 days, so overnight alerts are deleted before the morning shift
CERT-In requires a 24x7 staffed SOC for every registered company in India
Incidents must be reported within 72 hours, which an overnight delay always exceeds
1.explanation: The Direction requires covered entities to report specified incidents within six hours of noticing them; an alert left until morning may already have consumed that window. The 180-day figure is log retention, not deletion, and 72 hours is not the CERT-In deadline.

1.q: A SOC manager starts rewarding Tier 1 analysts for closing alerts well inside their time budget. What risk does this create?
options: Tier 2 becomes overloaded because analysts escalate everything to save time
Real alerts get closed as false positives because speed is rewarded over accuracy
Detection engineers stop receiving alerts because rules are disabled to cut volume
Case records grow too long because analysts paste every log line into notes
1.explanation: The time budget is a ceiling that triggers escalation, not a target; rewarding speed pushes analysts to close cases they should escalate. Over-escalation is the opposite pressure and is not what a closure reward encourages.

1.q: A large tiered SOC finds that details noticed by Tier 1 are often missing by the time a case reaches Tier 3, and analysts leave after months of repetitive queue work. Which redesign addresses both problems most directly?
options: Adding a fourth tier between Tier 2 and Tier 3 to review every escalation
Raising the Tier 1 time budget so analysts can investigate each case deeper
Functional teams where one analyst owns a case end to end, with triage automated
Outsourcing Tier 1 to a provider so that internal staff only handle Tier 2 work
1.explanation: Functional teams keep case ownership continuous, so context survives, and automation removes repetitive triage that drives burnout. Adding another tier creates one more hand-off, which makes context loss worse.

1.q: Banyan Microfinance's night shift has only two analysts. How is the SOC's work best organised for that shift?
options: One analyst acts as Tier 1 and the other as Tier 2, with Tier 3 left vacant
Both analysts triage only and leave every escalated case for the day shift
All alerts are queued unread overnight and triaged together each morning
Both analysts triage, either takes a case to closure, and on-call Tier 3 is paged
1.explanation: A two-person shift cannot run three tiers, so it uses a functional model: both triage, either can own a case through to closure, and a specialist is paged when forensics are needed. Leaving cases for the day shift recreates the overnight gap.

1.q: After automating most enrichment in a SOAR platform and abolishing the 'Tier 1' job title, a SOC manager proposes deleting the written escalation criteria. Why is this a mistake?
options: Someone still makes the first close-or-escalate decision on each alert and needs criteria
SOAR platforms cannot run unless escalation criteria are stored in their configuration
Auditors require the tier job titles to be kept in the organisation chart
Without Tier 1, Tier 2 can no longer declare incidents under the response plan
1.explanation: Automation and functional teams redistribute triage work but do not remove it; whoever makes the first decision still needs written criteria. The tier vocabulary describes the work, whatever the job titles say.

1.q: The US Senate committee analysis of the 2013 Target breach reported that automated intrusion warnings were raised but not acted on effectively. Which control from the lesson targets that failure most directly?
options: Adding more detection rules so that the intrusion produces stronger alerts
Restricting case-system access so that only senior analysts can read alerts
Extending log retention so that evidence is available for later investigation
Automatically notifying the SOC lead and on-call staff about unacknowledged critical cases
1.explanation: In that case the technology detected but the organisation did not act; alerting on unacknowledged high-severity cases attacks exactly that gap. More rules would only add alerts that could also go unanswered.

1.q: A new SOC writes a single escalation rule for every alert type: 'escalate anything suspicious'. What outcome does the lesson predict?
options: Tier 1 closures become more accurate, because analysts escalate more often
Detection engineering receives more tuning requests and false positives fall
Overload moves up to Tier 2, or Tier 1 grows unsure and reluctant to escalate
Case volume falls, because suspicious activity is defined narrowly by the rule
1.explanation: Vague criteria either send everything to Tier 2, recreating the overload one level up, or leave Tier 1 uncertain and hesitant. Good criteria are written per alert type and combine evidence, criticality, time sensitivity and effort.

1.q: After a CERT-In advisory, an analyst searches the estate for signs of a credential-theft technique that none of the SOC's rules has ever alerted on, starting from a written hypothesis. Which function is this?
options: Detection engineering, because it involves writing and tuning new rules
Threat hunting, a proactive Tier 3 search for activity no rule has flagged
Digital forensics, because it requires preserving disk and memory evidence
Tier 2 scoping, because it builds a timeline of an escalated incident
1.explanation: Hypothesis-driven searching for activity that no rule has alerted on is threat hunting. Detection engineering may later turn a finding into a rule, but the search itself is the hunt; scoping applies to an already escalated case.

1.q: Each week a senior analyst reviews a random sample of the cases Tier 1 closed. What is the main purpose of this review?
options: To catch mis-closures and turn them into training and tuning items
To measure each analyst's closure speed for the monthly league table
To re-open every sampled case so Tier 2 can investigate it fully
To delete closed cases older than 180 days from the case system
1.explanation: Quality review of closures is a control protecting the tier structure: a wrong Tier 1 closure hides a case from everyone above it, so sampled mistakes become training and rule changes. Ranking by speed would encourage the hurried closures the review is meant to catch.

1.q: A SOC analyst is working a case alone during a quiet shift. Which of these decisions is the analyst normally entitled to make without anyone else's approval?
options: Close the case as a benign true positive when the playbook criteria are met
Declare a major incident and invoke the organisation's response plan
Take a production database server offline to stop suspected data theft
Decide that the case is not reportable to CERT-In and close the matter
1.explanation: Analysts own dispositions within playbook criteria, escalation and pre-authorised first-response actions. Declaring major incidents, taking production servers offline and deciding reportability belong to other roles.

1.q: During a post-incident review, the SOC discovers that the proxy logs stopped arriving in the SIEM five weeks earlier. The queue looked unusually calm the whole time. Which role gap does this most clearly reveal?
options: Detection engineering, because the proxy rules were never tuned after deployment
Threat intelligence, because no advisory warned the SOC about proxy outages
Platform engineering, because nobody was monitoring ingestion for silent sources
Shift lead, because the handover did not list the open proxy-related cases
1.explanation: Monitoring ingestion so that a silent source is noticed is the platform engineer's job; a gap in ingestion is a gap in detection that analysts cannot see from the queue. Rule tuning cannot help when no data reaches the rules.

1.q: A draft RACI marks both the SOC and IT operations as 'A' for the activity 'Contain a compromised server'. What problem does this create?
options: Nobody does the work, because an A role is never also responsible
Both teams may claim ownership and argue during the incident itself
The matrix is invalid only because IT operations should be marked C
Legal must then be added as a third A to break any disagreement
1.explanation: A RACI must have exactly one Accountable per activity; two As lead to disputes during the incident, and zero leads to inaction. Adding a third A makes the problem worse, not better.

1.q: In the lab's triage.py, the only suppression silences the new-local-administrator rule for the account itadmin, with the reason 'approved build account, CHG-1042' and an expiry of 2026-12-31. Who owns it, and what must happen before it expires?
options: The shift lead owns it and extends it automatically at each handover
The analyst who first closed the alert owns it and may delete it at will
The platform engineer owns it, because suppressions are stored in the SIEM
Detection engineering owns it and must review it against the change ticket
1.explanation: The kit labels suppressions as owned by detection engineering, each with an owner ticket and an expiry, so the entry must be reviewed and justified again before 2026-12-31. Analysts benefit from the suppression but do not own it.

1.q: A retailer's contract with its managed provider says only 'monitoring of logs'. At 03:00 the provider sees ransomware staging on two file servers but does not isolate them. Which contract gap is most responsible?
options: The contract did not set out which log sources were in scope for monitoring
The contract did not require metrics or monthly service review meetings
The contract did not state what containment the provider may perform
The contract did not define how data is returned when the service ends
1.explanation: Nobody was accountable for isolating the servers because the contract never said whether the provider could do it. The other clauses matter too, but none of them would have changed what happened at 03:00.

1.q: In the lesson's example RACI, the row 'Isolate endpoint (EDR, pre-agreed)' shows SOC analyst R, incident responder A and IT ops / identity I. What does this mean in practice?
options: The analyst performs the isolation, the responder owns the outcome, and IT ops is told
The analyst must ask IT ops for permission before isolating any endpoint
The responder performs the isolation and the analyst is only consulted
IT ops owns the decision but delegates the technical work to the SOC
1.explanation: R means does the work, A means owns the outcome, I means told afterwards; because the action is pre-agreed, the analyst can carry it out without waiting for IT ops. Asking permission first would make IT ops C or A, which the row does not say.

1.q: A company hands its monitoring, investigation and response to an MDR provider, and the contract says the provider will help prepare CERT-In reports. Who is accountable for the company's CERT-In reporting obligation?
options: The MDR provider, because the contract transfers reporting to it
CERT-In itself, once the provider has submitted the incident details
Shared equally between the provider and the company's IT operations
The company, because outsourcing moves roles but not accountability
1.explanation: Outsourcing moves roles, not accountability: the organisation remains accountable for its own regulatory reporting, even when the provider supports it. 'Shared equally' breaks the one-accountable principle.

1.q: A new threat intelligence analyst loads every indicator from every commercial and community feed straight into the SIEM's matching rules. What is the likely result?
options: Better coverage with no extra cost, because each indicator is low-risk
Floods of low-value alerts, because the role's value lies in filtering
Fewer alerts, because broad indicator sets cancel each other out
Faster CERT-In reporting, because indicators come from national advisories
1.explanation: The threat intelligence role assesses which information is relevant; loading everything produces alert floods, while curated intelligence produces a few alerts that matter. Uncurated indicators are not free: each false match costs analyst time.

1.q: A SOAR platform holds credentials that can disable accounts and isolate hosts across production. Beyond building automations, what is the SOAR engineer's key safety responsibility?
options: Deciding which actions run without approval, which need an analyst's click, and logging all of them
Ensuring every automation runs fully unattended so containment never waits for a human
Storing the platform's credentials in each playbook so they never expire during an incident
Granting every analyst administrator rights so playbooks can be edited quickly at night
1.explanation: Because SOAR can change production systems, its engineer must define approval levels for each action and log every action. Running everything unattended removes the human check on powerful, sometimes irreversible changes.

1.q: At 02:15 a critical case has sat unacknowledged in the queue for forty minutes. Which role on the shift is primarily responsible for noticing this and calling the on-call incident responder?
options: The detection engineer who wrote the rule that raised the alert
The platform engineer responsible for the SIEM's ingestion health
The shift lead, who watches ageing cases and guards the escalation path
The SOC manager, who owns the SOC's metrics and service levels
1.explanation: The shift lead assigns work, watches the queue for ageing high-severity cases and is often the person who calls out the on-call responder. The SOC manager is accountable for service levels overall but is not watching the queue at 02:15.

1.q: An incident responder confirms that customer personal data was exfiltrated. Under the DPDP Act 2023 notification may be required. What is the SOC's proper part in that decision?
options: Notify the Data Protection Board directly, since the SOC found the breach
Give legal and compliance accurate, timely facts so they can decide
Wait until the investigation is fully closed before telling legal anything
Decide whether the data was sensitive enough to need any notification
1.explanation: Legal and compliance decide whether an obligation is triggered and what is said; the SOC's job is to supply accurate facts quickly. Waiting for full closure delays a decision that may have a short deadline.

1.q: The lesson observes that in almost every case the SOC holds the knowledge while another team holds the authority. Which practice follows most directly from this observation?
options: Moving all containment authority into the SOC so it no longer depends on others
Limiting what the SOC shares with other teams until an incident is confirmed
Letting each team decide its own actions during the incident as facts emerge
Agreeing authority with other teams in advance and passing knowledge to them fast
1.explanation: If knowledge and authority sit in different teams, the interface must move knowledge quickly and the authority must already be agreed, or decisions wait while the attacker does not. Moving all authority into the SOC would let it change systems it does not own.

1.q: A detection engineer adds a suppression for a noisy rule and is also the only person who ever reviews the suppression list. Which control does this arrangement lack?
options: Separation of duties, so someone else reviews suppressions that one person adds
Log retention, so suppressed alerts are kept for at least 180 days
Ingestion monitoring, so the suppressed log source is still reporting
Pre-authorisation, so the suppression is agreed with IT operations first
1.explanation: A suppression silences detection, so a single person adding and reviewing it is a risk; the person who adds one should not be its only reviewer. Retention and ingestion matter, but they do not check whether the suppression itself is justified.

1.q: Investigators expect that an insider fraud case may end up before a regulator or in court. Which specialist role should handle the acquisition of disk and memory evidence, and why?
options: The malware analyst, because evidence must first be detonated in a sandbox
The threat hunter, because the case started from a hypothesis about an insider
The forensic analyst, because acquisition must preserve the evidence's integrity
The SOC analyst on shift, because the evidence is already in the case record
1.explanation: The forensic analyst acquires and examines evidence in a way that preserves its integrity, which is what makes it usable before a court or regulator. The malware analyst examines suspicious files, not the overall evidence collection.

1.q: During a phishing incident, an incident responder with domain-admin rights resets a director's password and revokes her sessions himself, without involving anyone. Under the example RACI, what is wrong?
options: Nothing, because the incident responder is accountable for all containment
The analyst on shift should have done it, since containment is pre-agreed
Legal should have been consulted first, because the user is a director
IT ops / identity is A/R for account resets; the responder should be consulted
1.explanation: In the example matrix the identity team is Accountable and Responsible for resets and session revocation, with the responder only Consulted; acting alone bypasses the owner of the identity system. Only endpoint isolation is pre-agreed for the SOC.

1.q: A five-person SOC asks whether it really needs a role tree, since its members each do 'a bit of everything'. What is the best answer?
options: No, a role tree is only useful once each role has its own dedicated team
Yes, because it maps responsibilities, so each box needs a named owner
No, because small SOCs should outsource the engineering roles instead
Yes, because it fixes the number of staff each role must have
1.explanation: The role tree is a responsibility map, not a headcount chart; one person can sit in several boxes, but each box still needs someone who is answerable for it this month. It does not prescribe staff numbers.

1.q: A mid-sized bank wants its own staff, who know the business, to own investigations and response, but cannot staff nights and weekends. Which delivery model fits, and what must it design carefully?
options: Hybrid; the hand-offs between the internal team and the provider
In-house; the cost of hiring enough analysts for round-the-clock cover
Outsourced MDR; the business context the provider will lack
Outsourced MSSP; the response actions the provider will not take
1.explanation: A hybrid model keeps context and response inside while a provider covers hours, and its weak point is the hand-off between the two organisations. Full outsourcing would give away the business-context ownership the bank wants to keep.

1.q: In the lesson's 03:00 scenario, the night analyst recognised ransomware staging but escalated by chat to a colleague who had gone home. Which fix addresses why the shift lead never learned of it?
options: Training the analyst to recognise ransomware staging patterns earlier
Escalating only in the case system, with alerts on unacknowledged critical cases
Buying an EDR product with stronger ransomware detection signatures
Extending the CERT-In reporting window through a customer agreement
1.explanation: The analyst detected correctly; the failure was an escalation outside the case system, so nobody owned the case. Mandatory escalation through the case system with automatic alerts on unacknowledged critical cases fixes this without new technology.

1.q: Reading the example RACI from triage down to the CERT-In decision, how does accountability change from row to row?
options: It stays with the incident responder throughout, from triage to reporting
It moves towards the SOC as incidents become more severe and urgent
It moves away from the SOC as actions change production systems or make legal statements
It is shared equally across all four roles in the containment rows
1.explanation: The SOC is accountable for analysis and knowing; IT ops and identity own changes to their systems, and legal owns the reporting decision. Shared accountability would break the one-A rule.

1.q: An analyst closes an alert as a false positive and flags the rule. What does the detection engineer do with that feedback?
options: Deletes the rule at once, because any false positive proves it is broken
Forwards the alert to threat intelligence to add the host as an indicator
Asks the platform engineer to stop ingesting the log source that fired
Decides whether to change the logic, add a suppression or retire the rule
1.explanation: The detection engineer receives the feedback and chooses among changing the logic, adding a justified suppression or retiring the rule, testing changes against data that should and should not trigger it. Stopping ingestion would blind every other rule using that source.

1.q: A company hires its first 'SOC engineer' and gives them no written responsibilities beyond the job title. Which first step best prevents gaps that would only appear during an incident?
options: Map the responsibilities onto boxes of the role tree and record the owner of each
Let the engineer choose their own priorities after the first incident occurs
Rename the post 'detection engineer' so its purpose is obvious to everyone
Give the engineer SIEM administrator rights so they can cover any task
1.explanation: Titles vary widely; what matters is which responsibilities the person owns, written down against the role tree, so no box is left unowned. Renaming the post still leaves platform, SOAR and other boxes unassigned.

1.q: SIEM administrators can search every log, including personal data about staff and customers. Which set of controls does the lesson recommend for such privileged SOC roles?
options: Shared admin accounts so that actions can be traced to the team as a whole
Full access for all analysts so that investigations are never delayed
Password-only sign-in so analysts are not locked out during incidents
Least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and logged actions reviewed by another role
1.explanation: Privileged SOC roles are attractive targets, so they need least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and logging of their own actions, reviewed by someone outside the role. Shared accounts destroy individual accountability.

1.q: In the lab, triage.py contains RULE_META and SUPPRESS, prints a prioritised queue, and depends on minisiem.py loading all 340 events from four sources. Which mapping of these to role-tree boxes is correct?
options: RULE_META and SUPPRESS to threat intelligence; the queue to incident responders; loading to SOAR engineers
RULE_META to platform engineers; SUPPRESS to the shift team; loading to detection engineers
RULE_META and SUPPRESS to detection engineers; the queue to the shift team; loading to platform engineers
RULE_META and SUPPRESS to the SOC manager; the queue to hunters; loading to the shift lead
1.explanation: Rule severities, confidences and suppressions are detection-engineering artefacts, the printed queue is the shift team's work, and keeping all sources loading is platform engineering. Threat intelligence feeds requirements to rules but does not own the rule metadata.

1.q: A company is choosing between an MSSP and an MDR service. What distinguishes MDR from a plain MSSP monitoring service?
options: MDR covers only cloud workloads, while an MSSP covers on-premises systems
MDR adds investigation and response actions on top of monitoring
MDR transfers regulatory accountability for incidents to the provider
MDR replaces the need for an in-house incident response plan
1.explanation: An MSSP monitors security telemetry, while MDR adds investigation and response actions. Neither moves the organisation's accountability for its own reporting or response plan to the provider.

1.q: Why is 'are all log sources reporting?' one of the first checks at the start of every shift?
options: Because a gap in ingestion is a gap in detection that the queue cannot show
Because CERT-In requires a written ingestion report at each shift change
Because silent sources raise floods of false-positive alerts when they return
Because the SOAR platform stops all automations when any source goes quiet
1.explanation: If a source stops sending data, its rules cannot fire, and the queue simply looks calm; only a deliberate check reveals that the SOC is blind. CERT-In requires log retention, not shift-by-shift ingestion reports.

1.q: In the Banyan queue, R5 (log_cleared, 10.8) is at the top and R6 (beacon_regular_small, 3.6) is at the bottom, and both name WS-104. After taking R5, what is the most effective next investigative move?
options: Pull every alert sharing WS-104 and user divya into one case and rebuild the sequence in event-time order
Move to R2 next, because it holds the second-highest priority score in the queue at 7.2
Close R6 as routine telemetry traffic, because its low score shows the rule has little confidence
Suppress the second R3 hit as a duplicate so the queue only shows one alert per rule and host
1.explanation: The queue says where to start, not what the story is; grouping by shared entities and ordering by event time reveals the intrusion from 06:12 onwards. Working R2 next follows score order but ignores that R2 shares no entities with R5.

1.q: A rule for new local administrator accounts fires when an IT administrator runs an approved build script covered by a change ticket. How should the alert be dispositioned?
options: False positive, with a tuning request so the rule stops matching administrator scripts
Benign true positive, closed with the change ticket number recorded as the documented reason
Undetermined, because authorised and malicious account creation leave identical events
True positive, escalated so incident response can confirm the change ticket is genuine and approved
1.explanation: The rule detected exactly what it was built to detect, but the activity was authorised, which is the definition of a benign true positive. Calling it a false positive would wrongly imply the rule logic is broken.

1.q: A team routinely records authorised administrator actions as false positives instead of benign true positives. What is the most serious long-term consequence?
options: Closure notes become longer because each false positive needs a tuning ticket attached
Incident response receives more escalations because every false positive is reviewed by Tier 2
The per-rule false-positive rate is inflated, so detection engineers may weaken a healthy rule
Suppressions expire sooner because false-positive suppressions carry shorter review dates
1.explanation: Detection engineers tune rules using the false-positive rate; mislabelled BTPs make a correct rule look broken and invite changes that reduce coverage. The other options describe workload effects, not loss of detection.

1.q: Rule R4 (large_upload) matched the nightly backup job sending data to the approved storage endpoint. Which closure note meets the lifecycle's closure standard?
options: FP, closing: known backup traffic, no further action needed on this alert
FP: backup traffic, R4 is noisy for large uploads in general; suppressed R4 on all hosts with no expiry until detection engineering finds time to rewrite the rule properly
BTP: probably the backup job based on the destination name, closing to keep the queue short
FP: R4 matched the backup server's nightly upload to the approved endpoint, confirmed against backup schedule and change record; ticket raised for a narrow, expiring exclusion
1.explanation: A usable note states what happened, the evidence checked, the decision and what should change, so an engineer can act and a reviewer can verify. The broad suppression option removes coverage for every host, exactly what an attacker would hide behind.

1.q: triage.py gives R5 a priority of 10.8 from severity 4, confidence 0.9 and asset criticality 3. If the same log_cleared hit occurred on a host of criticality 1, what would its score be?
options: 10.8, because severity and confidence are properties of the rule rather than the host
3.6, so the same behaviour would rank alongside the beacon alert at the bottom of the queue
4.5, because the score is reduced by one criticality step for each level below the finance workstation
1.2, because confidence is applied twice when the asset is of low business importance
1.explanation: The score is the product severity x confidence x criticality, so 4 x 0.9 x 1 = 3.6. Asset context scales the priority; the rule's severity and confidence alone do not fix it.

1.q: A dashboard shows an alert in the In progress state, but the owner field is empty. How should a SOC lead interpret this?
options: It is effectively an unhandled New alert, because no named person is responsible for it
It is safe to leave, because the In progress state shows that triage has already begun
It should be moved to Pending, because unowned work is waiting for an external answer
It should be closed as undetermined, because the record cannot show who investigated it
1.explanation: Every state other than New and Closed needs a named owner; an ownerless In progress alert is New work disguised as handled. Pending is for waiting on an external answer and still requires an owner.

1.q: An alert has sat in Pending for two days waiting for a user to confirm whether they ran a script, and the playbook's time limit has passed. What should normally happen?
options: Close it as a benign true positive, since no complaint from the user suggests the run was intended
Leave it in Pending until the user replies, because closing without the answer would lose evidence
Close it as a false positive and raise a tuning ticket, since the rule produced an unanswerable alert
Escalate it as the playbook directs, because an unanswered confirmation is not evidence of safety
1.explanation: Pending must be time-limited, and the usual outcome when the answer never arrives is escalation, not closure. Silence from the user proves nothing about whether the activity was authorised.

1.q: Why should alert state transitions be timestamped by the case system in UTC rather than entered by the analyst?
options: Because analysts are not permitted to edit case records once an alert has been acknowledged by Tier 1
Because SIEM rules can only correlate events whose timestamps were written by the platform
Because those timestamps feed metrics and service levels, which need consistent, trustworthy times
Because UTC timestamps are required for the case system to sort the queue by priority score
1.explanation: System-written UTC transition times are the raw data for time-to-acknowledge and time-to-resolve metrics and for service-level timers. Typed times drift, vary by time zone and can be wrong.

1.q: Which suppression entry shows the properties of a well-formed suppression as described for the lab's triage helper?
options: R3, user matches *admin*, reason: admins create accounts often, no expiry date
R3, user = itadmin, reason: approved build account under CHG-1042, expires 2026-12-31
All rules, host = WS-104, reason: finance workstation is noisy, expires next quarter
R3, any user, reason: rule under review by detection engineering, expires when fixed
1.explanation: A good suppression names one rule, one field and one exact value, cites a change record as the reason and expires. The wildcard option is broad and permanent, removing coverage for any account whose name contains admin.

1.q: A Tier 1 analyst sends a chat message to a Tier 2 colleague about a suspicious alert, and the colleague replies that they will look later. The case record still lists the Tier 1 analyst as owner. What is the status of the escalation?
options: Not complete: ownership has not moved in the case system and no acknowledgement is recorded there
Complete: the Tier 2 colleague has accepted the work in writing, which transfers ownership in practice
Complete once the Tier 1 analyst sets the state to Escalated, even without a named receiver
Not required: chat escalations are logged by the platform, so the case record is not needed
1.explanation: Escalation is a transfer of ownership made through the case system and is complete only when the receiver acknowledges it there. A chat reply is a conversation, not a recorded hand-off.

1.q: R2 reports eight distinct users failing VPN logon from 203.0.113.66 before gopal succeeds from the same address. It shares no host or user with CASE-0001. How should the investigation treat it?
options: Merge it into CASE-0001, because two serious alerts on the same morning almost certainly share one actor
Close it as a false positive, because the account that succeeded is a standard user on a sales laptop
Record it as a true positive in a linked case, with any connection to CASE-0001 kept as an open hypothesis
Leave it undispositioned until CASE-0001 is closed, so both can be judged with the full set of evidence
1.explanation: The rule correctly detected a spray followed by a success, so the behaviour is a true positive, but without shared entities it is linked rather than merged, with the reason written down. Merging assumes a connection the evidence has not shown.

1.q: An analyst cannot decide whether an alert is malicious because process command lines were not being collected on the host. After recording the alert as undetermined, which feedback is most appropriate?
options: A tuning ticket asking detection engineering to lower the rule's severity until the data improves
A suppression for the host, since alerts that cannot be resolved only add noise to the queue
A playbook change telling analysts to close similar alerts as benign when evidence is missing
A telemetry-gap ticket, owned by the right team, requesting command-line collection on that host
1.explanation: Undetermined outcomes point at telemetry: the missing data is the finding and should be ticketed with an owner. Lowering severity or suppressing would hide the alert without fixing the blind spot.

1.q: In the Banyan case, fixed-size beacon requests from WS-104 began at 06:17, but the top-scoring alert was the log clearing at 08:17. What feedback does this true positive most clearly justify?
options: Raising the log_cleared rule's severity so that it scores above every other rule in the queue
Asking detection engineering whether the beacon detection should alert or score sooner than it did
Suppressing the large_upload rule on finance hosts, since it fired after the more useful beacon alert
Removing asset criticality from the score, since it pushed the finance host alerts too high
1.explanation: True positives point at coverage and speed; an earlier, low-scoring signal was available more than an hour before the loudest alert, which is a question for detection engineering. Raising log_cleared further does nothing to surface the earlier evidence.

1.q: A single rule matches the same host forty times in ten minutes for the same behaviour. What should the queueing stage do with these matches?
options: Deduplicate them into one alert carrying a hit counter, so the queue shows one item to work
Raise forty separate alerts, so each match receives its own disposition and closure note
Discard all but the first match, since later identical hits cannot add investigative value
Convert them into an incident automatically, since repeated matches confirm malicious activity
1.explanation: Deduplication collapses repeated hits of one rule on one entity into a single alert with a counter, preserving the information without flooding the queue. Discarding hits loses the count, and repetition alone does not make an incident.

1.q: R3 (new_local_admin) fired twice, at 07:02 and 07:03, both for the account svc_update on WS-104, from Windows Security events 4720 and 4732. What is the correct reading of the pair?
options: A duplicate pair caused by two collectors forwarding the same Security event to the SIEM
Two failed attempts to create svc_update, since a successful creation produces only one event
The account being deleted and recreated, which is typical of software update installers
An account being created and then added to a security-enabled local group, two linked steps
1.explanation: Event 4720 records a user account being created and 4732 a member being added to a security-enabled local group; together they show a new local administrator being set up. They are different events, so treating them as duplicate noise would miss a key step.

1.q: A targeted search on WS-104 shows a proxy fetch of invoice.docm at 06:12, a Sysmon event ID 1 for PowerShell at 06:14 and a 220-byte proxy request to a fixed URL at 06:17. Why does this strengthen the true positive disposition for R1?
options: Because any PowerShell start on a finance workstation is malicious regardless of its context
Because the 220-byte size matches a published signature for a known malware family
Because separate log sources independently agree on a plausible download, execution and callback sequence
Because the proxy records prove the user deliberately ran the macro inside the document
1.explanation: Corroboration across proxy, Sysmon and the follow-on proxy beacon, in a coherent time order, supports the disposition. The logs show sequence, not user intent, and PowerShell alone is not proof of compromise.

1.q: The lifecycle allows triage to go straight to the disposition decision, skipping investigation. When is that shortcut appropriate?
options: When the answer is already clear, such as a false positive caused by a data error, and it is still recorded
When the queue is long, since investigation can be deferred to the feedback stage after closure
When the alert has a low priority score, because low-scoring alerts rarely belong to larger cases
When the rule has a high confidence value, because confident rules do not need any corroborating evidence
1.explanation: Triage can close obvious cases directly, but the disposition and closure record are still required. Queue length and low scores are not reasons to skip investigation, as the low-scoring Banyan beacon alert shows.

1.q: triage.py shows R2 on host WS-107 even though VPN events carry no host field. What does this imply for the alert record?
options: The VPN logs are being parsed incorrectly and the host field must be reconstructed by the parser
The host came from a user-to-device mapping table, and the mapping method should be recorded
The host is the VPN concentrator, which the helper reports instead of the source IP address
The host is unreliable and should be removed, since enrichment must only use raw event fields
1.explanation: The helper maps gopal to a primary device via a PRIMARY_HOST table, which a real SOC would replace with DHCP, VPN or EDR data; recording the method tells later readers how much to trust it. Removing enrichment would discard useful context rather than qualify it.

1.q: The R6 line in the triage queue shows user=None (?). What is the correct explanation?
options: An unknown attacker account generated the beacon traffic and must be hunted in identity logs
The proxy source stopped sending user fields, which indicates a log-source health failure
The identity table has no entry for divya, so enrichment of the user failed for this rule
The rule groups by host and URL and returns no user, so enrichment has to tolerate the gap
1.explanation: R6 is a grouped rule keyed on host and URL, so there is no user value to enrich; the field is empty by design. The same identity table enriches divya successfully on the other WS-104 alerts.

1.q: A SOC manager worries that an insider on the team could close high-severity alerts as false positives to hide their own activity. Which lifecycle control best addresses this?
options: Raising the confidence values of high-severity rules so they always top the queue
Allowing only Tier 2 analysts to acknowledge alerts generated by high-severity rules
Sampling closed false positives on high-severity rules for evidence, with attributable state changes
Disabling the false positive disposition for high-severity rules so they must be escalated
1.explanation: Closure quality reviews that check the evidence behind sampled closures, combined with state changes attributable to named users, expose both drift and deliberate misuse. Removing the FP label would stop legitimate tuning feedback rather than detect abuse.

1.q: Post-incident reviews often find that the detection fired but nobody acted in time. Which lifecycle-level control most directly catches this failure as it happens?
options: Requiring every closure note to answer four questions before an alert can be closed
A meta-alert when a high-severity alert stays in New beyond its service level
Grouping new alerts automatically into open cases that share a host or user
Exporting the raw events of every high-severity alert with a hash and custody record
1.explanation: Monitoring the age of unacknowledged alerts detects warnings that exist but are not being worked. Closure-note standards and evidence export improve quality after someone acts; they do not notice that nobody has.

1.q: An alert scored 5.4 has waited an hour while a steady stream of new alerts scoring 5.5 to 6.0 keeps arriving above it. What does the lesson say queueing should account for?
options: Age, so that an older alert is not overtaken indefinitely by a stream of slightly higher scores
Nothing further, because the score already reflects severity, confidence and asset criticality fully
Volume, so that the 5.4 alert is closed automatically once newer alerts exceed a set count
Analyst preference, so that each analyst re-sorts the queue by the rules they know best
1.explanation: Age matters alongside score; without it, a moderate alert can starve in the queue. Leaving the order purely to score is exactly what allows that starvation.

1.q: A covered entity in India must report specified incidents to CERT-In within six hours of noticing them. Which property of the alert lifecycle record best supports showing that this was met?
options: A disposition label on each alert, showing which ones were confirmed as true positives
A ticketed feedback item for each closed case, showing that lessons were acted upon
Narrow, expiring suppressions, showing that no relevant alerts were silenced during the period
System-written timestamps for when the alert was raised, acknowledged and escalated
1.explanation: Demonstrating a reporting deadline depends on reliable, attributable times for when the SOC noticed and acted. Disposition labels say what was concluded, not when.

1.q: After the Banyan day, a manager reports that the SOC had seven incidents, one for each alert in the queue. What is wrong with that statement?
options: Nothing, because every alert from a correlation rule counts as an incident once it is queued
It undercounts, because the two R3 hits and each beacon request should be separate incidents
Alerts are claims to be tested; investigation grouped them into two cases, and only confirmed ones are incidents
It overcounts, because alerts on a single host can never form more than one incident
1.explanation: An alert is a claim; triage, investigation and disposition decide whether anything becomes an incident, and the seven alerts formed CASE-0001 plus a linked VPN case. The host-based option invents a rule the lesson does not state.

1.q: A rule that alerts on every powershell.exe start produces many false positives from administrative tools. Which fix best follows the lesson's guidance for false-positive feedback?
options: Suppress powershell.exe for all hosts until a better rule is written and tested by detection engineering
Require a suspicious parent-child relationship, such as Word starting PowerShell, not the name alone
Lower the rule's severity so its alerts sink below the threshold analysts usually reach
Reclassify the alerts as benign true positives so the false-positive rate stops rising
1.explanation: False positives point at detection logic, and adding context such as the parent process makes the rule precise without discarding coverage, as R1 does. A blanket suppression removes the coverage entirely.

1.q: A start-of-shift health query returns proxy last_seen 12:32, vpn 13:33, windows 08:17 and sysmon 06:14. What is the soundest conclusion before any investigation?
options: Endpoint telemetry may have stopped after 06:14, so a lack of Sysmon evidence later cannot be read as no activity
Sysmon is healthy, because its last event at 06:14 matches the R1 alert time, which shows the rule and agent are working
The proxy source is faulty, because it is the only source with far more events than the others
Nothing of note, because sources naturally report at different rates throughout a working day
1.explanation: The gap raises a question the analyst must answer, and until it is answered, absence of Sysmon events is not evidence of absence. Different volumes are normal; a source falling silent while others continue is the signal.

1.q: An analyst starts each shift by opening the queue and taking the top alert straight away. What is the main risk of skipping orientation?
options: The highest-priority alert may have been acknowledged already by the previous shift
The analyst will work alerts in score order rather than in event-time order
A source that has stopped sending looks exactly like a quiet night, so blind spots go unnoticed
The analyst cannot acknowledge any alert until the handover has been signed off in the case system
1.explanation: The queue cannot show what the SOC can no longer see; only a health check reveals a silent source. The other options describe minor or invented constraints rather than the core risk.

1.q: A new local administrator alert fires at 07:02, and the change calendar shows an approved IT task to build an account at 07:00. What should the analyst do?
options: Close it as a false positive, since the change calendar proves the rule fired in error
Check that the ticket matches the account and host, then record the change reference with the disposition
Escalate it immediately, because account creation on any workstation is always high impact
Suppress the rule for the whole morning, since approved work makes every alert in that change window benign
1.explanation: The change calendar can make the alert a benign true positive, but only if it actually covers this account and host, and recording the reference makes the decision defensible. In Banyan, svc_update was created by divya on a finance workstation, which a build ticket would not normally explain.

1.q: An analyst acknowledges R5 at the top of the Banyan queue and sees that five other lines name WS-104. What is the best next step?
options: Leave the other WS-104 alerts for colleagues, so the queue is shared fairly by priority
Take R2 next, since it is the oldest of the alerts scoring 7.2 and so should be handled first
Close the lower-scoring WS-104 alerts as duplicates of R5 to reduce the queue length
Open a case for the host and work the WS-104 alerts together rather than separately
1.explanation: Before starting, the workflow checks the queue for alerts sharing entities, and here they belong in one case. Splitting them across analysts hides the sequence; closing them as duplicates discards different evidence.

1.q: At 03:00 a Tier 1 analyst sees signs consistent with ransomware precursors, but the playbook says to escalate during business hours. What is the right action?
options: Follow the playbook and queue the escalation for 09:00, recording the evidence in the case meanwhile
Isolate the affected hosts personally before escalating, since waiting would allow encryption to begin
Escalate immediately through the emergency on-call path with the evidence, then raise a playbook change
Close the alert as undetermined until business hours, when Tier 2 can review the evidence
1.explanation: Playbooks support judgement and must never block an urgent response; the fix for the playbook comes afterwards. Taking response action outside one's authority is not the answer either.

1.q: An analyst has spent 30 minutes on an unclear alert, the planned time box for a first decision, and still cannot decide. What does the workflow call for?
options: Escalate or ask for help rather than continuing alone while the queue waits
Close it as undetermined so the time box metric for the shift is not breached
Keep investigating until a confident disposition is reached, however long it takes
Return it to New so another analyst picks it up later with a fresh view
1.explanation: A time box exists so an unclear alert does not absorb the analyst indefinitely; when it expires the analyst escalates or asks for help. Closing to meet a metric is evidence-free closure.

1.q: During the validate step for R1 (Word starting PowerShell on WS-104), the analyst asks what else would be true if the alert were real. Which check best answers that question?
options: Confirm that the R1 rule's severity and confidence values are set as detection engineering intended
Look for a document download shortly before the PowerShell start in the proxy logs for WS-104
Check whether other finance workstations also ran PowerShell during the same hour
Compare the R1 priority score with the other scores in the queue to judge its relative weight
1.explanation: If Word truly launched PowerShell from a malicious document, the document had to arrive somehow, so a preceding download is the expected corroborating evidence. Rule settings and queue scores say nothing about whether this event is real.

1.q: Which case note line correctly records an observation as a fact, kept separate from any assessment?
options: WS-104 is beaconing to a command-and-control server, confirmed by regular proxy traffic
The user probably opened a malicious invoice, which then started the beacon traffic
Proxy traffic looks suspicious and is consistent with known malware, so escalating
WS-104 made 18 requests of 220 bytes each to cdn-telemetry-sync.example from 06:17 UTC
1.explanation: The fact states what the logs show, with count, size, destination and UTC time. Calling it command and control is an assessment and should be labelled as one with its reasoning.

1.q: Six months after a case, a reviewer reads the note 'checked the proxy logs, nothing else found'. Why does this fall short of a defensible note?
options: Without the exact query text, nobody can reproduce what was searched or judge whether it was sufficient
Proxy logs are outside the analyst's remit and should be checked only by the network team
The note should state the analyst's tier, since conclusions carry weight according to seniority
Notes that report no findings should not be written, since only positive evidence is retained
1.explanation: Copying the query as run lets anyone rerun it and see its scope, which is what makes the note reviewable. The other options misstate who may search or what notes should hold.

1.q: A SOC with analysts in two countries finds that case notes from different sites disagree on when actions happened around a daylight-saving change. Which habit removes the problem?
options: Writing each site's local time with its time-zone name beside it in the note
Recording only the order of steps, since exact times are kept by the case system
Using UTC for every observation and action recorded in case notes
Converting all notes to head-office local time when the case is closed
1.explanation: UTC avoids confusion across sites and daylight-saving changes, and matches the lab data and tools. Labelled local times still need conversion and remain error-prone.

1.q: Weeks after evidence_export.py was run for CASE-0001, the exported file no longer matches its SHA256SUMS entry. What should the analyst conclude?
options: The manifest is out of date and should be regenerated from the current file before use
The file has changed since export, so its integrity cannot be relied on and the custody record must be examined
The mismatch is expected, because the custody utc field is rewritten each time the exported file is opened or copied
The events were re-indexed by the SIEM, which updates exported copies automatically
1.explanation: A digest mismatch means the bytes differ from what was recorded at export, so the item can no longer be shown to be unchanged. Regenerating the manifest would destroy the very check that reveals the problem.

1.q: A student runs evidence_export.py and finds that the utc field in custody.jsonl differs from the value shown in the lesson. What does this indicate?
options: The dataset differs from the course version, so the export should be repeated
The custody record is corrupt, because utc should equal the time of the first event
The system clock is wrong, because utc should match the end of the query window
Nothing is wrong, because utc records when the export was run rather than any event time
1.explanation: The utc field is the time of the export action, so every run will differ. The digest, not the utc field, is what matches only when the dataset is identical.

1.q: A case may lead to a disciplinary process. Why should the analyst export the relevant events during the shift rather than rely on finding them in the SIEM later?
options: Retention limits and re-indexing can remove or change the raw events the case depends on
SIEM searches cannot be cited in disciplinary processes unless the platform is certified
Exported files are smaller, so they are faster to search than the SIEM's original index
Exporting events automatically closes the case, which stops the service-level clock
1.explanation: SIEM data does not last forever and can change, so evidence is preserved early with a hash and custody record. The other options invent rules about certification or case closure.

1.q: Re-running the lab's evidence_export.py overwrites the exported file and appends a second custody line. How should a production evidence system behave instead?
options: Overwrite silently, since only the most recent export is relevant to the investigation
Delete the earlier custody line, so the record shows one clean export per item
Refuse to overwrite an existing evidence item, preserving the original and its record
Rename the old file without hashing it, so storage is not consumed by duplicate digests
1.explanation: The lesson notes that a production system would refuse to overwrite; evidence must stay as collected, with every custody action recorded. Deleting custody lines destroys the history the record exists to keep.

1.q: Which escalation note best lets a Tier 2 responder act without re-investigating CASE-0001?
options: WS-104 looks compromised, beaconing and a cleared log seen; please take over urgently
UTC timeline of WS-104 activity, affected user and criticality, evidence export reference, actions taken, recommendation, open unknowns
All 32 exported events pasted in full, so the responder can review them in their own order
Assessment: likely exfiltration; recommend isolating WS-104 at once; the timeline, evidence and remaining details are in the analyst's personal notes
1.explanation: A good escalation states what and when, which entities and how critical, the evidence, what was done, what is recommended and what is still unknown. A raw event dump shifts the analysis back to the receiver.

1.q: An analyst escalates a case in the case system, but the receiving team has not acknowledged it within the agreed time. Who owns the alert, and what happens next?
options: The receiving team owns it, because the escalation was recorded in the case system
The SOC lead owns it automatically, and the analyst returns to the queue
Nobody owns it until acknowledgement arrives, so it reverts to the New state
The original analyst still owns it and follows the escalation path to the next contact
1.explanation: Escalation is complete only on acknowledgement; until then ownership stays with the sender, who must chase it along the path to the next contact or on-call lead. Recording the escalation alone does not transfer responsibility.

1.q: An analyst sees the rule title beacon_regular_small and its low score of 3.6 and is inclined to close it as routine telemetry. Which part of the workflow most directly counters this anchoring?
options: The related-alert check on the same entities and asking what else would be true if it were real
Acknowledging the alert first, which records an owner and starts the service-level clock
Reading the handover, which lists the previous shift's open cases and pending decisions
Exporting the events with a hash, so the decision can be reviewed by someone else later
1.explanation: Anchoring is over-weighting the first impression; checking related alerts on WS-104 and testing the alert's implications pulls in contrary evidence. Acknowledgement and export are useful but do not challenge the first impression.

1.q: An analyst has decided early that a case is a benign software update and keeps finding evidence that fits. Which note-taking habit best guards against confirmation bias here?
options: Writing the note at the end of the shift, once the full picture has become clear
Recording only the evidence that supports the current assessment, to keep notes short
Separating facts from the assessment and writing down what evidence would refute it
Copying the previous shift's assessment so the case conclusion stays consistent
1.explanation: Labelling the assessment and stating what would disprove it keeps alternative explanations alive. Recording only supporting evidence is confirmation bias written down.

1.q: An analyst notices that one noisy rule produces hundreds of near-identical, mostly benign alerts each shift and that colleagues close them almost without looking. What is the best response?
options: Create a personal suppression for the rule, since the alerts are almost always benign
Report the rule so the feedback stage can tune it, alongside measures such as rotating duties
Close the alerts in bulk at the start of each shift, so attention is saved for other rules
Raise the rule's severity, so analysts treat its alerts with more care during triage
1.explanation: Alert fatigue leads to fast closure of the alert that matters; the defences are organisational, including tuning noisy rules through feedback, as much as individual. An unreviewed personal suppression removes coverage without an owner or expiry.

1.q: An analyst is called to an incident bridge halfway through handling an alert. What should they leave in the case note before going?
options: A disposition, so the alert does not breach its service level while they are away
Nothing, because the case system records each query the analyst has already run
A request for the alert to be reassigned, since interrupted work should be restarted
Where they are and what they were about to check, so they or a colleague can resume
1.explanation: Interruptions compound bias and lost context; a note of current position and next check lets work resume without starting again. Forcing a disposition to beat a timer is evidence-free closure.

1.q: An analyst with SIEM-wide search uses it to look at a colleague's browsing records out of curiosity, with no assigned case. How should this be judged?
options: As misuse, because powerful tools may be used only for authorised work on assigned cases
As acceptable, because the analyst's role grants access to all proxy data in the SIEM
As acceptable if no data is exported, because viewing results leaves no evidence copy
As a policy gap only, because the tool allowed the search and so no rule was broken
1.explanation: Searches must be limited to what a case needs, and personal data handled in line with policy and the DPDP Act 2023; the tool allowing a search does not make it authorised. Not exporting the data does not change that it was accessed without purpose.

1.q: Why does the analyst workflow place documentation inside the per-alert loop rather than at the end of the shift?
options: Because the case system locks notes once the analyst's shift has formally ended
Because notes written later are shorter, which makes them harder for reviewers to sample
Because notes reconstructed from memory are less accurate and complete than ones written while working
Because each loop step must be documented before the next alert in the queue can be acknowledged by anyone
1.explanation: The case note serves handover, escalation, review and possibly legal use, and memory-based notes lose queries, times and evidence references. The other options invent system behaviour.

1.q: A SOC wants to detect automatically that a log source has gone quiet, rather than relying on analysts noticing at the start of a shift. Which detection does this?
options: A rule that fires when the total number of alerts per hour falls below its usual level
A rule that fires when a source's event volume rises well above its normal daily rate
A meta-alert that fires when a high-severity alert stays unowned beyond its service level
An alert when a source's most recent event is older than its expected reporting interval
1.explanation: Comparing each source's last event time with its expected interval detects silence directly. A drop in alert totals is ambiguous, and the unowned-alert meta-alert covers a different workflow failure.

1.q: The handover says a case is pending a user's confirmation and that a host should be watched. What should the incoming analyst do first with this information?
options: Accept the summary as written and move straight to the top of the alert queue
Open the cases in the case system, confirm their current state and note what is now theirs
Close the pending case, since the user has had a full shift to answer the question
Ask the previous analyst to stay on until the pending case has been resolved
1.explanation: Orientation means reading the handover fully, then confirming each case's state in the system rather than trusting the summary, and taking ownership of what has passed over. Closing a pending case without an answer skips the playbook's time-limit rule.

1.q: While working a case on one host, an analyst sees a low-priority alert lower in the queue that fits the pattern under investigation and takes it ahead of higher-scoring alerts. Is this acceptable?
options: No, because the priority order is a control and must be followed exactly by every analyst
No, unless a supervisor first re-scores the alert so that it rises to the top of the queue
Yes, because the score is a starting point, provided the analyst records why in the note
Yes, and no record is needed, since the alert will be grouped into the case anyway
1.explanation: The score guides where to start, but an analyst may take an alert that fits an active pattern, and the reason belongs in the note so the choice is reviewable. Skipping the record makes the deviation unexplained.

1.q: In the fictional '2 a.m. handover gap' scenario, a night analyst recognised a ransomware precursor and messaged a colleague who had already gone home. The morning shift found encrypted file servers. What was the root failure?
options: Knowledge and responsibility moved only by chat, no case was opened, so nobody owned the alert
The detection rule failed to fire on the precursor activity until the encryption had already begun overnight
The night analyst misjudged the alert's severity and classified it as low priority
The on-call rota listed the wrong phone number for the escalation contact
1.explanation: The rule fired and the analyst recognised it; what failed was the transfer of knowledge and ownership, because a chat message creates no case and no accountable owner. Misjudged severity is wrong because the analyst correctly saw it as serious.

1.q: During the overlap the outgoing analyst says 'CASE-1047 is yours now' and the incoming analyst replies 'noted'. Nobody reassigns the case in the case system. Forty minutes later, who owns CASE-1047?
options: The incoming analyst, because the verbal briefing and reply transferred responsibility
The outgoing analyst, because ownership moves only on reassignment plus acknowledgement in the case system
The shift lead, because any case without a recorded owner defaults to the supervisor
Nobody, until the shift lead signs off the handover and the case system then reassigns the case automatically to the next shift
1.explanation: The lesson's rule is mechanical: until the case system shows a new named owner who has acknowledged it, the outgoing analyst still owns the case. A spoken 'noted' is not an acknowledgement and leaves exactly the ambiguous gap the procedure exists to close.

1.q: Why does the handover procedure require the incoming shift to read the published note and the queue before the verbal briefing begins?
options: So the incoming analysts can acknowledge every case in the case system before the outgoing shift explains any of them
So the outgoing analyst can skip the briefing entirely whenever the note is complete
So the briefing becomes a conversation about what is unclear instead of reading the note aloud
So the shift lead can measure how long each incoming analyst takes to read the note
1.explanation: Reading first means the incoming analyst arrives with questions, and the overlap is spent on gaps and misunderstandings. Acknowledging before the briefing is wrong because ownership is transferred at the end, after read-back.

1.q: A per-source query in the mini-SIEM shows proxy events until 12:32Z but the last sysmon event at 06:14Z. All four expected sources appear in the output. How should the outgoing analyst treat this in the handover?
options: Open a high-severity incident, because missing endpoint telemetry means the agents were tampered with
Leave it out, because every expected source appears in the output and is therefore still ingesting events normally
Report that endpoints were idle after 06:14Z, so no endpoint activity needs review
Record it in platform health as an open question, such as confirming the sysmon agent is still reporting
1.explanation: The difference may be normal for the data, so the right move is to state it as a question for the next shift rather than conclude either way. Omitting it is the strongest distractor, but a source being present says nothing about whether it is still reporting now.

1.q: After a shift with no new cases, an analyst decides not to write a handover note because 'there is nothing to hand over'. Why is this a mistake?
options: Because every shift must close at least one case before it is allowed to sign off
Because 'quiet' is itself information, and platform health and intel or changes still need reporting
Because a missing note automatically breaches the SOC's acknowledgement SLA for every case open during the shift
Because the incoming shift cannot log into the case system without the previous handover
1.explanation: Silence is ambiguous: the reader cannot tell a quiet shift from a forgotten note, and a quiet SIEM is only good news if the data is arriving. The SLA option is wrong because SLA timers attach to cases, not to handover notes.

1.q: While filling the seven-section handover template, an analyst has nothing to report under 'Pending decisions'. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Delete the heading so that the note stays short enough to read in two minutes
Merge the section into the headline so readers see that nothing is pending
Leave the section blank, since an empty section under a printed heading clearly tells the reader that nothing is pending
Keep the heading and write 'none', so the reader can tell nothing happened from a forgotten section
1.explanation: Writing 'none' distinguishes 'nothing to report' from 'the writer forgot'. A blank section is the strongest distractor, but blank looks identical to an omission, which is the ambiguity the template is meant to remove.

1.q: Why does the handover template list pending decisions and approvals as a separate section instead of folding them into open cases?
options: Because no analyst action is due while the SOC waits, so they get lost unless someone owns the chasing
Because approvals from other teams must be stored outside the case system for legal reasons
Because pending decisions never have deadlines and can safely be reviewed together at the end of the shift
Because only the shift lead is permitted to read the section that concerns other teams
1.explanation: When the SOC is only waiting, nothing in its own queue prompts action, so the item drifts; listing it separately assigns the chasing. The 'no deadlines' option is wrong because an unchased approval can delay containment of a live case.

1.q: At 01:30Z the night shift noticed a cyber incident at an Indian covered entity that falls under the CERT-In Directions of April 2022. The report has not yet been filed when the shift ends. Where and how should the handover capture this?
options: Under intelligence and changes, since it concerns a regulatory advisory from CERT-In rather than a live SOC case
Under pending decisions only, because legal decides whether the report is filed
Under active incidents, stating when the six-hour clock started and whether the report has been made
It can be left out, because regulatory reporting is the compliance team's job, not the SOC's
1.explanation: Regulatory clocks belong with the active incident, with the start time and report status, because the six hours run from noticing and the next shift may have little time left. Pending decisions is the closest distractor, but it hides the hard deadline away from the incident it belongs to.

1.q: According to the handover sequence figure, what is the most common way handovers degrade?
options: The shift lead signs off before the incoming analyst has read the queue
The incoming analyst reads the note before the outgoing analyst has finished it
Cases are reassigned to the incoming shift before the overlap period begins
Talking happens before writing, so the verbal briefing becomes the only record
1.explanation: Reversing 'write' and 'talk' leaves no durable record once the outgoing analyst leaves. Early sign-off is also a fault, but the lesson singles out talking before writing as the most common degradation.

1.q: In read-back, the incoming analyst says 'the identity team owes us a reply by 06:00 UTC'. The outgoing analyst corrects it to 04:00 UTC. Why does this step catch errors that a well-written note cannot?
options: Because read-back replaces the note as the official record of the handover
Because the writer cannot see how the reader interprets the note, and read-back exposes that interpretation
Because the case system only records deadlines that have been confirmed verbally by both analysts during read-back
Because the note is written in UTC while the read-back is done in local time
1.explanation: Read-back is an error-correction loop: the reader's restatement shows the writer what was actually understood. It does not replace the note, which remains the durable record.

1.q: A SOC moves from a single-site team to a follow-the-sun model with teams in Asia, Europe and the Americas. What change to handover practice does this make most important?
options: Dropping the overlap, since each region works daytime hours, fatigue is no longer a factor and notes can carry everything
Moving handovers to direct chat, because the teams rarely share a working language
Writing notes for a competent reader who was not there, because teams may never meet and lack local context
Letting each region keep its own template so notes match local working habits
1.explanation: Every follow-the-sun handover crosses a language, culture and time-zone boundary, so written quality matters even more and notes must not rely on local abbreviations or context. Dropping the overlap is wrong: it often becomes a scheduled video call.

1.q: A SOC's handover falls at 03:30 UTC, exactly when staff in India start work at 09:00 IST and authentication alerts spike. Handovers at this boundary are consistently rushed. What is the best fix?
options: Move the shift boundary away from the predictable busy period and keep a 15 to 30 minute overlap
Shorten the overlap so the handover is finished before the login spike begins
Suppress authentication alerts for the duration of the handover window each morning
Have the outgoing shift skip the verbal briefing on busy mornings and rely on the note
1.explanation: Boundaries should not coincide with predictable busy periods, and the overlap is the most valuable design choice. Suppressing alerts would create a blind spot, and shortening the overlap removes the time for briefing and read-back.

1.q: A SOC aligned to Indian Standard Time runs its day shift 08:30-16:30 IST. How should this shift be recorded in UTC in its handover notes?
1.explanation: IST is UTC+5:30, so 08:30 IST is 03:00 UTC and 16:30 IST is 11:00 UTC. 03:30-11:30 is the classic error of subtracting only five hours.

1.q: Which control would most directly have prevented a critical alert from sitting unowned after a shift change, as in the 2 a.m. handover gap?
options: A case-system alert when a critical or high case has no acknowledged owner a set time after handover
A weekly quality-assurance review of a sample of handover notes from each shift
A rule that escalations must be confirmed by a reply in the team chat channel
A longer retention period for handover notes so they can be reviewed after an incident
1.explanation: Alerting on unacknowledged critical cases makes the shift boundary observable while there is still time to act. Weekly QA is a good practice but finds the gap days later, and chat confirmation leaves the case outside the system of record.

1.q: An outgoing analyst pastes the titles of all 60 alerts from the shift into the handover note. What is wrong with this?
options: Alert titles may contain personal data and must never appear in handover notes
The case system cannot store notes longer than the standard template length
It hides the few items that matter; the note should summarise and prioritise while the queue holds detail
It forces the incoming shift to re-triage every alert from the beginning of the shift before it can work any new ones
1.explanation: A raw list buries the two alerts that matter among 58 that do not. The note's job is prioritised summary; the queue already holds the detail. Re-triaging everything is not implied by the list itself.

1.q: Why is step 1 of the procedure, bringing every open case up to date, described as the most important step?
options: Because updated cases allow the shift lead to sign off before the verbal briefing
Because a note that says 'see CASE-1042' is only useful if CASE-1042 records status, checks done and next action
Because the SLA clocks on each case pause while it is being updated by its owner
Because the incoming shift is not allowed to read any case that was updated by the outgoing shift during the overlap
1.explanation: The note links to cases instead of repeating them, so incomplete case records make the whole handover hollow. Updating a case does not pause SLA timers, and sign-off comes last, after ownership is acknowledged.

1.q: A draft handover entry reads: 'CASE-1042 High - credential stuffing, blocked.' Which rewrite best follows the lesson's guidance?
options: Attach the full raw WAF and portal logs to the note so the incoming analyst can draw their own conclusion about what happened and what to do next
Remove 'credential stuffing' entirely, because handover notes must contain only facts
Add the analyst's personal confidence level and rationale for the High severity rating
State facts and times, mark the assessment as suspected, give block time and change reference, and a next step with a deadline
1.explanation: Good entries separate observed facts (412 failed logins from two ranges) from labelled assessment, record the action taken with its reference, and state the next step and due time. Removing the assessment is wrong; it should be labelled, not deleted.

1.q: Why should handover notes live in the access-controlled case system instead of in email threads or broadly shared documents?
options: Because email cannot carry UTC timestamps reliably between time zones
Because the case system automatically deletes notes once the cases are closed
Because they summarise live incidents and may contain personal data, which must be protected and kept to what the next shift needs
Because the CERT-In Directions require every handover note at an Indian covered entity to be submitted and stored through the case system
1.explanation: Handover notes are sensitive: they describe live incidents and affected accounts, and under the DPDP Act 2023 personal data in SOC records must be protected. They are also retained as evidence, not deleted at closure.

1.q: What is the shift lead's role at the end of the handover procedure?
options: Confirm every open case has an acknowledged owner, check the on-call rota and raise platform issues, then record the handover complete
Rewrite the handover note in a standard format before the incoming analysts read it
Reassign all open cases personally so that analysts do not need to acknowledge them
Run the verbal briefing for each open case personally so that the outgoing analysts can leave on time and the incoming ones need not read the note
1.explanation: The lead closes the handover by verifying coverage. Reassigning cases personally is wrong because acknowledgement by the named new owner is what transfers responsibility.
