1.q: In a post-incident review, investigators want to know who was accountable for a case at 02:57 UTC and how long it sat after being reassigned. Why can a properly used case system answer this?
options: Because it stores the full transcript of the verbal briefing for every handover
Because reassignment and acknowledgement are separate timestamped events, giving an ownership audit trail
Because the shift lead's sign-off records the owner of every case at that moment
Because the handover note lists every case owner along with the exact time each of them joined and left the shift
1.explanation: Separate timestamps for reassignment and acknowledgement show who owned the case at any moment and the gap between the two, and they feed SLA timers. The sign-off is a single point in time and does not give per-case history.

1.q: To counter end-of-shift fatigue, many SOCs reserve the last 20 to 30 minutes of a shift for handover work. How are alerts handled during that window?
options: All new alerts, including high-severity ones, are held in the queue until the incoming shift has acknowledged all of its open cases
New alerts are assigned to the shift lead, who works them alone until the handover ends
The SIEM is paused so no new alerts are generated during the handover window
New low-priority alerts are left for the incoming shift, while high-severity alerts are still worked by whoever is best placed
1.explanation: Reserving time protects handover quality without creating a blind spot: only low-priority work waits. Holding all alerts is the close distractor, but it would let a high-severity alert sit untouched at the riskiest moment.

1.q: The lab's soc_metrics.py reports a mean time to acknowledge of 32.4 minutes but a median of 4.0, driven by one true-positive case that waited 150 minutes. Read through the lens of handovers, what does this suggest?
options: One outlier, plausibly a case that crossed a shift boundary without an owner, drags the mean while the median hides it
Most cases were acknowledged slowly, and the median understates the typical delay
The dataset is unreliable, because a mean cannot legitimately be eight times larger than the median of the same set of cases
The SOC's acknowledgement performance is good, since the median is what SLAs measure
1.explanation: A single long wait inflates the mean while the median stays low; the lab exercise asks you to treat it as a case lost at a shift boundary and write the missing handover entry. Means far above medians are normal with skewed data, so the 'unreliable' option is wrong.

1.q: A small in-house team staffs the SOC only during business hours and relies on an on-call rota overnight. How does this change the handover picture?
options: No handover is needed, because the on-call person only responds to pages overnight and never owns or works any cases
There is one handover per day, from the night coverage back to the day team in the morning
There are two handovers a day; the night coverage must know which cases are live and what authority it has
There are three handovers a day, the same as a standard three-shift 24x7 rotation
1.explanation: The handover happens twice: day team to night coverage and back. The night coverage needs to know live cases and its authority, and the morning team must learn what happened overnight.

1.q: What is the correct role of team chat in a SOC's handover and escalation process?
options: It is the primary escalation channel for critical cases because it is the fastest
It can point colleagues at a case, but the case itself and its ownership must live in the case system
It can replace the written note on quiet shifts, as long as the whole team is in the channel and has read the messages
It should be banned from the SOC, because messages cannot be retained as evidence
1.explanation: Chat is fast but does not persist, alert or transfer ownership, so it may say 'look at CASE-1042 now' but never replace the case. Critical escalations use the case system plus a phone call, so the primary-channel option is wrong.

1.q: The intelligence-and-changes section of a handover notes an authorised penetration test running 04:00-06:00Z. What does recording this, with its authorisation and contact list, mainly achieve?
options: It lets the incoming shift suppress every alert from the test's source addresses for the whole window without opening any cases
It moves responsibility for any alerts in the window from the SOC to the testing firm
It removes the need to open cases for alerts that occur during the testing window
It warns the next shift to expect unusual alerts and to check activity is in scope, rather than ignore or blindly escalate it
1.explanation: Changes and tests cause expected alerts; the authorisation and contacts let analysts verify activity against scope. Blanket suppression is the dangerous distractor, because real attacker activity during the window would then go unseen.

1.q: The SOC promises its business owners to contain compromised accounts quickly, and the identity team commits in writing to reset an account within one hour of a SOC request. In ITIL terms, what is the identity team's commitment?
options: A service level agreement, because it defines a measurable service level
A service level objective, because it is a specific measurable target
An operational level agreement, because it is between teams of the same organisation and supports the SLA
An underpinning contract, because the SOC depends on it to meet its own commitments to the business owners
1.explanation: An OLA is an internal agreement between teams that supports an SLA. An underpinning contract is the close distractor, but that term is for external suppliers such as a log-platform vendor.

1.q: An MSSP contract with an Indian customer covered by the CERT-In Directions says the provider will notify the customer of confirmed incidents 'within five hours of the incident being noticed'. What is the main problem?
options: The customer's six-hour CERT-In clock also runs from noticing, leaving it only about an hour to prepare and file the report
Nothing, because CERT-In's six-hour clock starts only when the provider notifies the customer, not when the incident is first noticed
The contract should use business hours, since CERT-In reports can only be filed during the working day
The provider, not the customer, becomes responsible for reporting to CERT-In once it has the facts
1.explanation: An SLA does not move the customer's regulatory obligation, so notification targets must leave enough time inside the six hours. The second option is the key misconception: the clock runs from noticing or being notified, not from the provider's hand-off.

1.q: A critical alert reaches the queue at 23:00 IST. The SLA says 'acknowledge within 30 minutes' using a business-hour timer for 09:00-18:00 IST on weekdays, and the next day is a working day. When is acknowledgement due?
options: 23:30 IST the same night
09:00 IST the next morning
18:00 IST the next day
09:30 IST the next morning
1.explanation: A business-hour timer stops outside the working day, so the 30 minutes only begin to count at 09:00 and expire at 09:30. That is exactly why critical work in a 24x7 SOC uses calendar-hour timers.

1.q: A case is created at 09:00:00 UTC. An analyst opens it to look at the details at 09:04 and assigns it to themselves at 09:12. Against a correctly defined SLA, what is the time to acknowledge?
options: 4 minutes, because the analyst had seen the alert by 09:04
12 minutes, because acknowledgement stops when a named analyst takes ownership
0 minutes, because the case was in the queue and visible from creation
8 minutes, measured from first viewing to the assignment of an owner
1.explanation: Time to acknowledge stops when a named analyst takes ownership, not when someone opens the alert to look at it. Counting first viewing would let the SOC appear responsive while nobody owned the case.

1.q: A Medium case created at 10:00 is upgraded to Critical at 13:00 when the analyst discovers the host is a domain controller. Which timer rule does the lesson recommend, and why?
options: Apply the stricter Critical target measured from the original creation time, so nobody gains time by starting low
Restart all timers from 13:00 using Critical targets, since the domain-controller risk only became known at that point
Keep the Medium targets, because severity at creation is what the SLA measures
Pause every timer during reclassification and resume with Critical targets afterwards
1.explanation: Measuring the stricter target from original creation removes the incentive to start cases at a low severity. Restarting at 13:00 is the plausible but gameable alternative, because it rewards initial under-classification.

1.q: Which of these is a legitimate use of an SLA clock pause?
options: Pausing a Critical case's time-to-notify timer while legal reviews and approves the exact wording of the notice sent to the customer
Setting a case to 'awaiting customer' near a breach so the analyst has time to finish triage
Pausing a High case's resolution timer after a recorded request for isolation approval, resuming automatically on reply
Pausing all open case timers during the shift handover so that work is not counted twice
1.explanation: A pause must be defined in the SLA, set by a recorded outbound request, and cleared on reply. Pauses should never apply to acknowledgement or notification for critical severities, which rules out the first option.

1.q: The Critical acknowledgement target is 15 minutes and the case platform warns the owner when 75% of a target has elapsed. An unowned Critical case reached the queue at 09:00. When should the warning fire?
options: At 09:05, a third of the way into the target
At 09:10, two thirds of the way into the 15-minute target
At 09:15, when the target is reached
At about 09:11, when 75% of the target has elapsed
1.explanation: 75% of 15 minutes is 11.25 minutes, so the warning fires at about 09:11 and the breach at 09:15. 09:15 is the breach point, where the shift lead is alerted, not the warning.

1.q: The lab's sla_check.py reports 'acknowledged within 15 min: 4/5 (80%)' and one breach: a true positive acknowledged after 150 minutes. How should the monthly SLA report present this?
options: Report 80% compliance only, since the median of 4.0 minutes shows the SOC performs well overall and the breach is noise
List the breached case individually with its disposition and a reason code, alongside the percentage
Exclude the breach as an outlier, because one case distorts a sample of five
Report the mean of 32.4 minutes only, because it already reflects the slow case
1.explanation: The single breach is the case that mattered most, and a percentage alone hides it. Reporting the mean is the close distractor, but it still does not show which case breached, whether it was real, or why.

1.q: A customer complains that their MSSP 'never finds anything useful', yet every monthly SLA report is fully green. What is the most likely cause, and the best remedy?
options: The SLA measures acknowledgement speed, not investigation quality; add quality reviews and service reviews of real cases
The SLA targets are too tight; relax them so that analysts have more time per alert
The customer misunderstands the report; add more charts so the green results are clearer
The provider is falsifying timestamps; move SLA calculation to the customer's own SIEM and audit the provider's case system
1.explanation: This is a 'watermelon' SLA, green outside and red inside, because the agreement measures the wrong things. Relaxing targets does not address what is measured; pairing speed with quality review does.

1.q: After a time-to-acknowledge target is introduced, analysts start clicking 'assign to me' on every new alert and looking at them later. Which change best counters this?
options: Tighten the acknowledgement target so analysts have less time to delay
Remove the acknowledgement target and measure only time to resolve
Allow each analyst to hold only one unacknowledged alert at a time
Also measure time to triage and review samples of acknowledged cases
1.explanation: Measuring time to an initial disposition and sampling cases exposes acknowledgement without action. Measuring only resolution invites the more dangerous distortion of closing cases early.

1.q: An MSSP pays penalties when time to resolve is missed. Its analysts begin closing difficult cases as false positives near the deadline. Why is this the most dangerous SLA distortion, and what is the control?
options: It inflates the false-positive share in monthly reports; the control is to remove false-positive metrics from the SLA entirely
It shortens resolution times too much; the control is to add a minimum time before closure
It turns real alerts into 'noise'; the control is quality review of closed cases and treating reopened cases as failures
It breaches the notification SLA; the control is to pause resolution timers on difficult cases
1.explanation: Early closure can bury a real intrusion, so closed cases are sampled and reopens count as quality failures. Pausing timers would just add a second gaming route, the abuse of pauses.

1.q: A SOC SLA starts the acknowledgement clock at the timestamp of the underlying log event rather than when the alert reaches the SOC queue. What is the effect?
options: Clock-synchronisation errors between systems no longer affect the measurement
Log collection and rule scheduling delays count against the SOC's acknowledgement time
The SOC gains time, because events are always logged after the alert is raised
Paused intervals can no longer be subtracted from the elapsed time
1.explanation: Starting at event time charges ingestion and rule delays to the SOC. Most SLAs start at queue arrival, the first moment the SOC can act, and measure the earlier delay separately as time to detect.

1.q: Why does the CERT-In requirement to synchronise ICT system clocks with NIC or NPL NTP servers (or servers traceable to them) matter for SOC SLAs?
options: It makes timestamps from different systems comparable, so start and stop events can be measured reliably
It allows SLA timers to run in IST instead of UTC for Indian customers, matching the regulator's own reporting clock
It makes the case system the legal source of time for regulatory reports
It removes the need to record the time zone alongside each timestamp
1.explanation: SLA timers subtract one event's timestamp from another's, often from different systems, so clocks must agree. The lesson still records every timestamp in UTC; synchronisation does not change the time zone.

1.q: Using the illustrative Banyan matrix, High-severity CASE-1042 is confirmed as an account takeover at 05:00Z. By when must the customer be notified?
options: 05:30Z, the High acknowledgement target measured from confirmation
07:00Z, two hours after confirmation, matching the High triage target
09:00Z, within four hours of confirmation
11:00Z, six hours after confirmation to align with CERT-In
1.explanation: High notification is 'within 4 h' of confirmation, and the notification column starts at confirmation, not at alert creation. The CERT-In six hours is a separate clock, running from noticing, that must be checked independently.

1.q: In the Banyan severity matrix, Critical and High targets are in minutes and hours, while Medium and Low are in business days. What does this design require of the case platform?
options: A separate case queue for each severity level
Manual timing of Medium and Low cases by the shift lead
That Medium and Low cases are never escalated outside business hours, even when new evidence shows they are more serious than first thought
Both calendar-hour and business-hour clocks, since high-severity work runs 24x7 while lower severities wait for daytime staff
1.explanation: The change of units is deliberate, and implementing it needs both kinds of timer. The 'never escalated' option is wrong: a Medium case can be reclassified upward at any hour, which then applies the stricter target.

1.q: A SOC's SLA promises to contain a compromised account within one hour, but containment depends on the identity team, which has no commitment to act on SOC requests. What does this reveal?
options: The SLA should be changed to business-hour timers so that the identity team can act on requests during its working hours
The SLA promises something the SOC cannot deliver, because it lacks a supporting OLA with the identity team
The containment target should be paused permanently until the identity team replies to each request
The identity team's delays should be recorded as SOC breaches to motivate faster action
1.explanation: An SLA can only be met if the agreements beneath it are met; the missing piece is an OLA. A permanent pause would just hide the dependency rather than fix it.

1.q: A fictional hospital's MSSP contract says only 'monitoring of logs'. Which gap matters most when an alert fires at 3 a.m.?
options: It does not say which logs, during which hours, how quickly alerts are examined, or who is called
It does not name the SIEM product or version the provider will use
It does not state how many analysts the provider employs in total
It does not require the provider to be based in the same country as the hospital, or to keep its analysts on site
1.explanation: Scope, hours, time targets and escalation contacts decide what actually happens at 3 a.m. The tooling and headcount options are operational details an SLA need not fix.

1.q: A SOC sets a Critical acknowledgement target of 2 minutes with a staffing level that can realistically deliver 10. What does the lesson predict?
options: Analysts will become faster over time, because tight targets drive improvement
The SOC will report frequent breaches, but detection quality will be unaffected
Constant breaches teach everyone to ignore breach alerts, and analysts acknowledge without looking
Customers will receive service credits, which in turn fund the extra staff needed to meet the target within months
1.explanation: Unrealistic targets both devalue breach alerts and push people to meet the number instead of doing the work. Targets should be set from measured alert volumes and staffing, with noisy detections fixed.

1.q: For the time-to-notify target in the Banyan matrix, what is the start event?
options: Creation of the alert in the SIEM
Confirmation of an incident
Acknowledgement by the case owner
Completion of the triage decision on the alert
1.explanation: Notification is measured from confirmation of an incident, which is why its column has a different start event from acknowledgement and triage. On the timer figure, escalation as an incident is what starts the notification clock.

1.q: A High case breached its two-hour triage target. The next day, further analysis shows it should have been Medium all along, and it is downgraded. Under the lesson's rules, what happens to the breach?
options: It is removed, because the Medium triage target of one business day was never actually exceeded once the severity was corrected
It is converted to a warning, because the original severity was wrong
It is transferred to the analyst who assigned the original severity
It remains recorded; a downgrade keeps any breach already recorded, though its reason code can note the misclassification
1.explanation: A downgrade keeps existing breaches, otherwise downgrading near or after a breach would become a way to erase failures. 'Misclassified severity' is one of the lesson's reason codes, so the review still explains it.

1.q: In a contractual dispute, the customer questions when a critical case was escalated. Which handling of SLA records best supports the SOC?
options: Timestamps typed by the analyst at each step, so the record reflects their own judgement
A summary of the case written by the shift lead after closure
Timestamps generated by the case system, kept with the case and protected from editing
Screenshots of the SLA dashboard taken at the end of each month
1.explanation: SLA records are evidence and must be system-generated, retained with the case and tamper-resistant. Hand-typed times are open to error and challenge, which is why the lesson rules them out.

1.q: A SOC detects a personal data breach at a customer. Under the DPDP Act 2023, the data fiduciary must inform the Data Protection Board and affected data principals. How does the SOC's SLA bear on this?
options: Its notification target to the customer's privacy or legal team determines how early that decision can be made
The SOC must notify the Data Protection Board directly within six hours under its SLA, on behalf of the fiduciary and the principals
The SOC's SLA replaces the fiduciary's obligation once the customer has been informed
It has no bearing, because personal data breaches are handled outside security monitoring
1.explanation: The SOC usually does not decide on DPDP notification, but its notification SLA controls how soon the fiduciary can. Six hours belongs to CERT-In reporting, not to the DPDP Act, and an SLA never replaces a legal duty.

1.q: An analyst argues that the CERT-In six-hour reporting clock only starts once the investigation has established root cause, so there is no need to involve legal early. How should the SOC's internal process be designed instead?
options: Start the internal clock at closure, since only a complete investigation can be reported accurately
Hand the case to legal only once the customer approves containment, since that approval marks the moment the incident is confirmed
Let the six-hour clock start at the next shift handover, so ownership is clear before reporting
Treat the clock as running from noticing and hand the facts to legal or compliance well inside it, for example within two hours
1.explanation: The six hours run from noticing or being notified, not from completing the investigation, so the internal target must leave time to prepare and approve the report. Waiting for closure could miss the deadline entirely.

1.q: A manager says, 'Our mean time to acknowledge was 32.4 minutes this month, so our SLA is met.' What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Mean time to acknowledge can only be calculated for true-positive cases
An SLA is checked case by case against a target, while MTTA is an aggregate that can hide individual breaches
The SLA should be measured with the median instead, which always matches the case-by-case compliance percentage
A mean above 15 minutes automatically means every Critical case breached
1.explanation: The SLA is the commitment and its per-case targets; metrics such as MTTA summarise performance over time. The median option is wrong because the lab median of 4.0 minutes looks excellent while a true positive still breached.

1.q: An MSSP's escalation procedure for Critical incidents is 'update the ticket and email the customer distribution list'. A ransomware precursor is confirmed at 03:00. What is the most important fix to the SLA?
options: Add a chat notification to the customer's team channel as well as the email
Shorten the Critical notification target so the email goes out sooner
Name an on-call contact on both sides and require a phone call that wakes them, plus the case update
Move Critical escalation to the next business morning, when the customer distribution list is actively monitored
1.explanation: A critical incident at 03:00 needs a named on-call person and a method that wakes them, not only a ticket or email. A shorter target does not help if nobody reads the message, and chat has the same problem.

1.q: Two SOCs both report "MTTR 40 minutes" in a quarterly benchmark. Why can you not conclude that they perform equally well?
options: Their MTTR definitions may use different start and stop points, such as creation vs acknowledgement or containment vs closure
MTTR is only comparable when both SOCs run the same SIEM product, the same correlation rules, the same case platform and the same shift pattern
One SOC must be reporting a median and the other a mean, because benchmarks always mix the two
MTTR is a lagging metric that only becomes comparable after a full year of case data
1.explanation: The "R" can mean respond, remediate, recover or resolve, and the clock may start at creation or acknowledgement, so equal numbers can measure different intervals. Mixing median and mean is possible but not guaranteed; the definition problem always applies.

1.q: A day's acknowledgement times are 3, 4, 6, 8 and 240 minutes. Which pair of summaries is correct?
options: Median 8.0 minutes, mean 52.2 minutes
Median 6.0 minutes, mean 52.2 minutes
Median 6.0 minutes, mean 65.3 minutes
Median 52.2 minutes, mean 6.0 minutes
1.explanation: Sorted, the middle value is 6, so the median is 6.0; the sum is 261, divided by 5 gives a mean of 52.2. Choosing 8 as the median picks the fourth value rather than the third.

1.q: In soc_metrics.py the 09:00 true positive was acknowledged after 150 minutes. If that delay were 1,500 minutes instead, what would happen to the reported median MTTA?
options: It would rise to 5.0 minutes
It would rise to roughly 302 minutes
It would stay at 4.0 minutes
It would fall to 2.0 minutes
1.explanation: The median depends only on the order of values; the outlier stays the largest value, so the middle value is still 4 minutes. Around 302 minutes is what the mean would become, not the median.

1.q: Why is MTTD harder to measure honestly than MTTA in a typical SOC?
options: MTTD can only be measured once analysts have acknowledged every alert within its SLA
MTTD is defined only for false positives, which are rarely investigated in depth
MTTD depends on the SIEM keeping raw events for no more than thirty days
The start of malicious activity is usually established only later, by investigation
1.explanation: MTTD starts at the attacker's first action, which is reconstructed during investigation, so it is retrospective and available only for investigated true positives. MTTA uses two system timestamps that exist as soon as a case is picked up.

1.q: A manager proposes counting benign true positives as false positives in the weekly false-positive share. What is the strongest objection?
options: It would lower the reported false-positive share and hide genuinely noisy rules
It would make correctly firing rules look noisy, risking them being disabled and losing coverage
It would break the median calculation, because BTP cases have no acknowledgement timestamp to measure from
It would double-count each BTP case in both the true-positive and false-positive totals
1.explanation: A BTP is a correct detection of authorised activity; labelling it FP makes a working rule look noisy and may lead to it being switched off. Merging BTPs would raise, not lower, the FP share, so the first option has the effect backwards.

1.q: The lab run reports a false-positive share of 40 per cent. What does this figure primarily point to?
options: An opportunity for detection engineering to tune the rules that produced those alerts
Tier 1 analysts misclassifying real incidents as false positives in order to protect their averages
An inflated MTTA, because false positives are the slowest cases to acknowledge
A coverage gap, because critical assets are not sending enough log sources
1.explanation: False positives are a property of detection rules and telemetry, so a high share is a tuning signal; closing FPs quickly and correctly is good analyst work. In the lab data the FP cases were among the fastest, so they do not inflate MTTA.

1.q: Using the lesson's model, where MTTR is measured from case creation, a night-shift staffing gap adds 60 minutes of queue wait to every case while investigation time is unchanged. What happens?
options: MTTA rises but MTTR is unchanged, because MTTR starts when the analyst acknowledges
MTTR rises but MTTA is unchanged, because the queue wait is not a timed interval
Neither changes, because the wait happens before the case is created in the system
Both MTTA and MTTR rise, because MTTR from creation already includes the queue wait
1.explanation: Acknowledgement time absorbs the wait directly, and resolution measured from creation contains it too, so a slow queue inflates both. MTTR would be unaffected only if the organisation measured it from acknowledgement, which is not this model.

1.q: The extended lab script prints median resolve TP 205.0 min (n=2) and FP 10.0 min (n=2), while the overall median MTTR is 20.0 minutes. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The overall median of 20 minutes is the right figure for planning true-positive workload
False positives consume more analyst time than true positives because their count is equal
A single blended MTTR describes no real case, so resolution should be reported by disposition
The TP median of 205 minutes is reliable enough to set a new true-positive resolution SLA directly from it
1.explanation: Blending 10-minute FPs with multi-hour TPs gives a figure that matches neither, so splitting by disposition and severity is more informative. With only two cases, the TP median is far too fragile to set an SLA.

1.q: Over one quarter, a SOC's MTTR falls sharply while the reopen rate rises and weekly case-review scores fall. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Detection rules were tuned successfully, so fewer complex alerts reach analysts and cases close faster
Analysts have become more efficient at investigation and evidence gathering
Cases are probably being closed before investigation is complete, a Goodhart's law effect
Telemetry coverage has improved, so each investigation needs less searching
1.explanation: Faster closure paired with more reopened cases and worse review scores signals premature closure driven by the speed target. Genuine efficiency gains would not normally reduce review quality or increase reopens.

1.q: Why should the timestamps behind SOC speed metrics be written automatically by the case system with an audit trail?
options: Hand-entered times drift and can be altered under pressure, so metrics built on them cannot be trusted
Hand-entered times cannot be stored in ISO 8601 format, so the metric scripts fail to parse them reliably
Automatic timestamps let the SOC compute MTTD in real time for every case as it opens
Automatic timestamps exclude false positives from MTTR without any extra filtering
1.explanation: A metric that depends on an editable field will eventually be edited, so system-generated, auditable UTC timestamps are required. Automation does not make MTTD real-time, because the activity start is still found by investigation.

1.q: A SOC has excellent MTTA, yet its payment servers send no logs at all. Which family of metrics would have exposed this weakness?
options: Speed metrics, such as MTTA split by severity
Coverage metrics, such as the share of critical assets sending logs
Volume metrics, such as alerts per rule per day
Quality metrics, such as reopen rate and review scores
1.explanation: Coverage measures what the SOC can see at all; speed, volume and quality metrics only describe alerts that were generated, so a silent asset never appears in them.

1.q: A SOC lead plans to publish a weekly leaderboard ranking analysts by personal MTTR. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Publish it, because individual MTTR is an objective and fair measure of analyst skill
Publish it, but rank analysts by median rather than mean so that single long outliers are ignored
Publish it, but exclude true positives so long investigations are not penalised
Do not publish rankings; use per-analyst data privately for coaching alongside case review
1.explanation: Speed rankings reward cherry-picking easy alerts and closing hard ones early, and punish the analyst who works the real intrusion. Switching to the median or excluding TPs still leaves the perverse incentive in place.

1.q: MTTA is stable most of the day but rises steeply between 02:00 and 06:00 UTC. What should the SOC lead investigate first?
options: A staffing or queue-coverage gap during those hours
Whether the early-shift analysts lack triage skills
Whether detection rules fire more false positives at night
Whether improved MTTD is pushing more alerts into that window
1.explanation: MTTA measures how long alerts wait for an owner, so a time-of-day rise reflects queue health and staffing rather than analyst skill. More FPs would add volume but is a weaker explanation than missing cover.

1.q: When metrics_ext.py imports CASES and p from soc_metrics.py, the three summary lines are printed before the per-case lines. Why?
options: metrics_ext.py explicitly calls a summary function defined in soc_metrics.py
Python prints the docstring and top-level output of every module it imports
soc_metrics.py has no if __name__ == "__main__" guard, so its top-level prints run on import
The from-import statement re-executes soc_metrics.py a second time after metrics_ext.py finishes running
1.explanation: Importing a module executes its top-level code, and without a main guard the print statements run as a side effect. No summary function exists, and the import runs once, at the point of import, not afterwards.

1.q: With the illustrative 15-minute acknowledgement target, four of the five lab cases are marked ok. Why is reporting "80 per cent compliance" on its own not enough?
options: Compliance percentages must be calculated from medians rather than from individual cases
The BTP case should have been excluded, which would make compliance 75 per cent
SLA compliance may only be reported over true positives, never over all cases
The single breach is a true positive, and the named breach list is what drives action
1.explanation: The percentage is accurate but hides that the one breach was a real incident waiting 150 minutes; the exception list puts that case in front of the reviewer. Excluding the BTP would give 3 of 4, still not the point.

1.q: A weekly export contains several cases that are still open at the end of the reporting period. How should they be handled in resolution metrics?
options: Include them with a resolution time set to the period end, so that MTTR covers every case in the export
Exclude them from resolution metrics, but report how many are open and the age of the oldest
Delete them from the export, because unresolved cases distort the mean resolution time
Give them the current median resolution time so the sample size stays the same
1.explanation: Open cases have no resolution timestamp, so they cannot enter MTTR honestly, but their count and age must be visible because long-open cases are often the important ones. Imputing an end time or median invents data.

1.q: Why are MTTD and time to contain normally computed only over true positives, while MTTA and MTTR can cover all cases?
options: A false positive has no attacker activity to detect or contain, so those intervals have no meaning
Containment times are recorded only by the EDR, which discards false-positive cases before they are exported
Including false positives in those intervals would artificially lower MTTA as well
Containment and detection SLAs apply only to benign true positives by convention
1.explanation: A false positive goes from acknowledgement straight to closure with no malicious activity start and no containment step. Acknowledgement and resolution exist for every case, so those can be computed over all cases or split by disposition.

1.q: A correlation rule has produced zero hits in the three months since a log parser was upgraded. What is the appropriate response?
options: Retire the rule, because three months of silence shows the threat is absent
Lower its severity so that it no longer affects the coverage figures
Test it, because a field-name change may have broken it without any error
Raise its acknowledgement SLA, because rarely firing rules need less urgency
1.explanation: Rules with zero hits may be broken by a renamed field rather than genuinely quiet, so they warrant testing and automated alerting. Retiring the rule on the assumption of absence could remove real coverage.

1.q: For SOC response-time data, why is the mean usually larger than the median?
options: The mean discards the smallest values before averaging
Times have a floor at zero but no ceiling, so a long tail pulls the sum up
The median is calculated only from false-positive cases
The mean is usually computed in seconds and the median in minutes
1.explanation: Response times are right-skewed: they cannot go below zero but a few cases can be very long, and the mean, which depends on the sum, follows those tail cases while the median does not.

1.q: A dashboard shows a median acknowledgement time of 3 minutes for critical true positives this week, with n=2, and a manager wants to plot it as a weekly trend. What is the main concern?
options: The mean should be plotted instead, because it is more stable at small sample sizes
Critical TPs should be merged with false positives so the sample becomes meaningful
The 90th percentile should be reported instead, because it stays reliable at any sample size, including n=2
With n=2 the median is fragile and a percentile meaningless, so trends need caution and n shown
1.explanation: Tiny samples make any summary unstable, so the sample size must be printed and trends treated with caution. The mean is even more sensitive to a single value, and a p90 of two cases is not meaningful.

1.q: Which of these is an acceptable entry for a SOC metrics definition sheet?
options: MTTR = resolved minus created, all cases, minutes, reported as median and mean
MTTR = how quickly the team responds to security incidents on average
MTTR = the resolution target agreed for high-severity cases in the SLA
MTTR = the duration the analyst writes into the case closure notes
1.explanation: A usable definition states the formula, start and stop points, population, unit and summary. The second option is a vague description, the third is a target rather than a measurement, and the fourth relies on an editable manual field.

1.q: What does the 2013 Target breach, as used in this lesson, illustrate about SOC metrics?
options: That detection technology failed to raise any warnings about the intrusion
That warnings were raised but not acted on, the failure that response metrics and exception lists expose
That short log retention made it impossible to reconstruct the timeline afterwards
That excessive false positives forced analysts to switch off the intrusion detection system before the breach
1.explanation: The Senate committee staff analysis reported that automated intrusion-detection warnings were generated but not responded to; the gap was in response, which acknowledgement metrics and breach lists make visible. It was not a failure to detect.

1.q: Which of these measures most deserves automated, near-real-time alerting rather than appearing only in a weekly report?
options: The monthly reopen rate for closed cases
The quarterly median MTTR split by severity
The time since each expected log source last sent an event
The year-on-year change in alerts per analyst
1.explanation: A silent log source creates a blind spot immediately and no speed metric will reveal it, so it needs its own alert. Reopen rate and quarterly trends are review measures where a weekly or monthly cadence is adequate.

1.q: Case records exported for metrics reporting contain user names, host names and sometimes email content. What does the lesson require for these exports?
options: Remove all timestamps so that the export no longer identifies individuals
Keep each export for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction
Apply no special controls, because metrics exports stay inside the SOC
Minimise the data and control access in line with the DPDP Act 2023
1.explanation: Metrics exports carry personal data, so they should contain only what reporting needs and be access-controlled under the DPDP Act 2023. Removing timestamps would destroy the metrics, and the 180-day rule concerns CERT-In log retention, not reports.

1.q: In weekly case review, senior analysts find that about one in five cases closed as false positive at Tier 1 should have gone to Tier 2, although none of them were reopened. Which quality metric captures this most directly?
options: Reopen rate for closed cases
False-positive share per rule
Escalation accuracy between tiers
Coverage of ATT&CK techniques
1.explanation: Escalation accuracy tracks how often Tier 2 finds that a Tier 1 closure should have been escalated. Reopen rate would miss these cases because none came back, which is why sampling-based review is needed alongside it.

1.q: After a log parser update, a well-tested detection stops firing and no component reports an error. Which part of the tooling map most likely broke?
options: The SIEM-to-case integration, because alerts are generated but rejected by the case API without notice
The SOAR-to-EDR response hook, because isolation commands are timing out
The pipeline's normalisation step, because a renamed field silently breaks rules that use it
The context-source lookup, because slow enrichment suppresses new alerts
1.explanation: Parsing and normalisation happen in the collection pipeline, and a field renamed there makes every rule using the old name match nothing, with no error. A failing case API would leave alerts visible in the SIEM, which is a different symptom.

1.q: During a busy shift, a Tier 1 analyst escalates a suspicious login to Tier 2 only by chat message. Why is this a problem for the SOC?
options: To the SOC record it never happened: no owner, timestamps or evidence in a case, and metrics miss it
It is acceptable as long as the chat platform keeps its messages for at least 180 days
It is the preferred method, because chat is faster than updating a case while an incident is still unfolding
It matters only for false positives, which need a documented disposition at closure
1.explanation: Case management is the single source of truth for handover, timestamps and metrics; an escalation outside it has no owner or audit trail. Chat retention does not make the message part of the case record.

1.q: A SOAR playbook is being designed for new phishing-related cases. Which action can safely be fully automated without a human approval gate?
options: Disabling the recipient's account as soon as a high-severity detection fires
Fetching the host's criticality and owner from the CMDB and writing them to the case
Isolating the host through the EDR as soon as the TIP marks the sender's IP as known-bad
Blocking the linked domain at the perimeter firewall for every user
1.explanation: Enrichment lookups are low-risk and reversible, so they can run automatically. Disabling accounts, isolating hosts and firewall blocks can disrupt the business on a false positive and belong behind an approval gate.

1.q: The kit's source-count search returns proxy 284, sysmon 33, windows 13 and vpn 10. What lesson about tooling does this distribution illustrate?
options: Proxy logs are low-value noise and should be dropped to reduce SIEM licence cost
Sysmon collection is broken, because it produced less than an eighth of the proxy volume
VPN logging is incomplete, because identity events should match endpoint volume
Web telemetry dominates volume, while endpoint and identity events are fewer but richer
1.explanation: Network and web telemetry is high-volume and cheap per event, which matters for SIEM sizing; dropping it would lose the best view of data leaving the organisation. Different sources naturally produce very different volumes.

1.q: A SOAR playbook automatically isolates any host on a single detection. Beyond outages from false positives, what risk does the lesson identify?
options: An attacker who understands the playbook could trigger it deliberately to disrupt the business
The playbook could leak the SOAR platform's stored API keys into the case notes
The playbook would stop the SIEM from correlating any further events from that host
The playbook would skip enrichment entirely, so isolated cases would reach analysts with no context
1.explanation: Automatic disruptive actions can be weaponised: someone who knows the trigger can cause outages on demand, which is why such actions require human approval. The other options are not consequences of auto-isolation itself.

1.q: In minisiem.py, the load command stores common fields as columns and also keeps a raw column. What does the raw column correspond to in a real SIEM?
options: A cache of recent search results kept to speed up repeated queries
The enrichment that the SOAR platform writes back after a lookup
The original event preserved alongside its parsed and normalised fields
A per-event hash used to prove evidence integrity in court
1.explanation: load keeps the original event as JSON in raw, which is how a SIEM preserves the source record next to the parsed fields. Enrichment comes later from triage tooling, and hashing for custody is a separate kit script.

1.q: Following an R1 office_spawns_script alert across the tooling map, at which point does the MTTA clock from the metrics lesson start?
options: When Sysmon on the workstation records the process creation
When the SIEM correlation rule matches the normalised event
When the analyst approves host isolation through the EDR
When the alert becomes a case with a creation timestamp
1.explanation: MTTA runs from case creation to acknowledgement, so the clock starts when the case management system records the case. The rule match produces the alert, but the timed interval begins with the case record.

1.q: During an authorised purple-team exercise, the red team stops the log forwarder on a server rather than clearing its event log. Which control is designed to catch this?
options: A detection rule for Windows Security event ID 1102, raised whenever an audit log is cleared
A health check that alerts when an expected source has sent nothing for N minutes
A Sigma rule for winword.exe spawning powershell.exe
A SOAR playbook that adds CMDB criticality to new cases
1.explanation: Stopping collection produces silence rather than an event, so only monitoring for missing data catches it. Event 1102 fires when the audit log is cleared, which did not happen here.

1.q: How should the credentials used by SOC integrations, such as the SOAR connector to the identity provider, be managed?
options: A dedicated least-privilege service account or key per integration, held in a secrets manager and rotated
One shared administrator key for all integrations, held in the SOAR platform so that rotation is a single change
Each analyst's personal credentials, so that every automated action is attributable
Keys embedded directly in playbooks, so they survive migrations between platforms
1.explanation: Each integration should have its own minimum-permission credential, stored and rotated securely, and its use logged. A shared admin key turns one compromise into access to everything the SOC controls.

1.q: Analysts copy indicators by hand between six separate consoles to work each case. What remedy does the lesson recommend?
options: Replace all of them with a single, more capable SIEM product that includes its own case management, EDR and SOAR
Add a dashboard console that aggregates screenshots of the other six
Integrate the tools into the case system or retire duplicates, since each manual copy adds delay and error
Assign one analyst to each console so nobody has to switch screens
1.explanation: Tool sprawl is fixed by integration and consolidation around the case system. Buying a new SIEM does not fix process, and another console or per-console staffing keeps the manual hand-offs in place.

1.q: The SIEM shows no alerts at all for an entire day. Why does the lesson argue that the team must understand how its alerts are produced?
options: Because a day with zero alerts always means the SIEM licence has lapsed
Because commercial SIEMs cannot run correlation rules against synthetic data, so quiet days cannot be tested
Because transparent scripts process events faster than production SIEMs do
Because without that understanding nobody can tell whether a quiet day is genuinely quiet
1.explanation: Treating the SIEM as a black box hides silent failures: a broken source or rule looks exactly like a safe day. That is why the course teaches each function on transparent scripts before production tools.

1.q: A student renames the user field in minisiem.py's events schema. Which effect best reflects how the course kit mirrors production fragility?
options: Only minisiem.py's own search command would stop working
triage.py, ioc_match.py and hunt.py would break together, as tools sharing one schema do
Only make_dataset.py would fail, and regenerating the dataset would restore the old name
Nothing would break, because each kit script keeps its own private copy of the data
1.explanation: Most kit scripts share minisiem.py's SQLite database and field list, just as production tools share a SIEM's normalised schema, so one schema change breaks every consumer. The scripts do not keep private copies.

1.q: Which normalised event would match the kit's correlation rule R1 office_spawns_script?
options: Sysmon event ID 3 in which winword.exe opens a network connection
Sysmon event ID 1 with parent image winword.exe and image powershell.exe
Windows Security event ID 1102 recorded on a finance workstation
Sysmon event ID 1 with parent image powershell.exe and image winword.exe
1.explanation: R1 looks for process creation (event ID 1) where Word is the parent and PowerShell or cmd is the child. The reversed parent-child pair describes a different behaviour, and event ID 3 is a network connection, not process creation.

1.q: Which capability does an EDR platform provide that a SIEM on its own does not?
options: Taking authorised response actions on the host, such as isolating it or ending a process
Correlating endpoint events with VPN and proxy logs on a single timeline for the investigating analyst
Retaining normalised events centrally for a defined retention period
Matching network traffic against signatures at the perimeter
1.explanation: EDR is both a detector and a response tool on the endpoint. Cross-source correlation and central retention are the SIEM's strengths, and signature matching of traffic is what IDS sensors such as Suricata do.

1.q: Which activity is an NDR sensor most likely to reveal that the organisation's EDR deployment would miss?
options: A Word macro spawning PowerShell on a managed laptop
A new registry run key created on a managed server
A process stopping antivirus on a managed workstation
Lateral movement from an unmanaged device with no agent
1.explanation: EDR only sees hosts where its agent runs, while network sensors see traffic from unmanaged devices and between servers. The other three happen on managed hosts, where the EDR agent records them directly.

1.q: The SIEM team owns the SIEM and the endpoint team owns the EDR. The connector between them failed and nobody noticed for a week. What process gap does this reveal?
options: The EDR lacked behavioural detection for the threats it was missing
The SIEM's retention period was too short to show the gap
Nobody owned the connector itself or had a health check defined for it
The SOAR playbooks lacked approval gates for response actions
1.explanation: Integrations fall between teams, so the tooling map assigns an owner and a health check to every arrow, not only every tool. The other options do not explain why a silent integration failure went undetected.

1.q: What is the main purpose of the failure-impact field in a tooling-map inventory entry?
options: To state concretely what visibility the SOC loses if the tool fails, which drives priority and budget
To record which team is to blame when the tool or its connector fails
To replace a health check for tools that cannot be monitored automatically, so outages are recorded by hand
To document personal-data flows as required by the DPDP Act 2023
1.explanation: A sentence such as "no endpoint process visibility for 2,000 workstations" makes the risk of a failure concrete, which helps prioritise fixes and justify spend. It complements, not replaces, a health check.

1.q: An Indian entity covered by CERT-In's April 2022 directions plans to keep SIEM logs for 60 days in an overseas cloud region to save cost. What is wrong with the plan?
options: Nothing, provided the logs are encrypted at rest in the overseas region
The directions require ICT system logs for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction
The directions require reporting within 6 hours, so 60 days of retention is excessive
The DPDP Act 2023 forbids retaining any log that contains personal data for longer than 30 days
1.explanation: The directions require covered entities to maintain ICT logs for a rolling 180 days within India, so both the period and the location fail. The 6-hour figure is the incident-reporting deadline, not a retention limit.

1.q: A compromised SIEM administrator account is used to delete detection rules. Which control gives defenders the best chance of noticing?
options: Letting Tier 1 analysts edit rules so that more people see each change
Keeping a backup copy of every rule inside the SOAR playbooks
Relying on the SIEM's own change history, which records every rule edit but which its administrators can edit
Logging admin activity to a store its admins cannot quietly alter, and alerting on rule deletions
1.explanation: Monitoring the monitors means sending the tools' administrative logs somewhere the same administrators cannot tamper with, and treating rule deletions as high-value detections. A history the attacker can edit offers no assurance.

1.q: During triage an analyst needs to know how critical host FIN-WS-12 is and which business unit owns it. Which context source answers this?
options: The threat intelligence platform
The malware analysis sandbox
The CMDB or asset inventory
The identity provider
1.explanation: The CMDB records assets, their owners and criticality. The identity provider answers questions about users and their roles, and the TIP answers whether an indicator is known.

1.q: Which part of the SOC tooling map does the kit script triage.py stand in for?
options: SOAR and context-source enrichment, adding asset criticality and user role and computing a priority
The collection pipeline, parsing two raw log formats into one normalised schema before any rules run
Detection engineering, testing rules against known-bad and near-miss events
Evidence preservation, writing a hashed chain-of-custody record for a case
1.explanation: triage.py attaches criticality and the user's department and role from tables standing in for a CMDB and identity provider, then scores priority. Parsing is normalise_demo.py, rule testing is test_rules.py and custody is evidence_export.py.

1.q: During a major incident the team suspects that the corporate chat and email platform may itself be compromised. What gap in the tooling map does this expose?
options: The SIEM does not retain chat logs long enough for investigation
The SOAR platform has no connector for paging on-call staff, so escalation waits for analysts to notice
The case system has no field to record the channel used
Escalation relies on one channel that may be compromised, so an out-of-band channel is needed
1.explanation: Communication tools belong on the map, and an escalation path with a single channel is a single point of failure, especially if an attacker can read it. Retention and case fields do not address reaching people safely.

1.q: An intrusion is discovered weeks late. According to the lesson, what should the SOC lead's first question be?
options: Which analyst was on shift when the first malicious activity occurred?
Which arrow on the tooling map failed to carry the evidence?
Which competing SIEM product would have detected the activity?
Which SLA target did Tier 1 breach during the incident?
1.explanation: Most SOC failures are integration failures, so the review starts by finding the broken link between tools, and the answer updates the map. Blaming the analyst or the product skips the systemic cause.

1.q: An organisation with no asset inventory, unclear escalation paths and untested rules plans to fix detection by migrating to a more expensive SIEM. What outcome does the lesson predict?
options: Detection will improve, because modern SIEMs include built-in asset discovery
MTTA will fall, because the new platform acknowledges alerts automatically
The same failures will recur on a costlier platform, because tools amplify process rather than replace it
Coverage will rise, because a migration forces every log source to be re-onboarded and every rule to be retested
1.explanation: Tools do not supply missing process: without context, clear escalation and tested rules, the new SIEM repeats the old failures. The map and process should be fixed first, then tools chosen to fill real gaps.

1.q: The API integration that turns SIEM alerts into cases starts failing without any notification. What symptom would the SOC experience?
options: Sources stop sending events and the SIEM shows rising ingestion lag
Cases still open, but their enrichment fields arrive empty
Alerts are generated in the SIEM but never reach an analyst as cases
The EDR stops isolating hosts after an analyst has approved it
1.explanation: The SIEM-to-case arrow carries alerts to humans; if it breaks, detection still happens but nobody works the alerts, and the queue simply looks quiet. Empty enrichment would point to the SOAR-to-context link instead.

2.q: An EDR console shows that rundll32.exe ran on a file server yesterday, yet a search of that server's Windows Security log finds no event 4688 for it. What should the analyst check first before drawing any conclusion?
options: Whether the Audit Process Creation subcategory was enabled on that server
Whether the EDR agent recorded the process under a different parent image
Whether the server's Sysmon configuration excludes rundll32.exe by name
Whether the 4688 was written to the System channel instead of Security
2.explanation: The Security log holds only what audit policy enables, so a missing 4688 first raises the question of whether process creation was audited at all. A Sysmon exclusion would affect Sysmon event 1, not the Security log's 4688.

2.q: A 4688 event confirms that powershell.exe started on a workstation, but the Process Command Line field is empty. Which explanation fits best?
options: PowerShell script block logging was disabled on the workstation
The process was started by a background service instead of a user with an interactive session
The policy to include command lines in process creation events is off
The event was truncated because the encoded command was too long
2.explanation: Event 4688 carries the command line only when the separate 'Include command line in process creation events' setting is enabled. Script block logging controls 4104 events and has no effect on the 4688 field.

2.q: A process command line shows powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand followed by a long Base64 string. Which telemetry source is most likely to give the analyst the readable code that PowerShell actually executed?
options: Security event 4688 with command-line auditing enabled
PowerShell Operational event 4104, script block logging
Sysmon event 1, including the ParentCommandLine field
Sysmon event 11, recording the script file that was created
2.explanation: Script block logging records script blocks as PowerShell processes them, so the decoded code appears in readable form. 4688 and Sysmon event 1 only repeat the encoded command line as it was typed.

2.q: The same account produces a 4624 with logon type 2 at 09:00 on the user's own desktop and a 4624 with logon type 10 at 00:40 from another workstation. What does the second event indicate?
options: A network logon, for example the account opening a file share
A service starting under the account's stored credentials
A console logon at the keyboard of the second workstation
A Remote Desktop session into the host using the account
2.explanation: Logon type 10 is RemoteInteractive, the Remote Desktop logon; at midnight from another machine it deserves a closer look. Type 3 is a network logon such as a file share access, and type 2 is the console.

2.q: Two analysts disagree about a cluster of failed logons (4625). One wants to know whether the attempts targeted real accounts. Which part of the 4625 events answers that question?
options: The logon type, which separates interactive from network attempts
The privileges list, which is filled in only for valid accounts
The status and sub-status codes, such as 0xC000006A for a bad password
The parent process field, which tells the analyst which program submitted the logon request to the operating system
2.explanation: The status and sub-status codes explain why the logon failed; 0xC000006A means the name was valid and the password wrong, which distinguishes it from attempts against non-existent accounts. Logon type says how the attempt was made, not whether the account exists.

2.q: An analyst wants to join every network connection and file write to the exact process instance that made them across a full day of Sysmon data. Which field is the reliable join key, and why?
options: ProcessGuid, because process IDs are reused and can be ambiguous
ProcessId, because it is unique for as long as the host is running
Image, because each executable path belongs to a single process
User, because each process runs in exactly one security context
2.explanation: Windows reuses process IDs quickly, so a PID can belong to several unrelated processes over a day; Sysmon's ProcessGuid identifies one process instance. Image and User are shared by many processes and cannot identify one instance.

2.q: A Sysmon event 1 shows Image C:\Users\Public\notepad.exe, but the analyst suspects the file is really a renamed copy of a different tool. Which field in the event best tests that suspicion?
options: CurrentDirectory, which shows where the process was started
IntegrityLevel, which shows whether the process was elevated
ParentImage, which shows which program launched the process
OriginalFileName, taken from the file's version resource
2.explanation: OriginalFileName comes from the binary's version resource, so it still names the original tool when the file on disk has been renamed. ParentImage describes the launcher, not the identity of the file itself.

2.q: During an investigation the team needs evidence that some process opened the Windows logon process to read its memory. Which Sysmon event type records that kind of activity?
options: Event 8, CreateRemoteThread
Event 10, process access
Event 7, image loaded
Event 3, network connection
2.explanation: Sysmon event 10 records one process opening another, which is how reading the logon process's memory shows up. Event 8 is a thread being started inside another process, a different action.

2.q: On a Linux server, an administrator logged in over SSH as their own account and then used sudo and su to become root before running a command. Which value in the auditd record still identifies the human who originally logged in?
options: The effective user ID of the command, which reflects root after the privilege change
The process ID of the shell that ran the command
The audit user ID (auid), which survives sudo and su
The session name written to the systemd journal
2.explanation: auditd records the audit user ID, which is set at login and survives sudo and su, so it still names the original account. The effective user ID would show root and hide who was behind it.

2.q: An analyst investigating SSH logons on a Red Hat-family server finds that /var/log/auth.log does not exist. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Red Hat-family systems write authentication events to /var/log/secure
SSH logons on Linux are recorded only when auditd rules are configured
The log was deleted, since every Linux distribution creates auth.log
Authentication events on Linux are kept only in the binary journal
2.explanation: Debian and Ubuntu use /var/log/auth.log, while Red Hat-family systems write the same sshd, sudo and PAM messages to /var/log/secure. Assuming deletion skips the simpler distribution difference.

2.q: A team deploys Sysmon with a tuned configuration and expects suspicious process launches to be stopped or flagged on the host. What is wrong with that expectation?
options: Sysmon blocks only processes that are listed in its exclude rules
Sysmon raises the alert once the event is copied into the Windows Security log and the host refreshes its audit policy
Sysmon needs an EDR licence before it can raise any detections
Sysmon is a sensor: it records activity but neither blocks nor alerts
2.explanation: Sysmon writes events to its own channel and does nothing else; detection happens later in SIEM rules. Exclude rules decide what is not recorded, they never block execution.

2.q: When stacking Sysmon parent-child pairs across a fleet, an analyst counts both total events and COUNT(DISTINCT host) per pair. Why is the distinct host count the more telling figure?
options: It removes duplicate events created when Sysmon and 4688 both fire
It shows how widespread a pair is, so pairs unique to one host stand out
It corrects the fleet-wide count for repeated process IDs, which otherwise makes identical launches look more common
It weights each pair by how many users were logged on to each host
2.explanation: Normal software produces the same pair on many hosts, while an attack usually produces a pair seen on only one; the distinct host count measures that spread. A pair can occur many times on one machine, so the raw count alone can hide rarity.

2.q: In the lab dataset, a single Sysmon event shows WINWORD.EXE as the parent of powershell.exe on WS-104, a pair seen on no other host. Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: A document opened in Word likely ran a macro that launched PowerShell
The user started PowerShell from Word's built-in scripting console
An Office update routine invoked PowerShell to install new components
Word crashed and Windows Error Reporting started PowerShell to recover
2.explanation: Word has no ordinary reason to start a command interpreter, so the pair is the classic sign of a malicious document running a macro (user execution leading to PowerShell). An update routine would appear on many hosts, not just one.

2.q: A process event shows powershell.exe -NoP -W Hidden -EncodedCommand followed by an encoded string. What can the analyst conclude from this command line alone?
options: The script downloaded a second-stage payload from the internet
The script ran with administrative rights because of the -NoP flag
The options hide what is run, but not what the script actually did
The script was blocked, since hidden windows are refused by default
2.explanation: No profile, a hidden window and an encoded command together suggest an effort to conceal, but the command line cannot reveal the script's behaviour; a 4104 record would. -NoP only skips loading the profile and grants no privileges.

2.q: A Security event 1102 appears on WS-104 at 08:17, but the host's earlier events had already been forwarded to the SIEM. What does this mean for the investigation?
options: The SIEM copies are unreliable, because clearing also rewrites forwarded events
The 1102 can be ignored, since nothing that mattered was actually lost
Only events written after 08:17 can be trusted for the investigation
Earlier events survive centrally, and the 1102 itself records the clearing
2.explanation: Clearing the local log cannot reach copies already in the SIEM, and the 1102 is itself evidence of defence evasion worth investigating. Ignoring it would discard a strong indicator, even though no data was lost.

2.q: On a finance workstation, a 4720 creates an account named svc_update from a regular user's session, and a 4732 adds it to the local Administrators group one minute later. Why do these events justify concern?
options: Service accounts must be created on domain controllers, never locally
A service-like name created outside IT suggests a persistence account
Event 4732 is only written when a group change fails a policy check
Local accounts cannot be used for logons until a reboot has occurred
2.explanation: An account that imitates a service name, created from a user's session and immediately made an administrator, is a typical way to keep access (create local account). Event 4732 records a successful group addition, not a failure.

2.q: Every suspicious event on WS-104 carries the user name divya. A manager concludes that divya ran the attack herself. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
options: The user field is copied from the proxy and may name another person
The user field is blank for every process started by a macro
The event records a security context; malware in her session runs as her
The recorded name identifies the owner of the parent process, regardless of the child process's security context
2.explanation: An event records the security context the process ran under, not the person at the keyboard, so malware launched from divya's session runs as divya. The user field is not taken from the proxy in endpoint events.

2.q: A SOC lead argues that endpoint events need not be sent to the SIEM because the EDR console already holds rich telemetry. Which risk does this decision create?
options: EDR telemetry may age out and cannot be correlated with proxy or identity data
EDR agents stop recording events once a SIEM forwarder is not present
EDR consoles record only alerts and never keep raw process telemetry
EDR data may have to be copied manually during an investigation because it can only be admitted as evidence once indexed by a SIEM
2.explanation: EDR consoles often keep raw telemetry for a limited period and in their own format, so it cannot be joined with network and identity sources. EDRs do keep raw telemetry, which is why the decision is about forwarding and retention.

2.q: After a missed detection, an engineer proposes enabling every Sysmon event type with no filtering and auditd rules for every system call. What is the main operational objection?
options: Sysmon refuses to load a configuration that has no exclude rules
Unfiltered data can overwhelm collection and budgets and drown key events
The audit subsystem prevents recording program execution once another system call category is enabled in the same policy
Broad logging erases ProcessGuid values, breaking parent-child joins
2.explanation: Unfiltered sources produce enormous volume that strains collection and licence budgets while burying the events that matter; logging should be driven by the execution, change and access questions. Sysmon and auditd have no such technical refusals.

2.q: An attacker with administrative rights on a host wants to stop Sysmon from recording without leaving a gap that looks obvious. Which defensive measure gives the SOC the best chance of noticing?
options: Configuring Sysmon to record image loads for every process on the host
Increasing the size of the local Sysmon/Operational channel on disk
Alerting on Sysmon state and configuration change events and on source silence
Relying on the attacker's own commands appearing in the 4688 events
2.explanation: Sysmon logs its own state and configuration changes (events 4 and 16), and a host whose events stop arriving is either off or tampered with. A bigger local log does nothing once the sensor is stopped or reconfigured.

2.q: On a laptop examined in person, the Sysmon/Operational channel clearly contains the suspicious process events, yet SIEM searches for that laptop return nothing. Audit policy and the Sysmon configuration are both correct. Where does the gap most likely lie?
options: In the audit policy, which must also enable Sysmon's own channel
In the Sysmon driver, which records events only after a reboot
In the SIEM parser, which necessarily rejects the entire channel when a forwarded event is missing a process identifier
In collection: the forwarder is not shipping that channel to the SIEM
2.explanation: Evidence must be observed by a source, allowed by its configuration and shipped by the forwarder; here the first two are satisfied locally, so the missing link is collection. Audit policy governs the Security log, not Sysmon's channel.

2.q: A single PowerShell launch produces a 4688, a Sysmon event 1, a 4104 record and an EDR process event. How should a SOC view this overlap?
options: As deliberate redundancy that adds resilience at a cost in volume and duplicates
As a misconfiguration, since only one source should record each process
As proof of tampering, because duplicate records indicate log injection
As a reason to disable 4688, since Sysmon fully replaces the Security log
2.explanation: Overlapping sources mean that if one is disabled or not forwarded, another may still hold the evidence, at the price of extra volume and deduplication work. Disabling 4688 throws away that resilience against Sysmon being stopped.

2.q: In the lab's WS-104 timeline, nothing is recorded between the Word-to-PowerShell event at 06:14 and the account creation at 07:02. Which additional collection would most directly explain what happened in that gap?
options: Linux auditd execve rules on the company's file servers
More 4624 logon auditing on all workstations in the finance team
Sysmon network, file and registry events plus PowerShell 4104 logging
Firewall logging of denied inbound connections at the perimeter
2.explanation: The dataset holds only Sysmon process creations and a few Security events, so what PowerShell did inside the host went unrecorded; network, file, registry and script block events would fill that gap. More logon auditing would not show the script's actions.

2.q: An analyst sorting a host's evidence into execution, change, access and defence finds a 7045 in the System log showing a new service. Which category does it belong to, and why does that matter?
options: Access, because a service always logs on with its own account
Change, because it leaves persistence behind that must be cleaned up
Defence, because services are installed mainly by anti-malware tools
Execution, because the service binary has already run on the host
2.explanation: A service installation modifies the host and is a common persistence trace, so it is a change that often turns suspicion into a confirmed incident needing clean-up. Installation itself does not prove the binary ran.

2.q: A SOC in India plans endpoint log retention. Which approach is consistent with the lesson's guidance?
options: Keep all endpoint logs indefinitely, since security purposes override DPDP
Keep endpoint logs only for 30 days, to minimise the personal data held
Keep only alerts, since raw endpoint events are not personal data at all
Keep logs for a rolling 180 days in India, with defined purpose and access
2.explanation: CERT-In's April 2022 directions require ICT logs for a rolling 180 days within India, and the DPDP Act 2023 calls for a defined purpose and limited access; retention is agreed with legal and compliance. Thirty days would fall short of the CERT-In requirement.

2.q: An attacker with administrative rights on a workstation has stopped Sysmon and cleared the Security log. Why can the web proxy's logs still be relied on for that host's activity?
options: The proxy keeps its own records, which the workstation cannot edit
The proxy reads the workstation's event logs before they are cleared
The proxy log is encrypted with a key held only by the endpoint agent
The proxy restarts Sysmon automatically when its events stop arriving
2.explanation: Network logs are written by separate devices, so control of the workstation does not let the attacker alter them; they are an independent second witness. The proxy has no access to the host's event logs.

2.q: A compromised workstation connects to dozens of other workstations on port 445, yet the perimeter firewall and the web proxy show nothing unusual. What best explains this, and which source would reveal it?
options: The traffic was encrypted, so only full packet capture could reveal it
The firewall logs only denied traffic; enabling allow logging would reveal it
The traffic is east-west; internal flow records or an NSM sensor would see it
The proxy filtered SMB requests; its category logs would reveal the activity
2.explanation: Workstation-to-workstation traffic never crosses the perimeter or the proxy, so only internal vantage points such as flow exporters or internal sensors see it. Allow logging on the perimeter firewall would still not see traffic that does not pass through it.

2.q: A firewall line reads: DROP IN=eth0 SRC=203.0.113.66 DST=10.40.0.5 PROTO=TCP DPT=3389. Which reading is correct, and what would raise its importance?
options: An internal host tried outbound SSH and was blocked; repeats would matter
An external host's RDP attempt was dropped; the source appearing elsewhere would matter
An external host's RDP session was allowed; a large byte count would matter
An internal host's DNS query was dropped; NXDOMAIN replies would matter
2.explanation: SRC is the external 203.0.113.66, DPT=3389 is Remote Desktop and the action is DROP; such lines are common, but the same address appearing in another source, such as the VPN log, sharply increases their value. The action field rules out an allowed session.

2.q: A syslog firewall entry begins with 'Nov  3 12:16:21 fw01 kernel:'. What limitation of this timestamp must the analyst account for before correlating it with UTC events?
options: It records the time the SIEM received the line, not when it was written
It is rounded to the minute, so the seconds shown are only approximate
It is always expressed in UTC, so it must be converted to local time
It carries no year and no time zone, so both must be assumed or known
2.explanation: The classic syslog timestamp omits the year and the time zone, so the analyst must know the device's zone (the kit treats it as IST) before aligning it with UTC data. Nothing in the format marks it as UTC.

2.q: An external partner reports malicious traffic from the organisation's single public address. The perimeter firewall performs NAT for all internal hosts. What does the analyst need to identify the internal machine?
options: The partner's own packet capture of the reported connection
The DNS resolver's logs of queries for the partner's domain
The firewall's translation records or its pre-NAT address fields
The proxy's URL category assigned to the partner's domain
2.explanation: With NAT, the outside address is shared by many hosts, so only the firewall's translation log or pre-NAT fields map the connection back to one internal address. DNS logs might suggest candidates but cannot tie a specific connection to a host.

2.q: To save storage, a firewall logs every denied connection but only a sample of allowed ones. Why is this especially damaging for incident investigation?
options: The connections of an attack that succeeded are exactly the ones not recorded
Denied connections lose their meaning without a paired allowed event for every source and destination recorded by the firewall
Sampling changes the rule numbers recorded in the denied connection logs
Allowed connections are needed to compute the NAT table for denied ones
2.explanation: A successful intrusion consists of connections the firewall allowed, so partial allow logging removes the evidence that matters most. Denied entries stand on their own and do not depend on allowed ones.
