2.q: A proxy that does not perform TLS inspection handles a user's HTTPS request to a file-sharing site. What can its log show about that request?
options: The full URL path and the name of the file that was uploaded
The HTTP method and response status of each request in the session
Nothing at all, because encrypted sessions bypass the proxy entirely
The destination host name and port from the CONNECT request
2.explanation: Without inspection the proxy sees only the CONNECT request, which gives host and port; the URL, method and status travel inside the encrypted tunnel. The session still passes through the proxy, so it is logged.

2.q: A bank's SOC proposes TLS inspection on its secure web gateway to gain full URL visibility. Which approach reflects the lesson's guidance on this decision?
options: Inspect all traffic without exception, since partial inspection creates blind spots
Treat it as a privacy and legal decision, exempting categories such as banking and health
Inspect only internal traffic and exempt external endpoints as a group because external services may use certificate pinning
Avoid inspection entirely, since SNI already reveals the full URL of each request
2.explanation: TLS inspection gives full visibility but is a significant privacy, legal and technical decision; sensitive categories are normally exempted and some applications break. SNI gives only the host name, not the full URL.

2.q: A DNS resolver log shows one workstation receiving hundreds of NXDOMAIN responses within minutes, each for a different random-looking name. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: Malware trying algorithmically generated domains to find its controller
A browser prefetching links from a page of search results
A misconfigured DHCP server handing out the wrong DNS suffix
A user mistyping the address of the company's intranet site
2.explanation: Bursts of NXDOMAIN for random-looking names are a classic sign of malware cycling through generated domains until one resolves. Prefetching resolves real, readable names that mostly exist.

2.q: Malware on a workstation resolves its controller's name using DNS over HTTPS to a public provider. What effect does this have, and which control addresses it?
options: The resolver logs the query as TXT; alerting on TXT volume addresses it
The query appears in DHCP logs instead; collecting lease logs addresses it
The resolver's logs never see the query; forcing all name resolution through approved resolvers addresses it
The query is rejected by the firewall by default; no further control is needed
2.explanation: Encrypted DNS to an external provider bypasses the organisation's resolver and its logs, which is why many organisations block outbound DNS except from their own resolvers. The query never reaches the internal resolver, so no TXT record is logged there.

2.q: A network team exports sFlow from its core switches and asks whether a single short connection from a server to an external host is guaranteed to appear in the data. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, because every flow exporter records each connection's 5-tuple
Yes, provided that the connection carried more than one packet of data
No, because sFlow records only connections to internal destinations
No, because sFlow samples packets, so a short connection may be missed
2.explanation: sFlow samples packets rather than tracking every flow, so brief connections may leave no record at all. sFlow does see external destinations; the limitation is sampling, not direction.

2.q: Investigators need to know, months after the fact, which internal hosts a file server exchanged large volumes with. No URLs or content are required. Which source is best suited to this?
options: Full packet capture from the data centre's core switch
Flow records such as NetFlow or IPFIX from internal devices
Web proxy logs with the authenticated user recorded
IDS alerts produced by signatures on the perimeter link
2.explanation: Flow records are compact, cheap to keep for months and available on internal segments, and they answer who talked to whom and how much. Packet capture is usually kept for days because of its storage cost.

2.q: In Zeek output, an analyst has a suspicious entry in conn.log and wants the matching TLS server name and any DNS lookup for the same connection. What lets them link these records?
options: The connection's uid, which Zeek writes into each related protocol log
The file hash in files.log, which Zeek copies into every other log
The SNI value, which Zeek uses as the primary key for conn.log
The sensor's capture interface, which is unique to each connection
2.explanation: Zeek gives each connection a unique identifier (uid) that ties its entries across conn.log, ssl.log, http.log and other logs. File hashes apply only to transferred files, not to every connection.

2.q: A Suricata alert names a signature for known command-and-control traffic from a workstation. How should a SOC analyst treat this alert?
options: As confirmed compromise, because signature matches are exact by design
As raw telemetry equivalent to a flow record for the same connection
As low confidence until the analyst confirms whether the traffic was encrypted when the sensor captured it
As someone else's detection logic that still needs validation as an alert
2.explanation: IDS alerts are detections produced by a rule author's logic, not raw telemetry, so they need the same validation as any SIEM alert. Signatures can and do match benign traffic.

2.q: A manager asks why the SOC does not simply capture all packets everywhere and keep them for a year. Which answer reflects the trade-offs described in the lesson?
options: Packet capture cannot record traffic that passes through a SPAN port
Packet capture records only headers, so it adds nothing beyond flows
Storage cost, wholesale personal data and encryption limit its value
Packet capture is illegal in India unless approved by CERT-In in advance
2.explanation: Full capture is expensive to store, collects personal data wholesale and offers limited insight into encrypted traffic, so SOCs capture selectively at key points or on demand. It records full payloads, not just headers.

2.q: A workstation makes a TLS 1.3 connection without Encrypted Client Hello. Which metadata can a passive sensor on the path normally still observe?
options: The server certificate, because TLS 1.3 sends it before encryption begins
The SNI host name in the ClientHello, along with addresses, timing and size
The requested URL path, because TLS 1.3 leaves the HTTP request line visible
Nothing beyond the 5-tuple, because TLS 1.3 encrypts the whole handshake
2.explanation: In TLS 1.3 the server certificate is encrypted, but the SNI in the ClientHello still usually names the destination, and addresses, timing and volume remain visible. ECH would conceal the real SNI, but it is not in use here.

2.q: A hunt reports: WS-104 https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping n=18 mean_gap=300s cv=0.004. How should this be interpreted?
options: Requests every five minutes with almost no variation, typical of software on a timer
Eighteen requests clustered within 300 seconds, typical of a page loading assets
Requests every five minutes with high variation, typical of a user refreshing a page
A single 300-second session split into 18 parts, typical of a large download
2.explanation: A coefficient of variation near 0 means the gaps barely vary, so a mean gap of 300 s describes a check-in every five minutes, which is machine behaviour. A high CV, not 0.004, would indicate human irregularity.

2.q: A beacon hunt flags hosts whose request intervals have a coefficient of variation below 0.2 rather than requiring perfectly identical gaps. Why is the threshold set this way?
options: Proxy timestamps are rounded to minutes, which hides sub-minute regularity
Perfect regularity would flag every routine site visited by all hosts
Malware may add jitter, which raises the CV without making it human-like
The CV cannot be computed when two consecutive gaps are exactly equal
2.explanation: Implants often add random variation to their interval, which raises the CV; a threshold catches such beacons while still excluding irregular human browsing. Routine human browsing is irregular, so perfect regularity would not flag it.

2.q: In a proxy log, which pattern best suggests exfiltration rather than ordinary use?
options: Many small inbound downloads from the same content delivery network during normal working hours
A large response received by a host from a software update server
Repeated failed requests with status 404 to a single internal web server
An unusually large volume sent from an internal host to a rare destination
2.explanation: Clients normally download far more than they send, so a large outbound volume to an unfamiliar destination reverses the usual pattern. A large download from an update server is the ordinary direction of traffic.

2.q: A suspicious connection came from 10.40.0.23 at 08:12 UTC. Which combination of evidence correctly attributes it to a machine and a person?
options: The current DHCP lease for 10.40.0.23 and the user logged on right now
The DHCP lease valid at 08:12 and the endpoint logon events for that host
The asset register's default address for each host and its listed owner
The firewall's post-NAT address and the proxy's URL category for the site
2.explanation: IP addresses are reassigned, so attribution needs the lease that held at the time of the event plus logon evidence from that host for the same time. Today's lease and current logons may describe a different machine and user.

2.q: An analyst writes one SIEM query that joins the lab's proxy and VPN events on the field src_ip to find users who connected from the same address. Why will the results be misleading?
options: VPN events record src_ip in IPv6 notation, so no proxy values can match
Proxy events leave src_ip empty whenever the user is authenticated
In proxy events src_ip is the internal workstation; in VPN events it is the user's external address
The SIEM drops src_ip from VPN events because they are written in syslog format
2.explanation: The same field name means different things in the two sources: an internal workstation address in proxy events and the remote user's external address in VPN events, so a naive join compares unlike values. The lab's proxy events do carry src_ip.

2.q: In the lab data, WS-104 made the most proxy requests of any host. Why is that fact on its own weak evidence, and what made WS-104 stand out instead?
options: A busy user is not a suspect; its rare single-host destinations and regular timing did
Request counts are unreliable in proxies; its blocked categories made it stand out
Volume is meaningless without payloads; its decrypted traffic made it stand out
Busiest hosts are usually servers; its workstation naming made it stand out
2.explanation: High volume is normal for a busy user; the evidence lay in three destinations visited by WS-104 alone and in the machine-regular timing of one of them. The dataset holds no payloads, so decryption played no part.

2.q: The lab's rule R6 prints the hit ('WS-104', 'https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping', 18, 220, 220). What does this tuple tell the analyst, and what does the rule leave unchecked?
options: 18 distinct hosts sent 220 requests; it leaves the destination's reputation unchecked
18 requests took 220 seconds each; it leaves the request sizes unchecked
18 requests were blocked with status 220; it leaves the user's identity unchecked
18 hits with bytes_out from 220 to 220; it leaves the request timing unchecked
2.explanation: The tuple is host, URL, hit count and minimum and maximum bytes_out, so the requests were identical in size; R6 tests size regularity only, and the interval check comes from hunt.py. The figures are bytes, not seconds or status codes.

2.q: WS-104's proxy log shows a request for https://banyan-payroll-update.example/invoice.docm at 06:12, and endpoint data shows Word starting PowerShell at 06:14. What is the most reasonable joint reading?
options: The download came from the company's own payroll system and is routine
A look-alike domain served a macro-enabled document that then ran PowerShell
The PowerShell process downloaded the document after Word had been opened
The proxy prevented the document from reaching the host, so the later Office process is unrelated to the web request
2.explanation: The domain imitates the company's name, the .docm extension is a macro-enabled document, and Word starting PowerShell two minutes later fits a phishing download followed by macro execution. The order of events rules out PowerShell fetching the document.

2.q: Malware on a workstation contacts its controller over a non-web protocol directly through the perimeter firewall, never touching the proxy. Which telemetry could still record this traffic?
options: The firewall log and flow records, but not the web proxy log
The web proxy log, because it records every outbound connection
The DHCP server log, because it records each outbound session
Only the endpoint, because firewalls log non-web protocols as denied
2.explanation: Traffic that bypasses the proxy appears only at devices it does pass through, such as the firewall and flow exporters. The proxy logs only requests sent to it, and DHCP records address leases, not sessions.

2.q: An analyst investigating whether Asha opened a share on FS01 searches only DC01's Security log for her 4624 events and finds no type 3 logon. Where should the 4624 type 3 for that share access have been written?
options: On FS01, because the machine accepting the session records the logon and its type
On DC01, but only when the Kerberos Authentication Service audit subcategory is on
On WS-101, because the client that requested the share records the network logon
On DC01 as a 4769, since the DC writes logon types into its service ticket events
2.explanation: The target of a logon writes the 4624 with the logon type; the DC records only ticket requests such as 4768 and 4769. A 4769 on DC01 would exist, but it carries no logon type and is not a session record.

2.q: A 4624 on WS-101 shows the Subject account as the workstation's own system account and the New Logon account as asha. Which statement about who logged on is correct?
options: The Subject account logged on, and asha is the account whose token it later borrowed
Asha logged on; the Subject is only the local account that requested the logon
Both accounts logged on, because Windows records a pair of sessions for every 4624
Neither can be stated until the matching 4672 confirms which account got the session
2.explanation: In a 4624 the account actually logged on is under New Logon; the Subject is the local requester, often the system itself. Reading the Subject as the user is a classic beginner's error.

2.q: A file server shows forty 4625 events in ten minutes from one address, each for a different user name, all with status 0xC0000064. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Several real users mistyped their passwords after a password policy change
Accounts were locked out and the clients kept retrying their saved credentials
Someone is trying user names that do not exist, which real users rarely do
Disabled leavers' accounts are still configured in a scheduled script somewhere
2.explanation: 0xC0000064 means the user name does not exist, so a burst across many names suggests name guessing or a stale script. Mistyped passwords on real accounts would show 0xC000006A instead.

2.q: A junior analyst tries to link a session on WS-101 to a session on FS01 by matching the Logon ID value in both machines' 4624 events. Why will this fail?
options: Logon IDs are only written to 4634 logoff events, never to 4624 logon events
The Logon ID is a domain-wide value, so every session on every host shares it
Logon IDs appear only in DC events, so the workstation records cannot be matched
A Logon ID is local to one machine and resets on reboot, so it is not cross-host
2.explanation: The Logon ID ties events within one session on one machine, such as a 4624 to its 4672 and 4634. It is not a cross-host identifier; correlation across hosts uses account, time and client address.

2.q: DC01 records a burst of 4769 events from one workstation within a minute, each for a different service account, and every one shows Ticket Encryption Type 0x17. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: A routine Group Policy refresh renewing service tickets for every domain service
An attempt to obtain service tickets for offline password cracking (Kerberoasting)
A password spray against service accounts that is failing Kerberos pre-authentication
A client that cannot reach the DC and is falling back from Kerberos to NTLM logons
2.explanation: Bulk RC4 (0x17) service-ticket requests for many service accounts from one client is the well-known Kerberoasting signal (T1558.003). A spray would show pre-authentication failures such as 4771, not successful 4769 ticket issues.

2.q: A user maps a share by typing the file server's IP address instead of its name. Which domain controller event would you expect in place of the usual 4769 for cifs/FS01?
options: 4776, because Kerberos finds no matching service principal and NTLM is used instead
4771, because the DC rejects Kerberos pre-authentication for address-based requests
4768, because the client requests a fresh TGT for every share reached by address
4648, because supplying an address counts as logging on with explicit credentials
2.explanation: Reaching a server by IP address prevents Kerberos from matching an SPN, so the client falls back to NTLM and the DC writes 4776; the 4624 on FS01 then shows the NTLM package. 4771 is a pre-authentication failure, not a protocol fallback.

2.q: A service account that has only ever produced type 5 logons on application servers appears in a 4624 type 10 on a finance workstation. How should this be treated?
options: As routine, because services restart under their configured account after patching
As a cached logon, because type 10 means no domain controller could be reached
As a scheduled job launched using a stored credential, because Windows records that job category as logon type 10
As a Remote Desktop session by a service identity, a baseline deviation to investigate
2.explanation: Type 10 is RemoteInteractive (Remote Desktop), and a service account interactively reaching a workstation breaks its type 5 baseline. Cached logons are type 11 and batch jobs are type 4.

2.q: A domain user mistypes her password at the console of her workstation. Which pair of events best describes what the domain controller and the workstation record?
options: DC writes 4769 for the host service; workstation writes 4624 with an elevated token
DC writes 4740 lockout immediately; workstation writes 4625 with status 0xC0000234
DC writes 4771 pre-authentication failed; workstation writes 4625 with 0xC000006A
DC writes 4776 for NTLM; workstation writes 4648 with the explicit credentials used
2.explanation: A wrong password fails Kerberos pre-authentication, so the DC writes 4771 (or a failed 4768) and the workstation writes 4625 with 0xC000006A. Lockout (4740, 0xC0000234) only follows after the threshold is exceeded.

2.q: A user's Entra ID sign-in log shows six attempts in four minutes that passed the password check and then failed MFA, with no final success. What is the right response?
options: No action is needed, because MFA held and the attacker never obtained a session
Block the source address and keep monitoring, since no account was compromised
Treat the password as compromised: reset it and contact the user by another channel
Pause MFA challenges temporarily and monitor the next password-only attempt to see whether it comes from the same network
2.explanation: Passing the first factor proves someone knows the password, and repeated prompts suggest MFA request generation (T1621). Even though MFA held, the password must be reset and the user contacted separately; blocking the address alone leaves the known password in use.

2.q: Why should an analyst not filter out Entra ID non-interactive user sign-ins as background noise?
options: They are the only records that carry the conditional access policy result
They record directory changes such as role assignments and MFA registrations
They are written only for administrator accounts, so each one is high value
They show tokens being used, where replay from an unexpected place becomes visible
2.explanation: Non-interactive sign-ins are made by clients using tokens they already hold, so stolen-token reuse from an unusual location shows up there. Directory changes belong to the audit log, not the sign-in categories.

2.q: An organisation's lockout threshold is five failures per account, and a sprayer tries one password against 300 accounts from a single address. Which detection logic is most likely to catch it?
options: Counting distinct user names that failed from each source address in a time window
Alerting when any single account exceeds five failures within thirty minutes
Alerting on every 4740 lockout event written by the domain controllers
Counting failures per account per day and flagging the top ten accounts
2.explanation: Spraying keeps each account under the lockout threshold, so per-account counts and lockout alerts stay silent; per-source distinct-user counts expose it. Per-account thresholds catch guessing against one account, not spraying.

2.q: An IdP shows failures against 2,000 accounts from 700 different addresses, each account tried once or twice with a different password per account. Which technique best fits?
options: Password spraying (T1110.003), because each account receives very few attempts
Credential stuffing (T1110.004), using breached pairs from many sources at once
Password guessing (T1110.001), because the attempts are spread over many accounts
MFA request generation (T1621), because the attacker is cycling user prompts
2.explanation: Many accounts, a different password per account, and many sources is the credential stuffing shape. Spraying instead tries one or a few common passwords across accounts, typically from one or few sources.

2.q: In the Banyan data, a VPN failure for divya appears at 06:42:21, while the Windows log shows her interactively logged on at WS-104 since 03:18. What does this combination tell the analyst?
options: Divya was connecting to the VPN from her desk and mistyped her password once
The VPN concentrator replayed her earlier desktop logon after a session timeout
Her WS-104 logon must have ended, so the VPN attempt marks her leaving the office
Someone other than divya was trying her account from the external spray address
2.explanation: She was already at her workstation, and the failure came from the external address 203.0.113.66 within the eight-user spray, so another party was using her name. A single desk typo would appear as a 4625 at WS-104, not a VPN failure from outside.

2.q: At 04:05 the Banyan data shows a single 4625 for ben at WS-102 with status 0xC000006A and logon type 2, after his successful logon there at 03:48. What is the most defensible disposition?
options: Suspicious, because any failure after a success suggests a second person at the desk
Benign: one wrong password at his own console after a success, with no follow-up
Malicious, because 0xC000006A shows the attacker knew a valid account name
Undetermined until his account is reset and the workstation is reimaged
2.explanation: A single wrong-password failure at the user's own console, after a success and with nothing following, matches unlocking a screen with a typo. Valid-name knowledge only matters when failures form a pattern across accounts or sources.

2.q: In your copy of the kit you raise rule R2's distinct-user threshold from 5 to 9 and rerun the rules. Why does the 203.0.113.66 hit disappear?
options: Only eight distinct users failed from that address before gopal's success
The rule now counts nine failures for one user before accepting any subsequent successful login
SQLite rejects HAVING thresholds larger than the number of VPN events
Gopal's own failure no longer counts once the threshold exceeds eight
2.explanation: R2 fires when the count of distinct failing users from the success's source meets the threshold; the spray reached eight, so a threshold of nine misses it. This also shows a sprayer that stays under a known threshold evades the rule.

2.q: The Banyan query reads logon_type and status with json_extract(raw, ...) because they are not normalised SIEM columns. What broader lesson does this illustrate?
options: Drop the normalized columns once the same records have been loaded as raw JSON, since every correlation can perform ad hoc extraction
Logon type and status are too low-value to normalise in an identity pipeline
A field not normalised at ingestion is recoverable only if the raw event was kept
SQLite cannot index JSON, so identity fields must always be queried from raw
2.explanation: The values could be recovered only because the raw event was stored alongside the normalised fields. Dropping raw data would make such fields unrecoverable, which is the opposite of the first option.

2.q: Why does the Banyan triage script keep a PRIMARY_HOST mapping such as divya to WS-104?
options: VPN concentrators log the internal host name only when the session is successful
VPN events carry no host, so alerts need a user-to-laptop map to show an asset
The mapping replaces geolocation, which VPN records never include for users
Windows logons lack a host field, so the script must infer it from the user
2.explanation: A VPN concentrator sees a remote client and its external address, not an inventory asset, so the script maps users to their usual laptops. Windows events do carry the host, so the last option is wrong.

2.q: An impossible-travel alert fires because a user signed in from Mumbai and, twenty minutes later, from an address geolocated to Frankfurt. What is the best first step?
options: Disable the account at once, because two distant successes prove token theft
Close the alert, because geolocation is unreliable and the heuristic is noisy
Block the Frankfurt address range at the firewall and the identity provider
Treat it as a prompt: check for VPN, proxy or mobile egress, then the user
2.explanation: Unfamiliar or impossible travel is a heuristic, often caused by VPNs, mobile networks and cloud proxies, so it is a triage prompt, not a verdict. Closing it outright discards a possibly real signal without checking.

2.q: A Linux server's deploy account has authenticated only with SSH keys for a year. Today auth.log shows "Accepted password for deploy" from an unfamiliar address. Why is this significant?
options: The unfamiliar address establishes malicious access even if the server has previously permitted password logins
It indicates a non-existent user, which SSH reports as Accepted password
The authentication method changed from key to password, breaking the baseline
It shows the account was locked out and then unlocked by an administrator
2.explanation: A server that normally sees only key-based logons should not suddenly accept a password; the method change plus an unfamiliar source deserves investigation. Password logins are not malicious in themselves, only unusual for this account.

2.q: A SOC collects Security logs from domain controllers but not from servers or workstations. What will it be unable to see?
options: Logon types and the target-side sessions created on the machines being accessed
Which client address requested Kerberos tickets for each account in the domain
Kerberos pre-authentication failures caused by wrong passwords on domain accounts
NTLM credential validation for domain accounts presented to member servers
2.explanation: DCs hold ticket and credential-validation requests (4768, 4769, 4771, 4776) including client address, but logon types and sessions (4624, 4625) are written on the targets. The other options are all recorded on the DC.

2.q: A user reports a new MFA method she did not add. You want the record of when that method was registered in Entra ID. Where should you look?
options: The interactive sign-in log, filtered to the user's successful MFA results
The non-interactive sign-in log, where token refreshes record method changes
The service principal sign-in log, because MFA registration runs as an app
The Entra ID audit log, which records directory changes such as new methods
2.explanation: Directory changes such as role grants and new authentication methods are recorded in the audit log, the IdP's counterpart of 4720 and 4732. Sign-in logs show authentication attempts, not registrations.

2.q: On a file server, a 4624 for the account svc-backup is immediately followed by a 4672 with the same Logon ID. The account is not in the administrator baseline. What does this indicate?
options: The new session holds administrator-equivalent privileges the baseline does not expect
The account used explicit credentials to run a process under a different identity
The session was created from cached credentials because no DC was reachable
The account's password was validated by NTLM rather than by Kerberos on the DC
2.explanation: 4672 means special privileges were assigned to the new logon, and the shared Logon ID ties it to that 4624; for an account outside the admin baseline that is worth investigating. Explicit-credential use is 4648, a different event.

2.q: Gopal's VPN success at 06:46 from 203.0.113.66 follows an eight-user spray. Which additional fact from the Windows log makes it more serious than the VPN records alone show?
options: Gopal had a 4625 at WS-107 that morning, proving his password was being guessed
Gopal had never logged on to any workstation, so the VPN was his first session
Gopal was already logged on at WS-107, so this was a concurrent second use of his identity
Gopal's 4624 at WS-107 was type 10, showing he normally works through Remote Desktop
2.explanation: His account was in use at WS-107 from 03:33, so a VPN session from an unplaced external address is a simultaneous second use of his identity. The Windows log shows only a type 2 success for gopal, no 4625 and no type 10.

2.q: After a VPN spray ends in one account's compromise, which pair of controls most reduces the chance of the same attack succeeding again?
options: Block the observed source address and use a lower per-account lockout threshold to prevent repeated failures against one user
Requiring MFA on the VPN and enforcing a banned-password list for all accounts
Geo-blocking unplaced countries and shortening VPN session lifetimes
Alerting on every VPN failure and renaming accounts to non-guessable names
2.explanation: The spray worked because one password was guessable and the VPN accepted a single factor; MFA and banned passwords address both causes. Blocking one address is the weakest response, since sprayers simply change source.

2.q: A field engineer's laptop shows a 4624 type 11 for his domain account while he is at a customer site with no corporate connectivity. What does this logon type tell you?
options: He connected through Remote Desktop to the laptop from another machine
A scheduled task started under his stored credentials while he was away
A process cloned his token and used other credentials for outbound access
He logged on interactively with cached domain credentials, no DC being reachable
2.explanation: Type 11 is CachedInteractive: an interactive logon verified against cached domain credentials because no domain controller could be contacted, which fits an off-network laptop. Remote Desktop is type 10, batch is type 4 and NewCredentials is type 9.

2.q: An attacker with read access to an S3 bucket of KYC documents downloads every object without changing any configuration. The account has a trail recording management events only. What will CloudTrail show?
options: Nothing of the downloads, because object reads are data events not recorded by default
Each GetObject call, because every trail records S3 reads as management events
A single summary event per bucket, written hourly as an Insights record
The downloads only in Event history, which includes data events for 90 days
2.explanation: S3 object-level reads are data events and must be explicitly selected on a trail; with management events only, the exfiltration leaves no audit trace. Event history covers management events only, not data events.

2.q: An AWS account with no trail configured discovers a suspicious IAM change thought to have happened about 120 days ago. What can the investigator expect from CloudTrail Event history?
options: The change, because Event history keeps IAM events for 400 days by default
Nothing, because Event history keeps only the last 90 days of management events
The change, but only if the investigator searches the region where workloads run
A digest file proving the change happened, even though the event itself expired
2.explanation: Event history holds 90 days of management events, so a change from 120 days ago is gone unless a trail delivered it to S3 earlier. The 400-day figure belongs to Google Cloud's Admin Activity logs.

2.q: An analyst investigating a suspected rogue CreateUser in an account whose workloads all run in ap-south-1 searches Event history in that region only and finds nothing. What is the most likely explanation?
options: CreateUser is a read-only call and is therefore excluded from Event history
IAM events are written only when a trail has data events enabled for IAM
IAM is a global service whose events are recorded in us-east-1, not ap-south-1
CreateUser is logged only in the region of the user's eventual console sign-in
2.explanation: Global services such as IAM and the global STS endpoint record their events in US East (N. Virginia). CreateUser changes state, so it is a management write, not a read-only call.

2.q: A CloudTrail record's sourceIPAddress contains a value such as an AWS service's name rather than an IP address. How should the analyst interpret it?
options: The record is corrupt and should be excluded from the investigation timeline
The caller hid its address with a proxy, which is a sign of defence evasion
It represents a private VPC endpoint whose actual address CloudTrail replaces with the service name in every record
An AWS service made the request on the principal's behalf, so no address is given
2.explanation: For calls made by AWS services on your behalf, sourceIPAddress contains the service name. Treating that field as always an address is listed among the common mistakes; it is not evidence of evasion.

2.q: A suspicious AttachRolePolicy call shows userIdentity.type AssumedRole with a sessionContext naming the role ops-admin. What should the analyst do to identify the real actor?
options: Treat ops-admin as the actor, because roles are assigned to named individuals
Find the earlier AssumeRole event that created this session and see who called it
Read the accountId field, which names the person who owns the role session
Look up the userAgent string, which records the operator's corporate login
2.explanation: An AssumedRole identity is a session, not a person; the AssumeRole call that issued it reveals who obtained it. accountId identifies the AWS account, not the human.

2.q: Within ten minutes one IAM user's access key produces AccessDenied errors against IAM, EC2, S3, KMS and Lambda, a pattern never seen for that user before. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A stolen credential is being used to explore what it is permitted to do
A recent service control policy change is blocking the user's normal job
CloudTrail is logging read-only calls as errors because of a selector change
The user's MFA session expired and every service rejected the old token
2.explanation: A burst of AccessDenied across many services from one principal is a classic sign of a stolen key mapping its permissions. A policy change would affect the services the user normally uses, not a sweep of unfamiliar ones.

2.q: During an incident you need to know who read secrets from an Azure Key Vault last week. The vault has never had a diagnostic setting. What can you establish?
options: All reads, from the subscription Activity Log's Administrative category
All reads, from the Entra ID sign-in log of each user that accessed the vault
Only reads in the last 24 hours, kept by Key Vault's built-in resource log buffer
Nothing about secret reads, because resource logs are not collected without one
2.explanation: Resource logs, including Key Vault secret access, are not collected at all unless a diagnostic setting routes them. The Activity Log records control-plane operations, not reads of secret values.

2.q: You want one Azure detection that covers every new Azure RBAC grant on any resource in a subscription. Which Activity Log operation should it match?
options: Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete outside the change window
Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write for any resource group in scope
Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write outside the change window
Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/action on the subscription scope
2.explanation: In the operation name pattern, /write creates or changes, so roleAssignments/write covers every new RBAC grant whatever the resource. The delete variant matches removals, not grants.

2.q: A Google Cloud project's security team wants to see who reads objects in a Cloud Storage bucket holding customer data. Which audit log type must they make sure is enabled?
options: Admin Activity, which records every API call made against a project's buckets
System Event, which records actions taken by Google systems on stored data
Data Access, which records reads of user data and is off by default for most services
Policy Denied, which records requests blocked by VPC Service Controls perimeters
2.explanation: Reads of user-provided data are Data Access audit logs, disabled by default for most services because of volume. Admin Activity covers configuration and metadata changes, not object reads.

2.q: You are writing a rule for AWS administrators signing in to the console without MFA. Which fields of the ConsoleLogin record must the rule test?
options: errorCode for Success and requestParameters.MFAUsed for No
eventType for AwsApiCall and sessionContext.mfaRequired for false
readOnly for true and userIdentity.accessKeyId for an empty value
responseElements.ConsoleLogin for Success and additionalEventData.MFAUsed for No
2.explanation: ConsoleLogin results are in responseElements.ConsoleLogin and MFA use in additionalEventData.MFAUsed, with eventType AwsConsoleSignIn. errorCode is absent on success and does not hold the value Success.

2.q: A workload account's CloudTrail delivers to an S3 bucket in the same account. An attacker gains administrator rights there. Which design change best protects the audit trail?
options: Deliver to a separate log-archive account with Object Lock and integrity validation
Enable CloudTrail Insights so unusual API volumes in the account are flagged
Turn on data events for the trail bucket so every deletion is itself recorded
Shorten the delivery interval so log files reach the bucket every minute
2.explanation: An administrator of the account can delete logs stored in it, so a separate, restricted archive account with immutability and integrity validation keeps the trail out of reach. Logging deletions still lets the attacker delete the evidence.

2.q: Months after an incident, a defence lawyer claims the CloudTrail log files presented were edited after the fact. Which feature lets the investigator answer this?
options: The ninety-day Event history view, which provides a comparable integrity guarantee for evidence stored in any external archive
Log file integrity validation, whose signed hourly digests hold each file's hash
Multi-region trails, because duplicate copies exist in every enabled region
CloudTrail Insights, which flags unusual changes in the volume of log files
2.explanation: Integrity validation produces signed digest files containing hashes of the delivered logs, so modification or deletion after delivery can be proven or disproven. Event history would not even cover events that old.

2.q: A trail's PutEventSelectors call changes it to stop recording data events for a sensitive bucket, made by a principal that never manages logging. How should this be classed?
options: Routine cost tuning, since data events are optional and expensive to keep
Privilege escalation, because event selectors grant new permissions to users
Data exposure, because the call makes the bucket readable by other accounts
Logging tampering, an attempt to blind defenders before acting (T1562.008)
2.explanation: PutEventSelectors sits with StopLogging, DeleteTrail and UpdateTrail as logging tampering under T1562.008; from an unexpected principal it should alert. Bucket exposure would appear as PutBucketPolicy or PutBucketAcl.

2.q: Why is a multi-region trail preferred even when an organisation runs workloads in only one AWS region?
options: It is the only kind of trail that can record data events for S3 objects
An attacker may start resources in unused regions, which it also captures
Single-region trails cannot deliver log files to a bucket in another account
It lengthens Event history retention from 90 days to 400 days in each region
2.explanation: Attackers may start resources in regions nobody watches, and a multi-region trail covers all of them, including global-service events in us-east-1. It does not change Event history retention.

2.q: The pipeline identity ci-deploy calls CreateAccessKey for the user finance-reports from 203.0.113.80 via the CLI, and it succeeds. Which reading and follow-up is best?
options: Likely persistence via a second credential; trace every later use of the new key ID
Treat the pipeline as the expected rotation owner and check only whether the previous key was disabled on schedule
A failed escalation attempt; check errorCode for AccessDenied on related calls
Data exposure of finance reports; review PutBucketPolicy calls by finance-reports
2.explanation: A build identity creating a key for a different user from an unexpected address gives someone a second way in (T1098); later records' userIdentity.accessKeyId reveal what the key did. The call succeeded, so it was not a failed attempt.

2.q: Your SIEM maps CloudTrail into ECS fields. Why should the original JSON record still be retained?
options: The normalized schema requires timestamps without their source time zone, so eventTime can only be understood from the raw JSON
The raw record is needed to compute cloud.provider, which ECS cannot hold
Fields such as requestParameters and sessionContext rarely survive normalisation
ECS discards sourceIPAddress, so address pivots work only on the raw record
2.explanation: Nested, API-specific details like requestParameters and sessionContext are seldom preserved intact by normalisation, yet they show exactly what changed and which role session acted. sourceIPAddress maps cleanly to source.ip.

2.q: When normalising CloudTrail to ECS following the normalise_demo.py pattern, how should event.outcome be derived?
options: From readOnly: true maps to success and false maps to failure
From whether errorCode is present: absent is success, present is failure
From eventType: AwsApiCall is success and AwsServiceEvent is failure
From responseElements: any non-empty value means the call succeeded
2.explanation: errorCode appears only when the call failed, so its presence or absence sets event.outcome. readOnly says whether the call changed state, not whether it worked.

2.q: The Banyan source count returns proxy 284, sysmon 33, windows 13 and vpn 10. Banyan is known to use Microsoft 365 for mail. What should the analyst do with this finding?
options: Nothing, because email activity is covered by the proxy logs of users' browsers
Assume Microsoft 365 is safe, since no alerts have come from that environment
Rebuild the dataset, because the query proves the cloud records failed to load
Record the missing cloud and SaaS audit logs in the coverage map with owner and date
2.explanation: No cloud audit source is present, so changes in the tenant would be invisible; the gap belongs in the coverage map with an owner and a date, not just noted. An absence of alerts from an unmonitored source proves nothing.

2.q: In Google Cloud you need to find who changed a project's IAM policy with SetIamPolicy last month. Which logName suffix should your query filter on?
options: cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fdata_access, because IAM policies are user data
cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fpolicy, since a policy-change operation automatically appears in Policy Denied even when it succeeds
cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity, because changing configuration is Admin Activity
cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fsystem_event, because IAM changes are made by Google
2.explanation: SetIamPolicy modifies configuration, so it is an Admin Activity log, always written and kept 400 days. Data Access covers reads of configuration and user data, and Policy Denied records blocked requests, not changes.

2.q: A CERT-In covered entity uses AWS and Azure with only default logging. Which statement about the 180-day log retention requirement is correct?
options: Both defaults fall short at 90 days, so trails and diagnostic settings must be set up
Both defaults meet it, because providers keep control-plane logs for a year
Only Azure falls short, because CloudTrail Event history keeps 400 days
Neither applies, because the directions exempt logs stored by cloud providers
2.explanation: CloudTrail Event history and the Azure Activity Log both keep 90 days, below the 180 days CERT-In requires, so routing to longer storage is the customer's job. The 400-day default belongs to Google Admin Activity.

2.q: In the Azure Activity Log, a single VM deployment produces several entries with statuses such as Started and Succeeded. Which field lets you group them as one operation?
options: The category, which is Administrative for every entry of the deployment
The caller IP address, which is identical for each entry of one operation
The resource ID, which is unique to each status entry of the operation
The correlation ID, which groups the entries that belong to one operation
2.explanation: The correlation ID ties together the entries belonging to one operation. Category and caller IP are shared by many unrelated operations, so they cannot isolate one.

2.q: A business unit creates a new member account in the company's AWS Organization on a Friday evening. Which setup ensures its API activity is logged from the first call?
options: An organisation trail in the management account, covering every member account
A single-region trail created by the account owner once workloads are deployed
Event history in the new account, enabled by the first administrator who signs in
CloudTrail Insights in the management account, flagging the new account's calls
2.explanation: An organisation trail applies to every member account, so a new account is covered from creation. A trail created later by the owner leaves the first calls, often the most sensitive, unrecorded.

2.q: An alert points to suspicious activity in an Azure subscription. Following the lesson's investigation sequence, what should the analyst establish first?
options: Which resources were changed, so the writes can be reverted before anything else
Which human sits behind the service principal, by finding the principal's owner
What is logged, since when, and whether logging itself was changed near the time
What the user's Entra ID sign-ins show about how the session was obtained
2.explanation: The first step is confirming visibility, including whether a diagnostic setting was deleted or logging stopped; otherwise later conclusions rest on gaps. Resolving the principal and checking sign-ins come after.

2.q: Which control most directly prevents a compromised administrator in a member account from switching off its audit logging in the first place?
options: An alert on StopLogging and DeleteTrail events sent to the SOC queue
A service control policy or Azure Policy that denies disabling of logging
Log file integrity validation with hourly signed digest files enabled
A longer retention period for the trail bucket in the same account
2.explanation: SCPs or Azure Policy can deny the logging-disable actions outright, so even an account administrator cannot perform them. An alert detects the tampering after it happens rather than preventing it.

2.q: An attacker uses a stolen cloud access key to open a security group to the internet and copy a database snapshot, without touching any company endpoint. Where is this activity visible?
options: In EDR telemetry, because cloud CLIs always run on corporate laptops
In the firewall logs, because cloud API calls pass the corporate perimeter
In VPN logs, because stolen access keys work only over the remote-access VPN
In the provider's audit logs, since every such change is a recorded API call
2.explanation: In the cloud identity is the perimeter and every change is an API call, so without malware the evidence lives only in the provider's audit logs. The attacker's calls need not cross the corporate network or any company endpoint.

2.q: A Banyan Windows event 4720 on WS-104 shows user: divya and target_user: svc_update. Which reading of this event is correct?
options: The account svc_update created a new account for divya on WS-104
The account divya was created on WS-104 and renamed to svc_update
Something acting under divya's authority created the new account svc_update
The account svc_update logged on to WS-104 using divya's credentials
2.explanation: In account-management events `user` is the subject (the identity performing the action) and `target_user` is the object acted upon, so divya's identity created svc_update. Reading it as divya's account being created swaps actor and victim, the exact trap the lesson describes.

2.q: An analyst finds VPN events with src_ip 203.0.113.66 and then searches the proxy log's src_ip for the same address. It returns nothing. What is the best explanation?
options: The proxy parser failed on those events and dropped the src_ip field from them
The proxy records external client addresses in its host field rather than in src_ip
Proxy src_ip holds internal workstation addresses, so an external VPN client address cannot appear there
The attacker routed the web traffic around the proxy, so no proxy events were written
2.explanation: The same field name has a different perspective in each source: on the VPN it is the external client, on the proxy the internal workstation. The empty result is correct, not a parse failure; there is no evidence of missing events, only of a pivot that cannot match.

2.q: A rule alerts on any VPN login where country != "IN". It fires on gopal's successful login, whose country value is "??". What is the underlying problem?
options: The placeholder for an unknown location is being compared as if it were a real country code
The gateway has mislabelled an Indian address, so the country field must be corrected
The rule should have compared src_ip instead, because country is never recorded by VPNs
The rule is correct, because "??" is the gateway's code for an anonymising network
2.explanation: `??` means the gateway could not geolocate the address; it is a placeholder, not a country, and should be mapped to null and handled deliberately. Nothing in the lesson says it denotes an anonymiser or a mislabelled Indian address.

2.q: A query counting distinct source addresses per user over Windows logons shows every user with an extra address, and a join on src_ip links unrelated local logons together. What causes this?
options: Interactive logons record src_ip as the literal string "-", which is being treated as an address
Windows writes the domain controller's address into src_ip on every interactive logon
DHCP reassigned the workstations' addresses during the day, multiplying the distinct values
The SIEM stores src_ip as text, so identical addresses are counted as different values
2.explanation: A local (type 2) logon has no remote address, so Banyan records `-`; counted or joined as a value it creates a phantom shared entity. DHCP churn would add real, different addresses, not one common value linking every local logon.

2.q: A correlation rule searches all sources for event.outcome: failure. Months later someone notices it has never matched a Sysmon process event. Why?
options: Sysmon writes its outcome in upper case, so the comparison with failure is case-sensitive
Sysmon process events have no outcome field at all, so the rule silently excludes that source
Sysmon process events only record successes, so a failure value can never occur there
The rule's time window is too short for Sysmon's delayed delivery of process events
2.explanation: Missing is not the same as false: the field inventory shows Sysmon events carry no `outcome`, so they can never satisfy the condition. The useful question is which sources populate a field before asking which events match; case differences would not explain total absence.

2.q: A dashboard charts the values of the field status across all sources and plots 200 next to 0xC000006A. What is wrong with this chart?
options: The Windows value is hexadecimal and must be converted to decimal before charting
The two values are HTTP status and Windows NTSTATUS codes that merely share a field name
The proxy value should be grouped by URL before it can be compared with Windows
The Windows value is a parse error and should be filtered out of the dashboard
2.explanation: On the proxy `status` is an HTTP code; on 4625 it is an NTSTATUS code meaning a wrong password for a valid user. They must live in separate fields with documented meanings. Converting hex to decimal would still compare unrelated encodings.

2.q: A firewall drop event is recorded on fw01 and describes a packet from 203.0.113.66 to 10.40.0.5. How should a normaliser place these three values?
options: fw01 in host.name as the observer; the two addresses in source.ip and destination.ip
fw01 in source.ip as the sending device; 10.40.0.5 in host.name as the target
fw01 in destination.ip as the device that received the packet; 203.0.113.66 in host.name
All three in host.ip, because each is a host that took part in the connection
2.explanation: The firewall is the observer, not a participant, so it belongs in `host.name`, while the connection's ends go in `source.*` and `destination.*`. Treating the firewall as one end of the connection is the observer-versus-participant trap.

2.q: To attribute proxy traffic to a machine, an analyst joins every proxy event of the day with src_ip 10.40.0.23 to WS-104, because that address was WS-104 at 03:26 UTC. What is the main risk?
options: Proxy src_ip is the external address, so 10.40.0.23 cannot belong to a workstation
The proxy rewrites src_ip to its own address after the first request from each host
DHCP may hand the address to another machine later, so the join needs a time window
IP addresses are stable all day, so the join is sound and there is no real risk
2.explanation: IP addresses change with DHCP leases, NAT and VPN pools, so a join on IP must be bounded by time, and a stable identifier is better where available. Proxy src_ip is internal, so the second option reverses the field's semantics.

2.q: An analyst wants to link a network connection to the process that made it, minutes after a process start event. Why is Sysmon's ProcessGuid a better join key than the PID?
options: The PID is recorded only in Windows Security logs, never in Sysmon events
ProcessGuid includes the host name and user, so no other field is needed
The operating system reuses PIDs, while ProcessGuid identifies one process instance
PIDs are randomised on each event, so the same process shows different PIDs
2.explanation: A numeric PID may belong to a different program a few minutes later; Sysmon added ProcessGuid precisely to identify a single process instance. PIDs are not randomised per event; they are stable for a process but reused after it exits.

2.q: One source records the user as BANYAN\divya, another as divya@banyan.example, and the account was renamed last year. Which join key is most reliable for linking her activity?
options: The lower-cased user name with domain prefixes and suffixes stripped from both values
The workstation name WS-104, because divya always signs in to the same machine
The source IP address, joined over the whole day to cover every logon she made
The account's SID or directory object ID, which stays the same when names and formats differ
2.explanation: The lesson's rule is to join on the most specific stable identifier: SIDs and cloud object IDs survive renames and formatting differences. Stripping prefixes still fails across a rename and can merge different people who reuse a name.

2.q: In ECS, the VPN's external client address and the proxy's internal workstation address can both be mapped to source.ip without creating a semantic collision. Why?
options: ECS allows any address to go in source.ip as long as event.module records the source
ECS converts private addresses to public ones during ingestion, so the values align
source.ip means the initiator of the connection, and both values are the initiators seen by their devices
The two values never occur in the same search, so the shared name causes no harm
2.explanation: ECS names carry semantics: `source.ip` is the initiator from the observing device's viewpoint, which both values are, while the observer itself goes in `host.name`. Relying on `event.module` to disambiguate would mean the name itself carries no meaning.

2.q: Three products report a successful logon as SUCCESS, Succeeded and the number 0. After normalisation, what lets one detection rule handle all three?
options: Writing the rule with a regular expression that matches all three spellings
Copying the original value into event.original for the rule to read
Storing each product's value in its own vendor-specific outcome field
Mapping each to the controlled ECS value success in event.outcome
2.explanation: ECS defines `event.outcome` with the controlled values success, failure and unknown, so rules no longer depend on vendor spelling. A multi-spelling regex works only until the next product appears, which is the problem controlled values remove.

2.q: A new Windows parser maps both the creator and the newly created account of event 4720 into a single user field. What is the consequence for investigations?
options: Nothing is lost, because event.code 4720 already tells the analyst which value is which
The subject/target distinction is destroyed, so actor and created account can no longer be told apart
The event becomes unsearchable, because ECS rejects a user field holding two values
Only the group membership is lost, because 4720 never records the creating account
2.explanation: The raw Windows record keeps Subject and New Account in separate sections; flattening them loses which identity acted. ECS keeps them apart as `user.name` and `user.target.name`. The event code says what happened, not which name belongs to which role.

2.q: normalise_demo.py outputs a firewall drop at 06:46:21Z from 203.0.113.66 to 10.40.0.5 port 3389 and a VPN login success at 06:46:00Z from the same address as gopal. What is the sound analyst conclusion?
options: gopal opened a remote desktop session to 10.40.0.5 through the VPN, and the firewall logged it as allowed
The firewall blocked gopal's VPN login, and the VPN gateway then retried it successfully 21 seconds later
The two events are unrelated, because firewall and VPN events can never share a source address
Shortly after that address logged in to the VPN as gopal, it tried to reach an internal host's remote desktop port and was blocked
2.explanation: Once both share `source.ip` and UTC time, the drop of a TCP 3389 attempt follows the VPN login by 21 seconds from the same address. The action is `drop`, so no remote desktop session was established.

2.q: Why does the normalised firewall event from normalise_demo.py contain no user.name, and what follows for the investigation?
options: The parser dropped the user field by mistake; it should be restored from event.original
A packet filter does not know who sent a packet; linking the address to a person needs a pivot through an identity source
ECS forbids user.name on network events, so the user is stored in host.name instead
The firewall recorded the user, but the regular expression did not capture that token
2.explanation: Normalisation does not invent information; the raw firewall line never contained a user. Getting from 203.0.113.66 to gopal requires the VPN log. There is no user token in the raw line for the parser to have missed.

2.q: In a copy of the lab script, the firewall parser is called with tz=timezone.utc instead of IST. What happens to the investigation?
options: The event shifts to 01:16:21Z, before the VPN login, so the recorded order would suggest the firewall saw the connection attempt first
The drop is stamped 12:16:21Z, five and a half hours after the VPN login, and the link between them disappears
Nothing changes, because the parser converts every time to UTC whatever offset it is given
The script fails with an error, because a syslog line cannot be parsed without its own zone
2.explanation: Declaring the IST wall-clock reading to be UTC leaves 12:16:21 unchanged as UTC, 5 h 30 min late, so the 21-second link vanishes. Conversion only works if the declared offset is the true one; the script runs without error, which is why the mistake is silent.

2.q: The VPN parser outputs event.action: "login" although the raw VPN JSON contains no action field. Why is this acceptable?
options: ECS requires event.action on every event, so parsers insert a default value when it is missing
The parser author knows this gateway emits login records, so the parser states what the source implies
The value is copied from the result field, which the gateway uses to record the action
It is not acceptable: a parser must never output a field that the raw event did not contain
2.explanation: Parsers carry knowledge about their source; here the record type is fixed, so stating the action is an accurate translation rather than invention. `result` holds the outcome (SUCCESS), not the action.

2.q: The raw line "Nov  3 12:16:21 fw01 kernel: DROP ... SRC=203.0.113.66 ..." is classic syslog. Which two facts must from_syslog() supply from configuration rather than read from the line?
options: The host name and the action
The month and the destination port
The source address and the protocol
The year and the time zone
2.explanation: Classic syslog timestamps carry month, day and time but no year and no zone, so the parser takes 2026 and IST from configuration. Host, action, addresses and port are all captured by the regular expression.

2.q: After a firewall vendor upgrade, event volume from the firewall looks normal, but every rule that uses source.ip on that source has stopped matching. Which monitoring would have caught this first?
options: Event volume per source, alerting when the number of events per hour falls
The count of alerts per rule, reviewed in the monthly detection report
Per-source parse-error rates and the fill rate of critical fields such as source.ip
The disk usage of the SIEM index that stores the firewall's events
2.explanation: A format change can stop a parser extracting a field while events keep arriving, so volume looks healthy. Fill-rate and parse-error monitoring detect the silent gap. Volume monitoring is exactly the metric this failure does not move.

2.q: A detection engineer must pick which field a rule should trust for the client's identity in web traffic. Which choice follows the lesson's guidance?
options: The observed source address of the TCP connection, which the sensor measures itself
The HTTP user agent, because it identifies the client software precisely
The requested host name, because the client must send it to reach the site
The user name typed at the login prompt, because it names the person
2.explanation: User agents, requested host names and typed user names are supplied by the remote party and are claims an attacker can craft. The sensor-measured connection address is observed, not self-reported, so rules should prefer it.

2.q: Two analysts dispute whether a long command line in a normalised event was truncated. What practice lets them settle it?
options: Keeping the raw event alongside the normalised one, for example in event.original
Re-running the parser on the normalised event to regenerate the full value
Comparing the event with the field dictionary entry for that command line
Querying the source's ingest time to see whether the event arrived complete
2.explanation: Normalisation is not lossless: parsers drop unknown fields and truncate long values, so the raw event must be kept for verification. Re-running a parser on already-normalised output cannot restore what was lost.

2.q: In the Banyan dataset the encoded PowerShell command is shown as <redacted-for-course>. What can an analyst still learn from that Sysmon event?
options: Its shape: hidden, no-profile PowerShell with an encoded command launched by WINWORD.EXE
Nothing reliable, because a redacted command line removes all evidential value
The decoded payload, because redaction only applies to the analyst's display
Only the user, because image and parent image are redacted with the command line
2.explanation: A redacted field can still be analysed for its shape: the flags -NoP -W Hidden -EncodedCommand and the parent WINWORD.EXE are suspicious in themselves. Image and parent image remain present in the event.

2.q: Module 3's correlation rule links the proxy download of invoice.docm to the Sysmon event at 06:14 UTC in which WINWORD.EXE launches powershell.exe. Which fields make that link?
options: The shared src_ip, because both the proxy and Sysmon events record it
The full document URL and download path, which the endpoint event copies from the original proxy request
The Sysmon ProcessGuid, which the proxy also records for each request
The shared host WS-104 and user divya, together with the short time gap
2.explanation: The field inventory shows Sysmon events carry host and user but no src_ip or url, and the proxy has no ProcessGuid. The shared host and user, plus time proximity, are the identifiers that join the two sources.

2.q: A proxy event for WS-104 shows an unusually large bytes_out value. Mapped to ECS as source.bytes, how should it be read?
options: The workstation sent a lot of data, which suggests an upload worth investigating
The workstation received a large file, which suggests a big download from the site
The proxy forwarded a large response, so the value measures server load
The value is in kilobytes, so it must be multiplied before it can be assessed
2.explanation: `bytes_out` is counted from the client, so it is bytes the workstation sent; large values suggest uploads, possibly exfiltration. Reading it as a download is the direction-and-unit trap the lesson lists.

2.q: A SOC in India stores command lines, URLs and user names from its sources. What does the lesson say this implies?
options: These fields are technical metadata, so privacy law does not apply to them once they are inside a SIEM
The fields must be deleted after normalisation, because only the ECS form may be kept lawfully
The fields must be hashed before ingestion, which also keeps them usable for every investigation
These fields can hold personal data under the DPDP Act 2023, so access to raw fields and their retention should be controlled
2.explanation: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 the SOC processes personal data when it stores such fields, so access should be need-to-know and retention follow policy. Deleting raw events contradicts the advice to keep event.original.

2.q: An analyst merges two timelines and finds that every event from one source is exactly 5 hours 30 minutes later than the matching event in the other. What should be suspected first?
options: Clock drift on the slower source's hardware oscillator
IST local times have been treated as UTC in one source
A collection backlog delaying one source's events
An attacker changing the system time on one host
2.explanation: A constant gap equal to a whole zone offset, here IST's +05:30, is the signature of a zone error. Drift is usually small, not a round number and changes over time, so it does not produce an exact, constant 5.5-hour gap.

2.q: A Banyan report lists an alert at 00:20 IST on 4 November 2026. What is the corresponding UTC time?
options: 05:50 UTC on 4 November 2026
18:50 UTC on 3 November 2026
18:50 UTC on 4 November 2026
00:20 UTC on 4 November 2026
2.explanation: UTC = local time minus the offset: 00:20 minus 05:30 crosses midnight back to 18:50 on the previous day. Adding the offset instead gives 05:50, the most common conversion mistake.

2.q: In January 2027 a team imports December 2026 firewall logs written in classic syslog format, and the parser supplies the current year. What goes wrong?
options: The events are rejected, because classic syslog timestamps must include a year
The December events are dated December 2027, almost a year in the future
The events are dated correctly, because the month tells the parser the year
The events shift by the IST offset, because the year change resets the zone
2.explanation: Classic syslog has no year, so a parser assuming the current year stamps December events as December 2027. The month gives no information about the year, which is why replaying old logs around the new year is a known trap.

2.q: An analyst copies event times from the Windows Event Viewer screen on her IST laptop into a case note without any zone. What is the problem?
options: Event Viewer shows UTC, so the note is correct but will confuse readers who expect IST
Windows stores events in the source machine's local time, so the values cannot be converted
The note is fine, because Windows event times are always displayed with an offset suffix
Event Viewer shows the viewer's local time, so the note now holds naive times though the event stores UTC
2.explanation: Windows stores `TimeCreated SystemTime` in UTC but displays it in the viewing machine's local time; copied without a zone it becomes a naive timestamp. Export the XML or use a collector that preserves the UTC value.

2.q: An API returns the value 1793688360000 for an event time. A script converts it as seconds and produces a date tens of thousands of years ahead. What is the correct handling?
options: Treat the value as local IST epoch time and subtract the offset before converting
Treat the 13-digit value as milliseconds and divide by 1000 before converting
Treat the value as seconds but truncate it to 10 digits by dropping the last digits
Treat the value as microseconds and divide by one million before converting
2.explanation: A 13-digit epoch value is usually milliseconds; divided by 1000 it is 1793688360, which is 2026-11-03T06:46:00Z. Epoch time is defined from a UTC origin, so there is no local offset to subtract.

2.q: Three timestamps: 2026-11-03T06:46:21Z, 2026-11-03T12:15:30+05:30 and 2026-11-03T06:46:00Z. Which event happened first?
options: The one written 06:46:00Z, because it sorts first as text
The one written 06:46:21Z, because UTC events come before IST
The one written 12:15:30+05:30, because it is 06:45:30 UTC
They cannot be ordered, because they use different offsets
2.explanation: Converted to UTC, 12:15:30+05:30 is 06:45:30Z, half a minute before the VPN login. A text sort puts it last because "12" follows "06"; ISO strings sort correctly as text only when they share one format and offset.

2.q: In the lesson's Python demonstration, comparing a naive datetime with an aware one raises a TypeError. Why does the lesson call this refusal a feature?
options: It forces an explicit decision about the zone instead of silently guessing, as many tools do
It shows that naive values are always in local time and must be converted by hand
It proves the two values are different instants, so the comparison would be false anyway
It prevents comparing times from two different sources, which should never be done
2.explanation: A naive time does not identify an instant, so any comparison would require a hidden assumption. Many tools quietly treat naive times as UTC or local, which is how 5.5-hour errors enter timelines; naive values are not inherently local time.

2.q: An MSSP monitors a London client whose server logs local time without an offset. On the night clocks go back, a login is stamped 01:30. What is the problem, and how does storing UTC help?
options: 01:30 occurs twice that night, so the instant is ambiguous; UTC never repeats an hour
01:30 never occurs that night, so the event is invalid; UTC records it as missing
01:30 is an hour late, so the event is misdated; UTC adds the hour back in
01:30 is correct, so no problem arises; UTC adds only a display label
2.explanation: When clocks go back, one local hour happens twice, so a naive local time in that hour matches two instants. It is the spring-forward transition when an hour never happens. UTC has no daylight-saving changes, so the ambiguity disappears.

2.q: A Banyan partner sends a log with the date 03/11/2026. Why does the course prefer ISO 8601 dates such as 2026-11-03?
options: ISO dates are shorter, so they use less storage in the SIEM index
Year-first order removes the ambiguity between 3 November and 11 March
ISO dates are in IST by default, so no offset has to be added
Slash-separated dates are rejected by SIEM parsers even when the source documents the intended day and month ordering
2.explanation: 03/11/2026 is 3 November in India and the UK but 11 March in the United States; year-month-day removes the doubt. ISO dates have no default zone: the offset or Z must be written explicitly.

2.q: A Windows workstation's clock is seven minutes ahead of the domain controller. Users report they cannot log on to the domain. What is the most likely cause?
options: The SIEM discards the logon events because their timestamps appear to come from the future
TLS certificates on the domain controller have expired from the workstation's point of view
Kerberos rejects requests when client and DC clocks differ by more than its default five-minute tolerance
NTP blocks logons until the workstation's clock has been slewed back to the correct time
2.explanation: Kerberos depends on synchronised clocks, with a default tolerance of five minutes in Windows domains, so a seven-minute skew breaks authentication. SIEM ingestion has no effect on whether a logon succeeds.

2.q: For one source, the SIEM shows event times that are consistently a few minutes later than the times at which the events were ingested. What does this indicate?
options: The source's events are delayed in a collection queue
The source is logging local time without an offset
The SIEM's clock is running ahead of true time
The source's clock is running ahead of true time
2.explanation: Events cannot arrive before they happen, so event time later than ingest time means the source clock is ahead. A collection delay produces the opposite pattern: ingest time later than event time.

2.q: An analyst suspects skew between a client and a domain controller but has no NTP records. Which evidence best measures the offset between the two sources?
options: The client's events sorted alone, compared with their own ingest time
The gap between the first and last event recorded on each host that day
The time of the most recent reboot shown in the client's system log
The same authentication recorded on both the client and the domain controller
2.explanation: Anchor events known to be simultaneous, such as both ends of one connection or one authentication seen on both systems, reveal the offset directly. A single host's events alone cannot show its offset from another host.

2.q: Compared with a time-zone error, how does clock skew between two sources typically appear?
options: A smaller, irregular offset that changes over time
An exact whole-hour or half-hour constant offset
A gap of exactly one hour around daylight-saving dates
Events from one source dated in the year 1970
2.explanation: Skew is usually small, not a round number and drifts, while a zone error produces a constant whole offset such as 05:30. Dates in 1970 point to an epoch unit or zero-value error, not skew.

2.q: A Sysmon event on WS-104 has @timestamp 06:14:00Z but, after a network outage, reaches the SIEM at 07:40Z. A rule runs every five minutes over the last five minutes of event time. What happens, and what fixes it?
options: The rule fires at 07:45, because the SIEM re-runs all windows when late events arrive
The rule fires at 06:15, because the agent reports the event time before sending the data
The rule never fires; only moving WS-104 to UTC would let the event match the window
The rule never fires; selecting by ingest time, or a longer look-back with de-duplication, would catch it
2.explanation: Before 07:40 the data is absent; after it, the 06:14 event lies outside every five-minute event-time window, so it is stored but never alerted on. Scheduled rules do not retroactively re-run past windows, and WS-104's zone is not the issue.

2.q: For the Banyan case timeline, the PowerShell execution on WS-104 has @timestamp 06:14 UTC and event.ingested 07:40 UTC. How should the case record it?
options: Place it at 06:14 UTC (11:44 IST) and record the 86-minute gap as a collection delay
Place it at 07:40 UTC, because that is when the SOC could confirm the event happened
Place it at 07:40 IST, because ingest time is recorded in the SIEM's local zone
Place it midway between the two times, because neither can be fully trusted
2.explanation: Timelines are built on event time; ingest time answers when the SOC could have known and is used to measure detection delay. Sorting the narrative by ingest time would misplace the attacker's action.

2.q: An agent reads an event at 06:14:02Z from a log written at 06:14:00Z, buffers it during an outage, and the central store receives it at 07:40:00Z. Which ECS assignment is correct?
options: @timestamp 07:40:00Z, event.created 06:14:00Z, event.ingested 06:14:02Z
@timestamp 06:14:02Z, event.created 07:40:00Z, event.ingested 06:14:00Z
@timestamp 06:14:00Z, event.created 06:14:02Z, event.ingested 07:40:00Z
@timestamp 06:14:00Z, event.created 07:40:00Z, event.ingested 06:14:02Z
2.explanation: `@timestamp` is when the event originated, `event.created` when an agent or pipeline first read it, and `event.ingested` when it arrived in the central store. The last option swaps created and ingested, placing arrival before the read.

2.q: Source A records 06:46:21 (whole seconds) and source B records 06:46:21.900 (milliseconds). Which statement about their order is justified?
options: A's event came first, because 06:46:21 is earlier than 06:46:21.900
B's event came first, because millisecond sources log more promptly
A's event came first, because it is 900 milliseconds earlier than B's
Their order is unknown, because A's event could fall anywhere within that second
2.explanation: A whole-second stamp covers the entire second, so A may be at 06:46:21.999. Differences smaller than the coarsest precision involved cannot establish sequence, which is why reading 900 ms of order into it is wrong.
