2.q: Banyan has two failed logons, on WS-102 and WS-108, both at 04:05:00Z. What can an analyst conclude about their order?
options: WS-102 came first, because a sort keeps the order in which events were written
WS-108 came first, because its EventRecordID will be the higher number
Only that they fell in the same second; across sources the order is unknown
They were simultaneous, because one attacker tool generated both of them
2.explanation: Sorts leave ties in arbitrary or input order. Sequence numbers such as EventRecordID break ties only within one source's log, not between two workstations' separate logs.

2.q: Host A's clock is known to run about three seconds ahead of host B's. A file appears on B two seconds after A's log says it was sent. What should the analyst conclude?
options: The ordering is uncertain, because the gap is smaller than the known skew between the hosts
The send necessarily came first because the timestamps show a positive interval and only the receiving host records the arrival
The file arrived before it was sent, so one of the two logs must have been tampered with
The hosts are in different zones, so B's time must be converted before any comparison
2.explanation: Within one host, order is usually preserved despite clock error, but across hosts a skew of a few seconds can reverse cause and effect. Orderings closer than the known skew must be treated as uncertain, not as proof of tampering.

2.q: A timeline of a laptop's day shows its morning activity after its afternoon activity. The laptop was offline until late afternoon. What is the likely cause?
options: The timeline was sorted on ingest time rather than event time
The laptop's clock lost several hours during the offline period
The laptop logged in local time while the server logged in UTC
The SIEM deduplicated the morning events and replayed them later
2.explanation: Ingest-time order shows when the SIEM learned of events; a laptop that reconnected late delivers its morning events after the afternoon. A clock error would shift the stamps, not reorder them by delivery, so always state which time a timeline uses.

2.q: An attacker with administrative rights on WS-104 changes the system clock before acting. Which combination of controls best preserves a trustworthy timeline?
options: Disable NTP on workstations so that the attacker cannot use it to resynchronise the clock afterwards
Alert on Windows event 4616 outside maintenance and forward logs quickly to a store whose event.ingested gives an independent time
Rely on file-system timestamps on WS-104, because a clock change does not affect them
Collect only event 1102 from WS-104, because log clearing always follows a clock change
2.explanation: Event 4616 records system time changes, and rapid off-host forwarding gives a central, trusted ingest time the attacker cannot rewrite. File-system timestamps can also be altered by an attacker, so they are not an independent record.

2.q: A body corporate in India covered by the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 is choosing a time source for its servers. Which choice meets the Directions?
options: NTP servers of NIC or NPL, or servers traceable to them
Any public NTP pool, as long as all servers use the same one
Each server's own hardware clock, checked monthly by hand
The cloud provider's time service, whatever it is traceable to
2.explanation: The Directions require connecting to the NTP servers of the National Informatics Centre or National Physical Laboratory, or to servers traceable to them. A consistent public pool keeps clocks aligned but does not meet the traceability requirement.

2.q: A management report converts an event at 20:00 UTC on 3 November 2026 to IST. Why does the lesson insist on keeping both columns?
options: It becomes 14:30 IST on 3 November, so readers need the UTC value to know it was evening
IST switches to a seasonal daylight-saving offset, so both columns are needed to verify which local offset was applied on the date
The IST value cannot be converted back to UTC, so UTC must be preserved for later analysis
It becomes 01:30 IST on 4 November, so the event can appear on a different day in each column
2.explanation: Adding 05:30 to 20:00 UTC crosses midnight into 4 November, a frequent cause of events landing on the wrong day in daily reports. IST is a fixed offset with no daylight saving time.

2.q: A "spray then success" rule requires VPN failures to come before a success. The failures come from a source that logs naive IST times, wrongly parsed as UTC; the success is correctly in UTC. Why does the rule not fire?
options: The failures are stamped five hours and thirty minutes early, placing them too far before the rule's eligible window
The success is stamped 5 h 30 min late, so it appears after the window
The failures are stamped 5 h 30 min late, so they appear after the success
The failures lack an offset, so the SIEM discards them at ingestion
2.explanation: Treating an IST wall-clock reading as UTC makes each failure 5.5 hours later than its true instant, so they now follow the success and the order condition fails. The success was parsed correctly, so it does not move.

2.q: An NTP client finds its clock is a few seconds fast. Why does it normally slew the clock rather than jump it back?
options: A gradual adjustment resets the host's authentication clock tolerance without saving the corrected value to its configuration
So the stratum of the client is promoted to match that of the server
So time does not run backwards, which would disorder the host's own logs
So the network delay between client and server is no longer counted
2.explanation: Slewing adjusts the clock rate gradually so local time never goes backwards; a jump back would make later events appear earlier than earlier ones. Correcting the clock does not change the client's stratum.

2.q: A firewall sends its logs as syslog over UDP port 514 to a relay. The relay's disk fills up for three hours before anyone notices. What happens to the firewall messages sent during those three hours?
options: They are lost, and neither the firewall nor the relay records that delivery failed
They are held by the firewall and re-sent once the relay acknowledges it has space
They are delayed in the relay's memory queue and written when disk space returns
They are redirected by the relay to the SIEM directly, bypassing the full disk
2.explanation: UDP syslog is at-most-once: there is no acknowledgement or retransmission, so messages that cannot be accepted simply vanish without either side knowing. The firewall cannot buffer and re-send because it never learns that delivery failed.

2.q: After a server reboot, Filebeat resumes shipping a busy application log and neither re-sends old lines nor skips new ones. What makes this possible?
options: The SIEM acknowledges every event and tells Filebeat which ones it already holds
The SIEM de-duplicates any lines that Filebeat sends a second time after restart
Filebeat records the offset it has reached in each file in its registry
The application writes a sequence number on every line that Filebeat checks
2.explanation: Agents keep their own read position; Filebeat stores the offset per file in a registry and continues from it after a restart. Acknowledgements support at-least-once delivery but do not tell the agent where in a file to resume.

2.q: A rule fires on 'ten failed logons for one account in five minutes'. Investigation finds only six genuine failures, all forwarded by an agent during a brief network interruption between the agent and the SIEM. What best explains the alert?
options: Clock skew on the host made six events appear to fall inside the five-minute window
At-least-once delivery re-sent events whose acknowledgements were lost, storing some twice
The parser split each failure into two events because of a changed log format
Success events were lost during the interruption, reducing the total number of distinct attempts visible to the rule engine
2.explanation: An agent that retries until acknowledged will re-send events whose acknowledgement was lost, so some are stored twice and counting rules over-count. Clock skew would move events in time but could not raise six events to ten.

2.q: A SOC builds its list of expected log sources from the distinct hosts that appear in the SIEM over the last 30 days, and alerts when any of them goes silent. Which problem can this design never detect?
options: A domain controller that stops sending events in the middle of a working day
A workstation whose agent was stopped by a local administrator yesterday
A proxy whose hourly volume drops to a fraction of its usual rate
A newly deployed server that has never sent a single event to the SIEM
2.explanation: A host that has never sent anything never appears in a list built from the SIEM, so its absence is invisible; the inventory should come from the asset register or CMDB. The other three hosts were seen before and would show up as silent or low.

2.q: A correlation rule runs every ten minutes over the last ten minutes of data, looking for VPN failures followed by a success for the same user. VPN events are found to become searchable about an hour after they occur. What is the most likely result, and the right fix?
options: The rule fires twice for each pattern; add de-duplication on the VPN event identifier
The rule misses patterns because the window is evaluated before the events arrive; measure lag and set the window to allow for it
The rule works normally because the SIEM re-evaluates old windows when late events arrive
The rule fires on the wrong user; convert the VPN timestamps to UTC at ingest
2.explanation: When ingestion lag exceeds the rule's window, the window is evaluated while the relevant events are still in transit and the pattern is never seen; lag must be measured and windows set accordingly. Most scheduled rules do not automatically re-run over past windows.

2.q: After a proxy firmware update, proxy events keep arriving at their normal hourly volume, yet rules keyed on the user field stop firing. Which health check is designed to catch this?
options: Field completeness and parse-error counts for the proxy source
Last-seen time per proxy host compared with its quiet interval
Hourly volume per source compared with the same hour last week
Queue depth on the relay that receives the proxy's syslog
2.explanation: Events that are present but missing rule-critical fields are a completeness failure, caught by checking that fields such as user are populated and that parse errors are zero. Volume and last-seen checks pass because events are still arriving on time.

2.q: A workstation configured for source-initiated Windows Event Forwarding cannot reach its collector for several days. What is the eventual risk to its Security events?
options: The collector pulls the missing events automatically once the workstation reappears
The workstation copies unsent events into its own Forwarded Events log for later
Group Policy disables Security auditing on the host until the collector is reachable
Unsent events are lost once the local Security log reaches its maximum and overwrites the oldest
2.explanation: A workstation that cannot reach the collector keeps its events in the local log, which by default overwrites its oldest entries when full; after a long enough outage, unsent events are gone. Forwarded Events is the log on the collector, not a buffer on the source.

2.q: A SOC collects an identity provider's audit records with an API poller. Which failure mode is characteristic of this collection method?
options: An endpoint agent upgrade can silence the provider's servers until every installation is rolled back by the SOC collection team
Packets are dropped in transit because the protocol has no acknowledgement
Provider throttling or publication delay makes the poller fall behind, adding lag
The provider's local log wraps before the forwarding subscription is renewed
2.explanation: Pull-based API collection depends on the provider's rate limits, pagination and the delay before audit events are published, so the poller can fall behind or its cursor can stick. Agent upgrades and UDP drops belong to other collection methods.

2.q: A network appliance cannot host an agent but supports syslog over UDP, TCP and TLS. Which collection design best fits the lesson's recommendations?
options: Syslog over TLS to a relay with a disk-backed queue
Syslog over UDP to the SIEM, with a larger receive buffer
An API poller that reads the appliance's logs every hour
A collector-initiated Windows Event Forwarding subscription
2.explanation: TLS syslog (RFC 5425) adds confidentiality, integrity and a connection that fails visibly, and a disk-backed relay queue turns downstream outages into delay. UDP stays at-most-once regardless of buffer size.

2.q: A syslog relay's disk-backed queue can hold about four hours of the traffic it receives. The SIEM is unavailable for six hours, and the sending devices cannot be slowed down. What is the expected outcome?
options: No loss, because back-pressure makes the devices hold events until the SIEM returns
Roughly two hours of events are lost and the rest arrive late
All six hours are lost, because a queue that overflows discards its whole contents
No loss, because the relay switches to an in-memory buffer when the disk queue is full
2.explanation: Buffers turn loss into delay only up to their capacity; with four hours of queue and a six-hour outage, about two hours cannot be held. Back-pressure cannot help when the senders, such as UDP syslog devices, cannot be told to wait.

2.q: A relay holds syslog in an in-memory buffer while the SIEM is down for maintenance. During the outage the relay process is restarted to apply a patch. What happens, and which design change prevents it?
options: The events are re-read from the devices on restart; no change is needed
The events are kept in the operating system's page cache; enable swap on the relay
The buffered events are lost; use a persistent, disk-backed queue
The buffered events are forwarded twice; add de-duplication in the SIEM
2.explanation: An in-memory buffer loses its contents when the process restarts, while a persistent disk-backed queue survives restarts. Syslog devices do not keep a copy to re-send, so nothing can be re-read from them.

2.q: An analyst finds that the field extraction for a proxy source has been wrong for months. On which kind of platform does a corrected extraction apply to the historic data immediately, without reprocessing what is stored?
options: One that parses at ingest and stores only the extracted fields
One that parses at ingest and tags events that fail to parse
One that de-duplicates events on a stable identifier before storage
One that stores the raw text and extracts fields at search time
2.explanation: With schema-on-read, fields are extracted when a search runs, so a new extraction applies to old data at once. Schema-on-write platforms that keep the raw event can re-parse, but only by reprocessing stored data.

2.q: Why does a well-designed pipeline keep the original raw event alongside the fields it parsed at ingest?
options: So that events can be re-parsed when a parser was wrong, and the original record can be shown as evidence
So that searches run faster, because the raw text is indexed more efficiently than parsed fields
So that storage costs fall, because the raw event compresses better than the parsed fields
So that the pipeline can switch from at-least-once to exactly-once delivery when needed
2.explanation: The raw event allows re-parsing after a parser error and is the evidence an investigation must be able to show. Keeping it adds storage rather than saving it, and it does not change delivery guarantees.

2.q: A vendor changes its log format. Which parser behaviour turns this change into loss that nobody notices?
options: Storing unrecognised events with an error tag and the unparsed message kept
Discarding unrecognised events without counting or reporting them
Rejecting the batch and raising an error that the SIEM team can see
Extracting the fields at search time from the stored raw message
2.explanation: A parser that silently drops what it cannot read makes a format change invisible: volume falls and no rule fires, with no error anywhere. Tagging and keeping failed events lets the parse-error count reveal the problem.

2.q: A health monitor applies a single 60-minute silence threshold to every source and host. What is the main weakness of this design?
options: It cannot measure ingestion lag, because silence and lag use different timestamps
It ignores volume drops, because a silence check only looks at event counts per day
It requires the asset inventory to be built from the SIEM rather than the CMDB
Normal quiet intervals differ by source, host group and time of day, so it misfires both ways
2.explanation: A workstation is quiet at night while a domain controller never is, so one threshold raises false alerts for some sources and is too slow for others; silence must be judged against what each source normally does.

2.q: In the Equifax breach, a traffic-inspection device had an expired certificate and encrypted traffic passed uninspected for about ten months. Which control would most directly have shortened that period of blindness?
options: Writing more correlation rules over the inspected traffic in the SIEM
Extending log retention so that older traffic could be searched later
Monitoring the device's output and certificate validity as a source-health signal
Adding a second SIEM to receive a copy of every inspected session
2.explanation: The sensor and pipeline existed, but nobody watched whether the telemetry itself was healthy; a health check on the device's output (and its certificate) would have flagged it. More rules or retention over data that was never produced do not help.

2.q: During working hours a finance workstation stops sending events, and the last event received from it records its security agent's service being stopped. How should the SOC treat this?
options: As a possible defence-impairment action, triaged in the SOC queue with priority
As an operations ticket for the desktop team, since agents often fail on upgrade
As benign until the next day's volume baseline confirms the host is still quiet
As closed, because the stop event proves the forwarding pipeline is working
2.explanation: Stopping security tools is a recognised adversary behaviour (ATT&CK T1562.001), so silence from a sensitive host after an agent stop is a security signal, not only an operations issue. Waiting a day gives an intruder the blind window they wanted.

2.q: An intruder clears the Security log on a host that forwards its events in near real time. What can the SOC still rely on?
options: Nothing from that host, because clearing the log also removes the forwarded copies
The events forwarded before the clear, together with the 1102 event recording it
Only the events written after the clear, because the agent restarts its read position
A full copy of the cleared log, because Windows archives it to the collector first
2.explanation: Near-real-time forwarding means earlier events, and usually the 1102 log-clear event itself, have already reached the SIEM even though the local copy is gone. Clearing a local log does not touch what the SIEM already stores.

2.q: In an Active Directory domain, workstations forward events to a Windows Event Collector over WinRM on port 5985 (HTTP). An auditor says the events are therefore sent in clear text. Is the auditor right?
options: Yes, because port 5985 carries unauthenticated HTTP and only 5986 is protected
Yes, because WEF sends events as plain syslog once they leave the workstation
No, because inside the domain Kerberos authenticates and encrypts the channel
No, because WEF tunnels its traffic through SMB signing on port 445 by default
2.explanation: Within a domain, WinRM's HTTP channel is authenticated and encrypted with Kerberos, so port 5985 does not mean clear text. Port 5986 (HTTPS) is the alternative, typically outside a domain, not the only protected option.

2.q: A SOC has scheduled source-health searches for every source but has never seen one of them raise an alert. What should it do to turn these checks into a trusted control?
options: Lower every threshold until the checks start to raise occasional alerts
Wait for a real outage and review whether the checks fired at the time
Move the checks from a fifteen-minute schedule to a daily schedule
Stop forwarding on a test workstation and confirm that the alert fires
2.explanation: A health check that has never been seen to fire is an assumption; deliberately breaking forwarding on a test host proves it works end to end. Waiting for a real outage tests it only when a failure would already be costly.

2.q: An engineer proposes dropping a high-volume, low-value endpoint event type at the agent to save bandwidth and licence. What is the key consideration before approving it?
options: Data dropped at the agent is gone for good, so the decision must weigh detection value and be recorded
Dropped events can be re-sent later from the SIEM archive, so the decision is easily reversed
Filtering at the agent increases ingestion lag for every other event type on the host
Filtering at the agent only affects the parse-error count, not what the rules can see
2.explanation: Filtering at the source is permanent for that data: it never reaches any buffer or archive, so it needs a risk decision based on which detections depend on it. Nothing downstream can re-send what was never collected.

2.q: An Indian entity covered by CERT-In's April 2022 directions keeps firewall logs for 90 days. Apart from limiting investigations, why is this a problem?
options: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 requires all logs to be kept for a year
ISO 27001 certification is withdrawn automatically for retention below 120 days
CERT-In requires covered entities to export firewall logs to it every 90 days
The directions require ICT system logs to be kept for a rolling 180 days within India
2.explanation: CERT-In's directions require covered entities to keep ICT logs for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction, so 90 days is a regulatory gap. The DPDP Act sets purpose limitation and safeguards, not a one-year log retention period.

2.q: Which of these sources is the strongest case for agent-based rather than agentless collection?
options: A firewall appliance that exports its logs only through syslog
An application on a Linux server that writes logs only to a local file
A SaaS platform whose audit records are available through an API
A web proxy appliance supplied by a vendor with a closed operating system
2.explanation: Agents can read sources that are never exposed over the network, such as a local application log file. Appliances and SaaS platforms cannot host an agent and are collected by syslog push or API pull.

2.q: How is exactly-once delivery usually approximated in a real collection pipeline?
options: By sending over UDP with a buffer large enough that no packet is ever dropped
By switching from UDP to TCP, which guarantees each event is stored only once
By using at-least-once delivery plus de-duplication on a stable event identifier
Use at-most-once delivery and retry each event a fixed number of times without writing a durable event identifier at the receiver
2.explanation: End-to-end exactly-once is hard, so pipelines retry until acknowledged and then remove duplicates using a stable event ID. TCP makes the connection reliable but cannot stop a retry after a lost acknowledgement from storing an event twice.

2.q: A health dashboard shows a server's events still arriving at normal volume, last seen two minutes ago, but the ingestion lag has grown steadily from one minute to forty minutes over the morning. The server's clock is NTP-synchronised. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A backlog is building in a buffer, which will turn into loss if the buffer fills
The server's events are being duplicated by an at-least-once forwarder
The timestamp parser stopped extracting occurrence times and reliably replaced them with a fixed delay added at indexing time
The server has been quiet, and the lag reflects its normal overnight interval
2.explanation: Steadily growing lag with normal volume and a correct source clock points to events queuing somewhere downstream; it is often the first sign of a backlog that becomes loss when the buffer is full. Duplication would raise volume rather than lag.

2.q: In the lab, the first step after regenerating banyan_events.jsonl is to compute and record its SHA-256 digest. What does this achieve?
options: It lets minisiem.py load the file faster, because hashed files skip JSON validation
It detects duplicate events, because repeated lines change the digest in a known way
It shows that the evidence analysed is exactly the evidence that was generated
It converts the line endings to Unix format so that every learner's file matches
2.explanation: A recorded hash proves the input is unchanged and, with the fixed seed, identical for every learner; in an investigation it shows the evidence analysed is the evidence collected. A hash detects that a file changed, not what changed, such as duplicates.

2.q: The lab's first health check is that the generator wrote 340 events and minisiem.py loaded 340. What is the production equivalent of this check?
options: Comparing events sent by each forwarder with events indexed by the SIEM, per source and per hour
Comparing the SIEM's total daily event count with the licence limit agreed with the vendor
Comparing the number of hosts in the SIEM with the number of hosts seen the previous day
Comparing each event's own timestamp with the time it became searchable in the SIEM
2.explanation: Sent-versus-indexed counts per source and hour directly reveal loss between forwarding and storage. Comparing event time with search time measures lag, not loss.

2.q: The source-inventory search uses MIN(ts) and MAX(ts) on the timestamp column, which minisiem.py stores as text. Why do these return the correct first and last times?
options: SQLite converts text that looks like a date into a datetime value automatically
The index on the timestamp column stores the values in numeric time order
MIN and MAX call julianday() implicitly whenever a column holds timestamps
ISO 8601 UTC strings in one fixed format sort as text in time order
2.explanation: Timestamps such as 2026-11-03T06:14:00Z in a single fixed format and time base sort lexically in chronological order, which is one reason to normalise time representation. SQLite does not silently convert text to dates.

2.q: The lab's silence check reports Sysmon silent for 439 minutes, well above a 60-minute threshold. What is the correct next step before raising an outage?
options: Raise a priority outage at once, since any endpoint source silent for hours is an incident
Compare the result with what the source normally does; here the generator only models morning activity
Lower the threshold for Sysmon so that shorter silences are also flagged in future
Remove Sysmon from the expected-source inventory, since it stops early every day
2.explanation: A silence check yields a candidate that the baseline resolves; reading make_dataset.py shows it writes routine process starts only within two hours of logon, so the silence is a property of the dataset. Removing the source would blind the check to a real future outage.

2.q: The hourly-volume query uses SUM(source='proxy') to produce a proxy column. Why does this count proxy events per hour?
options: In SQLite the comparison evaluates to 1 or 0 for each row, so the sum counts matching rows
SUM on a text column counts the number of rows whose value is not NULL
The expression filters the table to proxy rows before the GROUP BY is applied
SQLite treats the string 'proxy' as a column alias holding the per-hour count
2.explanation: A comparison in SQLite yields 1 when true and 0 when false, so summing it per group counts the rows that match, giving one column per source. It does not filter rows; other sources stay in the group and contribute 0.

2.q: In Drill A, the hourly count of WS-104's proxy events lists hours 03, 04, 05, 06, 09, 10, 11 and 12. Why could an analyst reading this output miss the outage?
options: The ROUND function merged the 07 and 08 hours into the neighbouring hours
substr(ts,12,2) truncated the 07 and 08 timestamps so they did not match
GROUP BY returns no row for an hour with no events, so the gap shows as a missing line, not a zero
The query applied a LIMIT that cut off the two hours with the lowest counts
2.explanation: An aggregate over existing rows cannot print an hour that has none, so the eye must notice an absent line; a dashboard built on an expected list of hours shows such hours as zero. The query contains no ROUND or LIMIT that could hide them.

2.q: Drill A removes two hours of WS-104's proxy events, and the proxy total falls from 284 to 270. Why is the largest-gap check more sensitive to this fault than the source total?
options: The gap check counts events twice, so any missing event doubles its effect on the result
A small change in the source total is lost in daily variation, while WS-104's gap jumps far above the clean worst case
The gap check compares event time with ingestion time, so it measures lag rather than volume
The source total is computed only once a day, while the gap check runs every hour
2.explanation: Fourteen missing events barely change a total of 284, but WS-104's largest gap rises from 75 to 145 minutes, far above the 88-minute worst case of any host on the clean day. The gap check uses consecutive event times from one host, not ingestion time.

2.q: What does LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY host ORDER BY ts) contribute to the largest-gap search?
options: The delay between each event's timestamp and the time it was loaded
The timestamp of the earliest event from each host in the dataset
The number of minutes since each host's last event and the reference time
For each event, the timestamp of the previous event from the same host
2.explanation: LAG returns the previous row's value within the partition, so for each proxy event it gives the prior event from the same host and the gap between consecutive events can be computed. It does not use ingestion time, which minisiem.py does not record.

2.q: The completeness check shows no_outcome = 284 for all 284 proxy events. How should this be interpreted?
options: As normal for this source, because proxy events carry an HTTP status instead; alert only if the baseline changes
As a parser failure, because every event should populate outcome for detection rules to work
As evidence that proxy events were duplicated during ingestion into the teaching SIEM
As a sign that the proxy dropped events whose outcome field could not be determined
2.explanation: Many NULLs are by design: proxy events record status rather than outcome. A completeness check needs a per-source baseline and alerts when the numbers change, not when they are non-zero.

2.q: In the Windows source, three events have a NULL src_ip and ten have the literal value '-'. A completeness check counts only NULLs and reports 3 of 13 missing. What is wrong with this result?
options: Nothing, because '-' is a valid address that Windows writes for local loopback logons
It over-reports, because the three NULL events should be excluded as log-clear noise
It under-reports, because '-' is a placeholder meaning no network source and should count as empty
It double-counts, because each '-' event also produces a matching NULL event
2.explanation: The ten '-' values come from interactive (type 2) logons with no network source; a NULL-only check treats them as populated. Placeholders that mean empty must be counted as empty, decided per source.

2.q: Which change in the lab's completeness numbers should raise a health alert?
options: Proxy no_event_id stays at 284 of 284 events on the following day
VPN no_user rises from 0 to most of its events after a firmware upgrade
Sysmon no_src_ip stays equal to the number of Sysmon process events
VPN no_host stays equal to the total number of VPN events received
2.explanation: The user field is fully populated in every source on the clean day and most detections pivot on it, so a jump in empty user values is a real regression. The other three are unchanged by-design values from the baseline.

2.q: normalise_demo.py parses the firewall line 'Nov  3 12:16:21 fw01 ...', from a firewall configured in India Standard Time, as 06:46:21Z. If the parser had instead assumed the time was UTC, what would happen?
options: The event would be rejected, because a BSD syslog line without a zone cannot be parsed
The event would be stored a day early, because the missing year defaults to the previous one
Nothing would change, because 203.0.113.66 links the two events regardless of their times
The drop would be placed at 12:16:21Z, five and a half hours after the VPN login, breaking the correlation
2.explanation: A wrong time-zone assumption shifts the firewall event by the UTC+05:30 offset, so it no longer sits beside the VPN login and every time-window correlation fails silently. The parser would still accept the line; the error is silent, not a rejection.

2.q: After normalisation, the VPN record shows gopal logging in successfully from 203.0.113.66 at 06:46:00Z, and the firewall record shows a TCP drop from 203.0.113.66 to 10.40.0.5 port 3389 at 06:46:21Z. Which statement do the records support?
options: The address that logged in to the VPN as gopal had a connection to an internal RDP port dropped 21 seconds later
The firewall dropped the address first, and the VPN login 21 seconds later was its successful retry
The firewall allowed RDP from 203.0.113.66 to 10.40.0.5 after the VPN login succeeded
The two records come from different addresses and cannot be correlated without a user field
2.explanation: In a common schema and time base the records share source.ip, and the VPN login at 06:46:00Z precedes the firewall drop on port 3389 at 06:46:21Z. The firewall action was drop, not allow, and the login came first.

2.q: Which two problems with the BSD-style firewall syslog line does normalise_demo.py have to fix before the event can be stored in the common schema's time base?
options: It has no host name and no protocol, which the parser adds from configuration
It has no source address and no port, which the parser looks up from the VPN
It has no year and no time zone, so the parser supplies the year and applies UTC+05:30
It has no message text and no severity, which the parser derives from the facility
2.explanation: The RFC 3164-style timestamp lacks a year and an offset, so the parser adds 2026 and converts from IST. The line does contain the host (fw01), addresses, protocol and port, which the parser extracts with a regular expression.

2.q: In Drill B, a healthy minisiem.db with 340 events is in the folder; a load of a file containing one truncated record fails with a JSONDecodeError, and the table then holds 0 events. What is the cause?
options: The JSON decoder deleted every row that shared a source with the truncated record
SQLite rolled the whole database back to an empty file when the error was raised
The truncated record overwrote the other records because it had no closing brace
load drops the existing table before inserting, and the error stops the inserts, so good data is destroyed first
2.explanation: load drops and recreates the events table and only then inserts; the decode error ends the run before any rows are written, leaving an empty store. The decoder only rejects the bad line; it does not touch the database.

2.q: Which set of production defences addresses the failure that Drill B demonstrates?
options: A lenient parser that silently discards bad records, so that one line cannot stop a batch
Tagging and counting unparsable records, writing new data before replacing old, and alerting when volume falls to zero
Turning off JSON validation at ingest so that truncated records are stored as they arrive
Reducing the batch size so that each failed load empties a smaller part of the table
2.explanation: The defences are to keep and count bad records, never destroy good data before new data is safely written, and alert on a source dropping to zero. A lenient parser that silently discards records is the other failure mode, not a fix.

2.q: In Drill C the load reports 345 events. Which search result shows that five of them are duplicates?
options: COUNT(*) returns 345 while COUNT(DISTINCT raw) returns 340
COUNT(DISTINCT host) returns more hosts than the inventory holds
MAX(ts) returns a later time than the clean dataset's last event
SUM(user IS NULL) returns five more empty values than the baseline
2.explanation: The raw column holds each event exactly as delivered, so the difference between rows and distinct raw events counts the copies. Duplicates repeat existing hosts, times and users, so the other checks would not change.

2.q: The lab de-duplicates by comparing whole raw records. Why does the lesson call this a teaching shortcut rather than a production method?
options: Comparing raw text is too slow for SQLite on more than a few thousand rows
The raw column is truncated to 60 characters, so different events look the same
Two genuine events can share every field, so production uses an event ID assigned at the source or forwarder
Raw records change on each delivery attempt, so true duplicates never match exactly
2.explanation: Real events often lack a unique identifier and two separate events can be identical, so whole-record matching could merge genuine events; production pipelines de-duplicate on a stable event ID. The 60-character substring was only for display in the search.

2.q: The five duplicated events in Drill C are proxy events from the 07:00 hour. Which kind of detection or metric do they affect most?
options: A single-event rule that fires on any Security log clear, even when the endpoint forwards the same record twice
A rule that alerts on any new administrator account being created
A silence check comparing each source's last-seen time with a threshold
A count of proxy requests per host per hour, which over-reports that hour
2.explanation: Duplicates rarely matter for single-event detections but inflate counts, so per-host hourly request metrics over-report the 07:00 hour. Last-seen times are unchanged because the copies repeat existing timestamps.

2.q: Why does make_faults.py copy minisiem.py into each of the outage, broken and dup folders?
options: Each drill needs a modified version of the loader that tolerates its fault
The script reads banyan_events.jsonl and writes minisiem.db in the folder it runs in, so drills leave the healthy database alone
SQLite cannot open the same database file from more than one folder at once
Copying the script resets its random seed so each faulty dataset is regenerated
2.explanation: Because minisiem.py works on files in its own folder, a copy per drill gives each fault its own database and keeps the clean one intact. The copies are unmodified; the point is to test the same ingestion path.

2.q: On some day, one workstation's Sysmon stops sending entirely, and the Sysmon source total falls from 33 to 29, well within normal day-to-day variation. Which lab view would reveal the problem?
options: Per-host count and last-seen for Sysmon, checked against the inventory of eight workstations
The hourly volume pivot for all sources, read across the morning hours
The source inventory with first-seen and last-seen times per source
The field-completeness counts of NULL values per source
2.explanation: Source-level counts can hide a single silent host; breaking Sysmon down by host against the eight expected workstations shows one missing. The source inventory would still show Sysmon present with plausible times from the other hosts.

2.q: The troubleshooting table lists the error 'no such function: LAG'. What is the cause?
options: The search was run before load, so the events table does not exist yet
The SQL statement was split by the shell because of missing double quotes
The SQLite library in that Python is older than 3.25, which added window functions
The search is running against a fault-drill database that lacks the ts column
2.explanation: LAG is a window function that SQLite supports from 3.25; older libraries do not recognise it, which is why setup prints sqlite3.sqlite_version. Running search before load gives 'no such table: events' instead.

2.q: Why do the fault drills feed their damaged datasets through exactly the same minisiem.py load step as the clean data?
options: Because the generator cannot produce faulty data, so a different loader is not available
Because the same loader is faster, which keeps the drills within the lab's time budget
Because a different loader would detect the faults automatically and spoil the exercise
Because the aim is to test whether the health checks notice problems, not to test a different pipeline
2.explanation: The drills damage the input while keeping the pipeline unchanged, so any result shows whether the checks themselves notice the fault; a check never seen to fire is an assumption. The plain loader does not detect faults, which is part of the lesson.

2.q: In Drill A's chart, WS-104 has no proxy events at 07 and 08 UTC. What should the analyst check first to tell a switched-off host from a pipeline problem?
options: Whether the proxy's events from other workstations also stopped in those two hours
Whether WS-104's Windows logon and Sysmon events also stopped in the same period
Whether the dataset hash still matches the one recorded in step 1
Whether the duplicates query finds repeated WS-104 events at 06 UTC
2.explanation: If the host's other telemetry also stopped, it was probably off; if it continued, the proxy configuration or relay path for that host is suspect. Other workstations' proxy events only show the problem is not proxy-wide, which the per-host view already implies.

2.q: The lab's silence check uses the last event in the dataset, 13:33Z, as its reference time. Why must a production silence check use the current time instead?
options: If the whole pipeline stops, the latest stored event stops advancing too, so every source looks recently active
The latest stored event is always in local time, so it cannot be compared with UTC timestamps
julianday() works only with the current time and returns NULL for stored timestamps
Using the latest event would double-count sources that sent several events in the final minute
2.explanation: Measuring silence against the newest stored event cannot detect a total stop, since the reference freezes with the data; 'now' keeps advancing and exposes it. julianday() accepts stored ISO timestamps, as the lab's own query shows.

3.q: Banyan adds a second firewall model and points it at the syslog input already used by the first firewall. Its events are stored, but a rule that searches the firewall index for blocked connections never returns them. What is the most likely cause?
options: The new device inherited the shared input's default source type and index
The new device's events were dropped by an ingest-time filter on the input
The new device sends over UDP, so its events were lost before they arrived
The new device's events are still waiting in the indexing refresh interval
3.explanation: An input applies its default source type and index to everything that arrives on it, so a new device on a shared port is labelled and routed as the old one, with the wrong time rules and container. A drop filter would mean the events were never stored, but here they are present.

3.q: An analyst knows a server sent authentication events at about 09:30 today, but a search of 09:00-10:00 returns none. Searching all time finds them, with ingest time 09:30 today and event time in 2019. What does this pattern indicate?
options: The events were routed to an index the analyst has no permission to read
The indexing layer delayed the events beyond the search window and applied a default event time when the new index was made available
The events were filed by a wrong or misread timestamp from the source side
The events were duplicated upstream and the copies replaced the originals
3.explanation: The events arrived on time (ingest time 09:30) but were filed under a wrong event time, from a bad source clock or a timestamp the SIEM misread, so a search of the right window cannot find them. An access problem would hide them from the all-time search as well.

3.q: Events from twenty branch routers are relayed through one central syslog server to the SIEM. Every event shows the same value in the host field. What explains this?
options: The routers share one source type, which overwrites the host label
The SIEM recorded the relay as host instead of reading it from the message
The relay merges events from all routers into a single multi-line record
The routers are synchronised to the same clock, and SIEM host attribution treats matching clock sources as a shared device identity
3.explanation: For relayed data the sender the SIEM sees is the relay, so unless the ingestion layer takes the host name from inside each message, every event is labelled with the relay's name. A shared source type sets parsing rules, not the host label.

3.q: A source averages 1,000 events per second with an average event size of 800 bytes. Approximately how much raw data per day will it add before indexing overhead or replication?
options: About 0.8 GB per day
About 6.9 GB per day
About 86.4 GB per day
About 69.1 GB per day
3.explanation: 1,000 x 800 bytes = 800,000 bytes per second; multiplied by 86,400 seconds this is about 69.1 x 10^9 bytes, or 69.1 GB per day. 86.4 GB/day is the figure for 2,000 EPS at 500 bytes, not this source.

3.q: An application's audit records are written as several records per block. A threshold rule counting failed logons from it fires far less often than the application's own report suggests it should. Which ingestion fault best explains the under-count?
options: The breaking rule splits each record into several one-line events
The breaking rule merges several real records into one stored event
The input truncates each record at the platform's maximum event size
The routing rule sends the records to a cheaper, slower storage tier
3.explanation: If the breaking rule merges several records into one stored event, a count-based rule sees one event where several logons failed, so it under-counts. Splitting records would produce more events, not fewer, and tiering affects search speed, not counts.

3.q: In Splunk, events from a newly onboarded source land in the correct index but are cut in the middle of records and carry wrong _time values. Which single setting most likely explains both symptoms?
options: The sourcetype assigned to the data, which selects breaking and time rules
The index assigned to the data, which selects its retention and access
The host value assigned to the data, which selects the relay to trust
The _indextime recorded for the data, which selects the search window
3.explanation: In Splunk the source type selects the line-breaking and timestamp rules, so a wrong source type corrupts both at once. The index is correct here and governs retention and access, not how events are broken or timed.

3.q: Proxy logs make up most of Banyan's ingest volume and the finance team wants costs cut, but beaconing detection relies on every proxy record. Which option reduces cost while keeping every record available to an investigator?
options: Aggregate the proxy logs into hourly request counts per host
Drop proxy requests to well-known content delivery networks
Trim the URL and user-agent fields from every proxy record
Route the proxy logs to a cheaper storage tier with slower search
3.explanation: Moving data to a cheaper tier keeps every record and only slows searching, the lowest-risk option. Aggregation destroys the per-request timing that beaconing detection needs, and dropping or trimming permanently removes evidence.

3.q: Rendered Windows events include a long block of descriptive text that is identical in every event of the same ID. Which volume-reduction step targets this with the least loss of evidence?
options: Aggregating the events into counts per event ID per host per hour
Drop the event IDs that take the most space and keep full descriptions for every other event type in the channel
Trimming the repeated description while keeping the structured fields
Routing all rendered Windows events to an archive-only storage tier
3.explanation: Removing repeated boilerplate while keeping structured fields cuts size without removing what detections use. Aggregation and dropping lose individual events, and an archive-only tier keeps everything but makes it hard to use for detection.

3.q: During a cost review an engineer proposes an ingest-time rule that drops all PowerShell Operational events because they are 'noisy'. What is the most defensible way to handle the proposal?
options: Treat it as a detection change: list dependent rules, assign an owner and review date
Approve the drop if a temporary recovery buffer keeps rejected events for seven days, without checking the rules that consume them
Approve it if the endpoint agent still keeps the events in its local event log
Treat it as housekeeping and record it in the SIEM platform's change log only
3.explanation: A drop rule removes evidence for every future detection and investigation; this one would also remove script-block events recording an intruder's commands. It must be decided per event type with dependent detections, an owner and a review date. Local logs on endpoints roll over and are not centrally searchable.

3.q: After reloading the Banyan dataset, a health query returns total 341 and distinct_raw 340 from SELECT COUNT(*) total, COUNT(DISTINCT raw) distinct_raw FROM events. What does this show?
options: One event failed to parse and was stored twice, once raw and once parsed
One event was stored twice because the ingestion layer does not de-duplicate
One event was dropped and replaced with a placeholder row by the loader
One event's raw text was truncated at the maximum event size and split
3.explanation: Two rows share identical raw text, so one event was stored twice. load() has no de-duplication, so a duplicate line, as at-least-once delivery can produce, is stored and counted. A truncated and split event would give two different raw values, not identical ones.

3.q: In a scratch copy of the kit, one truncated JSON line is inserted into banyan_events.jsonl. After load raises a JSONDecodeError, a count of the events table returns 0, although the file has 340 valid lines. Why is the table empty?
options: SQLite rolls back the whole transaction when any inserted row is invalid
The idx_ts index cannot be built when one row has no timestamp value
The table is dropped first and all lines are parsed before any insert
The search command refuses to read a table left by an incomplete load
3.explanation: load() runs DROP TABLE IF EXISTS first, then parses every line into a list in memory before inserting, so an exception on one line aborts the load after the old data is already gone. No row was ever inserted, so there was nothing for SQLite to roll back.

3.q: A threat model notes that anyone able to write to an upstream log file can insert one malformed record into a feed. Which ingestion property most directly prevents this from blinding the SOC to the whole feed?
options: Recording ingest time beside event time on every stored event
De-duplicating events on a stable identifier before they are written
Routing the feed to a container with restricted search access
Quarantining and counting bad records while ingesting the rest
3.explanation: Isolation contains a fault to the one bad record: it is quarantined, tagged and counted while the rest of the feed keeps flowing. Without it, all-or-nothing ingestion is a denial-of-service condition. De-duplication improves count accuracy but does nothing for malformed input.

3.q: In minisiem, logon_type and the VPN country are present in the dataset but are not among the twelve stored columns. What is the practical consequence for a detection rule that needs them?
options: The rule must extract them from raw at search time, which is slower and fragile
The rule cannot use either field because a value without a dedicated column is discarded before the original event can be searched
The rule can use them directly, because SQLite creates columns on first use
The rule must wait for a reload, because raw is only populated on request
3.explanation: The fields survive only inside the raw column, so a rule must pull them out with json_extract at search time, which is slower and easier to get wrong. They are not discarded, precisely because the original line was kept.

3.q: The minisiem volume query shows the proxy producing about 83 per cent of stored bytes while Sysmon events are the largest on average. Before trimming proxy data, what should the SOC establish first?
options: Whether Sysmon events could be trimmed instead because they are larger
Which detections, such as beaconing or large uploads, depend on proxy fields
Whether the proxy can send its events in a more compact binary format
Which proxy users generate the most requests so they can be excluded
3.explanation: High-volume network data often feeds important detections, so any reduction must start by asking which rules and investigations use it. Trimming the largest events per record ignores that proxy data dominates total volume, and excluding heavy users removes the very activity beaconing produces.

3.q: A covered entity in India routes its VPN logs into a container with a 30-day retention because the container is cheap. Why is this routing decision a compliance problem and not just a storage choice?
options: The DPDP Act 2023 forbids storing VPN logs outside a restricted container
MITRE ATT&CK T1562 requires authentication logs to be kept for one year
CERT-In's 2022 directions require ICT logs to be kept for a rolling 180 days
ISO 27001 requires every security log to be kept in a hot searchable tier
3.explanation: The container carries the retention period, and CERT-In's April 2022 directions require covered entities to keep ICT system logs for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction, so routing a regulated source to 30-day storage breaks that duty. T1562 is an adversary technique, not a retention rule.

3.q: A platform team moves Windows Security events from index wineventlog to a new index win_security to separate retention. Nothing errors, but several rules stop producing alerts. What most likely happened?
options: The new index has a shorter refresh interval, so events arrive too quickly
The new index inherited a different source type, breaking timestamp rules
The rules still name the old index, so they now search an empty container
The new index restricts access, so rules run as the analyst cannot read it
3.explanation: Detection rules usually name the container they search, so when routing changes and the rules do not, they search where the data no longer is and fall silent without any error. Changing the index does not by itself change the source type or its time rules.

3.q: A VPN appliance buffers events during an outage and delivers a two-hour batch late. The SIEM stores only event time. What can the SOC not determine as a result?
options: Whether the batch's events occurred during the outage window
Whether a correlation rule ran before the batch's events had arrived
Whether the batch's events can be searched by their original time
Whether the late records were assigned to the expected source type when the collector sent the queued batch to the SIEM
3.explanation: Without ingest time a late batch looks identical to a timely one, so the SOC cannot measure lag or tell whether a rule evaluated its window before all events arrived. Event time still places the events correctly in time and still allows searches by when they happened.

3.q: A SIEM's syslog input accepts UDP from any address on the internal network. A red-team report shows forged events planted in it from a test workstation. Which control best addresses the weakness?
options: Authenticate the input with TLS client certificates and restrict which networks reach it
Raise the input's maximum event size so forged records are split and easier to spot
Route the input's events to a restricted container that only the SOC can search
Record ingest time on the input so that forged events show an unusual lag value
3.explanation: Forged events succeed because the input accepts anyone who can reach it; authenticating senders and restricting the network, plus alerting on unexpected senders, closes that gap. Restricting who can search the data does nothing to stop forged data being written.

3.q: Source-health monitoring alerts when any source's event count drops sharply, and nothing else. Which ingestion attack does this configuration fail to detect?
options: An intruder stopping the endpoint agent on a compromised server
An administrator deleting the input that receives firewall events
A flood of junk events that exhausts licence and delays real events
A routing change that makes one event type disappear from its index
3.explanation: Flooding raises volume, so monitoring that only watches for falls misses it while the backlog delays the events that matter and the licence quota drains. A stopped agent, a deleted input or a routing change that removes an event type all reduce volume and would be caught.

3.q: A health check compares event time with ingest time. Several events from one host carry event times three days after their ingest times. How should the SOC treat this?
options: As normal lag, since buffered events always arrive with later timestamps
As expected, because ingest time is assigned before the event is created
As harmless, because the events are still searchable within all-time scope
As a red flag for a wrong clock or deliberate time manipulation to investigate
3.explanation: An event cannot be ingested before it happened, so a negative gap means either a faulty clock or timestamps set to file events where nobody looks; both deserve investigation. Normal lag produces event times earlier than ingest times, not later.

3.q: During onboarding of a new EDR feed, the engineer wants to prove that no events are being silently lost between source and SIEM. Which check gives that assurance most directly?
options: For a fixed window, compare the source's sent count with the SIEM's stored count
For a fixed window, compare the stored count from the new endpoint feed with the same window on the preceding business day
For a sample of events, compare the host field with the source's own host name
For a sample of events, compare event time with the source's own system clock
3.explanation: Reconciling what the source says it sent against what the SIEM holds for the same window directly measures loss. Comparing with yesterday only shows a change in volume, and host and time checks test labelling, not completeness.

3.q: During a large incident the SIEM is under heavy load. A forwarder confirms delivery of a critical event, but an analyst's search run seconds later does not return it. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The event was delivered but routed to a container the analyst cannot read
The event is stored but not yet searchable because indexing has lagged
The event was rejected by the input because it exceeded the size limit
The event was de-duplicated against an earlier copy and discarded
3.explanation: Indexing is not instantaneous: new data becomes searchable after a refresh interval, and that delay grows under heavy load, so a delivered event can be briefly unsearchable. A rejected or discarded event would not resolve itself, while this one appears once indexing catches up.

3.q: minisiem's load() creates only one index, idx_ts on the ts column. Why is a time index the first choice for almost every SIEM store?
options: Because event time is the only field present in every source type
Because SQLite requires an index on a time column before inserts
Because almost every search is bounded by a time range
Because indexing by time makes duplicate events easy to remove
3.explanation: SIEM searches are almost always limited to a time window, so organising and indexing by time lets the engine skip everything outside it. SQLite requires no index at all, and a time index does nothing to identify duplicates.

3.q: An analyst used to Splunk's _indextime is investigating ingestion lag in Elastic data that follows the Elastic Common Schema. Which field holds the comparable value?
options: @timestamp
@timestamp, the mapped occurrence time
event.dataset
event.ingested
3.explanation: The Elastic Common Schema defines event.ingested for the time the event reached the pipeline, the counterpart of Splunk's _indextime. @timestamp is the event time, and TimeGenerated is Microsoft Sentinel's event-time column.

3.q: Banyan's proxy logs reveal which websites individual staff visit. The SOC needs them for detection, and the privacy officer cites the DPDP Act 2023. Which ingestion design best serves both needs?
options: Drop the URL field at ingest time so no browsing history is ever stored
Route proxy logs to a container whose search access is limited to the SOC
Route the proxy logs to a shared default index and rely on each analyst to limit searches to records relevant to their own team
Aggregate proxy logs into daily totals so individual visits are not kept
3.explanation: Separate containers allow access to sensitive data to be limited to those who need it, which supports DPDP safeguard duties while keeping the evidence. Dropping URLs or aggregating would protect privacy but destroy the detail that detections such as beaconing need.

3.q: A rule searching for source.ip = 203.0.113.66 misses firewall events. Inspecting one of them shows the raw text contains SRC=203.0.113.66 and the stored fields include src=203.0.113.66 but no source.ip. Where does the fault lie?
options: In parsing, because the address was never extracted from the raw text
In normalisation, because the value was extracted under another name
In ingestion, because the event was routed to the wrong container
In event breaking, because the address was split into another event
3.explanation: The value was extracted, so the parser did its job; it was simply stored as src instead of the common name source.ip, which is a normalisation problem. A parsing failure would leave no extracted address field at all.

3.q: A firmware update makes a firewall insert a new IFACE=eth0 token near the start of every message. Which parser design is most likely to keep extracting SRC, DST and DPT correctly?
options: A position-based dissect parser that assumes each token remains in its original place after a firmware upgrade
A regex that captures the fourth, fifth and sixth words of the message
A delimited parser that treats each space-separated token as a column
A key-value parser that looks up each value by its label after splitting
3.explanation: A label-based key-value parser finds values by key, so inserted or reordered tokens do not matter. All three positional designs, including dissect, assume a fixed layout and shift or fail when a token is inserted before the values they want.

3.q: A parser's pattern has no ^ or $ anchors. It occasionally produces plausible-looking source and destination fields from log lines of a completely different program. What change addresses the root cause?
options: Anchor the pattern so it must match the whole record or nothing
Make the quantifiers greedy so the pattern consumes the whole line
Move the pattern into grok so it uses tested named sub-patterns
Add a type conversion so that extracted ports become integers
3.explanation: An unanchored pattern can match a fragment of a line that only resembles the expected format, producing wrong but plausible fields; anchoring forces a full match or none. Grok sub-patterns improve readability but still match fragments if the overall pattern is unanchored.

3.q: A parser uses the pattern .*SRC=(\S+) to extract the source address. An application field that users can control is logged after the header, and one record contains the text SRC=198.51.100.9 inside it. What will the parser capture?
options: The first SRC= value, because regex engines stop at the first match
Neither value, because two SRC= tokens make the pattern fail to match
The last SRC= value, because the greedy .* consumes as much as it can
Both values, because the capture group repeats for each occurrence
3.explanation: The greedy .* takes as much text as possible and gives back only what is needed, so the group captures the last SRC= occurrence, here the forged one in the user-controlled field. That is why attacker-influenced text must never be able to override header fields.

3.q: A parsing worker's CPU suddenly stays at 100 per cent and the feed backs up. The trigger is one very long user-agent value. Which parser property is the most likely cause?
options: A greedy capture that stores the whole user-agent value in a single field
A key-value split that treats each space in the user-agent as a new token
A missing type conversion that leaves the user-agent stored as a string
A pattern with nested quantifiers that backtracks exponentially on that input
3.explanation: Nested or overlapping quantifiers can take exponential time on certain inputs (catastrophic backtracking, CWE-1333), stalling a worker. Specific character classes, anchoring and parsing timeouts are the defences. A greedy capture is linear work and does not explain a stalled worker.

3.q: A source's records have a fixed header (time, host, program) followed by a message whose tokens vary between event types. Which parsing design best balances speed and robustness?
options: Dissect for the fixed header, then a key-value or regex step for the message
Dissect for the whole record, declaring every token in one fixed order
One regular expression for the complete record, with optional groups to describe every possible message type
A JSON decoder for the header, then a CSV reader for the variable message
3.explanation: Dissect is fast and readable but only suits a layout that never varies, so it fits the fixed header, while a key-value or regex step handles the variable message. Using dissect for the whole record would break on the first event type whose tokens differ.

3.q: A key-value parser splits on spaces and then on '='. A record contains msg=user login failed, and the stored msg field holds only 'user'. What went wrong?
options: The parser split each token on its last '=' instead of its first
The value contained spaces and was not quoted and handled as one value
The key msg appears only in some records, so the parser skipped it
The parser converted the value to an integer and truncated the rest
3.explanation: Key-value parsing breaks on values containing the separator; an unquoted value with spaces is split into several tokens, leaving only the first word under msg. The source must quote such values and the parser must honour the quoting. Splitting on '=' is unrelated to the space problem.

3.q: A DNS log is parsed with line.split(','). Occasionally the user and query-name fields hold the wrong values. Raw records show a quoted field containing a comma. What is the correct fix?
options: Split on the comma only a fixed number of times from the left
Replace every comma inside the line with a space before splitting
Switch to a key-value parser that splits each token on '='
Use a real CSV reader that understands quoting before unpacking
3.explanation: A naive split ignores quoting, so a comma inside a quoted value shifts every later column; a real CSV reader such as Python's csv.reader handles quoting correctly. Limiting the number of splits still breaks when the quoted comma falls before a later column.

3.q: VPN events arrive as JSON and decode without error. A rule written as result == "success" never fires, although many logons succeed. What does this illustrate?
options: Structured formats remove pattern matching but still need interpretation
Structured JSON records must be matched by a second positional parser because standard decoders discard the original field values
JSON decoding fails silently on nested objects and drops the result key
Structured formats need anchored regexes to locate keys in the document
3.explanation: Decoding gives fields for free, but someone still has to know what they mean and how values are written; the VPN writes SUCCESS in upper case, so a rule expecting lower case never matches. The decoder did not lose anything.

3.q: After a parser change, a firewall source starts storing destination ports of 99999 and timestamps in 1970. How should these values be interpreted?
options: As evidence of port scanning from hosts with misconfigured clocks
As normal edge values that type conversion stores without comment
As signs of a parsing or source fault that validation should flag
As placeholders the parser inserted for fields that were missing
3.explanation: Type conversion is the first validation: a port above 65535 is impossible and an epoch-zero date usually means a failed time extraction, so both point to a parser or source fault. Treating them as attack evidence would build conclusions on corrupt fields.

3.q: A firewall record matches the parser's header pattern and most fields are extracted, but SRC, the field this source's rules depend on, is absent. Following the decision pipeline in the lesson, how should the event be stored?
options: Discarded, because an event without a source address cannot be detected on
Tagged _parse_failure and stored with only its original text
Stored as a clean event with source.ip set to 0.0.0.0 as a placeholder
Tagged _parse_warning and stored with the fields that were found
3.explanation: The record was understood but is incomplete, so it is stored with its extracted fields and a _parse_warning tag. _parse_failure is for records whose header does not match at all, and inventing a placeholder address would create false matches.

3.q: To reduce noise, an engineer proposes discarding any event that a parser cannot interpret. From a security standpoint, what is the strongest objection?
options: Unparsed events must be retained to calculate future platform licensing costs for all sources
An adversary could hide activity simply by making records fail parsing
Discarding events breaks the time index for the rest of the feed
Unparsed events are the only ones that carry the original raw text
3.explanation: If unparsable events vanish, any record malformed enough to fail parsing disappears, giving an adversary a way to hide; keeping and counting them preserves the evidence and exposes the attempt. Raw text should be kept on every event, not only unparsed ones.

3.q: The lesson's harness reports FAIL with TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable for three of five lines fed to the demo parser. What does this error tell the analyst?
options: The pattern did not match and the code indexed the result without checking
The pattern matched but one capture group returned an empty string value
The timestamp conversion failed because the year was missing from the line
The JSON output step failed because a field contained an unsupported type
3.explanation: re.match returns None when the pattern does not match, and the demo uses m[1], m[2] and so on without checking, so indexing None raises this TypeError. The message is the same for every failure, which is why it says nothing about which assumption broke.

3.q: With the kit's demo firewall parser in production, which kind of activity against internal hosts would the SOC be blind to, based on the harness results?
options: RDP connection attempts arriving from external addresses on port 3389
Drops logged on days of the month with two digits, such as 13 November
ICMP ping sweeps, because those drops carry TYPE and CODE but no DPT
TCP drops logged with the standard SRC, DST, PROTO and DPT key order
3.explanation: The demo pattern requires DPT=, and ICMP drops have TYPE and CODE instead, so every ICMP drop fails to parse and a ping-sweep rule sees nothing. The original RDP line and the two-digit day both parsed successfully in the harness.

3.q: The tolerant header pattern accepts an optional log prefix with (?:\[[^\]]*\] )?. Why is [^\]]* used inside the brackets instead of .*?
options: Because .* cannot match the hyphen inside a prefix such as [FW-IN]
Because [^\]]* cannot run past the closing bracket of the prefix
Because .* would create a capture group that shifts the later fields
Because [^\]]* converts the prefix into a separate named field
3.explanation: The negated class stops at the first closing bracket, so the optional group matches exactly the prefix and cannot swallow the action and message that follow; it is also cheaper to evaluate. .* inside a non-capturing group would not shift group numbers, but it could consume far more than the prefix.

3.q: parse_kv.py builds its key-value dictionary with tok.split("=", 1). What does the second argument achieve?
options: It skips tokens that contain no equals sign at all
It keeps only the first token that contains an equals sign
It converts each value to an integer where possible
It splits on the first '=' only, so values may contain '='
3.explanation: maxsplit=1 splits each token at its first equals sign only, so a value that itself contains '=' (for example a URL query string) stays intact. Skipping tokens without '=' is done by the separate if "=" in tok filter.

3.q: An ICMP drop has no destination port. A colleague suggests the parser store destination.port = 0 so that every firewall event has the same fields. Why is this a poor choice?
options: An invented value creates false matches for rules and searches on that port
Port 0 is outside the valid port range and is rejected by type conversion
Port 0 forces the event to be tagged _parse_failure by field validation
An invented value prevents the event from being re-parsed after a fix
3.explanation: A missing port is absent, not zero; storing 0 makes ICMP drops match any search or rule that looks at port 0 and corrupts port statistics. The tolerant parser correctly adds destination.port only when DPT is present. Port 0 is a valid integer, so conversion would not reject it.

3.q: parse_dns_csv checks len(row) != 6 before unpacking the row into six variables. What would happen on a five-column line if that check were removed?
options: The last variable would silently receive an empty string
The csv module would pad the row with None to six values
The unpacking would raise an exception instead of tagging the event
The parser would silently shift the values into incorrect fields, then retain the row without recording a parsing error
3.explanation: Unpacking five values into six names raises a ValueError, turning one short line into a crash rather than a tagged _parse_failure with an error message. Python neither pads the row nor shifts values silently.

3.q: A SOC wants one metric that shows within an hour when a vendor change has broken a parser. Which metric best fits?
options: Total events stored per source type per day
_parse_failure events per source type per hour
Average event size per source type per hour
The daily count of detection alerts triggered in each source type
3.explanation: Tagged failures counted per source type per hour rise sharply when a format changes, showing which source broke and when. Total event counts may stay unchanged when parsing fails, because the events are still stored, just without fields.

3.q: In the course case study, a VPN vendor changed its log format; the parser kept matching but stopped extracting user names, and brute-force rules were silent for a month. Which monitoring would most likely have caught this on the first day?
options: A source-availability panel that alerts when the VPN appliance stops producing events for any reason
An alert when the VPN source's daily ingest volume doubles
An alert when the VPN source's ingest lag exceeds an hour
A field-completeness panel tracking user.name on VPN events
3.explanation: Events kept arriving and parsing, so volume and lag looked normal; only the share of VPN events with a populated user.name changed, which is exactly what a field-completeness panel shows. A silence alert never fires because the source never went quiet.

3.q: A _parse_failure appears in production for a new record variant, and the parser is fixed. What should happen to that record to prevent the same silent break recurring?
options: Add it, with its expected output, to the parser's golden sample set
Delete it, since the fixed parser will handle future records anyway
Keep it only in the quarantine container until the retention expires
Add a drop rule for its exact text so it cannot trigger failures again
3.explanation: Adding every production failure to the golden samples, with its expected output, means every later parser change or upgrade is tested against it. Deleting or dropping it removes evidence and leaves no regression test.

3.q: A parser bug stored a week of firewall events without fields. After the fix, the team reviews that week for missed detections. What design decision makes this review possible?
options: Recording ingest time beside event time on every stored event
Selecting the parser by explicit source type at ingestion
Keeping the original raw record on every event, parsed or not
Running the parser's golden samples on every platform upgrade
3.explanation: Because the raw event was kept, the faulty week's events can be re-parsed or re-ingested and the rules re-run. Golden samples prevent future breaks but cannot recover fields for events already stored without them.

3.q: A web proxy logs the client's user-agent string inside a free-text message after its own header fields. A tester shows that a crafted user-agent can change the stored client address. Which defence addresses this CWE-117 weakness most directly?
options: Anchor the user-agent pattern at the end of the line with a $ symbol
Never let a value from a free-text field overwrite a header field
Convert the user-agent to lower case before running the parser
Raise the maximum event size so the crafted text is not truncated
3.explanation: Log injection works when attacker-controlled text inside a field is read as another field; extracting header fields first, taking attacker-influenced fields last by explicit delimiters and never letting them overwrite header values prevents it. Anchoring alone does not stop a greedy pattern picking up injected keys.

3.q: The parser health dashboard shows a sudden burst of _parse_failure events from a single workstation, while all other hosts of the same source type parse normally. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Suppress the host's failures until the vendor publishes a new log format
Re-route the host's events to a cheaper tier until the burst subsides
Rewrite the parser to accept any record from that host without checks
Investigate the host, since deliberate parse evasion is one explanation
3.explanation: A vendor format change would affect every host of that source type; failures confined to one host may mean someone is crafting records to defeat rules keyed on parsed fields, so the host deserves investigation. Suppressing or accepting everything would remove the signal.
