3.q: The lesson runs parse_kv.py with python -I but runs parse_harness.py without it. Why does the harness need to run without isolated mode?
options: Isolated mode drops the script's folder from the import path, blocking normalise_demo
Isolated mode disables exception handling, so the try/except block would not work
Isolated mode prevents scripts from printing JSON output to the terminal
Isolated mode forbids importing standard-library modules such as json and re
3.explanation: -I removes the script's own directory from Python's import path, and the harness must import normalise_demo.py from the same folder; parse_kv.py imports nothing local, so it can run isolated. Isolated mode does not affect exception handling or standard-library imports.

3.q: Before normalisation was introduced, an analyst searched src_ip = "203.0.113.66" and got only firewall drops, although the same address had logged in to the VPN. What best explains the result?
options: The VPN stored the address under its own field name, so the search silently skipped it
The VPN login was rejected at parse time because its JSON carried a UTC timestamp
The firewall events were indexed first, and the search discarded later VPN events as duplicate records from the same address
The search engine discards duplicate addresses that appear in more than one source
3.explanation: Each source was parsed correctly but used its own name (clientIP for the VPN), so a search on one name returns a partial answer that looks complete. A UTC timestamp is not a parse failure; the VPN already logged in UTC and was passed through.

3.q: A new engineer onboards the VPN and maps its clientIP field to destination.ip instead of source.ip. Nothing errors. What is the most likely security consequence?
options: VPN events fail schema validation and are routed to the pipeline error index
Rules that watch source.ip for sprayers stop seeing VPN attacks, with no alert raised
The firewall begins to drop VPN traffic because the two sources now share one field
Only dashboards break; correlation rules read the raw event and are not affected
3.explanation: A mapping error is a silent detection gap: the address is stored under the wrong role, so any rule keyed on source.ip simply never matches VPN events. Rules run on normalised fields, not raw text, so they are affected, which is why mappings must be reviewed and tested like code.

3.q: The firewall line reads 'Nov  3 12:16:21 fw01 ...' and the stored event shows @timestamp 2026-11-03T06:46:21Z. What did the mapping have to rely on to produce that value?
options: The VPN event's timestamp, used as a reference to estimate the firewall's offset
The time at which the SIEM received the line, substituted for the event time
Configuration knowledge that the device runs in IST and of which year it was
The syslog header's embedded zone marker, which the parser converted to UTC
3.explanation: The line has neither year nor zone, so the parser applied the device's configured zone (IST, UTC+05:30) and the current year. Classic syslog headers carry no zone marker, and substituting receive time would replace event time with ingest time.

3.q: In the normalised firewall event, DPT=3389 is stored as the integer 3389 rather than the string "3389". Which query does this choice protect?
options: A free-text search for the word 3389 anywhere in the raw event
A grouping of events by host.name for a daily dashboard panel
A lookup of the destination address in a geolocation database
A filter for destination ports in a numeric range such as 1-1023
3.explanation: Type normalisation lets range and numeric comparisons work; as strings, '3389' would sort and compare as text. Free-text search on the raw event works either way, so it is not the query the integer type protects.

3.q: Ten Windows logon events in the lab hold '-' in src_ip. A rule groups failed logons by src_ip and alerts when one address exceeds a threshold. What is the risk if the mapping leaves '-' as it is?
options: The dash is treated as one very busy address, creating a false cluster of events
SQLite rejects the dash in a text column, so those ten events are never loaded
The classifier treats the dash as a routable external address because it cannot match one of the configured internal prefixes
The rule ignores them, since a dash is read by SQL as a null value by default
3.explanation: A placeholder stored as a value makes unrelated interactive logons look like one source address. SQL does not treat '-' as null; it is a normal string, which is why the mapping should convert placeholders to a true null.

3.q: In the Banyan data, proxy src_ip values are always 10.40.0.x while VPN src_ip values are external. A rule says 'alert on many failures from one src_ip'. What should the rule author conclude?
options: The proxy values are mapped wrongly and should be moved to destination.ip
Both are the initiator, but one address means very different things on each source
The VPN values are unreliable because external addresses are always behind NAT
The rule is safe on both sources, since normalisation has made the meanings identical
3.explanation: Both fields correctly hold the initiator, but an internal proxy client or NAT address may be shared by many people, while one external VPN address may be one attacker. Normalisation fixes names, not the need to know each source; the proxy mapping itself is correct.

3.q: One user appears as DIVYA in Windows, BANYAN\divya in another log and divya@banyan.example from the identity provider. A search for user = 'divya' finds only one form. What is the mature mapping fix?
options: Keep all three forms and ask analysts to list every variant in each query
Replace user names with numeric account IDs and drop the original strings
Normalise case and move the domain into its own field such as user.domain
Store the identity provider form only and discard the Windows user fields
3.explanation: Normalising case and splitting the domain gives one person one searchable identity while keeping the domain information. Asking analysts to list variants pushes the problem back onto every query and rule author, which is exactly what normalisation exists to avoid.

3.q: The lab's field coverage matrix shows host empty for VPN, src_ip empty for Sysmon and outcome empty for proxy and Sysmon. Which field can a rule join on across all four sources?
options: host, because every event is observed on some machine
src_ip, because every network event has an initiator
outcome, because every source records success or failure
user, because all four sources fill it in every event
3.explanation: The matrix shows user filled by proxy, Sysmon, VPN and Windows, so it is the only identifier available everywhere. host looks universal in principle, but the VPN record belongs to a person and carries no host.

3.q: A rule correlating a suspicious VPN login with later endpoint activity 'on the same host.name' has never fired, even in a test of the scenario. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: VPN events carry no host; add the user's primary host through identity enrichment
The VPN logs in UTC while endpoints log locally; convert the VPN to local time
Endpoint events are too many to join; sample them before the rule is executed
host.name is case sensitive; compare both sides in upper case to fix the join
3.explanation: The coverage matrix shows host empty for every VPN event, so a host join can never match; enrichment such as triage.py's PRIMARY_HOST fills the gap. Converting to local time would break correlation, since every source should be in UTC.

3.q: The coverage matrix query uses COUNT(host), COUNT(user) and so on, grouped by source. Why does this produce the information the matrix needs?
options: COUNT(column) counts distinct values, showing how varied each field is
COUNT(column) counts only non-null values, showing which sources fill a field
COUNT(column) counts rows in the index, showing which fields are searchable
COUNT(column) counts parse failures, showing which fields need new mappings
3.explanation: In SQL, COUNT(column) ignores nulls, so comparing it with COUNT(*) per source shows how often each field is populated. Distinct counts would need COUNT(DISTINCT column) and would measure variety, not coverage.

3.q: A single rule filtering event.category: authentication AND event.outcome: failure returns failed logons from Windows, the VPN, a cloud identity provider and SSH. What makes this possible?
options: Each product writes the same event.action verb, which the rule matches
The SIEM translates the query into each vendor's own field names at run time
Categorisation fields take values from a small fixed set that mappings must use
The rule reads event.code, which holds one shared ID for every failed logon
3.explanation: ECS categorisation fields have fixed allowed values, so every source mapped to them can be queried by meaning. event.action keeps each source's own verb and event.code each source's own identifier, so neither is shared across products.

3.q: An administrator account 'ravi' creates a new account 'svc_update'. In an ECS-style mapping, how should the two accounts be stored?
options: Both in user.name as a list, ordered by their appearance in the raw event
svc_update in user.name and ravi in a source-specific namespace field
ravi in host.name, since the action was performed on the admin's machine
ravi in user.* as the actor and svc_update in user.target.* as the affected account
3.explanation: ECS keeps the acting account in user.* and the affected account in user.target.*, so 'who did it' and 'who it was done to' never collide. Putting both in one field would make it impossible to tell actor from target in searches and rules.

3.q: An architect must decide when to add the geolocation and ASN of each external address seen at the VPN. Which choice best serves an investigation months later?
options: Enrich at ingestion and record the reference data version, so the context of that day survives
Enrich at search time, so every investigator always sees the most current location data
Skip enrichment and let analysts look addresses up by hand whenever an alert is opened
Enrich at search time and cache the result, so that repeated queries become faster
3.explanation: Geolocation and ASN describe the address at that moment and can change, so ingest-time enrichment with a record of the data version preserves what was true and what the analyst knew. Search-time lookup would show today's assignment, which may differ from the one at the time of the event.

3.q: A SOC enriches host ownership only at search time. Last week WS-104 was reissued to a new employee. What problem appears when the team reviews an incident on WS-104 from last month?
options: The old events are deleted, because their enrichment no longer matches the CMDB
The old activity appears to belong to the new owner, rewriting the history
The query fails, because the lookup table no longer contains the old owner
Nothing changes, because search-time enrichment is frozen when events arrive
3.explanation: Search-time enrichment joins current reference data, so historical events are shown with today's owner. It is ingest-time enrichment that freezes context at arrival, which is why ownership at the time of an incident may need to be captured at ingestion.

3.q: The kit's triage.py holds ASSETS, USERS and PRIMARY_HOST dictionaries and adds their facts to each rule hit without changing the events table. How should this enrichment be classified?
options: Ingest-time, because the dictionaries are loaded when minisiem loads events
Parse-time, because the facts are extracted from the raw JSON of each event
Search-time, because the lookups run when rules run and nothing is written back
Ingest-time, because each hit's context is fixed once the triage line is printed
3.explanation: The dictionaries are consulted when the rules are evaluated and the stored events stay unchanged, which is search-time enrichment. Ingest-time enrichment would write the context into the stored event when it arrived.

3.q: A team proposes enriching events with asset and identity context before mapping them to the common schema, to save a pipeline stage. What is the strongest objection?
options: Enrichment before normalisation makes events too large to store in the index
Enrichment sources only accept UTC times, which parsing has not yet produced
Asset and identity context must be retrieved at search time, since the collection pipeline cannot call a lookup before storing the record
Lookups would need one key per vendor field name instead of one normalised key
3.explanation: The asset lookup keys on host.name, identity on user.name and geo or intelligence on source.ip; before normalisation each lookup would have to know every vendor's name for those fields. Ingest-time enrichment in the pipeline is normal, so the third option is false.

3.q: During onboarding, a Windows-only field has no equivalent in the common schema and no current search uses it. What should the mapping do with it?
options: Keep it under a source-specific namespace or in the raw event for later use
Drop it, because unmapped fields add storage cost without detection value
Map it to the nearest common field, so that it becomes searchable everywhere
Copy it into event.action, which exists to hold source-specific information
3.explanation: Fields with no common name are kept under a namespace such as winlog.* or in the raw event, because the field nobody needs this year may be what an incident needs next year. Forcing it into the nearest common field would corrupt that field's meaning.

3.q: A manager says detection coverage is fine because 'we adopted ECS last quarter'. What is the most useful response?
options: Agree, because ECS field names guarantee that every source fills each field
Ask for a source-by-source audit of mappings, since the schema is only a vocabulary
Recommend replacing ECS with OCSF, which enforces mappings during ingestion
Agree, provided that the SIEM vendor certifies its own parsers for ECS output
3.explanation: A schema defines names; normalisation is the mapping of each source onto it, and that is where mistakes live, so mappings need auditing per source. Switching schemas does not remove the mapping work, and the lesson stresses that consistency matters more than which schema is chosen.

3.q: Pipeline monitoring shows that, overnight, the share of events with an empty user.name from the VPN rose from 0% to 95%, while event volume is unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Users have stopped logging in to the VPN and only health checks remain
The identity provider is down, so user enrichment could not be applied
The VPN vendor changed its log format, so the mapping no longer finds the user
The SIEM index is full, so it is truncating fields from incoming events
3.explanation: A sudden rise in empty key fields from one source with stable volume usually means a format change broke the parser or mapping. user.name comes from the event itself, not from enrichment, so an identity provider outage would not empty it.

3.q: Two products both expose a field called 'src'. In one it is the connecting client; in the other it is the appliance that generated the log. How should the mapping author avoid an error?
options: Map both to source.ip, since the schema defines src as the initiator in all cases
Map both to host.name, because the device name is the safer of the two meanings
Leave both unmapped and rely on full-text search of the raw events instead
Read each vendor's field documentation and test the mapping with known events
3.explanation: Mapping must follow meaning, not name: only documentation and test events reveal that one 'src' is the client and the other the reporting device. Mapping both to source.ip would put the appliance's address in the initiator role for one product.

3.q: A triage line shows 'host=WS-107 (sales laptop) user=gopal' for a VPN alert, although VPN events never carry a host. How should the analyst treat the host value?
options: As an inference from the user's primary host, to be confirmed before acting on it
As an observed fact, because the VPN concentrator recorded the client device name
As an error, because enrichment must never add fields the source did not provide
As proof of compromise of WS-107, because the alert has already linked the two
3.explanation: PRIMARY_HOST fills the gap from identity data, so WS-107 is an assumption about where gopal usually works, not a record of the connecting device. Adding context the source lacked is the purpose of enrichment, but good enrichment labels inferred context as inferred.

3.q: Months after onboarding, the team discovers that a proxy mapping swapped two fields. What makes it possible to correct historical events rather than only new ones?
options: The correlation engine stores every rule result, which can be replayed later
The raw event was kept beside the normalised fields, so history can be re-normalised
The coverage matrix records old values, so the swapped fields can be restored
The ingest-time enrichment saved a copy of each field before the mapping ran
3.explanation: Normalised fields are an interpretation; the raw record is the evidence and allows re-parsing and re-normalising after a mapping mistake. The coverage matrix only counts populated fields and holds no event values.

3.q: A SOC wants to enrich every event with each employee's department, manager, home address and salary band. Under the purpose-limitation principle of India's DPDP Act 2023, what is the sound approach?
options: Add all attributes, since data already held by HR may be reused for any purpose
Add no identity attributes at all, since any personal data in a SIEM is unlawful
Add only the attributes security decisions need and restrict who can view them
Add all attributes but hash them, so that analysts cannot read the raw values
3.explanation: Personal data should be processed for a specified purpose and limited to what it needs, so the SOC enriches with security-relevant attributes under access control and avoids turning the SIEM into general employee monitoring. Banning all identity context would remove information that triage genuinely needs.

3.q: Every source is stored in UTC except Windows, which was accidentally left in IST. A rule looks for a VPN success followed within 30 minutes by an account creation (4720). What happens to a real sequence of those two events?
options: It still matches, because the rule compares only the order of the two events
It matches twice, because the IST event is indexed under both of its times
It is rejected at ingestion, because mixed zones fail schema validation
It is missed, because the 4720 appears 5.5 hours later than it occurred
3.explanation: IST is UTC+05:30, so a Windows time stored as if it were UTC lands five and a half hours after the true moment, outside a 30-minute window. A wrong zone is stored silently, not rejected, which is why every source must be verified as UTC.

3.q: Some events fail processing in the ingest pipeline. Instead of dropping them, the pipeline stores them marked event.kind: pipeline_error. Why is this the better design?
options: The failures stay searchable and countable, so a broken source is noticed
The failures are automatically re-parsed by the SIEM with a fallback mapping
The failures are excluded from licensing, so ingest volume and cost are lower
The failures are treated as alerts, so every one is reviewed by an analyst
3.explanation: Marking rather than discarding failed events makes processing problems visible and measurable per source, instead of invisible gaps. Nothing in the marking itself re-parses events or turns them into analyst alerts; event.kind alert is a different value.

3.q: All six minisiem rules fired on the Banyan storyline. Which of them relates two different kinds of event to each other in time, making it correlation in the strict sense?
options: R2, which ties a VPN success to earlier failures from the same address
R5, which flags event 1102 because log clearing follows an intrusion
R1, which needs both a Word parent and a PowerShell child to be present
R4, which compares each upload's byte count against a fixed threshold
3.explanation: R2 joins two event types (failures and a success) on a shared address with an order condition. R1 checks two conditions, but both are fields of one process-start record, so it is still a single-event rule.

3.q: R2 counts COUNT(DISTINCT f.user) rather than COUNT(*) of failures before the success. Which situation does this choice prevent from firing the rule?
options: Eight accounts failing once each from one external address in a minute
One user mistyping a password ten times from the same address
A spray that continues against new accounts after the success
Five accounts failing from one address and then one succeeding
3.explanation: Counting distinct users separates a spray (many accounts, few tries each) from one person's repeated typos, which would give ten failures but only one distinct user. Eight accounts failing once each is exactly the spray the rule should catch.

3.q: R2 orders events with f.ts <= s.ts, comparing ts as text. Why does this give the correct order in the lab, and when would it silently fail?
options: SQLite converts text to dates automatically; it fails only if seconds are missing
The index idx_ts sorts by event time; it fails only when the index is rebuilt
UTC ISO 8601 strings sort in time order; mixed time zones would break it
Events are loaded in time order; it fails only if the file is shuffled first
3.explanation: Fixed-format UTC ISO 8601 timestamps sort lexically in chronological order, so text comparison works; a source left in local time would compare wrongly without any error. SQLite does not convert text to dates in a plain comparison.

3.q: R2 as written requires only that failures come at or before the success. On a year of production data, what is the main problem with this?
options: Failures that come after the success are counted twice in the result
Successes without any failures are reported as low-severity alerts
The distinct count stops working once more than one year is loaded
Failures from months earlier can join a success and raise false alerts
3.explanation: 'Before' is not a window: failures in January could join a success in November, giving false positives and a join that grows without limit. Failures after the success are discarded by f.ts <= s.ts, not double counted.

3.q: The last spray failure was at 06:42:49 and gopal's success at 06:46:00. Using the windowed R2 (julianday difference <= N/1440.0), what is the smallest whole-minute window N among these that still fires?
options: 4 minutes
3 minutes
2 minutes
10 minutes
3.explanation: The gap is 3 minutes 11 seconds, so a 3-minute window leaves every failure outside it and misses, while 4 minutes includes all eight. The 10-minute window also fires but is not the smallest; 2 minutes is the case the lesson shows missing.

3.q: A threshold rule fires on 5 or more distinct users failing from one address in clock-aligned ten-minute buckets. A spray of eight accounts runs from 06:48 to 06:52. What may happen, and why?
options: It fires twice, once for each bucket the eight failures touch
It may never fire, because the burst can split four and four across buckets
It fires once, because a tumbling window slides to cover the full burst
It fires late, because the first partial bucket remains open and is evaluated only after the hour closes
3.explanation: Tumbling buckets split a burst that straddles a boundary, so neither 06:40-06:50 nor 06:50-07:00 may reach five users. It is a sliding window, not a tumbling one, that moves with each event and avoids the boundary problem.

3.q: The cross-source query matches lower(p.parent_image) LIKE '%winword.exe%'. What would happen if lower() were removed and the pattern left in lower case?
options: Nothing, because LIKE in every SIEM is case-insensitive by definition
The query would also match WINWORD processes on unrelated hosts
It could miss the event, since the raw parent path is in capitals
The query would fail, because parent_image is not an indexed field
3.explanation: The raw path is WINWORD.EXE in capitals, and the lesson warns that a case-sensitive comparison would miss it, so case must be normalised or compared case-insensitively. Host scope is set by the join on host, not by the case of the pattern.

3.q: The combination query joins a Sysmon process start to proxy beacons and finds WS-104 with 12 beacons in 60 minutes. Why can these two sources be joined on host?
options: Sysmon events carry the proxy's URL, which identifies the requesting host
Both sources share src_ip, which minisiem converts to host at search time
The proxy records the process ID, which matches Sysmon's process start
Both Sysmon and the proxy fill the host field with the same host name
3.explanation: The field coverage matrix shows host populated by both Sysmon and the proxy, so the join key exists on both sides with one representation. Sysmon events in this dataset have no src_ip, so an address join would not work.

3.q: The VPN spray and gopal's login (06:42-06:46) overlap in time with the WS-104 intrusion. What may an analyst conclude from the data alone?
options: Nothing links them yet; they share no entity, so a link needs other evidence
Both belong to a single incident because they happened on the same morning and in the same network segment
The spray compromised WS-104, because divya was one of the sprayed accounts
They are unrelated, because VPN events cannot ever be correlated with hosts
3.explanation: Overlap in time without a shared entity is coincidence until enrichment or threat intelligence connects them. Divya's account failed in the spray but never succeeded from that address, and VPN events can be linked to hosts through enrichment, so the last option is too strong.

3.q: In the entity aggregation query, R3 fired twice for one account creation on WS-104. Why does the query count distinct rules per host rather than total hits?
options: Because SQLite cannot count rows that come from a UNION ALL subquery
Because repeated hits of one rule are weaker than hits from unrelated rules
Because R3 hits must be removed, since 4732 duplicates the 4720 event
Because counting hits would make WS-104 score lower than other hosts
3.explanation: One behaviour producing two hits adds little; four different rules on one host are independent lines of evidence. The R3 hits are not duplicates to delete: 4720 and 4732 record different steps, an account created and then added to a group.

3.q: A SOC with 300 rules plans to write a pairwise correlation rule for every pair of behaviours that might occur together. Why does entity risk aggregation usually scale better?
options: Pairwise rules cannot join events that come from two different log sources
Aggregation replaces the need for single-event rules, so fewer rules run
Each rule contributes to an entity's total, instead of one rule per pair
Aggregation needs no time period, so it never misses slow-moving attacks
3.explanation: Pairs grow quickly (six rules already give fifteen), while aggregation lets every rule add to the entity it names and alerts when one entity collects several. Aggregation depends on the single-event rules as inputs and still works within a period.

3.q: In production, a host's last Sysmon event is a suspicious PowerShell start at 06:14, while its proxy traffic continues until 12:32. How should an absence rule treat this?
options: Ignore it, because proxy activity proves the endpoint agent is still healthy
Raise it only at the end of the day, when the daily event totals are compared
Treat it as normal, because endpoint sources report far less often than proxies
Alert, because endpoint telemetry went quiet while the host stayed active
3.explanation: An absence rule compares each source's last-seen time, ideally per host, with its expected interval, and endpoint silence while the host is still active is exactly what it exists to catch. In the lab this is a generator artefact, but in production it could be telemetry being disabled.

3.q: R5 fires because event 1102 shows the Security log on WS-104 was cleared at 08:17. What evidence of the earlier activity on that host should still be available?
options: The events already forwarded to the SIEM before the log was cleared
The cleared local log, which Windows keeps in a hidden backup copy
Nothing, because 1102 instructs the SIEM to purge that host's events
Only the 1102 event itself, as clearing removes all prior forwarded data
3.explanation: Clearing the log locally does not remove copies already sent to the SIEM, which is a strong argument for central collection. A 1102 event has no effect on the SIEM's stored data.

3.q: A scheduled rule runs every 10 minutes with a 10-minute look-back. A laptop that was offline for an hour uploads its events in one batch. What is the risk, and the usual fix?
options: The events are counted twice; shorten the look-back to five minutes
The events may never fall in a searched window; use a longer look-back with de-duplication
The events are rejected as late; switch every rule to streaming evaluation
The events overwrite newer ones; sort the batch by ingestion time first
3.explanation: Late events carry old event times, so a look-back equal to the interval can skip them entirely; a longer look-back catches them and de-duplication prevents double alerts. Shortening the look-back would make the gap worse, not better.

3.q: A team must choose between streaming and scheduled evaluation for a new correlation rule. Which statement correctly describes the trade-off?
options: Streaming uses the full query language; scheduled rules cannot use joins
Streaming re-reads stored history; scheduled rules keep state in memory
Streaming alerts within seconds but holds window state; scheduled waits for its next run
Streaming is only for single-event rules; scheduled is needed for every threshold
3.explanation: Streaming engines evaluate each event against open windows held in memory and alert quickly; scheduled searches are simpler and can use the full query language but alert only on the next run. The first option reverses which approach has the full query language.

3.q: A sequence rule sometimes misses real activity from one firewall, whose events appear to fall outside windows they belong in. What should be monitored to confirm the cause?
options: The number of distinct users per address reported by the firewall each hour
The share of firewall events marked as parse failures by the ingest pipeline
The bytes per event, since larger events take longer to index and search
The difference between event time and ingestion time for that source
3.explanation: A wrong source clock shifts events out of their windows, and per-source monitoring of event time against ingestion time reveals the skew. Parse failures would show missing or tagged events, not events that are present but displaced in time.

3.q: A correlation rule joins all proxy events to all Windows events on user over a 24-hour window, then filters for 4720 and large uploads. It times out in production. What is the best first change?
options: Filter each side to the event types the rule needs before joining them
Lengthen the scheduled interval, so that the join has more time to finish
Switch the join key from user to host, since host has fewer distinct values
Remove the time window, so that the engine does not need to compare times
3.explanation: Narrowing inputs first (4720 events on one side, large uploads on the other) makes the join small without changing what the rule detects. Changing the join key alters the rule's meaning, and removing the window makes the join larger and less correct.

3.q: An adversary sprays three accounts per address from many different addresses, staying under R2's threshold of five distinct users per address. Which detection change best addresses this?
options: Lower the threshold to one distinct user per address, keeping the address join
Add a rule that counts failures per account across many source addresses
Extend R2's window to a full week, so that each address accumulates more users
Restrict R2 to addresses outside India, since sprays come from other countries
3.explanation: Layering rules on another entity (the account, across addresses) catches activity spread to avoid a per-address threshold, alongside MFA that makes a sprayed password useless. A threshold of one would alert on every typo and flood the queue.

3.q: An auditor notices that R2's threshold was changed from 5 to 500 three months ago, and nobody can say who made the change. Which practice would have prevented or exposed this?
options: Running R2 more often, so that a raised threshold is noticed sooner
Copying R2 into each analyst's personal saved searches as a backup
Keeping detection content under access control, version history and review
Adding an absence rule that alerts when the VPN stops sending events
3.explanation: A silently disabled rule or raised threshold works for an attacker like deleting logs, so detection content should be controlled, versioned and reviewed like production code. An absence rule detects missing telemetry, not changes to rules.

3.q: A newly written rule for Office spawning script interpreters has returned no results in its first month. What is the soundest next step?
options: Record the empty result as evidence that no such attacks occurred
Delete the rule, since it uses compute without producing any value
Lower its severity, so that any future hits do not page an analyst
Test it with a known-bad event to confirm it can fire at all
3.explanation: An empty result may mean a broken rule, for example a case mismatch or a missing field, so it must be tested with a known-bad event and a near-miss benign one. Treating silence as proof of safety is one of the lesson's named mistakes.

3.q: In the Banyan storyline, which preventive control would remove the scenario behind R1 at its source rather than detect it afterwards?
options: Application control that stops Office from starting script interpreters
Require MFA on the VPN for every remote account and record the authentication result in the SIEM
A proxy block on uploads larger than 10,000,000 bytes to unknown sites
Forwarding the Security log so that a local clear cannot destroy it
3.explanation: R1 detects WINWORD.EXE starting PowerShell or cmd, and application control preventing that parent-child launch removes the behaviour itself. MFA is the preventive answer to R2's spray scenario, not to R1's.

3.q: The entity aggregation query combines R1, R3, R4 and R5 but leaves out R6, although R6 also names WS-104. Why was R6 left out?
options: R6 is a single-event rule, and aggregation only accepts threshold rules
R6 groups by host and URL and returns no timestamp column to aggregate
R6 uses proxy data, which has no host field filled in the coverage matrix
R6 fired 18 times, which would dominate the count of distinct rules
3.explanation: The aggregation needs host and ts from each rule, and R6's output has host, URL and statistics but no time; giving it one (such as the first beacon) lets it contribute. The proxy does fill host, and distinct-rule counting is unaffected by R6's hit volume.

3.q: R2 returns ('203.0.113.66', 8, 'gopal', '2026-11-03T06:46:00Z'), and the raw events show gopal himself among the failures at 06:42:42. What exactly does the value 8 represent?
options: Failed attempts against gopal's account before his successful login
Accounts other than gopal that failed from the address before 06:46
Distinct accounts, gopal included, that failed from the address by then
Total VPN events from the address, both failures and the success
3.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT f.user) counts every distinct account with a failure from that address at or before the success, and gopal's own failure is one of the eight. The rule does not exclude the successful user, so 'accounts other than gopal' would give seven.

3.q: R2's self-join pairs each VPN success with every earlier failure from its address. On a production VPN with millions of events, what keeps this join practical?
options: Replacing COUNT(DISTINCT) with COUNT(*), which avoids a sort step
Joining on user instead of src_ip, which has far fewer distinct values
Running the rule once a day, so that fewer joins are executed overall
Bounding the join with a time window and an index on the time column
3.explanation: A time window limits how many failures each success can pair with, and a time index (minisiem creates idx_ts at load) lets the engine find them quickly. Swapping COUNT(DISTINCT) for COUNT(*) would change what the rule detects, losing the spray logic.

3.q: The kit's test_rules.py tests R2 with a spray of five users that must match and a spray of four users that must not. What does the second test add?
options: It confirms the threshold boundary, so a near-miss does not raise an alert
It measures how fast the rule runs when fewer failures are in the table
It checks that the rule ignores VPN failures that come after the success
It proves the rule handles accounts whose names are in upper case
3.explanation: Pairing a known-bad case with a near-miss benign case pins the threshold exactly: five fires, four does not. The four-user test varies only the count, so it says nothing about failures after the success or about case handling.

3.q: The overnight alert queue for endpoint detections is completely empty, while proxy alerts arrived as usual. Before the shift lead records a quiet night, which dashboard panel should be consulted?
options: The log-source health panel showing last-seen time per source
The detection performance panel showing alerts per rule
The activity panel showing outbound bytes per host
The management panel showing the trend in MTTA
3.explanation: A source that stops sending produces no alerts, and an empty queue for it looks exactly like a quiet night; only a last-seen health panel distinguishes the two. Alerts per rule would also show zero and cannot say whether the data was there.

3.q: In the Banyan lab data the 06 UTC hour, which contains the phishing download, the PowerShell launch and the VPN spray, holds 47 events, while 04 UTC holds 65. What does this show about a static threshold on total event volume?
options: It would fire for 06 UTC because several sources were active at once
It would fire for 04 UTC only after the proxy events were excluded
It would flag the routine 04 UTC peak before the intrusion hour
It would need a baseline from the same hour on the previous day
3.explanation: The busiest hour, 04 UTC, is routine start-of-day activity, and the intrusion hour sits inside the day's normal range, so a volume threshold draws attention to the wrong hour. Activity from several sources does not raise 06 above the peak.

3.q: After a vendor changes its log format, events keep arriving at normal volume but rules that use user.name stop matching. Which panel would have revealed the break?
options: Events per hour per source against a baseline
Field fill rate for user.name per source
Last event time per source with a threshold
Alerts raised per correlation rule per day
3.explanation: The volume and last-seen measures stay normal because events still arrive; only the percentage of events with user.name populated falls. A drop in alerts per rule is a late, indirect symptom that does not identify the parsing cause.

3.q: A team member proposes a panel titled 'Top browsers in use'. Following the panel design procedure, nobody can say who would read it or what they would do differently if it changed. What is the correct outcome?
options: Build it with a weekly refresh so it costs little search capacity
Build it and give it an owner who will review it each quarter
Move it to the management dashboard where trends are expected
Stop at the audience step and do not build the panel at all
3.explanation: If no audience or action can be named, the procedure stops before the panel is built, because it would be decoration. A slow refresh or an owner reduces cost and drift but does not give the panel a purpose.

3.q: While designing a health panel, the team defines a precise condition: 'Sysmon from any workstation has sent nothing for more than 15 minutes during office hours'. What should happen to that condition besides colouring the panel red?
options: It should be shown as a single threat-level gauge for managers
It should also become a meta-alert so that nobody has to watch
It should be replaced by a relative baseline learned over a month
It should be hidden behind a drilldown to protect personal data
3.explanation: When a threshold can be stated precisely, it should also raise an alert so the panel becomes a convenience rather than the only safeguard. A relative baseline is less suitable for a health floor, which the lesson recommends keeping static.

3.q: The outbound-bytes panel lists WS-104 with total_out 48,263,095 and max_out 48,200,000, while every other host is below 100 KB. Why is showing max_out beside total_out valuable here?
options: It shows that almost all of the total came from one single request
It shows that WS-104 sent several medium uploads over the day and reached the same total as one large transfer
It shows that the proxy truncated large requests at a fixed size
It shows that the total includes bytes received as well as sent
3.explanation: A maximum almost equal to the total means one request carried nearly all the data, the 48.2 MB upload, which points the drilldown at a specific event. Many medium uploads would give a maximum far below the total.

3.q: A SOC wall screen shows a stacked area chart of events by source. The proxy forms a thick band and the VPN is barely visible. What is the main risk of this design?
options: Stacking doubles the counts of sources that share an hour
The proxy band hides whether the chart has refreshed recently
Area charts cannot show values below one event per hour
Small series such as the VPN, which carried the spray, are hidden
3.explanation: Stacked and cumulative charts make low-volume sources invisible, yet in the Banyan data the small VPN source held the password spray. Stacking does not double counts; it adds series on top of each other.

3.q: The per-source hourly query returns rows for Sysmon up to 06 UTC and then no Sysmon rows at all. The chart drawn from it simply shows nothing for Sysmon after 06. What design change makes this silence hard to miss?
options: Sort the rows by count so that the smallest sources appear at the top
Switch the chart to a pie of total events per source for the day
Draw explicit zeros for empty buckets and show last-seen per source
Raise the refresh interval so that the missing rows reappear sooner
3.explanation: Absence appears only as a missing row, so a chart that drops empty buckets hides it; explicit zeros and a last-seen time make it visible. A daily pie still shows Sysmon with a share and gives no sign that it stopped.

3.q: A queue panel reports '5 open high-severity alerts'. Which addition most improves the shift lead's ability to act on it?
options: The age of the oldest alert and the SLA time remaining
The total number of alerts closed in the current month
A breakdown of the five alerts by ATT&CK tactic name
The number of events that the alerts were built from
3.explanation: Five alerts is fine if raised ten minutes ago and alarming if the oldest is six hours old, so age and SLA time remaining drive the action. A monthly closed count is a trend measure and says nothing about the current queue.

3.q: The 'failures per hour' panel shows 2 failures at 04 UTC and 8 at 06 UTC. An analyst wants a panel that explains why 06 is unusual. Which design follows the lesson's reasoning?
options: A line of failures per minute for 06 UTC with a shaded normal band
A top-N of source addresses by distinct users failed and later success
A pie chart of failures split between the Windows and VPN sources
A single number for the day's failure total coloured by a threshold
3.explanation: Distinct users failed per address, plus whether a success followed, shows a spray from one address; and once stated that precisely it is rule R2's logic and should be a rule. A per-minute line still shows only counts, not who or from where.

3.q: A SOC replaces its static failed-logon threshold with a baseline learned from the previous 30 days. Which weakness of this approach should the team keep in mind?
options: It cannot adapt to the organisation's daily working rhythm
It fires too often at night when logon volume is naturally low
It requires every panel to be expressed in the IST time zone
It treats an attacker already present in that period as normal
3.explanation: A relative baseline learns whatever happened during the learning period, including an intruder who was already active. Adapting to the daily rhythm is its strength, and being too sensitive at night is the weakness of static thresholds.

3.q: Which combination of thresholds does the lesson recommend as a practical compromise for a SOC's dashboards?
options: Use per-source baselines for collection health and vendor-supplied static thresholds for business activity
Static limits everywhere, with values reduced during night shifts
A static floor for source health and reviewed baselines for activity
Baselines everywhere, retrained automatically after each incident
3.explanation: Health has a clear fixed expectation such as at least one event per 15 minutes, while activity varies with the organisation's rhythm and suits baselines reviewed by a person. Reversing the two loses the clarity of the health floor.

3.q: During an incident one panel is in UTC and shows the Security log cleared at 08:17, while another is in IST and shows the VPN success as gopal at 12:16. An analyst concludes that the log was cleared before the VPN logon. What is correct?
options: Wrong: 12:16 IST is 06:46 UTC, about 90 minutes before the clearing
Right: 08:17 UTC is earlier than 12:16 on any clock used in India
Wrong: 12:16 IST is 17:46 UTC, many hours after the log clearing
It cannot be checked without the raw events from both sources
3.explanation: IST is UTC plus 5 hours 30 minutes, so 12:16 IST is 06:46 UTC and the VPN logon came roughly an hour and a half before the 08:17 clearing. Adding instead of subtracting the offset gives the wrong 17:46 figure; mixed zones are a classic cause of misordering.

3.q: Correlation searches have started skipping runs since a new 20-panel dashboard was put on a wall screen with a 30-second refresh and opened by ten analysts in their browsers. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Move the correlation searches to run only outside office hours
Refresh panels only as fast as their decisions require
Split the dashboard into two dashboards of ten panels each
Replace the panels with stacked charts that use one query
3.explanation: Every refresh costs search capacity, and dashboards can consume more than the rules; trend panels may refresh hourly and health or queue panels every minute or two. Splitting the dashboard keeps the same number of queries running.

3.q: A heavy panel times out during peak load and renders as an empty table. Why is this dangerous, and what is the defence?
options: Empty tables trigger false meta-alerts; suppress alerts during peaks
Timeouts corrupt saved searches; restore them from version control
Nothing can look like no events; show errors visibly and monitor failures
Timeouts expose raw data; restrict the panel to administrator roles
3.explanation: A panel that fails returns nothing, which a viewer may read as a quiet period, so panels must display errors and search failures and timeouts must be monitored. A timeout does not damage the saved search itself.

3.q: A dashboard built for the help desk includes a panel drawn from security logs that help-desk staff are not permitted to search directly. What principle does this break?
options: Dashboards must keep one time zone across all their panels
Panels should show rates against a baseline, not raw counts
Dashboards must refresh no faster than their decisions require
Role-based access applies to dashboards exactly as to search
3.explanation: A dashboard is a pre-built query over sensitive data, so it must not expose what its viewers could not search themselves. The other options are sound design rules but do not concern who may see the data.

3.q: A proposed wall-screen panel in the open-plan SOC lists each user's browsing destinations by name. Which design satisfies the purpose while respecting data protection?
options: Show host names with counts and keep details in a logged drilldown
Show the full list but rotate it off the screen every few minutes
Show the full list only in UTC so that times cannot be linked to staff
Show user names with destinations hashed so they remain searchable
3.explanation: Data minimisation under the DPDP Act 2023 and good practice means showing only what the purpose requires on shared screens and putting detail behind access-controlled, logged drilldowns. Rotating the list still exposes it to everyone in the room.

3.q: An insider with SIEM editing rights quietly raises the threshold on a health panel so that a stopped agent no longer turns it red. Which control most directly addresses this?
options: Refreshing the health panel more often during the night shift
Logging and reviewing dashboard and threshold changes like rule changes
Replacing the health panel with an events-per-hour volume chart
Showing the panel only in the management dashboard for the CISO
3.explanation: Silently changing a threshold or deleting a panel can hide activity as effectively as deleting logs, so dashboard changes need logging, versioning and review. Faster refresh just redraws the altered threshold more often.

3.q: Which description best fits an investigation (entity) dashboard as the lesson defines it?
options: A wall display of open alerts by severity watched throughout the shift
A weekly report of rules that fired most often, used to tune detection
A trend view of incidents by category prepared for the SOC manager
A set of panels opened during a case and filtered on one host or user
3.explanation: The investigation dashboard is opened rather than watched: an entity typed at the top re-runs every panel for it, so the first minutes of each case look the same. The wall display of open alerts is the queue dashboard.

3.q: The CISO asks for 'one dashboard that shows whether we are under attack'. What is the honest response the lesson recommends?
options: Build a green, amber and red threat gauge driven by alert counts
Offer the analysts' queue dashboard with a summary panel added
Explain that no dashboard proves absence; offer owned measures and briefings
Offer a live attack map of blocked internet connections by country
3.explanation: No dashboard can prove the absence of an attack; management is better served by a small set of measures with owners plus regular narrative briefings. A threat gauge invites exactly the false reassurance the request implies.

3.q: A vendor demo features an animated world map of 'attacks' in real time. Why would it have contributed little to spotting the Banyan VPN compromise?
options: The map would show the spraying address only after it was blocked
A valid-account VPN logon does not register as an attack at all
The map draws only countries with more than one thousand events
Geolocation of documentation addresses always resolves to India
3.explanation: The most dangerous activity, a successful logon with a valid account through the VPN, is not classed as an attack, and internet-noise geography says little about risk. Geolocation is approximate, not reliably India; that is a different weakness.

3.q: For an analyst activity dashboard, which panel is likely to be most informative according to the lesson's 'show' guidance?
options: New values never seen before, such as a new parent of an Office app
Total events ingested per day across all log sources combined
A pie chart with one slice for each of the twelve event types
Threats blocked this month by the perimeter firewall and proxy
3.explanation: Change, such as a never-before-seen parent process for Word or a new admin account, is more informative than totals and leads straight to an entity to examine. Ingest totals are vanity metrics that change no decision.

3.q: On the lab day the Security log on WS-104 was cleared (event 1102) at 08:17 UTC. Which arrangement best ensures the SOC notices this kind of tampering without depending on someone looking at a screen?
options: A volume chart of Windows events per hour on the wall display
A management trend of incidents by category reviewed monthly
A threat gauge turns amber when Windows event volume drops and stays visible on the team's overview screen
An owned health panel whose thresholds are also backed by alerts
3.explanation: Attackers who clear logs or stop agents benefit from health panels that are unowned or unalerted, so health thresholds need owners and alerts behind them. A wall volume chart still relies on someone happening to look.

3.q: A queue panel shows, for each confirmed incident, the time elapsed since it was noticed, against CERT-In's six-hour reporting direction. How should the SOC regard this panel?
options: As the official record that the incident has been reported
As the trigger that sends the report to CERT-In automatically
As a reminder of the deadline that does not replace the process
As a detection that confirms which incidents are reportable
3.explanation: The panel helps the shift lead keep the six-hour obligation in view, but reporting remains part of the incident process. It neither files the report nor decides reportability.

3.q: Applying the review question 'if this number doubled or dropped to zero, what would I do?' to an analyst panel showing 'events ingested today', the honest answer is 'nothing'. What should happen to the panel?
options: Move it to the engineering dashboard if capacity planning needs it
Keep it but add a shaded baseline band for the same day last week
Convert it into a correlation rule that fires on unusual totals
Replace it with a cumulative chart of ingest since the month began
3.explanation: A number that changes no analyst decision is decoration; if it serves capacity planning it belongs on the engineering dashboard. A baseline band makes the vanity total look more meaningful without giving analysts an action.

3.q: A ticket names the host as 'ws-104'. In minisiem, host='ws-104' returns a count of 0, while the same search with lower(host) returns 58. What should the analyst conclude before writing anything in the case notes?
options: The host was renamed during the day, so its earlier events use another name
The lower() function also matched other hosts whose names contain 104
The = operator compared case exactly, so the zero reflects the query
The host sent no events, and lower() matched only the raw JSON column
3.explanation: In SQLite = compares text including case, so 'ws-104' does not match the stored 'WS-104'; an empty result should first be treated as a question about the query. lower(host)='ws-104' is an exact match after case folding and cannot match other hosts.

3.q: The Banyan dataset has 340 events, nine of them from 203.0.113.66, yet src_ip <> '203.0.113.66' returns 295 rather than 331. What explains the 36 missing events?
options: Events with a NULL src_ip are neither equal nor unequal, so they drop out
Events whose src_ip is the placeholder '-' are treated as matching NULL
The <> operator ignores case and so removes addresses that look alike
Proxy events carry the address in the raw column and are not compared
3.explanation: A comparison with NULL is unknown, so rows without the field fail both = and <>; here that is all 33 Sysmon events and three Windows events. The '-' placeholder is a real string, so those Windows logon events are kept.

3.q: An analyst checks Windows events for missing source addresses with source='windows' AND src_ip IS NULL and gets 3, although 13 Windows events show no usable address. Why the difference?
options: Ten Windows events were dropped at load because their address was invalid
IS NULL only matches fields stored in the raw JSON, not in the columns
Three events have no address at all and ten were stored with src_ip 'None'
Logon events store the placeholder '-', which is a value and not NULL
3.explanation: The 4624 and 4625 events carry '-' as a real string, while 4720, 4732 and 1102 have no src_ip at all, which SQL represents as NULL. 'None' is only how minisiem prints NULL, not a stored string.

3.q: An analyst writes WHERE COUNT(DISTINCT user) >= 5 to find addresses that failed against many accounts, and the query errors. What is the fix?
options: Move the condition into ORDER BY so that it is applied after sorting
Put the condition in HAVING, which is applied after the grouping
Replace COUNT(DISTINCT user) with COUNT(user) inside the WHERE
Add a LIMIT so that the aggregation runs on fewer rows at a time
3.explanation: WHERE filters events before grouping and cannot test an aggregate; HAVING filters the grouped rows and can. Swapping to COUNT(user) is still an aggregate and still invalid in WHERE.

3.q: Two VPN failure patterns appear: one address failing 8 times for one account, and another failing once each for 8 accounts. Which aggregation separates a password spray from a user mistyping a password?
options: COUNT(DISTINCT user) grouped by source address
COUNT(*) grouped by source address and outcome
MAX(ts) minus MIN(ts) grouped by user account
SUM(bytes_out) grouped by source address
3.explanation: A spray is one address against many accounts with few attempts each, which a distinct count of users exposes; both patterns give the same COUNT(*) of 8. Time span alone does not tell the two apart.

3.q: On the Banyan table, SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(src_ip) FROM events returns two different numbers. What does the difference measure?
options: The number of events with the placeholder '-' as address
The number of duplicate addresses across all four sources
The number of events where src_ip is absent, which is 36
The number of addresses that appear in only one event
3.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows while COUNT(field) counts rows where the field is not NULL, so the gap of 340 minus 304 is the 36 events without src_ip. Placeholder '-' values are non-NULL and are counted by both.

3.q: Stacking proxy URLs by distinct hosts shows cdn-telemetry-sync.example visited by 1 host, 18 times. Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: It confirms command-and-control activity because only one endpoint accessed the destination within the observation window
It is rare in breadth but frequent in count, worth a pivot, not proof
It is ordinary browsing because 18 requests is a low daily volume
It is a proxy logging error because the requests are so regular
3.explanation: One host contacting one domain regularly fits automated traffic, but a newly installed legitimate agent would look the same; stacking yields candidates for a pivot, not a verdict. Calling it confirmed C2 skips that check.

3.q: Why does query thinking place 'inspect raw events' before 'aggregate'?
options: Aggregation is not possible until the raw events are loaded in memory
Inspection is cheaper, so it reduces the cost of the later aggregation
Raw events must be exported to the case before they may be counted
A summary of broken data looks as tidy as a summary of good data
3.explanation: Looking at a few full events reveals empty fields, unexpected case or the wrong event type, none of which a neat count would show. Inspection is about validity, not about reducing the cost of the aggregation.

3.q: A colleague in Bengaluru reports that suspicious activity began 'around 11:40'. The analyst searches minisiem with ts BETWEEN '2026-11-03T11:35:00Z' AND '2026-11-03T11:50:00Z' and finds ordinary proxy traffic. What is the most likely problem?
options: The BETWEEN filter excludes events whose seconds are not zero
The ts column is indexed and cannot be searched with BETWEEN
The window was written in IST but the data is stored in UTC
The proxy source is too noisy for a fifteen-minute window
3.explanation: A local time typed against UTC data is 5 hours 30 minutes off and returns other, plausible-looking events; 11:40 IST is 06:10 UTC, when the phishing download and PowerShell occurred. BETWEEN on ISO text compares whole strings, seconds included.

3.q: A new log source is ingested with timestamps like 2026-11-03T12:14:00+05:30 while existing events use the Z suffix. Why does this threaten time-range searches in minisiem?
options: String comparison orders ts correctly only with one format and zone
SQLite rejects timestamps that include a numeric zone offset
The index on ts is rebuilt and ignores rows with offsets
BETWEEN treats any offset as UTC plus the offset twice
3.explanation: ISO 8601 text sorts chronologically only when every value has the same format and zone, which is why normalisation converts times to UTC at ingest. SQLite accepts the text; it simply compares it as a string and misorders it.

3.q: A hunt query uses image LIKE '%powershell%' over 30 days of endpoint data on a production SIEM and runs far longer than expected. What is the main cause?
options: LIKE is case-insensitive and so compares each character twice
The leading wildcard stops index use and forces a full read
The pattern also matches the parent_image column of each event
Wildcards are evaluated after GROUP BY and so see every group
3.explanation: A pattern that begins with % prevents most platforms from using an index, so every event in the range must be read; on billions of events this decides whether the search finishes. LIKE tests only the column it is applied to.

3.q: To remove internal traffic from a proxy hunt, an analyst adds url NOT LIKE '%banyan.example%'. What happens to requests to https://banyan-payroll-update.example/invoice.docm?
options: They are removed because the pattern matches any URL containing banyan
They are removed because LIKE ignores the hyphen when matching text
They are kept only if the request returned more than zero bytes out
They are kept because the look-alike name does not contain banyan.example
3.explanation: The look-alike domain contains 'banyan-payroll-update.example', not the string 'banyan.example', so the exclusion leaves it in. Wildcards match exact substrings, which is why patterns must be checked against what they should and should not match.

3.q: The VPN country field has no column in the minisiem events table, yet the analyst needs it for the successful logons. How can it be retrieved, and what does this show?
options: With json_extract on raw, showing why keeping the original event matters
With a join to a geolocation table, showing why lookups need maintenance
With LIKE on the src_ip column, showing that addresses encode countries
With a reload of the dataset, showing that columns are added on demand
3.explanation: json_extract(raw, '$.country') reads a field that normalisation did not map to a column, which is only possible because the raw event is stored. A geolocation lookup would estimate a country, not return the value the VPN recorded.

3.q: gopal's VPN session at 06:46 came from 203.0.113.66 with country '??', and at 07:22 his workstation WS-107 browsed the intranet. What conclusion do these pivots support?
options: gopal ran the spray himself and then returned to his own desk
The VPN logon was legitimate because his workstation was active
A precise question for gopal and the VPN team about who held the session
Proof that WS-107 is compromised and must be isolated immediately
3.explanation: The data cannot say who used which session; it turns the alert into a specific, answerable question about a VPN session from an unknown location while his desk machine was in use. Treating desk activity as proof of legitimacy ignores the spraying source address.

3.q: In the pivot map of the investigation, an arrow runs from the beacon domain to 'Host WS-104', although the invoice download on that host happened earlier than the first beacon. What do the arrows represent?
options: The order in which events occurred on the network
The direction of data transfer, annotated with the original sender and the observed network destination
The parent-to-child relationship between processes
The order of discovery, labelled with the pivot field
3.explanation: Each arrow points from the value already known to the value the next search revealed, so it records the analyst's path, not chronology. Event order is established afterwards from the timestamps of the events found.

3.q: The beacon thread centres on WS-104 and the VPN thread on the gopal account and WS-107. Why would a host-based correlation rule not link the two?
options: The VPN source did not record a host, so it was discarded at load
The threads share no host; only pivots on user and address connect them
Host names in VPN events are in lower case and fail exact matches
The threads fall into different UTC hours and exceed the rule window
3.explanation: The two threads involve different hosts, so grouping by host keeps them apart and only pivots by user and source address reveal the full scope. VPN events lack a host field but are still loaded and searchable.

3.q: When pivoting from WS-104 to everything else it did, the analyst first excludes the proxy source. What must the analyst remember about that choice?
options: A separate proxy pivot is still needed; it reveals the 48 MB upload
The exclusion also removes Sysmon events that lack a src_ip value
Excluding proxy events changes the host value in Windows events
Proxy records must be excluded to correct a case-sensitivity issue that would otherwise affect every source in the query
3.explanation: Excluding the noisy proxy makes the endpoint and Windows events readable, but the 48,200,000-byte upload at 08:12 exists only in proxy data, so it needs its own pivot. source<>'proxy' tests source, which every event has, so no Sysmon rows are lost.

3.q: Which part of the query in Pivot 1 turns a list of beacon requests into the information needed to scope the activity in time?
options: COUNT(*) per host, giving the 18 hits on the domain
GROUP BY host and user, giving one row per account
MIN(ts) and MAX(ts), giving first and last seen times
A LIKE filter on the URL, which collects variations of the domain path without aggregating their timestamps
3.explanation: First and last seen, 06:17 to 07:42, define the span during which the host beaconed, which is what scoping requires. The count shows intensity, not when the activity started and stopped.

3.q: Why do pipeline languages such as SPL, KQL and ES|QL have no separate equivalent of SQL's HAVING clause?
options: They compute aggregates in the time picker before any filtering
They do not allow filtering on values produced by aggregations
They apply every filter to raw events and never to summary rows
A filter stage placed after the stats stage filters aggregated rows
3.explanation: Each pipeline stage transforms the output of the previous one, so a filter after summarize or stats naturally acts on the aggregated rows. Pipelines can therefore filter aggregates; they just need no special clause for it.

3.q: A hunter's search over 90 days of all sources, filtered only by a URL wildcard, keeps timing out. Which change is the single most effective first step?
options: Add ORDER BY ts so the platform reads events in time order
Narrow the time range, since storage is organised by time
Return all matching rows and count them in a spreadsheet
Add a join to the asset table to enrich each matching event
3.explanation: Nearly every platform organises storage by time, so a tighter range most reduces the data read; filters on indexed fields come next. Sorting adds work rather than limiting what is read.

3.q: An analyst wants to know how many proxy requests each host made yesterday and exports every matching event to the browser to count them by eye. What does the lesson recommend instead?
options: Let the SIEM aggregate by host and return only the summary rows
Export the events in smaller batches and count each batch in turn
Inspect the first ten events and extrapolate to the whole day
Run the export at night when correlation searches are paused
3.explanation: Aggregating on the platform returns a handful of rows instead of a million, which is faster and readable. A small limit is right for inspecting the shape of events, not for counting them.

3.q: Rule R2's self-join of VPN failures to later successes runs instantly on the ten lab VPN events. How should the same logic be prepared for a production VPN log?
options: Join every success to every failure across the full retention period
Replace the join with a wildcard search on the source address field
Run the join in the browser after exporting all VPN events daily
Restrict to a short window and to failures above a threshold first
3.explanation: Joining large sets is expensive in every product, so the inputs must be reduced first by time window and threshold. A wildcard search cannot express the relationship between failures and a later success.

3.q: A SIEM lets analysts search authentication records, browsing history and command lines across the organisation. Which control best reflects the lesson's view that search access is privileged?
options: Allow searches only in UTC so that personal times are not revealed
Use role-based restrictions and log each search's user, query and time
Limit every search to 10,000 rows so that bulk extraction is prevented
Require searches to be run from saved queries approved by managers
3.explanation: Role-based access plus an audit of who searched what and when lets misuse beyond the monitoring purpose be detected, as the DPDP Act 2023 expects. A row limit slows extraction but leaves the searches themselves unaccountable.

3.q: A team builds a multi-user search portal that takes a user name from an alert and pastes it straight into the SQL text before running it. What is the main security problem?
options: User names in alerts are case-sensitive and will often fail to match
Pasted values bypass the index on ts and make every search slower
Untrusted input placed in query text allows query injection
Alert values are stored as NULL and so match nothing at all
3.explanation: Values from alerts or emails are attacker-influenced, and pasting them into query text lets them change the query; multi-user systems must use parameterised queries and sandbox what queries can do, as minisiem's load does with its inserts. Case mismatch is an accuracy issue, not a security one.

3.q: At handover an analyst's case note says 'Searched for other hosts contacting files-share-drop.example, found nothing'. What would turn this note into usable evidence?
options: A screenshot of the empty result with the analyst's name on it
A statement that the search was repeated twice with the same result
The exact query, its time range and when it was run
The total number of proxy events present in the dataset
3.explanation: Only the recorded query, range and run time let a colleague review and reproduce the result, and check whether the empty answer came from the query rather than the data. A screenshot shows the outcome but not what was actually asked.

3.q: A SIEM keeps 30 days of searchable data. An exfiltration alert fires today, and later evidence suggests the attacker's foothold was gained about 40 days ago. What is the most serious consequence for the investigation?
options: The SOC can describe recent attacker actions but cannot show how access was gained, so it cannot be sure the entry point is closed
The exfiltration alert itself is unreliable, because correlation rules need the full dwell time of data to fire correctly
The SOC must restore the deleted indices from the hot tier's replicas before it can begin any form of scoping
The incident cannot be reported to a regulator, because reports must include the complete attack timeline from the start
3.explanation: Intrusions are found after they start; with 30 days held, the quiet initial-access stage from 40 days ago is gone, so the root cause and the way in cannot be established. Replicas are copies of current data, not of deleted indices, so they cannot bring it back.

3.q: Of the four reasons a SOC retains telemetry, which one most directly requires that the data sit on fast, frequently searched storage?
options: Legal and regulatory retention, because a regulator can request logs at any moment
Operational audit, because SLA reports are generated from the raw events every day
Detection lookback, because first-seen and baseline rules query history every few minutes
Investigation and scoping, because analysts need every raw event older than the dwell time
3.explanation: Scheduled rules that compare the present with recent history run constantly, so their lookback period must be on the hot tier. Investigation needs older, complete data but searches it far less often, so it can live on slower tiers.

3.q: In the lab purge experiment with a 07:00Z cutoff, the beaconing rule R6 returns zero hits although WS-104 kept beaconing until after 08:00Z. Why?
options: The purge also removed the proxy source's parsing metadata, so later beacon events no longer match the URL field
Only 9 of the 18 beacon requests survive, below the rule's threshold of 10, because its lookback straddles the cutoff
The surviving beacon requests were compressed into a summary table, which the rule's SQL does not read from
R6 depends on the R1 hit for the same host, and R1 lost its only matching event in the purge
3.explanation: A shorter retention window can silently break any rule whose lookback crosses the boundary: half the beacons were deleted, leaving a count under the threshold. The rules in minisiem are independent queries over the events table; R6 does not chain to R1.

3.q: A policy states that firewall logs are deleted after 90 days. An auditor finds some events that are 90 days and several hours old still present. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The lifecycle job failed and the excess events are evidence that the retention policy is not being enforced at all
Legal hold is applied automatically to every index older than the policy age until a reviewer releases it
The SIEM counts retention from ingestion time, and every firewall event arrived several hours after it was written
Data ages in whole indices, and an index is deleted only when its newest event passes the age, so retention acts as a minimum
3.explanation: Rollover groups events into time-based units that move and are deleted as a whole, so the oldest events in a unit outlive the nominal age slightly; this is why retention statements should be written as minimums. A failed job would leave data far older, not hours older.

3.q: An investigator needs logs from eleven months ago, which sit as snapshots in object storage in the frozen tier. What must happen before they can be searched?
options: Nothing extra: the lifecycle policy automatically moves data back to hot when an analyst queries it
They must be rehydrated: restored or mounted into a searchable tier, which takes time and may cost money
They must be re-collected from the original hosts, since frozen snapshots hold only summaries
Their legal hold must be lifted first, because frozen data is locked against any read access
3.explanation: Lifecycle arrows run one way; bringing archived data back into a searchable tier is a separate, deliberate rehydration step. Frozen snapshots hold the data itself, not summaries, and a legal hold blocks deletion, not reading.

3.q: An organisation covered by the CERT-In Directions of April 2022 plans its log retention. Which statement correctly reflects what the Directions mean for the covered ICT logs?
options: They must be kept for at least a rolling 180 days, within Indian jurisdiction, and be producible to CERT-In
They must be kept on the hot tier for 180 days so that a six-hour report can include every event
They may be kept for at most 180 days, after which the data protection law requires their deletion
They must be kept for 180 days only if an incident has been reported to CERT-In in that period
3.explanation: The Directions set a 180-day rolling floor, require the logs to be maintained within Indian jurisdiction and to be provided to CERT-In on reporting or request. They do not dictate a storage tier, and 180 days is a minimum, not a maximum.

3.q: A card-processing environment subject to PCI DSS keeps audit logs for three months on searchable storage and a further nine months in an archive that can be restored. How does this compare with the standard's log history requirement?
options: It falls short: all twelve months must be held on the hot tier so they can be searched immediately
It falls short: the standard sets 180 days of searchable data, so three months is not enough
It exceeds it: the standard requires only three months, so the nine archived months are optional
It meets it: twelve months in total with the most recent three immediately available for analysis
3.explanation: PCI DSS requires at least twelve months of audit log history with at least the most recent three months immediately available. The rest may sit on a slower tier; 180 days is the CERT-In figure, not the PCI DSS one.

3.q: An engineer proposes keeping all raw web proxy logs indefinitely 'because security monitoring is a legitimate purpose'. What is the strongest objection?
options: Indefinite retention breaches the CERT-In Directions, which forbid keeping logs for longer than 180 days
Indefinite retention prevents legal holds, because a hold can only be applied to data that has a deletion date
Proxy logs hold personal data; privacy law expects deletion once the purpose is met, so the policy needs a ceiling as well as a floor
Raw proxy logs become unreadable after a year because parsers change, so keeping them longer has no value
3.explanation: Under the DPDP Act 2023 personal data should be kept only as long as its purpose needs, so a security purpose justifies retention but not forever; the design needs both a floor and a ceiling, often extending lookback with summaries instead. CERT-In sets a minimum, not a maximum.

3.q: A lawsuit about an employee's actions is expected. The relevant endpoint logs will be deleted by the lifecycle policy in five days. What is the correct action?
options: Extend the retention period of the whole SIEM until the lawsuit ends, so nothing relevant is deleted
Disable the lifecycle policy until legal confirms which data is needed, then re-enable it
Apply a legal hold to that specific data through the documented process before the policy reaches it
Rehydrate the logs into the hot tier, since hot data is exempt from the deletion phase
3.explanation: A legal hold suspends deletion for the specific data, not for the whole SIEM, and must be in place before the policy deletes it. Extending everything or disabling the policy over-retains personal data and is not how holds are meant to work.

3.q: For one data class, investigators need 270 days of history, but the privacy and cost limits agreed so far allow only 180. How should the retention design handle this?
options: Resolve the conflict explicitly, for example by summarising or tiering to cut cost, or by documenting why the purpose justifies longer retention
Use the shorter limit automatically, because the privacy ceiling always overrides investigative and legal requirements
