options: The string starts with Mozilla/5.0, which only scripts send nowadays
The string names Linux, which few customers of the portal would use
It lacks engine and version tokens and requested no page assets
It is identical on every line, which browsers never repeat exactly
4.explanation: Real browser strings carry engine and version tokens, and browsers fetch stylesheets, scripts and images after a page; this client did neither. Every mainstream browser string begins with Mozilla/5.0, so that prefix proves nothing.

4.q: A client requesting thousands of pages identifies itself as a major search engine's crawler. How can the analyst verify the claim rather than trust the header?
options: Check whether the client fetched robots.txt before any other page
Run a reverse DNS lookup on its address, then a forward lookup of the returned name
Compare the user-agent string with the search engine's published version
Confirm that its requests include a Referer from the search engine's domain
4.explanation: The reverse-then-forward DNS check, recommended by the search engines themselves, ties the address to the operator; an impersonator fails it. Fetching robots.txt or copying the published user-agent string is behaviour any impersonator can imitate.

4.q: A WAF vendor reports SQL injection attempts against the portal's login form, but the analyst's search of the access log finds no injection markers on `/login`. What is the most likely reason?
options: The web server rejected the requests before writing them to the access log
The attempts were encoded, and the access log decodes values before storing
Login requests are written only to the error log, not to the access log
The form parameters travel in the POST body, which the access log does not record
4.explanation: The access log records the request line, so it shows injection only in the URL; POST body parameters require WAF, application or database logs. The access log stores the request as received, still encoded, so it does not decode anything.

4.q: Within three seconds one external source requests `/.env`, `/backup.zip`, `/wp-login.php` and `/phpmyadmin/`, all answered 404 with the same byte count. Which question decides whether this becomes a case?
options: Whether any of the probed paths answered 200, or the source went on to do more
Whether the source's user agent matches a commercial scanning product
Whether the portal runs WordPress, since one of the paths targets it
Whether the requests arrived over HTTP/1.1 rather than a newer protocol
4.explanation: Content discovery like this hits every public server daily; it becomes a case when a probe is served or the same source follows up. Whether the site runs WordPress does not matter, since scanners request such paths regardless.

4.q: Over a day the same path, `/branches/old-office`, returns 404 to forty different clients, most of whom send a Referer from the portal's own pages. What best explains the pattern?
options: A distributed scan rotating source addresses to avoid per-source thresholds
A crawler re-indexing the portal from many cloud addresses at once
A broken link on the site that visitors keep following
A cache misconfiguration that serves 404s to returning visitors
4.explanation: One real site path failing for many unrelated clients who arrived from your own pages is the mark of a broken link. A distributed scan would request many different well-known paths without a Referer from the site.

4.q: At 14:00 the portal returns 502 and 503 to every client on every path for six minutes, and the change calendar shows an application release at 13:58. How should the analyst read the spike?
options: As a denial-of-service attack timed to coincide with the release window
As a deployment or back-end outage, not activity by any one source
As injection probes reaching failing code, as the 500 class indicates
As rate limiting triggering on every client after the release
4.explanation: Errors across all clients and paths at once, matching a change record, point to an outage rather than one actor. Rate limiting would show as 429 per source, not 502 and 503 for everyone.

4.q: A developer explains that the portal catches every exception and shows a friendly error page with status 200. Why should the analyst raise this with the application owner?
options: Because 200 responses are excluded from SIEM ingestion by default
Because the friendly page leaks stack traces to the client
Because browsers cache 200 responses and repeat the failing request
Because application failures become invisible in the access log
4.explanation: The status records what the web server returned, so failures dressed as 200 cannot be told apart from successes, removing the 5xx signal injection triage relies on. A friendly page is the opposite of leaking stack traces.

4.q: Discovery paths, a traversal attempt and two SQL-shaped requests arrive from one address during the night. Before reading any status codes, what should the analyst establish first, and why?
options: Whether the address belongs to an authorised scanner in its window, since its lines look identical to an attacker's
Whether the address is on a threat-intelligence blocklist, since unlisted sources are rarely hostile
Whether the address geolocates abroad, since domestic sources are covered by the scan schedule
Whether the address previously visited the portal, since first-time visitors are always scanners
4.explanation: A scheduled scan by the organisation's own team produces exactly the same lines, so authorisation is checked first, against the schedule or a signed authorisation rather than assumed. Absence from a blocklist says nothing about intent.

4.q: A saved search for `UNION SELECT` returns nothing, yet a colleague finds injection attempts in the same log. Which approach would have caught them?
options: Searching the error log instead, because injection is never written to the access log
Searching only lines with status 500, because injection always causes a server error
Decoding the request and normalising case before matching the keywords
Searching the User-Agent field, because scanners announce injection there
4.explanation: Attempts arrive as UNION%20SELECT, with inline comments or mixed case, so detection must decode and normalise before matching. Restricting to 500s would miss attempts that were served or rejected.

4.q: Over ten minutes one source receives hundreds of 401 responses for `/admin/`, which is protected by web-server HTTP authentication. What does the pattern most likely indicate?
options: Content discovery looking for administration interfaces
Password guessing against the HTTP authentication
A misconfigured health check polling the wrong path
Rate limiting refusing the client after too many requests
4.explanation: Many 401s for one protected path from one source is the shape of credential guessing against web-server authentication. Rate limiting would answer with 429, and discovery spreads across many different paths.

4.q: The access log suggests the portal's statement page may build its SQL query unsafely. A colleague proposes replaying the logged requests against the portal to confirm. What is the right response?
options: Replay them from a lab address so the WAF does not block the confirmation
Replay only the request that returned 500, as that one already reached the query
Replay them outside business hours to keep impact on customers low
Hand it to the application security team, since testing needs written authorisation
4.explanation: Sending requests to the portal to check a vulnerability is testing, which requires written authorisation under the application security team's rules of engagement. The analyst's role is to read logs of requests others sent; timing or source address does not make unauthorised testing acceptable.

4.q: After an administrator adds a response-time field in the middle of the portal's log format, a content-discovery alert built on field positions stops firing entirely. What lesson does this illustrate?
options: Positional parsers break silently when the format changes, so format changes need monitoring
Custom log formats are not supported by SIEM parsers and must be avoided
Response-time fields are written only for successful requests, hiding 404s
Format changes take effect only after the next log rotation, so alerts pause
4.explanation: Access-log fields carry no names, only positions, so inserting a field shifts everything after it and saved searches quietly read the wrong values. Custom formats are fine as long as parsers are updated with them.

4.q: An incident lead asks whether workstation 10.40.0.23 connected to 198.51.100.80 at 10:02. The perimeter firewall's logs contain no line for that pair. What should the analyst verify before answering 'no connection'?
options: Whether the firewall's state table had reached its maximum size at that moment
Whether the destination address was covered by the firewall's DNAT rules
Whether the rule that would have allowed the traffic had logging enabled
Whether the workstation's own Windows Firewall was configured to log drops
4.explanation: Firewalls log decisions only for rules with logging switched on, and allowed traffic is the most common gap, so silence may just mean an unlogged allow. DNAT applies to inbound traffic to published servers, not to an outbound workstation connection.

4.q: An external vulnerability report lists port 3389 on Banyan's public address as 'filtered' rather than 'closed'. What does that tell the analyst about the perimeter firewall's handling of that port?
options: The firewall silently dropped the SYN, so the scanner received no reply
The firewall answered the SYN with a TCP reset sent from the public address
The firewall sent an ICMP unreachable message back to the scanner
The firewall allowed the SYN, but no service was listening behind it
4.explanation: A dropped SYN gets no answer and times out, which scanners report as filtered. A reset or ICMP unreachable is a reject, which tells the scanner immediately and is reported as closed.

4.q: A netfilter line begins `kernel: DROP IN=eth0 SRC=203.0.113.66 ...`. A colleague says the word DROP is the kernel's verdict and so needs no further checking. What is the accurate view?
options: Correct, because the LOG target writes the verdict of the rule that matched
DROP is free text the administrator set as the LOG prefix, so confirm it against the rule base
Correct only if the line also carries an OUT= value showing the egress interface of the packet
DROP is added by syslog when the receiving server cannot parse the action field
4.explanation: The LOG target only logs; the text before IN= is the --log-prefix chosen when the rule was written, and the packet is dropped by a separate rule. A prefix is only as truthful as whoever configured it, so check the rule base.

4.q: After normalising the kit's logs, the analyst sees a successful VPN login as gopal from 203.0.113.66 at 06:46:00Z and a dropped inbound RDP attempt from the same address to 10.40.0.5 at 06:46:21Z. Why does this one drop deserve attention?
options: Because any inbound RDP attempt shows that the target host has already been compromised
Because the drop proves the VPN account's password was guessed
Because RDP drops are written only when the target host is listening
Because joining it to the VPN success by address and time makes it part of a case
4.explanation: A lone dropped RDP attempt from the internet is background noise; the same address succeeding at the VPN 21 seconds earlier links the two lines and makes them part of a story. Nothing in either line proves the password was guessed.

4.q: A netfilter line reads `IN=eth0 OUT= SRC=192.0.2.77 DST=203.0.113.10 ... DPT=21 SYN`, where 203.0.113.10 is the firewall's own public address. What does the empty OUT= field indicate?
options: The firewall could not determine an egress route and therefore dropped the packet
The packet was a reply within an established session, so no route was needed
The packet was addressed to the firewall itself rather than forwarded through it
The logging rule was placed before routing, so the interface was not yet known
4.explanation: OUT= is empty when the packet is destined for the firewall's own address (input) rather than forwarded to another network. The SYN flag shows it was the opening packet of an attempt, not a reply in an established session.

4.q: A partner reports abuse from `203.0.113.10:40112` at 10:02:41 IST. Every Banyan workstation shares that public address. How does the analyst identify the responsible machine?
options: Find the session record with that translated port and time, then map its internal address to a host via DHCP
Search the firewall log for 203.0.113.10 at that time, then list every workstation that was online in that minute
Ask the partner for the user agent, then match it against the proxy log of all users
Search DHCP logs for port 40112, since DHCP assigns source ports along with addresses
4.explanation: Only the firewall's session log holds both identities, so joining on public port and time yields the internal address and port, and DHCP ties that address to a machine. Searching the public address alone matches every outbound connection from the company.

4.q: The firewall clock is four minutes fast and the session logs are forwarded without correction. Why is this especially damaging when answering external reports about Banyan's public address?
options: Session records older than four minutes are discarded by the collector when the clocks disagree
Public source ports are reused quickly, so the report can map onto the wrong connection
The SIEM rejects firewall events whose timestamps are ahead of its own clock
NAT translations expire four minutes early, so long sessions are cut off
4.explanation: Attribution relies on public address, public port and time together; with ports reused quickly, a few minutes of error can match the report to a different internal connection. Clock drift does not cause records to be discarded or translations to expire early.

4.q: Outbound deny lines from fw01 show an internal source address but no translated source address or port, while allow lines show both. Why?
options: Deny records are written before syslog adds the NAT fields to the message
The firewall hides translated addresses on denies to avoid disclosing its public range
Translation fields appear only in session-end records, which denies also produce
A denied first packet never creates a translation entry, so there is nothing to record
4.explanation: The first packet must match an allowing rule before any translation exists; a denied packet is never translated, so it is logged with its internal source only. Denied attempts do not produce session-end records with bytes and duration.

4.q: Within three seconds one external source is dropped on ports 21, 23, 25, 135, 445, 1433, 3306 and 3389 of Banyan's single public address. Which pattern is this?
options: A vertical port scan mapping the services of one host
A horizontal sweep looking for one service across hosts
Out-of-state packets from sessions that timed out
Beaconing from an implant testing several ports
4.explanation: One source, one destination and many destination ports in seconds is a vertical scan. A horizontal sweep keeps the port fixed and varies the destination host instead.

4.q: Internal firewall logs show workstation 10.40.0.57 attempting TCP 445 on 60 other internal hosts in two minutes. How should this compare with an identical sweep of Banyan's public range from the internet?
options: Both are routine background, since sweeps on 445 run continuously everywhere
The external sweep is more serious, since it comes from an unknown party outside Banyan's control
The internal sweep is more serious, suggesting a compromised host seeking its next target
Both are equally serious, since the pattern and the port are identical
4.explanation: Internet-wide sweeps of public addresses are constant background, but an internal source sweeping internal hosts points to lateral-movement reconnaissance from a compromised machine. Direction is the deciding branch, not the shape alone.

4.q: A workstation is denied outbound on TCP 445 to the same external address three times in nine seconds, and again the next morning. What is the most proportionate next step?
options: Isolate the workstation at once, because outbound SMB is proof of worm activity
Seek the owner's explanation and check on the endpoint which process makes the attempts
Allow port 445 outbound for this host, because the denies show a business need
Ignore the denies, because the firewall blocked every attempt successfully
4.explanation: Outbound attempts on a blocked port fit malware but also a misconfigured application or a laptop looking for a home-network share, so the owner and endpoint telemetry decide. Treating it as proof skips the benign look-alike; ignoring it drops a real lead.

4.q: Allowed-session logs show 10.40.0.23 contacting 198.51.100.200 every 300 seconds (give or take one), sending 612 to 618 bytes each time. What does this analysis establish on its own?
options: That the host is running command-and-control malware and should be handed straight to the endpoint team for containment
That the destination is a software update service, since the bytes are constant
That the firewall's idle timeout is 300 seconds and is recreating the session
That a program checks in on a schedule; rarity, proxy and DNS context and the owning process decide intent
4.explanation: The regular gaps and near-identical sizes show a beacon but not whether it is malicious, because update checks and telemetry share the rhythm. Rarity across the estate, destination context and the owning process are the next steps.

4.q: A beacon-hunting rule requires identical intervals between sessions to the same destination. Why might it miss real implants?
options: Implants often add random jitter, so the rule should look for a narrow spread of gaps
Implants always use UDP, which session logs do not record with durations
Implants rotate destination ports on every check-in, which breaks grouping
Implants send their check-ins only through DNS, which bypasses the firewall
4.explanation: Real implants commonly randomise their timing slightly, so the signal is a tight distribution of gaps rather than exact repetition. Grouping is by source and destination address, so port changes would not hide the rhythm.

4.q: During the beacon investigation the analyst finds that 40 other Banyan hosts also open five-minute sessions of the same size to 198.51.100.200. How does this change the assessment?
options: It confirms malware, because the implant has clearly spread from 10.40.0.23 to 40 more Banyan hosts on the internal network
It shows the firewall duplicated one host's records across several sources
It weakens the rarity argument; widespread software is likelier, to be confirmed by destination and process
It changes nothing, because rarity plays no part in judging beacons
4.explanation: A destination contacted by many hosts in the same rhythm fits update checks, telemetry or monitoring agents, so rarity no longer supports maliciousness; identifying the vendor and the process confirms it. Jumping to a 40-host infection skips that check.

4.q: The firewall drops a packet from 10.40.0.23 to 198.51.100.80:443 flagged `ACK PSH`, logged with the prefix FW-DROP-INVALID. The host had an allowed session to that server earlier. What is the most likely explanation?
options: An attacker injecting data into the host's established HTTPS session
A session that outlived the idle timeout, so no state entry matched
A covert channel hiding data in TCP flags to bypass the rule base
A port scan using ACK packets to map the firewall's rule set
4.explanation: ACK or PSH packets without a state entry are dropped as invalid, usually because the session expired or routing was asymmetric; with a prior legitimate session this is noise. An ACK scan would come from an external source across many ports.

4.q: A next-generation firewall session shows `sent=2.1GB received=40MB` for a workstation's connection to an unfamiliar cloud address. Before reporting exfiltration, what must the analyst confirm?
options: That the session ended with tcp-fin rather than a reset
That the destination port was 443 rather than a non-standard port
That the workstation's NAT port was not reused during the session
How this vendor defines sent and received relative to the initiator
4.explanation: Vendors define the byte-direction fields differently, and reading them backwards turns a download into an apparent exfiltration. How the session ended or which port it used does not tell you the direction of the transfer.

4.q: Every night at 02:00 the file server sends about 30 GB to one external address that no other host contacts, with almost nothing received back. What is the sensible first step?
options: Confirm with the system owner whether this is a scheduled backup or sync
Block the destination at once, because the bytes ratio proves data theft
Close the alert, because large transfers at night are always backups
Raise the firewall's idle timeout so the transfer is logged as one session
4.explanation: A large outbound transfer to a rare destination fits data theft but more often a backup or sync; the owner, schedule and host role decide. Assuming either answer without that check is the mistake the lesson warns against.

4.q: An external address is dropped 300 times on assorted ports of Banyan's public range, and an hour later appears in a single allowed session to 203.0.113.14:8443. Why does this sequence merit a detection rule of its own?
options: Because allowed sessions from scanned addresses are always successful exploits
Because the drops prove the firewall's rule base was misconfigured
Because the source may have found an open path after probing
Because an allow after drops means the state table was flushed
4.explanation: 'Allowed after denied' can mean the source found a reachable service after its probing, which deserves investigation of what that session reached. It is not proof of exploitation, and the drops show the controls working rather than a misconfiguration.

4.q: An investigator asks which file a workstation downloaded during an allowed 52 KB HTTPS session found in the firewall log. What can the firewall log provide?
options: The file name, taken from the TLS server name recorded with the session
The time, addresses, ports and bytes; the file needs proxy or endpoint logs
The full URL, because stateful firewalls record the request line of each session
Nothing useful, because firewall logs record denied traffic only
4.explanation: A firewall that is not inspecting applications is content-blind: it establishes that a session happened, when and how much moved, but not URLs or file names. Content-aware sources such as proxy and endpoint logs supply those.

4.q: An attacker with administrative control of a workstation clears its event logs. Why do the perimeter firewall's logs remain trustworthy evidence of that workstation's connections?
options: Because the firewall's records are copied to the workstation and cannot be cleared there
Because firewall logs are signed with the workstation's machine certificate
Because firewalls record the content of each connection as well as its metadata
Because the firewall writes its log independently, out of the attacker's reach
4.explanation: Firewall logs are produced on a separate system that the compromised workstation does not control, which makes them reliable for establishing that connections happened. They are content-blind, so they do not record what each connection contained.

4.q: Banyan tightens egress so that workstations may reach the internet only on 80 and 443 via the proxy, with denies logged. What new detection benefit does this bring?
options: Malware attempts to use other ports become visible deny lines
Encrypted sessions on 443 become readable in the firewall log
Inbound scans of the public range stop appearing in the logs
Beacons on 443 are blocked automatically by the deny rule
4.explanation: With only needed outbound ports permitted, anything else a host tries is denied and logged, turning malware's attempts into evidence. Egress filtering does nothing to decrypt traffic and does not block beacons that use an allowed port.

4.q: A red-team report says unsolicited inbound packets were refused by fw01's final catch-all rule, yet the SIEM shows no drops at all for that window. What is the most likely cause?
options: The catch-all rule rejected rather than dropped, and rejects are never logged
The packets were matched to existing state entries and therefore not logged
Logging for the implicit default deny rule was never switched on
The firewall logged the drops under the destination's internal address only
4.explanation: The default deny at the end of the rule base often has to have logging enabled separately, so traffic refused there can leave no trace. Rejects can be logged just like drops, and unsolicited packets have no state entries to match.

4.q: Why does a stateful firewall's log normally contain one or two records per connection rather than a line for every packet that crosses it?
options: Because packets after the first are discarded once the rule base has been evaluated
Because rules are evaluated for the first packet and later packets match the state table
Because syslog merges packets with the same 5-tuple into one message before sending
Because only TCP packets carrying the SYN flag are ever permitted through a stateful firewall
4.explanation: The rule base decides on the first packet; later packets in both directions are matched against the state entry, so the firewall logs decisions at session start, end or both. Later packets are forwarded, not discarded.

4.q: Counting distinct destination ports and distinct destinations per source in the drop log shows 198.51.100.140 with one port (23) and eight destinations, 203.0.113.11 to 203.0.113.18. How should it be classified?
options: A vertical scan of one Banyan host, to be escalated as targeted reconnaissance
Out-of-state noise from an expired Telnet session to several servers
An internal host attempting outbound Telnet against policy
A horizontal sweep of the public range, background unless linked to other evidence
4.explanation: One port across many hosts is a horizontal sweep, and a sweep of public addresses from the internet is everyday background until other evidence connects it to Banyan. A vertical scan would show many ports on a single host.

4.q: The SOC wants a rule that detects one internal workstation probing many other internal hosts, but its only firewall data comes from the perimeter firewall. What is the fundamental problem?
options: Perimeter firewalls never see east-west traffic, so internal or flow logs are needed
Perimeter firewalls log internal traffic only when it is denied, not allowed
Internal addresses are translated by NAT, hiding which workstation scanned
Perimeter firewalls record internal scans, but only in session-end records
4.explanation: Traffic between internal hosts never crosses the perimeter, so it cannot appear in its logs; segmentation with logging between zones, or flow logs, is required. Source NAT applies only to traffic leaving for the internet.

4.q: A firewall blocks all direct outbound traffic from workstations except DNS queries to the internal resolver. Why can an implant on a workstation still deliver data to an outside party over DNS?
options: The resolver relays the full query name, including encoded leftmost labels, to the zone's authoritative server
The resolver opens a direct TCP session between the workstation and the outside server on port 53 for the query
The root servers cache the encoded labels and forward copies to every registered domain owner
The stub resolver bypasses the internal resolver whenever a query uses the TXT record type
4.explanation: Recursion carries the whole name to whoever runs the zone's authoritative server, so labels can carry data without any direct connection. No direct workstation-to-server session is ever opened; the internal resolver relays both directions.

4.q: A resolver log shows that every suspicious query in an alert came from 10.40.0.5, the address of a branch office's local DNS forwarder. What is the best next step to identify the infected machine?
options: Treat the forwarder as the infected host and reimage it immediately
Search passive DNS for the suspicious names to find the client address
Use the forwarder's own query logs, DHCP leases or Sysmon event 22 to attribute the queries
Lower the TTL on the suspicious names so the client re-queries the central resolver directly
4.explanation: Behind a forwarder all queries appear to come from the forwarder, so attribution needs its logs, DHCP leases or endpoint DNS telemetry. Passive DNS records name-to-address answers, not which internal client asked.

4.q: A resolver log shows WS-104 looking up an unfamiliar domain, and the analyst needs to know whether the browser or a script made the query. Which source answers this directly?
options: The Zeek dns.log entry with its RD and RA flags
Sysmon event ID 22, which records the Image that made the query
The recursive resolver's query log with the response code
A passive DNS lookup of the domain's historical answers
4.explanation: Sysmon event 22 (DNSEvent) includes the process image, the only one of the three vantage points that names the asking process. Resolver and sensor logs identify the client address but not the process.

4.q: A workstation sends DNS queries on UDP port 53 straight to an internet address rather than to the internal resolver. Which source is most likely to reveal this, and why?
options: The internal resolver's log, because it records every query for every external zone, including ones sent elsewhere
Sysmon event 1, because it records each DNS packet as a process creation
Passive DNS, because it stores every query made by the organisation's hosts
A network sensor or firewall log, because the internal resolver never sees queries that bypass it
4.explanation: Queries sent directly to an outside server never touch the internal resolver, so only on-path sources such as a Zeek sensor or firewall logs see them. The resolver log is blind to traffic that bypasses it.

4.q: In a ten-minute window one client makes 60 queries: 55 return NXDOMAIN for 54 different unpronounceable names of similar length, and one similar-looking name returns NOERROR with 198.51.100.14. What is the most useful next pivot?
options: Add the 54 failing names to a blocklist and close the alert
Ask the user whether they mistyped several addresses during the window
Search firewall and proxy logs for connections from the client to 198.51.100.14
Raise the NXDOMAIN threshold, since failed lookups carry no network traffic and the noise hides real alerts
4.explanation: The burst fits DGA behaviour, and the single successful resolution is the likely controller, so its answer address is the pivot into connection logs. Blocking failing names is pointless because those names were never registered.

4.q: A DGA detection requires, per client per window, nx >= 25 AND nx_ratio >= 0.5 AND names >= 20. Which benign case is excluded specifically by the names >= 20 condition?
options: One application repeatedly retrying a single dead hostname
A busy server with a few failures among thousands of successes
A user making occasional typing mistakes in the browser
A CDN host name that is long and high in entropy
4.explanation: A retry loop can produce many NXDOMAINs at a high ratio but for one name only; requiring many distinct names removes it. The busy server is excluded by the ratio condition, not the distinct-name count.

4.q: Why does a DNS tunnel that sends data upstream normally use a different query name for every chunk of data?
options: Authoritative servers refuse to answer the same name twice within one TTL
RFC 1035 forbids a client from repeating a query name in the same session, so the resolver would drop the repeat
Root servers rate-limit repeated names, so new names avoid throttling
A repeated name would be answered from the resolver's cache and never reach the authoritative server
4.explanation: Caching means a repeated name is served locally for the TTL, so the data would never arrive at the zone owner; fresh names force recursion each time. RFC 1035 sets size limits, not a ban on repeated names.

4.q: An analyst measures Shannon entropy of leftmost labels and finds banyan-payroll-update scores 3.54 while the random qxv7rk2mzt9bwp scores 3.81. What does this show about entropy as a detection feature?
options: Entropy is unreliable only for hexadecimal labels and should be computed in Base32 so that word-based names score higher
Entropy rises with length for varied text, so on its own it cannot separate word-based malicious names from random ones
Dictionary-word domains are always benign, so the 3.54 score is a false positive
Entropy values above 3.5 bits per character prove the name was machine-generated
4.explanation: The lookalike made of words scored almost as high as the random string because entropy grows with varied, longer text, so entropy must be combined with rarity, volume and other features. A 3.5 threshold would flag the word-based name too, so it proves nothing.

4.q: A string of 32 characters drawn uniformly from the hexadecimal alphabet is measured with Shannon entropy. Which value is it expected to approach?
options: About 4 bits per character, the ceiling for a 16-symbol alphabet
About 5 bits per character, because its length is 32
About 2 bits per character, like a short English word
About 0 bits per character, because only digits and letters a-f appear
4.explanation: With 16 equally likely symbols the maximum is log2 16 = 4 bits per character, which a long uniform hex string approaches. Five bits would need 32 distinct, equally frequent symbols, which a 16-symbol alphabet cannot provide.

4.q: A protective DNS alert flags long, high-entropy labels from a single host. Which finding most strengthens the case for DNS tunnelling rather than CDN traffic?
options: The names resolve successfully with NOERROR
The parent domain is under a well-known cloud provider used by every host, which is how tunnels usually hide their traffic
Hundreds of distinct names under one young parent zone, asked by that host only, with a high TXT share
The queries are of type A and AAAA with short CNAME chains
4.explanation: Many unique subdomains under one unfamiliar parent from one client, plus TXT for the return path, is the structural tunnel signature. A well-known parent used estate-wide is the CDN look-alike, not evidence of a tunnel.

4.q: A host produced 1,000 unique query names under one parent zone, each carrying about 150 encoded characters in its labels. What is the reasonable upper estimate of data that could have left?
options: About 1.5 kilobytes, because only the final label carries data
About 150 kilobytes of encoded text
About 150 megabytes, because each name triggers a full TXT response
Nothing measurable, because DNS queries carry no payload
4.explanation: The total length of the encoded names bounds upstream data: 1,000 x 150 characters is roughly 150 kilobytes of encoded text. Upstream data rides in the names, so response sizes do not inflate it to megabytes.

4.q: During triage a mail gateway and a finance workstation both show many TXT queries. Which interpretation follows the lesson's triage logic?
options: Both are suspicious, because TXT records exist only to carry tunnelled data and no legitimate mail process ever needs them at all
Neither is suspicious, because TXT is used for SPF and DMARC policy
The gateway is suspicious because servers should never query TXT records
The gateway's TXT queries fit SPF and DMARC checks, while a high TXT share from a workstation to one zone needs investigation
4.explanation: Client role decides: mail servers routinely query TXT for email policy, ordinary desktops rarely do, so a workstation's TXT share to one parent is the signal. Saying TXT is only for tunnels ignores its legitimate SPF and DMARC use.

4.q: Every workstation in the estate queries three random single-label names a few seconds after the browser starts, all returning NXDOMAIN. How should this be classified?
options: Benign browser probing for networks that rewrite NXDOMAIN answers
An estate-wide DGA infection that needs immediate containment
A DNS tunnel, because the labels are random and the answers fail
Misconfigured DHCP options pointing hosts at a broken resolver
4.explanation: Browser probes come from every host, at launch, as a few random single-label names, which is the documented benign look-alike. A DGA burst is many names from one client at machine speed, not a handful from every host.

4.q: A SIEM's DNS pipeline drops NXDOMAIN responses to reduce storage. Which detection does this change break most directly?
options: Unique-subdomain counts for tunnels that receive NOERROR answers
Short-TTL churn detection for fast-flux hosting
NXDOMAIN-ratio detection of DGA malware
Newly-seen-domain alerts for names that resolve successfully
4.explanation: DGA detection depends on counting failed lookups for many names, so discarding NXDOMAINs removes its evidence. Fast-flux and tunnel detections use successful answers and are less affected.

4.q: A SOC reports no DNS tunnelling alerts in six months. Under which condition is that absence meaningful?
options: When the resolver logs only successful responses to save space
When the protective DNS service has a large blocklist of known-bad zones, so tunnels to those zones are stopped before any alert
When Sysmon event 22 is enabled on servers but not on workstations
When egress controls block outbound port 53, DoT and public DoH so that all DNS passes through the logged resolver
4.explanation: Resolver logs only mean everything when every query is forced through the resolver; otherwise DoH, external resolvers or hard-coded IPs leave no trace. A blocklist stops known zones but says nothing about traffic that bypasses the resolver.

4.q: An analyst sees a domain whose answers change on almost every query and carry a TTL of 30 seconds. Which conclusion is the most defensible?
options: It proves the domain is a DGA domain, because DGAs use short TTLs
It is one trait of fast-flux hosting, but load-balanced services also use short TTLs, so more context is needed
It proves DNS tunnelling, because short TTLs defeat resolver caching and force every query out to the authoritative server
It is harmless, because only NXDOMAIN answers matter in DNS analysis
4.explanation: Short TTLs with churning answers fit fast flux (T1568.001) but also legitimate load balancing, so rarity and reputation must decide. DGAs are characterised by many failing names, not by short TTLs.

4.q: After a DGA-infected host is detected, the team blocks the one domain that resolved and closes the case. What is the main flaw?
options: The algorithm will produce new candidate names, and the process on the host has not been found or removed
Blocking a domain at the resolver also blocks every CDN that shares its address, so the block must be rolled back first
The NXDOMAIN names must be registered by defenders before the case can close
The block will not apply until the domain's TTL has expired across the internet
4.explanation: A DGA generates fresh names daily, so blocking is only containment; the responsible process must still be identified and eradicated. Registering the failing names is a sinkholing tactic, not a requirement for closing a case.

4.q: In the lab's domain-stacking query, the clause substr(url, 9, instr(substr(url,9),'/')-1) is used. What would go wrong if the dataset contained plain http:// URLs?
options: The query would fail with a syntax error, because instr needs three arguments when the input string starts with http://
COUNT(DISTINCT host) would double-count every http request
Domains would be returned with the trailing slash included
The fixed offset of 9 assumes the 8-character https:// prefix, so http:// domains would lose their first character
4.explanation: Position 9 skips exactly 'https://'; 'http://' is 7 characters, so extraction would start one character into the host name. The instr length expression already stops before the slash, so no trailing slash is included.

4.q: The lab's domain stacking returns six domains seen on all eight hosts and three seen on one host only, first seen at 06:12, 06:17 and 08:12. What does ordering by host count and then first_seen achieve?
options: It sorts domains by traffic volume so the largest upload is listed first
It puts the rarest names first in time order, approximating a newly-observed-domain view
It removes the baseline domains from the result entirely
It proves the three rare domains were resolved by the internal DNS server
4.explanation: Sorting by distinct hosts brings rare names to the top and first_seen orders them chronologically, a stand-in for first-seen alerting. It does not filter out the baseline, and proxy data cannot prove any resolver lookup took place.

4.q: Which detection would have caught banyan-payroll-update.example even though its entropy was unremarkable?
options: An NXDOMAIN-ratio rule on the client's queries
A label-length rule alerting on labels longer than 50 characters, since brand lookalikes are usually long
Names containing the brand string that are not under the organisation's own registered domains
A TXT-share rule for workstations querying one parent zone
4.explanation: The domain imitates banyan.example under a different registered domain, so a brand-string check outside owned domains flags it, along with rarity and recency. It resolved, was short and used ordinary lookups, so NXDOMAIN, length and TXT rules miss it.

4.q: Banyan collected no resolver logs. Which evidence would resolver logs have added that the proxy data cannot provide?
options: The 48.2 MB size of the upload to files-share-drop.example
The 220-byte size of each beacon request
The authenticated user name attached to each web request
Names that were looked up but never reached the proxy, and the addresses returned for them
4.explanation: A DNS view adds lookups that never became web requests, such as a fallback DGA or DNS channel, plus answer addresses for pivoting. Upload and beacon sizes are proxy evidence that DNS logs do not contain.

4.q: On a managed workstation, a browser sends DNS over HTTPS to a public provider. Why does the lesson treat this as a control problem even though DoH is not malicious?
options: It bypasses the internal resolver, so its queries escape logging and protective DNS
It is forbidden by RFC 1035 for clients inside a corporate network
It forces all queries to use TCP port 853, which firewalls cannot inspect
It disables the browser's TLS certificate validation for every site
4.explanation: DoH hides queries inside HTTPS to an outside provider, so the resolver's logging and blocking never apply; defenders disable it by policy and block known endpoints. Port 853 is DoT, not DoH, which travels on 443.

4.q: A team wants one estate-wide threshold for 'too many distinct names per client per hour'. Why is this likely to fail?
options: Distinct-name counts cannot be computed in SQL without a window function, which most SIEM back ends still do not support
Mail gateways, servers and workstations have very different DNS profiles, so one threshold produces noise or misses
Distinct-name counts are only meaningful for NXDOMAIN answers
Registered-domain grouping makes per-client counts impossible
4.explanation: Baselines must be per client role: a mail gateway's normal volume would swamp a workstation threshold. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) with GROUP BY works fine in SQL, so the problem is the baseline, not the query.

4.q: A detection groups DNS queries by full query name to look for tunnelling. Why should it also group by registered domain?
options: Registered-domain grouping removes all CDN traffic automatically, leaving only the tunnel's parent zone in the result
Full query names are not stored by recursive resolvers
A tunnel's thousands of unique full names each appear once, but collapse into one large row per parent zone
Grouping by full name hides NXDOMAIN answers from the result
4.explanation: Each tunnelled chunk is a different full name, so per-name counts look small; grouping by the parent zone reveals the volume. Registered-domain grouping does not remove CDN traffic; rarity and reputation do that.

4.q: A DNS log entry shows 'qname: 4f6a3c9e...2d.t.example, qtype: TXT, rcode: NOERROR' from a workstation, the only such query from any host. Under the lesson's triage table, which check most directly separates a tunnel from a one-off oddity?
options: Counting how many distinct names under t.example this client queried in the same window
Checking whether the TXT answer exceeded 255 bytes
Confirming that the RCODE was NOERROR rather than SERVFAIL
Measuring the entropy of the registered domain t.example
4.explanation: A single strange name is noise; hundreds of unique names under the same parent from one client is the tunnel pattern, so the distinct-name count is decisive. The registered domain itself is short and ordinary, so its entropy says little.

4.q: A newly onboarded Squid proxy uses the default native access.log format. An analyst writes an exfiltration rule on its single byte field. What is the problem?
options: The byte field in that format is recorded in kilobytes, so thresholds are off by 1,024
The byte field in the default format is the reply size sent to the client, so it measures downloads, not uploads
The byte field counts request and reply bytes combined in one total, so uploads cannot be isolated from downloads
The byte field is only populated for CONNECT tunnels, not for ordinary requests
4.explanation: Squid's default native format logs the size of the reply delivered to the client, so it is good for downloads and poor for uploads; measuring uploads needs a custom format. The field is in bytes and is not a combined total.

4.q: A host produces a steady stream of HTTP 407 responses in the proxy log at regular intervals. What is the most accurate reading?
options: The destination server is rejecting the host's requests as forbidden
The proxy has blocked the destination by URL category
The destination server is temporarily overloaded and asking the client to retry later, which points to a capacity problem rather than the host
Software that is not proxy-aware or lacks proxy credentials, which may be a broken updater or an implant beaconing
4.explanation: 407 is the proxy's own Proxy Authentication Required answer, and regular 407s are a beacon-shaped pattern whether from an updater or an implant. A forbidden answer from the server or a policy block would be 403, not 407.

4.q: A proxy does not perform TLS inspection. An implant beacons over HTTPS to a rare domain every five minutes. Which analysis remains possible from the proxy log?
options: Rarity, timing regularity and tunnel volume from the repeated CONNECT records
Per-request URL paths such as /api/v2/ping and the HTTP methods used for each beacon
The inner HTTP status code and content type of every beacon request
Malware scanning and DLP inspection of the beacon's request bodies
4.explanation: Without inspection the proxy still logs CONNECT host:port, tunnel totals and timing, so rarity, rhythm and volume analysis work. Paths, methods, inner status and content scanning require inspection.

4.q: Without TLS inspection, a client keeps one long-lived CONNECT tunnel open for an hour and sends many beacon requests inside it. What is the consequence for beacon detection?
options: Each inner request still produces its own log line with a timestamp, so the beacon rhythm remains visible
The proxy reports an error and terminates the tunnel after the first request
Many requests may be hidden inside one tunnel record, so per-request rhythm is not visible
The tunnel is logged as a 407 because the proxy cannot authenticate it
4.explanation: An uninspected tunnel is logged once with its totals, so a long-lived tunnel can hide many requests and per-request timing disappears. Separate log lines per inner request only exist with inspection.

4.q: The lab query 'SELECT json_extract(raw,'$.status') AS status, COUNT(*) n FROM events WHERE source='proxy' GROUP BY status' returns a single row: 200 | 284. What does this mean for the investigation?
options: The attacker's requests all succeeded, so evidence must come from rarity, rhythm and volume rather than status codes
No malicious activity occurred, because blocked or failed requests would show non-200 codes and the attack would have been stopped
The proxy did not log status codes, and 200 is a default placeholder value
The proxy performed no TLS inspection, because inspected traffic returns 407
4.explanation: Status 200 means the requests worked, not that they were benign; with one status value the lab's evidence lies in rarity, rhythm and volume. Success codes are evidence of activity succeeding, so the second option is the misconception.

4.q: In the lab, minisiem.py stores ts, host, user, src_ip, url and bytes_out as columns. How can an analyst read the proxy status code, which is not a normalised column?
options: By rerunning minisiem.py load with a --status flag to add the column
With json_extract(raw, '$.status'), because the whole original event is kept in the raw column
By joining the events table to a separate status table created during load
It cannot be read; fields outside the normalised columns are discarded on load to keep the database small
4.explanation: minisiem.py keeps each original event in a raw column, so SQLite's json_extract can read any field such as status. Nothing in the lesson describes a status flag or a separate status table.

4.q: Hunt H1 reports 'n=18 mean_gap=300s cv=0.004' for WS-104's ping URL. What does the CV value tell you about the timing?
options: Gaps varied between roughly 0 and 600 seconds around the mean
Only 0.4 percent of the requests arrived on schedule
The beacon used 20 percent jitter, which H1 then corrected for before computing the mean gap of 300s
The standard deviation of the gaps is about 1.2 seconds, so the contact is machine-regular
4.explanation: CV is standard deviation divided by mean, so 0.004 x 300 s is about 1.2 seconds of spread, consistent with gaps like 06:17:00, 06:22:01, 06:27:03. A wide 0-600 s spread would give a CV near 0.5 or more.

4.q: An implant beacons every 300 seconds with 20 percent random jitter. Why does the lesson recommend scoring several features rather than relying on near-zero interval CV?
options: Jitter makes the requests use different domains each time, defeating rarity
Jitter raises the CV, so regularity alone can be defeated, while rarity, constant sizes and persistence still betray the beacon
Jitter causes the proxy to log the requests as CONNECT tunnels instead of URLs
Jitter pushes the CV above 1.0, which is indistinguishable from human browsing
4.explanation: Jitter is designed to defeat naive regularity checks, but a jittered beacon still has rare destinations, small constant sizes and persistence, and its CV stays well under 1. Jitter changes timing, not the destination domain.

4.q: The lab's rule R6 returns ('WS-104', 'https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping', 18, 220, 220). What feature does R6 add beyond hunt H1?
options: Size regularity: every request falls within a narrow byte range, here exactly 220 bytes
Rarity: the URL is visited by only one host in the estate
Upload volume: total bytes sent exceed a fixed threshold
Scope: no other host contacted the same URL
4.explanation: R6 checks at least 10 hits with sizes within 50 bytes, and the minimum and maximum of 220 show identical request sizes. Upload thresholds are R4's job and scope is H3's.

4.q: WS-104's average upload is 984,961 bytes while other hosts average about 2,000 to 2,500 bytes. Why is the mean a poor baseline here?
options: The mean ignores requests with zero bytes_out, which inflates the result for hosts that mostly send empty requests
The mean is computed per URL rather than per host in minisiem.py
The mean cannot be computed on integer columns in SQLite
One 48,200,000-byte request distorts it, suggesting every request is about a megabyte when almost all are small
4.explanation: A single huge upload dominates WS-104's mean; maxima, percentiles or per-destination totals describe volume better. The query in the lesson groups by host, so the per-URL claim is false.

4.q: All other proxy requests in the dataset together sent 560,116 bytes, and the single upload sent 48,200,000. Rule R4 uses a fixed threshold of bytes_out > 10000000. What is the main weakness of R4 in production?
options: It cannot detect any upload smaller than 48 MB
It only works when TLS inspection is enabled
Legitimate large uploads to sanctioned storage would trigger it, so it needs per-user baselines and destination category
It counts download bytes rather than uploaded bytes, so it would mostly fire on large software updates and file downloads
4.explanation: A fixed threshold is blunt: sanctioned large uploads are common, while first-time uploads to unsanctioned file sharing are not, so baselines and category sharpen it. The lab's bytes_out is the upload direction, so downloads do not trigger it.

4.q: Hunt H3 matches known-bad domains with patterns like url LIKE '%://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/%' rather than '%cdn-telemetry-sync.example%'. Why?
options: LIKE patterns without a slash are not supported by SQLite
Anchoring on the scheme separator and trailing slash prevents false matches on look-alikes such as cdn-telemetry-sync.example.org
The trailing slash is needed so that only HTTPS URLs are matched
It makes the LIKE search case-insensitive, so any upper-case spellings of the domain such as CDN-TELEMETRY-SYNC.EXAMPLE also match
4.explanation: Matching '://' before and '/' after the domain stops a longer name that merely contains it as a substring from matching. The scheme separator matches http and https alike, so it does not restrict to HTTPS.

4.q: The proxy shows the beacon and upload logged under the user divya. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Requests left WS-104 carrying divya's session identity, which software running in her session inherits, so the process must be found on the endpoint
Divya deliberately sent 48.2 MB to an external file-sharing service
Divya's credentials were stolen and used from another machine
The proxy authenticated divya interactively before each beacon request
4.explanation: Proxy identity is the session's identity, and an implant in that session inherits it, so the endpoint pivot decides which process acted. The requests came from WS-104 itself, so use from another machine is not supported.

4.q: Which wording of the 08:12 finding best matches the strength of the proxy evidence?
options: Divya exfiltrated the payroll database to files-share-drop.example
The beacon channel was used to steal customer records
48.2 MB of company data was confirmed stolen and must be reported as a breach of personal data under the DPDP Act within the deadline
Likely exfiltration: 48,200,000 bytes were sent from WS-104 under divya's identity to a file-sharing domain; the content is unknown
4.explanation: The proxy proves size, destination, host and session identity, not what the data was or who acted, so 'likely exfiltration' with stated unknowns is right. The other options assert content or intent that the proxy cannot show.

4.q: In the persistence query for 06:17 to 07:43, only the WS-104 ping URL reached five or more hits. Why does the lesson still apply rarity before this kind of frequency check?
options: Frequency queries cannot run in SQLite without first filtering by rarity, because GROUP BY with HAVING needs a pre-filtered table
Popular destinations such as webmail or update services can also be contacted often and regularly, so frequency alone misleads
Rarity determines the correct time window for the frequency query
Frequency checks only work on domains that appear on a single host
4.explanation: A regular series to a domain every host uses is usually an update or sync service, so rarity first removes those benign frequent contacts. It is analytic order, not an SQL restriction.

4.q: The lab proxy records contain full URLs such as https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping. What does this indicate about Banyan's proxy?
options: It is a transparent proxy that does not need any client configuration
It logs only CONNECT tunnels and reconstructs paths afterwards
Its HTTPS traffic is visible at request level, as with TLS inspection
The beacon used plain HTTP disguised with an https:// prefix
4.explanation: A full HTTPS path per request is only available when the proxy is a party to the encryption, which the lesson places in the inspected column. Uninspected tunnels yield host and port only, and paths cannot be reconstructed afterwards.

4.q: The question 2 query finds one .docm URL with bytes_out = 812. Why is this byte value small even though a document was delivered?
options: bytes_out counts client-to-server bytes, and a download's request is small; the file size would be in a bytes-in field the lab lacks
The proxy compressed the document to 812 bytes before logging it
The download failed partway through, so only 812 bytes of the file were received on WS-104 and the rest of the document never arrived
Macro-enabled documents are always smaller than one kilobyte
4.explanation: bytes_out measures what the client sent, so a GET is tiny; the document's size would appear as bytes in. The status was 200, so the download did not fail.

4.q: Why does the lesson treat a file extension in the URL as a weaker delivery indicator than a gateway's MIME type and malware verdict?
options: Extensions are removed from URLs by TLS inspection
MIME types are recorded only for uploads, which makes them more precise
Extensions can only be matched with regular expressions, not LIKE
The adversary chooses the URL path freely, while content type and scanning reflect what was actually served
4.explanation: An extension is just part of a path the adversary picks, so it can be omitted or faked; content type and scanning describe the response itself. The lesson's own query matches extensions with LIKE, so the regular-expression claim is false.

4.q: Building the WS-104 timeline, an analyst notes a mail.banyan.example visit at 06:04 and the invoice.docm download at 06:12. What can the proxy evidence support about the delivery route?
options: It proves the document link arrived by phishing email at 06:04
It proves the user typed the lookalike URL manually
The sequence fits a phishing link, but confirming that the link was in an email needs mail logs
It proves the download was triggered by the PowerShell process
4.explanation: The proxy shows a mail visit followed by a download, which fits phishing, but only mail logs can show the link in a message. PowerShell started at 06:14, after the download, so it cannot have triggered it.

4.q: The timeline query uses ts BETWEEN '2026-11-03T06:00' AND '2026-11-03T06:30' on text timestamps. Why does this comparison return the correct rows?
options: SQLite converts ISO 8601 strings to Unix time before comparing
ISO 8601 strings in one format and one time zone (UTC, Z) sort lexically in time order
BETWEEN ignores the date part and compares only the time
minisiem.py stores timestamps as integers, so the strings are converted to Unix time on load
4.explanation: Same-format, same-zone ISO 8601 strings sort in chronological order as text, so string comparison works. Mixing time zones or formats would break this, which is why consistent UTC matters.

4.q: In the merged timeline, Word downloads the document at 06:12, PowerShell starts at 06:14 and the first ping appears at 06:17. Which source shows that PowerShell's parent was Word?
options: Hunt H2's rare parent-child pair WINWORD.EXE -> powershell.exe from endpoint process telemetry
The proxy's user agent field on the 06:17 ping request
Windows event 4720 created at 07:02
The R6 size-regularity rule output for the ping URL
4.explanation: Process lineage comes from endpoint process creation data, which H2 summarises as a parent-child pair seen on one host. The lab proxy has no user agent field, and 4720 is account creation.

4.q: WS-104's hourly proxy counts are 3, 3, 1, 14, 11, 3, 5, 2, 5, 2 for hours 03 to 12. What best explains the 06 and 07 peaks?
options: The 48.2 MB upload was split across many smaller proxy requests during those two hours
Divya's working day started at 06:00, so normal browsing increased
The proxy duplicated log lines during a restart in those hours
The five-minute beacon, about twelve requests per hour, was active from 06:17 to 07:42
4.explanation: A 300-second beacon adds about twelve requests per hour, which accounts for most of the 14 and 11 in hours 06 and 07. The upload was a single request at 08:12, not spread across these hours.

4.q: A SOC wants its proxy logs to cover all web egress, including staff working from home. Which combination of controls achieves this?
options: Enable TLS inspection on the on-premises proxy only
Block direct outbound HTTP/HTTPS from workstations and extend coverage to remote users with a cloud SWG or always-on VPN
Require proxy authentication and rely on firewall logs for remote users
Publish a WPAD file and allow workstations to fall back to direct connections
4.explanation: Completeness requires that traffic cannot bypass the proxy and that off-network users still pass through a gateway. Inspection or authentication improves record content but does not stop bypass, and a direct fallback defeats coverage.

4.q: An organisation is deciding whether to enable TLS inspection on its proxy. Which consideration does the lesson place alongside the technical benefits?
options: Inspection removes the need to retain proxy logs for 180 days
Inspection makes proxy logs exempt from personal data rules
Decrypted browsing is personal data under the DPDP Act 2023, so purpose, exemptions such as banking and health, and access controls must be documented
Inspection must be applied to all categories without exemption to be lawful
4.explanation: Inspection is a privacy and legal decision as well as technical, needing documented purpose, exemptions and restricted access. It does not change CERT-In's 180-day retention requirement or remove DPDP obligations.

4.q: In Banyan's case, H3 reports 'none found' for other hosts contacting the three known-bad domains. Which additional indicators should a thorough scope search also use?
options: Destination IP addresses, the /api/v2/ping path on other domains, the user agent if logged and the 220-byte request size
Only the full URLs already in the alert, since domains are the strongest indicator and IP addresses change too often to be useful
The hourly request counts of every host compared with WS-104's
Every URL ending in .docm visited by any host in the last year
4.explanation: Scope should use every indicator a case produces, because an adversary may reuse infrastructure or paths under new domains. Searching only the known URLs repeats H3 and can miss the same implant on another domain.

4.q: In minisiem, SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE event_id='4720' returns 0, yet the analyst knows an account was created. Which follow-up query best diagnoses the problem?
options: Rerun the same query with LIKE '%4720%' to catch any formatting differences
SELECT typeof(event_id), COUNT(*) FROM events GROUP BY 1, to see how the field is stored
Reload the dataset, because a zero count means the 4720 event was never ingested
Widen the time range, because the account creation probably falls outside the loaded day
4.explanation: typeof() shows the event IDs are stored as integers, so the text '4720' never equals the integer 4720 in a table without declared column types. A substring LIKE might appear to work but hides the type mismatch rather than diagnosing it.

4.q: An analyst excludes 'internal traffic' from a proxy hunt with WHERE url NOT LIKE '%banyan%'. In the Banyan dataset, what is the most serious consequence?
options: The query becomes slow because a leading wildcard prevents any index use
Requests to cdn.example.org are wrongly treated as internal and dropped
Upper-case host names such as CRM.BANYAN.EXAMPLE slip through the exclusion and flood the hunt with internal noise
The request to the look-alike banyan-payroll-update.example is removed along with genuine internal sites
4.explanation: The phishing domain was chosen because it contains 'banyan', so a substring exclusion removes the request that started the intrusion. Performance is a minor concern by comparison; the fix is an anchored suffix test on the extracted domain such as LIKE '%.banyan.example'.

4.q: An indicator search url LIKE '%cdn%' returns 64 proxy requests: 18 to cdn-telemetry-sync.example and 46 to cdn.example.org, which all eight workstations use. If the 18 beacon requests are the only genuine matches, what are the query's precision and recall?
options: Precision about 0.28, recall 1.0
Precision 1.0, recall about 0.28
Precision about 0.72, recall 1.0
Precision about 0.28, recall about 0.72
4.explanation: Precision is true matches over returned rows (18/64, about 0.28); recall is true matches over all genuine matches (18/18 = 1.0). Swapping the two definitions gives the second option, which describes a query that misses events rather than one that over-matches.

4.q: Timestamps are stored as strings like 2026-11-03T07:02:00Z. A query uses ts BETWEEN '2026-11-03T06:00' AND '2026-11-03T07:02' and returns 15 events for WS-104 instead of 17. Why are the 07:02 events missing?
options: BETWEEN is exclusive at both ends in SQLite, so the events in the upper minute are never included in the result
The 'Z' suffix makes the stored values UTC while the bounds are read as local time
The short upper bound is a prefix of the stored value and therefore sorts before every 07:02 timestamp
String comparison treats the 'T' separator as a wildcard, so seconds are ignored
4.explanation: In string ordering a prefix sorts before the longer string that begins with it, so '...T07:02' is less than '...T07:02:00Z' and both 07:02 events fall outside the range. BETWEEN is in fact inclusive; the fix is a half-open range in the full stored format ending at 07:03:00Z.

4.q: A team counts events per hour with consecutive windows. Why does the lesson recommend half-open intervals (start <= ts < end) for this?
options: They allow the database to use the time index, which BETWEEN cannot
They automatically convert timestamps to UTC before comparison
Consecutive windows tile cleanly, so no event on a boundary is counted twice or dropped
They exclude both edges, removing duplicate events logged at exactly the hour
4.explanation: Including the start and excluding the end means an event at exactly 08:00:00 belongs to one window only. Inclusive edges on both sides would double-count it; half-open intervals do not exclude both edges.

4.q: WS-104 has 4 Windows events and 49 proxy events. Joining them only on host and then reporting SUM(p.bytes_out) gives a total four times too large. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Bound the join with a time window and aggregate or count distinct values rather than raw joined rows
Replace the JOIN with a LEFT JOIN so unmatched proxy rows are kept once
Add ORDER BY p.ts so that duplicate proxy rows are grouped together
Move the host condition from ON into WHERE so it is applied after the join and each proxy row is counted once
4.explanation: Each proxy row matched all four Windows rows (196 rows), so sums and counts are multiplied: fan-out. Bounding by time and aggregating each side or counting distinct values fixes it. A LEFT JOIN keeps more rows and does not remove the multiplication.

4.q: An analyst wants every 4720, 4732 and 1102 event listed with the count of proxy requests in the 15 minutes before it, including events with none. They write a LEFT JOIN but put p.source='proxy' in the WHERE clause. What happens?
options: Windows events without matching proxy rows show a count of zero, as intended
The query fails with an error, because WHERE cannot reference a column from the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN
Each Windows event is repeated once per proxy row, inflating the result
Windows events with no qualifying proxy row are discarded, turning the outer join into an inner join
4.explanation: For unmatched rows the right-hand columns are NULL, so a WHERE test on them is not true and the row is filtered out. Conditions on the right-hand table must sit in ON to keep unmatched left rows. The query runs without error, which is what makes the mistake dangerous.

4.q: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user) FROM events WHERE user NOT IN (SELECT target_user FROM events) returns 0, while the NOT EXISTS version returns 8. What explains the zero?
options: NOT IN compares case-sensitively, so no user name matched the subquery's format
The subquery contains NULLs, and comparing a value with NULL is unknown, so no row satisfies NOT IN
NOT IN is evaluated before DISTINCT, so duplicate users cancel each other out
The subquery returns svc_update, which matches every user through implicit wildcarding in the comparison
4.explanation: 338 of the 340 target_user values are NULL. x NOT IN (list) is true only if x is known to differ from every element, and a comparison with NULL is unknown, so nothing qualifies. NOT EXISTS ignores NULLs because they never match; case sensitivity has nothing to do with it.

4.q: A shift lead asks 'did the phish hit anyone else?'. Which element of the query specification determines that the result should have one row per host and user, and therefore the GROUP BY?
options: The grain
The population
The window
The condition
4.explanation: Grain states what one result row represents, which fixes the GROUP BY. The population names sources and time range; the condition is the predicate on the domain; neither decides the level of aggregation.

4.q: The question is 'which workstation sent more than 1 MB in total to a destination no other workstation uses?'. Why does the lesson build it from a CTE that counts distinct hosts per domain, joined back to the events?
options: Because SQLite cannot use COUNT(DISTINCT) and SUM in the same SELECT
Because the CTE caches the proxy events in memory, which makes the query run much faster on the full events table
Because destination breadth belongs to the domain grain while the byte total belongs to the host and domain grain
Because HAVING cannot refer to a column derived from the URL
4.explanation: Breadth is a property of a domain across all hosts; the 1 MB total is a property of one host and domain pair. Computing breadth separately and joining it keeps the two grains apart. SQLite does allow COUNT(DISTINCT) and SUM together; the issue is grain, not syntax.

4.q: An exfiltration query flags any single proxy request with bytes_out above 1,000,000. An attacker uploads 40 MB as many 900 KB requests to one destination. How should the query be changed to catch this?
options: Lower the per-request threshold to 500 KB so each piece exceeds it
Filter on a URL path containing 'upload' instead of on bytes
Count requests per host per hour and alert above the busiest hour seen so far
Sum bytes_out per host and destination and apply the threshold to the total in HAVING
4.explanation: A threshold at the event grain misses activity split across many events; summing at the host and destination grain catches the total regardless of chunk size. Lowering the per-request threshold only moves the cut, and the attacker can shrink the pieces again.

4.q: The beacon to cdn-telemetry-sync.example made 18 requests totalling 3,960 bytes. What does this tell you about choosing a query to find similar beacons?
options: A destination-breadth query is useless, because beacons always use popular domains
Volume thresholds will not find it; a query on the regularity of intervals between requests is needed
A byte threshold of about 200 per request reliably separates beacons from browsing
Counting requests per host per day is enough, because beacons always generate the most requests of any process
4.explanation: The beacon sends tiny amounts, so a volume query never catches it; its signature is the near-constant gap between requests, which LAG() measures. Fixed byte sizes are one implant's habit, not a reliable discriminator, and ordinary browsing produces many more requests per day.

4.q: An analyst measures beacon regularity with LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY host ORDER BY ts) instead of PARTITION BY host, url. What is the likely effect?
options: The query fails because LAG requires at least two partition columns
The gaps become shorter but remain perfectly regular, so the beacon is still just as obvious in the interval distribution
The beacon's requests are interleaved with the host's ordinary browsing, so its regular gaps are broken up and hidden
Only the first request of each URL is kept, so the gap count drops to one per URL
4.explanation: The partition must be the series being measured. With host alone, each beacon request's predecessor may be an unrelated browsing request, so the measured gaps vary widely and the regularity disappears. The gaps do not stay regular, which is why the second option is wrong.

4.q: In the LAG() interval query, 18 beacon requests produce 17 gaps and the outer query filters WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL. Why is that filter needed?
options: To exclude requests whose timestamps failed to parse
To remove the beacon's final request, which has no following request
The first request in each partition has no predecessor, so its gap would be NULL
To drop requests from hosts that never repeated a URL
4.explanation: LAG() returns NULL for the first row of each partition because nothing precedes it, so 18 requests yield 17 gaps. The last request does have a predecessor; it is the first, not the last, that lacks one.

4.q: A short-string time range returned 15 of the 17 WS-104 events in the intended window, and every returned event was in that window. How should the result be described?
options: Precision 1.0 and recall about 0.88: no false matches, but missed matches
Precision about 0.88 and recall 1.0: some false matches, but nothing missed
Precision and recall both about 0.88, because one error affects both
Precision 1.0 and recall 1.0, because 15 events is close enough to 17
4.explanation: All returned rows are genuine (15/15 = 1.0 precision), but 2 of 17 genuine matches were missed (recall 15/17, about 0.88), and one of them was the 4720 account creation. A boundary error is a recall failure, not a precision failure.

4.q: A scoping query for 'other hosts that contacted the beacon domain' returns no rows. What should the analyst do before writing 'no other hosts affected' in the case notes?
options: Rerun the query with a longer time range until at least one row appears
Replace the exact domain comparison with a substring match to be safe
Accept the result, because a query that runs without an error has already been validated by the platform
Confirm the query returns the known positive, WS-104, when that host is not excluded
4.explanation: Zero is a result to explain, not proof of absence. Running the query against a case you know must match shows that type, boundary or NULL problems are not hiding results. Switching to a substring match trades a recall check for false matches.

4.q: A rule filters target_user LIKE 'svc_%' to find service accounts. Which account name would it also match, unintentionally?
options: svcXupdate
svc
SVC-update in a case-sensitive database
admin_svc_update
4.explanation: In LIKE, the underscore matches exactly one character, so 'svc_%' matches 'svcXupdate' as well as 'svc_update'. 'svc' is too short to match, and 'admin_svc_update' does not start with 'svc'. A literal underscore needs an escape clause or exact comparison.

4.q: After a host-and-domain upload query returns one row, the analyst reruns it without the final HAVING SUM(bytes_out) > 1000000. What is this test for?
options: To check that the query still runs when no threshold is present
To see what the threshold removed and judge whether rows just below the cut look like the rows above it
To measure how much faster the query runs without aggregation
To convert the result from a precision measure to a recall measure
4.explanation: Removing the last filter exposes what it discarded; here two other single-host destinations appeared far below 1 MB, showing the cut is meaningful. If excluded rows resembled kept ones, the threshold would be arbitrary. It is a validity check, not a performance or syntax check.

4.q: A KQL detection fires when summarize dcount(user) by src_ip reaches 10 on a very large table. Some sprays against exactly 10 accounts are not alerted. What is the most likely reason?
options: dcount() counts only users that succeeded, ignoring failures
summarize sorts the result, dropping rows past a default limit
dcount() returns an estimate on large data sets, so a count near the threshold may fall just below it
KQL treats src_ip as text, so addresses written with leading zeros split into separate groups and lower the count
4.explanation: KQL's dcount() is approximate on large data, which matters when the threshold sits close to the true count. It does not filter by outcome; the estimation error near the cut is the relevant caution from the lesson.

4.q: In an SPL pipeline, a host value filter in the initial search matches 'ws-104', but a later where clause comparing host to 'ws-104' returns nothing. What explains the difference?
options: where can only compare numeric fields, so host comparisons always fail
The search command runs after where, so the field has not been extracted yet
SPL lower-cases all field values at index time, so where needs an upper-case literal
Field-value matching in search is not case-sensitive, while comparisons in where are
4.explanation: The same condition behaves differently in two places in one SPL pipeline: search matches values case-insensitively, where compares them case-sensitively, so 'ws-104' does not equal 'WS-104' in where. where handles strings; the issue is case.

4.q: An hourly bucket query shows WS-104 making 1 to 5 proxy requests an hour, except 14 of 37 in the 06 hour and 11 of 36 in the 07 hour. What is the correct conclusion?
options: WS-104 is compromised, because a third of all proxy traffic in an hour is proof of beaconing from that host
The proxy dropped other hosts' traffic in those hours, inflating WS-104's share
The 06 and 07 hours are where to look next; the buckets show when activity changed, not why
WS-104's user simply started work later than everyone else
4.explanation: Bucketing compares one entity with the estate over time and tells the analyst when to look; it does not explain the cause. Treating the spike as proof overstates the evidence, and the other explanations have no support in the data.

4.q: The lesson extracts the domain with substr(url, 9, instr(substr(url, 9), '/') - 1). Why is this described as a teaching shortcut rather than a production method?
options: It works only because every URL in the dataset starts with https:// and has a path; production SIEMs parse URLs into fields at ingest
It is slower than LIKE because it scans each URL twice
It returns the path instead of the host for URLs containing query strings
SQLite's substr counts from zero, so the result is shifted by one character on other platforms
