4.explanation: The fixed offset of 9 assumes the eight-character 'https://' scheme and a trailing slash; http URLs or URLs without a path would break it. Production platforms parse URLs at ingest and those fields should be queried. SQLite's substr is 1-based, so the last option is wrong.

4.q: A windowed join uses julianday(w.ts) - julianday(p.ts) <= 15/1440.0 together with p.ts < w.ts. What relationship does this express?
options: Proxy events up to 15 seconds before or after each Windows event
Proxy events within the 15 minutes before each Windows event
Proxy events in the same 15-minute bucket as each Windows event
Proxy events up to 15 hours before each Windows event
4.explanation: julianday() gives fractional days, and a day has 1,440 minutes, so 15/1440.0 is fifteen minutes; p.ts < w.ts makes it strictly before. It is a sliding window relative to each event, not a fixed bucket, and the unit is minutes, not seconds or hours.

4.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023's purpose limitation and on a shared SIEM, which practice for investigative proxy queries does the lesson recommend?
options: Run broad searches over all history at once, so that no personal data ever has to be queried a second time
Export full proxy logs to the analyst's workstation to avoid loading the SIEM
Mask user names in results, which removes the need for search auditing
Search for a defined purpose, return only the fields needed and time-bound every search
4.explanation: Proxy logs reveal what named employees browsed, so queries should serve a defined purpose and return minimal fields, on platforms that audit searches; time-bounding also stops unbounded queries starving scheduled detections. Broad or exported searches widen personal-data exposure.

4.q: A containment decision rests on the statement 'no other host contacted the beacon domain'. What makes that query result acceptable as evidence?
options: The query is saved with the case together with its specification, absolute time range and run time, so it can be reproduced
The query was written in the platform's native language rather than SQL
The result was confirmed by a second analyst running a different, broader query
The query returned within the platform's performance limit
4.explanation: Queries are part of the evidence chain: a reviewer must be able to rerun exactly what produced the result. A second broader query may help, but without the saved query, its range and its run time, the original statement cannot be checked.

4.q: The lab baselines each log source on its own before merging anything into a timeline. What error is this order mainly designed to prevent?
options: Running queries that are too slow because they join every source at once over the full dataset
Losing events whose timestamps are in different time zones
Anchoring on the first suspicious event and then reading every later event as confirmation
Counting the same event twice when it appears in more than one source
4.explanation: Judging each exception against its own source's normal pattern before merging limits confirmation bias: a failed logon is judged against other logons, not against the phishing story. Performance and duplication are not the reason the method fixes this order.

4.q: Two 4625 events at 04:05 show logon type 2 and status 0xC000006A, one each for ben on WS-102 and hema on WS-108, both of whom logged on successfully earlier. How should they be classified?
options: Noise: single wrong-password failures at the users' own keyboards, the shape of a mistyped password
Suspicious: two simultaneous failures on two hosts indicate coordinated password guessing
Suspicious: status 0xC000006A means the account does not exist, so someone is probing for valid user names
Unexplained: failures cannot be judged without the domain controller's logs
4.explanation: 0xC000006A means a valid account name with a wrong password; one failure each, interactive, on the user's own workstation after a successful logon, is a typo pattern. Guessing would show many failures or many accounts from one source, and the code does not mean an unknown account.

4.q: On WS-104, events 4720, 4732 and 1102 are all recorded under the account divya. Which statement can the analyst make from these logs alone?
options: divya created svc_update and cleared the log, so she should be treated as an insider
divya's password was stolen through the VPN spray and reused on WS-104
svc_update was used to clear the Security log, since it had just become an administrator and divya had no such rights
The actions were performed under the divya account; the logs do not show that the person divya performed them
4.explanation: Windows records the security context in which an action ran, not who sat at the keyboard; malicious code running in divya's session would produce the same events. svc_update never acts in any source, and the VPN thread shares no entity with WS-104.

4.q: A Sysmon stack groups process starts by parent and child and orders by number of hosts. Four Explorer-launched pairs appear on all 8 hosts; WINWORD.EXE to powershell.exe appears once on one host. Why is ordering by host count useful here?
options: It sorts processes by risk score so the most dangerous pair is listed first
Pairs seen on few hosts rise to the top, separating rare behaviour from the estate-wide baseline
It removes duplicate process starts caused by Sysmon logging each event twice when a parent spawns many children
It ensures that events are read in chronological order across hosts
4.explanation: Stacking counts how widespread each pattern is; routine applications appear on every host, so a pair on a single host stands out as an exception. The query has no risk score and does not order by time.

4.q: PowerShell's parent is WINWORD.EXE, but a search for any Word process start returns 0 rows. How should the analyst handle this?
options: Discard the PowerShell event as unreliable, because its parent was never logged
Record it in the note's gaps as a collection limitation, for example a filtered event or late-starting agent
Conclude that PowerShell spoofed its parent process ID, which proves a sophisticated attacker was on the host
Ignore it, because Sysmon never logs Office application starts
4.explanation: A missing parent start is a gap to state, not a reason to drop the evidence or to invent an explanation such as parent spoofing. The baseline shows Sysmon does log Office starts (excel.exe, outlook.exe), so the last option is false.

4.q: VPN logs show 203.0.113.66 failing once against each of eight accounts, seven seconds apart in alphabetical order, then succeeding as gopal four minutes later. What does this pattern indicate?
options: A brute-force attack on gopal's account, because it is the only one that succeeded
A misconfigured VPN client retrying cached credentials for every user
Normal remote working from a shared office network with an unresolved country
A password spray, with the success meaning one credential may be compromised
4.explanation: One attempt per account across many accounts at machine-regular intervals is a spray; the subsequent success suggests a valid credential was found. Brute force would show many attempts against one account, and eight users do not share one address while failing in alphabetical order.

4.q: The only ordinary VPN session in the dataset is gopal from 198.51.100.104 at 13:33. What should the findings note do with this observation?
options: Record the thin baseline as a gap, because one session cannot show what normal VPN use looks like
Use it as the baseline for normal remote access and flag every other address that connects to the VPN as malicious
Omit it, because a successful session is not an exception
Merge it into the spray thread, since it is also gopal
4.explanation: With a single normal session there is no real baseline for VPN use, and that limitation is itself a finding for the gaps section. Treating one session as the norm would overstate certainty, and the 13:33 session from an Indian address shares nothing with the spraying address.

4.q: gopal logged on interactively at WS-107 at 03:33, and WS-107 browses internal sites from 07:22, while a VPN session as gopal from 203.0.113.66 began at 06:46. VPN events carry no host field. What is the right conclusion?
options: The VPN session ran on WS-107, which was then used to reach the intranet sites from 07:22
gopal cannot have been at his desk, so the 07:22 browsing is the attacker
There is a conflict the logs cannot resolve; it must go to the user and the VPN team
The VPN session was gopal working from home before travelling to the office
4.explanation: The data shows an office workstation in use and a remote session from an unknown location under the same account, but with no host on the VPN event nothing ties the two together. Each other option asserts a link or explanation the logs do not support.

4.q: The 06:46 VPN success falls in the middle of the WS-104 activity (06:12 to 08:17). How should it be placed in the analysis?
options: As a separate thread, because it shares no host, user or address with the WS-104 events
As the initial access step of the WS-104 intrusion, because the timing fits the activity window
As noise, because successful logons are part of the baseline
As a duplicate of the 4720 event, because both occur near 07:00
4.explanation: Different account, no host on the VPN event, and an address seen in no other source: proximity in time is not a link. Merging it into the WS-104 story on timing alone is exactly the narrative bias the method guards against, yet it is still a spray-then-success, not noise.

4.q: The scope check starts from a VALUES list of the three suspicious domains and LEFT JOINs the proxy events to it. What does this construction guarantee?
options: Only domains contacted by more than one host are returned
Every listed domain appears in the output, so a domain with zero hits shows as zero instead of disappearing
The proxy events are deduplicated before counting hosts
Domains are matched case-insensitively against the URL
4.explanation: Driving the query from the list means each domain yields a row even with no matches, making a zero visible rather than missing, which matters when negative results are findings. It does not deduplicate or change case handling.

4.q: Scope checks find 203.0.113.66 in no source except VPN and no activity by svc_update anywhere. How should these results appear in the findings note?
options: They should be left out, because only positive results are findings
As proof that the attacker never used the new account or reached any internal systems at any point during the whole incident
As known-negative findings, qualified by the dataset ending at 13:33 and having no server or domain controller logs
As open questions only, because negative results carry no information
4.explanation: Empty scope checks are findings in their own right, but their reach is limited to the sources and time span analysed. Stating them as proof ignores the missing server and domain controller logs and the end of the data; omitting them hides useful information.

4.q: In the findings register, the 4720/4732 account creation is rated High while the 18 regular requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example are rated Medium. What justifies the difference?
options: The account events come from Windows, which is a more trusted source than the proxy
The beacon happened earlier in the timeline, so it has had more time to be explained away by the endpoint team as benign software
Medium is used for any finding involving more than one event
The 4720 event is the fact itself, while a beacon is inferred from regularity and another explanation remains possible
4.explanation: Confidence reflects how directly the log shows the finding: a 4720 records an account creation, while regular small requests are consistent with an implant but could in principle be an unknown legitimate agent. The upload is a proxy finding rated High, so source trust is not the criterion.

4.q: The findings register rates every line High or Medium and has no Low rows. Where does a low-confidence item belong according to the lab?
options: In the summary, flagged with a warning so the handler sees it first
In the recommended actions, as something to block pre-emptively
Nowhere; low-confidence items are discarded before writing
Under gaps and open questions rather than among the findings
4.explanation: A finding is a statement supported by cited evidence; something the analyst cannot support well enough is a question to resolve by other means, so it goes under open questions. Discarding it would hide a lead, and acting on it in the summary would overstate it.

4.q: When the manual analysis is compared with the six saved rules, which finding has no rule at all, and what surfaced it?
options: The invoice.docm download from the look-alike domain, found by the baseline of domains used by only one host
The cleared Security log, found by reading all 13 Windows events
The regular beacon, found by the per-user byte totals
The VPN spray, found by grouping VPN events by country
4.explanation: R1 to R6 cover the PowerShell spawn, spray, new admin, upload, log clearing and beacon; the 06:12 phishing download had no rule and was found because its domain was used by one host. Log clearing is covered by R5 and the beacon by R6.

4.q: divya sent 48.26 MB through the proxy while every other user sent 57 to 83 KB. A banded count then shows 65 requests under 1 KB, 218 between 1 and 5 KB, none between 5 KB and 1 MB, and one above 1 MB. What does the band check add?
options: It shows that divya's other requests were also unusually large
It proves the 48.2 MB request contained personal data
It confirms the large request stands alone rather than being the tail of a gradual spread of sizes
It shows that the beacon is responsible for most of divya's volume
4.explanation: With nothing between 5 KB and 1 MB, the single request above 1 MB is a clear outlier, not the top of a continuum. The check says nothing about the content of the upload, and the beacon's requests total under 4 KB.

4.q: Orientation shows the last Sysmon event at 06:14 while other sources run until 13:33. What follows for the analysis of WS-104 after 06:14?
options: No further processes ran on WS-104, because Sysmon would have logged them
The absence of process events after 06:14 is not evidence that nothing executed; it is a telemetry gap
Sysmon events after 06:14 must have been deleted by the 1102 log clearing, which also wipes the Sysmon channel
Process activity can be reconstructed from the proxy log's user field
4.explanation: With no process telemetry for most of the day, the account creation and upload cannot be tied to processes, and the silence cannot be read as absence. Event 1102 records clearing of the Security log, not Sysmon's log, so the deletion claim is unsupported.

4.q: The merged timeline's activity column uses COALESCE(domain, 'event ' || event_id, 'vpn from ' || src_ip). Why does this work across all four sources?
options: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument, so each row shows the field that its source actually populates
COALESCE concatenates all three values so each row shows its full context
COALESCE converts NULLs to empty strings, which prevents the GROUP BY from failing whenever a source lacks one of the fields
COALESCE picks the longest of the three strings, which is the most descriptive
4.explanation: Proxy rows have a domain, Windows and Sysmon rows have no domain but an event ID, and VPN rows have neither but a source address; COALESCE takes the first non-NULL. It does not concatenate the arguments or pick by length.

4.q: The timeline query groups by source, host, user and activity and selects MIN(ts), MAX(ts) and COUNT(*). What is the main purpose of grouping at this grain?
options: To remove the Windows events, which have no activity value
To hide repeated events that are probably duplicates introduced by the log collector during ingestion
To ensure only one row per host appears on the timeline
To collapse repeated activity such as the 18 beacon requests into one row with first and last time
4.explanation: The beacon becomes one row from 06:17 to 07:42:02 with n = 18, keeping the timeline readable while preserving its span and count. WS-104 still has several rows, one per activity, and the repeats are real events, not duplicates.

4.q: The Sysmon event shows powershell.exe -NoP -W Hidden -EncodedCommand with the encoded content redacted in the course data. How should the findings note treat what the command did?
options: State that it downloaded the beacon, since the first beacon request began three minutes later from the same host
Rate the PowerShell finding Medium, because its content is unknown
List it as an open question for the endpoint team to recover from host PowerShell logging or the document
Omit the event until the command is decoded
4.explanation: The logs show that hidden, encoded PowerShell ran from Word (a High-confidence fact) but not what it did; that belongs in open questions with a route to resolve it. Linking it to the beacon on timing is an inference the data does not establish.

4.q: Why does each row of the findings register list exactly one log source, even though the incident spans several sources?
options: Because the SIEM can only export one source per query
Because correlation is expressed through shared entities across rows, keeping each row's evidence reproducible from one query
Because findings from different sources must be reported to different teams
Because rows mixing sources would automatically be rated Low confidence
4.explanation: Each evidence cell condenses one query's result, so every row can be reproduced; the cross-source story emerges from rows sharing host WS-104 and account divya. It is a design choice for traceability, not a tool limitation or a confidence rule.

4.q: Which recommended action best matches the VPN spray-then-success thread in the findings note?
options: Reset gopal's credentials, review MFA on the VPN and block 203.0.113.66
Isolate WS-107, because gopal's workstation must be the source of the session
Disable svc_update, because the spray created that account
No action, because the thread is unlinked to WS-104
4.explanation: A possibly compromised VPN credential calls for a reset, MFA review and blocking the spraying address, plus a conversation with gopal. Nothing ties the session to WS-107 or to svc_update, and being a separate thread does not make it benign.

4.q: The dataset runs from 03:07 to 13:33 UTC on 3 November 2026. A draft note says 'svc_update was never used'. How should it be corrected?
options: No correction is needed, because the scope query returned zero
Change it to read that svc_update was used only on WS-104, where it was created and added to the Administrators group
Qualify it: svc_update performed no logged activity in the analysed sources within the 03:07 to 13:33 UTC window
Replace it with an estimate of when svc_update will be used
4.explanation: Conclusions apply only to the data's span and sources; there are no server or domain controller logs and nothing after 13:33. A bare 'never' overstates the negative result, and nothing shows svc_update acting on WS-104 either.

4.q: The lab runs minisiem.py rules only at the very end. Why not start from the rule alerts, as the Module 3 lab did?
options: Because the rules require the timeline query to have been run first
Because running rules first would modify the event table
Because the rules are less accurate than manual queries on this dataset
Because rules find only what someone wrote a rule for; independent analysis can then check the rules and find what they miss
4.explanation: Starting from raw sources lets the analyst find gaps in rule coverage (here the phishing download) and judge the rule hits independently. The rules and manual analysis agreed on six findings, so the rules are not less accurate; they are narrower.

4.q: The Windows query pulls logon_type with json_extract(raw, '$.logon_type'), and the 4720, 4732 and 1102 rows show None. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The JSON path is misspelt, so every row in the result should show None
Those event types do not carry a logon type field in their raw events
The events were tampered with when the log was cleared
json_extract cannot read integers, only strings
4.explanation: json_extract returns NULL when the field does not exist in that event; the 4624 and 4625 rows do show logon_type 2, so the path is correct and integers are read fine. Account-management and log-clearing events simply have no logon type.

4.q: Which sentence belongs in the FINDINGS section of the note, rather than in the summary's interpretation?
options: 07:02-07:03 windows: 4720/4732, svc_update created and added to Administrators on WS-104 under account divya
WS-104 shows a complete intrusion sequence from phishing to defence evasion
The attacker established persistence and then exfiltrated payroll data
divya fell for a phishing email and ran a malicious macro
4.explanation: A finding states what an event records, with time, source and entities. 'Intrusion sequence' is the summary's interpretation, and the claims about payroll data or divya's own actions go beyond what the logs show (the upload content and the person at the keyboard are unknown).

5.q: A colleague proposes lowering the base severity of R4 large_upload from 3 to 2 because most large uploads at Banyan turn out to be legitimate. What is the best response?
options: Keep severity at 3, since exfiltration would be serious and irreversible, and express the doubt through the rule's confidence and tuning
Lower it to 2, because a rule whose alerts are usually benign should not occupy the same severity band as genuine, confirmed threats in the queue
Lower it to 1 and treat it as informational, because the upload threshold already filters out most of the harmless traffic
Raise it to 4, because any rule that might detect exfiltration must sit at the top level whatever its false-positive rate
5.explanation: Severity answers 'how bad if true'; a true exfiltration is irreversible, so 3 stands. Noise belongs in confidence (0.5 in triage.py) and tuning. Lowering severity because a rule is noisy hides a dangerous behaviour at the bottom of the queue.

5.q: One alert shows an exploitation attempt against a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability on a server that was patched last month. Another shows a normal-looking VPN login with a password known to be stolen. How should their alert severities compare?
options: The exploit attempt is more severe, because alert severity should always inherit the CVSS base score of whichever vulnerability was targeted
The stolen-credential login can be more severe: severity judges the consequence of the behaviour, and the patched attempt likely failed
Both should be rated equally High, because each represents an external actor attempting to gain access to the environment
Neither can be rated until confidence is known, because severity must be adjusted downward for unconfirmed alerts first
5.explanation: CVSS scores a vulnerability's properties, not what a detected behaviour achieved. A failed attempt on a patched host has low consequence, while a valid-credential login may be the start of an incident. Severity is judged as if the alert is true, independent of confidence.

5.q: R2 vpn_spray_then_success has base severity 4. A detection engineer adds a second rule that fires on the spray alone (five or more failing accounts from one source, no success). What base severity logic is most defensible for the new rule?
options: The same value of 4, because both rules detect the same password-spraying technique from the same source address
A higher value than R2, because a spray seen early gives the SOC more time to respond and is therefore the more important and urgent signal to act on
A lower value than R2, because without a success the behaviour is only an attempt against the boundary, not credentials in an outsider's hands
No severity at all, because a spray without success cannot be a true positive and should therefore be suppressed outright
5.explanation: The consequence changes at the moment a login succeeds: R2 is rated 4 because valid credentials are compromised. A spray-only rule describes an attempt and sits lower, often feeding context. A failed spray is still a true positive of an attempt, so suppressing it outright is wrong.

5.q: In the Banyan severity scale, the Critical row lists no rule anchors and has the kit value 'case only'. What is the main reason for this design?
options: The minisiem engine cannot store a value above 4, so Critical must be tracked manually outside the lab kit
Critical alerts are handled by a separate incident team, so detection engineering is not permitted to assign that level to any rule it writes
Sigma has no critical level, so rules imported from Sigma could never be mapped to the top of the scale
A single detection rarely proves active harm, so Critical is reserved for case-level judgment, which keeps the top level rare and meaningful
5.explanation: Critical means active harm or loss of control now, which usually needs combined evidence from a case. Keeping it out of base severities prevents inflation. Sigma does define a critical level, so that distractor is factually wrong.

5.q: An analyst raises an R1 alert on WS-104 from 3 to 4 'because WS-104 is a finance workstation'. The SOC uses triage.py's model, where priority() multiplies severity by asset criticality. What is the problem?
options: The host's importance is counted twice: once in the raised severity and again by the criticality factor in the priority formula
R1 cannot be raised at all, because base severity set by detection engineering is fixed for every alert the rule creates
Raising severity is fine, but the analyst should also lower the asset criticality of WS-104 so that the overall priority score stays stable
The change is only a problem if the confidence for R1 is below 0.5, which would make the raised value statistically unreliable
5.explanation: In the context-in-priority model, severity describes the behaviour and criticality is applied in priority(). Raising severity because of the host and then multiplying by criticality double counts the asset. Alert severity can be raised, but for facts about the behaviour, not the host.

5.q: During a rule review you find rk_office_spawns_shell.yml carries 'level: high' while RULE_META gives R1 a base severity of 3 (Medium in this module's mapping). What should the reviewer do?
options: Leave both values as they are, since Sigma levels and SIEM severities are independent and never need to agree
Assess R1 against the SOC's own definitions, then either align the Sigma level or record why the difference is intentional
Always adopt the Sigma value, because community rule authors have seen the behaviour across many organisations
Average the two values into 3.5 so that both the SIEM and the case-management system show a compromise rating
5.explanation: Severity living in several places drifts, and analysts then see different values in different tools. The fix is a decision against the SOC's definitions, ideally a single source of truth, with the reasoning recorded. Copying community defaults unchanged describes an average organisation, not yours.

5.q: The WS-104 alerts individually range from 2 (R6) to 4 (R5), yet the WS-104 case is rated Critical. Which statement best justifies this?
options: Case severity is always one level above the highest alert in the case, so a case containing an R5 alert becomes Critical
The case contains more than five alerts, and any case above that count is automatically promoted to the highest level
Together the alerts show a chain of execution, persistence, a large upload and evidence destruction on a payments approver's host
WS-104 has asset criticality 3, and any case on a criticality-3 host is rated Critical regardless of the alerts it holds
5.explanation: Case severity reflects the combined consequence: a document running PowerShell, a new account, beaconing, a 48.2 MB upload and a cleared log describe probable data theft with evidence destruction. It is not a fixed offset from the maximum, nor a count rule, nor driven by host criticality alone.

5.q: Which of the following is a legitimate reason for an analyst to lower an alert's severity below the rule's base severity?
options: The queue is very long and the alert's SLA timer is about to breach, so a lower level buys more time
The rule has a low confidence value, so its alerts are probably benign and deserve a lower severity
The alert fired at night, when fewer users are active and any consequence would therefore be smaller
An approved change record explains the behaviour, or there is evidence that the attempt was blocked
5.explanation: Lowering is justified by facts about this alert, such as an approved change, a blocked attempt or a test system. Queue length and deadlines are explicitly not legitimate reasons, and low confidence belongs in the confidence input rather than in severity.

5.q: The R3 alert at 07:02 shows divya, a payments approver, creating the account svc_update, 48 minutes after R1 fired on the same host. Which triage outcome is most defensible?
options: Raise from 3 to 4 with a recorded note citing the out-of-role account creation and the earlier R1 alert, and link it to the WS-104 case
Keep at 3 without a note, because account creation is routine for administrators on any host and the base severity already covers that risk
Lower to 2, because a single account creation does not prove persistence and the confidence of R3 is only 0.6
Raise directly to Critical, because any new account on a finance workstation is proof of active harm in progress
5.explanation: Corroboration on the same host and behaviour outside the user's role are both raise facts, and the change must be recorded with old and new values and the reason. Critical is a case-level judgment, so jumping the single alert to Critical overstates what it proves.

5.q: The kit's SUPPRESS list covers R3 alerts for the account itadmin under change CHG-1042, while the R3 alert for divya is raised. Why do two alerts from the same rule receive opposite treatment?
options: Because itadmin's alerts have lower base severity than divya's, since base severity is assigned per user account
Because context explains itadmin's activity as approved work, while divya's account creation is out of role and corroborated
Because suppression applies only to alerts generated outside business hours, and itadmin worked during the night
Because R3 has two separate thresholds, one for administrators and one for ordinary users, built directly into the rule's detection logic
5.explanation: The same detected behaviour is judged against its context: an approved change explains itadmin's activity, so it is suppressed, while divya's lacks any such explanation and has supporting evidence. Base severity belongs to the rule, not to a user.

5.q: At the end of a busy shift an analyst wants to downgrade a High case to Low, noting only 'looks benign'. Under the governance practice described in the lesson, what should happen?
options: The analyst may proceed, because analysts own alert severity and may move it in either direction on their own judgment
The change should be blocked permanently, because a High case can only ever be closed by formal escalation to the incident response team
The downgrade needs a second person such as the shift lead and a specific recorded reason, since lowering is where incidents get lost
The analyst should leave the severity unchanged but close the case, because closure does not require a severity change
5.explanation: A common rule is that analysts may raise severity alone, but lowering High or Critical needs a second person and a recorded reason. Raising is cheap and safe; quiet downgrades are how real incidents get closed. Closing a High case without review sidesteps the same control.

5.q: The SIEM already holds a copy of WS-104's Security log, yet R5 log_cleared (event 1102) is rated High. What makes the behaviour severe?
options: Clearing the log deletes the SIEM's copy as well, so all historical evidence for the host is lost from every system
Event 1102 is generated only by malware, so its presence is definitive proof that the host is compromised
Clearing the log stops the endpoint from sending any further events, so the host becomes permanently invisible
It implies an actor with administrative rights wants to hide activity, and the on-host history is lost irreversibly
5.explanation: Severity looks at what the event enables and implies: the actor already holds administrative rights and is destroying evidence, and on-host history cannot be reconstructed. The SIEM's collected copy is not deleted, and 1102 can also be produced by legitimate administration.

5.q: A new rule detects a process that has never been seen in the Banyan estate before. An engineer argues it should be High 'because it is extremely rare'. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Rarity is evidence about whether the alert is real, so it informs confidence; severity must come from the consequence if true
Rare events can never be severe, because attackers prefer common tools that blend into normal administrative activity
Rarity should lower severity, because rare behaviour produces few alerts and therefore needs little analyst attention
Rarity is only meaningful for network events, so a host-based process rule must take its severity from the vendor's default rating instead
5.explanation: Severity is a judgment about consequence, not about how unusual the event is or how often it fires. Rarity supports the likelihood that the alert is true, which is confidence. A rare process could be harmless or dangerous; its consequence decides severity.

5.q: A misconfigured application triggers the same rule 500 times in ten minutes on one host. How should severity be handled?
options: Raise the severity to the top level, since 500 alerts in ten minutes show that the behaviour is far more serious than a single occurrence would be
Deduplicate into one alert with a count; volume does not make one behaviour more severe, and if volume matters, write a rule for that pattern
Lower the rule's base severity permanently, since a rule able to fire 500 times is clearly mis-rated for the environment
Rate each of the 500 alerts separately, because every alert must keep its own independent severity and triage record
5.explanation: A burst is one behaviour seen many times. Treat it as one alert with a count. Where volume itself is meaningful, as in a password spray, a separate rule should detect that pattern. Permanently lowering base severity because of one misconfiguration confuses noise with consequence.

5.q: A SOC manager wants to move from four to eight severity levels 'for more precision'. What is the strongest objection?
options: Most SIEM products cannot store more than five severity values, so the extra levels would be silently truncated
Eight levels would require each rule to be rewritten in Sigma, which supports only the four standard severities
Many levels tend to produce arguments about adjacent levels rather than better decisions, so analysts agree less often
More levels would remove the need for confidence values, which would make priority calculation impossible
5.explanation: A scale is useful only if two analysts would pick the same level for the same alert. Beyond about five levels, the boundaries become arguable and consistency drops. Sigma actually defines five levels, so the distractor about Sigma is false.

5.q: Which proposed definition of the High level best meets the guidance for a usable severity scale?
options: High: serious alerts that need prompt attention from an experienced analyst on the current shift
High: any alert from a rule with confidence above 0.8 on a host with asset criticality of 3
High: alerts that the vendor marks as high, unless the shift lead decides that they look harmless
High: attacker has, or very likely has, execution or valid credentials inside; a blocked attempt is not High
5.explanation: A good definition states the consequence if true, so an analyst can test an alert against it, and says what the level is not. 'Serious' is untestable, the confidence-and-criticality version mixes in other inputs, and vendor defaults describe an average organisation.

5.q: To quieten the queue, a team moves several noisy rules to the informational level. What risk does the lesson highlight, and how is it addressed?
options: The rules may still detect real behaviour, so they should keep contributing to an entity risk score or a hunt
Informational alerts breach SLAs automatically, so each must still be acknowledged within fifteen minutes
Informational rules cannot be re-enabled later, so the detection logic should be exported before moving them
Moving rules to informational lowers their confidence, so their precision must be recalculated from scratch
5.explanation: Informational is not a dumping ground: a demoted rule can still be detecting real activity. If it no longer creates queue work, it should feed context such as an entity risk score or a hunt. The other options describe behaviour the lesson does not claim.

5.q: A quarterly review finds that 92% of alerts at the High level were closed as benign over the last three months. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The High level is working correctly, because a cautious SOC should expect most High alerts to be benign
Severity inflation, or a confidence problem being expressed as severity, so rules at that level need review
The analysts are under-trained, because a benign rate that high can only result from wrong dispositions
The asset criticality values are wrong, because criticality is the main driver of how alerts are closed
5.explanation: Comparing the severity distribution with real dispositions is the recommended check; a level where most alerts close as benign suggests inflated base severities or noisy rules whose doubt should be in confidence. Analyst quality may be worth checking, but it is not the most likely explanation from this metric alone.

5.q: An intruder works slowly with legitimate administration tools and keeps uploads below the R4 threshold, so only Low alerts are produced. Which defence most directly counters this?
options: Raise all Low rules to Medium, so that every alert they produce is guaranteed to be read by an analyst before the shift ends
Lower the R4 upload threshold to zero bytes, so that any upload at all generates a Medium alert
Aggregate Low and informational detections into a per-entity risk score so that weak signals on one host surface together
Disable Low rules entirely, since they are not read and only add storage cost to the SIEM
5.explanation: Adversaries who stay low are effectively exploiting the severity scale. Aggregating weak signals per user or host lets several Lows on one entity surface together. Raising every Low inflates the scale, and a zero threshold floods the queue.

5.q: For the WS-104 incident, which impact questions drive the Critical rating?
options: Functional impact, because the number of hosts affected determines how severe an incident is
Recoverability alone, because any incident that needs outside help is Critical by definition
Functional impact and host count, because one workstation compromised means business is stopped
Information impact and recoverability: a 48.2 MB upload from a payments approver and a cleared log
5.explanation: Functionally only one workstation is affected, but the potential data loss to an unfamiliar domain and the destroyed on-host log make information impact and recoverability severe. The lesson stresses that these, not the number of hosts, drive the rating.

5.q: Why should severity reclassifications be written to the case system's audit log rather than only to an editable severity field?
options: So the record cannot be rewritten after an incident and reviewers can see who changed what, when and why
So the SIEM can recompute rule confidence automatically every time an analyst edits a severity value
So the SLA timer restarts from zero whenever a severity is changed, giving the analyst a fresh deadline
So that analysts no longer need to write a reason, because the audit log captures the old and new values
5.explanation: The reclassification record is what makes severity trustworthy; protecting it in an audit log stops it being altered later and supports quality and post-incident review. The record still needs a reason, so the last distractor is wrong.

5.q: An analyst argues that every alert at an earlier ATT&CK tactic must be less severe than every alert at a later one. Which counter-example from the lesson shows why this is only a heuristic?
options: A cleared log is always the least severe event, because it happens at the end of an intrusion
A successful initial access on a domain controller outranks reconnaissance-stage noise anywhere
A beacon is more severe than exfiltration, because command and control precedes data theft
A password spray is more severe than a new local admin, because it targets many accounts
5.explanation: Later intrusion stages are usually more severe because more of the attacker's work is done, but what is touched also matters: initial access on a domain controller can outrank later-stage activity elsewhere. The other options misstate the stage ordering or the lesson's ratings.

5.q: In which situation is the 'context in severity' model, where the same rule yields High on a domain controller and Medium on a kiosk, most appropriate?
options: When the SOC uses triage.py's priority() formula, which already multiplies by asset criticality
When the SOC wants severity statistics to be directly comparable across every host in the estate
When SLA commitments are written per severity level and must reflect business impact directly
When the CMDB is incomplete, so that asset criticality cannot be looked up during triage at all
5.explanation: Folding context into severity suits organisations whose SLA contract is defined by severity. Combining it with a formula that also multiplies by criticality double counts the asset, and comparable statistics across hosts are the advantage of the other model.

5.q: A password spray against the VPN and a technique requiring hands-on work on each individual host are both detected. Considering the breadth dimension only, which statement is correct?
options: The hands-on technique has the larger breadth, because each compromised host gives deeper access
Breadth is identical, because each detection was triggered by a single source address
Breadth cannot be assessed for remote-access events, only for host-based endpoint telemetry
The spray has the larger potential blast radius, because it can be repeated cheaply across many accounts
5.explanation: Breadth asks how many accounts, hosts or departments a behaviour can reach. A behaviour that scales cheaply, such as spraying many VPN accounts, has a larger blast radius than one needing manual effort per host. Depth of access is a different dimension.

5.q: During triage an analyst decides an alert matches the rule's typical case and keeps its base severity. According to the severity lifecycle, what should happen?
options: The decision to keep is noted in the triage record, because keeping the base value is also a decision
Nothing is recorded, because the reclassification log is only for alerts whose severity actually changed
The alert is automatically raised one level, because every triaged alert must move away from the base value
The rule's base severity is updated to match, because the analyst has just confirmed it is correct
5.explanation: In the lifecycle figure all three branches, including keep, pass through the recorded reclassification step. Base severity changes only through rule review, not because one alert matched its typical case.

5.q: Using triage.py, where R4 has (severity 3, confidence 0.5) and an unknown host falls back to criticality 2, what does priority('R4', 'UNKNOWN-9') return?
options: 3.0, because 3 x 0.5 x 2 is multiplied and rounded to one decimal place
4.5, because unknown hosts inherit the criticality of the most recent known host
0.0, because a host missing from ASSETS contributes a criticality of zero to the product
6.0, because unknown hosts are treated as criticality 4 until they are registered
5.explanation: priority() uses ASSETS.get(host, ('unknown asset', 2)), so an unregistered host gets criticality 2: 3 x 0.5 x 2 = 3.0. The kit does not treat unknown assets as high; that is a recommendation in the lesson, not the code's behaviour.

5.q: R2 (event at 06:46) and R1 (event at 06:14) both score 7.2, yet triage.py prints R2 first. What causes this?
options: triage.py breaks equal scores by the newest event timestamp first, so the 06:46 VPN alert is placed above the older R1 alert
sorted(..., reverse=True) compares the next tuple element, the rule-name string, so 'R2 ...' sorts above 'R1 ...'
R2's unrounded score is slightly higher than R1's, and the difference disappears only when printed
R2 involves an external address, and triage.py adds a hidden bonus to alerts from external sources
5.explanation: Python compares tuples element by element; with equal scores it compares the rule-name strings, and in reverse order R2 precedes R1. The tie is broken alphabetically, not by time. Both products are exactly 7.2, and no external-address bonus exists in priority().

5.q: A newly deployed rule ships with confidence 0.0 by mistake. What happens under a multiplicative priority model, and what is the safeguard?
options: Its alerts score as if confidence were 1.0, so a minimum value is unnecessary but a maximum is needed
Its alerts rise to the top, because a zero factor is treated as missing data and the remaining factors are simply summed instead
Every alert from the rule scores 0 and sinks to the bottom, so models need floors such as a minimum confidence
The SIEM rejects the rule, because a multiplicative model cannot be evaluated when any factor equals zero
5.explanation: In a product, a zero erases everything: however severe, the alerts score 0. Multiplicative models therefore need floors, such as a documented default confidence for new rules and a minimum criticality for any asset.

5.q: A SOC is choosing between the kit's product (severity x confidence x criticality) and a weighted sum of the same inputs. Which trade-off is stated correctly?
options: A product lets several mediocre inputs add up to an alarming score, while a weighted sum lets one low input cancel all the others
A weighted sum always gives identical ordering to a product, so the choice affects only presentation
A product is preferred because it never produces ties, unlike a weighted sum on integer scales
A weighted sum stops one low input cancelling a high one, but several mediocre inputs can add up to an alarming score
5.explanation: In a weighted sum a High severity cannot be wiped out by a low factor, which some SOCs want, but mediocre factors accumulate. In a product each factor scales the others and ties are common on small scales; the kit itself shows a 7.2 tie.

5.q: Analysts on one shift close many genuine R3 alerts as 'false positive' to clear the queue quickly. What is the longer-term effect if confidence is measured as precision?
options: R3's measured confidence falls, lowering the future priority of every alert it produces, including real ones
Nothing changes, because confidence is fixed by detection engineering when a rule is first written
R3's severity is automatically reduced, because the SIEM moves rules with many false positives down one severity level each quarter
R3's confidence rises, because a larger number of closed alerts makes the precision estimate more reliable
5.explanation: Precision is true positives divided by all dispositioned alerts, so careless false-positive closures depress it and push the rule's future alerts down the queue. Severity is a separate input and does not change from dispositions.

5.q: A rule has produced ten alerts in ninety days, one of them a true positive. A colleague wants to set its confidence to 0.1 immediately. What is the best assessment?
options: Correct, because precision is exact once any true positive exists and needs no further evidence
The sample is too small for a reliable precision, so a documented default is better until more alerts accrue
Confidence should be set to 1.0, because the rule has been proven able to catch at least one real attack
Confidence should be set to 0.0, because nine false positives out of ten alerts means the rule is useless and should be disabled
5.explanation: Precision from very few alerts is weak evidence; ten alerts with one true positive is noisy. A documented default is held until enough history accumulates. Setting 0.0 would also erase every future alert under a multiplicative model.

5.q: An alert arrives for host PAY-NEW-03, which is not in the CMDB. triage.py gives it criticality 2. Why does the lesson call this default 'arguable', and what is recommended?
options: Because 2 is too high for unknown hosts, which are nearly always decommissioned test machines
Because the default should be 1, so that unregistered hosts never compete with known business assets
Because an unknown host may be a forgotten box, a new payment server or an intruder's device, so treat it as high and register it
Because unknown hosts should be excluded from scoring entirely until the CMDB team has classified them
5.explanation: Calling an unknown host average hides real uncertainty; it may be critical or even attacker-controlled. Many SOCs treat unknown assets as at least High criticality until classified and raise a task to register them.

5.q: If the account that succeeded after the VPN spray had been divya (a payments approver) instead of gopal, how would the kit's priority() score that R2 alert, and why is that a problem?
options: 10.8, because priority() reads the USERS table and lifts alerts for payments approvers automatically
0.0, because priority() cannot score an account-based alert unless the account owns a registered host
12.0, because identity criticality is added on top of the asset criticality whenever the account is a privileged one
It depends only on the host mapped to the account, so the score ignores what the compromised account can reach
5.explanation: priority() never reads USERS; R2 is scored with the criticality of the host mapped in PRIMARY_HOST. For credential compromise, what matters is what the account can reach, so the lesson recommends taking the higher of asset and identity criticality. The exact value depends on that host mapping.

5.q: The WS-104 queue lines score 10.8, 7.2, 5.4, 5.4, 4.5 and 3.6. Counting each rule only once per entity, what is the WS-104 entity risk?
5.explanation: The raw sum is 36.9; the two R3 alerts come from the same rule, so de-duplication counts 5.4 once, giving 31.5. 10.8 is only the highest single alert, which is exactly what per-alert scoring is limited to.

5.q: Why should entity risk scores decay over time?
options: Because SIEM storage limits require older alerts to be deleted before their risk can be counted
So that old activity does not keep an entity at the top of the queue for weeks after it was handled
Because older alerts have lower confidence by definition, so their severity must be reduced each day
So that the same rule firing repeatedly within a short window counts more heavily than a single alert
5.explanation: Decay prevents stale activity dominating the ranking long after it mattered. Repeated firing of one rule is handled by per-rule de-duplication, which works in the opposite direction to the last distractor.

5.q: R6 beacon_regular_small has low severity and confidence. How does entity risk scoring change the case for keeping it enabled?
options: It does not; low-scoring rules should be disabled once entity scoring is in place to reduce the load
It forces R6 alerts to page an analyst individually, so they can no longer be missed in the queue
R6 can contribute risk quietly and surface only when other evidence accumulates on the same entity
It raises R6's base severity automatically, because aggregated rules are treated as High by default
5.explanation: Entity scoring lets weak rules stay on without each alert creating work: their scores add to the entity's risk and surface when corroborated. Severity is not changed by aggregation, and paging on each R6 alert is what entity scoring avoids.

5.q: For months, alerts have arrived faster than the SOC can work them, and items below a score of 4 are never opened before automatic closure. What does the lesson say is the honest response?
options: Keep the current order, since low-scored items are only being deferred and will be reached and worked properly in a quieter week
Lower the severity of the affected rules so that the queue statistics reflect what is actually being handled
Raise the confidence of the low rules so that their alerts climb above the cut-off and are eventually worked
Tune or retire the rules filling the tail, automate their handling or add capacity, instead of pretending they are handled
5.explanation: When arrivals persistently exceed capacity, the priority order becomes a decision about what will never be examined. The options are tuning, retiring, automating or adding capacity. Altering severity or confidence to fit capacity changes the facts, not the workload.

5.q: A Medium alert scored 5.4 keeps being pushed down by a steady stream of 5.5-6.0 alerts and has waited nine hours. Which queue mechanism is designed for this?
options: Ageing, which raises an item's effective priority the longer it waits so it cannot be starved
Deduplication, which merges the waiting alert into the newer alerts that keep arriving above it
Severity inflation, which lifts the waiting alert's base severity so that it outranks the newer items
Tie-breaking, which compares rule names so that the waiting alert is placed above alerts with equal scores
5.explanation: Ageing addresses starvation by increasing effective priority with waiting time, and it should be shown next to the score. Tie-breaking only applies to equal scores, and changing severity to move an item misuses the definition.

5.q: With the SLA dashboard turning red, a shift lead suggests temporarily lowering R3's confidence to 0.3 so that its alerts fall below the cut-off. What is the correct objection?
options: Confidence can only be changed by the CMDB owner, so the shift lead lacks authority over that value
Time pressure may change the order of work but must not alter severity or confidence, which are facts about alerts
Lowering confidence to 0.3 would have no effect, because priority() ignores confidence values below 0.5
The change is acceptable provided it is reversed at the end of the shift and clearly noted in the handover report for the next lead
5.explanation: Time and capacity are handled by ageing, deadline proximity and capacity decisions, not by editing inputs. Confidence reflects measured precision; manipulating it hides real alerts and corrupts future scores. Confidence is owned by detection engineering, not the CMDB, and priority() uses it at any value.

5.q: At 08:30 analyst B takes R2 (score 7.2) ahead of higher-scored WS-104 alerts. What makes this a legitimate override?
options: R2 is the oldest alert in the queue, so the standard oldest-first rule requires it to be worked before any of the WS-104 alerts
R2 has a higher base severity than every WS-104 alert, so it should have been ranked first anyway
A successful external login after a spray suggests a live session that quick, pre-authorised containment can cut off
Analyst B is more familiar with VPN alerts, and analysts should take the alert types they know best
5.explanation: The model cannot see that an external actor with valid credentials may still hold a session and that disabling the account is fast; that context justifies the override, with a written reason. R1 at 06:14 is older than R2, R5 shares R2's severity of 4, and choosing familiar work is an illegitimate reason.

5.q: Why must the reason for working an alert out of score order be written down?
options: Because SIEM products refuse to assign an alert to an analyst unless an override reason is supplied first
Because the written reason is used to recompute the rule's confidence after the alert has been closed
Because without a note the alert's SLA timer cannot be paused while the override is in progress
Because legitimate and illegitimate overrides look alike from outside, and the note lets a shift lead tell them apart
5.explanation: Picking easy alerts to improve closure counts looks the same as taking an urgent one from outside. The recorded reason makes overrides reviewable. Confidence comes from dispositions, not override notes.

5.q: R1 fired on WS-104 at 06:14; the VPN spray from 203.0.113.66 began at 06:42 and also targeted divya. How should the R2 case and the WS-104 case be handled?
options: As separate cases that cross-reference each other, since the spray began after R1 and cannot have caused it
As a single merged case, because both involve divya and the spray must have delivered the malicious document
As unrelated cases with no link, because the two alerts were raised on different hosts by different rules
As one case led by R2, because the external spray is the root cause of everything seen on WS-104
5.explanation: The timeline rules out the spray causing the WS-104 activity, so they are different stories; but they touch the same person, so each case notes the other in case later evidence links them. Ignoring the shared target loses that thread.

5.q: A minisiem search of VPN events from one external address shows eight different users failing at seven-second intervals, then one of them succeeding four minutes later. What is the best interpretation?
options: A single user mistyping a password repeatedly, followed by a successful login after a password reset
A password spray across many accounts followed by a successful login with valid credentials
A brute-force attack against one account, shown as eight failures before the correct password was found
A VPN concentrator health check, which cycles through test accounts at fixed intervals
5.explanation: Few attempts against many different accounts from one source, in a fixed rhythm, is the spray pattern; the later success means an outsider holds a valid account. Brute force targets one account with many guesses, which the varied usernames rule out.

5.q: Which explicit tie-breaker order does the lesson recommend for alerts with equal priority scores?
options: Rule name, then host name, then event time, so that the ordering is deterministic and reproducible
Severity, then asset criticality, then confidence, so that the score's own inputs decide among equals
Time waiting, then SLA deadline, then severity, so that equal items are ordered by risk and age
Newest event first, then the analyst's preference, so that the freshest evidence is always examined
5.explanation: Ties should be broken by waiting time, then SLA deadline, then severity. Sorting by rule name, as the kit effectively does, is deterministic but orders work by a label rather than risk or age.

5.q: A routine CMDB update mistakenly lowers a payment server's criticality from 3 to 1. Why does the lesson treat this as a security concern?
options: Because the SIEM stops collecting logs from any asset whose criticality is set below 2
Because a criticality change automatically lowers the base severity of rules firing on that server
Because criticality changes disable entity risk scoring for the affected host until the CMDB team has reclassified it
Because every alert about the server silently drops in priority, so such changes should be logged and reviewed
5.explanation: Criticality multiplies every alert's score for that host, so a wrong value (accidental or malicious) pushes real alerts down. Changes to criticality and confidence should be reviewed like rule changes. Severity and log collection are not affected by the CMDB value.

5.q: A SOC considers deriving priority from a lookup matrix of severity against criticality, using confidence only as a gate, similar to ITIL's impact-urgency grid. What is the main trade-off?
options: It is easy to explain and audit, but coarse compared with a continuous score
It removes ties completely, but cannot be used once entity risk scoring is enabled
It is more precise than multiplication, but requires confidence to be measured hourly
It eliminates the need for asset criticality, but makes severity harder to define
5.explanation: Matrices are transparent and auditable but coarse, since many alerts land in the same cell. They still use criticality, and coarse cells actually produce more ties, not fewer.

5.q: R1 office_spawns_script fires often on developers' workstations where macros are part of normal work, but rarely and usually maliciously in Finance. How can the scoring model reflect this?
options: Lower R1's base severity for everyone, because the developer alerts show the behaviour is usually harmless
Keep confidence per rule and per business unit, so the same rule carries lower confidence for developers
Raise the asset criticality of developer workstations, so that their R1 alerts are not drowned out
Suppress R1 globally and rely on entity risk scoring to surface any genuinely malicious documents
5.explanation: Confidence can depend on context as well as on the rule; keeping it per business unit expresses that developer alerts are less likely to be malicious without lowering severity, which describes harm if true, or distorting criticality.

5.q: Without an entity-grouping stage, what failure is most likely for the six WS-104 alerts?
options: The alerts would all receive a score of zero, because ungrouped alerts lack an entity criticality value
The SIEM would merge them into one alert automatically, losing the individual event timestamps
Different analysts on different shifts each close one as suspicious with no further evidence, missing the chain
The R5 alert would be dropped from the queue, because only one alert per host can be shown at a time
5.explanation: Working alerts rather than entities splits an intrusion across people and shifts, so nobody sees the sequence. Grouping by host, account or source address puts the related alerts in front of one analyst.

5.q: During a quiet intrusion on a finance server, a burst of hundreds of noisy alerts suddenly appears on unrelated hosts. Which defences from the lesson best protect against this being a distraction?
options: Raising the confidence of every rule involved in the burst so that the queue reflects the increased activity
Lowering the criticality of the unrelated hosts so that their alerts fall to the bottom of the queue
Disabling the noisy rules until the burst ends, then re-enabling them once the queue has been cleared
Entity grouping, so the burst collapses into a few entities, and analysts who scan the queue beyond the top
5.explanation: An adversary can pull attention away with high-volume noise. Grouping by entity keeps the burst from crowding the queue, and analysts reading below the top items still spot the quieter intrusion. Editing confidence or criticality on the fly corrupts the model.

5.q: In the prioritisation pipeline, analysts' dispositions feed back into rule confidence. What happens if this feedback loop is missing?
options: Confidence values go stale, so the first scoring step's numbers gradually stop reflecting how rules really perform
The queue stops sorting altogether, because priority() needs a fresh confidence value computed for every new alert it receives
Severity values start drifting upward, because dispositions are the only control on severity inflation
Entity risk scores can no longer be calculated, because they depend on the disposition of each alert
5.explanation: The feedback loop is the slowest in the pipeline: closures update confidence, which changes next week's scores. Without it the values set once become stale. Scoring and entity aggregation still run, just on outdated inputs.

5.q: The triage helper prints `host=WS-107 (sales laptop)` for the `R2` VPN alert, yet the VPN events behind that alert carry no host field at all. How should the analyst record this host value in the case?
options: As an assumption from a user-to-device mapping, to be confirmed through VPN client, DHCP or EDR records
As an observation, because the triage helper joined it directly from the alert's own event fields and VPN records
As irrelevant, because VPN alerts are about addresses and accounts rather than about devices
As confirmed, because the sales laptop is the only device the inventory lists for that user
5.explanation: The helper filled WS-107 from its PRIMARY_HOST table, which maps users to their usual device; nothing in the VPN events observed that device. Treating it as confirmed because the inventory lists one device still confuses a usual mapping with evidence about this session.

5.q: In the enriched triage queue, the `R6 beacon_regular_small` line shows `user=None (?)` while every other WS-104 line names `divya`. What is the correct reading of this gap?
options: The beaconing ran under a system account, so no person was involved in that activity
The identity table is stale and must be rebuilt before the R6 alert can be triaged
The rule groups proxy events by host and URL, so its hit carries no user to enrich
The user field was deliberately removed from proxy events to protect personal data
5.explanation: R6 aggregates by host and URL, so the hit has no user value and the helper honestly prints None. Reading the gap as a system account confuses a missing field with evidence that no user was involved.

5.q: `ioc_match.py` prints `EXPIRED ipv4 198.51.100.104 conf= 40 hits= 1 ... src=open feed`, and the matching event is `gopal`'s 13:33Z VPN session with country `IN`. What should the analyst do with this result?
options: Block the address at the VPN gateway, since any match on a reported indicator is actionable on its own
Treat it at most as a reason to look, since the indicator is old, weak and on shared hosting
Escalate gopal's evening session as a second compromise linked to the morning spraying
Ignore the line entirely, since expired indicators are removed from feeds automatically
5.explanation: The indicator's validity ended in June, it came from an open feed at confidence 40 and describes old scanning on shared hosting, and it lands on a routine login; the script itself says review before acting. Escalating it would treat a normal employee session as an attack on the strength of stale intelligence.

5.q: A vendor's sha256 indicator for the malicious `invoice.docm`, confidence 90, returns `no match` with zero hits against the Banyan events. What does this result tell the analyst?
options: That the document on WS-104 was a different variant from the one the vendor reported
That the vendor's confidence was overstated and the indicator should be removed from the feed
That WS-104 never opened the malicious file, which lowers the priority of the R1 alert
Nothing yet, because the dataset holds no file hashes and so could never have matched
5.explanation: A non-match is only meaningful when the searched data could have contained the indicator; this dataset has no hash field at all. Concluding a different variant was used reads meaning into a lookup that had no chance of succeeding.

5.q: A prevalence query shows each of `banyan-payroll-update.example`, `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` and `files-share-drop.example` was reached by exactly one host, first seen within the same two hours. Why does this matter for triage?
options: It proves the domains are malicious, so intelligence lookups for them are no longer needed
It shows the proxy only logs one host per domain, so the counts cannot be relied upon
It marks them as rare, newly seen entities, unlike domains the whole office reaches daily
It shows the domains are internal services that only the finance team is permitted to use
5.explanation: Low prevalence and a recent first-seen time make an entity more interesting, in contrast to mail.banyan.example which every workstation reaches. Rarity raises attention but does not prove maliciousness, so it does not replace intelligence or validation.

5.q: While enriching the `R1` alert, a junior analyst proposes pasting `WS-104` and the username `divya` into a public reputation website to see whether anyone has reported them. What is the right response?
options: Do not submit internal entities to public services; answer them from internal sources instead
Submit them, but only through a browser private window so that nothing about the lookup is stored afterwards
Submit the hostname only, since usernames are personal data but hostnames are not sensitive
Submit them after the alert is confirmed, when the investigation no longer needs secrecy
5.explanation: Public services keep what is submitted and some expose it to others, so internal hostnames and usernames must never go there; the asset inventory, directory and SIEM history answer the questions. Submitting only the hostname still leaks internal names, so that compromise does not fix the problem.

5.q: An analyst closes a suspicious-login alert with the note: "Source IP geolocates to India, where the user lives, so the login was the user." What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
options: Geolocation is only accurate for IPv6 addresses, so an IPv4 result should be discarded
The analyst should have used the ASN instead, which reliably identifies the person behind an address
A login can only be attributed to a user after the address appears in a threat feed
Geolocation is an estimate, and VPNs, cloud and carrier-grade NAT break the address-person link
5.explanation: Shared infrastructure puts many unrelated users behind the same addresses and attackers can rent infrastructure in any country, so geolocation is a hint, not attribution. The ASN identifies the network operator, not the person, so it cannot fill that gap either.

5.q: An analyst enriching the spraying address `203.0.113.66` gets no geolocation or ownership result from the lookup service. In this course dataset, what should the enriched record say about the address's location?
options: The country of the organisation's VPN gateway, since the address connected through it
Unknown, while noting that the raw VPN events carry a synthetic country field of `??`
The country most often seen for spraying campaigns against the finance sector this year
The country of the user whose account succeeded, since the session belongs to that user
5.explanation: Documentation-range addresses have no real geolocation, so the honest value is unknown, and the dataset's own raw field also says ??. Filling in the user's country would invent a location and quietly assume the very thing triage is testing.

5.q: The `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` indicator from ISAC-A is marked TLP:AMBER. Which use of its context is consistent with that marking?
options: Quoting it in the public status update that tells customers about the incident
Including it in the case notes and the internal escalation on a need-to-know basis
Posting it to a vendor support forum to ask whether the product detects the loader
Adding it to the SOC's public blog post on finance-sector phishing campaigns
5.explanation: TLP:AMBER allows sharing inside the organisation on a need-to-know basis, so case notes and internal escalation are fine. A vendor forum looks like a technical channel but is outside the organisation, so posting there breaks the marking.

5.q: A SOC playbook queries the asset inventory, the directory and SIEM history before calling any external enrichment service. Which justification for this order is correct?
options: External services require the internal inventory and directory results as input before they will answer a query
Internal sources are always more accurate than commercial feeds for external addresses
Regulations forbid any external lookup until internal sources have been exhausted first
Internal sources are cheap, private and specific, so external calls are kept to what remains
5.explanation: Internal lookups leak nothing and describe your own environment, so they come first and external lookups are made only for what they could not answer. Internal sources are not always more accurate about external addresses, which is why external enrichment still has a place.

5.q: `R1` fires on a workstation that is missing from the asset inventory, so the triage helper gives it its default criticality of 2 and it sits below several WS-104 alerts. What should the analyst take from this?
options: The unknown asset is a finding in itself, and the default criticality may understate the alert
The alert can wait, since unlisted devices are usually test machines of low business value
The default value is safe, because the helper picks the middle of the scale for missing assets
The alert should be suppressed until the asset owner registers the device in the inventory
5.explanation: A device nobody recorded is worth a question, and a default criticality is a guess that can push a real attack down the queue. Calling the middle value safe ignores that the device could be anything, including a critical server never entered.

5.q: Two VPN logins for the same user both geolocate to the same country. One comes from a residential broadband provider, the other from a small hosting company's address range. Why is the network owner more informative here than the country?
options: The hosting company's range proves the second login came from a criminal group
The broadband range proves the first login came from the user's own home network and so must be legitimate
It shows a change in the kind of network used, which is worth noting though not attribution
It identifies the person behind each address, which a country lookup never can
5.explanation: The ASN says what kind of operator announces the range, so a shift from home broadband to a hosting provider is a meaningful anomaly when the country is the same. It is still a hint: neither value proves who is behind the address.

5.q: `ioc_match.py` reports `MATCH ipv4 203.0.113.66 conf= 60 hits= 9 src=ISAC-A`, and the nine hits are exactly the eight failures and one success behind `R2`. How much weight should this match carry?
options: Enough to close the case as a confirmed attack by the group named in the ISAC report
None, because an indicator that only matches the alert's own events adds no information
Enough to block all VPN access from that country for the rest of the incident
It supports the R2 alert, but IP indicators are moderate evidence and do not show who is behind them
5.explanation: A confidence of 60 on an address is moderate, because addresses are cheap to change and often shared, so the match supports the alert without proving attribution. It is not worthless either: an independent community report about the same address raises likelihood.

5.q: Of the Banyan intelligence results, why does `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` (confidence 85, ISAC-A, finance-sector loader command-and-control) justify raising the priority of `R6` and `R1`?
options: Because the domain matched 18 events, and match count is the main measure of an indicator's overall quality
Because high confidence, a fitting sector context and one-host prevalence all point the same way
Because AMBER-marked indicators are by definition more reliable than GREEN or CLEAR ones
Because any domain-type indicator outranks an IP indicator regardless of its confidence
5.explanation: The indicator is high-confidence, specific to finance-sector phishing which fits a microfinance company, and history shows only one host reaches it, so the evidence converges. The hit count reflects beacon frequency, not how good the indicator is.

5.q: To learn more about a suspicious domain during triage, an analyst plans to browse to it from a corporate workstation and to scan the address that attacked the VPN. Why is this outside the limits of enrichment?
options: Active contact can warn the attacker and touching third-party systems may be an offence
Browsing is acceptable, but scanning must wait until the alert has been formally confirmed
Both are acceptable if done from the SOC's own network rather than from a user workstation
Both are acceptable provided the results are recorded with their source and timestamp
5.explanation: Enrichment is passive: visiting, resolving or scanning can reveal that the SOC has noticed, and touching others' systems without authorisation can be an offence under the IT Act 2000. Recording provenance does not make an unauthorised active lookup acceptable.

5.q: For the `R1` alert involving `divya`, which set of identity attributes is appropriate for the analyst to pull into the case?
options: Role, department and privilege level, plus her full HR file in case it explains motive
Her salary band and performance ratings, since these indicate how attractive a target she is
Role, department, privilege level and, if needed for escalation, her manager
Only her display name, because any further identity data breaches data protection law
5.explanation: Triage needs to know what the account can do and who to escalate to; anything beyond that turns enrichment into a profile of the employee, against the minimum-necessary principle of the DPDP Act 2023. Taking only the name goes too far the other way and loses the privilege context triage depends on.

5.q: After an incident, the SOC finds that a production database had been re-labelled as criticality 1 in the CMDB a week earlier by an account that did not belong to its owner. Which control would most directly have reduced this risk?
options: Re-scoring every alert manually rather than using criticality from the inventory
Copying the CMDB into the SIEM each night so that analysts see the latest values
Restricting who can change criticality and logging and reviewing such changes
Raising every database's criticality to the maximum so that no change matters
5.explanation: Enrichment sources are part of the detection system, so changes to values that drive priority must be restricted and logged. Copying the CMDB faster would just deliver the tampered value to analysts sooner.

5.q: An address range was labelled "trusted partner" two years ago, and every alert from it is enriched into low priority. Nobody now remembers who added the label. What is the right way to manage such labels?
options: Give each label an owner, a reason and an expiry date, as a suppression entry has
Keep the label, since partner traffic is lower risk than ordinary internet traffic
Remove partner labels completely and treat all partner traffic as hostile
Move the label into the threat feed so it is reviewed alongside other indicators
5.explanation: A trust label silently lowers priority for everything it covers, so it can hide an attack from a compromised partner; like a suppression it needs an owner, a reason and an expiry. Removing all such labels overcorrects and discards legitimate context.

5.q: Overnight, a single intelligence feed starts producing twenty times its usual number of matches, mostly against well-known business services. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Escalate every new match, since a surge suggests a widespread campaign against the business
Lower the confidence threshold so that the extra matches are filtered from the triage queue
