Delete the feed's historic indicators and re-import them from the source's archive
Treat the surge as an alert about the feed and review its quality before acting on matches
5.explanation: A careless or poisoned feed can make legitimate services look malicious and push the SOC to block its own business, so a sudden spike should itself be investigated. Escalating every match would amplify the feed's error.

5.q: An analyst writes: "R1 is malicious: the host is criticality 3 and the user is a payments approver." What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: Criticality should be ignored for process-creation alerts, which concern only the endpoint and not the business
Enrichment shows how much the alert matters, not whether the activity happened or is malicious
A payments approver's workstation is routinely excluded from macro-execution rules
The conclusion is right, because high-impact alerts are treated as confirmed by default
5.explanation: Asset and identity context describe impact; whether Word really launched a malicious script is the validation question. Treating high-impact alerts as confirmed by default would escalate every false positive on important hosts.

5.q: Two alerts each report a workstation contacting a newly registered domain. In the first, one host has contacted it; in the second, every workstation in the office has. Which dimension of enrichment differs most between them?
options: Impact, because the domain's registration date sets the value of what could be lost
Likelihood, because a single contact proves the domain is malicious while many disprove it
Provenance, because the two counts come from different proxies with different retention
Scope, because prevalence shows whether the problem is one host or many
5.explanation: Prevalence answers scope: whether the activity is confined to one host or spread across the environment. It can inform likelihood too, but neither count proves or disproves maliciousness on its own.

5.q: The `banyan-payroll-update.example` indicator has source `internal`: Banyan's own team noted the look-alike domain when it was registered on 29 October. Why is such internal intelligence often especially valuable?
options: It is about threats aimed at your own organisation, so its relevance is high
It is shared with the whole sector, so it has been checked by many more analysts
It never expires, so analysts need not check its validity before acting
It carries a higher confidence score than any external source can assign
5.explanation: Internal intelligence describes threats aimed at you, such as a look-alike of your own name, so it fits the environment better than generic feeds. It still has a confidence and validity like any indicator; being internal does not exempt it from those checks.

5.q: A SOC automates enrichment so that a playbook sends the entities of every new alert to an external reputation API. What risk does this create, and what reduces it?
options: API rate limits may slow triage; caching every response for a year removes the problem
One badly written playbook can leak every alert's entities; use approved accounts, protected keys and a submission record
Automation removes the need for privacy checks, because no analyst sees the submitted data
External responses may arrive late; running the playbook only after escalation fixes it
5.explanation: Automation multiplies both value and risk: one faulty playbook can submit internal hostnames and usernames for every alert, so approved accounts, keys in a secrets manager and a record of submissions are needed. Claiming automation removes privacy checks gets it backwards, since the leak happens without anyone noticing.

5.q: In the decision graph for interpreting an indicator match, why is the validity check placed before the confidence and source check?
options: Because confidence is recalculated automatically whenever the validity date is extended
Because only valid indicators carry a TLP marking that permits them to be used in triage
Because an expired indicator's confidence is out of date by definition
Because validity is quicker to check, so it filters the queue before slower checks run
5.explanation: Once an indicator passes its valid_until date the source no longer vouches for it, so its confidence describes the past and cannot be weighed as if current. Speed of checking is not the reason; the order follows from what the confidence value means.

5.q: A night-shift analyst picks up an enriched alert showing `criticality 3` and `role: payments approver`, but the case does not say where either value came from or when it was last updated. What best practice was missed?
options: Re-running enrichment at every hand-over so that values are always freshly fetched
Recording only values from external sources, since internal values are self-evident
Limiting enrichment to one source per entity so that provenance is never ambiguous
Recording the source and age of each enrichment value so others can judge its trust
5.explanation: Without provenance the next analyst cannot tell a current CMDB value from a stale entry or a guess; context without provenance is just a claim. Re-running enrichment at every hand-over wastes effort and still leaves no record of where values came from.

5.q: Reproducing `R2`'s join for `203.0.113.66` lists eight failed users, and one of them is `gopal`, whose failure at 06:42:42Z came four minutes before his successful login. What should the analyst note about the rule's count of eight?
options: That the count is wrong and the rule actually saw only seven sprayed accounts
That gopal's failure proves he typed his own password wrongly a few minutes before succeeding
That the count includes the user who later succeeded, which the analyst should know
That the rule double-counts each user, so the real number of accounts is four
5.explanation: The rule counts distinct failed users at or before the success, so gopal's own failure is one of the eight; that is reasonable for spraying but is a property of the logic to record. It does not make the count wrong, and seven other accounts were still tried.

5.q: `R2` joins failures to a success with the condition `f.ts <= s.ts` and no other time limit. In a dataset covering several months, how could this rule produce a misleading alert?
options: Scattered forgotten-password failures from one address over weeks could add up to five users and fire it
A success followed later by failures would fire it, because the time comparison runs in both directions at once
Failures from different addresses would be merged, because the join ignores the source address
The rule would stop firing altogether once the database held more than one day of events
5.explanation: Without a window any earlier failure from the same address counts, so slow, unrelated failures, for example from a shared office NAT address, could reach the threshold. The join does match on src_ip, so failures from different addresses are not merged.

5.q: The eight failures behind `R2` fall within 49 seconds, exactly seven seconds apart, in alphabetical order of username. What does this pattern contribute to validation?
options: It shows the VPN gateway logs failures in batches sorted by username before writing them
It shows the rule's missing time window has caused unrelated failures to be grouped together
It suggests eight staff mistyped passwords together after a scheduled password change
It is the signature of automation, which removes the doubt raised by the missing time window
5.explanation: Fixed spacing and alphabetical order are what a script produces, not colleagues mistyping, so on this data the absent window does not undermine the alert. A batch of mistakes after a password change would not be evenly spaced and alphabetical.

5.q: To check for activity on WS-104 other than beaconing, one analyst runs `NOT (url LIKE '%ping%')` and gets 31 events; another runs `(url IS NULL OR url NOT LIKE '%ping%')` and gets 40. What explains the nine-event difference?
options: The first query is case-sensitive, so URLs containing PING in capitals were excluded
Events with no URL make the first condition unknown rather than true, so they are silently dropped
The second query counts beacon requests twice, once as NULL and once again as a non-matching URL value
The first query stops at the SIEM's default result limit, which the second query avoids
5.explanation: In SQL a comparison with NULL is neither true nor false, so the Windows and Sysmon events, which have no URL, fall out of the first query, including the 06:14Z PowerShell start. The second query does not double count; it explicitly lets the NULL rows back in.

5.q: An analyst validating `R1` checks only the normalised columns (time, host, user, image, parent image) and writes that "the PowerShell invocation looks ordinary." Why is this conclusion unsafe?
options: The normalised image path is often wrong, so the parent process cannot be trusted either
Sysmon never records command lines, so no invocation detail is available from any view
The command line, showing a hidden, encoded script, exists only in the raw event
The normalised view hides the user field, so the analyst cannot tell who ran the script
5.explanation: minisiem.py keeps twelve common fields as columns and command_line is not one of them, so the decisive -NoP -W Hidden -EncodedCommand detail is visible only by selecting raw. Sysmon did record the command line; the normalised view simply dropped it.

5.q: The proxy records the `invoice.docm` download on WS-104 at 06:12Z, and Sysmon records Word starting PowerShell on the same host at 06:14Z. Why is this pair much stronger evidence than either event alone?
options: They come from independent sources that cannot influence each other yet tell one story on one host
They come from the same SIEM, so the timestamps are guaranteed to share one clock
The proxy event confirms the PowerShell command was malicious by inspecting the content of the downloaded file
Two events always outweigh one, regardless of which sources produced them
5.explanation: The proxy knows nothing of Sysmon and vice versa, so consistent records from both, on the same host within minutes, are hard to explain away or forge. Being stored in the same SIEM does not make sources independent or clocks reliable; independence comes from the systems that produced them.

5.q: The VPN spraying from `203.0.113.66` happened while WS-104 was beaconing. A draft case note says: "The attacker who phished WS-104 also sprayed the VPN." How should this statement be handled?
options: Keep it, since two attacks in the same morning against one company must share an actor
Delete it, since activity without a shared entity must never be mentioned in a case
Keep it, provided the spraying address also appears in the proxy logs for WS-104
Record it as a hypothesis, because the events align in time but share no entity
5.explanation: The VPN lane shares nothing with the WS-104 lanes except the time window, so a link is a hypothesis to test, recorded as such. Deleting it goes too far; a hypothesis is useful as long as it is labelled and not presented as a finding.

5.q: `R3 new_local_admin` returns two hits on WS-104: event 4720 at 07:02Z and event 4732 at 07:03Z, both involving `svc_update`. How should the analyst validate them?
options: As two separate incidents, since two different Windows event IDs were recorded a minute apart on the host
As one action: the account was created and then added to Administrators a minute later
As a duplicate log entry caused by the SIEM ingesting the same event twice
As a false positive, since creating an account does not itself grant privileges
5.explanation: The raw events show account creation followed by group addition, one story that the rule counts twice; validating it as one action avoids inflating the case. They are not duplicates, because the event IDs and times differ.

5.q: `R6 beacon_regular_small` fires when a host makes ten or more requests to one URL with under 50 bytes of variation in size. What validation step is needed before calling a hit a beacon?
options: Checking that the URL uses HTTPS, since command-and-control traffic is always encrypted
Checking that the bytes sent are exactly identical, since any variation rules out a beacon
Checking that the requests are evenly spaced in time, which the rule never tests
Checking that more than one host contacts the URL, since beacons spread across a network
5.explanation: The rule ignores intervals, so a dashboard that refreshes repeatedly with similar sizes could satisfy it; regular spacing is what turns a match into evidence of automated check-ins. Requiring identical sizes would add nothing about timing and would miss real beacons with small jitter.

5.q: An analyst argues that the 06:14Z PowerShell start on WS-104 is suspicious because "nobody is at work at six in the morning." Banyan's staff work in IST. What is the correct assessment?
options: The event was at 11:44 IST, mid-morning, so the time is not suspicious in itself
The event was at 00:44 IST, after midnight, so the analyst understated the concern
The dataset uses local time, so 06:14 is genuinely early morning in the office
Time zone is irrelevant, because Sysmon timestamps are not reliable enough to use
5.explanation: The dataset is in UTC and IST is five and a half hours ahead, so 06:14Z is 11:44 in the office. Subtracting the offset instead of adding it gives the after-midnight answer, a common time-zone error.

5.q: Twenty-five minutes into validating an alert, the analyst has found suspicious signs but cannot obtain the endpoint data needed to confirm or refute it. The SOC's time box is 30 minutes. What is the appropriate outcome?
options: Close the alert as refuted, since the missing data means nothing could be proven
Mark it confirmed, since suspicious signs justify assuming the worst case
Keep working on it beyond the time box until the endpoint data becomes available
Conclude undetermined, record what is missing, and escalate or hand it over
5.explanation: Undetermined is a legitimate conclusion when recorded with what is missing, and the case then moves on through escalation or hand-over. Calling it refuted would close a possibly real attack on the basis of absent evidence.

5.q: To find out whether `gopal` made the 06:46Z VPN connection himself, which approach is safest?
options: Send him a chat message from the SOC account asking whether he personally used the VPN early this morning
Call him on a known phone number or via the service desk and ask a neutral, specific question
Reply to his most recent email asking him to confirm his VPN activity in writing
Reset his password first and then ask him through his corporate chat account
5.explanation: If his credentials are compromised, the attacker may answer messages sent to his accounts, so a verified out-of-band channel and a neutral question are needed. A chat message from the SOC still lands in an account the attacker may control.

5.q: An alert shows a database administrator exporting a large customer table at night, and the only person who could explain it is that administrator. What should the analyst consider before contacting them?
options: Whether the administrator's manager is available to sit in on the conversation
Whether the export is under the size limit below which contacting the user is required before any escalation
Whether this could be deliberate misuse, in which case the playbook escalates without alerting them
Whether the administrator has received security awareness training this year
5.explanation: When the person you would ask could be the one misusing access, asking alerts them; insider-risk cases are escalated according to the playbook so HR and legal can be involved. Bringing in their manager still tips off the subject.

5.q: During validation of the WS-104 alerts, an analyst proposes logging in to the workstation remotely to "have a quick look" at running processes. Why is this inappropriate at the validation stage?
options: It changes the host's state and may alert the attacker; host collection belongs to incident response
It is acceptable only if the analyst uses the user's own credentials, so that no new logon records are created
It is unnecessary because the SIEM already stores a full memory image of every host
It is inappropriate only outside office hours, when users cannot be informed beforehand
5.explanation: Validation works from the SIEM's copy of the evidence; logging in alters the host and can tip off the attacker, so collection is left to incident response and evidence preservation. Using the user's credentials would make things worse by blurring who did what.

5.q: While seeking refuting evidence for a suspicious script alert, an analyst finds a change ticket that describes exactly the observed activity. What should the analyst do before relying on it?
options: Close the alert as benign, since a matching change ticket is the strongest refutation available
Ask the user who ran the script to confirm the ticket by replying in the same channel
Escalate the alert anyway, since change tickets are never accepted as refuting evidence
Check the ticket at its source, such as who raised and approved it and when
5.explanation: An attacker who knows how the SOC validates may plant refuting evidence, so it must be checked at its source as carefully as confirming evidence. Rejecting all tickets goes too far, since genuine change records are exactly how benign activity is shown.

5.q: In the validation workflow, why is the raw event read before pivoting across other sources?
options: Because the SIEM deletes raw events once a pivot query has been run against them
Because a pivot built on a mis-parsed or missing field produces a story on a false basis
Because pivots can only use fields that appear in the raw event and not the normalised view
Because reading raw events is faster, so it should be done while the alert is still fresh
5.explanation: If the host, user, time or a key field is wrong or missing in the normalised view, every pivot built on it inherits the error, so the alert's own evidence is verified first. Pivots in minisiem.py actually use the normalised columns, which is why those must be checked against raw.

5.q: At step 2 of validation, reproducing the rule shows it matched a process whose parent was a different program that merely had the target name as a substring. What follows?
options: The analyst completes the pivot and refutation steps before deciding anything
The alert is escalated, since any rule match must be investigated in full
The alert is a false positive, and the later steps are unnecessary
The alert is a benign true positive, since the rule worked as designed
5.explanation: The workflow has an exit at every step: if the rule matched the wrong thing, the claim is false and there is nothing left to corroborate. It is not a benign true positive, because the rule did not detect the behaviour it was meant to detect.

5.q: Validation of an `R1`-style alert shows Word really did start PowerShell, and the application owner confirms it is an approved finance macro listed on the organisation's approved-macro register. How should the outcome be classified?
options: As a benign true positive: the rule worked as designed and the activity was authorised
As a false positive: the alert should never have fired on approved activity
As undetermined: an owner's statement can never refute a detection
As confirmed: any script started by Office is malicious by definition
5.explanation: The first two validation questions passed, so the rule matched what it was meant to match; the third showed the activity was authorised, which is a benign true positive. Calling it a false positive misdescribes the rule, which did nothing wrong.

5.q: An analyst runs a `LEFT JOIN` variant of `R2` that lists every successful VPN login with its count of preceding failures, and sees `gopal`'s 13:33Z session with 0 failures. What is the purpose of this check?
options: To show that gopal's evening session was also part of the spraying campaign
To recover the country field, which the normal join drops from VPN events
To remove the rule's dependency on the source address for counting failures
To test the rule's negative case: a routine session correctly does not fire
5.explanation: Checking cases that should not fire shows whether the rule separates normal and suspicious activity on this data; here the routine session has zero failures and stays quiet. The country field is in the raw event and needs json_extract, not a different join.

5.q: The pivot on `gopal` shows him browsing through the office proxy from his workstation before and after the 06:46Z VPN success from an address of unknown location. What does this establish?
options: Proof that gopal's account was compromised, so he need not be contacted at all
Strong corroboration that his credentials were used without him, still to be put to him safely
Proof that the VPN success was a logging error, since he could not have been in two places at the same time
Nothing useful, because proxy and VPN events cannot be compared across different sources
5.explanation: A user working at an office desk rarely needs an external VPN session from an unknown location, so this strongly suggests credential misuse, but he might have used a personal device; that question is put to him through a verified channel while his credentials are treated as at risk. Calling it proof skips that refutation step.

5.q: While validating `R1`, a pivot on WS-104 reveals the first request to `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` three minutes after the PowerShell start. According to the validation workflow, what happens next?
options: The domain is noted in the conclusion of R1 and left for the threat-intelligence team
The domain is blocked immediately, since it appeared within minutes of the script start
The domain becomes a new claim, and the workflow restarts at step 1 for it
The domain is ignored, since R1 concerns process creation rather than network traffic
5.explanation: A new entity found during a pivot becomes its own claim to state, reproduce, corroborate and conclude, which is how the R6 beacon was validated. Blocking at once acts on a timing coincidence before the claim has been tested.

5.q: After the Security log on WS-104 is cleared at 08:17Z (event 1102), the SIEM holds no further Windows events from that host. How should the analyst interpret the empty lane afterwards?
options: As possibly missing telemetry rather than proof that nothing more happened on the host
As evidence that the attacker left the host once the log had been cleared
As a sign the clearing failed, since a successful clear would also remove event 1102
As confirmation that the incident ended at 08:17Z and the case can be scoped to that time
5.explanation: An empty result means nothing until you know your query, time window and telemetry could have shown activity; after a log clear, a gap may mean missing records, not missing activity. Concluding that the attacker left reads the absence of evidence as evidence.

5.q: `R1`'s SQL matches events whose lower-cased `parent_image` contains `winword.exe`. Why did the analyst read the raw event to confirm the full parent path was the Office installation's `WINWORD.EXE`?
options: Because lower-casing the field can change the path and match a different drive letter
Because Sysmon records only the file name, so the full installation path must be reconstructed by hand
Because the rule matches only exact paths, so a renamed Word binary would never fire it
Because a substring match would also catch a different program whose name contains that string
5.explanation: A contains-test fires on any path with that substring, so confirming the real Office path rules out an impostor or unrelated program. The rule is the opposite of an exact-path match, which is exactly why the check is needed.

5.q: Validation notes for `R2` record that the rule has no time window and could fire on scattered failures over weeks, even though it fired correctly this time. What should happen to this observation?
options: Nothing, since the rule produced a true positive and should be left unchanged
It should be fed back to detection engineering as evidence for adding a time window
The rule should be disabled until the analyst rewrites it during the same shift
It should be kept only in the analyst's personal notes to avoid criticising the rule author
5.explanation: Rule weaknesses found during validation are tuning evidence for detection engineering, even when the alert itself was correct. Disabling the rule would remove a detection that has just caught a real attack.

5.q: WS-104 made 18 requests to `cdn-telemetry-sync.example` between 06:17:00Z and 07:42:02Z, each exactly 220 bytes, spaced about five minutes apart with only seconds of variation. Which feature most clearly separates this from a person browsing?
options: The total of 18 requests, since people rarely visit one site more than ten times
The use of a path containing api, which only automated software ever requests
The fixed interval combined with an identical request size across every request
The start time shortly after the office opened, which is typical of scheduled tasks
5.explanation: A steady five-minute interval with a constant 220-byte size is what an automated check-in produces, and human browsing does not. A request count alone can be reached by a busy user or a refreshing page, which is why R6 needs the timing check.

5.q: At 02:00 the R3 new_local_admin rule fires because the IT administrator account created a new local account. No change ticket exists, and the analyst closes the alert as a false positive because the administrator is trusted. What is wrong with this disposition?
options: The rule matched exactly what it was written to detect, and trust is context, not a record of authorisation
The alert should have been closed as a benign true positive because administrators routinely create accounts
The analyst should have added a suppression for the administrator account before closing the alert
Nothing is wrong, because an action by a known administrator cannot be malicious or a policy violation
5.explanation: An account really was created, so the rule did its job and the alert is not a false positive. Without a change record it cannot be a benign true positive either; it is a true positive or undetermined until the owner confirms. Calling it benign because the user is an administrator is the exact identity-as-authorisation error.

5.q: Investigation of an R4 large_upload alert shows that a misconfigured parser fills bytes_out with downloaded bytes, so big downloads look like uploads. Which response best fits this finding?
options: Add a scoped suppression for R4 on the affected host until the parser can be reviewed next quarter
Raise the R4 byte threshold so that the inflated values no longer cross it on ordinary downloads
Close it as a false positive and request a parser mapping fix, since every rule and investigator using bytes_out is misled
Close it as a benign true positive because the transfer really happened, was initiated by the user and matched the rule's intent
5.explanation: The rule matched bad data, so it is a false positive whose cause is in normalisation; fixing the data corrects R4 and every other consumer of the field. A suppression or threshold change would only hide the symptom for one rule while the wrong field keeps misleading other detections and investigations.

5.q: Two analysts disagree about R6 beacon_regular_small firing on a legitimate monitoring agent's heartbeat: one calls it a false positive, the other a benign true positive. What resolves the disagreement?
options: The number of times the heartbeat has fired this week, since recurring hits are always benign
The written statement of the rule's intent, because the disposition depends on what the rule was meant to detect
The asset criticality of the host, because low-criticality hosts produce benign true positives by definition, whatever the rule
The seniority of the analysts, because disposition labels are a matter of SOC convention only
5.explanation: If R6 is documented as detecting machine-regular small requests, the heartbeat is a benign true positive; if it is documented as detecting command-and-control beaconing, it is a false positive. Frequency does not decide intent, which is why every rule needs a written description of what it is for.

5.q: Why does the classification method ask whether the rule matched its intent before asking whether the activity was authorised?
options: Because authorisation records are stored in the SIEM and are faster to check than reading through the rule logic
Because a benign true positive must always be converted into a permanent exclusion in the rule
Because detection engineering only accepts tuning requests that include an authorisation check
Because it stops trusted actors' real events being called false, and the two outcomes need different fixes
5.explanation: Asking intent first prevents closing a real event as 'false' just because the actor is trusted, and it separates a broken rule (false positive, fix the rule) from a correct rule hitting approved activity (benign true positive, leave the rule). Authorisation evidence actually lives outside the SIEM, in change and test records.

5.q: An event ID 4732 alert shows a real group-membership change on a server. The analyst finds no change record, and the server owner is on leave until next week. What is the correct disposition for now?
options: False positive, because the rule should not fire on servers that have a named owner
Benign true positive, because server owners routinely make group changes during maintenance
Undetermined, with the missing authorisation evidence recorded and the case kept open or escalated
True positive closed with no further action, because the owner cannot be asked about the change before next week
5.explanation: The rule matched its intent, but there is no record to prove authorisation and no way to obtain one yet, so the evidence is insufficient: undetermined, recording what is missing. Benign requires a record, and an unconfirmed real event must not be closed without action.

5.q: In the first lab run, triage.py prints the full queue but no 'suppressed' line, even though SUPPRESS contains the itadmin entry. How should a reviewer treat that suppression?
options: As dead configuration to review: either the benign activity stopped, or it now arrives under a different field value
As proof that the suppression is working perfectly, since no build-account alerts reached the queue
As a parser fault, because a suppression that never prints a line proves the user field is not being loaded from the events at all
As safe to make permanent, because a suppression that never matches can never hide an attacker
5.explanation: The dataset contains no itadmin event, so the entry matched nothing. A never-matching suppression is harmless today but must be reviewed: remove it if the activity ended, or correct it if the activity now appears under another value and is reaching the queue anyway.

5.q: After the BLD-01 itadmin event is appended and triage.py is rerun, which observation best shows that the suppression is properly scoped?
options: The loader reports 341 events instead of 340 after the reload
The suppressed line prints every field of the BLD-01 hit, including target_user
The R5 log_cleared alert for WS-104 remains at the top of the queue at 10.8
Both R3 new_local_admin alerts for divya on WS-104 still appear at priority 5.4
5.explanation: Scope is shown by what the suppression did not hide: the only other R3 hits, the svc_update alerts on WS-104, remain in the queue. The printed suppressed line is the audit trail, which is valuable but says nothing about whether the condition was too wide.

5.q: In the over-suppression run, an analyst adds ("R3", "host", "WS-104", "too noisy", ""). Other WS-104 alerts still reach the queue. What is the most serious consequence for the investigation?
options: The R5 log_cleared alert drops in priority because R3 no longer contributes to the WS-104 host's combined entity risk score
The persistence step disappears, so the case cannot explain continued access and clean-up may leave svc_update in place
The BLD-01 build account alert reappears because two entries for the same rule conflict
The suppressed lines are no longer printed, so there is no trace of what the entry hid
5.explanation: The host-wide entry hides both svc_update alerts, the intruder's new local account. The intrusion may still be found from other alerts, but without that step the attacker's foothold may survive remediation. The suppressed lines are in fact still printed, which is what makes the damage discoverable.

5.q: A copy of triage.py is changed so that the itadmin entry's expiry is 2026-10-31, a date already past, and the suppressed line still appears. What explains this?
options: The date string is in the wrong format, so Python treats it as a date far in the future
The loader caches the previous SUPPRESS list until minisiem.py load is run again
The matching loop unpacks r, f, v, *_ so the reason and expiry are collected but never compared
Expiry is only checked once a day, so a suppression keeps working until the next scheduled run
5.explanation: The *_ collects the remaining tuple elements and ignores them, so the expiry is documentation, not enforcement. The ISO date format is fine; it is simply never read by the matching code.

5.q: With expiry enforced through date.fromisoformat(exp), the host-wide entry with an empty expiry makes the script stop with ValueError as soon as it checks an R3 hit on WS-104. Why is this behaviour desirable?
options: It enforces a stricter contract in which a suppression without a valid expiry cannot take effect at all
It converts the empty expiry into today's date, so the entry quietly expires on its own at midnight tonight
It hides all R3 alerts until the error is fixed, which prevents duplicate pages to on-call
It removes the host entry from the list permanently and records the change in version control
5.explanation: Every entry must now carry a parseable date, so an entry without an expiry fails loudly instead of suppressing forever. It does not silently convert or delete the entry, and it does not hide alerts; it stops the run so someone must fix the configuration.

5.q: An analyst asks for the suppression ("R2", "user", "gopal", ...) to stop a recurring VPN alert, but R2 alerts for that account keep reaching the queue. What is the most likely cause?
options: R2 is a correlation rule, and correlation rules are evaluated after the suppression check
R2's output has src_ip, users_failed, success_user and ts, so hit.get("user") is always None
The suppression needs a reference to a change ticket before triage.py will load it
The user value must be written in upper case because the comparison is case-insensitive
5.explanation: The check reads field names from each rule's output, and R2 has no user column, so the entry can never match. The kit does not validate tickets or case; this failure is noisy rather than blind, which is why every suppression should be tested against stored samples it should and should not hide.

5.q: Once expiry is enforced and the itadmin entry has expired, the BLD-01 alert returns at only 3.6, near the bottom of the queue. Why is its priority so low?
options: Expired suppressions are automatically demoted to the lowest severity until they are renewed
R3 has a lower severity on servers than on workstations in the minisiem.py rule table
The alert is marked as a duplicate of the WS-104 R3 alerts and is scored at a reduced weight
BLD-01 is not in the ASSETS table and gets default criticality, and itadmin is not in USERS
5.explanation: priority() multiplies severity, confidence and asset criticality; an unknown asset gets the default criticality, and the unknown user prints as '?'. Nothing in the kit demotes expired entries; the alert simply reappears with whatever score its entities earn, which is the intended prompt to renew or stop the activity.

5.q: A rule is suspicious on finance workstations but routinely fires on lab test machines. Why does the lesson call lowering its priority on the lab machines safer than suppressing it there?
options: Because lowering priority also lowers the rule's false-positive count in the SOC metrics
Because a low-priority alert can still be found and examined, while a suppressed one never reaches an analyst
Because suppressions cannot be scoped to a group of hosts, only to a single host name
Because priority changes do not need any review, while every suppression must first pass the four-eyes principle
5.explanation: Reducing confidence or recording low asset criticality moves the alert down the queue without hiding it, so a curious analyst can still find it. Both kinds of change should be reviewed; the point is visibility, not the approval process.

5.q: A SOC report shows one analyst closed forty false positives from the same rule this week. How should this be interpreted and acted on?
options: The analyst is closing too quickly and should be retrained on validation before closing alerts
The analyst should add a personal suppression so that the rule no longer reaches their queue
The rule should be disabled until the analyst has time to investigate each of the forty hits
It is a precision problem with the rule, to be tracked per rule and raised with detection engineering
5.explanation: False positives are tracked per rule, not per analyst: forty a week marks a detection-engineering priority, and the analyst closing them is doing the job. Disabling the rule would remove coverage entirely instead of improving its precision.

5.q: Which false-positive closure note gives detection engineering the most to work with?
options: "FP, closed. Activity looks normal for this user and host. No further action required."
"FP. Rule is too noisy and should be turned off on finance workstations as soon as possible."
"FP on R1 v3: parent_image holds the grandparent because the parent field was empty; raw event attached; 6th this week; propose parser fix."
"FP, user confirmed by chat that they opened PowerShell themselves. Closing to clear the queue."
5.explanation: A useful record names the rule and version, the specific mismatch, the evidence, the frequency and a proposed change. 'Looks normal' or a user's chat message gives no evidence about why the rule misfired, and a blanket shutdown proposal ignores coverage.

5.q: A Tier 1 analyst with SIEM write access spots an obvious flaw in a rule's condition. What is the appropriate way to get it fixed?
options: Raise a tuning request with the evidence; engineering reproduces it, tests against stored FPs and known TPs, and deploys through review
Edit the production rule immediately, since the analyst holds the best evidence about the misfire
Add a suppression for the affected pattern now and mention the flaw at the next shift handover
Close all future hits from the rule as false positives until the rule owner is available to review the evidence and change the condition
5.explanation: The analyst supplies the evidence, but the change is tested against both the false positive and known true positives and deployed through review, then confirmed in the queue. Silent edits or ad-hoc suppressions skip testing and can remove real coverage.

5.q: A rule that produced about thirty alerts a day suddenly produces none for three days, with no announced change. What should the SOC conclude?
options: The environment has become safer, so the rule's threshold can be lowered to restore its usual volume of about thirty a day
Nothing, because only increases in alert volume indicate a problem with a detection
The rule has reached its tuning goal and can be moved to a lower review cadence
The drop needs investigation, since a new suppression, a broken parser or a stopped log source can each cause it
5.explanation: A quiet queue is not necessarily a healthy one: an unexpected drop is as worth investigating as a spike, because it may mean the SOC has stopped seeing the activity. Assuming improvement, or adjusting thresholds before knowing the cause, risks building on a blind spot.

5.q: Detection engineering raises a counting rule's threshold because the real baseline is higher than assumed. Which risk does this tuning option introduce?
options: Other rules that share the same field begin to fire on the same events
Every future hit is hidden from the queue but still recorded in the audit trail
An attacker who keeps their activity just below the new threshold is no longer detected
The rule loses its written intent and can no longer be classified as FP or BTP
5.explanation: Raising a threshold trades noise for blind space just below it, which an attacker can deliberately occupy. Affecting other rules through a shared field is the side effect of fixing data, not of changing a threshold.

5.q: Why should a suppression record each match it suppresses rather than silently drop the alert?
options: So that a hunter or investigator can still find the evidence if the suppressed account or pattern is later abused
So that the suppressed alert can be re-raised automatically into the queue whenever the analyst queue is otherwise empty
So that the rule's precision metric includes suppressed hits as true positives
So that the reason and expiry fields are printed on screen each time the rule runs
5.explanation: The audit trail of suppressed matches keeps the evidence searchable, so a review can ask what suppressions hid. Nothing re-raises suppressed hits automatically, and they are not counted as true positives.

5.q: A SIEM administrator adds an exclusion for their own workstation across several rules late at night. Which controls would most directly expose or prevent this?
options: A higher severity for every rule on that workstation, so the exclusion is overridden
Monthly retraining of analysts on the difference between false and benign true positives
A rule that all suppressions must use the user field rather than the host field
Version-controlled suppressions with review, plus alerting or daily reports on changes to the list
5.explanation: Suppressions decide what the SOC cannot see, so they are an attack surface for insiders and intruders: restricted change rights, reviewed diffs and change alerting reviewed by someone else address that. Choosing a different field does not stop someone from excluding themselves.

5.q: A rule raised 20 alerts last month: 5 true positives, 10 false positives and 5 benign true positives. Counting benign hits as noise for the queue, what is its precision?
options: 25 percent
33 percent
50 percent
75 percent
5.explanation: Precision is TP / (TP + FP + BTP) when benign hits count as queue noise: 5 / 20 = 25 percent. The 50 percent figure would result from counting benign true positives as useful alerts, which is not the queue-noise definition used here.

5.q: You are asked to suppress R1 for one approved, signed finance macro on WS-104. Why is a host-only condition unacceptable, and what limits the kit's SUPPRESS design here?
options: A host entry would hide the macro's hits but also R5 and R4 hits; SUPPRESS cannot name a rule
A host entry would hide every R1 hit on WS-104, including real phishing; each SUPPRESS entry compares only one field
A host entry would never match because R1 output lacks a host field; the kit's SUPPRESS design supports only the user field
A host entry would hide only future hits; SUPPRESS cannot apply to alerts already in the queue
5.explanation: A host condition covers anyone and anything on WS-104, including the very Word-spawns-PowerShell event in the lab storyline. The safe condition combines host with user and image, but each SUPPRESS tuple tests a single field for equality. R1 does output host, and each entry already names its rule.

5.q: The BLD-01 itadmin event from the lab recurs, but CHG-1042 was closed in October. How should it now be classified?
options: False positive, because the change ticket no longer matches the rule's intent
Benign true positive, because the suppression entry still lists CHG-1042 as its reference and the account is a known build account
Not benign: without a current authorisation record it is a true positive or undetermined, and the owner is asked
Benign true positive, because the same build account performed the same action as before
5.explanation: The rule still matched its intent, so it is not a false positive. Authorisation must be a valid record, and a closed change no longer authorises the activity; a stale suppression entry or a familiar pattern is not proof.

5.q: A team proposes an allowlist that exempts the backup service account from every detection rule. Why does this break the suppression anatomy taught in the lesson?
options: Because service accounts cannot be suppressed at all, only interactive user accounts
Because allowlists must be written as exclusions in rule logic, never as suppressions
Because a suppression must always include the host field in addition to the user field
Because a suppression applies to one rule; a global exemption hides everything that account might ever do
5.explanation: Each suppression names one rule so that the documented benign pattern is hidden and nothing else; a cross-rule exemption makes the account an invisible place to stand. The anatomy calls for the narrowest identifying fields, not a mandatory host field.

5.q: To cut noise, an analyst proposes suppressing a script-execution rule wherever the process name is powershell.exe. Why is this a poor condition?
options: Attackers living off the land use the same tools as administrators, so a process name alone hides their activity too
Process names are not normalised by the parser, so the condition would never match anything
PowerShell alerts are always true positives and must never be classified as noise
The suppression would also hide events from unrelated rules that mention PowerShell anywhere in their command-line field
5.explanation: Wide conditions such as a process name alone match legitimate and malicious use equally, which is exactly what living-off-the-land techniques exploit. A suppression is scoped to its rule, so it would not hide other rules' alerts; the problem is how much of this rule it hides.

5.q: During a busy shift an analyst posts in the team chat: "can someone look at WS-104? lots of alerts". Two people react with a thumbs-up. Why has the case not been escalated?
options: Because chat messages are not retained long enough to count as evidence for the case or for its formal escalation record
Because no named receiver has accepted ownership through a channel they must watch, so the analyst still owns it
Because escalations must always be sent by email so that a written copy exists
Because the message did not include a priority score from the triage queue
5.explanation: Escalation is a transfer of ownership: a named receiver, an obligated channel, the evidence and an explicit acknowledgement. Reactions in chat are not acceptance. Email alone is not the requirement either; for urgent cases a page pointing to the case is.

5.q: An analyst pages the on-call IR lead for a SEV1 case, but no acknowledgement arrives within the escalation SLA. What should happen next?
options: Assume the IR lead has seen the page and begin containment on their behalf
Wait for the next shift handover, when the IR lead will be back at a desk
Follow the playbook: page the secondary on-call, then the SOC manager, while still owning the case
Close the page and reopen the case at a lower severity so that it fits the normal queue
5.explanation: Silence is not consent; it is a failed escalation, and ownership stays with the analyst until someone acknowledges. Taking containment decisions without authority, or waiting, both leave the case without a capable owner.

5.q: In the lab queue the R6 beacon_regular_small alert on WS-104 has the lowest priority, 3.6. How should this affect the escalation decision?
options: It should not: priority orders the work, but R6 shows a command-and-control pattern, which is a hard trigger
R6 should be escalated only if the higher-priority alerts on WS-104 turn out to be confirmed true positives first
R6 should go to the Tier 2 case queue rather than to on-call because its score is below 5
R6 should be closed as noise unless its priority rises above the R4 upload alert
5.explanation: The decision is made on the criteria, not on queue position: 18 small regular requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example indicate C2 and meet a hard trigger. Queue scores combine severity, confidence and criticality to order work; they are not escalation thresholds.

5.q: Five of the six alert types in the lab queue concern WS-104 and divya, and one concerns a VPN login as gopal. How should the analyst structure the escalation?
options: Six separate pages, one per alert type, so that each rule owner can respond independently
One case covering all six alert types, stating as fact that the VPN spray caused the phishing
Two unrelated cases, because the alerts involve different users and different hosts
One case for WS-104 and divya, with a linked case for gopal's VPN login and the connection stated as a hypothesis
5.explanation: Related alerts are grouped into one case before escalating, so the receiver sees the story rather than six pages. The link to the VPN spray rests on timing only, so it is a linked case stated as a hypothesis, neither merged as fact nor treated as unrelated.

5.q: A Tier 1 analyst's thirty-minute time-box expires on an unusual logon to a domain controller. The evidence is still inconclusive either way. What should the analyst do?
options: Return the alert to the queue with notes, because undetermined alerts simply wait there until more evidence arrives
Close it as undetermined, because the time-box defines the maximum effort for any alert
Escalate to Tier 2, because an undetermined alert on a crown-jewel asset meets the impact-based criteria
Page the CISO directly, because domain controllers are always handled as reportable incidents
5.explanation: For a high-impact entity, 'undetermined' is a reason to escalate rather than to wait; returning to the queue is the option for low-impact alerts. Paging the CISO skips the hierarchical route, and reportability is a separate later check.

5.q: The IR lead who owns the WS-104 case needs gopal's credentials reset and his VPN sessions reviewed. What kind of escalation is this request?
options: Hierarchical, because it moves the case to a higher tier with more authority
Functional, because it goes across to the identity team, which owns that capability
Hierarchical, because only the CISO can approve resetting a user's credentials
Functional, because it hands ownership of the whole case to the identity team
5.explanation: Functional escalation moves expertise across to a specialist owner, here the identity team. Ownership of the case stays with the IR lead: one owner, many contributors, each request tracked in the case.

5.q: Evidence suggests a production database server is compromised, and the analyst believes it should be isolated immediately. The analyst has no authority to isolate production systems. What is the right move?
options: Isolate it anyway and record the reason, since the evidence is strong and time matters
Wait until the investigation proves the compromise before mentioning isolation to anyone
Ask a colleague with the right privileges to isolate it informally and document it later
Escalate to the owner of that authority with the evidence and a recommendation to isolate
5.explanation: Actions beyond the analyst's remit are escalated: the analyst recommends and the authority owner decides. Acting without authority, or arranging it informally, bypasses accountability; waiting for proof delays a high-impact decision.

5.q: Triage of a data-access alert suggests that a senior executive may be copying customer records for personal use. How should the escalation be handled?
options: Through the route the playbook names, often the SOC manager with HR or legal, on a need-to-know basis
Through the normal on-call page, copying the whole SOC distribution list so that every shift is kept aware
By contacting the executive first to give them a chance to explain before escalating
By posting the evidence in the incident channel so the investigation can start immediately
5.explanation: Insider and executive matters are sensitive: they follow the named route and are kept need-to-know. Wide distribution or contacting the subject may warn them and spread sensitive details.

5.q: The WS-104 evidence shows divya opened a malicious document and her workstation is compromised. Why should the escalation avoid email threads that include her?
options: Because divya is the main suspect and must not learn that she is being investigated
Because her mailbox may be readable by the attacker, so the incident needs an out-of-band channel
Because email does not support attachments large enough to carry the case evidence
Because CERT-In requires incident communication to stay off corporate email systems
5.explanation: When normal channels may be compromised, discussing the incident there can tip off the attacker; that is why out-of-band communication is used. Divya is the victim of a phishing document, not presumed to be an insider.

5.q: A new analyst is unsure how to build a SIEM query to check whether an alert's source address appears elsewhere, and considers escalating the alert to Tier 2. What does the lesson advise?
options: Escalate it, because any doubt about an alert justifies handing it upward
Close the alert as undetermined, since the analyst cannot complete validation
Consult a colleague about the query; that is consultation, not a reason to escalate
Page on-call, because the tooling gap is itself a hard trigger for the SOC
5.explanation: Escalation is not a substitute for triage: uncertainty about a tool is solved by asking a colleague. The 'when in doubt, escalate' advice applies to doubt about a potentially serious alert, not to how to run a query.

5.q: The SOC first noticed a possibly reportable incident at 08:25Z. Assuming the CERT-In six-hour window starts then, which deadline should be written into the case?
options: 14:25Z, which is 19:55 IST
14:25Z, which is 08:55 IST
13:55Z, which is 19:25 IST
19:55Z, which is 14:25 IST
5.explanation: 08:25Z plus six hours is 14:25Z, and IST is UTC+5:30, giving 19:55 IST. The last option swaps the zones: 19:55 is the IST time, not UTC. Writing both forms in the case avoids exactly that confusion.

5.q: A possibly reportable incident is noticed at 21:10Z on 3 November. What is the six-hour deadline, expressed in IST?
options: 02:40 IST on 4 November
03:10 IST on 4 November
08:40 IST on 3 November
08:40 IST on 4 November
5.explanation: 21:10Z plus six hours is 03:10Z on 4 November; adding the 5:30 IST offset gives 08:40 IST on 4 November. 02:40 IST on 4 November is when the incident was noticed, not the deadline, and the deadline cannot fall on 3 November in IST.

5.q: An analyst notices a likely compromise but spends four hours confirming every detail before escalating. If the incident turns out to be reportable to CERT-In, what is the main consequence?
options: None, because the six-hour window starts when the compromise is confirmed by the analyst
The organisation has about two hours left for the legal decision and the report
The window restarts when the IR lead acknowledges the escalation, giving six more hours
The report can be filed late as long as the analyst's confirmation work is documented
5.explanation: The six hours run from noticing, not from certainty or containment, so four hours of confirmation leave only two for the POC and legal. Hard triggers exist partly to prevent this; acknowledgement does not reset the clock.

5.q: In the WS-104 hand-off, who decides whether the incident is reported to CERT-In, and who sends the report?
options: The Tier 1 analyst decides, because they noticed it first, and sends the report directly
The on-call IR lead decides and sends it, because they own the case after acknowledgement
CERT-In decides after receiving the analyst's case export, so no internal reporting decision is needed at all
The designated point of contact with legal advice decides, and the report goes through that POC
5.explanation: Reporting authority and technical authority sit with different roles: the IR lead raises the question, the CISO / legal POC decides and reports, and the analyst flags and supplies the time noticed and facts. The analyst never contacts CERT-In directly.

5.q: A case note written by a Tier 1 analyst reads: "Probably not reportable; anyway we have 72 hours." What is the problem with it?
options: It records an interpretation of legal obligations that belongs to accountable roles; the note should state facts and flags
It uses the wrong figure, and the correct fix is simply to replace 72 hours with the six-hour window in the same case note
It should have been written in the escalation's NEED field instead of in the case notes
It is acceptable as long as the IR lead countersigns the note before the shift ends
5.explanation: Analysts should not paraphrase or estimate legal obligations in case notes; an analyst's guess can mislead the decision. Correcting the number still leaves an analyst's legal interpretation in the record; the note should flag 'possibly reportable' and give the time noticed.

5.q: In the WS-104 escalation, the CONFIDENCE line says the link between the VPN spray and WS-104 rests on timing only. What failure does stating this protect against?
options: The receiver discarding the VPN evidence because it came from a different log source
The IR lead rejecting the escalation because its confidence is not high for every finding
A reasonable hypothesis being treated later as fact and sending the investigation down the wrong path
The CERT-In report being delayed until the two cases are proven to be connected
5.explanation: Separating confirmed facts from hypotheses keeps a plausible link from hardening into an assumption that misleads the investigation. The escalation still states high confidence that WS-104 is compromised; reporting does not wait for the link to be proven.

5.q: The WS-104 escalation's DONE line includes "No containment taken." Why is recording this deliberate non-action important?
options: It shows that the analyst followed the rule never to contain a host before CERT-In is notified
It proves that the evidence on WS-104 has not been altered by the SOC since the alert
It tells the CERT-In point of contact that the incident is still in the detection phase
It tells the receiver the host is still live, so containment remains an open, urgent decision
5.explanation: The receiver must know what has not been done: WS-104 is still live, which is why the NEED line asks for a containment decision within 30 minutes. There is no rule that containment waits for CERT-In, and non-action alone proves nothing about evidence integrity.

5.q: In the escalation decision path, the 'Possibly reportable?' check comes after the decision to escalate, not before it. Why?
options: Because only the CISO can open the reporting check, and the CISO is reached last
Because paging on-call should never be delayed while someone works out whether a regulator must be told
Because reportability can only be judged after containment has been completed
Because the time noticed is not recorded until the IR lead acknowledges the page
5.explanation: The most urgent cases leave the path immediately and are then checked for reportability; delaying the page for a legal question gives the attacker time. Reportability is not deferred until after containment; it travels early, right after the IR lead takes the case.

5.q: At 02:00 an analyst escalates a SEV1 case by sending an email to the IR lead and assigning a ticket to the IR queue. What is missing?
options: A page or call that interrupts a human, pointing to the case rather than repeating it
A copy of the full evidence pasted into the email so the IR lead need not open the case
A second ticket in the identity team's queue so that two owners can work in parallel
A message to the affected user asking them to stop using the workstation until morning
5.explanation: The case system is the record, but urgency needs a paging channel; email or a ticket alone is not enough out of hours. The page should link to the case, not duplicate it, and parallel owners are a failure, not a remedy.

5.q: In the lab case the Security log on WS-104 was cleared at 08:17Z. Which CERT-In Directions requirements help keep the incident timeline credible despite this?
options: Reporting within six hours and designating a point of contact for the organisation
Encrypting all endpoint logs and reporting each cleared log as a separate incident
Keeping ICT system logs for a rolling 180 days within India and synchronising clocks to specified NTP sources
Sending a copy of every Security log to CERT-In daily so that the regulator holds an independent record of each host
5.explanation: Retained logs and accurate clocks are what make a reported timeline trustworthy; a cleared local log shows why central collection matters. The six-hour and POC requirements concern reporting, not evidence integrity, and the Directions do not require daily log submission.

5.q: Further investigation shows that an escalated R4 upload went to an approved auditor's sharing site under a documented request. The analyst wants to lower the case's priority. How should this be done?
options: Lower it quietly in the case system, since de-escalation does not change ownership
Leave it at the original priority, because escalated cases must never be downgraded
Close the case as a false positive and remove the escalation from the record
De-escalate openly: record the evidence and reason in the case and inform the owner
5.explanation: De-escalation is legitimate when new evidence shows a case is less serious, but it must be recorded and the owner informed, never silent. It is also a real, authorised event, so 'false positive' would be the wrong label.

5.q: Unsure who is free, an analyst separately sends the same urgent case to two Tier 2 analysts without telling either about the other. Why is this a problem?
options: Because Tier 2 analysts may only receive cases through the IR lead
Because it creates two parallel owners, which is as bad as having none
Because the second escalation resets the escalation SLA for the case
Because cases with two receivers cannot be acknowledged in the case system
5.explanation: An escalation should end with one acknowledged owner; two people who each think they own the case may duplicate or contradict each other's work, or each assume the other is acting. The issue is ownership, not a system limitation or an SLA rule.

5.q: During a holiday weekend, a page for a hard-trigger alert goes to a phone number belonging to someone who left the company months ago. Which defensive control has failed?
options: 24x7 coverage of hard triggers with escalation contacts that are tested regularly
Written escalation criteria in the playbook for each alert type
Out-of-band communication prepared in advance for compromised channels
Recording the time noticed in the case template in UTC and IST
5.explanation: Attackers favour nights, weekends and holidays when escalation is slowest, so on-call contacts must be tested; a page reaching a former employee is a failed control. The criteria may be perfectly written and still fail if the route does not reach a person.

5.q: A post-incident review wants to know whether the escalation path, rather than detection, slowed the response. Which measurements answer that most directly?
options: The number of alerts per rule and the share closed as false positives
The time from the first malicious event to the alert firing in the SIEM
The time from trigger to escalation and from escalation to acknowledgement, checked against the SLA
The number of people copied on the escalation and the length of the package
5.explanation: Escalation SLAs measure trigger-to-escalation and escalation-to-acknowledgement times; the review also asks whether criteria were met earlier than the escalation happened. Event-to-alert time measures detection, and FP counts measure rule precision.

5.q: An analyst validates that Word spawned PowerShell on a finance workstation two minutes after a .docm download, but has not yet worked out what the script did. What should the analyst do?
options: Finish analysing the script first so that the escalation contains a confirmed and complete account of its effect on the host
Close the alert as a benign true positive if the user confirms they opened the document
Queue it for Tier 2 within the normal SLA, because no data has been seen leaving the host yet
Escalate now, because validated malicious execution is a hard trigger that does not wait for the full investigation
5.explanation: Hard triggers such as an Office application spawning a script interpreter are escalated as soon as they are validated; waiting for certainty only gives the attacker time and eats into any reporting window. A user opening the document is not authorisation for what it executed.

5.q: The VPN log shows one failure for each of eight accounts from 203.0.113.66 at 06:42Z, then a success for gopal from the same address at 06:46Z. Which statement must be written in the note as an inference with a confidence level rather than as a fact?
options: At 06:46:00Z the VPN logged a successful logon for gopal from 203.0.113.66
Between 06:42:00Z and 06:42:49Z the VPN logged eight failures from 203.0.113.66
The password for gopal was guessed by the address that ran the spray
The failures from 203.0.113.66 were logged seven seconds apart, one per account
5.explanation: The logs record failures and a success, not how the password was obtained; it could have been phished or reused rather than guessed, so the claim is a (strong) inference. The other three can be re-run with one query and are facts.

5.q: triage.py prints the R2 VPN alert as host=WS-107 (sales laptop) user=gopal. How should a defensible note record the host?
options: As the victim host in the timeline, because the triage helper attached it to the alert
As user gopal with primary device WS-107 per asset mapping, noting that VPN events carry no host
As unknown, and WS-107 should be left out of the case record entirely to avoid confusion
As the source host of the 06:46Z VPN session, confirmed by the helper's enrichment tables and the VPN logs
5.explanation: WS-107 comes from the hard-coded PRIMARY_HOST lookup, not from the VPN event, so it is enrichment and must be labelled with its source. Dropping it entirely loses useful context; copying it into the timeline turns a lookup into a fact.

5.q: A Banyan user says she opened an invoice "just before lunch". The proxy shows the download at 2026-11-03T06:12:00Z. How should the timeline line show the time?
options: 06:12:00Z (11:42 IST), keeping UTC first and adding local time because the user's account refers to it
11:42 IST only, because that is the time the user will recognise when interviewed
06:12 without a zone marker, since the case header already states that the SOC works in UTC
11:42:00Z, converting the time to IST but keeping the Z so that sorting still works
5.explanation: Every time is UTC with an explicit marker; local time may be added in brackets when it matters (IST is UTC+05:30, so 06:12Z is 11:42 IST). Writing 11:42 with a Z states a wrong UTC time, and an unmarked time is ambiguous.

5.q: A note ends: "Contained. Closing as TP." A reviewer flags the word "Contained". What is missing that the Actions section should record?
options: The confidence level that the containment worked, expressed as high, medium or low
The rule ID that triggered the alert and the priority score from the queue
A copy of the raw events that show the host was compromised before containment
What action was taken, by whom, who approved it and when, in UTC
5.explanation: Actions record what was done, by whom, approved by whom and when. "Contained" names none of these, so nobody can verify or reverse it. Confidence levels belong to inferences in the Analysis section, not to a record of actions.

5.q: During a backlog in the log pipeline, an event's host time is 06:14:00Z but the SIEM index time is 07:31Z. An analyst builds the timeline from index times without saying so. What is the main risk?
options: None, because index time is the more trustworthy clock and should always be preferred
The SHA-256 hash of the evidence export will change, invalidating the evidence reference recorded in the case
Events may be ordered and correlated wrongly, and a reader cannot tell which clock was used
The CERT-In six-hour reporting clock starts at index time, so the report becomes late
5.explanation: Event time, collector receipt time and index time can differ by seconds or hours; mixing them silently breaks ordering and correlation. The note must record which timestamp was used. Index time is not inherently more trustworthy, and it does not affect the hash of an existing export.

5.q: To keep a timeline tidy, an analyst rounds all eighteen beacon request times to the nearest minute. Why is this a mistake for this case?
options: Minute-level times cannot be written in ISO 8601 and so break sorting in the case tool
The second-level regularity of the requests is itself part of the evidence for beaconing
Rounding changes the SHA-256 hash of the exported evidence file stored in the case
CERT-In directions require every SOC record to keep timestamps to the millisecond
5.explanation: The lesson's rule is to keep the precision you were given: the machine-regular ~300 s gaps (CV 0.004) are what makes the traffic look like beaconing. Rounding the note does not alter the exported file's hash; it degrades the analysis.

5.q: A note says "see attached export, 32 events on WS-104". Which addition turns this into a usable evidence reference?
options: A copy of all 32 events pasted into the note so the reader does not need the file
The analyst's confidence that the export is complete, with a short reason for it
The file name, location, SHA-256 hash, the query or method that produced it, and the custody entry
The priority score of each alert whose events appear in the exported file
5.explanation: An evidence reference lets a reader find the item again and prove it is unchanged: name, location, hash, method and custody. The note points to the evidence; pasting the events in does not show integrity and makes the note try to be the evidence.

5.q: Before writing the timeline, an analyst runs sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS in the case folder and sees "WS-104_2026-11-03_events.jsonl: FAILED". What does this mean and what should happen?
options: The file differs from when the manifest was written; do not rely on it and record and investigate the mismatch
The manifest uses the wrong format for sha256sum, so the check should be repeated with Get-FileHash
The export missed some events; re-running the export with a wider window will fix the check
The file is unchanged but was moved; updating its path in custody.jsonl and re-running the check will make it pass
5.explanation: -c recomputes the hash of the named file and compares it with the manifest; FAILED means the content changed (one changed character is enough). The item cannot be relied on until explained. Get-FileHash gives the same digest, so switching tools would not change the result.

5.q: For CASE-0002 an analyst runs evidence_export.py CASE-0002 WS-107 and gets 10 events, all proxy requests. The case rests on VPN logons. What should the evidence list do?
options: List the 10-event export alone, since it is the hashed output of the approved export script
Re-run the export with the attacker's IP address in place of the host name to capture the VPN events
Omit the export and describe the VPN events in the analysis section instead
Add the VPN events as a separate item with the exact query and a hash of its saved output, and state the gap
5.explanation: The export selects by host and VPN events carry no host, so the case basis is missing from it. The VPN data needs its own reference (exact query plus hash) and the gap must be written down; an evidence list that silently omits a source is worse than one that names it.

5.q: Two hours after writing a note, an analyst finds the first beacon request was at 06:17:00Z, not 06:19Z as recorded. What is the correct way to fix the record?
options: Edit the original entry so that the case record shows only the correct time
Append a dated entry that corrects the earlier one, citing which entry and what changed
Delete the original entry and re-create it with the corrected time and the original note time
Leave the error, because a two-minute difference does not affect the disposition
5.explanation: Case notes are append-only: an explicit, dated correction preserves the fact that decisions may have been made on the earlier information. Editing or re-creating the entry hides what was believed at the time.

5.q: A note says only "Checked WS-104 for non-beacon activity: nothing else". The query actually run was SELECT ... FROM events WHERE host='WS-104' AND NOT (url LIKE '%ping%'). Why does the lesson insist on pasting the exact query?
options: Because the filter drops every event whose url is NULL, including Windows and Sysmon events, and only the exact text reveals it
Because paraphrased queries cannot be re-run in minisiem.py, which accepts only SQL taken from case notes
Because the LIKE operator is case-sensitive in SQLite, so the paraphrase hides missed upper-case URLs
Because the query text is needed to compute the SHA-256 hash recorded in the evidence reference
5.explanation: In SQL a comparison with NULL is neither true nor false, so NOT (url LIKE ...) silently excludes events without a URL, which is every non-proxy event. A paraphrase hides this flaw; the exact query lets the next analyst spot it. The hash is computed from the file, not the query text.

5.q: An analyst searched the proxy logs for any other host contacting the three suspicious domains and found nothing. How should this be recorded?
options: It need not be recorded, because a note should list findings and an empty search found nothing
As "no lateral spread", closing the scoping question for the case
As a negative result with the exact search and its scope, noting that hosts bypassing the proxy would not appear
As a low-confidence inference that the attacker targeted only WS-104
5.explanation: A negative result is a finding: it saves the next analyst repeating the search and bounds the case, but only within the data searched. "No lateral spread" overstates it, because non-proxied traffic is not covered.

5.q: Which NEXT line best serves the analyst who picks up the case at shift change?
options: Further investigation required; escalated to the appropriate team for follow-up
Case is serious and needs attention from senior staff as soon as possible
Waiting on endpoint data; will continue next shift once more information is available
T2: decode the PowerShell command from endpoint data; IR lead: decide isolation of WS-104; T1: confirm the 06:46Z VPN use with gopal's manager
5.explanation: Next steps must be specific and owned, so the next analyst can continue without asking questions. The other options name neither the work nor who owns it; "further investigation required" is explicitly not a next step.

5.q: WS-104 uploaded 48,200,000 bytes to files-share-drop.example, a domain seen nowhere else in the proxy data. Which analysis line follows the lesson's confidence vocabulary?
options: Confirmed exfiltration of customer data (high): 48.2 MB sent to an unknown domain
Probable exfiltration (medium): 48.2 MB uploaded to a domain seen nowhere else in proxy data; content unknown
Possible exfiltration (low): large uploads are common and the proxy cannot tell us anything useful
Exfiltration: clearly malicious, given the size of the upload and the timing before the log clear
5.explanation: The evidence points one way but a key piece (the content) is missing, which is the definition of probable/medium, and the reason is stated. "Confirmed ... customer data" asserts content nobody has seen; "clearly malicious" gives confidence without a level or reason.

5.q: The spray against the VPN and the phishing on WS-104 happened on the same morning. No event connects them. How should the CASE-0001 analysis record the relationship?
options: As a possible/low-confidence hypothesis that remains open, with the reason that no event links them
As a fact in the timeline, because both incidents fall within the same three-hour window
As probable/medium, because two attacks on one organisation in one morning are rarely unrelated, even with no linking event
It should not be mentioned at all, since anything without evidence must stay out of the record
5.explanation: A plausible link that the evidence neither establishes nor contradicts is possible/low and stays a hypothesis. Upgrading it on coincidence alone, or writing it as a fact, could steer containment toward the VPN; leaving it out loses an open question the next analyst should know about.

5.q: A weak note says: "Looks like she clicked a phishing mail this morning." The dataset shows a proxy GET of invoice.docm from banyan-payroll-update.example at 06:12:00Z. What is the main problem with "phishing mail"?
options: It uses an informal tone that is unsuitable for a record that may be read by a regulator
It names the user, which breaches the rule on minimising personal data in case notes
It presents an inference as fact: the data shows a web download, and how the user reached the link is not recorded
It omits the SHA-256 hash of invoice.docm, which is needed before any delivery method is stated
5.explanation: The observed fact is a web download; an email as delivery vector is an inference (and the initial-access email is listed as not yet known). Naming the user involved is acceptable and needed; the error is stating an unobserved mechanism as fact.

5.q: While working a case an analyst finds a PowerShell script on a share containing a plaintext service-account password. What belongs in the case note?
options: The password value, so that IAM can confirm which credential to rotate
The first and last characters of the password, enough to identify it without exposing it fully
Nothing about the credential, because notes should not contain any sensitive information
That a credential for that account was exposed, where it was found, and a request to rotate it
5.explanation: Record that a secret was exposed and where, so it can be rotated, but never the value itself, not even partially. Omitting the exposure altogether would leave the credential unrotated.

5.q: A CASE-0001 analysis line cites the ISAC-A feed entry for cdn-telemetry-sync.example, which is labelled TLP:AMBER. The rest of the note uses only internal data. What sharing label applies to the note?
options: TLP:CLEAR, because the SOC produced the note itself from its own logs
TLP:AMBER, because enrichment carries its sharing label forward into the note
TLP:GREEN, as a compromise between internal data and the AMBER feed entry
No label, because TLP applies only to intelligence feeds and not to case records
5.explanation: Sharing labels are carried forward: once AMBER intelligence is in the note, the note is AMBER. Downgrading to GREEN or CLEAR would allow sharing that the intelligence source did not permit.
