5.q: As CASE-0001 evolves over two days, which part of the record is it acceptable to rewrite rather than extend by appending?
options: The Timeline, so that it reflects only the facts currently believed to be correct
The Analysis, replacing superseded hypotheses so that the next analyst is not confused
The Summary, which is kept current so that a manager can read it alone
The Evidence list, removing items whose hashes no longer verify
5.explanation: The Summary is the only section rewritten as the case evolves; everything else grows by appending. Changed inferences get new analysis entries rather than edits, so the record still shows what was believed when decisions were made.

5.q: Why does the lesson recommend entering hosts, accounts, domains and hashes as typed entities (observables) in the case platform rather than only in free text?
options: Typed entities can be searched across cases automatically, so links to other cases surface
Typed entities are hashed by the platform, which replaces the need for evidence references
Free text in case platforms is not retained long enough to satisfy audit requirements
Typed entities are hidden from reviewers, which protects the personal data they contain
5.explanation: Structured observables are searchable across cases, which free text is not, so the next analyst can pivot on them. They do not replace hashed evidence references, which prove integrity of exported items.

5.q: A reviewer samples two closed R3 alerts. Note A is three lines: the hit was for the itadmin build account, it matches the documented suppression for change CHG-1042 valid to 2026-12-31, benign true positive, no action. Note B is two pages of narrative that never says what was checked. Which is defensible?
options: Note A, because it states what was checked, the reason for the disposition and the outcome
Note B, because a longer narrative shows the analyst spent more effort on the alert
Neither, because benign true positives must always be escalated to Tier 2 before closure
Both equally, because the disposition label is the only part a reviewer actually checks
5.explanation: Length is a poor proxy for quality: Note A traces the closure to a documented change and suppression, so a reviewer can judge it. Note B cannot be checked because it never says what was examined, however long it is.

5.q: During triage an analyst finds that a firewall's clock runs four minutes ahead of the NTP-synchronised domain controllers, and has corrected the firewall times by four minutes in the timeline. What else should the note contain?
options: Nothing further, because corrected times are now consistent and the offset no longer matters
The known clock offset, its size and source, and that the timeline times were corrected for it
A replacement of all firewall times with the domain controller times for the same events
A recommendation to discard the firewall data, since a drifting clock makes it unreliable as evidence
5.explanation: Known clock problems are recorded with the offset and whether you corrected for it, otherwise a reader comparing the timeline with the raw events sees unexplained differences. Drifting data is still usable evidence once the offset is documented; CERT-In's NTP synchronisation requirement exists to prevent such drift.

5.q: A CERT-In-reportable incident must be reported within six hours of being noticed. How do case notes make that obligation defensible later?
options: By recording the priority score at the time of the first alert, which proves the urgency assessment
By including the full raw events in every note so that regulators can check them directly
By showing, in UTC, when the activity was first seen and what was known at each point
By closing each alert as soon as the incident report is filed, so the case shows no open items
5.explanation: The reporting clock can only be met, and later defended, if notes record in UTC when activity was first noticed and what was known then. Scores and pasted raw events do not establish when the SOC became aware.

5.q: A colleague asks how to decide quickly whether a statement in a note is a fact or an inference. Which test does the lesson give?
options: Whether it has been confirmed by two analysts on the same shift
Whether it appears in the output of the triage helper or the intelligence matcher
Whether it carries a confidence word such as probable or possible
Whether someone could re-run a query or check an item to see it for themselves
5.explanation: A fact can be reproduced, for example with one minisiem.py search; an inference can only be argued. Tool output is not automatically fact either, as host=WS-107 shows, and a confidence word marks an inference but does not identify one that is missing it.

5.q: An analyst drafts: "User divya was careless and opened the attachment; her personal browsing history for the week is attached for context." What should change?
options: Nothing, because the user's behaviour is directly relevant to how the compromise occurred
State neutrally that divya opened the file, and remove the browsing history, which the investigation does not need
Replace the username with "a finance user" everywhere, since names may never appear in case notes
Keep the browsing history but mark the note TLP:RED so that only the SOC can read it
5.explanation: Notes record facts neutrally ("user divya opened the attachment") and minimise personal data to what the investigation needs, which the DPDP Act 2023 also requires. Usernames needed for the case are fine; a sharing label does not justify collecting unnecessary personal data.

5.q: triage.py scores each hit as severity x confidence x asset criticality. A new rule has severity 3 and confidence 0.6 and fires on WS-107, whose criticality is 2. Where would it sit in the lab queue?
options: At 3.6, level with R6 at the bottom of the queue
At 7.2, level with R1 and R2 in the middle of the queue
At 5.4, level with the two R3 hits
At 10.8, level with R5 at the top of the queue
5.explanation: 3 x 0.6 x 2 = 3.6, the same score as R6 (2 x 0.6 x 3). 5.4 would need criticality 3 on this rule; checking the arithmetic by hand against RULE_META and ASSETS is how you learn to trust or question the queue.

5.q: R1 on WS-104 (criticality 3) and R2 on WS-107 (criticality 2) both score 7.2. What does this tell you about the two rules' entries in RULE_META?
options: The two rules have identical severity and confidence, so the tie comes from the rules alone
R1's severity x confidence (2.4) is lower than R2's (3.6); the more critical asset makes up the difference
R1's severity x confidence must be higher than R2's, because R1 involves code execution
Nothing can be inferred, because the score also includes the intelligence feed's confidence
5.explanation: 7.2 / 3 = 2.4 for R1 and 7.2 / 2 = 3.6 for R2 (R2 is severity 4 x confidence 0.9). Equal scores can hide different rule weightings. The intelligence feed is not part of the triage score at all.

5.q: The queue puts R5 log_cleared (10.8) first and five other WS-104 alerts below it. What working order does the lab recommend?
options: Strictly by score from top to bottom, because priority already reflects the attack sequence
Lowest score first, because low-scored alerts are the ones most likely to be missed
Group all WS-104 alerts and close them together as one item without validating each
R5 first for urgency, then R2, then the WS-104 alerts in event-time order so each validation builds on the last
5.explanation: Queue order is about urgency, investigation order is about time. R5 is validated first because it may trigger escalation immediately, but the story is reconstructed forwards in time. The queue order was nearly the reverse of the attack: R5 was the last thing the attacker did.

5.q: The R6 beacon alert shows user=None (?). How should the analyst treat this in the note?
options: As evidence that no user was logged on, so the beaconing came from a system process
As a reason to lower confidence in the alert, because a real beacon would always show the logged-on user
As a gap in the rule, which groups by host and URL and never selects a user, and record it as such
As an error in the dataset that requires re-copying the lab kit before continuing
5.explanation: The rule's query never selects the user column, so None is the absence of a field, not a finding. Reading it as "no user logged on" turns a gap into a fact; it says nothing about the beacon's validity.

5.q: On R1, R3, R4, R5 and R6 the helper prints ip=n/a. What does this mean?
options: The rule's query did not select a source IP column, not that the activity had no IP
The events originated from inside the network and so have no external IP to classify
The IP was in a documentation range and has been hidden by the helper
The IP lookup failed because the intelligence feed was not loaded
5.explanation: n/a reflects what the rule returned: those rules do not select a source IP. Concluding that the activity was internal or IP-less would turn the helper's limitation into a finding.

5.q: A shift lead proposes a rule: "Only investigate alerts scoring 5.0 or above; close the rest as low priority." Applied to this lab's queue, what would be lost?
options: Nothing important, since R5, R1 and R2 already establish the compromise
The R3 account creation, so the persistence mechanism would go unrecorded
Only the R6 beacon, which is covered by the R1 alert on the same host anyway
R4 and R6, so the 48.2 MB upload and the command-and-control channel would never be validated
5.explanation: R4 scored 4.5 and R6 3.6, both under the cut-off, yet they reveal the probable exfiltration and the C2 beacon. R3 scored 5.4 and would survive. Priority orders the work; it must not decide what is ignored.

5.q: hunt.py reports WS-104 -> cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping with n=18, mean_gap=300s, cv=0.004. Why does this make R6 one of the strongest alerts despite its 3.6 score?
options: The low CV shows the requests were large, consistent with data exfiltration
The near-zero CV means machine-regular five-minute requests, starting just after PowerShell ran, to a domain on an ISAC-A C2 listing
Eighteen requests exceed the rule's threshold of eight, which automatically promotes the alert to high severity
A mean gap of 300 s matches the Windows default update interval, ruling out benign software
5.explanation: CV (standard deviation divided by mean) of 0.004 means almost no variation in the gaps: automated traffic. Corroborated by timing after the PowerShell start and an intelligence match (conf 85), it is strong evidence of C2. The score cannot know about such cross-source corroboration; CV says nothing about request size.

5.q: hunt.py's H1 lists host/URL pairs with at least 8 requests and an interval CV below 0.2. A user's browser polls a news site 40 times with CV 0.9. Why is it not listed?
options: Because news sites are on an allow-list built into hunt.py
Because 40 requests exceeds the maximum count the hunt considers suspicious
Because a CV of 0.9 means the gaps vary widely relative to their mean, so the traffic is not regular
Because CV is only computed for requests smaller than 1,000 bytes
5.explanation: H1's criterion is regularity: CV = standard deviation / mean of the gaps, and 0.9 is far above 0.2, typical of human-driven browsing. The hunt has no maximum count or byte filter described in the lab.

5.q: The queue contains two R3 new_local_admin hits on WS-104: event 4720 for svc_update at 07:02:00Z and event 4732 adding it to Administrators at 07:03:00Z. How should they be documented?
options: One note covering both alert IDs, because create-then-elevate is a single activity
Two separate incidents, because each rule hit must be counted for queue metrics
Close the second hit as a duplicate without a note, since the first note covers the account
Merge them into the R5 note, because all three alerts were generated under divya's account
5.explanation: The two hits are one activity, so one note covers both. Counting two incidents inflates metrics; closing one as a duplicate without a note loses the group change, which is what made the account an administrator.

5.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE user='svc_update' returns 0. Which statement belongs in the R3 note?
options: svc_update was never used, so the persistence attempt failed and the account can be closed as harmless
svc_update was created as a decoy, so further attacker activity will use a different account
The query is invalid because svc_update appears only in target_user, so the result should be discarded
No event in this dataset was performed by svc_update; this does not cover later activity, and the cleared Security log may hide events
5.explanation: A negative result is bounded by its data: this dataset's sources and time span, and a host whose Security log was cleared at 08:17:00Z. "Never used" overstates it. The query is valid for its purpose: it checks activity by the account, not activity on it.

5.q: Every alert in the queue was dispositioned as a true positive with high confidence except R4 large_upload, which was rated medium. Why?
options: Because R4's priority score of 4.5 is below the threshold for high-confidence dispositions
Because the proxy recorded the size and destination of the upload but not its content
Because files-share-drop.example matched only an expired intelligence indicator
Because large uploads to file-sharing sites are routine for finance workstations
5.explanation: The evidence points to exfiltration (48.2 MB, a domain seen nowhere else, five minutes before the log clear), but what left the host is unknown, which keeps it at medium. Confidence follows the evidence, not the score; the expired indicator in the lab is 198.51.100.104, not this domain.

5.q: To validate R4, the analyst runs SELECT host, MAX(bytes_out) FROM events WHERE source='proxy' GROUP BY host ORDER BY 2 DESC. What does this query contribute?
options: It confirms the upload's content type by comparing it with the request sizes of every other host's proxy uploads
It lists every upload made by WS-104 in time order for the timeline
It compares the upload with each host's largest request, showing 48,200,000 bytes against others under 4,000
It identifies which hosts contacted files-share-drop.example during the day
5.explanation: GROUP BY host returns each host's largest outbound request, giving an estate-wide baseline: WS-104's upload is about twelve thousand times larger than anything else. It neither orders events in time nor filters by destination domain.

5.q: gopal's VPN credential is assessed as compromised at 06:46Z. At 13:33:00Z gopal logs in again from 198.51.100.104, which matches only an expired, confidence-40 open-feed indicator. What disposition fits the 13:33Z session?
options: Undetermined: the expired indicator is not evidence on its own, but any session with a compromised credential is suspect until the user confirms it
Benign: the indicator has expired, so the address should be treated as clean and the session closed
Malicious with high confidence, because any match on an intelligence feed confirms attacker infrastructure
Out of scope, because the session occurred outside the 06:00-09:00Z window of the evidence export
5.explanation: ioc_match.py warns "expired indicator still matches: review before acting", so the match proves nothing, and the session could be gopal working from home. But once the credential is compromised, later sessions are suspect, so it stays undetermined pending confirmation. An export window does not define the scope of a case.

5.q: The CASE-0002 next steps say to contact gopal "via manager by phone (not email)" to confirm the 13:33Z session. What is the reasoning behind this channel?
options: Phone calls are automatically recorded and so serve as evidence for the case
Company policy forbids SOC analysts from emailing staff directly about incidents
Email is slower, and the CERT-In six-hour deadline requires a faster response
With gopal's credential compromised, an attacker may be able to read or answer email sent to the account
5.explanation: If the credential is compromised, messages to that account may be read or answered by the attacker, so confirmation goes out of band through a trusted channel. The choice is about trust in the channel, not speed or recording.

5.q: python evidence_export.py CASE-0002 WS-107 exports 10 proxy events and a verified hash. Why is that not sufficient evidence for CASE-0002?
options: Because the export window ends at 09:00Z and gopal's laptop was not powered on before then
Because the case rests on VPN events, which carry no host and so are not in a host-based export; they must be saved and hashed separately
Because proxy events from WS-107 must be exported under CASE-0001, where the proxy activity was found
Because the export script refuses to hash files for hosts with criticality below 3
5.explanation: The export selects by host, and VPN events have no host field, so the actual basis of the case is missing. The lab saves the VPN query output to a file, hashes it and records the exact query because no custody entry exists for it.

5.q: Two analysts save the same minisiem.py VPN search to a file, one on Windows and one on Linux, and get different SHA-256 hashes. What is the most likely cause and the right response?
options: One of the two files was tampered with; the case should be escalated at once as an evidence-integrity incident
sha256sum and Get-FileHash use different algorithms; re-hash both with the same tool
Python wrote CRLF line endings on Windows and LF on Linux; record the platform and method with each hash
The SIEM returns rows in random order; add ORDER BY to the query and re-run it
5.explanation: The content is the same but line endings differ, so the bytes and the hash differ. This is why an evidence reference records platform and method. Get-FileHash and sha256sum compute the same SHA-256 digest, and the lab query already orders by ts.

5.q: A learner's query SELECT ts, command_line FROM events WHERE source='sysmon' fails with "no such column: command_line". What should they do?
options: Re-run python minisiem.py load, since the column is created only on a fresh load
Read the field from the stored JSON with json_extract(raw,'$.command_line')
Query the image column instead, which holds the full command line for Sysmon events
Re-copy the lab kit, because a missing column means the dataset has been modified
5.explanation: minisiem keeps common fields as columns and the rest only in the raw JSON column, so command_line must be extracted with json_extract. Reloading would not add the column; image holds the executable path, not its arguments.

5.q: In Step 5 the analyst uses url NOT LIKE '%ping%' to hide the beacon. Lesson 7 warned that such a filter can silently drop events. Why is it safe in this query?
options: Because SQLite treats NULL as an empty string in LIKE comparisons, so no rows are lost
Because the time range in the query excludes all events that lack a URL
Because NOT LIKE in minisiem is rewritten to include NULL values automatically
Because the query is restricted to source='proxy', where every event has a URL, so no NULL URLs exist to drop
5.explanation: A comparison with NULL is neither true nor false, so NOT LIKE drops rows with a NULL url. Restricting to proxy events, which all carry a URL, removes that risk. On the full table the same filter would hide Windows and Sysmon events.

5.q: A learner runs python minisiem.py load in their working folder and sees "loaded 341 events". What should they do before triaging?
options: Re-copy the kit into a fresh folder, because the dataset has been modified and every later result may differ
Continue, because one extra event cannot change the triage queue or any hash
Run load a second time, since the first run appends to the table and the count then settles back on the expected 340
Delete the most recent line of banyan_events.jsonl to bring the count back to 340
5.explanation: The original dataset loads 340 events; any other number means it was changed, and a stray event can alter the queue, query results and export hashes. load drops and recreates the table rather than appending, and hand-editing the dataset only adds uncertainty.

5.q: Six alerts are grouped into CASE-0001 on WS-104. Why is R2 placed in its own case, CASE-0002, rather than added to CASE-0001?
options: Because VPN alerts always belong to the network team's case queue
Because R2 involves a different account and an external address, and no event links it to WS-104
Because R2's priority score is lower than R5's, and cases are grouped by score
Because CASE-0001 already has more than five alerts, the maximum per case
5.explanation: Cases group alerts that share entities and time. R2 shares neither host nor user with the WS-104 alerts, and no event connects them, so it gets its own case, cross-referenced as a possible link. Grouping is not based on score or case size.

5.q: CASE-0001's notes cite the ISAC-A match for cdn-telemetry-sync.example (TLP:AMBER). CASE-0002's notes cite ISAC-A's entry for 203.0.113.66 (TLP:GREEN) and an expired open-feed indicator (TLP:CLEAR). Which labels do the case records carry?
options: Both AMBER, because the two cases come from the same morning and the same SOC
Both CLEAR, because case records are internal documents and TLP applies only to feeds
CASE-0001 AMBER and CASE-0002 GREEN, each inheriting the most restrictive label of the enrichment it uses
CASE-0001 GREEN and CASE-0002 CLEAR, because labels are averaged across the enrichment used
5.explanation: Each note inherits the sharing label of the intelligence it contains: AMBER for CASE-0001, GREEN for CASE-0002 (its most restrictive item). Labelling CASE-0002 AMBER merely because it is cross-referenced would over-restrict it; ignoring labels would breach the source's terms.

5.q: The 1102 log-clear event at 08:17:00Z on WS-104 shows user divya. Which disposition statement is most defensible?
options: TP, high confidence: the log clear ran under divya's account; whether divya personally did it is a separate, open question
TP, high confidence: divya cleared the Security log to hide her own activity and should be suspended
FP: users sometimes clear logs by accident, and divya is a payments approver with admin rights
Undetermined: a log clear cannot be judged without first decoding the PowerShell command
5.explanation: The user field shows the account context, not the person; code running in divya's session would produce the same record. A log clear after account creation on a user workstation is never routine, so TP is high confidence, but blaming divya turns an inference into a fact.

5.q: hunt.py's H3 found no host other than WS-104 contacting the three suspicious domains. How should the scoping result appear in CASE-0001?
options: As confirmation that the incident is fully contained to WS-104, closing the scoping task
As a reason to downgrade CASE-0001's severity, since only one host was affected
As evidence that the domains were not real attacker infrastructure, given the single host
As a negative result limited to proxied traffic: hosts whose traffic bypasses the proxy are not covered
5.explanation: H3 searched proxy data, so its negative result bounds the case only for traffic through the proxy. Recording it with that limit saves repeating the search without overstating it as containment or as grounds for downgrading.

5.q: R1 is dispositioned TP with high confidence. Which pair of independent facts supports that confidence?
options: The 7.2 priority score and the payments-approver role of divya in the USERS table
The internal intelligence list entry and the fact that WINWORD.EXE is an Office binary
A proxy download of invoice.docm at 06:12:00Z and a Sysmon record at 06:14:00Z of Word starting hidden, encoded PowerShell
Eighteen beacon requests and the 48.2 MB upload later the same morning
5.explanation: High confidence comes from independent sources agreeing: the proxy shows the macro document arriving and Sysmon shows Word spawning hidden, encoded PowerShell two minutes later. Score and user role are enrichment, not validation; the beacon and upload support other alerts.

5.q: CASE-0002's analysis states that what the 06:46Z VPN session accessed is unknown. Which next step addresses that gap?
options: Re-run evidence_export.py for WS-107 with a wider time window to capture the session
Run hunt.py again to see whether the session produced beaconing traffic
Search the dataset's VPN events for destination fields recorded during the session
T2 requests the VPN session details for 06:46Z, such as the assigned IP and destinations, from the VPN platform
5.explanation: The VPN data in the SIEM has no destination fields, and a host export of WS-107 cannot contain VPN activity, so the answer must come from the VPN platform's session records. Searching the existing events again would only confirm the gap.

6.q: In the lab, the vendor's SHA-256 indicator for invoice.docm carries the highest producer confidence (90) yet ioc_match.py reports 'no match'. What is the most accurate explanation?
options: The attacker re-packed the document after reporting, so its delivered hash changed
The indicator's validity window had lapsed before the as-of date
The Banyan dataset contains no file-hash telemetry for it to match against
The feed stores the hash truncated, so the equality test always fails
6.explanation: The SOC collects no file hashes, so a computed indicator over file bytes cannot match: the indicator is not wrong, the SOC is blind to it. It is not expired (it had 89 days left), and the attacker's file was the reported one.

6.q: hunt.py reports 'WS-104 https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping n=18 mean_gap=300s cv=0.004'. How is the beaconing signal it relies on best classified structurally?
options: Computed, because it is a statistic derived from the request timestamps
Atomic, because it names a single URL matched by equality on one field
Behavioural, because it encodes a parent-child process relationship
Atomic, because the domain name alone identifies the C2 infrastructure it contacts
6.explanation: The coefficient of variation of request gaps is calculated from data, which makes it a computed indicator that does not depend on the domain's name. The URL appears in the output, but the detection is the statistic, not an equality test on the URL.

6.q: A defender can deny an adversary one of the following. According to the Pyramid of Pain, which denial imposes the greatest cost on the adversary?
options: Blocking the C2 domain so the loader must be pointed at a new registration
Blocking the source address so the spraying must move to another server
Detecting the fixed URL path so the beacon configuration must be edited
Detecting the access-then-spray-then-exfiltrate way of operating itself
6.explanation: TTPs sit at the top of the pyramid: changing how a group operates is the slowest and most expensive change. Network artefacts such as a fixed URL path are one level below tools and two below TTPs; domains and addresses are cheaper still.

6.q: The expired open-feed indicator 198.51.100.104 ('scanning, old, shared hosting', valid until 30 June) matches gopal's successful VPN login at 13:33 on 3 November. What is the soundest interpretation?
options: The attacker has returned on gopal's account through a second known-bad host
A likely stale-address false positive: review context, not proof of compromise
Proof that the 13:33 session was legitimate, since the indicator expired months ago
A confirmed match that should trigger an automatic block of the address
6.explanation: Addresses decay fastest, this one lapsed 126 days earlier, and shared-hosting addresses are reassigned, so the match is review-only context. Expiry does not prove innocence either; it simply removes the indicator's weight, leaving other evidence to decide.

6.q: Why is the Module 4 rule R1 office_spawns_script classed as a behavioural indicator rather than an atomic one?
options: It matches a single process name exactly in one field of the Sysmon log
It combines several fields of one event with logic describing an action
It is computed by hashing the image path of the spawned process
It was shared by a partner organisation with a confidence score attached
6.explanation: R1 joins conditions on event_id, parent_image and image to describe what the adversary does (Word starting a shell). A single-field equality test would be atomic; R1 needs logic across fields and process-lineage telemetry.

6.q: A feed reports cdn-telemetry-sync.example as loader C2 and you confirm 18 requests from WS-104. Following the 'climb the pyramid' habit, what is the most valuable next step?
options: Add the domain to the proxy blocklist and close the indicator as handled
Search other feeds for the same domain to raise its confidence score
Examine those requests for fixed paths, sizes and timing detectable without the name
Compute the SHA-256 of the proxy log lines so they can be shared with partners as hashes
6.explanation: Climbing means turning a short-lived atomic value into durable detections: the fixed /api/v2/ping path, constant 220-byte size and 300 s rhythm can be detected whatever domain is used next. Blocking the domain is useful but leaves the detection at the bottom of the pyramid.

6.q: Under the lesson's default-use table, how should a SOC normally act on a matched IPv4 indicator that belongs to a large cloud provider's range?
options: Alert and enrich, blocking only if fresh, well graded and not shared infrastructure
Block automatically, because address matches from cloud ranges have near-zero false positives
Ignore it, because addresses sit at the bottom of the Pyramid of Pain
Report it to the registrar's abuse process and block it for the full window
6.explanation: Addresses decay fast and shared or cloud infrastructure causes collateral damage when blocked, so alert-and-enrich is the default. Near-zero false positives describes a current file hash, not an address; ignoring it would discard useful context.

6.q: In the Banyan case, about 48 MB left for files-share-drop.example at 08:12. Why was this destination found even though no feed entry mentioned it?
options: ioc_match.py pivots from matched domains to related domains automatically
hunt.py's timing analysis flagged the upload as a regular beacon
The look-alike domain indicator also covered other attacker domains
The behavioural rule R4 large_upload flagged the unusually large upload
6.explanation: R4 looks for unusually large uploads regardless of destination, so it caught exfiltration no feed knew about. hunt.py detects regular timing, not a single large transfer, and ioc_match.py only tests the values in its feed.

6.q: Before activating a newly received indicator, which question best determines whether it can protect the organisation at all?
options: Which field in which collected log source it would have to match
Which threat actor the producer attributes the indicator to
Whether the indicator appears in more than one commercial threat feed
Whether its TLP marking allows it to be shared with partners
6.explanation: If you cannot name the field and confirm the source is collected, the indicator can never match, however good it is. Attribution, feed count and TLP matter for other decisions but do not decide whether a match is possible.

6.q: The lesson says file hashes 'never stop identifying the file, but stop finding it'. Which statement captures this correctly?
options: Hash collisions make old SHA-256 values unreliable after a few months
Hashes decay faster than addresses because files are deleted after use
A hash stays precise for that exact file, but campaigns move to re-packed variants
A hash identifies the whole malware family, so later re-packed variants still match it
6.explanation: A SHA-256 permanently identifies one byte sequence, but changing one byte produces a new hash, so the campaign's later variants no longer match. The strongest distractor is wrong because a hash identifies a single file, not a family.

6.q: What practical value does the atomic / computed / behavioural classification from Hutchins, Cloppert and Amin give a SOC?
options: It ranks indicators by how much it costs the adversary to replace them once detected
It describes how an indicator is matched and so what data must be collected
It sets the validity window that each indicator type must be given
It defines the TLP level at which each indicator type may be shared
6.explanation: The structural classes say how matching works (equality, a function over data, logic over fields), which decides the telemetry needed. Ranking by adversary cost is the Pyramid of Pain, a different model.

6.q: As of 3 November 2026 the lab producers gave 203.0.113.66 seven more days, the C2 domain 58 and the file hash 89. Which reasoning best explains why the address got the shortest window?
options: Addresses are atomic, and atomic indicators always expire after a week
The producer had the lowest confidence in the address of all the entries it published
The address had already matched, so its purpose was fulfilled
Attacker addresses are rented or compromised and recycled to new holders within days
6.explanation: Shelf life follows type: addresses are abandoned and reassigned quickly, so a match soon stops meaning what it did. Domains are atomic too yet got longer windows, so 'atomic means one week' is wrong; the windows are producer choices driven by decay rate.

6.q: Why does a look-alike of your own organisation's domain, such as banyan-payroll-update.example, warrant blocking and a relatively long period of relevance?
options: Its only purpose is to impersonate you, so it stays relevant while it is registered
Look-alike domains cannot be re-registered once reported to the registrar
Domains sit at the top of the Pyramid of Pain, so they are costly for the attacker to change
Blocking it has no business impact because it is hosted on shared platforms
6.explanation: A domain built to imitate your name has no legitimate use for your users, so blocking it is safe and it remains relevant as long as it exists. Domains are mid-pyramid, not at the top, and shared hosting is a reason for caution, not for blocking.

6.q: The address 198.51.100.200 appears in a firewall log. At what point does it become an indicator rather than an observable?
options: As soon as it is recorded in any security log source
When it appears in logs from more than one sensor
When it is paired with a judgement that it suggests malice, plus context
When it is converted into a hash so that it can be matched exactly across sensors
6.explanation: An observable is a fact seen in data with no judgement; it becomes an indicator when someone attaches the assessment that it suggests malicious activity, with context such as what, who, confidence and validity. Seeing it in several sensors adds observations, not judgement.

6.q: A manager wants a single metric for how well the SOC's threat feeds protect it. Which measure best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: The total number of indicators loaded into the SIEM each month
The number of distinct commercial and open feeds subscribed to
The proportion of feed indicators that carry a TLP:CLEAR marking
The share of indicators per pyramid level that telemetry can actually match
6.explanation: Coverage should be measured by pyramid level and matchability: ten thousand hashes you cannot match are worth nothing. Raw counts and feed numbers reward volume, not protection.

6.q: Suppose the attacker re-packs invoice.docm, hosts it on a fresh look-alike domain and uses a new C2 domain and address. Which lab detection would most likely still fire on WS-104?
options: The ioc_match.py entry for cdn-telemetry-sync.example
R1, Word starting PowerShell, regardless of file or origin
The vendor SHA-256 entry once hash telemetry is added
The ioc_match.py entry for banyan-payroll-update.example
6.explanation: R1 is a TTP-level behavioural rule that does not depend on any domain, address or hash, so it survives infrastructure and file changes. The re-packed file has a new hash, so even with hash telemetry the old SHA-256 would not match.

6.q: Why can an exact match on an IP address hosted on shared infrastructure be weak evidence of the actor behind activity?
options: Many unrelated tenants may sit behind it, so equality on it does not identify the actor
IP addresses are computed indicators and so are prone to calculation errors
Proxies always rewrite source addresses, so the logged value is never the true origin of the traffic
IP addresses are matched with LIKE patterns, which over-match by design
6.explanation: An atomic indicator is only as precise as what it names; a shared host, load balancer or NAT may front many parties. Addresses are atomic, not computed, and the lab matches src_ip by equality.

6.q: A SOC subscribes to a feed of 10,000 malware hashes but has no endpoint or mail-gateway hashing. Its lead reports 'strong coverage'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, because hashes have near-zero false positives and are highly precise
Agree, provided the hashes are refreshed at least weekly from the vendor
Disagree, because hashes are at the top of the pyramid and too costly for the SOC to match at scale
Disagree: coverage at that level is nil; raise a collection gap and weigh behavioural rules
6.explanation: Indicators that cannot match provide no coverage, so the right action is a collection-gap ticket, with behavioural detections reducing the risk meanwhile. Hashes are at the bottom of the pyramid, and refreshing unmatchable values changes nothing.

6.q: Why does the lesson warn that 'indicators can leak'?
options: Indicators stored in a SIEM can be overwritten by attackers who gain write access to its logs
Expired indicators are automatically published back to open feeds
A list of what you hunt for reveals what you know, so sharing must respect its TLP
Shared indicators expose the internal IP addresses of the matching hosts
6.explanation: An adversary who sees your hash and domain lists learns what you have detected and can change exactly those, which is why each indicator's TLP marking governs sharing. The other options describe risks the lesson does not raise.

6.q: On 12 November 2026, 203.0.113.66 (valid until 10 November) matches a fresh VPN login. How should the match be treated under the lesson's guidance?
options: As confirmation that the password-spraying campaign is still active against Banyan
As context for review, since the indicator's short validity window has lapsed
As grounds to block the address automatically for another seven days
As a false positive to be suppressed with no further review
6.explanation: Expired indicators must stop driving automatic action; addresses move on quickly, so the match needs a timestamp check and other evidence. Suppressing it without review is also wrong: it is still context worth a look.

6.q: R6 beacon_regular_small and hunt.py's H1 search detect C2 without knowing the domain. At which Pyramid of Pain level do they mainly operate?
options: Network/host artefacts: fixed path, small constant size and regular rhythm
Domain names: the destination host of the repeated requests
Hash values: the fingerprint of the beacon's payload bytes
IP addresses: the resolved server behind the beacon URL
6.explanation: Constant request size and machine-regular timing are artefacts baked into the tooling; changing them needs code or configuration changes. The rules deliberately do not depend on the domain or address.

6.q: A colleague argues that because behavioural rules exist, the C2 domain feed entry added nothing. What does the Banyan worked example show?
options: The colleague is right: behavioural rules alone found every stage of the Banyan intrusion
The feed was superior: it found the exfiltration destination before R4 did
Feed matches and behavioural rules covered different parts and worked together
Neither helped: all detections relied on the expired open-feed address
6.explanation: The C2 domain match confirmed the intrusion in seconds, while R4 found files-share-drop.example, which no feed listed. IOCs and TTPs complement each other; neither alone covered the case.

6.q: ioc_match.py prints 'expired indicator still matches: review before acting'. What should a production intelligence platform do with expired indicators?
options: Keep them active but lower their confidence by ten points
Re-issue them with a new validity window after each match
Convert them into behavioural rules so they stop decaying
Drop them or downgrade them to context only so they cannot drive actions
6.explanation: Expiry is a control: expired indicators must not trigger automatic actions, so they are removed or kept only as context. Extending a window on a match would let stale values perpetuate themselves.

6.q: Which indicator is the better candidate for automatic blocking: (a) the SHA-256 of a file still in circulation, matched by EDR hashing, or (b) a domain on a popular file-sharing platform used in one phishing run?
options: (a), because a current hash has near-zero false positives and blocking it hurts no business traffic
(b), because domains sit higher on the pyramid and last longer than hashes
(b), because domains are atomic and therefore cheaper to match accurately
Neither, because only TTP-level indicators may ever be blocked automatically, whatever their freshness
6.explanation: While the file circulates, a hash match means the same file, so blocking it is precise and safe where telemetry exists. Blocking a shared platform's domain would break legitimate traffic despite its higher pyramid level.

6.q: Why do behavioural indicators tend to produce more borderline matches than atomic ones?
options: They are matched with less precise field types in most SIEMs
They describe broad patterns that benign activity can also show, so matches need judgement
They depend on producer confidence scores that are often inflated
They expire faster than atomic ones, so many matches occur after their validity window has lapsed
6.explanation: A pattern such as Office starting a shell or many failures then a success can occur legitimately, so behavioural matches need tuning and analyst review. Behavioural indicators actually last longest, so faster expiry is wrong.

6.q: ioc_match.py shows 'conf= 85' for cdn-telemetry-sync.example. What does this number actually tell the consuming SOC?
options: That there is an 85 per cent probability the domain is malicious in its network
How sure the producer was of its own claim, on its own scale, when it made it
That 85 per cent of the producer's past reports have proved correct
That the domain has been seen by 85 independent sources across the sector
6.explanation: Producer confidence expresses the producer's certainty in their claim at the time, on their scale. It is not a probability calibrated for your network, and it says nothing about the producer's track record, which is what source reliability grades.

6.q: Report X comes second-hand from a sector group with years of accurate reporting. Report Y is an anonymous paste that includes a registration date and URL path you can verify in minutes. Which handling best reflects Admiralty practice?
options: Grade both by the source alone, so trust X and discard Y
Grade both by the information alone, so trust Y and discard X
Average the two source and information grades and act on whichever report scores higher overall
Treat X as a good source with unconfirmed claims and corroborate it; verify Y's details
6.explanation: The system grades source and information independently: X needs corroboration despite its strong source, and Y's verifiable content can be confirmed so its weak source matters less. Collapsing either into a single judgement loses exactly that distinction.

6.q: A new threat-sharing partner sends its first report. The analyst grades the source 'F'. What does this grade mean and imply?
options: Reliability cannot be judged yet; treat it as unknown and seek more evidence
The source is unreliable based on its track record, so its reports should be discarded
The source is fairly reliable but needs a second confirmation
The report is improbable and conflicts with existing evidence
6.explanation: F means reliability cannot be judged, typically for a new or unassessed source; it is not a bad grade. 'Unreliable' is E, and improbability is an information grade (5), not a source grade.

6.q: A domain arrives within one day via a vendor feed, an open feed and a sharing group. Tracing shows all three cite the same original vendor report. May the analyst grade the information '1'?
options: Yes, because three separate channels have each independently confirmed the same domain
Yes, provided at least one of the three channels is graded A or B
No: copies of one original are a single report, which is circular reporting
No, because information can only be graded 1 by the original producer
6.explanation: Grade 1 requires confirmation by an independent source; three copies of one report are one report. Local telemetry, such as a hunt finding, could provide genuine independent confirmation.

6.q: An analyst proposes averaging the Admiralty grades of all feed entries to report a 'mean grade' for each feed. Why is this unsound?
options: The letters and numbers belong to different scales that cannot be combined
Admiralty grades change too quickly for an average to stay meaningful
The grades are ordinal labels with no defined distance between values
Averages are only valid when every entry shares the same TLP marking
6.explanation: Grades order values (B is better than C) but define no distance, so arithmetic on them is meaningless; any numeric conversion is a written local policy choice. The scale-mixing point is true but does not explain why averaging a single axis fails.

6.q: The vendor's file hash (producer confidence 90) is graded B6 in the worked table. Why does the information grade fall to 6?
options: The SOC has no file-hash data, so the claim's truth cannot be judged locally
The vendor's past reporting has been inconsistent in malware analysis
The hash conflicts with the other feed entries and is therefore graded improbable
The hash's validity window expired before the as-of date
6.explanation: Grade 6 means truth cannot be judged: with no hash telemetry, Banyan cannot check the claim at all. The source letter stays B because the vendor is reliable for malware analysis; the hash still had validity remaining.

6.q: R2 fired on the same events that 203.0.113.66 matched, yet the worked table grades the address B2 rather than B1. What is the reasoning?
options: R2 was written using the indicator, so its alert is not independent corroboration of it
ISAC-A has only a fair track record, which caps information at 2
Expired indicators can never be graded above 2 in the Admiralty system
Local data confirms only that something there sprayed Banyan, not the wider claim
6.explanation: The claim graded is that the address is used for VPN spraying generally; Banyan's data supports it strongly but only for its own 06:42 events, and an address is a weak identifier of an actor. R2 was in fact written without knowledge of the indicator, so it is independent.

6.q: Under the course's illustrative scoring policy, an indicator has producer confidence 60, a source graded B, one independent local corroboration and is within its validity window. What is its local score and permitted action?
options: 60, context only because addresses cannot alert on their own
70, raise an alert for analyst review rather than block automatically
80, eligible for automatic blocking wherever the indicator's type allows it
50, context only until a second corroboration is recorded
6.explanation: 60 with no change for a B source, plus 10 for one independent corroboration, gives 70, which falls in the 50-79 alert band. Reaching 80 would need another corroboration; nothing in the policy caps an in-window address at context only.

6.q: How does STIX 2.1 express the confidence of an object such as an indicator?
options: As an optional integer property from 0 to 100
As a mandatory two-character Admiralty grade such as B2
As a TLP colour from CLEAR to RED
As a decimal probability between 0 and 1
6.explanation: STIX 2.1 defines an optional confidence property holding an integer from 0 to 100, which the lab feed's conf column imitates. TLP governs sharing, not confidence.

6.q: Using the half-life model s(t) = s0 x 0.5^(t/h), an address with a local score of 70 and a 7-day half-life receives no new sightings. What is its score after 14 days, and its action band?
options: 35, still in the alert band
52, still in the alert band
0, because it is fully expired
About 17, context only
6.explanation: Fourteen days is two half-lives: 70 x 0.25 = 17.5, which is below 50 and so context only. 35 is the value after one half-life; gradual decay never reaches zero in finite time.

6.q: The SOC has a confidence-95 indicator for commodity adware and a confidence-60 indicator for ransomware staging. How should confidence relate to prioritisation here?
options: Prioritise strictly by confidence, so the adware indicator goes first
Raise the ransomware indicator's confidence to reflect its severity
Keep confidence and impact separate and combine them only when prioritising
Discard the ransomware indicator because its score is below the block threshold
6.explanation: Confidence measures how sure you are; severity measures how bad the outcome would be. Inflating confidence to express severity corrupts the score, while ranking by confidence alone ignores impact.

6.q: What is the main weakness of hard expiry as used by ioc_match.py, compared with gradual decay?
options: It cannot represent different validity windows for different indicator types in one feed
An indicator counts at full weight one day and not at all the next, with nothing changed
It requires the analyst to recompute every score manually each morning
It lets expired indicators continue to drive automatic blocking
6.explanation: Hard expiry creates a cliff: 203.0.113.66 has full weight on 9 November and none on 11 November although the address did not change. Each entry carries its own valid_until, so per-type windows are possible, and the script marks expired matches for review.

6.q: How should a SOC grade its own internal incident team as a source of intelligence?
options: Always A, because internal sources have direct access to all the relevant evidence
Always F, because internal teams have no external track record
The same as the most reliable external feed it subscribes to
Often high for claims about its own environment, lower for the wider world
6.explanation: Reliability rests on track record and access: an internal team sees its own environment directly but has limited access to what happens elsewhere. A is reserved for sources with a long, checked record, not granted by habit.

6.q: An aggregator feed re-publishes indicators from several well-regarded sector groups but does no analysis of its own. How should its source reliability be graded?
options: On its own record and access; it does not inherit its upstream sources' grades
At the highest grade among the well-regarded upstream sources that it re-publishes
At the average grade of its upstream sources, weighted by volume
Always as E, because aggregators are inherently unreliable
6.explanation: Reliability reflects the source's own history and access; an aggregator has no access of its own, so it cannot borrow its upstreams' letters. E would be a judgement of a poor record, not something to apply automatically.

6.q: In the confidence-and-ageing workflow, what happens when a previously graded indicator is seen again in local data?
options: It is re-received at the top and its producer confidence is replaced
It re-enters at information grading, is re-graded and its age is reset
Its source grade is raised one letter for each new sighting
Nothing changes until its valid_until date is reached
6.explanation: The feedback loop runs back to Grade information: a genuine new sighting can change the credibility grade and restarts the age clock. Sightings support the claim; they do not rewrite the producer's number or the source's letter.

6.q: An open feed adds a major CDN's address range as 'malicious'. Which control most directly prevents this from becoming a self-inflicted outage?
options: Raising the producer confidence threshold for open feeds to 90
Applying a short hard-expiry window to every open-feed indicator so that bad entries age out within days
Checking candidates against an allowlist, with thresholds so low-graded sources cannot block alone
Converting open-feed indicators into behavioural rules before use
6.explanation: Feed poisoning is countered by grading open sources conservatively, never letting them block alone and checking candidates against a reviewed allowlist of critical ranges. A short expiry would still allow the outage while the entry was active.

6.q: Which sentence correctly separates likelihood from confidence in an analytic judgement?
options: We assess with moderate confidence that the intrusion is likely linked to the ISAC-A campaign
We are likely confident that the intrusion is possibly linked to the ISAC-A campaign
There is a high-confidence probability of 85 that the campaign is involved
The intrusion may be linked to ISAC-A reporting, which we believe strongly
6.explanation: 'Likely' states how probable the judgement is; 'moderate confidence' states how good the evidence is, and both appear distinctly. The other sentences blur the two or use undefined words such as 'may' and 'possibly'.

6.q: gopal's account was compromised by the 06:46 spray. At 13:33 his session matches the expired, F3-graded 198.51.100.104. Why can the intelligence not settle whether this was the attacker returning?
options: Because an address match is only valid if it occurs within one hour of the indicator's first hit
Because the VPN logs do not record the source address of successful logins
Because open-feed indicators must always be ignored in incident response
Because an expired F3 claim about shared hosting says almost nothing about that day's user
6.explanation: The indicator is low-graded, expired 126 days earlier and about shared hosting, so it carries no weight either way; other evidence such as the user and his device must decide. Open-feed matches are context, not something to ignore entirely.

6.q: Of the six steps from receiving an indicator to acting on it, which are implemented by ioc_match.py itself?
options: Source grading and information grading
Reading producer confidence and applying hard expiry against AS_OF
Local corroboration and action by threshold
All six, with results printed on each line
6.explanation: The script reads the producer confidence and compares valid_until with AS_OF to mark EXPIRED. Grading, corroboration and thresholds are the analyst's and platform's work, recorded alongside the indicator.

6.q: cdn-telemetry-sync.example has a local score of 95 and a 30-day half-life. If 30 days pass with no new sighting or report, what action does the illustrative policy permit?
options: Automatic blocking, since it started well above the threshold
An alert for analyst review, since it remains in the 50-79 band
Context only, at about 47, unless new evidence resets the clock
Removal from the platform, because decay has reached zero
6.explanation: One half-life halves 95 to about 47.5, which is below 50 and therefore context only. A starting score does not protect an indicator from decay, and halving never reaches zero.

6.q: A SOC confirms a feed indicator locally and also finds that another feed entry was a false positive. What should it do with this knowledge?
options: Report sightings and false positives back to the producers within each indicator's sharing rules
Keep both findings internal so that producers cannot adjust their scores
Publish both findings on an open feed so the wider community benefits
Lower the producer confidence values in its own copy of the feed and move on without telling anyone
6.explanation: Feedback to producers, respecting TLP, improves grading over time and is how sources earn or lose their letter. Publishing openly could breach the indicators' sharing restrictions.

6.q: Which piece of local evidence would count as independent corroboration of a feed claim that a domain is C2?
options: An alert from a SIEM rule generated automatically from that feed entry
The same domain appearing in a second feed that cites the original report
A high producer confidence value attached to the domain by the feed
A hunt finding a machine-regular beacon to it by timing analysis alone
6.explanation: A timing hunt that does not use the domain list confirms the claim from your own data, independently of the feed. A rule generated from the same entry merely re-expresses the indicator, and a citing feed is circular reporting.

6.q: A low-confidence indicator matches a session belonging to a named employee. What does the lesson require?
options: Suspend the account until the employee proves the session was theirs
Escalate to HR, since any intelligence match on an employee is grounds for investigation
Never use it as a basis for disciplinary action; handle it as personal data with care
Delete the match record immediately to protect the employee's privacy
6.explanation: People are in scope: low-confidence intelligence must not drive disciplinary or legal action, and such matches are personal data under the DPDP Act 2023. Deleting the record would destroy the audit trail the lesson asks you to keep.

6.q: In a private copy of the kit you run ioc_match.py with AS_OF set to 9 November 2026 and then 11 November 2026. Which line changes status between the two runs?
options: cdn-telemetry-sync.example moves from MATCH to EXPIRED
203.0.113.66 moves from MATCH to EXPIRED
198.51.100.104 moves from EXPIRED to MATCH
banyan-payroll-update.example moves from MATCH to EXPIRED
6.explanation: 203.0.113.66 is valid until 10 November, so it is current on 9 November and expired on 11 November. The two domains remain valid for weeks longer, and 198.51.100.104 expired on 30 June in both runs.

6.q: The internal team's note on banyan-payroll-update.example is graded B1 in the worked table. What justifies the information grade of 1?
options: Its verifiable registration date and the local download followed by R1 confirm it
Internal sources are always graded 1 for information about their own domains
Its producer confidence of 70 is above the policy threshold for confirmed information
The domain appears in both the internal note and ISAC-A's feed
6.explanation: Grade 1 needs independent confirmation: the registration date is checkable and Banyan's own data shows the 06:12 download followed by R1 at 06:14. Producer confidence is a separate number, and internal sources earn no automatic grade.

6.q: In the Banyan data, 284 events carry a URL (9 distinct) and 304 carry a source address (11 distinct strings). After canonicalisation, dropping placeholders and gating internal values, how many values can tell the SOC anything new from outside sources?
options: Twenty, one lookup for every distinct value observed
Nineteen, every distinct value left after removing the placeholder
Eight: six external host names and two external addresses
Eleven, because only the address strings need external reputation
6.explanation: Of 20 distinct values, '-' is a placeholder, 8 addresses are in 10.40.0.0/24 and 3 URLs are under banyan.example, leaving 6 external host names and 2 external addresses. Nineteen would still send internal values outside, which is both wasteful and a disclosure.

6.q: Why should an enrichment cache be keyed by the pair (canonical value, source) rather than by the canonical value alone?
options: Different sources can legitimately disagree about one value, and both answers must survive
Keying by value alone would make it impossible to store negative results for any entity at all
Sources require the cache to prove which key was used before they bill a lookup
A value cannot be canonicalised until the pipeline knows which source will receive it
6.explanation: The ISAC data and an external reputation service may disagree about the same domain; a value-only key would let one answer overwrite the other. Negative results can be stored under either key design, so that distractor misses the point.

6.q: On 15 November a pipeline serves a cached 'MATCH, confidence 60' for 203.0.113.66, fetched on 3 November and stored with a 14-day TTL. The indicator's valid_until is 2026-11-10. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because the cache entry is still inside its 14-day TTL
The hit count has changed since 3 November, so the match must be recomputed
Address TTLs should be longer than 14 days, so the cached entry is in fact far too young
Validity was not re-checked against the as-of date; the correct status is EXPIRED
6.explanation: The cache TTL and the indicator's validity are independent clocks; the rerun with AS_OF 2026-11-15 shows the same nine events now come back EXPIRED. Being inside the TTL only means the lookup is recent, not that the indicator is still valid.

6.q: An approved external reputation service answers a worker's request with HTTP 429 and a Retry-After header. What should the worker do?
options: Retry immediately up to five times, then record the value as clean
Stop sending to that source, wait at least the requested time, then retry with growing backoff
Send the same value to a free public service that publishes submissions, so the answer arrives sooner
Record 'no data from source' and cache that negative result with a long TTL
6.explanation: A 429 (RFC 6585) is an instruction to slow down; the worker obeys Retry-After and lengthens the wait on repeated refusals. Recording 'no data' would misrepresent a refusal as an answer, and immediate retry loops get integration keys suspended.

6.q: Two honest pipeline runs over identical Banyan events disagree: one marks 203.0.113.66 MATCH, the other EXPIRED. Which provenance field, read with valid_until, explains the difference?
options: query_time_utc, because it records when the event itself occurred
as_of, because validity status is evaluated against that date
pipeline_version, because an expiry change implies a different release
retrieved, because one answer must have come from a stale cache
6.explanation: Validity is recomputed from valid_until and the as-of date, so 3 November gives MATCH and 15 November gives EXPIRED with identical data and code. query_time_utc records when the pipeline asked, not the date the validity test used, and it is not the event time.

6.q: An external source fails to answer within the pipeline's timeout while an alert is being enriched. How should the result be handled?
options: Record the value as clean as of that time, since no adverse data was returned
Record 'no data from source' and negative-cache it with the usual negative TTL for that type
Hold the alert out of the queue until the source answers or the shift ends
Record 'source unavailable at time T', let the alert proceed and flag it for re-enrichment
6.explanation: A timeout is no answer, which an analyst reads differently from 'no data' and completely differently from 'clean'. Enrichment must never block an alert from reaching the queue, so holding it is wrong too.

6.q: A community feed mistakenly lists a major public DNS resolver as malicious. Which design choice in the lookup cascade stops this from producing an alert storm?
options: Consulting allowlists and warning lists before the internal TIP's intelligence
Caching TIP matches with a long TTL so the entry is looked up less often
Placing external reputation services ahead of the TIP so wider data overrides it
Negative-caching every resolver lookup so repeated queries are suppressed
6.explanation: Allowlists sit before intelligence precisely because feeds contain mistakes about widely shared benign values. Caching the bad match for longer would only prolong the storm, and reordering towards external services increases exposure without fixing the error.

6.q: Why does the lesson recommend a shorter TTL for negative results than for positive ones?
options: Negative results take more cache storage because they include the full query
Sources rate-limit repeated negative lookups more harshly than positive ones
A value nobody has reported today may be reported once a campaign is noticed
Negative results cannot be reproduced later, so they lose value quickly
6.explanation: A negative answer ages faster: reporting often lags the start of a campaign. It is recorded as 'no data from source X as of T', never 'clean'. Storage size and rate-limit treatment are not the reasons given for the shorter TTL.

6.q: cdn-telemetry-sync.example reached Banyan through ISAC-A data marked TLP:AMBER. A contracted external reputation service is available. What should the privacy gate decide?
options: Submit it externally, because the gate only blocks internal values
Submit only the host name without the URL path, which removes the restriction
Submit it to a free public service instead, because the contract only covers paid lookups
Match it internally only; the AMBER marking forbids passing it to that third party
6.explanation: The gate checks the most restrictive marking already attached to a value; sending an AMBER value to an outside enrichment service passes it beyond the recipient organisation. Being external is not enough, and stripping the path does not change the marking on the domain itself.

6.q: A pipeline sends the src_ip value '-' (present in 10 Banyan events) to a reputation service. What is the correct diagnosis?
options: It is an internal address token, and sending it outside discloses Banyan's internal addressing
It is a placeholder, not an entity; it should be dropped and counted at canonicalisation
It is a defanged indicator that must be refanged before the lookup
It should be routed to internal sources, since its owner is unknown
6.explanation: '-' is a placeholder some source writes when it has no value; looking it up wastes a request and pollutes the cache. Counting dropped values matters because a rise signals a parsing problem. It is not an address of any kind, internal or defanged.

6.q: A team proposes running the full lookup cascade first and applying the privacy gate only to results, just before they are attached to the alert. What is the fundamental flaw?
options: Internal and restricted values will already have been sent to sources before the gate runs
The gate becomes redundant, because the cache already filters out internal values
Results cannot be classified after the lookup, because sources strip the original TLP markings
Running the gate late breaks deduplication, since the gate is what removes repeats
6.explanation: The gate protects the stages after it: classification must happen before any lookup so no value reaches a source it should not. A gate on results cannot undo a disclosure. The cache does not classify values, and deduplication is a separate earlier stage.

6.q: Which starting TTL policy for positive cache entries best follows how fast the underlying facts change?
options: One TTL for every entity type, so results stay consistent across alerts
Long for IP addresses and short for hashes, since file contents are rebuilt often
Long for file hashes, medium for domains and short for IP addresses
Short for file hashes, because a hash can come to name different content
6.explanation: A SHA-256 always names the same content, domain reputation shifts over days to weeks, and address reputation can change within hours as cloud and residential ranges are reassigned. A hash never names different content, although its verdict can be revised.

6.q: The internal TIP marks an indicator as a false positive while several cached results derived from it are still inside their TTL. What should the pipeline do?
options: Leave the entries alone and let them expire naturally when their TTL runs out
Flush every cached result derived from that indicator, regardless of remaining TTL
Halve the stored confidence of the cached results so that analysts weigh them less from now on
Add a negative cache entry beside each positive one so both answers are kept
6.explanation: Revocation or a false-positive verdict invalidates derived results immediately; waiting for the TTL keeps serving a known-wrong answer. Keeping both answers is right for different sources, not for a single source that has withdrawn its own claim.

6.q: The internal TIP has been unreachable for six hours while external lookups kept working. What does the lesson's degradation guidance require?
options: Nothing beyond routine logging, because external services cover the missing community intelligence
Holding new alerts out of the queue until TIP matching can be applied again
Recording every value enriched during the outage as clean for the TIP source
Raising a pipeline health alert, since lost intelligence matching is a coverage gap
6.explanation: Silently lost TIP matching is a coverage gap that belongs in the shift handover and any overlapping case record. External services do not hold the curated community data, and enrichment must never hold alerts back or turn 'unavailable' into 'clean'.

6.q: An enrichment record for cdn-telemetry-sync.example contains the line 'we assess the beacon as malicious with high confidence'. What is wrong with this record?
options: The confidence should be written as a number so it can be compared with 85
The SOC must reuse the source's confidence of 85 in the record rather than writing its own wording
It mixes the SOC's analytic judgement into provenance, which should hold the producer's words
Provenance records may describe the domain but must not mention the beacon
6.explanation: 'ISAC-A reports C2, confidence 85' is provenance; the SOC's assessment belongs in the case notes, citing the record as evidence. Adopting the source's confidence as the SOC's own would blur the same line from the other side.

6.q: A domain enriched yesterday is enriched again today and the source now gives a different answer. How should the case records be handled?
options: Append the new record and keep both, because the change itself is information
Overwrite the old record so analysts only ever see the current answer
Keep the original record and discard the new one to preserve the timeline
Merge the two into one record carrying the average of both confidences
6.explanation: Provenance is append-only: a change of verdict tells the analyst something, and both records stay reproducible. Overwriting loses exactly the history a reviewer needs to understand why a decision was made at the time.

6.q: A SOC allowlist contains a content-delivery host added two years ago, with no owner, reason or review date. Why is this a security problem rather than just untidiness?
options: It raises external quota use, because allowlisted values are re-checked externally on every alert
It causes cache misses, because allowlisted values are never written to the cache
It makes cache keys ambiguous, because the allowlist uses its own canonical form
It is an unaudited suppression that can hide malicious use of that host indefinitely
6.explanation: Allowlist entries stop the cascade at stage 1, so an ownerless entry with no expiry becomes a hiding place; adversaries may even try to get their own infrastructure allowlisted. Allowlisted values short-circuit lookups, so they do not raise quota use.

6.q: Which pipeline health signal most directly suggests that a trusted feed has stopped updating?
options: A rising number of values dropped at the canonicalisation stage
A falling hit rate for lookups answered by the internal TIP
A rising cache hit rate for file-hash lookups across the day
A rising count of 429 refusals from the external reputation service
6.explanation: If the TIP's feeds stop refreshing, fewer current indicators exist to match, so its hit rate falls. Rising drops at canonicalisation point to a parsing problem, and 429 counts reflect external quota pressure, not feed freshness.

6.q: An alert involves the account name of an employee. Which enrichment approach fits the lesson's privacy rules and the DPDP Act, 2023?
options: Query an external breach-lookup service so the alert has complete context
Copy the employee's full HR record into the alert for the analyst's convenience
Enrich only from internal sources, adding only attributes the security decision needs
Hash the account name before sending it to external services, which fully anonymises the lookup
6.explanation: Personal identifiers are enriched internally and minimised to what the decision requires, for a lawful purpose with reasonable safeguards. Hashing a known name before sending it outside still discloses a lookup about an identifiable person and is not what the gate permits.

6.q: Which of these lookup results can correctly short-circuit the cascade for that value?
options: 10.40.0.23 resolved by the CMDB as an internal host with a known owner
A cache entry for a domain whose TTL ran out an hour ago
An ISAC-A match where policy lets stage 4 add registration age
An allowlist entry for a public resolver when the task is a hunt
6.explanation: An internal address is definitively internal; no external source can add anything useful. An expired cache entry is no longer definitive, a stage-3 match may still need permitted stage-4 fields, and an allowlist entry is definitive only for its own purpose.

6.q: During an incident, 300 high-severity alerts share four external values and the external service's daily quota is nearly spent. Which approach handles the rate limit best?
options: Increase retry frequency so the pending requests are answered sooner
Query the service once per event, so that every one of the 300 alerts carries its own fresh answer
Lower the TTLs during the incident so answers are refreshed more often
Look up each distinct value once, reuse cached answers and spend budget on high severity first
6.explanation: Deduplication and caching are the first rate-limit controls, and a per-source budget spent in priority order keeps quota for what matters most. Per-event lookups and shorter TTLs multiply requests exactly when the quota is scarcest.

6.q: One proxy event records 'Files-Share-Drop.example.' and another 'files-share-drop.example', and the pipeline performed two separate external lookups. Which stage failed?
options: Classify and gate
Canonicalise and deduplicate
Record with provenance
Attach and feed back
6.explanation: Host names should be lower-cased with the trailing dot removed so equal values compare equal and are looked up once. The gate classified both correctly as external; the duplication happened earlier, at canonicalisation.

6.q: The analyst confirms that the 198.51.100.104 match was gopal's ordinary VPN session. What is the appropriate feed-back step?
options: Record the outcome against the indicator in the TIP and tell the open feed where a channel exists
Add the address to the allowlist permanently, with no owner or expiry, so that it can never match again
Delete the match from the case record so the false positive does not mislead reviewers
Submit the address to public reputation services so they can correct their own verdicts
6.explanation: Rejected matches become feedback to the source and are recorded in the TIP; any allowlist entry needs an owner and an expiry. A permanent ownerless entry is a hiding place, and deleting the record destroys provenance.

6.q: Why is a little random jitter added to retry backoff in an enrichment pipeline with many workers?
options: So cache entries written after retries expire at slightly different times
Because the Retry-After header requires clients to choose a random delay
So many workers refused together do not all retry the source in lock-step
So that the wait grows longer after each consecutive refusal from the source
6.explanation: Jitter spreads retries so simultaneous refusals do not produce a synchronised burst that triggers the limit again. Growing the wait after each failure is the backoff itself, not the jitter, and Retry-After states a delay rather than demanding randomness.

6.q: Why does the default cascade consult the internal TIP and community data before an approved external service?
options: External services are generally less accurate than any internal source
A TIP answer is always definitive, so the external stage is never needed once the TIP has replied
External services cannot return reputation information about domains
Cost and exposure: the TIP stays in-house, while external lookups spend quota and reveal the query
6.explanation: The cascade runs from cheapest and most private to most expensive and most exposed; the TIP is curated, marked and internal. A stage-3 match is often not final, since policy may let stage 4 add fields, so 'always definitive' is wrong.

6.q: 203.0.113.66 sent the password-spraying login attempts against Banyan's VPN. Which MISP attribute type should Banyan's event use for it?
options: ip-dst, because the address appears in the alert raised on Banyan's VPN gateway
ip-src, because the address was the source of the activity against the victim
A domain-ip object, because every address must be paired with a host name
ip-dst, because consumers will want to block outbound traffic to the address
6.explanation: ip-src marks an address seen as the source of activity, such as a spraying host; ip-dst is for addresses the victim connected to, such as C2. Recording it as ip-dst sends consumers to the wrong field of their logs.

6.q: 203.0.113.66 was part of a serious intrusion, yet the worked example leaves its IDS flag off. What is the reasoning?
options: Attributes in High threat-level events are never flagged, to avoid duplicate alerts
Addresses cannot be correlated in MISP, so flagging them would have no effect
The feed marked the address TLP:GREEN, which prevents setting the IDS flag
The flag follows specificity, not severity; addresses change and may be reassigned
6.explanation: An address is cheap to change and may later belong to someone else, so automated matching weeks later would block innocent traffic; a last-seen time gives context instead. TLP and the IDS flag are independent settings, and addresses do correlate.

6.q: Banyan saw cdn-telemetry-sync.example in its own proxy logs. ISAC-A had already reported it under TLP:AMBER with the context 'C2 for loader seen in finance-sector phishing'. What is the best contribution Banyan can make?
options: Add a sighting on ISAC-A's existing attribute to say it was seen here too
Copy ISAC-A's context into Banyan's TLP:GREEN event so peers see the full picture
Re-publish ISAC-A's event with distribution All communities to maximise reach
Create a TLP:CLEAR event containing the domain and ISAC-A's description of it
6.explanation: A sighting tells the producer and its community the value was seen elsewhere without redistributing anything. Copying ISAC-A's AMBER context into a GREEN event re-shares another organisation's information under a looser marking, one of the most damaging sharing mistakes.

6.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes MISP distribution from TLP?
options: Both are enforced by the platform, which blocks any synchronisation that would break either of them
TLP is enforced by the platform, while distribution only advises human readers
Distribution is enforced by MISP synchronisation; TLP tells people what they may do with data
They are two names for one setting, so choosing one automatically sets the other
