6.explanation: MISP will not synchronise an event to an instance its distribution excludes, while the TLP tag instructs people on onward sharing in e-mail, tickets and reports. Neither sets the other, which is why both must be set and kept consistent.

6.q: A reviewer finds an event tagged tlp:red with distribution set to All communities. What is the correct assessment?
options: It under-shares, because TLP:RED data would normally be published more widely
It is consistent, because the TLP tag always overrides the distribution setting during synchronisation
It is a contradiction that will leak: the platform will propagate it far beyond the marking
It is harmless, because publishing and distribution are unrelated in MISP
6.explanation: Distribution is what MISP enforces, so All communities propagates the event across connected instances regardless of the tag. The opposite case, TLP:CLEAR restricted to your organisation, is the one that merely under-shares.

6.q: An analyst records the C2 domain only in the event's info title rather than as an attribute. What is the consequence?
options: The domain is invisible to correlation, detection exports and tag-based filtering
Correlation still finds the domain, because it scans event titles for values
The domain is shared only within the creating organisation, not the community
MISP converts the domain into an attribute automatically when the event is published
6.explanation: Correlation and exports read attribute values and flags; filtering reads machine tags. A value hidden in the title or a free-text comment is seen by none of them. The title is shared with the event, so it is not kept local either.

6.q: A consumer receives a partner event whose analysis field is set to Initial. How should the consumer treat it?
options: As confirmed intelligence, because the producer chose to publish it
As unusable until the producer changes the state to Completed
As an unpublished draft that has reached the consumer by mistake and should be deleted
As early, possibly wrong information that should not be acted on as if Completed
6.explanation: Analysis (Initial, Ongoing, Completed) tells consumers how mature the information is; Initial means early and possibly wrong. That calls for caution, not dismissal, and analysis state is separate from the published state.

6.q: One event stores 'CDN-Telemetry-Sync.example.' and another stores 'cdn-telemetry-sync.example', but MISP shows no correlation between them. What is the most likely cause?
options: Correlation is disabled for domain attributes in MISP's default instance configuration
Basic correlation is exact value matching, so inconsistent spelling defeats it
A warninglist suppressed the domain because it contains the word 'cdn'
Events with different TLP tags are never correlated with each other
6.explanation: Correlation compares stored values literally, so case or a trailing dot can break the link; Lesson 3's canonicalisation discipline applies. Warninglists flag listed values such as known resolvers, not values that merely contain a word.

6.q: An analyst is about to add the address of a well-known public DNS resolver, seen in Banyan's DNS logs, to the event. Which MISP mechanism warns them that this value produces false positives?
options: A warninglist match on the value
A sighting recorded by a consumer
A galaxy cluster attached to the event
A decay model applied to the attribute
6.explanation: Warninglists are maintained lists of values known to cause false positives, such as public resolvers, and MISP warns when an attribute matches one. Sightings are consumer feedback after the fact, and decay models score attributes down over time.

6.q: Why is attaching the ATT&CK cluster T1204.002 to Banyan's event valuable to a detection engineer at a peer organisation?
options: It identifies which domain to add to the proxy block list
It enforces the TLP tag on every attribute in the event
It ties changeable indicators to a behaviour that a behaviour-based rule can detect
It raises the event's threat level so that consumers across the community prioritise it
6.explanation: Galaxy clusters link indicators, which change, to behaviours, which do not, so the engineer knows which behaviour rule should fire whatever the next campaign's domain is. The cluster carries no blocking value and has no effect on markings or threat level.

6.q: Why model a delivered file as a MISP file object rather than as separate filename, size and hash attributes?
options: Objects bypass the event's distribution setting, so file details can be shared more widely
Object contents are excluded from correlation, which reduces noisy links
Objects are the only way to set an IDS flag on hash values
It keeps values that describe one thing together, linkable and exportable to STIX 2.1
6.explanation: An object groups related attributes from a template and can be linked to other objects by typed references, matching STIX 2.1's model. Its contents are attributes too, so they correlate and export like any other; objects do not bypass distribution.

6.q: Several consumers record false-positive sightings against an IDS-flagged attribute in a producer's event. What does this most appropriately lead to?
options: MISP deleting the attribute automatically once a threshold is reached
The producer reviewing the attribute and withdrawing or correcting it
All correlations involving the attribute being removed instance-wide
The event's TLP tag being relaxed to tlp:clear for wider review
6.explanation: Sightings are a feedback channel: an indicator several consumers mark as false positive should be reviewed or withdrawn by its producer. The lesson describes no automatic deletion, and markings are unrelated to quality feedback.

6.q: Banyan's enrichment pipeline pulls attributes from its MISP instance. Which attributes should be allowed to generate alerts or blocks automatically?
options: IDS-flagged, current, specific attributes that still pass allowlists and validity checks
Every attribute in any event whose threat level is set to High
Every attribute that correlates with at least one other event on the instance
Any attribute carrying a tlp:clear tag, since it may be used and acted on without restriction
6.explanation: All attributes may be matched for enrichment, but automated action should come only from flagged attributes, and the pipeline still applies its own allowlists and validity checks. Threat level, correlation and TLP say nothing about whether a value is specific enough to block.

6.q: Two banks investigating the same fraud campaign want to share an event with each other and nobody else on their shared ISAC instance. Which distribution choice fits?
options: This community only, on the shared ISAC instance
Connected communities
Your organisation only
A sharing group of the two organisations
6.explanation: A sharing group is a named list of organisations allowed to receive the data, suited to cases where the whole instance is too wide and one organisation too narrow. This community only would reach every organisation on the ISAC instance.

6.q: An analyst has created and saved a new event with distribution set to This community only. Has it been shared with the community yet?
options: Yes, every save immediately synchronises the event to all organisations within its distribution
Yes, but only to organisations that already have a correlating event
No, publishing is the release step that triggers synchronisation and notifications
No, sharing always requires a manual STIX export sent to each partner
6.explanation: Creating or editing an event does not share it; publishing marks it ready and triggers synchronisation within its distribution and any configured notifications. Many organisations put a second-analyst review before that step.

6.q: An ISAC-A event is synchronised onto Banyan's MISP instance. Which field still lets a Banyan analyst judge who produced the intelligence?
options: The owner organisation, because it identifies who holds this synchronised copy of the event
The creator organisation, which remains the original producer after synchronisation
The event UUID, because it encodes the producer's reliability grade
The sharing group name, because only producers can create sharing groups
6.explanation: The owner organisation is whoever owns this copy on this instance, while the creator remains the original producer across synchronisation. The UUID only makes the event recognisable across instances; it carries no grading.

6.q: Why does the worked Banyan event deliberately leave out 198.51.100.104?
options: It was an expired open-feed entry that matched an ordinary employee session
It came from a TLP:CLEAR feed, and MISP cannot store TLP:CLEAR values
Addresses may only be recorded inside objects, never as plain attributes
It is an internal address, and internal addresses never leave Banyan
6.explanation: The address is not part of the intrusion; including it would spread a false association to every consumer. It is an external documentation address, and TLP:CLEAR data can be stored in MISP like any other.

6.q: An event with distribution Connected communities contains one attribute that must stay on the creating organisation's instance. What does MISP allow?
options: Turning the attribute's IDS flag off, which keeps it out of synchronisation
Disabling correlation on the attribute, which also stops it being shared
Giving that attribute a more restrictive distribution than the event
Nothing; attributes must inherit the event's distribution, so the event must be split
6.explanation: Attributes have their own distribution, which can inherit the event's or be more restrictive, so one event can share most content while keeping a value local. The IDS flag governs detection use and disabling correlation governs linking; neither restricts sharing.

6.q: An attribute arrives tagged with a PAP value that permits only passive use. How should Banyan's enrichment pipeline treat it?
options: Ignore the tag, because PAP only controls onward sharing to other people
Read it as the source's reliability grade and weight the match accordingly
Use it to choose which instances the attribute is synchronised to
Have the privacy gate block active queries about it to external services
6.explanation: The Permissible Actions Protocol states what recipients may do with an indicator, such as whether they may actively query it externally, which connects directly to Lesson 3's privacy gate. Onward sharing is TLP's job, reliability is the Admiralty scale's, and synchronisation is distribution's.

6.q: A partner event carries Admiralty-scale tags grading the source B and the information 2. How should an analyst read this?
options: TLP level B with handling priority 2 for the information
The source is usually reliable and the information is probably true
Threat level B and analysis state 2 as set by the producer
Distribution allowed to travel two hops from community B
6.explanation: The Admiralty taxonomy encodes Lesson 2's grading: a letter for source reliability (B, usually reliable) and a number for information credibility (2, probably true). TLP, threat level and distribution are separate fields with their own vocabularies.

6.q: Two unrelated-looking events correlate on an address belonging to a major cloud provider, and an analyst concludes they are the work of the same actor. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Correlation only links domain attributes, so the address match must be a display error in MISP
Cloud provider addresses cannot be stored as attributes in MISP events
A correlation counts only after at least one sighting has confirmed it
A correlation is a lead, not attribution; shared infrastructure can host unrelated actors
6.explanation: Correlation links identical values, and an address on shared cloud infrastructure may serve entirely different actors. Such values are also prime candidates for warninglists or correlation exclusions to avoid over-correlation.

6.q: An integration needs only to pull IDS-flagged detection exports from MISP and add sightings. How should its API key be managed?
options: Scope it to the minimum role needed, keep it in a secrets manager and rotate it
Use an administrator's key so the integration never fails on a permission check
Store it in the pipeline's configuration file in the code repository for traceability
Share one key across all integrations so that audit logs show a single identity
6.explanation: API keys carry their user's permissions, so a minimal role limits the damage if one leaks; secrets storage and rotation reduce exposure further. A shared key destroys the per-integration attribution that activity logging relies on.

6.q: MISP is configured with a decay model. What happens to an attribute that is several months old and has received no sightings?
options: It is deleted automatically once its first-seen date passes a threshold
Its distribution narrows step by step until it is local to the producer
Its score drops over time, and only sightings would refresh it
Its IDS flag is cleared from the stored event the next time it syncs
6.explanation: Decay models apply the shelf-life idea from Lesson 1, scoring old attributes down unless sightings refresh them. They change how much an attribute counts, not its distribution, its stored flag or its existence.

6.q: Banyan publishes its intrusion event to its sector ISAC community. Does this satisfy its incident-reporting obligation to CERT-In?
options: Yes, because sharing through a sector ISAC community counts as reporting to CERT-In
No, reporting specified incidents to CERT-In is a separate legal obligation
Yes, provided the event is tagged tlp:clear so CERT-In may read it
Only if the event's distribution is set to All communities
6.explanation: Community sharing in MISP does not replace legal reporting under CERT-In's directions. No marking or distribution setting turns a community event into a regulatory report, and the shared event must also respect DPDP Act limits on personal data.

6.q: A consumer's proxy-blocking export includes Network activity domains and excludes External analysis references. A producer files a campaign's C2 domain under External analysis. What is the likely result?
options: The domain is blocked twice, once from each category in the export
The domain fails to correlate with other events containing the same value
The domain loses its TLP tag when it is exported to the consumer
The domain never reaches the proxy-blocking control that needed it
6.explanation: Category and type determine which exports and controls a value reaches, so a mis-categorised C2 domain is filtered out of the blocking export. Correlation works on the value regardless of category, so it would still link.

6.q: A team lead proposes adding three more free open feeds because more indicators should mean better coverage. Which question should the SOC answer before subscribing to any of them?
options: Which intelligence requirement each feed helps answer, and how much it overlaps with feeds already consumed
Whether the SIEM licence can absorb the extra indicator volume without raising the ingestion cost
Whether each feed publishes more indicators per day than the feeds the SOC already subscribes to
Whether the feeds can be connected directly to the firewall blocklist so that every match is stopped at once
6.explanation: Feeds should be driven by requirements and judged on relevance and uniqueness; overlapping feeds add duplicates and false positives faster than useful indicators. Indicator volume is the misleading measure the lesson warns against, and wiring feeds to a blocklist skips every cleaning stage.

6.q: One feed lists `CDN-Telemetry-Sync.example.` with a trailing dot and another lists `cdn-telemetry-sync[.]example`. If the platform stores both values exactly as received, what is the most likely effect when a host contacts that domain?
options: Neither entry matches, because the SIEM rejects every indicator that contains upper-case letters or brackets
Only the first entry matches, so the second feed is wrongly judged to have a zero hit rate
Duplicate records survive, so one connection can appear as several independent confirmations of the indicator
Both entries are merged automatically at match time, so normalisation at ingestion adds nothing
6.explanation: Case, a trailing dot and defanged notation make one indicator look like two; without canonical forms they are not deduplicated and the same event looks independently confirmed. Matching engines do not silently merge raw strings, which is exactly why normalisation must happen once, in code, at ingestion.

6.q: Two feeds describe the same canonical domain. Feed X marks it TLP:GREEN with first-seen 2 November; feed Y marks it TLP:AMBER with first-seen 30 October. How should the merged record be built?
options: Keep the newer record only, with TLP:GREEN and first-seen 2 November, because it reflects the latest view
List both sources, keep first-seen 30 October and carry TLP:AMBER, the more restrictive marking
List both sources, keep first-seen 2 November and carry TLP:GREEN so the indicator can be shared widely
Keep two separate records so that each feed's TLP marking and dates remain exactly as published
6.explanation: Deduplication keeps information: every source, the earliest first-seen, all context, and the most restrictive TLP of the contributors. Choosing TLP:GREEN would breach the AMBER producer's sharing terms, and keeping two records defeats the purpose of deduplication.

6.q: During deduplication, an address arrives from an open feed with confidence 60 and from a commercial feed with confidence 60. A colleague wants the merged record to show confidence 120, capped at 100. Why is this wrong?
options: Confidence is a property of the feed rather than of the indicator, so it should not be stored on the merged record
STIX 2.1 forbids confidence values above 90 on any indicator received from more than one source
The open-feed value should replace the commercial one because open feeds are published faster
Both feeds may have copied one original observation, so two entries are not two independent confirmations
6.explanation: Merging must not sum confidences: feeds copy each other, so agreement can be one observation seen twice (circular reporting). The suggestion that confidence belongs to the feed is backwards; the lesson stresses that confidence belongs to each indicator.

6.q: At a feed review, feed A matched 40% of its indicators against your telemetry, but nearly all matches were large cloud and CDN addresses closed as false positives. Feed B, a sector ISAC feed, had no matches. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Feed A is relevant to your traffic but not useful; feed B's lack of hits does not by itself show poor quality
Feed A should be kept because a high hit rate is the clearest single measure of a feed's quality
Feed B should be cancelled, because a feed that never matches your telemetry cannot be relevant to the organisation
Both feeds perform equally, since hit rate and false-positive share cancel each other out over time
6.explanation: Hit rate measures relevance to your traffic; the false-positive share of those hits shows whether that relevance is useful. A high rate can simply reflect shared infrastructure, and zero hits may mean intelligence about threats that have not reached you yet.

6.q: A consumer wants to download only the intelligence objects a provider has added since its last poll, over an authenticated HTTPS connection. Which part of the standards stack provides this?
options: The STIX `valid_from` property, which tells the client which objects are newer than the last download
The STIX `pattern_type` property, which tells the client which objects it is permitted to download
A TAXII collection, which the client is granted access to and polls for objects added after a given time
A STIX relationship object, which links each new indicator to the report that the client last downloaded
6.explanation: TAXII transports STIX content: a client is given access to collections and requests objects added after its previous request, so transfer is secure and incremental. `valid_from` describes when an indicator becomes meaningful, not what the client has already fetched.

6.q: A provider offers the same indicators as a CSV list and as STIX 2.1 over TAXII. The SOC only matches indicators today. Why is the STIX option still the better choice?
options: CSV lists cannot hold domain names, so only IP addresses and hashes would survive the import
STIX keeps validity, confidence and relationships that later ageing and scoring logic will need
STIX indicators are always more accurate because each one is vetted by an OASIS review panel
CSV files cannot be loaded into a SIEM lookup table without first being converted to JSON
6.explanation: Flattening to a list throws away `valid_until`, `confidence` and relationships, exactly the fields a feed-management pipeline uses to age and score. OASIS standardises the format, not the accuracy of any producer's content.

6.q: A producer revises an indicator, shortening its `valid_until` and lowering its confidence. The new object has the same `id` as before and a later `modified` time. Why does keeping the same `id` matter to the consumer?
options: It signals that the producer has withdrawn the indicator and that all earlier matches should be discarded
It shows that the indicator has been independently confirmed by a second producer since its creation
It lets the TAXII server skip the object, because objects with known identifiers are never resent
It lets the consumer recognise the object as an update of an indicator it holds, not a new indicator
6.explanation: A STIX id is stable across versions, so a consumer can replace the older version with the revised one; `modified` tells it which is newer. A changed version is still sent by TAXII, and a revision says nothing about independent confirmation or withdrawal.

6.q: In the feed-management pipeline, the allowlist filter is applied before scoring. What failure does this ordering prevent?
options: A high-confidence entry for the organisation's own mail domain reaching the detection and blocking path
Two spellings of the same domain being counted as two separate indicators in the threat intelligence platform
An expired indicator being matched against historical events during a retrospective hunt
A TLP:AMBER indicator being shared with a community that is not entitled to receive it
6.explanation: Filtering before scoring means no score, however high, can push your own or shared infrastructure into automatic action. Duplicate spellings are handled earlier by normalisation and deduplication, not by the allowlist.

6.q: A platform marks indicators as expired only while it imports each weekly feed file. What problem does this design create?
options: Indicators are expired too early, because import time is always later than each producer's own `valid_until`
Indicators whose validity ends between imports stay active for alerting and blocking until the next import
Expired indicators are deleted at import, so retrospective hunts lose the infrastructure they need
Every indicator is re-scored at import, so confidence values drift upward with each weekly run
6.explanation: Age changes daily even when the feed does not, so validity must be evaluated at match time, as the lab matcher does against `AS_OF`. Marking expiry does not imply deletion; the defect here is stale indicators remaining actionable between imports.

6.q: Attackers have hosted phishing pages on a large, legitimate cloud storage service that the business also relies on, and the service's domain is on the SOC allowlist. How should the allowlist entry behave?
options: Remove the domain from the allowlist so that every feed match against it blocks the service immediately
Suppress every match on the domain completely so that analysts are not distracted by known services
Keep the entry but delete the matching events so that the SIEM does not store unneeded data
Keep the domain out of automatic action while still logging matches so they can be reviewed and hunted
6.explanation: An allowlist removes a value from automatic action, not from visibility, precisely because trusted platforms are abused by attackers who expect to be allowlisted. Removing the entry would risk an outage of a service the business depends on; suppressing matches entirely would create a blind spot.

6.q: An auditor finds the allowlist entry `partner-portal.example — excluded after false positive`, with no other fields. What is missing according to good allowlist practice?
options: A STIX identifier and pattern, so that the exception can be exported to other organisations in the ISAC
The confidence value of the feed entry that originally caused the false positive
An owner and a review date, so that someone revisits whether the exception is still justified
The TLP marking of the partner portal, so the exclusion can be shared with the ISAC
6.explanation: Documented exceptions, like Module 5 suppressions, need a reason, an owner and an expiry that is actually reviewed; this one has only a reason. STIX identifiers and TLP markings describe intelligence objects, not the governance of an exclusion.

6.q: After a feed listed a shared CDN address and the SOC's automatic block cut off dozens of business websites, management asks for a safer way to block on intelligence. Which design fits the lesson?
options: Blocks pass change control and cover only current, high-confidence, allowlist-checked indicators, with their effect monitored
Blocks are applied automatically only to indicators that appear in at least two independent feeds, regardless of age or allowlist status
Blocks are applied automatically to all commercial-feed indicators, since vendors curate and expire their entries
Blocks are removed entirely and intelligence is used only in quarterly reports to the risk committee
6.explanation: The lesson's control set is change control, current high-confidence allowlist-checked indicators, and monitoring of the block's effect. Requiring two feeds is weak because feeds copy each other, and trusting all vendor entries ignores per-indicator confidence and the allowlist.

6.q: Which statement best explains why a sensible age policy gives different default lifetimes to IP addresses, domains and file hashes?
options: Hashes expire fastest because a file hash can be reassigned to a different file within days
Domains expire fastest because registrars must delete malicious domains within a fixed period
Addresses are reassigned within days, domains last longer but can be re-registered, and hashes stop matching once the file changes
All types should share one lifetime, because the producer's `valid_until` already describes the decay of every indicator type equally
6.explanation: Each type decays differently: addresses are recycled quickly, domains more slowly with re-registration risk, and hashes never match a different file but are trivially replaced. A hash cannot be reassigned, and a producer's `valid_until` is an override where given, not a reason to ignore type differences.

6.q: To reduce clutter, an engineer proposes deleting every indicator as soon as it passes its `valid_until`. Months later, an incident is found to have started long before detection. What capability has the deletion removed?
options: The ability to block the incident's infrastructure at the firewall during the current response
The ability to check whether the incident's infrastructure appeared in logs at the time it was active
The ability to share current indicators with the ISAC under the original TLP marking
The ability to normalise newly arriving indicators into the platform's canonical schema
6.explanation: Ageing out retires indicators from action but keeps them for history and retrospective hunting; deletion destroys that look-back. Blocking long-expired infrastructure today is exactly what expiry is meant to stop, so it is not the capability lost.

6.q: The lab matcher is rerun with `AS_OF = date(2026, 11, 15)`. The line for `203.0.113.66` changes from `MATCH ... hits= 9` to `EXPIRED ... hits= 9`. How should the analyst interpret this?
options: The nine events are no longer evidence of spraying, so the incident record for 3 November should now be closed as resolved
The ISAC has withdrawn the indicator, so the address was probably never involved in password spraying
The hit count is now unreliable, because expired indicators are matched against a different set of events
The address should no longer drive alerts or blocks, but the 3 November events still support the spraying case
6.explanation: Expiry describes an indicator's future usefulness, not the truth of the past: the same nine events still show eight failures and a success for gopal. Closing the case would wrongly let expiry rewrite evidence; nothing indicates the ISAC withdrew anything, the date simply passed 10 November.

6.q: In the lab output, the vendor's SHA-256 indicator has the highest confidence in the feed (90) but reports `no match`. What does this line tell the analyst?
options: Nothing about whether the file was present, because the dataset contains no file hashes to match against
The malicious document never reached the organisation, since a confidence of 90 makes a missed match unlikely
The vendor's indicator is probably wrong, because high-confidence indicators normally match at least once
The hash has expired, because the matcher reports `no match` for indicators past their validity
6.explanation: The matcher cannot match hashes because the telemetry never collected them, so the result is silent about presence. Expired indicators are reported as `EXPIRED`, not `no match`, and confidence says nothing about whether your telemetry could see the field.

6.q: The lab kit matches a domain indicator against proxy URLs using the pattern `%://<domain>/%`. For the indicator `evil.example`, which statement about this matcher is correct?
options: It matches `http://notevil.example/x`, because the domain text appears inside the host name
It matches `https://evil.example/login` but misses `https://cdn.evil.example/a`, so subdomains go undetected
It matches `http://site.example/evil.example/`, because the domain appears between two slashes in the URL path
It matches `https://cdn.evil.example/a`, because any host ending in the indicator satisfies the pattern
6.explanation: Requiring `://` before and `/` after the domain stops look-alike hosts and path mentions from matching, but it also means a subdomain such as `cdn.evil.example` is not matched; a production matcher would extract and compare host names and parent domains. `notevil.example` fails because `://` must come directly before the indicator.

6.q: One feed provides the SHA-1 of a malicious document and another provides its SHA-256. How should normalisation and deduplication treat these two values?
options: Merge them into one indicator record, because both hashes identify exactly the same malicious file
Keep only the SHA-256, because SHA-1 values are converted to SHA-256 during normalisation
Lower-case both and store each under its own algorithm type, never comparing one with the other
Truncate both to the same length so that they can be compared by their common prefix
6.explanation: Hashes are normalised to lower-case hexadecimal with the algorithm recorded as the type, and values of different algorithms are never compared or merged as equal. A SHA-1 cannot be converted into a SHA-256; the file would have to be rehashed.

6.q: An analyst wants to submit indicators from a TLP:AMBER ISAC feed to a public online sandbox to gather extra context. What is the main problem?
options: Public sandboxes only accept file hashes, so the network indicators would be rejected
The sandbox would lower the indicators' confidence, which would change their scores in the platform
TLP:AMBER indicators may only be shared after their `valid_until` date has passed
Sending them to a public service may breach the community's sharing terms and alert the adversary
6.explanation: TLP restricts onward sharing; pushing AMBER material into public or third-party services can breach the terms, cost the membership and tip off the adversary. TLP restrictions do not lapse when an indicator expires.

6.q: At renewal time, overlap analysis after normalisation shows that 85% of a paid commercial feed's indicators are already present in the SOC's free feeds. Which evaluation criterion does this measure, and what does it suggest?
options: Uniqueness: most of the paid feed duplicates data already held, so its value must come from curation and context
Timeliness: the paid feed is slower than the free feeds, so it should be replaced by them immediately at renewal time
Accuracy: the overlapping indicators are probably false positives, so the feed should be cancelled
Ingestibility: the overlap shows the vendor's schema is unstable and causes repeated parsing errors
6.explanation: Overlap after normalisation measures uniqueness; feeds copy each other, so a paid feed must justify itself through what it adds, such as context, confidence and expiry. Overlap says nothing about which feed saw indicators first, so it does not measure timeliness.

6.q: An open feed generated automatically from honeypots lists thousands of addresses with a category but no confidence and no first-seen date. What use of its entries fits the lesson?
options: Load them into the firewall blocklist, because honeypot observations are direct evidence of malicious intent
Treat them as leads for enrichment and hunting rather than as grounds for blocking
Discard the feed, because indicators without stated confidence cannot be stored in a threat platform
Assign every entry a confidence of 100, because honeypots only receive malicious traffic
6.explanation: Open feeds are cheap and broad but thin: an entry means the address did something classified as bad at some point, and may since have been reassigned. That makes it a lead, not a blocking decision. Discarding it outright wastes its breadth and speed.

6.q: Overnight, a community feed doubles in size and 30% of its new entries match the SOC's allowlist of shared cloud and DNS infrastructure. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Raise the confidence of the feed's other entries, because the producer is clearly increasing coverage
Remove the matching entries from the allowlist so that the new indicators can take effect
Treat it as possible poisoning or a producer error, hold the feed from action and investigate
Accept the update, since the allowlist will stop those entries and the rest can go to blocking
6.explanation: Sudden changes in feed size or in the share of entries hitting the allowlist are signals that the feed path itself may be compromised or broken; feeds are part of the attack surface. Relying on the allowlist alone would let the rest of a suspect update reach blocking unchecked.

6.q: A scoring model multiplies the producer's confidence, the SOC's own rating of the source's reliability, and a recency factor. Why use all three rather than the producer's confidence alone?
options: Producer confidence is always overstated, so the other two factors exist only to reduce it
Recency and reliability are already contained in STIX `confidence`, so the model avoids missing values
Multiplying three factors guarantees that no indicator from an ISAC can fall below the detection threshold
The producer's view, your trust in that producer, and the indicator's age each change independently
6.explanation: Confidence is the producer's judgement; source reliability is your own assessment from Lesson 2; recency falls daily as the indicator approaches and passes its validity. Each can change without the others, so combining them keeps the score explainable. STIX confidence does not encode your view of the source or the passage of time.

6.q: The SOC confirms an incident and extracts the attacker's domains and hashes. Where and how should this internal intelligence be recorded?
options: In the same platform and fields as external feeds, so it is matched, aged and shared in the same way
Only in the incident ticket, because internal indicators are too narrow to be worth matching again
In a separate spreadsheet with no expiry, because internally proven indicators never become stale
Directly in the firewall blocklist, because internal intelligence does not need allowlist checks
6.explanation: Internal intelligence is highly relevant but narrow, and it is only useful if it goes through the same matching, ageing and sharing process as external feeds. Proven indicators still age, since infrastructure is abandoned and reassigned, so a no-expiry spreadsheet is wrong.

6.q: A SIEM alert reads "Threat intel match: malicious IP (confidence 75)" on a user's outbound connection. Strictly, what has the match itself established?
options: That the user's workstation is communicating with an attacker's command-and-control server
That a value in your logs equals a value another party reported in connection with past activity
That the producer has confirmed the address is still malicious at the time of the user's connection
That the same threat actor named in the feed is now targeting the organisation
6.explanation: A match only shows equality between your log value and someone else's earlier observation; maliciousness, compromise and actor identity are inferences the analyst must support with local evidence. The producer's confidence refers to its own past observation, not to your connection today.

6.q: A feed entry for a cloud-hosted IP address was added three years ago and has no `valid_until`. It now matches a connection from a finance workstation. How should the analyst classify the indicator?
options: Current and reliable, because an indicator without a `valid_until` never expires
Expired, because any indicator older than one year passes its validity automatically
Not formally expired, but quite possibly stale, which the analyst must judge for this match
Both expired and stale, because cloud addresses are always removed from feeds after one year
6.explanation: Expiry is a formal property based on a stated validity; with none set the indicator is not expired. Staleness is the analyst's judgement, and an old cloud address has very likely been reassigned. Treating a missing expiry as "valid forever" is the strongest distractor and the most common error.

6.q: A domain in a feed is valid until next year. Since the feed was published, the domain lapsed and was re-registered by an unrelated small business for its online shop. Which statement is correct?
options: The indicator is expired, because re-registration automatically ends its validity in the feed
The indicator is still reliable until next year, because the producer's validity period overrides later changes
The indicator is neither expired nor stale, because domain indicators are high on the Pyramid of Pain
The indicator is unexpired but stale, because the domain no longer identifies the attacker's infrastructure
6.explanation: Expiry and staleness do not always coincide: the validity date has not passed, yet the domain now belongs to someone else, so matches are likely collateral. A producer's validity window is a policy tool, not a guarantee that the infrastructure is unchanged.

6.q: A file hash cannot be reassigned to a different file. In what way does a hash indicator still lose value over time?
options: The attacker can change the file slightly, so the old hash stops matching new samples while the feed keeps it
Hash algorithms are re-keyed periodically, so old hash values no longer correspond to the same file
Endpoint tools discard hashes older than a fixed period, so old indicators can no longer be compared
The same hash begins matching legitimate files once the original malware is removed from circulation by vendors
6.explanation: Recompiling or changing a single byte produces a new hash, so the indicator simply stops matching anything new; it decays rather than becoming wrong. Hash functions are not re-keyed, and a hash does not start matching different files.

6.q: An IP indicator matches an employee's connection. Following the lesson's analytical approach, what should the analyst establish before asking what the address did?
options: The threat actor the producer associated with the address in its original report
What kind of address it is: cloud, hosting, VPN service, residential or mobile carrier
Whether the employee has administrative rights on the workstation that connected
How many other organisations in the ISAC have reported the same address during this month
6.explanation: The type of address determines how likely a collateral match is, because shared infrastructure serves many unrelated users. The named actor is attribution, which adds little to the decision and can anchor the analyst.

6.q: An indicator for a mobile carrier's public address matches a sales employee's laptop tethered to a phone. Why is this match especially likely to be collateral?
options: Mobile carrier addresses are reserved documentation ranges that cannot appear in real traffic
Feeds never include mobile carrier addresses, so the indicator must have been mistyped
Carrier-grade NAT places many subscribers behind few public addresses, so one listed address covers many users
Mobile connections are encrypted end to end, so the feed producer could not have observed the original activity
6.explanation: Carrier-grade NAT makes one public address shared by many subscribers, so a listing for one misbehaving user turns everyone behind it into potential matches. Feeds can and do include carrier addresses; the problem is sharing, not a typo.

6.q: A feed entry's context field reads "scanning (old, shared hosting)". What should this text alone tell an analyst who sees a match?
options: The producer gives two reasons to doubt the match: the observation is old and the address is shared
The match should be escalated at once, because scanning is usually the first stage of a targeted intrusion
The address belongs to the organisation's own hosting provider and should be added to the allowlist
The indicator is a sinkhole run by a researcher, so any connection to it indicates an infected host
6.explanation: The producer itself flags age and sharing, both of which make collateral matches likely; this is why context strings matter. Nothing in the text says the address belongs to your provider, and escalating on the word "scanning" ignores the warnings the entry gives.

6.q: In the lab dataset, gopal's VPN account shows a failure and then a success from `203.0.113.66` at 06:42 and 06:46, and a success from `198.51.100.104` at 13:33. Which statement correctly justifies resetting gopal's credential?
options: The 13:33 session matched an indicator in the feed, so the account was in contact with known malicious infrastructure
Both sessions matched feed indicators, so the combined confidence of 100 makes compromise certain
A successful login followed a password spray from an address under a current ISAC indicator with matching context
The 13:33 session came from an unusual address, so any later session from a new address requires a reset
6.explanation: The account is at risk because of the spray and the 06:46 success, which rule R2 detects and a current ISAC indicator supports. The 13:33 match is an expired, low-confidence, shared-hosting entry on a routine session, and confidences from different indicators are never added.

6.q: An analyst disabled gopal's account and wrote in the case: "Disabled because the user connected from malicious IP 198.51.100.104." The action was broadly appropriate. Why is the record still a problem?
options: It cites a stale collateral match instead of the spray, misleading later readers and unfairly marking the employee
It should have named the threat actor behind the spray so that the record is complete for later auditors and regulators
It reveals a TLP:CLEAR indicator, which may not be written into internal case records
It is acceptable, because the outcome was correct and case records are not reviewed afterwards
6.explanation: Doing the right thing for the wrong reason produces a case record that misleads everyone who relies on it and can follow a named employee long after the match is shown to be stale. TLP:CLEAR places no restriction on internal records, and adding unsupported attribution would make the record worse.

6.q: An analyst decides that because the lab's `198.51.100.104` line is `EXPIRED`, nothing about it needs to be looked at. According to the analyst question sequence in this lesson, what is wrong with that decision?
options: Expired matches must be re-imported with a new `valid_until` before they can be closed
Expired matches should be escalated automatically, because old infrastructure is often reused by attackers
Expired matches must first be reported to the feed producer before any further review is allowed
Expiry removes the match from automatic action, but the analyst should still review whether the events fit
6.explanation: The flow's dashed path sends an expired match from "no automatic action" to the question of whether the events fit the context; it is removed from automation, not from attention. Automatic escalation of old infrastructure would reverse the purpose of expiry.

6.q: In the lesson's question sequence for an indicator match (indicator current, shared infrastructure, events fit the context), which question is the only one that can lead to action?
options: Whether the indicator is current, because an unexpired indicator is sufficient grounds to block
Whether the infrastructure is shared, because unshared infrastructure proves the activity is malicious
Whether corroboration exists, because two feeds agreeing on a value settles the decision
Whether the events fit the context, because only it looks at your own users, hosts, time and behaviour
6.explanation: The first two questions judge the indicator and the infrastructure; only the third examines your environment, and no path reaches action without it. Agreement between feeds may be circular reporting, so it cannot settle the decision on its own.

6.q: On 3 November, which path through the question sequence does the lab match on `203.0.113.66` follow?
options: Current: no; then no automatic action, with the events reviewed and recorded as collateral
Current: yes; shared infrastructure: no; events fit the context: yes; act proportionately
Current: yes; shared infrastructure: yes; seek corroboration; events fit: no; record collateral
Current: yes; shared infrastructure: no; events fit the context: no; record collateral match
6.explanation: On 3 November the indicator is valid until 10 November, and eight failures followed by a success fit the ISAC's "password spraying against VPNs" context, so the outcome is proportionate action. The expired-and-collateral path describes `198.51.100.104`, not this address.

6.q: After the lab review, a manager writes: "The vendor hash for invoice.docm had no match, so WS-104 was not affected by the malicious document." What is the best response?
options: The conclusion is unsupported: the telemetry holds no hashes, and the logs show the download and Word spawning PowerShell
The conclusion is correct, because a vendor indicator with confidence 90 would certainly have matched if the file was there
The conclusion is correct for now, but the vendor should be asked to lower the indicator's confidence
The conclusion is unsupported, because the vendor indicator expired before the download took place
6.explanation: A match needs the adversary's use, telemetry recording the field and a matcher comparing it; the second condition fails here, while other events show divya downloading the file and Word spawning PowerShell on WS-104. The hash line reports `no match`, not `EXPIRED`, so expiry is not the reason.

6.q: A targeted attacker registers fresh domains and rents new servers for each victim. What does this imply for a SOC that relies mainly on indicator feeds?
options: Feeds will list the new infrastructure within hours, so matching will catch the intrusion slightly later
The attacker will be caught through circular reporting, because several feeds will share the new indicators quickly
The infrastructure will not be in any feed before it is used, so behaviour-based detections must cover the gap
Hash indicators will still match, because fresh infrastructure does not change the files the attacker uses
6.explanation: Infrastructure built for one victim cannot be in anyone's feed before it reaches that victim, which is why behaviour detections such as R1 (Office spawning a shell) matter: they fire without intelligence. Attackers who rotate infrastructure can just as easily change file hashes.

6.q: An address appears in the platform from an open feed, two commercial vendors, an ISAC alert and a national advisory, and its score has risen accordingly. Provenance shows every entry derives from one researcher's blog post. How should the analyst assess it?
options: As five independent confirmations, which justifies the high score and immediate blocking
As highly reliable, because a national advisory would only cite independently verified indicators
As unreliable, because indicators copied by several producers are normally deliberate disinformation
As a single observation repeated through copying, so the agreement adds no independent confirmation
6.explanation: This is circular reporting: one original observation reaching you through sources that copied it, with nobody downstream re-checking it. Copying does not make the observation false either; it simply adds no confirmation, and an advisory citing others is not independent verification.

6.q: Which combination of sources gives the strongest support that an address really is malicious?
options: Three commercial feeds that each list the address with a confidence above 80
Your own proxy logs showing suspicious behaviour and a separate organisation's incident involving it
An ISAC alert and a national advisory that both cite the same vendor's report on the address
An open feed entry and a commercial feed entry that both describe the address as a scanner
6.explanation: Agreement is strong only when the observations are independent; your own telemetry and another organisation's incident are separate views of the activity. Multiple feeds, even with high confidence, may all derive from one source, as the advisory-citing-vendor option shows.

6.q: One vendor report attributes activity to APT29, another to Cozy Bear and a third to Midnight Blizzard. What is the most careful interpretation?
options: The three reports describe three unrelated groups, because each vendor tracks a different actor
The three names are formal aliases of one group, so the reports are certain to describe exactly the same activity
The names come from vendor schemes whose boundaries may differ, so a shared name implies overlap, not identity
The disagreement shows the attribution is wrong, so all three reports should be discarded
6.explanation: Vendors name groups in their own schemes and draw boundaries differently; ATT&CK lists associated names to help translation, but that is a claim of overlap, not proof that the reports describe the same activity. Assuming either full identity or complete unrelatedness overstates the evidence.

6.q: During the spray case, a manager asks the analyst to delay containment until the responsible group has been identified. Which reply best reflects the lesson?
options: Containment does not depend on attribution: reset the credential, review the session, enforce MFA and block the current address
Attribution must come first, because the response to a named group differs fundamentally from the response to an opportunist attacker
Attribution can be inferred quickly from the address, since ISAC indicators always state the responsible actor
Containment should wait for the ISAC to publish an attribution, because acting early may alert the adversary
6.explanation: For the spray the response is the same whoever ran it, so defenders should act on behaviour and evidence. Infrastructure is rented and shared, so an address cannot reliably identify an actor, and delaying containment for attribution leaves the compromised account open.

6.q: An analyst already convinced that an incident is under way reads every indicator match as support and dismisses the `EXPIRED` flag on one of them as "probably a feed glitch". Which bias is this?
options: Availability bias, because a recent dramatic breach makes the incident seem more likely
Anchoring, because the analyst gives too little weight to the first piece of information received in the case
Circular reporting, because the analyst counts the same match several times
Confirmation bias, because evidence that fits the belief is accepted and contrary evidence explained away
6.explanation: Favouring evidence that fits an existing belief and explaining away inconsistent evidence is confirmation bias. Anchoring is over-weighting the first information received, not under-weighting it, and circular reporting is a property of sources, not a cognitive bias.

6.q: An alert's title names a well-known state-sponsored group, and the analyst frames the entire investigation around that group even after later evidence points to an ordinary password spray. Which bias does this illustrate?
options: Confirmation bias, because the analyst ignores evidence that the alert was generated incorrectly
Anchoring, because the first information received is given undue weight in later judgements
Availability bias, because the group's name is easy to remember from training material
Producer bias, because the vendor that wrote the rule wanted to attract attention to its research
6.explanation: Over-weighting the first piece of information, here the actor name in the alert title, is anchoring. Availability bias concerns events that are vivid or recent, such as a breach in the news, rather than the first information encountered in a case.

6.q: Applying Analysis of Competing Hypotheses to the `198.51.100.104` match, an analyst lists "attacker reusing old infrastructure" and "employee working from home". How does the technique decide between them?
options: By choosing the hypothesis with the most evidence consistent with it, since the bare match fits both
By choosing the hypothesis favoured by the feed's context string, since the producer saw the activity
By looking for evidence inconsistent with each: timing, country and normal pattern contradict only the attacker hypothesis
By choosing the more severe hypothesis, since a SOC should always assume the worst case until it is proven otherwise by evidence
6.explanation: ACH focuses on disconfirming evidence: both hypotheses fit the bare match, but the session timing, the Indian country field, the user's usual behaviour and the absence of other suspicious activity are inconsistent only with the attacker explanation. Counting consistent evidence is exactly the habit ACH is designed to correct.

6.q: What does a key assumptions check ask an analyst to do?
options: Write down what the conclusion assumes, such as "the feed entry is still accurate", and ask what follows if it is false
Confirm that every indicator in the case has a stated confidence and `valid_until` before closing it
Check that the SIEM's assumptions about time zones and field mappings match those used by the feed producer for each entry
Ask a second analyst to repeat the investigation independently and compare the two conclusions
6.explanation: The technique makes hidden assumptions explicit and tests the conclusion against each one being wrong. Peer review is valuable but is a different practice, and checking indicator fields is part of feed management rather than of examining assumptions.

6.q: A board member asks whether subscribing to the sector ISAC feed will tell the organisation if it has been compromised. Which answer is accurate?
options: Yes, because a clean ISAC match report confirms that no known threat has reached the organisation
Yes, provided the feed is STIX/TAXII, since STIX indicators include the victim's compromise status
No, because ISAC feeds carry only strategic reports and never contain matchable indicators
No; it says what others saw and what to hunt for, but only our own evidence shows what happened to us
6.explanation: Intelligence supplies others' observations, context, confidence and values worth hunting; whether you are compromised, and what your users were doing, can only be answered from your own telemetry. A clean match report is not proof of absence, and ISAC feeds do carry indicators, as the lab feed shows.

6.q: Which judgement about the lab case is written the way the lesson recommends?
options: The spray and the WS-104 phishing were carried out by the same advanced actor, as the timing proves
Moderate confidence that the spray and the WS-104 phishing are the same actor: same morning, but no shared infrastructure
High confidence of attribution to a known threat group, since the ISAC indicators were involved in both incidents that morning
The 198.51.100.104 match is probably fine, and the spray is probably bad, based on the feed results
6.explanation: A good judgement uses a defined confidence level, states the reasons in the same sentence and separates what was observed from what is inferred. Claiming timing "proves" the same actor overstates the evidence, and the lab evidence supports no attribution at all.

6.q: To feed the next feed review with evidence about intelligence limitations, which measurement does the lesson recommend tracking?
options: The total number of indicators each feed delivers per month, as a measure of coverage
The number of distinct threat actors named across all feeds during the review period
The share of intelligence matches closed as collateral, broken down by feed and by indicator type
The average confidence value of each feed's indicators, as a measure of the producer's accuracy
6.explanation: Collateral-match share by feed and type shows which sources and indicator types produce false accusations and fatigue, which is what a review needs to decide. Raw volume and the producer's own confidence values describe the feed, not how it performs against your telemetry.

6.q: A managed security service provider receives an indicator from an ISAC marked TLP:AMBER+STRICT. One of its clients is in the same sector and would benefit from blocking it. What does the label allow?
options: Passing it to the client on a need-to-know basis, because AMBER labels always include clients
Using it inside the provider's own organisation only; the client cannot be told without the ISAC's permission
Passing it to the client provided the indicator is re-labelled TLP:AMBER before forwarding
Passing it to any sector peer, because STRICT only forbids publication on public channels
6.explanation: AMBER+STRICT restricts sharing to the recipient's own organisation; it is plain TLP:AMBER that extends to clients. A recipient cannot re-label the item itself, because only the source sets or changes the label, so the provider must ask the ISAC.

6.q: An analyst wants a second opinion on a suspicious file received from a peer group at TLP:GREEN and uploads it to a public online sandbox whose submissions are visible to its users. How should this be assessed?
options: Acceptable, because TLP:GREEN permits sharing with the wider cyber defence community
Acceptable, because the sandbox is a security tool and its users are defenders
A breach of the label, because GREEN excludes publicly accessible channels whatever the motive
A breach only if the file contains personal data; otherwise GREEN allows the upload
6.explanation: TLP:GREEN allows community sharing but explicitly not via public channels, and a public sandbox that shares submissions is one. The 'community' distractor is the strongest, but a public service open to anyone is not the vetted community the label means.

6.q: A case summary contains twelve TLP:GREEN indicators, three first-party indicators and one quoted TLP:AMBER domain. Without asking any source, what label must the summary as a whole carry?
options: TLP:AMBER, because a combined product takes the most restrictive label among its parts
TLP:GREEN, because the majority of the items are GREEN or first-party
TLP:GREEN with the AMBER domain marked inline, because labels apply per item
TLP:AMBER+STRICT, because mixing labels requires the next stricter level
6.explanation: The strictest label inside a product governs the whole product, so one AMBER item makes the summary AMBER. Inline marking does not help a GREEN release, because the GREEN audience may not receive the AMBER item at all; removing it is what would allow GREEN.

6.q: A TLP:AMBER report from a partner is eight months old and the campaign it describes appears to be over. A colleague proposes publishing its indicators in a public blog post. What is the correct course?
options: Publish, because TLP restrictions lapse once the information is no longer operationally sensitive
Publish after removing the partner's name, because anonymised AMBER content becomes CLEAR
Re-label it TLP:GREEN first, then publish it once the community has had time to act
Ask the partner in writing for permission to widen the label, and publish only if it agrees
6.explanation: Age never changes a TLP label; only the source can widen it, and a short written request with the reason is the normal route. Removing the partner's name does not change the label either, because the restriction attaches to the information, not to the attribution.

6.q: A list of suspicious domains arrives by email from a contact at a vendor, with no TLP label and no statement of terms. How should the SOC treat it?
options: As TLP:CLEAR, because TLP 2.0 defines unlabelled content as unrestricted
As TLP:GREEN by default, because that is the community default in TLP 2.0
According to the context and agreement it came under, and ask the sender how it may be shared
As TLP:RED, because unlabelled information must always be treated as the most restrictive level
6.explanation: A missing label is not permission: the recipient should treat the item according to the relationship and any agreement in place and ask the sender. Defaulting to RED is a plausible distractor, but the lesson's rule is to use context and ask, not to apply any fixed label automatically.

6.q: A MISP event is tagged tlp:red from the TLP taxonomy, but its distribution setting is 'All communities'. What will happen when the instance synchronises?
options: The event is shared according to the distribution setting, so the RED tag will not stop it spreading
MISP blocks synchronisation, because the TLP tag always overrides the distribution setting on every event
The event is shared only with the named recipients listed in the RED tag
MISP downgrades the tag to tlp:clear to match the distribution setting
6.explanation: In MISP the TLP tag is a taxonomy label for humans, while the distribution setting controls synchronisation, so the event goes everywhere the distribution allows. The two settings must be made to agree by the person publishing; the platform does not enforce the tag.

6.q: A manager asks whether marking a PDF TLP:RED will stop a recipient from forwarding it. Which answer is accurate?
options: Yes, because TLP-aware mail gateways refuse to forward RED documents
No; TLP is a human-readable promise, so compliance rests on recipients and community sanctions
Yes, provided the label is written in the subject line as well as in the header of every page of the document
No, because TLP labels are only meaningful inside a sharing platform such as MISP
6.explanation: TLP does not encrypt or restrict anything technically; it states the source's expectations, and enforcement rests on recipients and on the community excluding members who break it. Labels are meant for emails and documents as much as platforms, so the MISP-only distractor is wrong.

6.q: To be safe, a SOC labels every outbound report TLP:RED, including routine phishing indicators meant for sector peers. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Peers will act on the indicators more quickly, because RED signals urgency
Nothing changes, because recipients may use RED information to block threats across their community
The reports become more trusted, because RED shows the source has verified them
Recipients cannot act on them widely, so they either ignore the reports or quietly break the label
6.explanation: Over-labelling is a failure in its own right: RED limits use to named recipients, so the information cannot reach those who must act, which pushes recipients to ignore it or breach it. The guidance is to choose the least restrictive label that keeps the risk acceptable.

6.q: A threat report is TLP:GREEN for sharing purposes but is also classified 'Confidential' under the analyst's company policy, which forbids sending it outside the company. May the analyst send it to a peer at another organisation?
options: No; TLP does not replace internal classification, and the stricter of the two rules applies
Yes, because TLP is the external sharing standard and takes precedence over internal policy
Yes, provided the peer belongs to the same ISAC and the label is kept on the document
Only after re-labelling it TLP:AMBER, which reconciles the two schemes
6.explanation: TLP is not a classification scheme and does not override internal classification, contracts or privilege; the stricter rule governs what the analyst may do. Re-labelling does not help, because the internal policy forbids any external release.

6.q: A TLP:AMBER advisory adds the line 'for incident response staff only'. A SOC manager wants to circulate it to the whole IT department on a need-to-know basis. What applies?
options: The manager may circulate it, because AMBER already permits need-to-know sharing across the organisation
The added limit is advisory only and can be ignored if the IT staff need the information
The added limit must be respected alongside the label, so circulation is restricted to incident responders
The added limit makes the advisory TLP:RED, so only the named recipient may read it
6.explanation: TLP 2.0 lets a source state additional limits, and recipients must honour them in addition to the label. The extra limit narrows the audience inside AMBER; it does not convert the item into RED.

6.q: An internal wiki page from 2021 lists indicators marked TLP:WHITE. Under TLP 2.0, how should a recipient treat that marking today?
options: As TLP:GREEN, because TLP 2.0 withdrew WHITE and moved its content to community-only sharing
As TLP:CLEAR, because TLP 2.0 renamed WHITE to CLEAR with the same unrestricted meaning
As unlabelled, because version 1.0 labels have no meaning under version 2.0
As TLP:AMBER, because legacy labels must be handled at the next more restrictive level
6.explanation: TLP 2.0 renamed TLP:WHITE to TLP:CLEAR; the meaning (disclosure not limited, subject to copyright) is unchanged. The version change added AMBER+STRICT and clarified wording, it did not invalidate or tighten old WHITE markings.

6.q: A SOC consumes three community feeds but never reports anything back. Its manager asks what contribution would add most value at the lowest cost. Which is best?
options: Re-publishing the commercial feed it buys, so the community receives more indicators
Bulk-exporting every indicator from its SIEM alerts each week without vetting them
Publishing full incident reports, including victim details, so peers can see the whole picture
Sending sightings and false-positive reports back to the sources whose indicators it uses
6.explanation: Sightings and false-positive reports are the cheapest and most valued contribution: they corroborate or clean the community's intelligence. Bulk unvetted dumps trade quality for volume, re-publishing a commercial feed usually breaches its licence, and victim details should be stripped.

6.q: A source listed a domain with moderate confidence. Two other ISAC members each report, independently, that the domain was seen beaconing from one of their hosts. Why does this matter to the source?
options: It lets the source upgrade the label from TLP:AMBER to TLP:GREEN automatically
It proves the attribution to a named threat actor that the source suspected
Independent corroboration is what justifies raising the confidence in the indicator
It obliges the source to report the domain to CERT-In within six hours
6.explanation: Confidence rises when independent sources corroborate a claim, and sightings are exactly that evidence. Corroboration of the indicator does not on its own prove actor attribution, and labels change only by the source's decision, not automatically.

6.q: At 10:00 a SOC in an organisation covered by the CERT-In directions of April 2022 notices unauthorised access to a server. By 14:00 the scope is still unclear. What should the team do about reporting?
options: Submit an initial report with what is known before 16:00 and send updates as the investigation proceeds
Wait until scope is confirmed, because an incomplete report would mislead CERT-In
Report only once the root cause is known, because the six-hour window starts at confirmation of the incident
Notify the sector ISAC instead, which forwards reportable incidents to CERT-In
6.explanation: The six hours run from noticing the incident, so the reportability decision is made early on incomplete information, with an initial report followed by updates. The clock does not start at confirmation, and an ISAC post is voluntary sharing, not the mandatory report.

6.q: An Indian body corporate covered by the CERT-In directions keeps its firewall logs for 90 days in a cloud region outside India. Against the directions, what is wrong?
options: Nothing, provided the logs can be handed to CERT-In within six hours of a request
Only the location; 90 days meets the requirement if the logs are moved into India
Only the duration; logs may be stored anywhere if they are kept for 180 days
Both: logs must be kept securely for a rolling 180 days and within Indian jurisdiction
6.explanation: The directions require ICT system logs to be maintained securely for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction. This setup fails on both duration and location, so each single-fix distractor leaves one breach in place.

6.q: A mandatory CERT-In report about an intrusion includes a C2 domain that a partner shared with the SOC at TLP:AMBER. What should the SOC also do?
options: Remove the domain from the report, because mandatory reports must respect inbound TLP labels
Tell the partner that its indicator was included in a mandatory report
Re-label the domain TLP:CLEAR, because reporting to a government body makes it public
Nothing further, because legal reporting duties release the SOC from the partner's label
6.explanation: A mandatory report is not a community release; the SOC is required to provide the information, but it should inform the source when the source's material is included, as good sharing agreements anticipate. Reporting does not make the item public or change its label.

6.q: In the outbound pipeline, why is 'Inherited limits' checked before 'Strip and minimise' rather than after?
options: Some content cannot be shared at all, so there is no point sanitising it before that is known
Stripping changes the TLP label, so the inherited label must be recorded before it is lost
Inherited limits are set by the approver, who must sign off before anyone edits the content
Sanitisation tools need the TLP tag on each item to decide which fields to remove
6.explanation: Checking inherited limits first can end the process or narrow the audience, so it avoids wasted sanitisation of content that may not leave at all. Stripping does not change any label itself; the outbound label is chosen afterwards from what remains.

6.q: A draft community note would be TLP:AMBER because it includes one partner's AMBER domain; everything else is first-party. The SOC wants the widest possible audience now. Which approach follows the pipeline?
options: Label it TLP:GREEN and add a line asking recipients not to forward the AMBER domain
Send it at TLP:AMBER to the whole sector, because AMBER permits sharing with clients
Remove the AMBER domain, release the rest at GREEN, and ask the partner separately for permission
Label it TLP:AMBER+STRICT so that the AMBER domain is protected inside a GREEN release
6.explanation: The label depends on what remains after stripping, so removing the restricted item allows a GREEN release while a separate request seeks permission. A GREEN note cannot carry AMBER material with a 'do not forward' line, and AMBER does not cover sector peers.

6.q: Which item in a draft peer warning about a phishing campaign should be removed or generalised before release?
options: The SHA-256 hash of the malicious attachment
The sender address pattern used by the lure emails, including the look-alike domain they came from
The ATT&CK technique ID for the initial access method
A file path showing where the attachment was saved, which contains the user's profile name
6.explanation: Recipients need attacker-side facts such as hashes, sender patterns and techniques; a file path containing a user profile name is victim-side detail and identifies a staff member. The hash is the most tempting distractor, but it describes the malicious file, not the victim.

6.q: A password spray came from a residential IP address that is probably a compromised home router. How should it appear in a shared note?
options: As an attacker IP with long validity, because spray sources are valuable blocklist entries
As an 'observed source' with a short validity, recognising it may belong to an innocent person
Omitted entirely, because any IP address is personal data and may never be shared
As the attacker's home address, so that peers can report it to law enforcement
6.explanation: Attacker-side data can still be personal data and can belong to a victim of compromise, so the lesson advises describing it as an observed source with short validity. Omitting all IPs goes too far; observation-based wording keeps the defensive value while avoiding accusation.

6.q: A SOC wants to share a phishing email sample with its ISAC. The email greets the recipient by first name and quotes a real customer's loan account number. What should happen before it is shared?
options: Nothing, because the content was written by the attacker and is therefore attacker-side data
Only the recipient's name needs removing; customer data inside a lure is the attacker's responsibility
Both the recipient's name and the customer's details must be redacted, keeping the lure's structure
The sample must not be shared in any form, because lures always contain personal data
6.explanation: Lures often carry victims' personal data, and under the DPDP Act's purpose limitation peers need the lure's theme and structure, not the names or account numbers in it. Treating attacker-written text as automatically safe is the strongest distractor; refusing to share at all discards useful attacker-side detail.

6.q: A SOC's commercial feed licence allows use for its own defence but forbids redistribution. Several of the vendor's indicators fired during an incident. What can the SOC put in its community note?
options: Its own observations of the activity, naming the vendor as the source only if the licence permits
The vendor's indicators unchanged, because indicators are facts and cannot be licensed
The vendor's indicators, provided the note is labelled TLP:AMBER rather than GREEN
Nothing about the incident, because any mention of the activity would breach the licence
6.explanation: Re-publishing a vendor's indicators, even unchanged, can breach a no-redistribution licence, and a TLP label does not change licence terms. The SOC can share its own sightings and first-party observations, which are its own information.

6.q: A draft note removes the victim's name but says: 'a microfinance lender in Pune, attacked 3 November with a lure quoting its branch manager's loan scheme'. What is the problem?
options: None; removing the organisation's name is sufficient anonymisation
The combination of sector, city, date and lure details can still identify the victim
The note should include the company name, because peers need it to verify the report
The date must be removed, but sector and city are always safe to include
6.explanation: Anonymisation is more than deleting a name: combinations of sector, location, date and lure content can identify a victim who has not agreed to be named. No single field is always safe; it is the combination that must be assessed.

6.q: A legitimate small-business website was compromised and used to host a lure. How should a SOC describe it in a shared note?
options: As a malicious site operated by the attacker, so peers block it permanently
By naming the business as complicit, so that peers pressure it to clean up
Not at all, because compromised sites cannot be included in any shared intelligence without the owner's consent
By the observation, for example that it served the lure on a stated date, without accusing the owner
6.explanation: Naming a victim of compromise as malicious causes harm and legal risk; the lesson advises describing observations, not accusations. The URL remains useful attacker-side intelligence, so excluding it altogether discards value.

6.q: An MSSP analyst wants to warn client B using details from client A's incident, including the names and phone numbers of client A's affected staff. Which response is correct?
options: It needs client A's permission or full de-identification, and the personal data must not be passed on
It is allowed, because the MSSP holds the data lawfully under its contract with client A
It is allowed if labelled TLP:AMBER+STRICT, because client B then cannot share it further
It is allowed if client B signs a non-disclosure agreement with the MSSP first
6.explanation: Client A's incident details belong to client A, and disclosing personal information obtained under a service contract without consent can be an offence under section 72A of the IT Act 2000. Labels or an NDA with client B do not supply client A's or the individuals' consent.

6.q: ioc_match.py matches domain indicators against the url field with the pattern %://value/%. A proxy event has the URL https://ads.example/track?ref=cdn-telemetry-sync.example. Will it count as a hit for that feed domain?
options: Yes, because the domain string appears somewhere in the URL
No, because the pattern only matches requests whose host is the domain itself
Yes, because LIKE matching ignores the scheme and path separators
No, because ioc_match.py matches domains against the src_ip field instead
6.explanation: The pattern requires '://' immediately before the domain and '/' after it, so only requests to that host count; a mention in a query string does not. That design avoids false sightings from referrers and tracking parameters, which is why 'appears anywhere' is wrong.

6.q: The vendor's SHA-256 indicator shows 'no match' with zero hits in ioc_match.py. How should this result be recorded?
options: As clean: the file was not present on any Banyan host
As a false positive to report back to the vendor
As no data: the dataset has no file-hash field, so the indicator could not be tested
As expired, because indicators with no hits are retired from the feed
