6.explanation: The Banyan events contain no hash field, so a hash indicator cannot match whatever the truth; 'no match' here is a telemetry gap, not a clean result. Reporting a false positive would be wrong because nothing was ever tested.

6.q: The beacon domain shows 18 hits. Grouping the raw events by host and user returns a single row: WS-104, divya, 18. Why does this grouping matter for the sighting report?
options: It shows the activity is one infected host, which tells the source more than a raw hit count
It proves the user deliberately contacted the domain, which must be stated in the report
It means the hits are duplicates and the true sighting count is one
It shows the feed's confidence of 85 should be lowered because only one host was affected
6.explanation: Verifying a match in the raw events turns '18 hits' into 'one workstation over about 85 minutes', which is the useful fact for scope and for the source. The 18 events are separate beacon requests, not duplicates, and one host does not undermine the indicator.

6.q: intel_grade.py grades banyan-payroll-update.example B3 MEDIUM, yet the raw events show the .docm download at 06:12:00Z and WINWORD spawning PowerShell (rule R1) on the same host at 06:14:00Z. What is the correct analyst action?
options: Edit grade() so that any R1 hit on the same host upgrades a domain to credibility 1
Leave B3 unchanged, because only the script's output counts as evidence
Downgrade it to B6, because the script could not connect the domain to a rule
Record a manual upgrade to B2 with the host-and-time reasoning, leaving the script unchanged
6.explanation: R1's output names the host and time but not the URL, so the script cannot see the link; the analyst's inference supports 'probably true' (2) and is recorded as an override with its reason. Editing the script to force a higher number hides the judgement instead of documenting it.

6.q: The feed gives 203.0.113.66 a confidence of only 60, but intel_grade.py grades it B1 HIGH. What explains the difference?
options: The script multiplies the feed confidence by the number of sightings
ISAC-A is rated A for reliability, which overrides the feed's number
Rule R2 independently detected the spray from that address, which local evidence treats as confirmation
The address is labelled TLP:GREEN, and GREEN items automatically receive a higher grade than AMBER items
6.explanation: Credibility 1 is assigned when the value is sighted and a behavioural rule that knows nothing about the feed also names it, so local corroboration raises your confidence above the source's. ISAC-A is rated B, not A, and TLP has no bearing on the grade.

6.q: On 16 November the ageing line shows 203.0.113.66 as EXPIRED (valid until 10 November), although it is graded B1 HIGH. What decision does the lab record?
options: Retire it from blocking and alerting, keep it for retrospective searches and the case record
Keep blocking it, because a HIGH grade outweighs the source's validity estimate
Delete it from all systems, because expired indicators must not be retained
Extend its validity by 30 days, because Banyan's own rule confirmed it
6.explanation: Grade and validity are separate questions: HIGH says the address was attacker infrastructure, expiry says it may have changed hands. Deleting it would lose history for retrospective searches, and only the source can extend the validity of its own indicator.

6.q: A new minisiem rule fires next week on behaviour involving an indicator from the open feed. Which part of that indicator's grade should change as a result?
options: The reliability letter, because the open feed has now been proven right
The credibility digit, because the evidence for this particular claim has changed
Both the letter and the digit, because grades are recalculated together
Neither, because grades are fixed once recorded in the case
6.explanation: Credibility is a property of the claim and should move with the evidence; reliability is a property of the source and changes only as its track record changes over time. One correct item does not re-rate a whole source.

6.q: The expired open-feed address 198.51.100.104 matches one successful VPN logon for gopal at 13:33Z. What does the lab conclude?
options: The session is malicious, because the address appears in a threat feed
The session is legitimate, because the indicator expired before the incident
The indicator should be re-activated, because it matched during the incident
The indicator says nothing reliable; the session is a case question for the user and VPN logs
6.explanation: An expired, low-confidence 'scanning' indicator cannot judge a single successful logon either way, so neither 'malicious' nor 'legitimate' follows from it. Because gopal's account was sprayed that morning, the session must be checked directly with the user and the VPN logs.

6.q: Using the lab's grade() logic, an indicator from the open feed (reliability C) is sighted, a correlation rule names it, and it is still valid. What verdict does the script print?
options: C1 -> MEDIUM
C1 -> HIGH
C3 -> MEDIUM
C1 -> UNGRADED (keep feed score)
6.explanation: Sighting plus a rule hit gives credibility 1, but HIGH requires reliability A or B; a C source with credibility 1-3 falls into the MEDIUM branch. C3 would apply only if no rule named the value.

6.q: The hash indicator is graded B6 UNGRADED (keep feed score). Why does the script keep the vendor's confidence of 90 rather than assign its own verdict?
options: Because a reliability of B always defers to the source's number
Because the vendor's TLP:AMBER label forbids local re-grading
Because with no hash telemetry the claim cannot be judged locally, so any grade would be false precision
Because the hash indicator is still valid for another 76 days, which locks the vendor's original score in place
6.explanation: Credibility 6 means 'cannot be judged': no local evidence exists either way, so the honest result is to keep the source's score and fix the telemetry gap. Validity and TLP are separate fields that have nothing to do with the grade.

6.q: banyan-payroll-update.example is valid for 14 more days on 16 November, but the domain may still be live when it expires. What may the Banyan SOC do?
options: Nothing; validity periods are fixed when an indicator enters the feed
Extend the validity itself, because the indicator is Banyan's own first-party intelligence
Ask ISAC-A to extend it, because ISAC-A shared the indicator with Banyan
Mark it TLP:CLEAR so other feeds can extend its validity
6.explanation: The look-alike domain's source is 'internal', so Banyan is the source and sets its validity; it can extend it after re-checking that the domain is live. ISAC-A is the source of other indicators, not this one, and TLP has nothing to do with validity.

6.q: The incident shows event 4720 creating the local account svc_update, followed by 4732 adding it to Administrators. How useful is the name svc_update as an indicator for peers?
options: A strong blocking indicator, because account names like this are unique to one threat actor and never reused
Useless, because account names can never be shared as intelligence
Useful only if paired with the internal host name where it was created
Weak on its own, since attackers pick routine-looking names, but a fair hunting lead in peers' 4720 events
6.explanation: Attackers choose names that blend in, so the name alone is weak evidence, yet peers can search their own account-creation events for it. Adding the internal host name would leak victim-side data without improving the peers' hunt.

6.q: The lab gives files-share-drop.example a 30-day validity but gives the account name svc_update no expiry. What reasoning justifies the difference?
options: Domains always expire after 30 days by registry rules, while account names are permanent
The domain is AMBER and the account name is GREEN, and GREEN items do not expire
The domain is live infrastructure that can change hands; the name describes past behaviour as a hunting lead
The domain was seen once, whereas the account name was seen in two events
6.explanation: Validity reflects how long an indicator stays useful to act on: infrastructure decays and must be re-checked, while a name describing what the attacker did remains a valid search term. Both are first-party items, and registry rules or hit counts are not the reason.

6.q: An early version of scrub_check.py compared each word to the user list without stripping trailing characters. Which line of the draft would it have missed?
options: '...then success for gopal.' because the word read as 'gopal.' does not equal 'gopal'
'...opened by divya on WS-104' because user names before a host name are skipped
'Beacon every 300 s from 10.40.0.23' because IP addresses are not words
'svc_update created and added to Administrators' because underscores split the word
6.explanation: The regex keeps full stops inside a word, so a name ending a sentence becomes 'gopal.' and fails an exact comparison; rstrip('.-') fixes this. The 10.x address is caught by a separate pattern, and svc_update is not in the user list at all.

6.q: scrub_check.py prints '0 finding(s) in note_green.txt - clear to review for release'. What does that result mean?
options: The note is approved for release to sector peers
The note contains no TLP:AMBER material
The note contains no personal data of any kind
The checker found none of its patterns; a person must still read and approve the note
6.explanation: The checker only matches dataset user names, WS- host names and 10.x addresses; it knows nothing of TLP labels or other personal data. Zero findings removes one blocker, but approval still requires a human review.

6.q: After scrub_check.py flagged four identifiers in note_draft.txt, which further problem in the draft could only a human reviewer catch?
options: The draft named the internal address 10.40.0.23 in the beacon line, which reveals Banyan's network layout
The draft included cdn-telemetry-sync.example, received at TLP:AMBER, in a TLP:GREEN note
The draft named the workstation WS-104 on the second line
The draft named the user gopal at the end of the spray line
6.explanation: The checker has no notion of inherited labels, so the AMBER domain passed unnoticed; the other three options are exactly the findings the tool reported. The lesson also notes the draft wrongly offered the expired spray address as a live indicator.

6.q: svc_update appears in note_green.txt and the checker does not flag it. Why is it acceptable to share?
options: It names an account the attacker created, so it is attacker-side data, not a staff member's identity
It passed the checker, and anything that passes the checker is safe
Service accounts are excluded from personal data under the DPDP Act
It was created after the CISO's approval of the note, so it is automatically covered by the release decision
6.explanation: The account belongs to the intrusion, not to a person at Banyan, so it is attacker-side. Passing the checker is not the reason: the checker would also miss names absent from the dataset, which is why human judgement decides.

6.q: Why is TLP:GREEN the correct label for the final peer note in the lab?
options: Because the CISO approved it, and every note the CISO approves is released to sector peers at GREEN
Because the scrub check reported zero findings, which permits GREEN
Because every item is first-party or arrived at GREEN, once the AMBER domain was held back
Because sector peer notes must always be GREEN under TLP 2.0
6.explanation: The outbound label follows from the most restrictive label on anything included; with the AMBER item removed, GREEN fits. Approval and a clean scrub are necessary steps, but neither sets the label.

6.q: The GREEN note still lists 203.0.113.66, which expired on 10 November. How is it presented, and why?
options: As a live block recommendation, because it was graded B1 HIGH
It is not listed; expired indicators may never appear in shared notes
As ISAC-A's indicator with ISAC-A's permission, because it arrived at AMBER
As context with its expiry stated, so peers can search historical logs rather than block it
6.explanation: An expired indicator keeps value for retrospective searches, so the note states the short life ('review after 2026-11-10') instead of recommending a block. The address arrived at GREEN, so no special permission was needed.

6.q: Which feature of note_amber.txt makes it most valuable to ISAC-A beyond simply confirming the domain?
options: It re-labels the domain TLP:GREEN so ISAC-A can publish it
It adds context the source lacked, the macro-to-PowerShell-to-beacon sequence, and asks to widen the label
It includes the infected user's name and workstation so that ISAC-A can independently verify every detail
It reports the domain to CERT-In on ISAC-A's behalf
6.explanation: A good sighting confirms with timing and volume, adds new context and explicitly requests permission to widen the label. A recipient cannot re-label the item itself, and personal data such as the user name has no place in the report.

6.q: ISAC-A refuses permission to re-share cdn-telemetry-sync.example at TLP:GREEN. What can the peer note still usefully say about the command-and-control activity?
options: The domain with its middle characters masked, which removes the AMBER restriction
The domain, provided the note credits ISAC-A as the original source
The behaviour, such as fixed-size HTTPS beacons about every 300 seconds after an Office macro, without the domain
Nothing at all, because any information Banyan observed that is linked to an AMBER indicator inherits the AMBER label
6.explanation: Banyan's own observations of the behaviour are first-party and give peers something to hunt for, while the restricted value stays out. A masked or credited domain is still the AMBER information, and the label does not extend to everything Banyan observed itself.

6.q: A real outbound note mentions a contractor whose name never appears in the dataset's user field. What will scrub_check.py do, and what does the lab recommend?
options: Miss it, since the user list comes from SELECT DISTINCT user; load identity lists and still read every note
Flag it, because the regex treats every capitalised word in the note as a possible user name and reports it
Flag it, because the checker compares words against the CMDB by default
Miss it, which is acceptable because contractors are not covered by the DPDP Act
6.explanation: The checker only knows names present in the dataset, so anyone absent from it slips through; the lab suggests loading lists from the CMDB and identity provider and reading notes yourself. Contractors are individuals and their names are personal data like any other.

6.q: A student's intel_grade.py output shows 'rules -' for cdn-telemetry-sync.example, while the lesson shows R6. What is the most likely cause?
options: The script is not in the same folder as ioc_match.py
RULES in minisiem.py was edited, or minisiem.db is stale and needs reloading
CHECK_DATES was changed, which alters which rules are evaluated
The domain expired, so the script hides its rule hits
6.explanation: Rule names come from running minisiem's RULES against the database, so a changed rule set or a stale database removes the R6 match. A folder problem would raise ModuleNotFoundError instead, and CHECK_DATES affects only the ageing line.

6.q: A teammate argues that cdn-telemetry-sync.example should go in the GREEN peer note because it is graded B1 HIGH and valid for 45 days. What is the flaw in the argument?
options: The grade is wrong; a domain seen on one host cannot be HIGH
The validity is wrong; the domain expired on 16 November
B1 indicators must be reported to CERT-In before they can be shared with peers
Grade and validity decide whether to act on it; the TLP label alone decides who may be told
6.explanation: Grade, validity and label are independent: a strong, valid indicator received at AMBER still cannot enter a GREEN release without the source's permission. The grade and validity in the argument are correct, which is what makes it tempting.

6.q: A SOC never retires indicators from its VPN blocklist, reasoning that a confirmed attacker address is always worth blocking. What risk does the lab identify?
options: Addresses change hands over time, so the list eventually blocks legitimate users
Blocklists that grow too long stop matching any new attacker addresses
Keeping expired indicators breaches the source's TLP label
Retired indicators can no longer be used for retrospective searches
6.explanation: Rented or compromised addresses are reassigned, so never-expiring entries accumulate and start blocking innocent users. Retiring from blocking while keeping the record avoids that without losing history; TLP governs sharing, not retention.

7.q: R5 log_cleared matches nothing more than Security event ID 1102, yet the lesson treats it as durable rather than brittle. What is the reason?
options: Event 1102 is rare in normal estates, so the rule rarely needs tuning
The rule is behavioural in substance, because clearing is a technique
The matched value is set by the operating system, not by the attacker
The rule runs on forwarded logs, so the attacker cannot delete the hit
7.explanation: An attacker who clears the Security log cannot make Windows record that action under a different ID, so the matched value is an operating-system fact rather than an attacker-controlled one. Rarity affects precision, not durability; what makes signatures brittle is attacker control of the value.

7.q: Dropping R6's size-spread condition and keeping only 'hits >= 10' returns three host-and-URL pairs on the Banyan data, of which only the WS-104 beacon is the intrusion. What is this variant's precision for the storyline?
options: About 0.33, because one of the three alerts is a true positive
1.0, because the variant still catches the only real beacon
About 0.67, because two of the three pairs belong to WS-103
0, because the two benign pairs outnumber the true positive
7.explanation: Precision is TP / (TP + FP) = 1 / (1 + 2), about 0.33. Catching the only beacon describes recall (1.0 here), not precision.

7.q: An engineer 'tightens' R6 by keeping the spread condition and raising the volume threshold from 10 to 20 requests. The query now returns no rows. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Precision has reached 1.0, because the rule no longer produces false positives
The new number encodes nothing about beacons and exceeds the beacon's 18 requests
The spread condition and the volume condition cancel out when combined in HAVING
The dataset is too small for any aggregation rule to return results reliably
7.explanation: The beacon made 18 requests, so a threshold of 20 removes the true pair: recall falls to zero and there are no alerts for which to have a precision. Good tightening adds a condition that discriminates the threat; this one only demands more of it.

7.q: A rule examines one million process-creation events a day, of which ten are malicious. It catches all ten and wrongly flags 0.1% of benign events. Roughly what share of its alerts are real?
options: About 99.9%, matching its accuracy on benign events
About 50%, since misses and false alarms balance out
About 10%, because ten alerts are true out of a hundred
About 1%, because roughly 1,000 benign events are flagged
7.explanation: 0.1% of 999,990 benign events is about 1,000 false positives, so precision is 10 / 1,010, about 0.01. The 99.9% figure is the true-negative rate on benign events, not the share of alerts that are real; the low base rate is what drags precision down.

7.q: In an authorised exercise, a red team copies PowerShell to a file named updater.exe and starts it from a Word macro; R1 stays silent. Which design change addresses this most directly?
options: Add updater.exe to the rule's list of child process names
Match the executable's embedded original file name, not its path
Lower the rule's severity so that more of its hits are reviewed
Replace the contains match with an ends-with match on the path
7.explanation: The image path is attacker-controlled; the embedded original file name (Sysmon's OriginalFileName) stays PowerShell.EXE after a rename, so matching on it removes the cheap evasion. Adding updater.exe only chases this one name, and the attacker can pick another.

7.q: R1's SQL tests lower(parent_image) LIKE '%winword.exe%', while the kit's Sigma version uses ParentImage|endswith '\WINWORD.EXE'. Which parent path would the SQL match but the Sigma rule would not?
options: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE
D:\Apps\Office16\WinWord.exe
C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office15\winword.exe
C:\Users\Public\Downloads\notwinword.exe
7.explanation: LIKE '%winword.exe%' is a contains match, so notwinword.exe matches; the Sigma ends-with match on '\WINWORD.EXE' requires the backslash immediately before the name. The case variants match both rules, because both normalise or ignore case.

7.q: A colleague proposes removing lower() from R1 because 'SQLite LIKE already ignores case'. Why does the lesson keep the explicit normalisation?
options: LIKE ignores case only when the field is indexed, which minisiem.db does not do
LIKE's case behaviour can be changed and other query languages differ, so intent must be explicit
Without lower(), the rule would match lowercase paths but miss the stored uppercase ones
lower() makes the query faster, because SQLite compares lowercase strings more cheaply
7.explanation: SQLite's LIKE ignores ASCII case by default, but that default can be changed and other languages (and SQLite's own = operator) are case-sensitive, so explicit normalisation survives translation. The third option describes what a case-sensitive comparison would do, not today's LIKE behaviour.

7.q: How does the lesson classify R2 vpn_spray_then_success in terms of family and logical shape?
options: An anomaly rule expressed as a single-event match on VPN failures
A signature rule expressed as an aggregation of logon event counts
A behavioural rule expressed through a threshold plus a sequence
An anomaly rule expressed through a per-user baseline of failures
7.explanation: Spraying followed by a valid logon is a behaviour; it is computed as a threshold (failures for at least five distinct users from one address) and a sequence (the success comes after them). No baseline of normal is measured, so it is not an anomaly rule.

7.q: R3 new_local_admin matches Windows events 4720 and 4732, specific IDs, yet the lesson calls it behavioural. Why?
options: It captures account creation or elevation, regardless of the name chosen
It compares the new account with a baseline of administrator accounts
It requires the two events to occur in sequence within a time window
It matches the account names that attackers commonly give new users
7.explanation: The rule captures the persistence step itself (creating or elevating a local account), which does not depend on the account name the attacker picks. It uses no baseline, and matching popular attacker account names would make it a brittle signature.

7.q: An attacker who understands R6 wants their beacon to fall outside the rule while still checking in to the same URL. Which change defeats the rule most cheaply?
options: Moving the check-in URL to a domain that is not on any intelligence feed
Adding random padding so request sizes vary by more than 50 bytes
Clearing the Security log after every check-in to remove the evidence
Starting the beacon from wscript.exe instead of from PowerShell
7.explanation: R6 fires on ten or more requests to one URL whose sizes vary by less than 50 bytes, so size jitter alone defeats it. A new domain evades a feed signature, not R6, which does not use any feed; the launching process is invisible to a proxy-based rule.

7.q: During exfiltration an attacker sends 48 MB in many requests of about 5 MB each instead of one large upload. Which kit rule is evaded, and why?
options: R4, because each request stays under its fixed 10,000,000-byte threshold
R6, because the requests are too large to count as small check-ins
R4, because its per-host baseline has learned the attacker's normal volume
R2, because the transfer no longer follows a burst of failed logons
7.explanation: R4 is a single-event match on bytes_out greater than 10,000,000, so splitting the upload into smaller requests keeps every event under it. R4 uses a fixed number, not a per-host baseline, which is why the third option is wrong.

7.q: Suppose the Banyan macro had started wscript.exe instead of PowerShell. Which statement about the storyline holds?
options: R1 still fires, because it matches any child process of WINWORD.EXE
No kit rule sees the intrusion, because the first alert never happens
Only R2 still fires, because the VPN activity is independent of the host
R1 is silent, but R6 still sees the check-ins and R5 the log clearing
7.explanation: R1 lists only powershell.exe and cmd.exe, so wscript.exe slips past it, but the later 220-byte beacon and the 08:17 log clearing are caught by R6 and R5. Layering families means one rule's evasion lands in another rule's view; R1 does not match any child.

7.q: The lesson tunes R5 for recall and accepts occasional false positives from approved maintenance. What reasoning supports that choice?
options: Log clearing is common, so analysts are used to triaging these alerts quickly
Signature rules cannot be tuned for precision, so recall is the only choice
A missed clearance means evidence vanished unseen, a rare and high-value event
Maintenance clearances are attacker-controlled, so they must be investigated
7.explanation: A false negative on R5 means an attacker removed evidence undetected, which is far costlier than an occasional maintenance alert on a rare event. Log clearing is not common where logs are forwarded, and signature rules can be tuned like any other.

7.q: A new anomaly rule flags hosts whose daily outbound destinations differ markedly from their history. Its false-positive rate is modest, but the estate is large and real intrusions are rare. What role should it most likely have?
options: Paging an analyst on every hit, since anomalies catch unknown threats
Feeding a risk score or hunting queue rather than paging anyone directly
Replacing the behavioural rules, since it does not depend on technique lists
Running only on hosts that have already produced a behavioural alert today
7.explanation: Because the threat's base rate is tiny, even a modest false-positive rate makes most hits noise, so broad anomaly rules usually contribute risk or feed hunts. Catching the unknown is their strength, but it does not justify paging on every hit, and they complement rather than replace behavioural rules.

7.q: A per-host upload baseline is measured over the month before deployment. Later it emerges that an intruder was exfiltrating small amounts throughout that month. What is the consequence for the rule?
options: The rule fires more often, because the baseline is inflated by attacker data
The rule switches to signature mode until the baseline is recalculated
The intruder's activity was learned as normal and will not stand out
Nothing, because baselines measure volume and exfiltration is not volume
7.explanation: If the attacker was present during the learning period, their activity becomes part of the baseline, so it no longer counts as a departure from normal. An inflated baseline makes the rule fire less, not more.

7.q: A rule passes design review, deploys cleanly and shows no errors, but has never fired in six months, including during a purple-team test of its technique. Which design question was most likely skipped?
options: Which legitimate look-alike produces the same pattern in this estate
Which context would make the activity more or less suspicious
Which error, a false positive or a false negative, is worse here
Whether the needed telemetry and fields are collected under those names
7.explanation: A rule written for a field that is not collected, or is parsed under another name, passes review and never fires. Skipping the look-alike question causes false positives, not total silence during a real test of the technique.

7.q: Before deployment, Banyan finds that a vendor update agent on every workstation polls one fixed URL with identical 300-byte requests every few minutes. What is the most sound response for R6?
options: Add an allowlist for known agents or a condition such as a recently first-seen destination
Raise the hits threshold until the update agent's daily request count no longer qualifies
Widen the size-spread limit so that identical requests no longer count as regular
Remove the size condition, since the agent shows that constant size is not discriminating
7.explanation: The agent is a legitimate look-alike, so the rule needs context that separates it from a beacon, such as an allowlist of known agents or a first-seen destination. Raising the hit count risks dropping real beacons (as the threshold-20 variant did) and says nothing about what makes a beacon malicious.

7.q: The Sysmon summary groups the dataset's 33 process creations: 32 are applications started by explorer.exe and one is WINWORD.EXE starting PowerShell. What should an engineer conclude before using R1 in a real estate?
options: R1 will have near-perfect precision anywhere, because Word rarely has children
The pair discriminates well here, but Word's legitimate children must be measured first
The summary proves R1 has full recall, because only one Word child exists
R1 should also match explorer.exe children, since they make up most starts
7.explanation: In this synthetic estate the parent-child pair is a near-perfect discriminator, but a real estate must first be measured for how often Word legitimately starts children. One observed Word child says nothing about recall against techniques the data does not contain.

7.q: Which proposed extra condition for R6 is the best example of tightening a rule in the way the lesson recommends?
options: Require at least 30 requests per host and URL before the rule fires
Require total bytes_out per pair to exceed the daily average for all hosts
Require that the destination was first seen in the estate recently
Require the requests to fall within the analysts' daytime working hours
7.explanation: A recently first-seen destination is a fact that tends to be true of new C2 infrastructure and rarely of long-standing update services, so it adds discriminating information. Raising the request count merely demands more of the beacon and could drop the 18-request one entirely.

7.q: An engineer loosens a behavioural rule by adding three more child processes to its match list. What is the expected effect on its two summary measures?
options: Recall tends to rise and precision tends to fall
Precision tends to rise and recall tends to fall
Both measures rise, since more techniques are covered
Neither changes until the base rate itself changes
7.explanation: Widening the condition moves more true events inside the alert boundary (recall up) but also more benign ones (precision down), which is why each addition needs a look-alike check. Both rising together is possible only if no benign activity matches the new values.

7.q: A SOC can count a rule's true and false positives from analyst verdicts, but struggles to state its recall in production. Why is recall the harder measure?
options: Recall needs the base rate, which SIEMs do not record for each rule
Recall only applies to anomaly rules, which have no fixed definition of a hit
Recall changes whenever thresholds change, so it never stays stable
Recall needs the false negatives, and missed attacks are rarely known
7.explanation: Recall is TP / (TP + FN), and false negatives are attacks that raised no alert, which the SOC usually never learns about; it is estimated through testing and feedback. Precision changes with thresholds too, so instability is not what makes recall hard.

7.q: An intruder stops the Sysmon service on a workstation before acting further. From a detection-design view, what is the most important consequence?
options: Rules that rely on process-creation telemetry go blind, so source-silence rules matter
Behavioural rules switch to Security log events automatically and keep working
Only anomaly rules are affected, because their baselines need continuous data
Nothing changes for R1, because it matches events already stored in the SIEM
7.explanation: Every rule assumes its data arrives; without Sysmon, R1 and other process-creation rules cannot fire on new activity, which is why absence rules that notice a source going quiet belong in the design. Rules do not switch data sources by themselves, and past events do not cover future actions.

7.q: Banyan plans to widen R1 so that Excel, as well as Word, counts as a suspicious parent. What should be measured first?
options: How many PowerShell versions are installed on each workstation
How often Excel legitimately starts child processes in the estate
How many proxy requests Excel sends compared with Word
How many intelligence feeds list Excel-based campaigns
7.explanation: Widening the parent list raises recall but brings in Excel's legitimate look-alikes, such as finance macros, so its own children must be measured before deployment. Proxy volumes and feed listings say nothing about the process relationship the rule relies on.

7.q: Which statement of 'the behaviour' best satisfies the first design question in the lesson?
options: Detect the invoice.docm malware delivered from the payroll lure
Detect PowerShell sessions opened by the user account on WS-104
A document editor starting a command or script interpreter
Any process that contacts banyan-payroll-update.example
7.explanation: The behaviour should be stated in terms of the technique, not a particular sample, host or domain, so that it survives changes in the lure and infrastructure. The other statements tie the rule to attacker-chosen values from one incident.

7.q: R4's fixed 10 MB threshold works on the Banyan data because no other workstation sent more than 3,999 bytes in one request. Why does the lesson warn against copying this design into a real business?
options: Real proxies log request sizes in kilobytes, so the threshold must be rescaled
Fixed thresholds cannot be written in SQL, so production SIEMs reject them
A threshold rule is a signature and therefore has narrow recall by definition
One number rarely fits every host, so a per-entity baseline is usually needed
7.explanation: Normal upload volume differs between hosts and users, so 'large' is better judged against each entity's own history over a learning period. Calling a threshold a signature misreads the family: R4 is an anomaly-style rule.

7.q: A reviewer wants a selection that matches only when CommandLine contains both ' -nop' and ' -w hidden'. The draft lists both values under CommandLine|contains. What is wrong, and what fixes it?
options: Nothing is wrong: values listed under one field must all match the same event
A list means OR, so the draft matches either value; adding |all makes it AND
contains cannot take a list, so each value needs its own separate selection
A list means AND already, so the draft is too strict and needs a 1 of condition
7.explanation: In Sigma a list of values under one field is OR, so the draft fires on either string; the all modifier (CommandLine|contains|all) requires every value. Two fields in one map are AND, but two values under one field are not.

7.q: Converted with -t splunk --without-pipeline, the log-cleared rule becomes EventID=1102. If deployed as is, what is the main risk?
options: Splunk rejects the query, because EventID is not a valid SPL field name
The query matches nothing, because Splunk stores event IDs only as text
The query is restricted to the Security log but uses the wrong severity
The query is unscoped: an event 1102 from any log or source would match
7.explanation: Without a pipeline, nothing from logsource reaches the query, so service: security is lost and any event numbered 1102 in any log matches. The query is syntactically valid SPL; the problem is what it searches, not whether it runs.

7.q: Converting the log-cleared rule with -p splunk_windows produced source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=1102. Which two changes did the pipeline make?
options: It turned service: security into a source condition and renamed EventID
It added a severity filter from level and appended the rule's tags
It converted the YAML list into IN and doubled the backslashes
It validated the condition and removed the unused falsepositives
7.explanation: The splunk_windows pipeline mapped the logsource to the Splunk source WinEventLog:Security and the generic EventID field to Splunk's EventCode. Rendering lists as IN and escaping backslashes is the backend's job, not the pipeline's.

7.q: A rule converted with a community pipeline is deployed, passes review and is green on the dashboard, but never fires, even when an administrator clears a test log. What is the most likely cause and the right check?
options: The rule's level is too low; raise it and the SIEM will start alerting
sigma check missed a condition error; re-run it with verbose output
The pipeline does not match how the data is indexed; test on a known event
The backend rejected the query silently; reinstall the Splunk backend
7.explanation: A pipeline written for someone else's indexing produces valid queries with the wrong source or field names, a silent false negative found only by searching for a known event. Level affects triage, not matching, and a condition error would have stopped conversion.

7.q: A copy of the office rule has the condition 'selection_parent and selection_childs'. What happens when it is checked and converted?
options: sigma check passes, and the converter silently drops the unknown name
sigma check reports an issue, but conversion produces a parent-only query
sigma check reports a condition error, and conversion fails with it too
sigma check reports a YAML error, because the file can no longer be parsed
7.explanation: The check reports one condition error ('selection_childs' not defined), and converting the file fails with the same message, so a broken condition cannot reach the SIEM through the converter. The YAML itself is still valid, so it is not a parse error.

7.q: A rule's technique tag passes sigma check without any InvalidATTACKTagIssue. What has that result actually established?
options: The tag is well formed and known to the ATT&CK data bundled with pySigma
The tag is the correct mapping for the behaviour the rule detects
The tag will stay valid in every future ATT&CK and pySigma release
The tag matches the tactic implied by the rule's logsource category
7.explanation: The tag validator checks format and known IDs against the ATT&CK data in the installed pySigma version; whether the tag is the right mapping is a judgement. Because the bundled data changes between releases, a clean result today is not a guarantee for future versions.

7.q: An analyst copies rk_office_spawns_shell.yml to build an Excel variant and edits only the title and detection. Why must the id also change?
options: sigma check rejects any two files in a directory with the same title
The backend uses the id as the Splunk search name and would collide
The id encodes the logsource, so a new detection needs a new UUID
Deployment and deduplication tooling would treat both as one rule
7.explanation: The id is a UUID that identifies a rule permanently, even across title changes, so tools that deploy and deduplicate rules would merge or overwrite two files sharing one. It does not encode the logsource.

7.q: Which parts of a Sigma rule actually determine the query text that a converter produces?
options: detection and level, because severity decides which events are kept
logsource and detection; the other fields travel as metadata
title, tags and detection, since tags select the backend's mapping
detection alone; logsource is documentation for human reviewers
7.explanation: logsource drives which pipeline transformations apply and detection is rendered into the condition; identity, context and triage hints do not change which events match. logsource is not mere documentation, as the splunk_windows conversion showed.

7.q: A v2 office rule adds filter_approved: CommandLine|contains '\finance\approved\' with 'and not filter_approved'. Why does the lesson call this filter a deliberate flaw?
options: contains is not allowed in filters; only endswith is valid after not
The filter makes the rule fail sigma check, so it can never be deployed
Filters cannot reference fields that the selections do not also use
Anyone starting a process can put that string in its command line
7.explanation: CommandLine is attacker-controlled, so an attacker who includes the folder string hides the alert; exceptions should key on things the attacker controls less, such as a signed script or approved host group, with an owner and expiry. The tested variant passed sigma check, so it is not a validation problem.

7.q: The Splunk output for the office rule is ParentImage="*\\WINWORD.EXE" (Image IN ("*\\powershell.exe", "*\\cmd.exe")). A reviewer flags the doubled backslashes as a converter bug. How should this be answered?
options: SPL string escaping requires them, so the query is correct
It is a bug in the backend and the query will match nothing
They come from the YAML file, which must use single backslashes
They mark the endswith modifier and replace the leading wildcard
7.explanation: Backslashes are doubled because SPL requires them to be escaped inside strings; the endswith modifier is represented by the leading * wildcard, not by the backslashes.

7.q: Running 'sigma convert -t splunk rk_office_spawns_shell.yml' with neither -p nor --without-pipeline ends in an error. What is the purpose of that refusal?
options: The Splunk backend cannot render rules with more than one selection
It forces a choice between a pipeline and explicitly using none
The rule lacks a service key, which the Splunk backend requires
It signals that the rule failed validation and must be fixed first
7.explanation: The error says a processing pipeline is required and points to 'sigma list pipelines splunk': the tool makes the operator state whether data mapping is wanted. The same rule converts fine with --without-pipeline, so it is neither a validation nor a selection-count problem.

7.q: With -p splunk_cim the office rule became Processes.parent_process_path="*\\WINWORD.EXE" (Processes.process_path IN (...)). When is this the right pipeline for Banyan's SOC?
options: Always, because CIM field names are the Splunk standard for all data
Only for Sysmon data, because CIM is a Sysmon acceleration mapping
When Banyan's process data is actually mapped to the CIM data model
Never, because data-model fields cannot be searched with wildcards
7.explanation: A pipeline describes how data is stored; splunk_cim fits only if the process events are normalised into the CIM Processes fields. On raw data indexed differently, the valid-looking query would find nothing. Sysmon acceleration is a different pipeline (splunk_sysmon_acceleration).

7.q: The office rule uses category: process_creation with product: windows, while the log-cleared rule uses product: windows with service: security. What is the main trade-off between these styles?
options: The category style is portable across sources; the service style names one log
The category style needs no pipeline; the service style always needs one
The category style is for behavioural rules; the service style for anomalies
The category style matches any product; the service style any operating system
7.explanation: process_creation can be satisfied by Sysmon event 1, an EDR process event or Security event 4688, so category rules port well; a service names a specific log and is more precise about what is meant. Both styles depend on a pipeline to become scoped queries.

7.q: A new analyst argues that because the log-cleared rule says service: security, it can never match an event from another log, whatever tool converts it. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: service only applies to Linux products, so it is ignored for Windows
Sigma ignores logsource entirely and always searches every index
The restriction applies only when the rule's level is set to high
logsource is a statement; only a pipeline turns it into a filter
7.explanation: logsource declares intent; whether the query is restricted depends on the processing pipeline, as the unscoped EventID=1102 output without one shows. It is not ignored either: with splunk_windows it became a source condition.

7.q: Image|endswith: '\cmd.exe' is used in the kit rule rather than Image|endswith: 'cmd.exe'. What does the leading backslash achieve?
options: It escapes the dot so that it matches a literal full stop
It ensures the match is a whole file name, not a suffix of one
It makes the comparison case-sensitive for Windows paths
It tells the backend to render the value as a regex
7.explanation: Requiring the path separator before the name means C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe matches but a hypothetical notcmd.exe does not. Sigma matching stays case-insensitive, and regular expressions need the re modifier.

7.q: A team translates minisiem's R1 into Sigma and finds the Sigma version fires on fewer events, though both convert and run without errors. Which explanation best fits the lesson's comparison?
options: The Sigma version is case-sensitive, so mixed-case paths are missed
Sigma drops the OR between child images when there are two selections
The SQL uses a contains match where Sigma uses a stricter ends-with match
The SQL reads Sysmon and Security logs, while Sigma reads Sysmon only
7.explanation: R1's LIKE '%...%' tests are contains matches, while the Sigma rule uses endswith on full path components, so translation changed the match semantics and therefore precision and recall. Sigma string matching is case-insensitive by default, so case is not the difference.

7.q: A draft rule has selection: Image: '\cmd.exe' with no modifier. It passes sigma check but never fires on real cmd.exe starts. Why?
options: Values without a modifier are treated as regular expressions
Plain values are case-sensitive, and paths are stored in capitals
Single-value selections need a list to be rendered by the backend
A plain value must equal the whole field, not just its final part
7.explanation: Without a modifier a string must match the entire field (ignoring case), so '\cmd.exe' never equals 'C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe'; endswith is needed. Plain values are case-insensitive by default, so capitals are not the problem.

7.q: Both kit rules carry status: experimental. What does this tell a consumer of the rules?
options: The rules are new and not yet proven in production use
The rules use syntax that sigma-cli does not yet support
The rules may only be converted without a pipeline
The rules have failed review and must not be deployed
7.explanation: status records maturity: experimental means newly written and not yet proven, unlike test or stable. Both rules pass sigma check and convert normally, so it says nothing about syntax or pipelines.

7.q: The v2 office rule converts to (ParentImage IN (...)) (Image IN (...)) NOT CommandLine="*\\finance\\approved\\*". Which reading of the last part is correct?
options: NOT comes from the filter's name prefix, and the trailing * from endswith
NOT comes from a not in the condition, and the leading * from the list
'and not filter_approved' became NOT, and contains became * on both sides
The filter became NOT only because its field is absent from the selections
7.explanation: The condition's 'and not filter_approved' is rendered as NOT, and the contains modifier becomes wildcards before and after the value. Filter names like filter_ are a readability convention; the condition, not the prefix, decides the logic.

7.q: Banyan's SOC expects to replace its SIEM within two years and wants to protect its investment in detection content. Why does Sigma help?
options: Sigma rules run directly on any SIEM, so no conversion step is needed
Rules describe what to detect, and a new backend renders them for the new SIEM
Sigma stores the SIEM's past alerts, so history migrates with the rules
Sigma replaces processing pipelines, so field names never need mapping
7.explanation: Sigma separates what to detect from how one product searches, so rules kept as code can be converted for the new platform with its backend and a pipeline matching its data. Sigma is not a SIEM and does not run queries; pipelines remain necessary for field mapping.

7.q: The office rule's falsepositives entry reads 'Legitimate macros that launch scripts (rare; document and allow-list)'. How should an analyst use it when the rule fires?
options: As the rule's severity, to decide whether the alert is high or low
As a filter the converter applies automatically to suppress macros
As proof that the alert is benign whenever a macro was involved
As the first thing to rule out: is there an approved macro here?
7.explanation: falsepositives is a triage hint telling the analyst which benign explanation to check first; it does not become query text. Exceptions must be written as named filters to affect matching, and a macro being involved is exactly what a malicious document looks like too.

7.q: A SOC keeps its Sigma rules in a shared repository. Which control best addresses the risk that a careless or malicious change creates a blind spot that looks like tuning?
options: Restricted merge rights, required review and automated check and conversion
Publishing every rule publicly so that peers can spot harmful filters
Setting every rule's status to stable so that edits need a version bump
Converting rules only without a pipeline so filters are always visible
7.explanation: The repository shapes what the SOC sees, so it should be protected like code: limited merge rights, review of diffs and automated sigma check and conversion on every change. Publishing rules tells adversaries what you match on, and a status label enforces nothing.

7.q: A rule's condition is '1 of selection_*' and it defines selection_cmd, selection_ps and filter_admin. When does it match, before any filter is applied?
options: When every selection whose name starts with selection_ matches
When exactly one of the three search identifiers matches
When at least one of selection_cmd or selection_ps matches
When selection_cmd matches, since it is the first one listed
7.explanation: '1 of selection_*' means at least one selection whose name matches the pattern, so filter_admin is not included and either selection suffices. 'all of selection_*' would require every matching selection.

7.q: An advisory includes a Sigma rule for a technique Banyan cares about. What is the sound way to adopt it?
options: Deploy it unchanged, since rules in advisories are already validated
Read it, convert it with Banyan's own pipeline and test it on Banyan data
Convert it without a pipeline so that the author's mapping is preserved
Run sigma check on it and deploy it once the summary reports no issues
7.explanation: A public rule encodes someone else's log sources, field names and assumptions, so it must be judged, converted with a pipeline matching local indexing and tested on local data. A clean sigma check proves structure, not that the rule finds events in your environment.

7.q: The office rule puts ParentImage and Image in two named selections joined by 'and'. A reviewer suggests merging them into one map. What is the accurate assessment?
options: The merge would change the logic, because a single map means OR
The merge would fail sigma check, because one map allows one field
The merge would widen the rule to match either field on its own
The logic is the same; separate names aid review and later changes
7.explanation: A map is AND, so one map with both fields means the same as the two selections joined by and. Separate names make the intent clearer and make it easy to add parents or a filter later.

7.q: A Sysmon process-creation event shows WINWORD.EXE as the parent of powershell.exe, and rule R1 fires on that parent-child pair. Which mapping does this observation support on its own?
options: T1204.002 Malicious File and T1059.001 PowerShell, under Execution
T1566 Phishing under Initial Access, plus T1059.001 PowerShell under Execution
Only the Execution tactic, because techniques require knowledge of attacker intent
Only T1059 at parent level, because sub-techniques are too specific for a rule tag
7.explanation: The event shows a user-opened document (Word as parent) running PowerShell, which supports both Execution techniques. Phishing describes how the document arrived, which a process event cannot show, so adding T1566 tags the incident rather than the observation.

7.q: R1 matches Word starting either powershell.exe or cmd.exe, but the kit's Sigma rule is tagged only with attack.t1059.001. What is the practical consequence for coverage reporting?
options: A matrix built from tags will overstate coverage, because cmd.exe is not a technique
The rule will fail sigma check, because its tags do not match its selection fields
A matrix built from tags will omit T1059.003, although the rule does cover it
The rule will stop matching cmd.exe, because the backend converts only tagged images
7.explanation: This is under-mapping: the logic covers the Windows Command Shell sub-technique but the tags do not say so, so tag-driven coverage reports miss it. Tags have no effect on matching, and sigma check validates tag form, not agreement with the logic.

7.q: R4 flags a 48,200,000-byte HTTPS upload to files-share-drop.example. The lab has proxy sizes but no destination categorisation. Which tag is the most defensible?
options: T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage, because the hostname suggests a file-sharing site
T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service, noting that the destination type is unconfirmed
T1071.001 Web Protocols, because the upload travelled over HTTPS to an external host
T1048 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, because the upload bypassed the C2 channel
7.explanation: The rule sees only size and URL; whether the site is cloud storage is enrichment it does not have, so the parent technique with a recorded doubt is honest. Choosing the cloud-storage sub-technique from a hostname would be a guess presented as fact.

7.q: The proxy shows WS-104 downloading invoice.docm from a look-alike domain, and the lab collects no mail logs. How should this step be mapped in the coverage work?
options: T1566.002 Spearphishing Link, since a web download proves the user clicked a link
T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment, since a .docm file is a typical attachment
Leave it unmapped, because no detection rule fires on the download event
T1566 at parent level, with the delivery vector recorded as unconfirmed
7.explanation: Without mail telemetry the route by which the URL reached the user is unknown, so either sub-technique would be a guess. The step must still appear in the matrix, as a gap, precisely because no rule covers it.

7.q: T1078 Valid Accounts is listed under several tactics, including Initial Access, Persistence and Privilege Escalation. A rule detects a stolen password used over the VPN from outside. Which tactic should the tag carry?
options: Every tactic the technique is listed under, since ATT&CK lists it under each of them
Persistence only, since a working password lets the attacker return later
The tactic the login achieves in the scenario the rule targets, here Initial Access
No tactic at all, since multi-tactic techniques should be tagged by ID alone
7.explanation: A tactic is the goal inferred from what the action achieves in context; an external VPN login gets the attacker in. Listing every tactic would claim coverage of persistence and escalation scenarios the rule does not observe.

7.q: A manager says: 'We have nothing for T1059, so write a rule that searches process events for the string PowerShell.' What is the main problem with this approach?
options: It maps downwards from an ID to a keyword, producing a brittle name-matching rule
It targets a technique instead of a tactic, which is too narrow for coverage goals
It ignores sub-techniques, so the resulting rule cannot be tagged in Sigma at all
It relies on process events, which ATT&CK does not list as a data source for T1059
7.explanation: Good rules start from an understood procedure and its artefacts and are then mapped upwards. Starting from an ID and grepping for a word gives logic that matches names rather than behaviour and is easy to miss or trip.

7.q: R2 fires only when at least five distinct users fail from one IP and a VPN success follows from that IP. Why can its alert be cited as evidence for more than password spraying?
options: Because counting distinct users also demonstrates T1110.001 Password Guessing
Because any VPN event is evidence of T1133, whether it succeeds or fails
Because the source IP belongs to a documentation range and is therefore external
Because the required success is itself use of a valid account via an external remote service
7.explanation: A failures-only rule would support T1110.003 alone; requiring the success makes the alert evidence of T1078 and T1133 too. Failed VPN attempts alone do not demonstrate use of an external remote service by the attacker.

7.q: R3 is named new_local_admin and matches Windows events 4720 and 4732, but the minisiem table has no group column. What does careful mapping reveal about R3?
options: It fires only on account creation, because 4732 is never written for local groups
It fires on additions to any security-enabled local group, not only Administrators
It cannot be mapped to Persistence, because account creation is a Discovery action
It misses additions to Administrators, because the group is in the raw event only
7.explanation: Without a group field the logic cannot restrict 4732 to the Administrators group, so its scope is wider than its name. The raw event does carry the group, which is why the data-source table marks this as a partial dependency.

7.q: For T1136.001, the lab collects the Security log, rule R3 exists and fired correctly on the Banyan dataset, and the kit has no test for R3. What status should the coverage matrix show?
options: Covered: the rule fired on real attack data, which is stronger than a unit test
Untested: a rule exists, but it has not been shown to fire and stay quiet on cases
Partial: the rule exists but the data source is missing the group field
Gap: without a test the technique counts as having no detection at all
7.explanation: Firing once on a dataset built to contain the attack does not show the rule rejects near misses, so the honest label is untested. Calling it a gap would understate what exists; calling it covered would overstate it.

7.q: In the Banyan matrix the T1059 PowerShell/cmd row is blue (partial) even though R1 has passing tests. Why is it not green?
options: R1's tests cover PowerShell only, so the cmd.exe branch is counted as missing data
R1 has no near-miss test, so its PowerShell coverage cannot be scored as tested
R1 maps to two tactics, and multi-tactic rows are always scored as partial
R1 only recognises Word as the parent, so shells started from other parents are not seen
7.explanation: The tested logic covers one parent application; PowerShell or cmd launched by other Office programs or script hosts falls outside it. R1 does have a near-miss test (explorer.exe as parent), so that is not the reason.

7.q: A team exports its coverage to ATT&CK Navigator and gives every technique that has any rule a score that renders green. What is the main risk of this layer?
options: Techniques with untested rules look covered, so the heat map claims more than was shown
Navigator rejects layers whose scores are not derived from tested rules only
Techniques with tested rules lose their colour, because scores overwrite each other
The layer cannot be version-controlled, because colours are stored outside the JSON
7.explanation: Navigator colours whatever score it is given; collapsing 'rule exists' into green hides the difference between untested and tested rules. Layers are JSON files that can be shared and version-controlled.

7.q: The data-source table shows that the Banyan lab collects no mail-gateway logs. What does this tell the detection team about phishing delivery?
options: It is a rule gap: a proxy rule for .docm downloads fully closes it
It is a tuning gap: R1 should be widened until it fires at delivery time
It is a telemetry gap: no rule can detect it until that data is collected
It is a mapping gap: tagging R1 with T1566 records that delivery is covered
7.explanation: Data-source mapping shows what cannot be seen at all; logic cannot compensate for missing telemetry. A proxy rule could catch some downloads, but it would not see the mail that delivered the link or attachment.

7.q: The Security-log-cleared rule depends on event 1102, which Windows writes into the log that has just been cleared. Which data-source condition makes this rule genuinely useful?
options: The Security log is sized large enough that it is never cleared automatically
The rule runs on the endpoint itself, where the cleared log is still available
Sysmon is installed, so process creation records the clearing tool's command line
The Security log is forwarded off the host to the SIEM in near real time
7.explanation: If the log lives only on the host, clearing it removes the evidence an investigator needs; forwarding preserves the 1102 event and what came before it. Running the rule locally does not help once the local log is gone.

7.q: A rule repository was mapped two years ago and its coverage report has not been rechecked since. Several ATT&CK releases have come out in between. What is the most important risk, and the control for it?
options: Rules may stop matching events; re-run the rules against the original dataset
Tags may now point to revoked or changed entries; re-validate them against the new version
Tactic IDs may be renumbered into kill-chain order; re-sort the coverage matrix
Navigator layers may expire; export a fresh layer file from each rule's tags
7.explanation: ATT&CK releases add, split, deprecate and revoke entries, so an ID can become wrong without the rule changing. Recording the version and re-validating tags against MITRE's published STIX data catches this; rule matching is unaffected by ATT&CK releases.

7.q: A vendor content pack, two community rules and an internal wiki page tag the same scheduled-task behaviour with three different technique IDs. How should the detection engineer settle the tag?
options: Use the ID that appears in the most sources, since agreement indicates accuracy
Use the vendor's ID, since commercial content is reviewed before publication
Look it up on the official ATT&CK site for the version in use and record that version
Keep all three IDs, so the rule appears in coverage under whichever is correct
7.explanation: Disagreements are resolved against the authoritative source for a stated version, not by majority vote or vendor trust. Keeping all three would inflate coverage and leave two false claims in the repository.

7.q: A SOC is building its first coverage matrix and proposes one row for every Enterprise technique. What is a better way to choose the rows?
options: From the threat model: sector groups, own incidents, exercises and regulator questions
From the rule repository: one row per technique already tagged in an existing rule
From the tactic list: one representative technique per tactic column of the matrix
From the data sources: one row per technique the current telemetry can observe
7.explanation: Rows should reflect the threats that matter, so that the important gaps stand out. Building rows from existing rules or existing telemetry hides exactly the techniques the SOC cannot yet see.

7.q: A colleague sorts a technique report by tactic ID, assuming that the lowest ID is the earliest stage of an intrusion. Which result shows why this assumption is wrong?
options: Reconnaissance (TA0043) and Resource Development (TA0042) sort to the end of the list
Initial Access (TA0001) sorts to the end, after Impact (TA0040)
Execution (TA0002) sorts before Initial Access (TA0001)
Exfiltration (TA0010) sorts after Command and Control (TA0011)
7.explanation: Tactic IDs are identifiers, not sequence numbers: the two pre-compromise tactics were added later and carry the highest numbers. Exfiltration actually sorts before Command and Control by ID, the reverse of what the last option states.

7.q: Which practice is the clearest example of coverage theatre in an ATT&CK-based report?
options: Leaving a technique red because its only rule has not yet been tested
Tagging a parent technique because the rule cannot tell sub-techniques apart
Recording the ATT&CK version used for each mapping in the coverage report
Counting community rules as coverage although their log source is not collected
7.explanation: A rule that reads data the SIEM never receives cannot fire, so counting it is reassurance without substance. The other options describe honest practice that understates rather than overstates coverage.

7.q: A technique's row shows a rule and a passing test suite, but the log source the rule reads was decommissioned last month. What status should the row now carry?
options: Covered, because tests prove the logic and the logic has not changed
Untested, because tests that use synthetic data are void without live data
A gap, because without data the rule cannot fire whatever its tests say
Partial, because two of the three conditions in the row are still met
7.explanation: Coverage is the weakest of data, rule and test, and data is the precondition for the other two. Passing unit tests prove the logic, not that the events still arrive.

7.q: A dashboard reports 'Execution: covered' because one rule is tagged attack.execution. Why is this a weak basis for planning detection work?
options: Tactic tags are not valid Sigma tags, so the rule may not be counted at all
Tactics are too coarse: one rule can hide many untouched execution techniques
Execution is a pre-compromise tactic, so coverage there has little value
Tactic coverage is already implied by technique tags and is double-counted
7.explanation: Gap analysis needs technique or sub-technique granularity; tactic-level colouring hides dozens of techniques with no detection. attack.execution is a valid Sigma tag, so the problem is granularity, not syntax.

7.q: During tuning, R1 is narrowed so that it matches only powershell.exe under Word, after cmd.exe caused noise. Its tags currently include T1059.001 and T1059.003. What must happen to the mapping?
options: Keep both tags, since the attacker may still use cmd.exe from a Word macro
Replace both with the parent T1059, since tuning has reduced the rule's precision
Leave the tags until the next ATT&CK release, when all mappings are re-validated
Remove the T1059.003 tag, since the rule no longer observes the Windows Command Shell
7.explanation: Tags must follow the logic: once cmd.exe is excluded, claiming T1059.003 would show coverage that no longer exists. Mappings change both with ATT&CK releases and with rule changes such as tuning.

7.q: A new Sigma rule's tags pass sigma check without warnings. What has this check established about the rule's ATT&CK mapping?
options: Only that the tags follow the naming convention, not that they are correct
That each tagged technique has a passing test case in the repo
That the technique tags are consistent with the rule's detection logic
That the tactic tags match the tactics listed for each tagged technique
7.explanation: sigma check validates the form of tags; whether a technique is right for the logic is a human review responsibility. Treating a clean check as validation of the mapping lets wrong IDs into coverage reports.

7.q: A reviewer receives a pull request whose rule has the tag attack.t1098 and nothing else about the mapping. What is missing for the mapping to be reviewable?
options: A Navigator layer file showing where the technique sits in the matrix
The ATT&CK version, the technique name and a sentence on why the logic shows it
A second technique tag, so the mapping can be cross-checked for consistency
The threat group that used the technique in the incident that inspired the rule
7.explanation: A mapping is a claim and needs its evidence: version, ID and name, and a rationale linking the observation to the technique. Without a rationale a reviewer cannot tell whether the tag matches the logic.

7.q: R6 finds 18 identical 220-byte HTTPS requests from WS-104 to one URL, starting shortly after the macro ran. Which mapping fits what the rule observes?
options: T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service under Exfiltration
T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel under Exfiltration
T1071.001 Web Protocols under Command and Control
T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol under Command and Control
7.explanation: Small, regular, identical requests are a beacon: C2 traffic carried over HTTP(S), which is T1071.001. Requests of 220 bytes move no meaningful data out, and HTTPS is an application-layer protocol, which rules out T1095.

7.q: A rule fires whenever WINWORD.EXE starts any child process, without checking which program the child is. How far up the ATT&CK stack can this rule's tags honestly go?
options: Not to T1059: the rule does not observe a scripting interpreter being run
To T1059 but not a sub-technique, since the child program is unknown
To T1059.001, since PowerShell is the most common child of a malicious macro
To T1059.001 and T1059.003, since together they cover the likely children
7.explanation: The observation is only 'Word started something', which does not demonstrate an interpreter at all, so even the parent T1059 is not supported. Tagging the likely child would be mapping what the attacker might do rather than what the rule sees.

7.q: A near-miss test inserts an event with source='appliance' and event_id=1102 and expects R5 to return []. It fails with 'Lists differ: [(None, None, '-')] != []'. What has the test revealed?
options: R5 matches any event with ID 1102, because its query has no condition on source
R5 matches only events with a placeholder user, because '-' is treated as a wildcard
The fixture is faulty, because a fresh table should not return rows with NULL fields
The oracle is wrong, because event 1102 always means a cleared Security log
7.explanation: The returned row shows R5 fired on an event from another source; the query only checks event_id=1102. The NULLs are expected, because the synthetic event did not set ts or host, so they do not indicate a fixture fault.

7.q: In the failing R5 case the returned row is (None, None, '-'). Why are the first two values None?
options: R5 selects only the user column, and unittest pads the other values with None
The appliance source has no timestamps, so SQLite discards the ts and host values
The test event did not set ts or host, so the helper inserted NULL for them
The FIELDS list does not include ts or host, so those columns are always empty
7.explanation: run() inserts e.get(f) for every field, and dict.get returns None for missing keys, which SQLite stores as NULL. R5 selects ts, host and user, so the row reflects exactly what the synthetic event supplied.

7.q: An analyst raises R2's threshold from five users to six without updating the tests. Running the kit's suite prints '..F....' and 'AssertionError: 0 != 1'. Which test failed, and what does it mean?
options: test_four_users_is_below_threshold: a four-user spray is now matched by mistake
test_five_users_then_success: a five-user spray the rule must detect now raises nothing
test_spray_without_success: eight failures now fire without any successful login
test_five_users_then_success: the rule now returns one row instead of none
7.explanation: The positive case at the threshold expects one row and got zero, so the documented five-user behaviour has been lost. The four-user near miss still passes, since six is even further from four.

7.q: Suppose R2's only positive test used eight failed users. Which unnoticed change to the rule shows why that test is not enough?
options: Lowering the threshold from >= 5 to >= 4 would make the eight-user test fail
Removing the success condition would make the eight-user test return no rows
Changing COUNT(DISTINCT f.user) to COUNT(f.user) would make the test fail
Raising the threshold from >= 5 to >= 8 would still let every test pass
7.explanation: A threshold is pinned only by testing exactly at it and just below it; a case well above the limit passes for any threshold up to eight. Lowering the threshold would not make the eight-user case fail either, so that option is false.

7.q: A colleague's test file contains its own copy of R1's SQL and runs that copy against synthetic events. Why is this design unsafe?
options: The copy runs in a separate database, so the test cannot see the synthetic events
The copy bypasses parameterised inserts, so the events are vulnerable to injection
The test keeps passing after the production rule changes, so it proves nothing about it
The copy doubles the test run time, so the suite stops being run on every change
7.explanation: The kit's run() executes RULES[rule] from minisiem.py so that any edit to the real rule is tested. A duplicated query can drift silently from production while its tests stay green.

7.q: The kit's run() helper opens sqlite3.connect(':memory:') and creates a new events table on every call. What property does this give the test suite?
options: Each test starts from an empty fixture, so tests are independent of order
Each test reads the real Banyan dataset, so results match production volume
Each test shares one table, so later tests can build on earlier test events
Each test writes to minisiem.db, so failures can be inspected after the run
7.explanation: An in-memory database created per call leaves nothing behind for the next test, so no test can pass or fail because of another. Sharing a table between tests would make results depend on run order.

7.q: A near-miss test for R1 changes the parent to explorer.exe, the child to notepad.exe and the host name at the same time, and the rule correctly stays silent. What does this pass prove?
options: That both the parent and the child conditions work, since both were changed
That the rule ignores host names, since the host was changed and it stayed silent
That the rule is fully specified, since three decision points were covered at once
Little: any one of the changed attributes may be the condition that suppressed it
7.explanation: A near miss should differ from the positive case in exactly one attribute, so that a pass shows that particular condition doing its job. With three changes, a broken parent check could be hidden by a working child check.

7.q: A test with five VPN failures on 1 October and a success from the same IP on 3 November expects R2 to stay silent, but R2 fires. What in the rule causes this?
options: Its GROUP BY includes s.ts, so each success is compared with every failure
Its only time condition is f.ts <= s.ts, so failures of any age are correlated
Its COUNT(DISTINCT f.user) counts the same user once per day of retention
Its join is on src_ip, so failures from other IPs are added to the count
7.explanation: The rule has no lower time bound, so a month-old failure counts as if it preceded today's login. Grouping by the success timestamp is correct design; the missing window is the defect.

7.q: The R5 'another source' test fails and a deadline is close. Which response is NOT legitimate?
options: Adding source='windows' to R5 and rerunning all existing and new tests
Deleting the test, so the build passes and the rule can ship unchanged
Recording a reviewed decision to accept the limitation as a known case
Holding the rule change until the team decides between fixing or accepting
7.explanation: A red test is a finding: fix the rule or document an explicit, reviewed acceptance of the limitation. Deleting an inconvenient test hides a known defect and removes the protection it would give later.

7.q: After adding source='windows' to R5, the new near-miss test passes. What else must be confirmed before the fix is complete?
options: That the Sigma version of the rule converts to the same SQL text as R5
That the fix also adds a lower time bound, as was needed for R2
That event 1102 no longer appears from the appliance source in the SIEM
That earlier positive cases still pass and the real dataset hit is still found
7.explanation: A fix that removes an over-match can also remove the true match, so the full suite and the known real hit must still pass; in the lesson 15 tests passed and the 08:17 WS-104 hit remained. Sigma conversion is a separate concern.

7.q: All unit tests for R1 pass. Which question about R1 does this green run leave unanswered?
options: Whether real Sysmon events reach the SIEM with the parent image in parent_image
Whether R1 stays silent when explorer.exe is the parent of PowerShell
Whether R1 still matches when the process paths are written in lower case
Whether R1 fires when Word starts PowerShell with both fields populated
7.explanation: Unit tests insert fields directly, so they prove logic, not that telemetry is generated, forwarded and parsed into the expected field. The other three are exactly what the R1 unit tests check.

7.q: Running minisiem's rules over the 340-event Banyan dataset gives 1, 1, 2, 1, 1 and 1 hits, all of them part of the attack. Why is this weak evidence that the rules are ready for production?
options: The dataset lacks negative cases, so the precision figure cannot be calculated
The dataset is synthetic, so the rules will not run against real event formats
The dataset was built to contain the attack, so it says little about everyday noise
The dataset is too small for SQLite to apply the GROUP BY and HAVING clauses
7.explanation: Replay is meant to measure volume on real production data from the systems the rule will watch; a purpose-built storyline nearly guarantees perfect precision. The dataset does contain benign events, so precision can be computed, but it is not representative.

7.q: A team wants an end-to-end check that R3 still works after a Windows agent upgrade. Which approach fits the lesson's guidance?
options: On a production server, add a test user to Administrators and check the alert
Insert a synthetic 4720 row into the SIEM index and check that the alert appears
Rerun the R3 unit tests after the upgrade, since they use the production rule text
In an isolated lab domain, create and then delete a logged test account, and check the alert
7.explanation: A benign stand-in on a lab machine makes Windows generate a real 4720, exercising collection and parsing; the test is recorded and the account removed. Inserting rows or rerunning unit tests skips the telemetry path that the upgrade may have broken.

7.q: In a detection-as-code pipeline, which order of checks matches the lesson's description of a rule change?
options: Peer review, deploy, replay on recent data, then unit tests on a schedule
Syntax check, unit tests, peer review, replay on recent data, then deploy
Unit tests, deploy, syntax check, then peer review of the alert volume
Replay on recent data, syntax check, deploy, then unit tests and review
