7.explanation: Cheap automated checks come first and block the change on failure; a reviewer reads rule and tests together; replay estimates volume before deployment; scheduled end-to-end checks follow. Deploying before tests or review lets defects reach analysts.

7.q: R4 fires when bytes_out > 10000000. Which pair of test cases pins its threshold precisely?
options: 10,000,000 bytes must fire and 9,999,999 bytes must not
48,200,000 bytes must fire and 1,000,000 bytes must not
10,000,001 bytes must fire and exactly 10,000,000 bytes must not
10,000,001 bytes must fire and 20,000,000 bytes must also fire
7.explanation: With a strict greater-than, the boundary lies between exactly ten million and one byte more, so those two values document it. Testing exactly ten million as a positive would encode the wrong operator.

7.q: In the lesson's test report, both failing results were negative cases. What is the usual reason defects cluster there?
options: Rules are written while looking at the attack example, so positives tend to pass
Negative cases use more fields, so they are more likely to contain typing errors
Positive cases are generated automatically, so they cannot disagree with the rule
Negative cases run after positive ones, so they inherit leftover fixture rows
7.explanation: The positive case is usually the event that inspired the rule, so it passes almost by construction; over-broad logic shows up only on what the rule should not match. Fixtures are rebuilt per call, so leftover rows are not a factor.

7.q: An engineer runs 'python -m unittest test_rules -v' from the parent folder of the kit instead of inside it. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The test module cannot be imported, because test_rules.py is not on the path
The tests run but skip R2, because its generator needs the kit's working folder
The tests run silently, because -v only prints names inside the kit folder
The tests pass but use the real dataset, because minisiem.db is found instead
7.explanation: The module name test_rules is resolved from the current directory, which is why the command must run next to test_rules.py and minisiem.py. The -v flag changes output detail, not where modules are found.

7.q: The kit's R6 negative case sends ten requests to one URL whose sizes grow by 40 bytes each, and the rule stays silent. Which decision point does this case isolate?
options: The count condition: ten requests fall below the minimum needed per host and URL
The URL condition: growing sizes indicate different endpoints on the same host
The timing condition: the requests are too close together to look like a beacon
The regularity condition: the size spread is 360 bytes, above the 50-byte limit
7.explanation: Ten requests satisfy the count condition (at least ten), so only the max-minus-min size check can explain the silence. R6 has no timing condition in the kit, so the last option does not apply.

7.q: The run() helper inserts events with '?' placeholders rather than formatting values into the SQL string. Why does this matter?
options: Placeholders let SQLite cache results, so each test runs against the same rows
Placeholders convert values to lower case, so case handling is tested for free
Values are passed as data, so event content cannot alter the SQL being run
Placeholders allow missing fields, which would otherwise raise a syntax error
7.explanation: Parameterised queries keep test data separate from SQL text, so a value containing quotes or SQL cannot change the statement. Case handling is done in the rule itself, not by the insert mechanism.

7.q: A new rule ships with three positive test cases and no negative cases, and all three pass. What risk does this leave open?
options: The rule may never fire, because positive cases cannot prove that it matches
The rule may be far too broad, matching large amounts of legitimate activity
The rule may be mis-tagged, because positive cases validate the ATT&CK mapping
The rule may fail in replay, because positive cases bypass the SQL engine
7.explanation: Positive cases prove the rule can fire; only negative cases, ideally near misses, show it does not fire on look-alike benign events. A rule that matches everything would pass all three positives.

7.q: How should end-to-end checks be scheduled relative to unit tests in a mature detection pipeline?
options: On every rule change, while unit tests run only after SIEM or agent upgrades
Once when a rule is first deployed, since telemetry does not change afterwards
Only during incidents, since lab emulation duplicates what unit tests already do
Periodically and after agent, parser or SIEM upgrades, while unit tests run on every change
7.explanation: End-to-end tests need lab infrastructure and are slower, so they confirm the pipeline periodically; unit tests are cheap and gate every change. Telemetry does change, through parser updates and new builds, so a single check at deployment is not enough.

7.q: An incident review finds that R1 missed a Word-to-PowerShell launch because the image path was in an unexpected form. The rule is fixed. What should accompany the fix?
options: A regression test that recreates the missed event, so the miss cannot return silently
A new near-miss test with explorer.exe as parent, to confirm the parent condition
A replay over the Banyan dataset, to confirm the fixed rule still finds one hit
A Sigma tag update, so the coverage matrix marks the technique as re-tested
7.explanation: Every missed detection or confirmed false positive should become a regression case that encodes the exact input that went wrong. The explorer.exe near miss already exists and tests a different condition.

7.q: Why should a rule's tuning change and its updated tests be committed together?
options: Split commits cannot be reviewed, because the platform links tests to rules by ID
The history then records both the change and the behaviour it was meant to keep
Tests in a later commit would run against the old rule text from the cache
Combined commits skip the syntax check, which speeds up urgent tuning
7.explanation: Changing rule and tests in one commit documents the intended behaviour alongside the change and ensures the pipeline tests the new logic. Skipping checks is never a goal of the practice.

7.q: The month-old-failures test for R2 fails. Someone argues the test is wrong because R2 'works as written'. What settles whether the rule or the test should change?
options: The SQL: whatever the query returns is by definition the rule's correct behaviour
The dataset: R2 is correct if it produces no false positives on the Banyan events
The oracle: the written statement that a spray means failures shortly before a success
The tag: R2 is correct if its behaviour matches the T1110.003 technique name
7.explanation: Expected results come from the analyst's documented intent, which here requires correlation within a short window; the test therefore defines what the tuned rule must do. The one-day Banyan dataset cannot expose the defect, so it cannot settle the question.

7.q: R1 is edited to fire only on workstations, adding lower(host) LIKE 'ws-%'. The existing positive test supplies only source, event_id, parent_image and image. What happens on the next run, and what does it show?
options: The positive test fails, showing the rule now depends on a field the test lacks
The positive test passes, because a missing field is treated as a wildcard match
The near-miss test fails, because explorer.exe events now lack a command line
Both tests error out, because the events table has no host column
7.explanation: The missing field is inserted as NULL, a NULL comparison does not match, so R1 returns [] and the assertion of one row fails. Tests that supply only the fields a rule reads therefore document, and enforce, its data dependencies.

7.q: Analyst dispositions show that R6 raised 140 alerts in 30 days and 131 were closed as false positive or benign. What does this precision figure tell the detection engineer about R6's recall?
options: That recall is also low, because a rule with many false positives usually misses many true positives too
That recall is high, because a rule broad enough to raise 140 alerts is unlikely to miss a real beacon
Nothing directly, because beacons R6 missed never became alerts and so never appear in the dispositions
That recall is about 0.06 as well, because precision and recall are computed from the same alert counts
7.explanation: Recall is the share of real occurrences caught, and misses never enter the queue; it has to be estimated from known-bad tests, emulation, hunting and incident review. Assuming broad rules have high recall is the strongest distractor, but breadth says nothing about which variants the logic actually matches.

7.q: Most of a rule's alerts are closed as benign true positives: the behaviour is exactly what the rule describes, performed by an approved administration process. Which kind of change does that disposition pattern point to?
options: Context for triage or a scoped, owned suppression for the approved instance, leaving the logic unchanged
Narrowing the rule's logic, because a benign true positive is an error in the rule's definition
A parser fix, because benign true positives usually come from fields that are normalised incorrectly
Raising the rule's threshold until the approved process no longer reaches it during normal operation
7.explanation: A benign true positive is noise for the queue but not an error in the rule: the rule matched its intent and only the instance is authorised, so enrichment or a scoped suppression is the fix. Narrowing is for false positives, where logic matches activity outside the rule's own intent.

7.q: When the engineer computes per-rule precision, 30 of a rule's 80 closed alerts are marked undetermined. How should those 30 be treated?
options: Counted as false positives, because an alert that cannot be confirmed was not worth the analyst's time
Counted as true positives, because an alert that cannot be ruled out must be assumed to be malicious
Split evenly between true and false positives so that the ratio is not biased in either direction
Left out of the ratio but reported, since many undetermined closures signal an evidence problem
7.explanation: Undetermined alerts belong in neither side of TP / (TP + FP), but a high number of them is a separate defect: the rule or its data does not give analysts enough evidence to decide. Counting them as false positives would push the engineer to tune away alerts that may have been real.

7.q: On the Banyan lab day every rule R1 to R6 has a precision of 1.00, because every hit belongs to the scripted intrusion. Why does the lesson call this figure 'almost worthless'?
options: The dataset's ground truth is unknown, so it is impossible to say which of the seven alerts are true positives
Seven alerts from one synthetic day are far too few, over far too short a period, to predict precision in production
Precision cannot be computed for aggregation rules such as R2 and R6, so the overall figure is misleading
A precision of 1.00 proves the rules are too narrow, so they must be loosened before they are deployed
7.explanation: Precision is only meaningful over enough alerts and a long enough period, including real administrative and seasonal activity; seven alerts on one day are anecdote. The ground truth is in fact known from make_dataset.py, which is exactly what lets the lab label hits as storyline or routine.

7.q: Rule A has precision 0.10 and raises about two alerts a month. Rule B has precision 0.50 and raises about two hundred alerts a day. Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on where tuning effort should go first?
options: Rule B, because once volume is taken into account it consumes far more of the analysts' time
Rule A, because its precision is five times worse and precision is the main measure of rule quality
Neither, because both are above the minimum precision a SOC should accept for a production detection
Rule A, because rarely firing rules hide their defects longest and should be fixed before frequent ones
7.explanation: Precision paired with volume gives the analyst time a rule consumes: 100 noisy alerts a day from B outweigh about two a month from A. Ranking by ratio alone, as the strongest distractor does, ignores the cost the queue actually pays.

7.q: A sweep of R4 (bytes_out > T) over the lab proxy data gives 1 TP at T = 10,000,000 and still exactly 1 TP at T = 3,900, 3,500, 3,000 and 2,000, while false positives rise from 0 to 141. What does the constant true-positive count show?
options: The sweep is broken, because lowering a threshold must always add true positives as well as false positives
The kit's threshold is too high, because the lowest value tested would catch the same attack and more
The upload is far above all routine requests, leaving a wide band where R4 is precise and complete
R4 has perfect recall for exfiltration, so its threshold can be set anywhere without affecting detection
7.explanation: Routine requests stay below about 4,000 bytes and the real upload is 48.2 MB, so any threshold in that band keeps the TP and the engineer picks a value with margins on both sides. It does not prove perfect recall: the sweep only measures the attack present in this data, not smaller uploads an attacker might choose.

7.q: A threat assessment notes that an attacker could exfiltrate in 9 MB requests, each just under R4's 10 MB threshold. The baseline shows that lowering R4 to 3,000 bytes would add dozens of false positives a day. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Lower R4 to 3,000 bytes and accept the noise, because the threat model must always override the baseline
Leave R4 unchanged, because the baseline shows any lower threshold would make the rule unusable
Lower R4 to 9,000,000 bytes, so that the specific variant in the threat assessment is caught exactly
Keep R4 and add a second rule that totals bytes per host and destination over a period such as an hour
7.explanation: The baseline shows how low the threshold can go before noise explodes; the threat model shows how low it needs to go. When they conflict, a different aggregation (total bytes per host and destination per hour) catches split uploads without drowning the queue. A 9 MB threshold only moves the evasion point slightly lower.

7.q: In the R6 sweep, raising the size-range limit from 50 to 3,500 bytes gives 3 alerts, and additionally lowering the minimum hit count from 10 to 5 gives 33 alerts for the same single beacon. What tuning practice does this result support?
options: Always lower the hit count before widening the size range, because count thresholds produce less noise
Change one parameter at a time and measure, because parameters interact and loosening two at once multiplies noise
Prefer the 33-alert setting, because a wider net is the only way to be sure of catching every beacon variant
Set both parameters from the beacon's own values, so that the rule matches the known implant exactly
7.explanation: Each loosened parameter added some noise, but together they produced 33 alerts with no extra true positives, so interactions must be measured one change at a time. Fitting the rule exactly to the known implant would raise precision but narrow it to one variant, trading recall for a tidy number.

7.q: A tuning request arrives saying only 'add WS-103 to R6's exclusions'. Why should the engineer set the proposed fix aside and work through the diagnosis questions in order, starting with the data?
options: Exclusions can only be applied after a data fix, because the SIEM rejects exceptions on unnormalised fields
Host exclusions are never acceptable in a detection rule, so the request must always be rewritten
Starting with the data is fastest, because parser fixes need no testing or review before deployment
The same symptom has several causes, and starting with suppressions piles exceptions around a defect never fixed
7.explanation: Too many alerts may come from bad data, logic broader than its intent, numbers off baseline or an authorised instance, and each needs a different change; the order runs from the most general, durable fix to the most specific. Exclusions are sometimes right (an authorised instance), and every fix still goes through tests and review.

7.q: False positives from a rule that tests a user field all come from one log source, where the parser leaves the field empty for a common event type. Which change does the diagnosis order call for, and why?
options: Fix the parser or normalisation, because the defect is in the pipeline and every rule using the field benefits
Add a filter excluding events with an empty user field, because that removes exactly the noisy alerts
Narrow the rule to the other log sources, because the faulty source cannot be trusted for this detection
Suppress the rule for that source until the vendor fixes its logging format in a future release
7.explanation: Wrong data is the first question in the diagnosis path, and its fix (parser or normalisation) is the most general: it repairs every consumer of the field. Filtering empty values or dropping the source hides the symptom for one rule and leaves the same blind spot for every other rule.

7.q: R6 alerts on WS-102 sending twelve identical 180-byte requests to a CRM status endpoint within one minute. Why is narrowing R6 preferred to suppressing WS-102 or the CRM URL?
options: A suppression cannot be scoped to one URL, so it would silence R6 for every host and destination at once
The burst is a benign true positive, so the change must apply to all hosts rather than to WS-102 only
R6 ignores time, so its logic is broader than its intent; a suppression would hide later real beacons
The data for WS-102 is wrong, so the parser has to be corrected before any change to the rule is made
7.explanation: R6 promises a beacon, a periodic check-in over time, but its query never looks at time, so any burst qualifies in any environment: logic broader than intent. Suppressing the host or URL leaves that defect and creates a blind spot for a real beacon there later. The burst is not a benign true positive, because it does not match the rule's intent at all.

7.q: A sanctioned software-update agent polls its vendor server every five minutes all day with requests of identical size, and R6 alerts on it. Which change is appropriate?
options: Add a further time condition to R6, because the agent shows the rule is still broader than its intent
A scoped, owned, expiring suppression or enrichment marking the sanctioned destination, with R6 unchanged
Raise R6's minimum hit count above the number of polls a day, so that only longer-lived beacons match
Widen R6's size-range limit, so that only implants with perfectly fixed request sizes still match
7.explanation: Unlike the one-minute burst, this traffic really is regular, small and persistent, so it matches R6's intent; only this instance is approved. That reaches the 'known authorised instance' question and calls for a scoped suppression or enrichment, not loosening R6 for everyone, which would weaken it against real implants too.

7.q: An analyst asks for R5 alerts to be suppressed whenever the user is a member of the IT operations team, because 'they are authorised'. What evidence does the diagnosis require before the activity can be treated as a known authorised instance?
options: A record of approval with an owner for the specific activity, not the user's identity or team
The analyst's confirmation that previous alerts for the same users were closed as benign
A check that the user's account has administrative rights on the hosts where the alerts occurred
A sweep showing that suppressing the team would raise R5's precision above an agreed target
7.explanation: 'Known authorised instance?' is answered only by a documented approval with an owner, never by who the user is; an attacker using an IT account looks exactly like that team. Past benign closures show a pattern but not that this activity is approved, and a precision gain says nothing about what the suppression would hide.

7.q: After a 30-minute span condition is added to R6's HAVING clause, the kit's test_regular_small_requests fails with 'AssertionError: 0 != 1'. Its fixture events have no timestamps. What is the correct interpretation and response?
options: The change broke detection of real beacons, so the span condition must be reverted before going further
The failure is a known side effect of aggregation tests, so the test can be skipped for this change
SQLite treats a missing timestamp as zero, so the span is negative and the threshold must be lowered
A missing ts makes the span NULL so the group is dropped; the fixture needs realistic timing
7.explanation: With no ts, julianday() returns NULL, the span comparison is NULL and the group never satisfies HAVING; the test assumed a rule that ignored time. A failing test must be investigated, never bypassed: here it is the test's assumption that is outdated, so the fixture gets ten requests five minutes apart. Reverting would only be right if a realistic known-bad sample stopped matching.

7.q: Why is 30 minutes, rather than (for example) 90 seconds, a defensible minimum span for the narrowed R6?
options: It is the smallest span that removes the WS-102 burst, so it changes the rule as little as possible
It matches the proxy's log rotation interval, so groups longer than 30 minutes would be split
It comes from the threat model: a five-minute beacon passes it after seven check-ins, and implants stay longer
It is the default beacon interval of common implants, so shorter spans would never be observed
7.explanation: The span must separate bursts from beacons based on how real beaconing behaves, not just clear the one burst that prompted the change; 90 seconds would also clear the burst but leave other short bursts alerting. The lesson does not tie the value to log rotation or to any implant's default interval.

7.q: Along with fixing the R6 fixture, the engineer adds test_short_burst_not_matched: twelve requests five seconds apart that must produce no alert. What is the main value of this new test?
options: It raises the suite's coverage figure so that the change passes the review step automatically
It records the reason for the change, so a later edit that drops the span fails the suite
It proves that R6 now catches every beacon with an interval longer than five seconds
It replaces replay, because a burst test shows the same effect as running the rule on past data
7.explanation: A near-miss test freezes the reason for the change into the suite: anyone who later removes or weakens the time condition gets a failure. It says nothing about recall for all beacon intervals, and it does not replace replay, which is the only way to see which past true positives a change would remove.

7.q: On the Banyan day the spraying address's failures run from 06:42:00 to 06:42:49 and the success is at 06:46:00. An engineer proposes adding a three-minute window between each failure and the success to R2. What would happen on this data?
options: The spray would still match, because the window is measured from the first failure, which is 240 seconds earlier
The spray would still match, because the window only limits how many failures are counted, not whether they join
Only the last few failures would join, so R2 would match with a lower distinct-user count than before
The spray would be missed, because even the last failure is 191 seconds before the success at 06:46
7.explanation: Every failure is at least 191 seconds (3 minutes 11 seconds) before the success, so no failure falls inside a 180-second window and nothing joins. The one sample observed gives a floor: the window must sit comfortably beyond the slowest known attack sequence, and noise is better fixed with entities or conditions than by shortening it.

7.q: Two test failures appear during tuning: R6's known-bad fixture fails after a span condition is added, and R2's five-user spray test fails after the window is set to two minutes. Why is the right response different in the two cases?
options: R6's fixture had unrealistic timing; R2's test is a realistic spray the rule no longer catches
R6's failure came from a SQL error while R2's came from a logic change, so only R2's needs investigation
R2's test was written by the kit's author while R6's was not, so only R2's result can be relied on
Both should be handled the same way, by adjusting the fixtures until the changed rules pass again
7.explanation: R6's fixture had no timestamps at all, an assumption made obsolete by adding a time dimension, so the test is fixed. R2's test spaces the success five minutes after the failures, a realistic sequence, so its failure is a real loss of detection and the change is stopped. Adjusting both fixtures blindly is exactly the bypass the lesson warns against.

7.q: The kit's R2 suite passes both against the original unwindowed rule and against a version with a ten-minute window. A new test, test_stale_failures_not_joined, fails against the original rule. What does this reveal?
options: The ten-minute window broke the threshold tests, and the new test was needed to make that failure visible
The original R2 joins a success to the previous day's failures, and no existing test required a window
The original R2 ignores the distinct-user threshold when failures and success fall on different days
The new test is wrong, because a correct R2 should join failures from any time before the success
7.explanation: The new test puts eight failures on 2 November and the success on 3 November; the kit's R2 still alerts, so it has no window, and the old suite could not tell. The ten-minute version passes every test, including the new one. A good R2 change keeps the threshold tests and adds this near miss so the window cannot silently disappear.

7.q: A proposed R6 change passes every unit test, including the new near-miss test. Why does the change-control path still require a replay over stored data before review?
options: Replay re-runs the unit tests on production hardware, which catches performance problems the tests miss
Replay is needed only for Sigma rules, because their converted queries may differ from the tested version
Only replay shows the effect on alert volume and which past true positives the new version would miss
Replay confirms the rule's ATT&CK mapping, which unit tests cannot check because they ignore metadata
7.explanation: Unit tests check the rule against its specification with small fixtures; replay runs it over a representative period of real stored data and shows the effect on the queue and on past true positives. It is not a performance test or a mapping check, and it applies to any rule change.

7.q: A week after a tuned version of a rule is deployed, its daily hit count has dropped from about fifteen to zero. How should the detection team respond?
options: Close the tuning ticket, because zero alerts shows the noise has been removed as intended
Lower the rule's priority, because a rule that no longer fires adds no value to the queue
Wait for a full quarter of data, because a week is too short to say anything about the change
Investigate whether the rule or its data is broken before treating silence as success
7.explanation: A rule whose hits fall to zero after a change may be broken rather than successful, and a silent rule produces no complaint; monitoring with rollback ready is the last step of the change path. Waiting a quarter is right for measuring precision of a rare rule, but not for a sudden drop from fifteen a day to nothing.

7.q: A team manages its detections as Sigma rules in version control. Which metadata change best records that a tuned rule is being deployed in a staged, reversible way rather than as finished work?
options: Updating the modified date and setting status to test, moving to stable only after monitoring
Updating the author field and setting level to low until the analysts accept the new version
Adding the ticket number to the rule's tags so the SIEM shows it beside each alert
Changing the rule's id so that the old and new versions can run side by side in production
7.explanation: Sigma records change in its metadata: a modified date and a status that moves from experimental through test to stable; staged deployment runs the new version at test status before it is trusted. Lowering level changes priority, not maturity, and the ticket belongs in the commit message rather than the ATT&CK-style tags.

7.q: An attacker with access to the SIEM console wants to avoid detection for a planned data theft. Which control most directly defends against the attacker quietly widening a suppression on R4?
options: A higher R4 threshold, so that suppressions are needed less often and attract more attention
Changes only through version control and review, alerting on any change made outside it
Weekly precision reviews, so that a rule whose precision changes suddenly is examined by the team
Encryption of the rule repository, so that the attacker cannot read the current R4 threshold
7.explanation: Widening a suppression or raising a threshold achieves more for an adversary than endpoint evasion, so the change path itself is the control: version control, mandatory review and a monitored audit trail, with out-of-band changes raising an alert. Precision reviews would not notice a suppression that removed a rare true positive; secrecy of the threshold does not stop the change.

7.q: Which pair of health signals does the lesson recommend for every detection engineering dashboard to catch tuning that has gone wrong?
options: Total alert volume across the SOC, and the average time analysts take to close an alert
The number of rules deployed each month, and the share of rules that have ATT&CK tags
Rules that stopped firing after a change, and suppression growth per rule with the events each matched
Per-rule precision over the last day, and the number of unit tests in the rule repository
7.explanation: A rule that goes silent may be broken, and a growing suppression may be hiding true positives; both are invisible in ordinary queue metrics. SOC-wide volume and closure time show workload, not which rule has lost detection.

7.q: A reviewer receives a pull request that changes R6's query but contains no change to test_rules.py. What is the main concern the lesson raises about such a change?
options: The rule cannot be converted to Splunk until its tests have been updated to the new query syntax
Unit tests compare query text, so an unchanged suite will fail as soon as the rule's text changes
The change cannot be replayed, because replay uses the test fixtures as its source of past data
The reason for the change is recorded nowhere a machine can check, so it can be silently undone
7.explanation: A rule change normally comes with a test change: a new near miss or boundary that encodes why the rule changed. Without it the purpose lives only in someone's memory. The kit's tests run the rule against events, not against its text, and replay uses stored historical data, not fixtures.

7.q: A rule for DNS tunnelling has been deployed for a month and has raised no alerts. The SIEM receives no DNS resolver or endpoint DNS logs. How should the SOC describe its position on DNS tunnelling?
options: It has tested coverage: a month of silence shows the rule works and the network is not being tunnelled
It has a data-source gap: zero hits are no evidence of no tunnelling, because the rule cannot see its data
It has a logic gap: the rule's conditions are too narrow and should be widened until it starts firing
It has untested coverage: the rule exists but needs known-bad and near-miss tests before it can be trusted
7.explanation: A rule with no telemetry returns zero hits, which looks exactly like a quiet day; 'no alerts' only means 'no attack' for behaviour you have proven you can see. The classification stops at the first failed condition, telemetry collected, so it is a data-source gap rather than untested coverage or a logic gap.

7.q: Windows Security event 4732 is collected and its raw JSON includes the group name, but minisiem's events table has no group column, so R3 fires on every local group addition. How is this gap classified, and who fixes it?
options: A logic gap, fixed by detection engineering adding a group condition to R3's existing query
A data-source gap, fixed by the infrastructure team enabling a different group-membership event
A scope gap, fixed by deploying event collection to the hosts where group changes are not logged
A field gap, fixed in the pipeline by parsing the group name into a column that the rule can test
7.explanation: The source and the event are collected, but a field the logic needs is not available as a field: a field gap, a data problem fixed in parsing. It is not a pure logic gap, because R3 cannot add a condition on a column that does not exist; the fix has to come first in the pipeline.

7.q: On WS-104, Sysmon process-creation events stop at 06:14, yet R3 shows svc_update was created at 07:02 and R5 shows the Security log was cleared at 08:17. What can the SOC not determine because of this gap?
options: Which process or program performed the account creation, the upload and the log clearing
Whether the account creation and the log clearing actually happened on WS-104 that morning
Which user account was logged on to WS-104 when the account creation and the log clearing occurred
Whether the 48.2 MB upload reached the external file-sharing destination recorded by the proxy
7.explanation: Windows Security and proxy events still record that the actions happened, on which host and by which user, but without process creation after 06:14 the actor process behind each action is invisible. This is a scope gap in an otherwise valuable source, and it hides most of the attacker's hands-on activity.

7.q: A coverage report states 'We have no detection for T1071.004 (DNS used for command and control).' The SIEM collects no DNS telemetry. Why does the lesson recommend rewording it as 'We collect no DNS telemetry, so DNS-based command and control is invisible'?
options: The rewording avoids citing an ATT&CK sub-technique, which reports to management should not contain
The rewording is shorter, and gap reports must fit on one line of the coverage matrix to be accepted
It names the real cause and its owner, instead of inviting detection engineering to write an impossible rule
The rewording turns a logic gap into a data-source gap, which lowers its priority in the gap register
7.explanation: The first wording invites 'why not write one?', a question detection engineering cannot answer because no query sees DNS that is not logged. The second states the problem as a data-source gap owned by whoever owns telemetry. Wording does not change the gap's type, only whether the report can be acted on.

7.q: The coverage matrix marks T1059.001 (PowerShell) as covered because R1 detects WINWORD.EXE starting PowerShell. Process creation with parent is collected. What kind of gap exists for an Excel macro that starts PowerShell?
options: A data-source gap: Excel process events are a separate source that would have to be collected first
No gap: the matrix records techniques, and the technique itself is already covered by R1
A field gap: the parent-image field is not parsed for Excel, so the rule cannot match it
A logic gap inside a 'covered' technique: the data exists but the rule ignores Excel
7.explanation: Process creation with the parent image is collected for any parent, so the only missing piece is logic: R1 is narrower than the behaviour it claims. A cell marked covered can hide such variants, which is why gap analysis walks the obvious variants of each technique rather than trusting the matrix.

7.q: A behaviour from the threat model has no telemetry collected and also no rule. Using the lesson's classifier, how should it be recorded, and why?
options: As a logic gap, because writing the rule is cheaper and can be done while telemetry is being requested
As a data-source gap, because each behaviour stops at its first failed condition and data comes first
As both a data-source gap and a logic gap, so that each owner receives a separate ticket at once
As untested coverage, because neither the data nor the rule has been shown to work on known-bad cases
7.explanation: The classifier stops at the first failed condition, because a later condition cannot be meaningfully tested while an earlier one fails: a rule cannot be tested against telemetry that does not exist. Recording it as a logic gap would send it to the wrong owner, who cannot close it.

7.q: A rule for new local administrator accounts exists, has been in production for a year and has fired several times, but nobody has ever run it against a known-bad case and a near miss. Where does it land in the lesson's classifier?
options: Untested coverage: a gap in evidence rather than in capability, closed by adding known-bad and near-miss tests
Covered, with evidence, because production alerts over a year show that the rule fires on real events
A logic gap, because a rule without tests must be rewritten before it can be counted at all
A field gap, because untested rules usually depend on fields whose parsing has not been checked
7.explanation: The data and the rule exist, so the only failed condition is the last one: known-bad and near-miss tests. Alerts in production show the rule fires on something, not that it fires on the attack and stays quiet on the look-alike; only the green box, with tests, should be called covered.

7.q: An inventory query on the Banyan dataset shows Sysmon carrying only event ID 1 and no flow or firewall source at all. A hunter wants to find hosts that connected directly to external addresses without using the proxy. What does the inventory imply?
options: It can be done with Sysmon event 1, because process creation records include each process's connections
It can be done from the VPN logs, because they record every connection made through the internal network
It cannot: there are no network-connection events or flow data, so direct traffic leaves no trace
It can be done from the proxy logs, by looking for hosts whose request counts fall below the baseline
7.explanation: Sysmon in this dataset records only process creation, and there is no flow, firewall or EDR data, so traffic that bypasses the proxy is invisible: a data-source gap. The VPN records carry no internal host or tunnel address, and a quiet host in the proxy logs is not evidence of direct connections.

7.q: R2 shows gopal's password used from the spraying address 203.0.113.66 at 06:46. That address appears in nine VPN events and nowhere else, and the VPN records have no internal host or tunnel address. Which telemetry would most directly close this gap?
options: VPN address-assignment logs together with firewall or flow records and internal authentication logs
Sysmon process creation on WS-107, gopal's workstation, for the hours after the VPN login
Proxy logs for 203.0.113.66, so that the attacker's web browsing after the login can be followed
A rule that alerts on every VPN login from an address that previously failed authentication
7.explanation: To answer 'what did the attacker reach with the valid account?' the SOC must tie the session to an internal address and then follow it through flow, firewall and internal authentication data. WS-107 activity is gopal's own routine use, not the attacker's session, and a new rule adds detection, not visibility into the session.

7.q: A colleague argues that Sysmon events ending at 06:14 are only an artefact of how the lab generator writes routine endpoint events, so they should not be recorded as a gap. Why does the lesson still treat it as one?
options: Generator artefacts are always caused by a collection fault that would also exist in production
Any source that stops during the working day must be recorded as a data-source gap by policy
The cutoff proves that the attacker deliberately stopped the Sysmon service on WS-104 at 06:14
For coverage it is identical to an outage: no process creation is recorded after 06:14
7.explanation: Coverage is judged by what the data lets the SOC see, not by why the data is missing: from 06:14 onwards no process creation exists, which hides the actors behind persistence, upload and log clearing. It is a scope gap, not a data-source gap, and the lesson explicitly says it is a generator property, not an outage or attacker action.

7.q: The proxy recorded WS-104 downloading invoice.docm from banyan-payroll-update.example at 06:12, two minutes before R1 fired, and it is the only macro-enabled document download of the day. How is this gap classified and closed?
options: A data-source gap: closing it needs a mail gateway, because the document arrived by email
A pure logic gap: data and fields exist, so a rule for macro-enabled Office downloads closes it
A field gap: the proxy must first parse a file-type field before any rule can test the download
No gap: R1 fired two minutes later, so the delivery step is already covered by an existing rule
7.explanation: The URL field already shows the .docm extension, so only the rule is missing; a rule on macro-enabled downloads, perhaps with a first-seen domain, would alert at delivery. R1 compensates for the gap, which lowers its priority, but compensation does not make the delivery step covered.

7.q: Rule R6 detects beaconing only through proxy logs. An implant that resolves its server over DNS and connects directly, bypassing the proxy, is in the threat model. Why should the detection team not try to close this gap with another proxy rule?
options: Proxy rules cannot inspect DNS names, so a resolver-based rule is needed on the existing proxy data
R6 already covers command and control, so a second rule would duplicate its alerts for the same beacon
The traffic never reaches the proxy and no DNS or flow data exists, so no rule of any kind can see it
The variant is too exotic for a microfinance threat model, so it should be accepted rather than closed
7.explanation: Writing rules to close data-source gaps is a listed mistake: no query can see traffic or DNS that is not logged, so the gap goes to the telemetry owner. R6 does not cover this variant at all, and the lesson treats DNS-based C2 as relevant, ranking it medium-high in the register.

7.q: In the Banyan gap register, the missing rule for .docm downloads is the cheapest gap to close, yet it ranks below the untraceable VPN session. What justifies that order?
options: Logic gaps always rank below data-source gaps, because data-source gaps take longer to close
The .docm download was a single event, while the VPN gap involved nine separate events from one address
The VPN gap was found first in the analysis, and the register keeps gaps in the order they were found
R1 compensates two minutes after delivery; nothing would catch the attacker in gopal's session
7.explanation: Prioritisation weighs likelihood, harm and compensating detections before cost: the VPN gap combines a likely technique for the sector, high harm and no compensation. Type alone does not decide the order (the 4625 logic gap ranks lowest, the DNS data-source gap third), and order of discovery is explicitly rejected as a method.

7.q: 'No process events after 06:14' ranks second in the Banyan register although R3, R4 and R5 partly compensate for it. Which factor most raises its priority?
options: Its breadth: one fix, full-day process telemetry, closes gaps in persistence, exfiltration and impairment
Its low cost: re-enabling an existing source needs only a rule change by detection engineering
Its lack of compensation: no other rule fires anywhere during the attacker's hands-on activity
Its type: scope gaps always outrank logic gaps because they affect every host in the estate
7.explanation: A data or scope fix is expensive but may close many gaps at once, which is part of the cost-and-breadth question. The gap is in fact partly compensated by R3, R4 and R5, and it is a pipeline or endpoint-team fix, not a rule change.

7.q: R1 currently compensates for the missing .docm delivery rule. A month later R1 is tuned and its parent condition changes. What does the lesson say this should trigger for the delivery gap?
options: Nothing, because the delivery gap's priority was fixed when it was entered in the register
Removal of the delivery gap from the register, because a tuned R1 is more precise than before
A re-assessment, because the compensation the gap relied on may have weakened or gone
An automatic downgrade of the gap to accepted, because tuning has been reviewed and approved
7.explanation: Compensations change: if R1 is tuned or broken, the gap it compensates becomes urgent, so compensating detections must be linked to the gaps they cover and re-assessed after major tuning changes. Higher precision after tuning says nothing about whether R1 still catches the delivery's follow-on step.

7.q: Two gaps receive scores of 7.4 and 7.1 from a team's likelihood-times-impact formula. What does the lesson advise about using these scores to order the work?
options: Always close the 7.4 gap first, because a consistent formula is what makes prioritisation defensible
Do not rely on the small numeric difference; compare written reasoning such as 'high, no compensation'
Re-score both on a ten-point scale, so that the difference between them becomes statistically clear
Close the cheaper of the two first, because cost decides between gaps with nearly equal scores
7.explanation: The exact arithmetic matters much less than recorded reasoning that can be challenged; 7.4 against 7.1 is false precision, while 'high, no compensation' against 'high, compensated by R1' is a real argument. Finer scales add more false precision, and cost is weighed after threat, not as an automatic tie-breaker.

7.q: A SOC manager decides not to fund DNS logging this year. For the DNS gap in the register to be recorded as 'Accept' rather than left as an unknown, what must the entry contain?
options: A documented risk decision by someone with authority to make it, with an owner and a date to reconsider it
A note that DNS-based command and control is outside the threat model, so the gap no longer needs a row
The name of a compensating rule, because a gap can only be accepted when another detection covers it
Approval by the detection engineering lead, because data-source gaps are owned by detection engineering
7.explanation: Accepting a gap is a dated, owned risk decision taken by someone with the authority, which makes it defensible if a regulator later asks; an unknown gap is not. A compensating rule defines the 'Compensate' decision, not 'Accept', and data-source gaps are owned by the telemetry owner, not detection engineering.

7.q: A team proposes publishing its complete gap register on the company intranet so that every department can see the SOC's progress. What concern does the lesson raise?
options: The register changes too often to publish, so readers would act on gaps that are already closed
Departments might request their own telemetry, which would distort the register's priority order
Publishing gaps breaches the CERT-In directions, which forbid disclosure of logging configuration
It maps where an attacker can act unseen, so it is sensitive and access must be restricted
7.explanation: Attackers exploit common gaps anyway, but a register tells an insider or intruder exactly where detection is absent, so it is confidential. The CERT-In directions mentioned in the lesson concern enabling and retaining logs, not secrecy of the register.

7.q: A vendor dashboard reports that the SOC detects 30% of all ATT&CK techniques and recommends raising the figure. Which critique follows from the lesson?
options: The percentage should be calculated per tactic, because techniques differ in how many sub-techniques they have
The figure is too low for any SOC, so the team should prioritise the cheapest techniques to raise it
Gaps should be measured against the organisation's threat model, not against every technique in the knowledge base
The dashboard ignores sub-techniques, so the true figure is likely to be much higher than reported
7.explanation: Counting the whole of ATT&CK is a listed mistake: a microfinance company should prioritise credential attacks on remote access, malicious documents and data theft, not techniques against industrial control systems. Raising the number by closing cheap, irrelevant cells is coverage theatre, not risk reduction.

7.q: After an upgrade, the endpoint agent is silently removed from a group of servers. Detections that depend on it simply stop producing hits. Which practice from the lesson would expose this new gap soonest?
options: Reviewing the gap register at its scheduled date, when every open row is re-assessed by its owner
Alerting on sources that stop reporting or fall below their baseline per host, and re-running scope checks
Watching per-rule precision, because rules that lose their data show a sharp fall in precision
Re-mapping every rule to ATT&CK after each upgrade, so that the coverage matrix stays current
7.explanation: Gaps open over time and are silent, so coverage must be monitored continuously: source-health alerts per host and rules whose hits fall to zero show the loss within hours or days. A scheduled register review would find it much later, and a rule with no data raises no alerts at all, so its precision does not visibly change.

7.q: The team believes it has closed the delivery gap with a new .docm download rule. According to the lesson, what is the strongest evidence that the gap is really closed?
options: Emulating the technique in an authorised lab and confirming the artefacts fire the rule
A peer review confirming that the rule's query is syntactically correct and mapped to ATT&CK
A month in production without false positives from the new rule on ordinary proxy traffic
Updating the coverage matrix so that the delivery cell changes from uncovered to covered
7.explanation: Emulation on authorised systems tests the whole chain, collection, parsing and logic, end to end, which is the strongest evidence a gap is closed. A quiet month shows good precision but not that the rule fires, and a matrix change without evidence is exactly coverage theatre.

7.q: A log source is collected and stored, but events arrive in the SIEM several minutes after they occur, after the scheduled rule that needs them has already run for that period. How does the lesson classify this?
options: As no gap, because the event is stored and will be found by any later search or hunt
As a logic gap, because the rule should be rewritten to search a longer period on each run
As a data-source gap, because a delayed source must be treated as if it were not collected
As a scope gap in time: the event is stored but not visible when the rule runs
7.explanation: Collection that does not cover the time the rule runs is partial collection, a scope gap in time, which the lesson ties to Module 2's collection-delay lesson. Widening the search period may be part of the fix, but the cause is in the pipeline, and storing the event later does not make the real-time detection work.

7.q: When building the business case to the network team for DNS resolver logging, which point from the lesson can strengthen the argument for an organisation operating in India?
options: CERT-In's 2022 directions require every organisation to deploy DNS tunnelling detection rules
CERT-In's 2022 directions require ICT logs to be enabled and kept for a rolling 180 days in India
CERT-In's 2022 directions require all logs to be retained for seven years before deletion
CERT-In's 2022 directions exempt organisations that already collect proxy logs from DNS logging
7.explanation: The lesson notes that the April 2022 directions require enabling logs of ICT systems and retaining them for a rolling 180 days within India, so a data-source gap can also be a compliance issue that helps fund the fix. The directions do not mandate specific detection rules or seven-year retention.

7.q: To close the 'Excel macro starts PowerShell' gap in R1, a manager proposes buying a new EDR product. Process creation with parent images is already collected for the period in question. What is the main flaw in the proposal?
options: It ignores that EDR telemetry would be a duplicate source, which the SIEM cannot deduplicate
It treats a field gap as a data-source gap, when the parent image must first be parsed correctly
It funds new telemetry for a logic gap that detection engineering could close in days with a rule and tests
It skips the risk decision, because every gap must be formally accepted before it can be closed
7.explanation: With the data already present, the gap is logic: R1 is narrower than the behaviour, so a rule change through the Lesson 5 change path closes it cheaply. Funding a log source to close a logic gap wastes money, just as writing rules for a data-source gap wastes engineering effort.

7.q: The Banyan data shows two failed console logons (4625) at 04:05 that were benign typos, and no rule looks for repeated local failures. Why does this gap rank lowest in the register?
options: The data is incomplete, because 4625 events are collected only for domain logons and not for console logons
Two failed logons are too few to support a rule, so the gap cannot be closed until more data exists
The 4625 events were benign, which shows that the technique is not used against this organisation
Console guessing is less likely for this organisation, and an account lockout policy limits it where configured
7.explanation: The gap is a real logic gap, since the 4625 events are collected and no rule looks at them, but likelihood for this sector is low and a lockout policy compensates. Benign typos on one day do not prove the technique is unused; they only show the data is available to write the rule.

7.q: The kit's R1 tests cover Word starting PowerShell and Explorer starting PowerShell, and both pass. Which later edit to R1 would leave every existing test green?
options: Deleting cmd.exe from the list of child images
Deleting the parent-image condition from the rule
Changing the parent image from Word to Excel
Deleting powershell.exe from the list of child images
7.explanation: No positive test exercises the cmd.exe branch, so removing it breaks nothing the suite checks. Dropping the parent condition would make the Explorer near-miss match and fail, and changing the parent or removing powershell.exe would break the Word positive.

7.q: Both kit Sigma rules declare level: high, yet RULE_META in triage.py gives R1 severity 3 and R5 severity 4, and no mapping is documented. How should the reviewer raise this?
options: Blocking: sigma check rejects rules whose level disagrees with the triage scale, so R1 cannot be deployed until the two values are aligned by hand
Note only: triage values are an operational choice and are expected to override the Sigma level freely
Should fix: the same level becomes two triage severities, so agree a written level-to-severity table that both files follow
Should fix: lower R1 to level: medium in Sigma, because triage.py is always the authoritative source
7.explanation: The defect is an undocumented inconsistency between two artefacts, so the fix is a mapping both follow; which side changes is for that mapping to decide. sigma check cannot see triage.py at all, so it does not block anything here.

7.q: triage.py computes priority as severity x confidence x asset criticality. R1 on WS-104 (criticality 3, confidence 0.8) scores 7.2, tied with the VPN spray alert. What happens if R1's severity is raised from 3 to 4?
options: It scores 9.6 and ties with the log-cleared alert at the top
It scores 9.6 and ranks clearly above the VPN spray alert
It scores 8.1 and ranks just above the VPN spray alert
It stays at 7.2, because confidence caps the final priority
7.explanation: 4 x 0.8 x 3 = 9.6, which breaks the tie with the 7.2 spray alert. The log-cleared alert scores 10.8 (4 x 0.9 x 3), so R1 does not tie with it; 8.1 would need confidence 0.9 with severity 3.

7.q: Reviewing rk_security_log_cleared.yml, an engineer recalls that published rules map clearing Windows event logs to T1070.001 and doubts the rule's attack.t1685.005 tag. What does the lesson say to do first?
options: Ask the author to switch the tag to attack.t1070.001, since most published material and older rules use that ID
Keep both attack.t1685.005 and attack.t1070.001 on the rule so that either ATT&CK version reports it as covered
Remove the tag until MITRE publishes a mapping note, then re-tag the rule during the next quarterly content review cycle for the SOC
Check the tag against the ATT&CK version the team has pinned, for example with pySigma's validator, and record that version
7.explanation: A tag you cannot verify is a finding, but unverified is not wrong: verify against the pinned dataset before asking for a change. Switching to T1070.001 on memory would have introduced an ID that the validator's ATT&CK 20.1 data rejects.

7.q: The validator, loaded with ATT&CK 20.1, accepts attack.t1685.005 and rejects attack.t1070.001. What finding about R5's tags remains after this check?
options: None remains: the validator has accepted the technique tag, so the ATT&CK tags row of the checklist can be ticked and closed
The rule does not record its ATT&CK version, lacks a tactic tag, and older content still using T1070.001 now disagrees in coverage
The rule must revert to T1070.001, because the validator's data is newer than the references the SOC has already published
The rule needs a second technique tag for T1070.001, because that ID still describes indicator removal in the current ATT&CK release
7.explanation: Verification removed the doubt about the ID but exposed that the mapping version is unrecorded, so the next reviewer will hit the same question; a tactic tag is also missing and older rules need re-mapping. The validator rejects T1070.001, so reverting or adding it would be wrong.

7.q: A reviewer proposes adding attack.defense-evasion as R5's tactic tag. Against the pinned ATT&CK 20.1 data, how should the author respond?
options: Use attack.defense-impairment, which the validator accepted, since it flagged attack.defense-evasion as invalid
Accept attack.defense-evasion, since every Indicator Removal technique still sits under the Defense Evasion tactic
Add no tactic tag at all, since a technique tag already implies its tactic in every ATT&CK version and backend
Tag both tactics, since the validator treats a tactic that is invalid in its version as an informational issue
7.explanation: In the lesson's probe, the validator accepted attack.defense-impairment and flagged attack.defense-evasion as invalid for the version in use, and T1685.005 sits under Defense Impairment. Omitting the tactic is the very gap the review raised.

7.q: sigma check on rk_office_spawns_shell.yml reports '0 condition errors'. What has this established?
options: The condition matches at least one event in the SOC's collected process telemetry
Each branch of the condition is covered by a positive test in the rule's test file
The condition means the same as the hand-written minisiem translation of the rule
Every name used in the condition refers to a selection that is defined in the rule
7.explanation: A condition error is a reference in the condition that does not resolve to a defined selection, so zero means the names line up. sigma check never sees the data, the tests or the SQL translation, which is why those remain human review items.

7.q: Which of these defects could sigma check on its own have reported during the automated gate?
options: R1 declaring level: high while triage.py gives the same rule severity 3
R5's minisiem SQL matching event 1102 from any source, not only the Security log
A probe rule tagged attack.t9999.999, a technique that does not exist in ATT&CK
R1 having no positive test for Word starting cmd.exe in test_rules.py
7.explanation: The ATT&CK validator in pySigma rejected the invented tag as InvalidATTACKTagIssue. The other three defects live in triage.py, minisiem.py or the test file, which sigma check does not read.

7.q: test_rules.py has test classes for R1, R2 and R6 but nothing at all for R5. How does the lesson classify this finding?
options: A note, since R5 is a single EventID condition whose behaviour is obvious to anyone simply reading it
Should fix, since sigma check already passed and so the rule is known to be well formed
Blocking under most teams' standards, since every rule needs a positive and a near-miss negative
No finding, since R5 produced one correct hit when the rules ran over the Banyan dataset
7.explanation: A positive plus a near-miss negative per rule is the minimum bar, so a rule with no tests at all cannot ship. A passing sigma check or one correct dataset hit says nothing about whether a broken R5 would be noticed.

7.q: Which single new test for R5 would both meet the minimum testing bar and have exposed the reviewer's data finding about R5's SQL?
options: An event with ID 1102 from a non-Security source that must not match
A Security event with ID 1103 that must not match the rule
A Security event with ID 1102 on a second host that must also match the rule
An empty events table on which the rule must return no rows
7.explanation: R5's SQL tests only event_id=1102, so a 1102 from another source would match and fail the test, revealing the missing source restriction. An ID-1103 negative checks the event ID, not the source, and would pass against the current SQL.

7.q: A Sigma selection contains ParentImage|endswith: '\WINWORD.EXE' and Image|endswith with the list '\powershell.exe' and '\cmd.exe'. Which process-creation event does it match?
options: Explorer as parent starting cmd.exe
Word as parent starting wscript.exe
PowerShell as parent starting Word
Word as parent starting cmd.exe
7.explanation: Separate fields in one selection must all hold, while a list under one field means any of its values. Word starting cmd.exe satisfies both fields; Explorer fails the parent field and wscript.exe is not in the child list.

7.q: The Sigma R1 uses ParentImage|endswith '\WINWORD.EXE', while minisiem's R1 uses lower(parent_image) LIKE '%winword.exe%'. How does the lesson treat this difference?
options: As a blocking finding: the SQL cannot match real Sysmon paths, because LIKE in SQLite is always case-sensitive
As translation drift recorded as a note: the SQL is a contains match and so slightly broader than the Sigma rule
As no finding: lowering the field and using LIKE gives exactly the same semantics as the Sigma endswith modifier
As a should-fix finding: the SQL is narrower than Sigma, so some Word-launched shells would be missed in triage
7.explanation: A contains pattern accepts winword.exe anywhere in the path, not only at the end, so the deployed query means slightly more than the portable rule; the lesson records it as a note. It still matches the real path, so it is neither blocking nor narrower.

7.q: During an authorised purple-team exercise a renamed copy of PowerShell, started from a Word macro, does not trigger R1. How does the lesson treat this weakness in review?
options: As a recorded known limitation, pointing to an original-file-name variant where telemetry supplies that field
As a blocking finding, because any rule that an attacker can evade must be rewritten before it is deployed
As a reason to add every renamed variant the red team used to the rule's list of child image names
As outside review scope, because evasion is assessed during hunting rather than during rule review
7.explanation: Image names are attacker-controlled, so name-based matching is a known limitation to document, with a pointer to a sturdier variant keyed on the PE original file name. Chasing the red team's chosen names does not fix the underlying weakness.

7.q: Which review comment best follows the lesson's location, observation, evidence, action, class shape?
options: The tags on the Office rule look incomplete to me; maybe worth having another look before this ships.
rk_office_spawns_shell.yml tags: rule matches cmd.exe but omits attack.t1059.003; add the tag. Should fix.
I would have written this rule using a different mapping style; please align it with how I tag rules.
Tags: should fix. Please review all ATT&CK tags in the file again and update anything that seems off to you.
7.explanation: The first comment names the file and field, states what the logic covers that the tags miss, and gives the action and class, so the author can act at once. The others are vague, personal or lack evidence.

7.q: An engineer with repository access quietly removes one value from a rule's child-image list. All unit tests still pass. Which control makes this change visible and attributable?
options: Running sigma check on every commit before the change is merged to main
Running the full unit test suite in the pipeline on every pull request
Raising the severity of the affected rule so that its alerts are noticed sooner
Mandatory second-person review of every change, recorded in version control
7.explanation: Review by someone other than the author, kept in the change history, is separation of duties: the edit has to be seen and approved by a second person. sigma check and the tests both pass for this change, so neither reveals it.

7.q: A change adds a suppression to triage.py with a clear reason and a change ticket, but no owner and no expiry date. How should it be classified?
options: A note, because the reason and ticket already document why it was added
Should fix, because the expiry can be added once the ticket is later closed
Blocking, because a suppression needs an owner and an expiry before it can ship
No finding, because suppressions are tuning choices outside the rule review scope
7.explanation: The lesson lists a suppression without owner or expiry among blocking findings, because an unowned, permanent suppression can blind the SOC indefinitely. The kit's own suppression carries CHG-1042 and an expiry of 2026-12-31 for that reason.

7.q: Why does the review checklist place the Logic and Data rows before Metadata, ATT&CK tags and Severity?
options: Logic and Data findings are always blocking while the other rows never are
The automated gates check metadata, so those rows can be skimmed quickly
Metadata and severity can be changed after deployment without a review
A rule that cannot match real data makes tags, metadata and severity moot
7.explanation: Logic and Data establish whether the rule can work at all; Tests then provide evidence for them, and the descriptive rows matter only for a working rule. Classification depends on the finding, not the row, and every row still needs a full review.

7.q: The worked review produced findings in several artefacts. Which one best shows a defect living in the gap between files, where no single-file automated check looks?
options: Sigma level high for R1 against RULE_META severity 3 in triage.py
An undefined selection name used in a Sigma rule's condition line
A YAML indentation error that stops a Sigma rule from being parsed
An invented technique ID such as attack.t9999.999 in a rule's tags
7.explanation: The severity finding exists only when the Sigma file and triage.py are read together. Undefined selection names, parse errors and invalid tags are all visible inside one Sigma file and are caught by sigma check.

7.q: Which question falls outside the reviewer's responsibility in the lesson's model of rule review?
options: Whether every field the rule uses exists after parsing
Whether the tests include a near-miss for each condition
Whether the SOC should detect this behaviour at all
Whether the level follows the documented severity mapping
7.explanation: Whether to detect a behaviour is settled at the requirement stage; the reviewer reads the requirement but judges whether this rule is safe and useful to deploy as written. Fields, near-miss tests and severity mapping are all checklist rows.

7.q: A rule that detects Word starting PowerShell is tagged with attack.t1204.002, attack.t1059.001 and attack.t1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact), because 'macro attacks often end in ransomware'. What should the reviewer ask for?
options: Keep T1486, because tags should reflect the attacker's likely final objective
Remove T1486, because tags must describe behaviour the rule itself observes
Replace T1486 with an Impact tactic tag, which is less specific but still valid
Keep T1486 but lower the rule's level, since impact is only a probable outcome
7.explanation: Tags are checked in both directions; one justified only by what an attacker might do later makes the coverage map claim detection of encryption that this rule never sees. A broader Impact tactic tag has the same flaw.

7.q: A reviewer raised 'this rule may flood the queue'. The author replies with a 30-day historical replay showing two hits, both confirmed true positives. What should the reviewer do?
options: Accept the evidence, resolve the finding and record why it was resolved
Keep the finding open until the rule has run in production for a month
Ask for a wider replay, since thirty days can never show expected volume
Escalate to the SOC manager, since authors may not close their own findings
7.explanation: The lesson says that when an author answers with data, such as a replay, the reviewer accepts it and records why. Holding the finding without a reason, or demanding more data by default, turns review into obstruction rather than evidence.

7.q: A one-line pull request raises a rule's failed-login threshold from 5 to 10. The author asks for a quick approval because 'it is only a number'. Why does the lesson reject rubber-stamping it?
options: Small changes skip the automated gates, so the reviewer must re-run sigma check on them by hand
Threshold edits always alter the rule's ATT&CK mapping, so its technique tags must be redone as well
Raising a threshold can silently remove detection, so its effect and boundary tests must be checked
One-line changes cannot be reverted cleanly, so they need more approvals than larger changes do
7.explanation: Removing a list value or raising a threshold narrows what the rule fires on while every existing test can still pass, so the reviewer checks the effect and that tests sit at the new boundary. Gates run on every change regardless of size.

7.q: The automated gates pass and the reviewer, after working through the checklist, has no findings. What should the review record contain?
options: A single approval comment, because no findings means nothing needs writing
The sigma check and unit-test output pasted in, which proves the rule works
A request for a second reviewer, because a clean review is likely incomplete
Which checklist areas were examined and what evidence was looked at for each
7.explanation: A review that only re-runs the gates is not a review; even a clean review records what was checked and on what evidence, so the approval can be relied on later. Pasting gate output repeats the automated step.

7.q: Why does the lesson advise rotating reviewers rather than letting authors review their own rules?
options: Version control systems refuse to merge changes approved by their author
The author's own tests and reading share the same blind spots as the rule
sigma check results differ depending on which engineer runs the validator
Authors are not permitted to read the triage configuration for their rule
7.explanation: Tests prove the rule does what its author intended, not that the intention was right, and self-review inherits that limit. Rotation also spreads knowledge across the team instead of leaving each rule with one person.

7.q: Converting rk_security_log_cleared.yml without a processing pipeline produced a query for EventID=1102 with no restriction to the Security log. What does the reviewer ask for?
options: Convert with a pipeline that matches how the SOC indexes Security events, and add the source restriction to the SQL
Add a second selection for EventID 104 so that the converted query covers the System log as well as Security
Accept the converted query, since 1102 is unique to the Security log and so the missing restriction is harmless here
Rewrite the Sigma logsource as category: process_creation so that the backend adds the correct index filter
7.explanation: Without a pipeline the logsource is not mapped to an index or source, so the query can match an event numbered 1102 from another source. The fix belongs in the conversion pipeline and in minisiem's R5 SQL; event IDs are not unique across all sources.

7.q: R7's first version ends with (julianday(p.ts) - julianday(d.ts)) * 1440 <= 10, and the test with a spawn exactly ten minutes after the download fails with '0 != 1'. Why?
options: julianday() returns floating-point days, so ten minutes computes to 10.000000074505806, which is not <= 10
julianday() ignores the trailing Z, so the spawn timestamp is read one hour later than the download time
SQLite evaluates <= as a strict comparison when both operands are the result of a floating-point product
The ordering check p.ts >= d.ts compares the strings byte by byte and fails when the minutes differ by ten
7.explanation: Ten minutes is 1/144 of a day, which has no exact binary representation, so the product lands a hair above 10. The ordering check passes for this pair, and <= is inclusive in SQLite; the failure is purely the floating-point error.

7.q: The fixed R7 tests CAST(strftime('%s', p.ts) AS INTEGER) - CAST(strftime('%s', d.ts) AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 0 AND 600. Which requirement clause does the lower bound of 0 enforce?
options: The rule must not alert on a spawn that happened on a different host
The rule must not alert when the download and spawn share a timestamp
The rule must not alert on a spawn that happened before the download
The rule must not alert on a spawn more than ten minutes after download
7.explanation: A negative difference means the process started before the download, so a lower bound of 0 rejects it and replaces the old p.ts >= d.ts check. BETWEEN is inclusive, so equal timestamps (a gap of 0) still match; the upper bound 600 handles the ten-minute clause.

7.q: Why does the lab add R7 as a new correlation rule instead of tuning R1 to require a preceding macro-document download?
options: SQLite cannot join two log sources inside a rule that already filters on Sysmon process events
R1 must still fire when a malicious document arrives by email or USB with no proxy event
R1 is mapped to Execution, and a rule may carry tags from only one ATT&CK tactic
Tuning R1 would change its rule ID, which would break the R1 test class in the kit
7.explanation: Requiring a download would blind R1 to every non-web delivery path, so R1 stays as the broad signal and R7 adds a higher-confidence one for the web-delivered case. SQLite self-joins work fine, as R7 itself shows.

7.q: After R7 is added, python triage.py stops with KeyError: 'R7'. What is the effect on the alert queue, and what does the lesson recommend beyond adding the entry?
options: Only R7's alert is dropped; add a default severity for any rule missing from RULE_META
R7's alert is ranked last; give R7 the same RULE_META entry as R1 to keep the order
Only alerts on WS-104 are dropped; enrich the host table so every hit has a lookup
No alert is ranked at all; add a test that every key in RULES has a RULE_META entry
7.explanation: The lookup RULE_META[rule] raises and ends the whole run, so every alert is lost, not just R7's. The integration fix is the missing entry plus a test that would catch the next rule added without one; a silent default would hide the gap.

7.q: With RULE_META R7 = (3, 0.9) on WS-104 (asset criticality 3), R7 scores 8.1 and ranks above R1's 7.2 for the same event. What justifies the higher confidence?
options: R7 carries a higher Sigma level than R1, and triage.py reads that level directly
Two independent observations, a download and a shell start, agree on host and time
R7 alerts on two hosts at once, which doubles the asset criticality used in triage
R7 is the newest rule, and new rules start at high confidence until they are tuned
7.explanation: Correlation needs both a macro-document download and an Office-spawned shell on the same host within the window, which is stronger evidence than R1's single event. Severity stays at 3 because the behaviour is the same; triage.py uses RULE_META, not the Sigma level.

7.q: In a throwaway copy, sed changes BETWEEN 0 AND 600 to BETWEEN -600 AND 600 and the suite is re-run. Which test should fail?
options: test_spawn_before_download_not_matched
test_spawn_after_window_not_matched
test_spawn_at_exactly_ten_minutes_matched
test_spawn_on_other_host_not_matched
7.explanation: The mutant accepts spawns up to 600 seconds before the download, so the test whose spawn is at 06:11, a minute before, now matches and fails. The upper bound is unchanged, so the after-window and boundary tests behave as before.

7.q: What does the mutation step in the lab demonstrate that a green run of the 14 tests cannot?
options: That R7 finds every malicious-document chain in real production data
That the Sigma correlation version behaves the same as the SQL
That the ten-minute window is the right length for real users
That the tests can fail, by catching a deliberately weakened rule
7.explanation: A suite that never fails proves nothing; weakening the rule on purpose and seeing exactly the matching test fail shows the tests have teeth. Mutation says nothing about production recall, the Sigma version or the window length.

7.q: A student mutates one clause of R7 in the throwaway copy, re-runs the suite and all 14 tests still pass. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The mutation was harmless, so the clause can be removed from the rule
The suite is working, because a passing run means the rule is fully correct
No negative test isolates that clause, so a test for it should be added
The copy is stale, so the student must re-run python minisiem.py load
7.explanation: Surviving mutants reveal untested logic; the fix is a near-miss test that fails when that clause is weakened. A survivor does not show the clause is unnecessary, and the unit tests use in-memory events, not minisiem.db.

7.q: On importing the edited minisiem.py, Python prints SyntaxWarning: "\w" is an invalid escape sequence. What is the likely cause?
options: SQLite's LIKE does not accept backslashes, and Python is warning you about that
The test file's WORD constant uses forward slashes instead of backslashes
The R7 SQL string lost its r prefix, so '%\winword.exe' is read as an escape
The JSONL dataset stores paths with doubled backslashes that Python rejects
7.explanation: Without the r prefix, \w inside a normal string is an invalid escape that recent Python versions warn about. In SQLite LIKE the backslash has no special meaning, so the raw string passes it through unchanged as intended.

7.q: R7 passes all 14 unit tests but python minisiem.py rules reports 0 hits for it on the Banyan data. Which approach does the lab suggest for finding the cause?
options: Confirm the dataset was reloaded, then run each clause separately with search
Delete the R7 test class, since tests that pass while the rule fails are wrong
Widen the window to 3600 seconds until the rule produces at least one hit
Run sigma check on the Sigma version, which reports why the SQL returns nothing
