7.explanation: The troubleshooting list points to a skipped load or a missing backslash in a LIKE pattern, and debugging clause by clause with search isolates which condition removes the chain. Widening the window hides the defect, and sigma check never sees the SQL.

7.q: The Sigma version of R7 passes sigma check and uses group-by: Computer. What does the review checklist's Data row raise that the validator could not?
options: temporal_ordered correlations are rejected by every backend, so the rule cannot be converted to any query
timespan must be expressed in seconds, so 10m is read as ten months by most conversion backends
The correlation needs its own logsource block, without which it would match every event in the SIEM
Proxy logs do not normally carry Computer, so the base rules share no group-by value without field mapping
7.explanation: Computer is a Windows event field; proxy events record the client differently, so a real SIEM needs the pipeline to map both into one field. minisiem avoids this only because normalisation already put both into host. sigma check validates structure, not field presence.

7.q: rk_macro_doc_then_shell.yml reports 0 errors and 0 issues from sigma check. What does this result establish?
options: The correlation produces the same single hit on WS-104 as the minisiem SQL
The portable rule is well formed, not that it runs correctly on your data
Every converted backend query has been tested against the Banyan dataset
The group-by field exists in both the proxy and the Sysmon log sources
7.explanation: sigma check parses and validates the rule; no conversion backend was installed in the lab, so no converted query was tested. Until one is, the SQL version proven by the unit tests is the trusted implementation.

7.q: The Sigma correlation uses type: temporal_ordered. If it were changed to a temporal type that does not require the listed order, which requirement clause would no longer be enforced?
options: Not alerting on a spawn that happened before the download
Not alerting on a spawn that happened on a different host
Not alerting on an ordinary .docx download from the web
Not alerting on a spawn more than ten minutes afterwards
7.explanation: temporal_ordered requires the base rules to match in the listed order, download then spawn; without order, a spawn followed by a download would also correlate. Host is enforced by group-by, the window by timespan and the file type by the base rule.

7.q: R7 matches lower(p.parent_image) LIKE '%\winword.exe' rather than '%winword.exe'. What does the backslash add?
options: It makes the comparison case-insensitive, matching Windows path behaviour
It stops a match on a different binary whose name merely ends in winword.exe
It anchors the match to the System32 folder where Office is installed
It escapes the % wildcard so that SQLite treats it as a literal percent character
7.explanation: Requiring the path separator before the name means the image must be exactly winword.exe, not something like notwinword.exe. Case-insensitivity comes from lower(), and in SQLite LIKE the backslash is an ordinary character, not an escape.

7.q: R7 joins proxy and Sysmon events on host. A reviewer learns that at another site the proxy records only the client IP address, which DHCP reassigns. What is the risk?
options: The join raises an SQL error at run time, so R7 stops and the pipeline reports the failure loudly
R7 alerts on every proxy event, because an IP never equals a host name in the comparison
Triage ranks R7 lower, because asset criticality cannot be looked up from an IP address
The join can fail silently or pair the wrong machines, so R7 misses or misattributes chains
7.explanation: A correlation key is only as good as its meaning in both sources; if the proxy's host is a reassigned IP, matches are lost or attached to the wrong workstation without any error. A failed equality returns no rows rather than every row.

7.q: In the lab's Sigma version the base rule rk_macro_doc_download has level low, even though a macro document started the Banyan intrusion. What justifies that level?
options: The proxy log source is unreliable, so its rules can never carry a higher Sigma level
Initial-access techniques are always rated low, because execution has not yet happened
Teams that exchange macro workbooks make the download alone common and weak evidence
The replay found only one .docm on the dataset, so the rule is too rare to be useful
7.explanation: The research replay found one .docm in a day of synthetic data, but real data would show many from business units that use macros, so the download alone should not alert at high severity; it gains weight only in the correlation.

7.q: A colleague proposes deleting test_spawn_at_exactly_ten_minutes_matched because 'the real chain on WS-104 is two minutes, so the edge never happens'. What is the best response?
options: Delete it: boundary cases rarely occur in production, so they add cost but little value
Replace it with a test at nine minutes, which exercises the window without float issues
Keep it, but mark it as an expected failure, since float error at the edge is unavoidable
Keep it: it is the only test that exposed the float bug and it guards against its return
7.explanation: The boundary test was invisible-to-everything-else evidence of a real defect, and keeping it stops the floating-point version from coming back. A nine-minute test would pass under the buggy code, and the integer fix makes the boundary exact, so no failure is expected.

7.q: Each R7 test is built from chain() with exactly one argument changed from the matching default. Why does the lab construct tests this way?
options: A failure then points at exactly one condition of the rule
Fewer events per test make the suite run measurably faster
The run() helper accepts at most one changed field per call
Changing several fields would make the SQL join return errors
7.explanation: If a near miss differs from the matching chain in one field only, its failure isolates that condition; changing several at once can let a test pass for the wrong reason. Speed and helper limits are not the motivation.

7.q: Besides fixing the boundary, which weakness of the original R7 does the integer-seconds condition also remove?
options: Reliance on host names being lower case, which breaks when a source writes WS-104 in mixed case
Reliance on SQLite's LIKE operator, which mis-handles backslashes when the pattern ends in an .exe image name
Reliance on comparing timestamp strings, which works only while every source writes the identical ISO format
Reliance on events arriving in time order, which fails when the proxy log is ingested late
7.explanation: The old p.ts >= d.ts compared strings, which orders correctly only if all sources use the same format; converting both to Unix seconds compares actual times. Host case and LIKE handling are not touched by the fix, and the query never relied on ingest order.

7.q: The lab's Sigma correlation declares level: high, its base rules are low and medium, and RULE_META gives R7 severity 3. What does the review record say about this?
options: The correlation level must equal the highest base-rule level, so it should be lowered to medium now
Severity is to be confirmed against the team's level table, re-opening the earlier mapping finding
RULE_META must be raised to 4, since every high Sigma rule maps to the top of the triage scale
Nothing, because a correlation's level is informational and never used by the triage process
7.explanation: The kit still has no written level-to-severity mapping, so the lab records R7's severity as provisional pending that table. Neither base-rule levels nor R5's high-equals-4 entry define a rule, which is exactly why the mapping is needed.

7.q: The R7 test class has positives for a .docm with Word starting PowerShell and an upper-case .DOCM with cmd.exe, plus a boundary positive. Which branch of R7's logic has no positive test?
options: An .xlsm download followed by Excel starting a shell
A Word parent that starts cmd.exe as the child process
A URL whose file extension is written in upper case
A spawn exactly 600 seconds after the download time
7.explanation: Every test uses the default Word parent and a .docm URL, so the Excel parent and .xlsm branches could be deleted with all tests still green. cmd.exe, upper case and the 600-second edge each have a test.

7.q: Banyan adds a requirement clause: R7 'must not alert when the document comes from the internal file server'. Following the lab's method, what should accompany the new SQL condition?
options: A positive test with an internal-server URL, to prove that the new condition runs
A replay of the Banyan dataset, since it already contains internal-server downloads
A near-miss test identical to the matching chain except for an internal-server URL
A raised R7 confidence in RULE_META, since excluding the server removes noise
7.explanation: Each must-not clause becomes a near-miss negative that differs from the matching chain in that one respect, so removing the condition would fail it. A positive cannot prove an exclusion, and the dataset replay is not a test.

7.q: After the fix, R7 produces one hit on the 340-event Banyan dataset. A manager concludes that R7's false-positive rate in production will be close to zero. What is the problem with that conclusion?
options: One hit proves recall, not precision; precision can be measured only after an incident
The dataset is synthetic, so no result from it says anything at all about the rule's own logic
The hit came from the unit tests, which use different events from those in the dataset
The dataset holds one true chain; volume must be estimated by replaying weeks of real data
7.explanation: One hit on a dataset built with one chain shows the rule finds it and leaves R1 to R6 unchanged, not how often benign activity matches. The lab's Step 2 replay is the method for estimating volume before deployment.

7.q: WS-104 downloads two .docm files, at 06:12 and 06:13, and Word starts PowerShell at 06:15. How many rows does the fixed R7 query return?
options: One, because the rule reports each spawn only once
Two, one for each download paired with the single spawn
One, because only the closest download is paired
Zero, because two downloads make the pairing too ambiguous
7.explanation: R7 is a self-join that pairs every qualifying proxy event with every qualifying Sysmon event on the same host, and both gaps (180 and 120 seconds) are inside the window. The SQL has no deduplication or nearest-match logic, so two rows result.

7.q: An adversary in an authorised exercise learns R7's ten-minute window and waits fifteen minutes after the download before opening the document. What detection coverage remains for that step?
options: R1 still fires on Word starting PowerShell, without the download context
R7 still fires, because the window is measured from the user's last logon
Nothing fires, because R1 was retired once R7 covered the same behaviour
R5 fires, because a delayed spawn is recorded as a log-clearing event
7.explanation: R7 is deliberately additive: R1 keeps alerting on the Office-spawned shell, just with lower confidence. The lab notes that window length is a tuning decision because an adversary can pace activity to sit outside it.

8.q: The VPN log shows a burst of 40 failed logons for one account from an external address, with no successful logon. How should this activity be classified under the lifecycle's terminology?
options: An adverse event that warrants triage; it becomes an incident only when an authorised role declares one
An incident, because any activity that threatens an account's confidentiality is by definition an incident
A routine event, because no logon succeeded and therefore no harm occurred
An indicator that an incident has already occurred on the VPN gateway itself
8.explanation: A failed-logon burst has potential for harm, which makes it an adverse event; incident status is a recorded declaration by the role the policy names, not a property of a single alert. Calling it an incident floods the IR process with triage-level work.

8.q: While WS-104 is being isolated, a responder finds a second beacon domain in the workstation's memory that the SOC had not seen before. What should happen next?
options: Continue eradication as planned and hunt for the new domain during the post-incident review
Block the new domain immediately and close the incident once the beacons stop
Return to analysis: hunt for the new domain across all hosts before eradication continues
Rebuild WS-104 at once so that the second channel is removed together with the disk
8.explanation: This is the lifecycle's 'new indicators, rescope' feedback path: a new indicator found during containment sends the team back to analysis so that other hosts using it are found. Blocking it and closing assumes WS-104 is the only host involved, which nobody has checked.

8.q: Which of the following is a precursor rather than an indicator in the SP 800-61 Rev. 2 sense?
options: Word starting PowerShell on a finance workstation shortly after a download
A sector advisory that payroll-themed phishing is targeting microfinance companies
A 48 MB upload from a workstation to a look-alike file-sharing domain
A new local administrator account created on a finance workstation outside change hours
8.explanation: A precursor warns that an incident may happen in future; the advisory describes a threat, not activity already seen in your environment. The other three are indicators that something may already be happening; a specific precursor can still be acted on, for example by watching for look-alike payroll domains.

8.q: Analysts see files on a shared file server being encrypted, and the encryption is spreading to more shares by the minute. The IR lead asks whether containment should wait until scoping is finished. What is the right advice?
options: Wait, because containing before scoping always tips off the attacker and loses other footholds
Wait until the hunt searches confirm whether any other hosts are involved in the activity
Take and hash a full disk image first, then contain once the evidence is preserved
Contain now, because serious ongoing harm outweighs the benefit of scoping first
8.explanation: Scope before containing is the default, but the lesson names active encryption as the exception where containment cannot wait. Preserving evidence matters, but it must never delay stopping serious harm, so imaging first is the wrong order here.

8.q: The hunt script reports no other hosts contacting the case domains and shows the Word-to-PowerShell pair on only one host. Which scoping statement should the analyst give the IR lead?
options: No other host is affected, so containment can safely be limited to WS-104
Within the telemetry available, the endpoint compromise appears limited to WS-104
The hunt proves that no other device on the network ever contacted the case domains
Scope cannot be stated at all until every host has been forensically imaged
8.explanation: A scoping statement is only as good as the telemetry behind it, so it must name its basis. 'No other host is affected' overstates what proxy and process records can show; refusing to state any scope until every host is imaged would stall a decision the IR lead needs.

8.q: A Tier 2 analyst is certain that a case is a serious intrusion. Who should record the decision that it is an incident?
options: The role named in the IR policy, usually the IR lead, based on the analyst's facts
The analyst who opened the first alert, because they know the evidence best
The SIEM, automatically, once the case priority score passes a set threshold
The legal team, because the declaration may start a regulatory reporting clock running
8.explanation: Declaration commits people and money and may start clocks, so the IR policy assigns it to a named role; the analyst supplies the facts and the time noticed. Legal assesses reportability, but it does not normally own the decision that a case is an incident.

8.q: In Banyan, the malicious document was downloaded at 06:12Z and, in the illustrative SOC times, the incident was noticed at 08:25Z. What is the gap and what does it represent?
options: 73 minutes; it measures how long containment took once the incident was declared
133 minutes; it measures how long the analyst took to escalate the case to the IR lead
73 minutes; it is the attacker's free time between initial access and detection
133 minutes; it is the attacker's free time before the SOC noticed the activity
8.explanation: 06:12Z to 08:25Z is 2 hours 13 minutes, or 133 minutes, during which the upload and log clearing had already happened. It is time between first malicious activity and noticing, not escalation or containment time; reducing it is the aim of most SOC improvement work.

8.q: The attacker cleared the Security log on WS-104 at 08:17Z (event ID 1102), yet the analysts could still reconstruct the earlier activity. Why?
options: Event ID 1102 records every deleted entry, so the cleared events can be restored from it
The R5 rule fired before the clearing and quarantined a protected copy of the log file on the host
The earlier events had already been forwarded to central logging before the log was cleared
The attacker cleared only the System log, so the Security log on the host stayed intact
8.explanation: Centralised telemetry, built during preparation, meant the events had left the host before 08:17Z. Event 1102 only records that the log was cleared; it does not contain the deleted entries.

8.q: For Banyan, the analyst recommends isolating WS-104, blocking both domains and the spraying address, and resetting both accounts as one coordinated set rather than one at a time. What is the main reason?
options: Each action needs separate approval, and one combined request is approved much more quickly
The SOC executes all containment itself, and one EDR job is simpler to run than several
Containing one foothold while another stays open warns the attacker and leaves a way back
The CERT-In report must list every containment action taken within one log entry
8.explanation: Piecemeal containment tells the attacker they have been seen while a second foothold (here gopal's VPN access) remains usable. The SOC normally advises rather than executes containment, so the EDR job option misdescribes its role.

8.q: WS-104 was isolated at 09:05Z. At 09:20Z the analyst re-runs the proxy search and still sees regular requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Either the isolation failed or another host is infected; the scope must be re-examined
The proxy logs are probably delayed, so recheck only after the next status update
The domain block failed, but the isolation of WS-104 can still be marked as verified
The requests are cached lookups that continue briefly and can be ignored after isolation
8.explanation: Verification means the detecting search should go quiet after the action; continuing beacons mean isolation did not work or a second host is beaconing, which sends the team back to analysis. Assuming log delay, without checking which host the requests came from, risks missing a second foothold.

8.q: Evidence from WS-104 has been exported and hashed, and the IR lead now asks how the workstation should be returned to service. What should the analyst recommend?
options: Remove the malware and the svc_update account, then return the cleaned device to divya for use
Rebuild it from a known-good image, then watch closely for the case indicators on its return
Rebuild it at once to get the user working, and recover any evidence later from backups
Return it after a full antivirus scan reports clean, keeping it isolated for one more day
8.explanation: Recovery should rebuild from known-good state rather than 'clean' a compromised machine, because unknown persistence may survive cleaning, and a returning host is a re-entry risk that needs close monitoring. Rebuilding before preserving evidence destroys what scoping and any legal process need.

8.q: The svc_update account and the malware have been removed from WS-104. What else must eradication include for this incident to be complete?
options: Deleting the Banyan events from the SIEM so that the case can be formally closed
Blocking every file-sharing service across the organisation on a permanent basis
Re-enabling the Security log on WS-104 and restoring all of the cleared entries from a backup
Fixing the weaknesses used: macro-enabled internet documents and a guessable VPN password
8.explanation: Eradication removes the attacker's presence and the weakness they used to get in; otherwise the same route works again. Re-enabling logging is useful hardening, but it does not close the entry points the attacker actually used.

8.q: In the post-incident review, the team notes that the beacon rule R6 had the lowest priority score in the queue (3.6) although it showed command and control. What is the appropriate outcome?
options: A tracked detection-tuning change that feeds back into Preparation for the next incident
Retiring R6 entirely, since the other five rules detected the incident without its help anyway
Lowering the priority of R1 so that R6 appears relatively higher in future queues
Accepting the score, because beaconing alerts are by nature low-severity findings
8.explanation: The 'improvements' arrow runs from Post-Incident Activity to Preparation; an under-prioritised C2 alert is a tuning lesson to act on. Lowering R1 would just hide a different true positive rather than fix R6's scoring.

8.q: triage.py prints a priority score from base severity, rule confidence and asset criticality. Two alerts come from the same rule, one on a finance workstation and one on a low-criticality kiosk. Which scores higher?
options: Both score the same, because the score depends only on the rule that fired
The kiosk, because low-criticality devices are the easiest for attackers to use
The finance workstation, because asset criticality multiplies into the score
Neither is fixed; the Tier 1 analyst sets each score by hand during triage
8.explanation: The score multiplies base severity by rule confidence and asset criticality, so the same rule on a more critical asset scores higher; this is why the asset table lifts every WS-104 alert. The score is calculated by the script, not set by hand.

8.q: Hunt H1 reports: WS-104 https://cdn-telemetry-sync.example/api/v2/ping n=18 mean_gap=300s cv=0.004. What does the cv value tell the analyst?
options: The requests are rare and irregular, which is typical of a person browsing to the site by hand
Only 0.4 percent of the requests reached the domain and the rest were blocked
The gaps between requests vary by about 0.4 seconds on average from 300 seconds
The gaps between requests are almost perfectly regular, typical of automated beaconing
8.explanation: The coefficient of variation is the standard deviation divided by the mean; 0.004 means near-identical gaps of about 300 seconds, the signature of a timer-driven beacon. It is a ratio, not seconds: 0.004 of 300 s is a deviation of about 1.2 s, not 0.4 s.

8.q: Hunt H2 reports: WINWORD.EXE -> powershell.exe hosts=1 n=1. How does this output help scoping?
options: It proves that PowerShell was never run on any other host for any purpose
It shows the Word-to-PowerShell pattern appears on only one host in the telemetry
It shows that Word launched PowerShell once on each of the hosts examined
It identifies the malicious document's hash so it can be blocked at the gateway
8.explanation: H2 lists parent-child pairs seen on only one host; this one occurred once, on one host, which supports limiting the endpoint scope to WS-104. It says nothing about PowerShell started by other parents, so it does not prove PowerShell was never used elsewhere.

8.q: A policy reviewer asks where containment and eradication sit in the CSF 2.0 structure used by SP 800-61 Rev. 3. Which answer is correct?
options: Mainly in RS.MI, Incident Mitigation, in the Respond Function
Mainly in RC.RP, Incident Recovery Plan Execution, in Recover
Mainly in DE.AE, Adverse Event Analysis, in the Detect Function
Mainly in RS.MA, Incident Management, in the Respond Function
8.explanation: Rev. 3 places containment and eradication mainly in RS.MI. RS.MA covers managing and coordinating the incident, which is close, but it is not where the actions that stop harm and remove the attacker are placed.

8.q: During the incident, an analyst notices that the 06:42Z spray failures raised no alert; only the 06:46Z success did. Under the Rev. 3 framing, what should be done with this observation?
options: Hold it for the post-incident meeting, which is where Rev. 3 places lessons learned
Put it in the next RS.CO status update so that executives can decide on a fix
Report it to CERT-In, because gaps in detection coverage must be notified
Record it now as an input to Improvement (ID.IM), since improvement runs throughout
8.explanation: Rev. 3 moves lessons learned out of a single closing phase: observations from Detect, Respond and Recover feed ID.IM as soon as they are noticed. Holding it for the final review is the Rev. 2 habit the new framing is designed to change.

8.q: Which statement about NIST SP 800-61 Revisions 2 and 3 is accurate?
options: Rev. 3 adds a fifth phase called Govern in front of the four Rev. 2 phases
Rev. 2 remains the current NIST guidance, and Rev. 3 is an optional draft profile
Rev. 3 supersedes Rev. 2 and frames incident response within the CSF 2.0 Functions
Rev. 3 retires the phase vocabulary, so playbooks must stop using 'containment'
8.explanation: Rev. 3 (April 2025) supersedes Rev. 2 and describes incident response through the six CSF 2.0 Functions. The classic phase names remain useful working vocabulary, so playbooks need not drop them; citing Rev. 2 as current NIST is the error.

8.q: At 02:00 local time, the night shift confirms command and control from a payments approver's laptop, but nobody on shift is authorised to approve isolating it, so isolation waits until 09:00. Which CSF 2.0 Function holds the root gap, and what fixes it?
options: Detect; add a rule that raises beaconing alerts to the highest priority in the queue
Govern; agree in advance who may authorise containment out of hours, and record it
Recover; keep a spare laptop ready so that isolation does not stop payment approvals
Respond; train analysts to isolate hosts themselves without waiting for any approval
8.explanation: Detection worked; the delay came from unclear authority, which is a Govern gap that shows up as delay in Respond. Letting analysts act without approval removes the control instead of fixing the missing pre-agreed authority.

8.q: Which mapping of a Banyan activity to a CSF 2.0 Category is correct?
options: Building the timeline and scoping the hosts: RS.AN, Incident Analysis
Rebuilding WS-104 from a known-good image: RS.MI, Incident Mitigation
Rule R1 firing on WS-104 in the alert queue: DE.AE, Adverse Event Analysis
Telling executives the status during response: RC.CO, Recovery Communication
8.explanation: Timeline and scoping are incident analysis, RS.AN. Rebuilding is RC.RP, R1 firing is continuous monitoring (DE.CM), and status communication during response is RS.CO, with RC.CO reserved for recovery communication.

8.q: The IR lead asks the SOC analyst to 'take care of containment' for Banyan. In most organisations, what does the analyst's work in this phase consist of?
options: Isolating hosts and disabling accounts directly from the SIEM console
Handing the case to IT operations and pausing monitoring until recovery
Advising on what to contain and in what order, preserving evidence and verifying actions
Drafting the CERT-In report, since containment is executed entirely by IT
8.explanation: IT operations, identity and network teams normally execute containment on the IR lead's authority; the SOC advises, preserves evidence where safe and verifies each action by re-running its searches. Pausing monitoring would remove the verification and re-entry watch.

8.q: During an ordinary shift with no open incident, an analyst notices that a proxy log source has been silent for two days and that a playbook lists a contact who has left the company. Where does reporting these fit in the lifecycle?
options: Outside the lifecycle, since no incident has been declared yet
Detection and Analysis, because the silent source is an indicator of compromise
Post-Incident Activity, because both are lessons learned from a previous case
Preparation, because the gaps would slow the handling of the next incident
8.explanation: Preparation is continuous SOC work, and reporting telemetry or contact gaps is part of it. A silent source might deserve a check, but on its own it is a coverage gap, not evidence of an intrusion.

8.q: WS-104 is isolated and the beacon has stopped. The identity team is ready to delete svc_update and IT is ready to reimage the disk, but the raw events have not yet been exported. What order should the analyst advise?
options: Reimage first, since recovery restores the business fastest and evidence can wait
Export and hash the raw events, then remove svc_update and rebuild the workstation
Delete svc_update first, because the unauthorised account is still a live threat
Postpone all eradication until the post-incident review has been completed
8.explanation: With harm already stopped by isolation, evidence should be preserved before eradication and rebuild change it. Deleting the account first sounds urgent, but on an isolated host it gains little and loses evidence of how it was created and used.

8.q: An attacker keeps both a workstation implant and a compromised VPN account, expecting defenders to contain the first and miss the second. Which practice counters this most directly?
options: Scoping across all telemetry before acting, then containing every foothold together
Rebuilding the first compromised host as soon as it has been identified
Increasing the status update cadence so that leadership notices sooner
Retaining logs for 180 days so that the second foothold can be found later
8.explanation: Multiple footholds defeat piecemeal containment; scoping first and then containing as a coordinated set closes them together. Long log retention helps later investigation but does nothing to stop the attacker using the second foothold now.

8.q: A department head whose team is not affected asks to be added to the HERON core update list 'just to stay informed'. How should the IR lead decide?
options: Add them, because wider awareness reduces rumours while the incident runs
Ask what they will decide or do with the information; if nothing, they do not need it yet
Add them to the core list, but strip hostnames and indicators from the copy that they receive
Refuse, because only the SOC and the IR lead may receive incident updates
8.explanation: Audiences are defined by what they must decide or do; with no answer, they do not need the information yet. Refusing everyone outside the SOC goes too far: executives, legal and action teams all legitimately receive updates.

8.q: The log says: 48,200,000 bytes uploaded 08:12Z to files-share-drop.example; content not yet known. Which wording is best for the executive update?
options: A small amount of data may have left the network; there is no sign it was sensitive
48.2 MB was exfiltrated over HTTPS to files-share-drop.example at 13:42 IST
No customer data was lost; the transfer went to an external file-sharing site
About 48 MB left the network to an unknown file-sharing site; content not yet known
8.explanation: Tailoring changes language and detail but never the facts: the executive version states the size in plain terms and keeps the biggest unknown explicit. 'No sign it was sensitive' and 'no customer data was lost' soften an unknown into reassurance the evidence does not support.

8.q: WS-104 was isolated at 09:05Z and no beacon has been seen since, but the endpoint sweep of other hosts is still pending. Which status-update sentence is accurate?
options: The known command-and-control channel has stopped since WS-104 was isolated at 09:05Z; scoping continues
The incident is now fully contained: WS-104 was isolated at 09:05Z and the beacon has stopped for good
The attacker has been removed from the network following isolation at 09:05Z
No further risk is expected; the remaining work is limited to collecting evidence
8.explanation: 'Contained' is a strong word that scoping does not yet support; the accurate sentence states what is known and that scoping continues. Early reassurance becomes a false statement to retract if a second host is found.

8.q: The 10:30Z HERON update is due, but nothing material has changed since 09:30Z. What should the author do?
options: Skip this update and send the next one when there is real news to report
Delay the update until the endpoint sweep result arrives later in the morning
Send 'no material change' at 10:30Z with the time of the next update
Ask the IR lead to suspend the cadence until the facts start changing again
8.explanation: The promised time lets everyone stop asking; missing it, even with no news, damages trust and brings interruptions. A 'no material change' update with the next time is a valid update; delaying for the sweep breaks the promise just the same.

8.q: At 09:50Z the SOC finds a second host beaconing to the case domain. The next scheduled update is at 10:30Z. What should the analyst do?
options: Tell the IR lead at once; a major change triggers an update outside the cadence
Include it in the 10:30Z update so that the agreed cadence is respected
Email the core list directly from the SOC so that everyone learns immediately
Wait until the second host is fully scoped so that the update is never retracted
8.explanation: A significant change such as a second infected host triggers an immediate update outside the cadence, coordinated through the IR lead. Emailing the list directly bypasses the hub and may use a channel the attacker can read.

8.q: Which finding most strongly requires moving all incident communication off the corporate mail and chat platform?
options: A new local administrator account appearing on a single workstation
Evidence that the attacker holds an identity-provider administrator account
A password-spray success against one standard user's VPN account from an external address
A malicious document opened by a user in the finance department
8.explanation: An attacker with administrative access to the identity provider or tenant can read anyone's mail and chat, so in-band channels are no longer safe for anyone. A local admin account on one workstation does not by itself prove tenant compromise.

8.q: After declaration, the IR lead creates a new chat space outside the corporate tenant and emails the join codes to the working group from corporate mail. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing, because the chat platform itself is outside the corporate tenant
Nothing, provided the invitations go only to the named core list
Sending join codes in-band lets an attacker reading mail learn of the channel or join it
Only that messages on external chat platforms cannot be used as evidence in the incident log
8.explanation: An out-of-band channel must be prepared in advance, and join codes must not travel through possibly compromised systems. Restricting the recipient list does not help if the attacker can read the sender's or a recipient's mailbox.

8.q: divya, the user whose session ran the malicious document, must be told to stop using WS-104 and expect a replacement. How should she be contacted?
options: By email to her corporate mailbox, marked confidential and urgent
By a message to WS-104 through the EDR console before it is isolated
By adding her to the out-of-band bridge so that she can follow the investigation as it unfolds
By phone, through her manager, with verbal instructions not to use or delete anything
8.explanation: Affected devices and accounts must never carry incident communication, and the user needs instructions, not investigative detail. Adding her to the bridge gives her far more than she needs to act.

8.q: The network team offers to block the beacon domain immediately, but WS-104's isolation is scheduled for an hour from now. There is no sign of ongoing destructive activity. What should the IR lead decide?
options: Block now, because every minute of beaconing raises the amount of data lost
Block now and tell divya by email so that she stops using the laptop meanwhile
Block the beacon domain now but leave the upload domain open so the team can watch the attacker
Hold the block and run it together with isolation, because an early block warns the attacker
8.explanation: Changing visible things before containment is coordinated tips off the attacker while their foothold is still live; communication and containment timing are planned together. The data-loss argument would matter if serious harm were ongoing, which the scenario rules out.

8.q: Which ticket title is the best choice for the network team's block request in the Banyan incident?
options: Block files-share-drop.example - finance data theft
HERON: block two domains and one address (list attached)
WS-104 compromise - block attacker domains urgently
Finance laptop hacked - network blocks needed today
8.explanation: A codename and a neutral description give the network team what it needs to act without revealing the incident's nature to anyone browsing the queue. Naming the host or 'data theft' discloses sensitive detail in an ordinary ticket.

8.q: The ISAC shared the indicator cdn-telemetry-sync.example under TLP:AMBER. Corporate communications wants to name the domain in a public statement. What is the correct position?
options: Not allowed: TLP:AMBER limits sharing to the recipient organisation and its clients on a need-to-know basis
Allowed, because an indicator loses its sensitivity once the incident is contained
Allowed, provided the statement credits the ISAC as the source of the indicator
Not allowed: TLP:AMBER restricts the indicator to the specific named individuals who originally received it
8.explanation: TLP:AMBER permits sharing within the recipient's organisation and with its clients on a need-to-know basis, so it must not appear in a public statement. Restriction to named individuals describes TLP:RED, which is stricter than AMBER.

8.q: A reportable incident is noticed at 21:10Z. What is the CERT-In six-hour point, in UTC and IST (UTC+05:30)?
options: 03:10Z the next day, which is 09:10 IST
03:10Z the next day, which is 21:40 IST
03:10Z the next day, which is 08:40 IST
02:40Z the next day, which is 08:10 IST
8.explanation: 21:10Z plus six hours is 03:10Z the following day; adding 5 hours 30 minutes gives 08:40 IST. The 09:10 IST option adds six hours instead of five and a half to the UTC time.

8.q: A Tier 2 analyst wants to hold back the time noticed from legal until the content of the upload is confirmed, 'so that we only report correct facts'. Why is this wrong?
options: It is not wrong; legal only needs the time once the investigation has ended
The deadline runs from noticing, so holding facts back consumes the reporting window
The deadline runs from the first malicious event, which has already passed anyway
CERT-In requires the SOC to file directly, so legal does not need the time at all
8.explanation: The six-hour window runs from noticing, not from the end of the investigation, so the time noticed and confidence-labelled facts must go to legal and the POC at once. The clock does not start at the first malicious event, and the SOC does not file the report itself.

8.q: In Banyan, who sends the report to CERT-In?
options: The SOC analyst who noticed the incident, to save as much time as possible
The IR lead, because the IR lead owns every incident communication
Legal, because legal assesses whether the incident is reportable
The designated point of contact, using the facts the SOC supplied
8.explanation: Reports to CERT-In go through the organisation's designated POC, on reportability advice from legal and with facts from the SOC. Legal decides whether the incident is reportable, but the POC is the authorised voice to CERT-In.

8.q: Which of these incident log entries follows the lesson's style for the log?
options: Around 09:20 someone checked and the beacon seems to have stopped, maybe reset gopal too?
09:20Z SOC-T2 FACT Beacon stopped and attacker gone; recommend closing HERON today.
09:20Z SOC-T2 FACT No requests to cdn-telemetry-sync.example since 09:05Z (proxy).
09:20Z FACT/DECISION No beacon since isolation; IR lead agreed to keep the blocks.
8.explanation: Each entry should have a UTC time, an author and one label, and a fact should give its source. 'Attacker gone' adds an inference to the fact, and a combined FACT/DECISION entry with no author mixes two kinds of entry.

8.q: Two analysts write executive updates from their own chat notes, and the executives receive two different figures for the size of the upload. Which practice prevents this?
options: Drawing every update from the single incident log and changing only the wording per audience
Assigning a separate analyst to write each audience's update in parallel
Sending the full technical update to every audience so that nothing is ever reworded or simplified
Inviting the executives onto the bridge so that they hear the facts first-hand
8.explanation: One incident log is the single source of truth; updates are pulled from it, never from memory or chat, and tailoring changes presentation, not facts. Sending the technical version to everyone avoids rewording but fails executives, who need impact and decisions in plain language.

8.q: The content of the 48 MB upload may decide whether the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires notice to the Data Protection Board. Who decides this, and what is the SOC's part?
options: The SOC decides, because only the SOC can see what the upload contained
Legal and the data protection function decide; the SOC works to establish and report the content
Nobody yet, because DPDP duties apply only after the investigation has closed
The CERT-In POC decides, because filing the CERT-In report also notifies the Data Protection Board
8.explanation: Whether and how the DPDP Act applies is assessed by legal and the data protection function; the SOC supplies facts, states unknowns and updates them when the content becomes known. The SOC never estimates legal obligations itself.

8.q: Update 2 says 'No other host seen contacting case domains (proxy telemetry; endpoint sweep pending)'. Why does the bracketed qualifier belong in the update?
options: To show legal which team is responsible if the statement is later found wrong
To satisfy a CERT-In format rule that each fact must name its data source
To tell readers what the conclusion rests on and what could still change it
To signal to executives that the SOC disagrees with the IR lead's scope
8.explanation: 'None found' in proxy records does not prove no other host is compromised, so the update states its basis and the pending check; that keeps it accurate and lets readers judge confidence. It is about confidence labelling, not assigning blame.

8.q: A message apparently from the IR lead appears in the incident chat asking a system administrator to 'disable the EDR agent on WS-104 for testing'. What should the administrator do?
options: Comply quickly, since the IR lead owns all decisions in the incident
Comply, provided the action is recorded in the incident log with the time and the requester's name
Ignore it, because EDR settings are never changed during an incident
Confirm through a known channel before acting, as for any change to a security control
8.explanation: Attackers exploit incident confusion with impersonation, so instructions affecting security controls are confirmed through a known channel. Ignoring it outright is wrong too: a genuine instruction could exist, and the attempt itself should be reported.

8.q: During HERON, which observation would most strongly suggest that the attacker is watching the investigation?
options: A new mailbox forwarding rule appearing on divya's account during the incident
A rise in the number of messages on the out-of-band bridge chat
Help-desk calls from finance staff about slow laptops that morning
Executives forwarding the executive summary to their deputies
8.explanation: The SOC monitors the incident itself, and a new forwarding rule on a compromised user's mailbox is a strong sign of an attacker reading mail. Executives forwarding the summary is a need-to-know problem, but it does not point to the attacker.

8.q: Why does the HERON communication plan brief the help desk with a routing script before WS-104 is isolated?
options: So that it can reset divya's password straight away when she phones
So that related calls go to IR and staff do not 'fix' affected machines and destroy evidence
So that it can tell callers what data the attacker took from the network
So that it can reimage WS-104 as soon as the network team confirms the device has been isolated
8.explanation: A forgotten help desk can destroy evidence with a well-meaning reboot or fix, so it needs a script that routes related calls to the IR team. Resetting the password is the identity team's coordinated action, not something the help desk should do on its own.

8.q: Before applying the blocks, the network lead asks for the name of the finance user whose laptop is involved. How should the IR lead respond?
options: Give the name, because action teams need the whole story to act correctly
Give no context at all, because need-to-know means action teams act without it
Give the name only if the network lead is already on the core distribution list
Give the domains and address with enough context to act; the user's identity is not needed
8.explanation: Action teams get what they need to act, not the whole story, and the user is a victim until proven otherwise. Need-to-know is not secrecy, so withholding all context goes too far: the team must still understand enough to apply the blocks correctly.

8.q: The IR lead decides on the out-of-band phone bridge to isolate WS-104. How should that decision be recorded?
options: Not at all, since out-of-band channels are meant to leave no record
Only if a regulator later questions the timing of the isolation
In the incident log, with the time and the IR lead as decision-maker
Only in the bridge platform's call history, which serves as the log
8.explanation: Out of band does not mean off the record; bridge decisions go into the single incident log under the name of the person who made them. A platform's call history is not the authoritative, labelled incident record.

8.q: An unfamiliar voice joins the HERON phone bridge, introducing themselves as a new member of the identity team. What should the bridge lead do?
options: Verify the person by calling back on a known number before continuing
Ask them to state the codename, since only real participants know HERON
Let them stay but avoid sensitive details until they have spoken
Close the bridge and create a new one, emailing fresh join codes
8.explanation: Out-of-band channels must be identity-checked, and a call-back on a known number verifies the person. An attacker with mail access may already know the codename and that the bridge exists, so knowing 'HERON' proves nothing.

8.q: After WS-104 is rebuilt, the team tells divya and the head of finance that service has been restored. Which CSF 2.0 Category does this communication belong to?
options: RS.CO, Incident Response Reporting and Communication
RC.CO, Incident Recovery Communication
RS.MA, Incident Management
RC.RP, Incident Recovery Plan Execution
8.explanation: Communication appears twice in CSF 2.0: RS.CO during response and RC.CO during recovery. Telling people that restored service is back is recovery communication; RC.RP covers the restoration work itself, not the messages about it.

8.q: The identity team resets gopal's password after the Banyan spray success, but the SIEM still shows VPN activity from 203.0.113.66 under his name twenty minutes later. What is the most likely gap in the containment?
options: The reset was applied to the directory but not replicated to the VPN appliance yet
The already-authenticated VPN session and issued tokens were never revoked or ended
The attacker had captured the new password because divya's workstation was not isolated
The VPN logs record the original login time, so later rows are a replay of old events
8.explanation: A reset stops the old password working for new sign-ins but does not necessarily end sessions that are already authenticated, so the VPN session and tokens must be terminated and revoked in the same action. Replication delay would affect new sign-ins, not explain an existing session continuing.

8.q: An analyst proposes isolating WS-104 at 09:00Z, then resetting gopal and divya at 10:00Z once the identity team is free. Why does the lesson treat this plan as flawed?
options: Isolation should always follow account actions, so the reset must happen first instead
The identity team cannot act on accounts belonging to a host that is already isolated
An hour between actions exceeds the containment window that NIST SP 800-61 prescribes
The visible isolation warns the attacker while the credential footholds remain open
8.explanation: Containing one foothold while others stay open tells the attacker which part of their access was found and leaves them a route to accelerate, migrate or destroy evidence; known footholds should be contained together. NIST does not prescribe a fixed window, and reversing the order would simply give the warning from the other side.

8.q: svc_update was created on WS-104 (event 4720) and added to the local Administrators group (4732). The identity team offers to disable it in the central directory. What should the analyst say?
options: It is a local account, so it must be disabled on the host through the EDR or management channel
Directory disablement is correct, but it must be followed by a forced group-policy refresh on WS-104
It should be deleted from the directory instead, since deletion is cleaner than disabling it
It should be left untouched until eradication, because changing it would tip the attacker off
8.explanation: A local account lives only in that machine's account database, so central directory action does nothing to it; it is disabled on the host and the same name is hunted for on other hosts. Leaving it active keeps the attacker's way back in, and deleting it would lose its history.

8.q: During containment the team must neutralise svc_update. Why does the lesson recommend disabling rather than deleting it at this stage?
options: Deletion would trigger event 1102 and erase the remaining Security log on the workstation
Disabled accounts cannot be re-enabled by an attacker who still holds local administrator rights
Disabling keeps the creation record, group memberships and profile available for investigation
Deletion is only possible after the host has been rebuilt from a known-good image in recovery
8.explanation: A disabled account retains the records the investigation needs, while a deleted one loses them; full removal belongs to eradication after evidence is captured. Deleting an account does not clear the Security log, and a disabled account can be re-enabled by an administrator, so that distractor overstates its strength.

8.q: Ransomware is actively encrypting a file share from a server with no EDR agent, and every minute adds damage. Which containment choice does the lesson support?
options: Wait for forensics to capture memory, because volatile evidence outweighs further encryption
Block the ransomware's known domains at the proxy and leave the server running for analysis
Power off or disconnect the server now, accepting lost volatile evidence to stop the harm
Reset all administrator passwords first so that the encryption process loses its permissions
8.explanation: Powering off is rarely the right first choice, but ongoing destruction is the stated exception: when every minute running costs more than the evidence is worth, stopping the harm comes first. Domain blocks do not stop local encryption, and waiting for capture lets the damage grow.

8.q: Why does blocking the three Banyan attacker domains at the proxy and DNS resolver, with block logging enabled, also help scoping?
options: Any other host that tries to reach those destinations shows up in the block logs
The blocks force the beacon on WS-104 to reveal its fallback domains in the proxy logs
Block logging records the full content of the attempted uploads for later impact review
The resolver returns the attacker's real server addresses, which can then be traced
8.explanation: Network blocks apply to every host at once, and logged block hits reveal hosts not yet known to be compromised. Nothing in a block forces malware to disclose other infrastructure; an attacker with other domains may simply switch, which is the weakness of indicator-based blocking.

8.q: Which statement best distinguishes short-term from long-term containment as the lesson defines them?
options: Short-term containment is done by the SOC; long-term containment is done only by forensic specialists
Short-term containment removes persistence; long-term containment rebuilds systems from clean images
Short-term containment covers hosts; long-term containment covers accounts, domains and networks
Short-term stops immediate harm fast; long-term keeps the business safe until rebuild
8.explanation: Short-term containment uses fast, usually reversible actions to stop harm now, while long-term containment covers the days until eradication and recovery are complete. Removing persistence and rebuilding are eradication and recovery work, not the two containment stages.

8.q: A long-term containment measure at Banyan is a temporary conditional access policy requiring step-up authentication for finance accounts. What does the lesson say every such measure needs?
options: Approval from the business owner, who holds a veto over any measure affecting finance
An owner and an end condition, so the temporary measure does not become permanent debt
A signed legal hold, because temporary policies change the evidence held by identity systems
A matching detection rule, so the measure can be removed automatically when alerts stop
8.explanation: Long-term containment measures are temporary by definition, so each needs an owner and an end condition or it becomes permanent technical debt. Business owners are consulted on timing and workarounds but do not usually hold a veto over stopping harm.

8.q: At 08:12Z WS-104 uploaded 48.2 MB to files-share-drop.example. If the SOC had noticed the upload while it was still running, how would the recommended order change?
options: Isolate WS-104 immediately, accept the tip-off risk, then coordinate the other actions straight after
Keep the coordinated window but shorten it, because the upload is already recorded in the proxy
Block only files-share-drop.example and wait, so the attacker does not notice the response
Power off WS-104, because a running upload means volatile evidence no longer has any value
8.explanation: Coordination is for the minutes you have, not a reason to wait: with data actively leaving, the active foothold is contained at once and the rest follows immediately. Power-off is reserved for destruction that cannot be stopped another way; EDR isolation stops the upload while keeping memory.

8.q: The Banyan VPN session from 203.0.113.66 and the WS-104 activity overlap in time but share no host or address. How should the recommendation treat the link between them?
options: As proven, because divya's account appears in the spray list and also ran the WS-104 payload
As irrelevant, because only footholds on the same host need to be contained in one window
As a separate foothold in the same window, with the link stated as an open question
As a false positive, because gopal's later success from 198.51.100.104 shows a genuine user
8.explanation: The evidence does not connect the two, so the VPN session is a separate foothold contained alongside WS-104, and the link is stated as unproven to stop a hypothesis being read as a finding. divya's spray attempt failed, so her appearance in the list does not prove a connection.

8.q: A tier-1 analyst wants to isolate the CFO's laptop through EDR right away, but is unsure whether the containment authority pre-authorises it. What does the lesson advise?
options: Isolate it anyway, because EDR isolation is reversible and therefore always pre-authorised
Ask the CFO directly by email whether a short interruption to their work is acceptable
Wait until the post-incident review clarifies the authority, then act on its conclusion
Treat it as not pre-authorised: recommend it, state the time pressure and escalate
8.explanation: When unsure, the analyst treats the action as needing approval, because a short wait rarely decides an incident while an unauthorised outage of a critical user can become an incident itself. Isolating a critical user's device is listed as needing incident lead approval, and emailing a possibly compromised user risks tipping off.

8.q: Banyan's head of finance objects that disabling divya, a payments approver, will stop a payment run. In the lesson's model, what role does the business owner play?
options: The owner holds a veto and may postpone containment until the payment run has completed
The owner is consulted on timing and workarounds, such as a deputy approving payments
The owner executes the account changes, because finance administers its own approvers
The owner has no role, because containment decisions belong only to the security team
8.explanation: Business owners are consulted where an action stops a process; they shape timing and workarounds and own continuity, but do not usually veto stopping active harm. The identity team, not finance, executes account actions.

8.q: In the lesson's comparison of containment options, which pairing correctly describes why wiping and reimaging WS-104 is not part of the Banyan containment recommendation?
options: It stops the attacker poorly on that host, and its business impact is lower than isolation
It sends a weak tip-off signal, so it should be saved for the end of the coordinated window
It keeps very little evidence, and belongs to recovery once evidence has been captured
It cannot be executed remotely, so it needs the user to bring the device to IT operations
8.explanation: Wipe and reimage stops the attacker on that host but rates very low for evidence and high for impact, so it is reserved for after collection, as a recovery step. It is rated as a strong signal, not a weak one, and it stops the attacker well on the host.

8.q: Why is EDR network isolation, rather than switch-port or VLAN isolation, the preferred first action for WS-104?
options: It keeps the host running and reachable through the EDR console for live collection
It blocks the attacker's local administrator account as well as the host's network traffic
It sends no signal to the attacker, because the beacon keeps reaching the attacker's server
It cuts the management channel too, which prevents the attacker using the EDR for access
8.explanation: EDR isolation blocks all traffic except the management console, so memory and processes are preserved and investigators can still reach the host; switch-port or VLAN isolation usually also cuts that channel. A beacon that stops checking in is noticeable, so isolation does send a signal.

8.q: Which set of actions does the lesson place in the silent preparation before the coordinated Banyan containment window?
options: Resetting divya first, blocking the domains, and asking IT operations to reboot WS-104 cleanly
Confirming out-of-band channels, exporting logs, briefing executors and arranging a payments workaround
Emailing gopal and divya about the investigation and asking them to stop using their accounts
Blocking 203.0.113.66 at the VPN, then watching whether the attacker changes source address
8.explanation: Only steps that send no signal happen before the window: out-of-band confirmation, log export, briefing executors by phone or bridge, and the finance workaround. Account resets and IP blocks are visible to the attacker, and emailing compromised users is a classic tip-off.

8.q: A mature team proposes delaying containment for a day to observe the Banyan attacker and map more infrastructure. According to the lesson, who may make that decision and when is it inappropriate?
options: The analyst who knows the evidence best; it is inappropriate only if the attacker is already dormant
The network team that would apply the blocks; it is inappropriate when indicators are still unknown
The SOC manager under pre-authorisation; it is inappropriate when no law-enforcement request exists
The incident lead with legal and business owners; it is inappropriate while data is leaving or harm continues
8.explanation: Deliberately leaving an intruder active is a decision for the incident lead with legal and business owners, sometimes at law enforcement's request, and not appropriate when harm is ongoing. It is never an analyst-alone decision, and a law-enforcement request is a possible reason, not a precondition.

8.q: After the Banyan window closes, IT ops replies that every action is done. What must happen before the analyst can call the footholds contained?
options: The incident lead must sign the post-incident review, which formally closes containment
The domain blocks must be removed, so that normal traffic can confirm the beacon has gone
Verification in the SIEM and EDR console that the beacon, sign-ins and VPN access have stopped
Eradication must be completed, because containment is only confirmed by a rebuilt host
8.explanation: An action approved but not confirmed is not yet containment: the analyst checks for successful requests to the domains, VPN authentication from 203.0.113.66, unexpected sign-ins by gopal or divya, and the EDR isolation status. Eradication and the review come later and are separate phases.

8.q: In the containment verification, the SIEM shows several blocked proxy requests from WS-104 to cdn-telemetry-sync.example after the window. How should the analyst read this?
options: As expected and useful block hits, provided no request to the domain actually succeeded
As proof that EDR isolation failed, so WS-104 must be powered off immediately
As a sign that the attacker has migrated, so the domain block can safely be removed
As a logging error, because an isolated host cannot generate any proxy events at all
8.explanation: The lesson notes that block hits are expected and useful during verification; what would show incomplete containment is a successful request to the blocked domains. Blocked attempts do not prove isolation failed, and removing the block would reopen the channel.

8.q: The Banyan containment recommendation ends with 'Decision requested within 15 minutes'. Which purpose of a good recommendation does this line serve?
options: It sets the maximum time NIST allows between detection and the start of containment
It makes the decision easy and time-bound, so the incident lead can approve in one reply
It authorises the analyst to execute the actions alone if no reply arrives in that time
It informs the attacker's likely dwell time, which the business owner needs for planning
8.explanation: The analyst's job is to make the decision easy: name action, target, impact, evidence consideration and owner, and ask for a decision by a stated time. A deadline does not convert a non-pre-authorised action into one the analyst may take alone, and NIST sets no such limit.

8.q: Which of the lesson's criteria from NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 is most directly at stake when choosing EDR isolation over power-off for WS-104?
options: Duration, because isolation is a permanent solution whereas power-off is an emergency step
Effectiveness, because power-off only partly contains a host that has a live C2 channel
Time and resources, because isolation needs no staff while power-off needs a site visit
The need to preserve evidence, because isolation keeps memory that power-off destroys
8.explanation: Both actions stop the host's network activity; the difference that drives the choice is evidence, since power-off destroys memory, processes and network state. Power-off is not partial containment, and isolation is a short-term, reversible action rather than a permanent solution.

8.q: gopal's VPN history shows a success from 203.0.113.66 at 06:46Z and another from 198.51.100.104 (country IN) at 13:33Z. What practical consequence does the lesson draw for containing his account?
options: Only the 06:46Z session needs ending, because the later session proves the account is clean
The 13:33Z session must be the attacker too, so gopal's laptop WS-107 should be reimaged
The reset may interrupt the genuine gopal, who must be contacted and given new credentials out of band
The account should be left active so that the attacker's next sign-in can be traced to its source
8.explanation: The later success may be the real user working remotely, so containment will interrupt a genuine person who must be reached by phone and re-credentialed out of band. A legitimate later session does not clean the account, and nothing in the evidence links WS-107 to the intrusion.

8.q: In the VPN query, eight different accounts fail from 203.0.113.66 at seven-second intervals, one attempt each, followed by gopal's success four minutes later. Which interpretation fits the lesson?
options: Password spraying (T1110.003) ending in a valid credential, a foothold to contain
A brute-force attack on one account, so locking gopal alone fully contains the activity
A misconfigured VPN client retrying cached credentials, so no containment is required
Credential stuffing from a breach list, so only accounts present in that list need resets
8.explanation: One attempt per account across many accounts at regular intervals is the shape of spraying, and the later success gives the attacker a valid credential with remote access. Brute force targets one account with many attempts, which is not what the rows show.

8.q: divya's account ran the WS-104 payload and is recorded as creating svc_update. The identity team resets her password and revokes her sessions. What does the lesson's foothold table warn about this action?
options: It must be delayed until after eradication, because the reset would erase the 4720 event
It does not clean WS-104, so the host still needs isolation and its own evidence collection
It also disables svc_update automatically, because that account was created by divya's session
It is unnecessary once WS-104 is isolated, since her credential cannot be used from elsewhere
8.explanation: The table notes that the reset does not clean WS-104: the host remains compromised and needs isolation and collection. A credential reset has no effect on a separately created local account, and an isolated host does not stop a stolen credential being used from another device.

8.q: Among the lesson's four attacker reactions to being tipped off, which one is the main reason defenders can declare victory too early?
options: Acceleration, because the attacker takes all reachable data before access is lost entirely
Destruction of evidence, because cleared logs hide the attacker's earlier activity on hosts
Migration, because the attacker visibly moves to a new domain that defenders then block
Dormancy, because the attacker goes quiet on known footholds while keeping a hidden one
8.explanation: Dormancy means silence on the known footholds while a hidden one stays open, which makes containment look complete when it is not. Migration is also a move to an unknown foothold, but the lesson ties premature victory specifically to dormancy.

8.q: In the recommendation-to-verification sequence, why does the SOC analyst appear at both the start and the end of the exchange?
options: Because the analyst holds the containment authority and must both approve and execute
Because the business owner requires the analyst to sign off any workaround it arranges
Because the analyst knows which indicators should go silent and can query the SIEM to confirm it
Because the executors cannot record action times, so the analyst logs them on their behalf
8.explanation: The analyst understands the evidence, so they write the recommendation and then verify that the beacon has stopped and no further sign-ins occurred. The incident lead, not the analyst, holds the authority, and executors report the time of each action themselves.

8.q: A colleague re-runs sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS on the WS-104 export and gets OK. They conclude the export is a complete and accurate record of everything WS-104 did that morning. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: Nothing, because SHA-256 collisions are infeasible and the file was hashed by the script
An OK result is only valid if the hash is computed in upper case, as Get-FileHash prints it
A match only shows the file is unchanged since hashing, not that the query or source was complete
sha256sum -c checks the manifest's format, not the file's content, so it cannot prove anything
8.explanation: A matching hash proves the item is unchanged since its digest was recorded; completeness depends on the documented query and the integrity of the SIEM before export. sha256sum -c does recompute each file's digest, and hexadecimal digests compare case-insensitively.

8.q: WS-104 is still running after EDR isolation. Following RFC 3227's order of volatility, what should the analyst ask the forensic team to capture first?
options: Memory, processes and network connections, which are lost at power-off
The disk image, because invoice.docm and the svc_update profile are on it
The SIEM, proxy and VPN logs, because retention may delete them soonest
Archived backups of WS-104, because they show the host before compromise
8.explanation: Collection works from the most volatile layer down; in practice that means memory, processes and connections first, since registers and cache are rarely collected. Remote logs are durable but retention-bound, and the SOC can preserve them in parallel without touching the host.

8.q: The process log for WS-104 shows PowerShell only as '-EncodedCommand <redacted-for-course>'. Why does the lesson link this to the urgency of memory capture?
options: Because encoded commands are written to temporary files that the next reboot deletes
Because the SIEM discards encoded parameters, so the disk image is the only other copy
Because memory capture is the only legal way to decode a command under section 63
Because memory may still hold the decoded PowerShell and beacon configuration
8.explanation: Running memory may hold the decoded script, the beacon's configuration and live connections, none of which survives a reboot. Nothing in the lesson says the SIEM discards parameters or that temporary files hold the decoded command.

8.q: A help-desk technician offers to reboot WS-104 and run a clean-up tool to make it usable for divya again. Which evidence-preservation action does the lesson recommend?
options: Let the clean-up run, as long as the technician records each step in the incident log
Issue a clear 'do not reboot, do not clean, do not reimage' instruction to help desk and user
Ask the technician to hash the disk before rebooting, so any change can be detected later
Allow a reboot but not the clean-up tool, since a reboot preserves the disk layer intact
8.explanation: A well-meant reboot or clean-up destroys the most volatile layers first, so telling the help desk and user not to touch the host is itself an evidence-preservation action. A reboot loses memory, and a hash only detects later change, it does not preserve memory.

8.q: After the export, the analyst copies the file and SHA256SUMS to a separate folder and changes 48200000 to 482000 in the copy. sha256sum -c reports FAILED. What does this exercise demonstrate?
options: That the original export is now unusable and must be re-run from the documented query
That even a single altered value, here shrinking the upload's size, is detected on verification
That sed edits change the line endings, which is what the manifest actually checks for
That the custody record must be updated with the new digest whenever a copy is edited
8.explanation: The change would turn a 48.2 MB exfiltration into a harmless-looking 0.5 MB transfer, and verification fails because any change produces a different digest. The original was untouched in its own folder, and recording a digest for an altered copy would defeat the purpose of custody.

8.q: A second run of evidence_export.py CASE-0001 WS-104 prints the same digest 8521c97c...19acf. Which property of the export makes this possible?
options: The script caches the first export and returns it unchanged if the same case is used
The custody file stores the digest, so the script copies it instead of re-hashing the file
The hash is keyed on the case identifier and host, not on the content of the exported events
The query parameters, the ordering and the line endings are fixed, so the bytes are identical
8.explanation: The export selects the raw events with a fixed window, orders them by timestamp and writes Unix line endings, so the same data produces the same bytes and therefore the same digest. The script overwrites the export and re-hashes it; it does not cache or copy a stored digest.

8.q: After exporting WS-107 into CASE-0001, SHA256SUMS lists only the WS-107 file. Where does the WS-104 digest still exist, and what lesson follows?
options: In custody.jsonl, which is append-only here and so is the authoritative record
In the WS-104 export file itself, which embeds its own digest in the last line
Nowhere, so the WS-104 export must be discarded and collected again from scratch
In minisiem.db, which stores every digest the export script has ever computed
8.explanation: The script rewrites SHA256SUMS on every run, but appends to custody.jsonl, which now has three lines including the WS-104 entry; the custody log carries the history. The lesson recommends one manifest entry per item and never letting a tool silently replace a record.

8.q: The WS-107 export contains gopal's proxy and process events but none of the suspicious VPN events from 203.0.113.66. Why?
options: The VPN events fall outside the fixed 06:00Z to 09:00Z window used by the export script
The script deliberately excludes authentication events to keep exports within size limits
VPN records in this dataset carry no host field, so a host-based export cannot select them
The VPN events were already exported with WS-104, so the script skips duplicate events
8.explanation: The export filters on host, and VPN records have no host value, so they need a separate documented query on source and src_ip, hashed and recorded the same way. The 06:42Z to 06:46Z spray events do fall inside the window, so timing is not the reason.

8.q: Which description of a chain of custody best explains why a gap in it matters even when the item's hash still matches?
options: The gap means the hash algorithm must be upgraded, because SHA-256 cannot cover gaps
The gap breaks the manifest's format, so sha256sum -c can no longer read the entry
The gap shifts legal ownership of the item to whoever held it last before the gap
Nobody can say who held the item then, inviting the claim that it was altered in that gap
8.explanation: The hash shows whether an item changed; the custody record shows who could have changed it. A period with no known holder invites a challenge regardless of the hash, which is why every access and transfer is logged.

8.q: The custody entry for the WS-104 export records the host and the start and end of the window. Which challenge does recording these query parameters answer?
options: Whether the file was altered after collection, by allowing the digest to be recomputed
Whether the export can be reproduced, by letting anyone re-run the same query and compare
Whether the analyst was authorised, by tying the export to the incident lead's approval
Whether the SIEM ingested every event, by proving that no events were dropped in transit
8.explanation: The documented query gives reproducibility: anyone with the same SIEM data can re-run it and obtain the same bytes. Detecting alteration is the digest's job, and no export parameter can prove the SIEM's own ingestion was complete.

8.q: The Banyan attacker cleared WS-104's Security log at 08:17Z, yet the incident timeline still contains the earlier events. What explains this?
options: The SIEM had already collected the events centrally, and the clearing was logged as 1102
Event 1102 restores the cleared entries automatically into the Windows Application log
The EDR agent replays the local Security log to the SIEM after every clearing event
The clearing only removes events newer than the last reboot, so earlier ones remained
8.explanation: Central collection had already copied the events off the host, so the local clearing damaged only the disk layer, and the clearing itself became a strong indicator as event 1102. Event 1102 records that the log was cleared; it does not restore anything.

8.q: Ten days after an intrusion, an investigation finds that the first proxy events have already aged out of the SIEM. Which log-preservation step, taken at the first sign of the incident, would most directly have prevented this?
options: Recording each source's time zone and clock offset so the timeline can be rebuilt
Waiting for a legal hold, which automatically extends retention for every log source
Exporting the relevant records with integrity and custody, and extending source retention
Forwarding proxy logs to the EDR console, which keeps all records for the case's life
8.explanation: Exported, hashed records no longer depend on retention, and extending retention keeps the wider data set available for scoping. Clock records improve timelines but do not stop deletion, and the SOC should not wait for a hold before preserving.

8.q: Legal counsel issues a legal hold for the Banyan incident. Which task correctly belongs to the SOC and IT operations rather than to legal?
options: Deciding whether the hold is needed and which records and custodians it should cover
Stopping automated deletion for the covered data and confirming in writing it is done
Determining whether the exported logs will be admissible under the evidence statute
Releasing the hold once the analysts consider the technical investigation complete
8.explanation: Legal decides whether a hold is needed, what it covers and when it ends; the SOC and IT operations implement it by suspending retention, clean-up and reimaging and confirming that in writing. Admissibility is also a legal question.

8.q: At the end of the case, an analyst wants to delete their working copies, chat logs and notes to tidy up. A legal hold is still in force. What does the lesson say?
options: Working files are not evidence, so they can be deleted once the final report is written
Only the exported evidence files are covered, so personal notes may be removed freely
Chat logs may be deleted, but tickets must be kept because they are system records
The SOC's own case records may fall within the hold and must be kept until it is released
